text: A 28-year-old man presented with dysphasia, dysarthria, descending symmetric flaccid paralysis of voluntary muscles, diplopia, decreased deep tendon reflexes, constipation. The probable diagnosis of botulism is made. Which membrane transport is affected?
expl: Option C: Diagnosis: Botulism , caused by botulinum toxin. Affected Process: Exocytosis , necessary for neurotransmitter release. Mechanism: SNARE proteins (e.g., Synaptobrevin ) are crucial for exocytosis of acetylcholine . Botulinum toxin degrades SNARE proteins , inhibiting neurotransmitter release and leading to paralysis. Why not others: Option A: Facilitated diffusion is not primarily involved in neurotransmitter release. Option B: Primary active transport is related to ion movement, not exocytosis. Option D: Simple diffusion does not apply to neurotransmitter release mechanisms. Key takeaways: Botulism inhibits exocytosis by degrading SNARE proteins, leading to paralysis. Tags: Inicet 2021 Level: Difficult Tag: Transmembrane transport Reference: Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology, 26 th Edition, Page no. 307

text: Neurological examination of a patient revealed the following Diplopia and suspected involvement of other cranial nerves, tingling and numbness in the lower extremities. Symptoms were getting worse upon taking hot bath. Defect of which of the following cells is the most likely cause?
expl: Oligodendrocytes are responsible for producing and maintaining myelin in the central nervous system (CNS) . The patient's diplopia (cranial nerve involvement), sensory symptoms (tingling, numbness), and worsening with heat (Uhthoff's phenomenon) strongly suggest demyelination , commonly seen in Multiple Sclerosis (MS) . MS is an autoimmune disorder characterized by loss of oligodendrocytes , leading to impaired nerve conduction. Incorrect Options: Option B: Ependymal Cells: These line the ventricles and produce cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) . Damage to these cells is associated with hydrocephalus or CSF flow obstruction , not demyelinating diseases. Option C: Astrocytes: Provide support, maintain the blood-brain barrier, and regulate ion balance . They are involved in reactive gliosis (scar formation) in MS but are not the primary cells affected . Option D: Microglia: These are the immune cells of the CNS , responsible for phagocytosis and inflammatory responses. While they play a role in MS-related neuroinflammation , the primary defect in MS is oligodendrocyte destruction . Key Takeaways: Oligodendrocytes produce CNS myelin; their loss causes MS. MS presents with diplopia, sensory deficits, and worsening with heat (Uhthoff's phenomenon). Other glial cells (ependymal, astrocytes, microglia) have different CNS functions and are not the primary cause of demyelination.

text: Migraine is due to
expl: Answer- C. Cortical spreading depression Cortical spreading depression is a self propagating wave of neuronal and glial depolarization that spreads across the cerebral cortex. The activation of trigeminal afferents by cortical spreading depression in turn causes inflammatory changes in the pain- sensitive meninges that generate the headache of migraine through central and peripheral reflex mechanisms.

text: A 35-year-old female presented with difficulty in walking, fatigue and reduced reflexes. She was diagnosed to be the case of Lambert Eaton syndrome. Antibodies are produced against which channels?
expl: Option A: In Lambert Eaton syndrome, antibodies are produced against the voltage gated calcium channels present on the presynaptic membrane, which destroy the channels leading to muscular weakness. Option B: Potassium channel. Potassium channels are responsible for repolarizing the membrane after depolarization by allowing potassium ions (K+) to flow out of the cell. Disease: Potassium channel autoimmune syndromes (e.g., Hypokalemic periodic paralysis). Option C: Sodium channel: Sodium channels play a crucial role in initiating action potentials by allowing sodium ions (Na+) to flow into cells during depolarization. Disease: Na+ channelopathies (e.g., Sodium channel myotonia or periodic paralysis). Option D: Chloride channel: Disease: Cystic fibrosis Mucoviscidosis (due to mutations in the CFTR chloride channel located on chromosome 6). Most common mutation is ΔF508 deletion which codes for phenylalanine. Key take aways: In Lambert-Eaton syndrome , antibodies are produced against calcium channels leading to impaired release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction and resulting in muscle weakness. Reference: Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology, 26 th Edition, Page no. 328

text: 34-year-old man was not able to recognize the face of his college friend although he was able to recognize his friend by his voice. Where could be the site of lesion in this case scenario?
expl: Option C: In humans, storage and recognition of faces are more strongly represented in the inferior temporal lobe. Damage to this area can cause prosopagnosia, the inability to recognize faces. Patients with this abnormality can recognize people by their voices, body language, etc. However, they cannot identify the familiar people by seeing their faces. Many of them show autonomic responses when they see familiar as opposed to unfamiliar face. The presence of an autonomic response to a familiar face in the absence of recognition has been explained by postulating the existence of a separate dorsal pathway for processing information about faces that leads to recognition at only a subconscious level. Option A: Parietal lobe - Involved in spatial awareness and sensory integration, but not specifically in facial recognition. Option B: Occipital lobe - Primarily responsible for visual processing, but damage here affects basic vision rather than the specific ability to recognize faces. Option D: Frontal lobe - Involved in decision-making, problem-solving, and social behavior but not directly responsible for facial recognition. Key takeaways : Damage to the inferior temporal lobe can lead to prosopagnosia , which is the inability to recognize faces while retaining the ability to recognize individuals through other cues, such as voice. This area is crucial for facial recognition. Tags: INICET nov 2021 Reference: Ganong’s Review of Medical Physiology 26 th Edition Page no. 672

text: A man suffered from road traffic accident that lead to trauma to the spinal cord. On investigation, a complete transection of one side of the spinal cord is suspected. For below the level of injury Which of the following statement is incorrect regarding this case?

options.A: Ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature
options.B: High dose of corticosteroids have been shown to be of value if administered soon after the onset of spinal cord injury
options.D: Weakness and spasticity in certain muscle groups on same side of body

ansText: Ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature
expl: Contralateral loss of pain and temperature occurs because the spinothalamic tract crosses to the opposite side at the spinal cord level. This means damage on one side results in loss of these sensations on the opposite side of the body, below the lesion. Corticosteroids are effective in reducing inflammation if administered early, as they suppress immune cells and reduce capillary permeability, preventing further damage from swelling and inflammation. Ipsilateral loss of fine touch, vibration, and proprioception occurs due to damage to the fasciculus gracilis or fasciculus cuneatus (dorsal column), which ascends without crossing until it reaches the medulla. This leads to loss of stereognosis on the same side of the lesion. Ipsilateral weakness and spasticity arise from damage to the corticospinal tract (a motor pathway) that affects the same side of the body. Since corticospinal fibers cross at the medulla, any damage below this level affects motor control ipsilaterally. Why not others: Contralateral pain and temperature loss happens due to spinothalamic tract involvement. Corticosteroids prevent secondary damage from inflammation and swelling. Ipsilateral stereognosis loss is due to the dorsal column damage, and ipsilateral motor weakness is caused by corticospinal tract disruption. Key Takeaways: Spinal cord hemisection results in contralateral loss of pain/temperature and ipsilateral loss of fine touch, proprioception, and motor control. Early corticosteroid therapy can reduce secondary damage in spinal cord injuries. text: A patient who had a stroke 2 days ago now presents with uncontrollable, violent, and jerking movements of the limbs on one side of the body. What is the most likely site of the lesion?
expl: Explanation: The patient's presentation is consistent with hemiballismus , a hyperkinetic movement disorder marked by involuntary, forceful, flinging movements of the extremities on one side. This condition typically follows a vascular insult (stroke) that damages the subthalamic nucleus . Basal Ganglia and Movement Disorders: Hypokinetic Disorders Parkinsonism: Caused by dopamine deficiency in the substantia nigra pars compacta . Clinical features: Akinesia, bradykinesia, cogwheel rigidity, resting tremor, shuffling gait, stooped posture, micrographia, reduced facial expression, and mood/cognitive changes. Hyperkinetic Disorders Hemiballismus: Lesion of the subthalamic nucleus → decreased inhibition of the thalamus → excessive, uncontrolled movements. Huntington’s Disease: Degeneration of striatal neurons in the indirect pathway → choreiform, dance-like movements. Dystonia: Dysregulation of the direct pathway → sustained, twisting, and abnormal postures. Anatomical Role of Basal Ganglia Structures: Striatum (Caudate + Putamen): Major input center receiving cortical signals. (Options C & D ruled out) Globus Pallidus (GPe, GPi): Processes inhibitory and excitatory motor signals. GPi exerts tonic inhibition on the thalamus. Substantia Nigra: Pars compacta: Dopamine production (degenerates in Parkinsonism). Pars reticulata: Inhibitory output to the thalamus via GABA. (Option B ruled out) Subthalamic Nucleus: Provides excitatory glutamatergic input to GPi and SNr. Damage → loss of inhibition → hyperkinetic state → hemiballismus. (Correct Answer) Key Neurotransmitters: Dopamine: From substantia nigra (pars compacta), modulates direct & indirect pathways. GABA: Major inhibitory transmitter (striatum, GPi, GPe, SNr). Glutamate: Major excitatory transmitter (cortex → striatum; subthalamic nucleus → GPi/SNr). Explanation of Incorrect Options: Substantia nigra (Option B): Lesions here reduce dopamine and produce Parkinsonism (hypokinetic features: rigidity, tremor, bradykinesia), not violent flinging movements. Putamen (Option C): As part of the striatum, it primarily influences voluntary motor control, but isolated lesions here are not associated with hemiballismus. Caudate nucleus (Option D): Involved in cognitive and limbic aspects of motor control; its degeneration is classic in Huntington's disease, producing chorea rather than hemiballismus.

text: A 40 year old man presents to the clinic with a sudden onset of facial weakness on the right side. He is unable to close his eye, and his mouth droops on the same side. He reports no other symptoms, and there is no history of trauma. On examination, he can't raise his right eyebrow or smile symmetrically, the most likely diagnosis is?
expl: Bell's palsy is characterized by unilateral facial paralysis involving both the upper and lower face . It results from damage or inflammation of the facial nerve (CN VII) , affecting the ability to close the eye, raise the eyebrow, and smile. Characteristics features of Bell's palsy Inability to raise the eyebrow or close the eye on the affected side. Drooping of the mouth on the affected side. Upper and lower face are both affected (distinguishing it from a stroke). The onset is usually rapid, occurring over hours to days. No other neurological deficits or history of trauma. Bell's phenomenon is a normal reflex that occurs when the eyes roll upward and outward when a person tries to close their eyelids Why Not Other Options B (Stroke): A stroke typically spares the forehead due to bilateral cortical innervation of the upper facial muscles, so the patient would be able to raise their eyebrow. C (Trigeminal neuralgia): Causes severe facial pain but does not result in facial weakness or paralysis. D (Myasthenia gravis): Causes fluctuating muscle weakness but would not typically cause sudden, complete facial paralysis on one side. Key Takeaways Bell's palsy involves complete unilateral facial paralysis affecting both the upper and lower face, unlike stroke which spares the forehead. Tags: Inicet nov 2021 Reference: John E. Hall/Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology, 14 th Edition, page no. 696 to 708, & based on clinical knowledge.

text: A 32-year-old man presents with progressive weakness in both lower limbs that started 5 days ago and has now ascended to involve the upper limbs. He reports a history of diarrheal illness 2 weeks earlier. On examination, there is flaccid quadriparesis, areflexia, and bilateral facial weakness. Nerve conduction studies show demyelinating polyneuropathy. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: Guillain-Barré syndrome is an acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (AIDP) that often follows infections such as Campylobacter jejuni gastroenteritis . It is characterised by rapidly progressive, symmetrical, ascending muscle weakness , areflexia , and sometimes cranial nerve involvement (commonly facial palsy). Autonomic dysfunction may also occur. Nerve conduction studies typically show slowed conduction velocities due to demyelination. This clinical presentation is classic for GBS . Explanation of other options: Myasthenia gravis (Option A): Causes fluctuating muscle weakness with diurnal variation, but reflexes are preserved, and it is not preceded by infection in most cases. Poliomyelitis (Option C): Presents with asymmetrical flaccid paralysis and preserved sensation, unlike GBS, which is symmetrical. Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (Option D): Associated with paraneoplastic syndromes (especially small-cell lung carcinoma), shows proximal weakness that improves with activity , not ascending paralysis.

text: Which of the following statements is correct concerning a 50-year-old male who was diagnosed with a submandibular gland tumor, underwent surgical removal, and subsequently suffered lingual nerve damage?

options.A: The taste sensation of the posterior one-third of the tongue is lost
options.B: The taste sensation of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is lost
options.C: A general sensation of the posterior one-third of the tongue is lost
options.D: A general sensation of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is lost

ansText: The taste sensation of the posterior one-third of the tongue is lost
expl: Explanation : The lingual nerve , a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3) , is responsible for providing general sensation (touch, pain, and temperature) to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue . Additionally, it carries taste fibers from the chorda tympani (a branch of the facial nerve, CN VII ), which are involved in taste perception in the same region. Damage to the lingual nerve primarily affects general sensory input from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. This is the most consistent and reliable symptom following lingual nerve injury. Clinical Insight: During submandibular gland surgery , the lingual nerve is particularly vulnerable due to its close anatomical relationship with the gland. Postoperative complications commonly include: Loss of general sensation in the anterior two-thirds of the tongue . Occasional loss of taste in the same area if the chorda tympani is also damaged . Explanation for other options: The taste sensation of the posterior one-third of the tongue is lost (Option A) : Incorrect. This region is innervated by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) for both taste and general sensation , and is not affected by lingual nerve injury. The taste sensation of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is lost (Option B) : incorrect . The lingual nerve does carry chorda tympani fibers for taste, but taste loss only occurs if the chorda tympani is also injured . However, general sensation loss is the more reliable and consistent symptom of lingual nerve damage. General sensation of the posterior one-third of the tongue is lost (Option C) : Incorrect. This area is also innervated by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) , and is not impacted by damage to the lingual nerve.

text: A patient who recently had a leg amputation reports feeling pain in the missing limb, a phenomenon known as phantom limb pain. This phenomenon is based on which of the following mechanism.
expl: Phantom limb pain arises due to cortical plasticity , which refers to the brain's ability to reorganize itself after injury or amputation. After the loss of a limb, the cortical representation of that limb is taken over by adjacent areas in the brain. This can lead to misinterpretation of signals, resulting in sensations like pain, itching, or tingling in the missing limb. Rewiring of neural circuits occurs, and neurons that were previously connected to the amputated limb now respond to stimuli from other parts of the body, but the brain may still perceive these signals as coming from the missing limb. This process is an example of the brain's adaptability but can cause discomfort as the brain attempts to process signals without proper input from the absent limb. Why Not Other Options B (Weber French Law) : Deals with the relationship between stimulus magnitude and perception, irrelevant to cortical reorganization. C (Principle of Labeled Time) : Involves temporal coding of sensory information, not applicable to phantom limb pain. D (Muller's Specific Nerve Energy) : Relates to how specific nerves produce distinct sensations, regardless of stimulus, which doesn't explain cortical reorganization. Key Takeaways Cortical plasticity leads to phantom limb pain, where the brain reorganizes and adjacent regions take over the area once representing the amputated limb. This reorganization may cause sensory confusion , leading to the perception of pain or sensations in the missing limb. Tags: Neet 2023 Topic: Sensory receptor Level: Good to know Reference: John. E. text: A 45-year-old male presents with double vision and difficulty swallowing. He has a history of autoimmune disease and notices that his symptoms worsen as the day progresses. Neurological examination shows ptosis and muscle weakness, which improve after a brief period of rest. There are no sensory deficits, and deep tendon reflexes are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Myasthenia gravis (MG) presents with fluctuating muscle weakness that worsens with activity and improves with rest . Common symptoms include ptosis, diplopia , and difficulty swallowing . MG is caused by autoantibodies against acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction. No sensory deficits or reflex abnormalities , which aligns with MG. Presentation weak neck muscles give cause the head to fall forward or backward Drooping eyelids (ptosis) Inability to move eyes side to side double vision (diplopia) difficulty speaking (dysarthria) difficulty swallowing (dysphagia) Worsening of symptoms as the day progresses is typical in MG. Why not othchroers: A) Guillain-Barre Syndrome (GBS): It is is a rare autoimmune disorder in which the body's immune system mistakenly attacks the peripheral nervous system. It often follows an infection, surgery, or vaccination. It Causes ascending weakness with areflexia , not the fluctuating weakness seen in MG. Symptoms do not improve with rest. B) Multiple Sclerosis (MS): It is a chronic autoimmune disease of the central nervous system (CNS), primarily affecting the brain, spinal cord, and optic nerves. It is demyelinating disorder causing sensory disturbances and varied neurological deficits, not pure muscle fatigability seen in MG. D) Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome (LEMS): In LEMS, the immune system attacks voltage-gated calcium channels (VGCCs) on nerve terminals, reducing the release of acetylcholine. It Causes proximal muscle weakness , improving with exercise . Unlike MG, ptosis and diplopia are uncommon early in LEMS. Key Takeaways: Myasthenia gravis presents with fluctuating muscle weakness , worsens with activity, and improves with rest , affecting the ocular and bulbar muscles . Other conditions (GBS, MS, LEMS) show different patterns of weakness and involve distinct neurological signs. Tags: Inicet may 2022 Tag: Special senses Level: Must know Reference: Guyton & Hall, Chapter 46, pg. 598; Ganong's review of medical physiology, 26th edition, Page 324, 325

text: 49-year-old male developed chest pain, nausea and uneasiness. On investigation, ECG shows ST segment elevation. The probable diagnosis is Myocardial infarction. The best cardiac marker marker is:
expl: Option C: Troponin I is the best cardiac marker for diagnosing myocardial infarction. Timing: Troponin I rises in 2-4 hours after injury and remains elevated for 7-10 days . Specificity: It is highly specific for cardiac injury. Other Markers: LDH: Normally, LDH2 > LDH1 , but in myocardial infarction, this reverses (LDH Flip). CK-MB: Good for detecting re-infarction , rising in 2-4 hours and falling in 2-3 days . Myoglobin: One of the earliest markers to rise (within 1 hour ) but lacks specificity, falling within 24 hours . Why Not Others: Option A: LDH: Not specific for myocardial infarction and has a delayed rise compared to troponin. Option B: CK-MB: Good for re-infarction but less sensitive and specific than troponin I for initial diagnosis. Option D: Myoglobin: Rises early but lacks specificity for myocardial infarction, as it can be elevated in other conditions. Key takeaways: The best cardiac marker for diagnosing myocardial infarction is Troponin I, as it rises within 2-4 hours and remains elevated for 7-10 days. Tags: Good to know Topic: Cardiac Electrophysiology Level: Good to know Reference: Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology, 26 th Edition, Page no. 1394

text: A 28-year-old woman presents with progressive fatigable weakness, particularly involving her eyelids and extraocular muscles. By the evening, she develops ptosis and diplopia, which improve after rest. Reflexes and sensation are normal. The ice pack test on the eyelid improves ptosis. Which of the following best describes the underlying mechanism of her condition?

options.A: Autoantibodies blocking acetylcholine receptors at the presynaptic terminal
options.B: Autoantibodies blocking acetylcholine receptors at the postsynaptic terminal
options.C: Autoimmune destruction of voltage-gated calcium channels at the presynaptic terminal
options.D: Autoimmune destruction of voltage-gated calcium channels at the postsynaptic terminal

ansText: Autoantibodies blocking acetylcholine receptors at the postsynaptic terminal
expl: Explanation: The clinical presentation is classic for myasthenia gravis (MG) , an autoimmune disorder of the neuromuscular junction . In MG, autoantibodies target nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the postsynaptic membrane , reducing the number of functional receptors. This leads to impaired neuromuscular transmission and fatigable weakness , which improves with rest (as acetylcholine accumulates) and with the ice pack test (cold reduces acetylcholinesterase activity, increasing acetylcholine availability). Explanation of other options: Presynaptic receptor block (Option A): MG is not a presynaptic disorder; presynaptic pathologies include botulism. Presynaptic Ca 2+ channel destruction (Option C): This describes Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS) , where impaired calcium influx reduces acetylcholine release. Postsynaptic Ca 2+ channel destruction (Option D): No such mechanism exists in neuromuscular junction diseases.

text: A man presents to the hospital with complaints of drooping of eyelids and increasing eye irritation. He reports his symptoms to be worsening as the day goes on, particularly during outdoor activities. What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
expl: Explanation: The clinical presentation of ptosis and fatiguability is suggestive of myasthenia gravis. Myasthenia gravis Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disorder with antibodies directed against acetylcholine receptors at the postsynaptic neuromuscular junction. Primarily leads to weakness of the voluntary muscles, particularly the ocular and facial muscles. Clinical features Fatiguability: Symptoms worsen with activity and improve with rest. Ptosis Diplopia Generalised muscle weakness. Disorders related to Neuromuscular junction: Explanation: Botulism Toxicity (Option C): Botulinum toxin inhibits acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction. It results in muscle weakness, but symptoms typically include descending paralysis and can affect multiple muscle groups. Tetanus Toxicity (Option D): Tetanus caused by Clostridium tetani leads to severe muscle spasms and rigidity. Symptoms often include lockjaw, muscle stiffness, and generalised spasms, rather than ptosis or symptoms that worsen with the day.

text: A 45-year-old man presents with muscle cramps, which are worse at the night. Fasciculations are frequent and multiple. The probable diagnosis of amyotropic lateral sclerosis is made. In this disease due to overactivity of NMDA receptors (shown in figure) there will be?
expl: Option B: In Amyotropic lateral sclerosis due to overactivity of NMDA receptors there will be enhanced calcium ion influx. NMDA receptor is a receptor of glutamate. Riluzole is a NMDA receptor blocker used in the treatment of amyotropic lateral sclerosis. Option A: Decreased chloride ions influx : Chloride influx is typically associated with inhibitory neurotransmission (e.g., GABA receptors), not NMDA receptors, which are excitatory. GABA receptor stimulation leads to increased Cl- influx. Option C: Enhanced potassium ions influx : Potassium typically moves out of neurons during repolarization, not into the cell via NMDA receptors, though NMDA receptors are permeable to K+. Option D: Decreased sodium ion influx : NMDA receptors also allow sodium influx, but the primary issue in ALS is excessive calcium influx, not reduced sodium influx. Key takeaways : In amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), overactivity of NMDA receptors leads to enhanced calcium ion influx , which contributes to neuronal damage and excitotoxicity. text: A 42-year-old male presented with convulsions, awful taste, dilated pupil and increased reflex. The probable?
expl: Option C: Strychnine is a competitive antagonist of glycine receptors . Glycine is an inhibitory neurotransmitter, particularly in the spinal cord and brainstem. It normally prevents excessive neuronal firing by inhibiting motor neurons. Strychnine toxin acts by blocking the action of glycine at the post-synaptic receptors in the motor neurons of the anterior horn of the spinal cord. Option A: Agonist of Dopamine : Dopamine is a neurotransmitter involved in various functions such as movement control, reward, and motivation. Strychnine does not interact with dopamine receptors. Option B: Agonist of Serotonin : It is involved in mood regulation, sleep, and more. Serotonin agonists enhance serotonin activity. Strychnine does not stimulate serotonin receptors. Option D: Antagonist of Acetylcholine : Antagonists of ACh receptors block cholinergic transmission, which could lead to paralysis or reduced muscle activity. Strychnine primarily affects glycine receptors, not acetylcholine receptors. Key takeaways : In strychnine poisoning, the toxin acts as an antagonist of glycine leading to increased neuronal excitability and convulsions. Reference: Ganong’s Review of Medical Physiology 26 th Edition Page no. 350

text: A 35-year-old man presented with ptosis, dysarthria and descending flaccid paralysis 5 days after consumption of canned beverage. On examination, there is decreased deep tendon reflexes. The probable diagnosis is botulism. The botulinum toxin degrades SNARE proteins like synaptobrevin (shown in the figure). Which of the following neurotransmitter will not be released?
expl: Option D: Botulinum toxin inhibits Ach release by cleaving SNARE proteins, which are necessary for vesicles containing acetylcholine to fuse with the presynaptic membrane. It binds to acetylcholine receptors on the nerve terminals at neuromuscular junction, which results in blockage of release of the acetylcholine, leading to flaccid paralysis. A. GABA : Inhibitory neurotransmitter released in the CNS, not affected by botulinum toxin. GABA is not typically involved in neuromuscular transmission, and its inhibition does not directly lead to flaccid paralysis. B. Serotonin : Primarily involved in mood and cognition, not impacted by botulinum toxin. Its dysfunction does not explain the motor symptoms observed in this patient. C. Glycine : Inhibitory neurotransmitter in the spinal cord, not directly affected by the toxin. Glycine is more implicated in diseases like tetanus , where glycine release is inhibited, leading to spastic paralysis (in contrast to the flaccid paralysis seen in botulism). Key Takeaways: In botulism , botulinum toxin blocks the release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, causing flaccid paralysis. text: A patient experiences phantom limb pain following the amputation of the right limb. What would a PET scan most likely reveal in such a case?

options.A: Expansion of right somatosensory fibres for the hand into neighbouring areas
options.B: Neighbouring fibres of the right somatosensory area extending into the right-hand area
options.C: Expansion of the right sensory cortex
options.D: Expansion of the left sensory cortex

ansText: Neighbouring fibres of the right somatosensory area extending into the right-hand area
expl: Explanation: After amputation, the brain undergoes cortical reorganisation. In this case, the neighbouring somatosensory fibres that previously represented adjacent body parts extend into the region that formerly represented the right hand. This reorganisation is associated with the perception of phantom limb pain. Explanation for other options: Expansion of right somatosensory fibres for the hand into Neighbouring areas (Option A): Somatosensory fibres specifically responsible for the right hand expand into neighbouring regions. However, it is not the fibres themselves that expand; rather, it is the cortical representation that changes. Expansion of right sensory cortex (Option C): Implies a general enlargement of the right sensory cortex. However, the expansion is not global; rather, it involves the Neighbouring cortical areas invading the region corresponding to the amputated limb. Expansion of left sensory cortex (Option D): The left sensory cortex is responsible for processing sensory input from the right side of the body. The reorganisation occurs in the sensory cortex corresponding to the amputated limb (in this case, the right cortex, which processes left-sided sensations). Learning objective: Phantom Limb Pain Perceived due to cortical plasticity In the phantom limb phenomenon, the limb does not exist (amputated), but the patient complains that he feels pain or itch in the limb. Based on the evidence, brain reorganisation occurs when sensory input is cut off. For example, in leg amputees, the ventral posterior thalamic nucleus can perceive the signal that once received input from the leg and foot, now responds to stump (thigh) stimulation. Management : Epidural Anaesthesia: Used during amputation surgery to reduce acute pain and subsequent need for opioids, lowering phantom pain incidence. Spinal Cord Stimulation: Electric current stimulates spinal pathways, reducing phantom limb pain and causing a tingling sensation instead in the phantom limb

Management : Epidural Anaesthesia: Used during amputation surgery to reduce acute pain and subsequent need for opioids, lowering phantom pain incidence . Spinal Cord Stimulation: Electric current stimulates spinal pathways, reducing phantom limb pain and causing a tingling sensation instead in the phantom limb

text: A military after amputation tells the doctor that he still feels the pain in the amputated part. Which is incorrect statement regarding this case?

options.A: Reduced incidence of phantom pain following epidural anaesthesia during surgery is reported
options.C: Lateral dorsal thalamic nucleus is one example where this change can occur
options.D: Spinal cord stimulation has been shown to be effective therapy for phantom pain

ansText: Lateral dorsal thalamic nucleus is one example where this change can occur
expl: Reduced incidence of phantom pain has been reported after epidural anesthesia during amputation surgery, as it may prevent acute surgical pain. Phantom pain is based on cortical plasticity , where adjacent areas take over the cortical representation of the amputated limb. The ventral posterior thalamic nucleus , not the lateral dorsal thalamic nucleus, is one example where cortical changes can occur. Spinal cord stimulation has been shown to effectively reduce phantom pain. Electric current passed next to spinal cord interferes with the impulses ascending to the brain and lessens the pain felt in the phantom limb. Why Not Others A : Correct, as evidence supports the reduction of phantom pain with epidural anesthesia. B : Correct, phantom pain is associated with cortical plasticity. C : Incorrect, the ventral posterior thalamic nucleus is involved, not the lateral dorsal. D : Correct, spinal cord stimulation is an effective therapy for phantom pain. Key Takeaways Phantom pain is due to cortical plasticity and can be managed with spinal cord stimulation . The ventral posterior thalamic nucleus is involved in phantom pain, not the lateral dorsal nucleus . text: A 32-year-old male presents after a penetrating spinal cord injury. Examination reveals: 1.Ipsilateral loss of proprioception, vibration sense, and fine touch below the level of the lesion. 2.Contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation starting one or two segments below the lesion. Which of the following syndromes best explains these findings?
expl: Explanation: Brown-Séquard syndrome results from hemisection of the spinal cord (lateral half). Key features: Ipsilateral (same side) deficits: Loss of proprioception, vibration, and fine touch due to dorsal column-medial lemniscal tract injury (fibers cross in the medulla). Contralateral (opposite side) deficits: Loss of pain and temperature starting 1-2 segments below lesion due to spinothalamic tract damage (fibers cross within 1-2 spinal segments). Motor deficits may also occur on the ipsilateral side due to corticospinal tract involvement. Explanation of Other Options: Weber's syndrome (Option A) : Midbrain lesion involving corticospinal tract + oculomotor nerve (CN III) . Clinical features: Contralateral hemiparesis + ipsilateral oculomotor palsy. Does not involve the spinal sensory cross-pattern . Dejerine syndrome (Option B) : Medial medullary syndrome (medulla infarct). Features: Contralateral hemiparesis + ipsilateral tongue weakness + medial lemniscus involvement. Wallenberg syndrome (Option D) : Lateral medullary syndrome (posterior inferior cerebellar artery infarct). Features: Ipsilateral facial pain/temp loss + contralateral body pain/temp loss, ataxia, dysphagia. Key Takeaway Points: Spinal Cord Syndromes Comparison Clinical Pearls: Spinothalamic fibers: cross 1-2 segments above entry → contralateral pain/temp loss. Dorsal columns: cross at medulla → ipsilateral proprioception/vibration loss below lesion. Motor fibers (corticospinal): cross at pyramidal decussation → ipsilateral weakness if lesion is below medulla. Common Causes of Brown-Séquard: Penetrating trauma (knife/gunshot) Multiple sclerosis (rare hemisection) Tumors causing lateral cord compression

text: A 38-year-old woman was rushed to the emergency department after getting stabbed with a sharp weapon. On MRI, complete transection of one side of spinal cord is suspected. Which of the following is least likely to be seen in this patient?
expl: Option C: Brown-Sequard Syndrome results from hemisection of the spinal cord, causing: Ipsilateral Loss of Proprioception : Due to damage to dorsal columns. Contralateral Loss of Pain and Temperature : Due to damage to the spinothalamic tract. Ipsilateral Flaccid Paralysis : At the level of the lesion due to lower motor neuron damage. Contralateral Spastic Paralysis : Below the level of the lesion due to upper motor neuron damage. Why not other options: Option A: Ipsilateral loss of proprioception : This is expected in Brown-Sequard syndrome due to damage to the dorsal columns on the same side as the lesion. Option B: Contralateral loss of pain : This occurs because the spinothalamic tract, responsible for pain and temperature sensation, crosses over to the opposite side before ascending. Option D: Contralateral loss of temperature : Similar to pain, the loss of temperature sensation occurs contralaterally due to the crossing of the spinothalamic tract. Key Takeaways: In a patient with suspected complete transection of one side of the spinal cord, the least likely finding would be contralateral flaccid and spastic paralysis, as paralysis is typically ipsilateral due to damage to the corticospinal tract on the same side as the injury (Brown-Sequard syndrome). text: A 55 y of came to emergency department after suffering a stroke. She has difficulty maintaining balance and posture, and upon neurological examination, it is noted that she has proximal limb weakness, especially when trying to stand or walk. His fine motor control in his hand remains intact. There are no signs of sensory loss or cranial nerve involvement. So, which pathway is most responsible for this?
expl: The reticulospinal tract is primarily involved in controlling balance and posture by influencing the muscles of the trunk and proximal limbs . It plays a significant role in maintaining muscle tone and helps coordinate movements necessary for standing and walking. Why Not Other Options A (Lateral Corticospinal tract): Responsible for fine motor control , particularly of distal muscles, such as those in the hands. Since fine motor skills are intact, this pathway is not the primary issue. B (Rubrospinal tract): Involved in the control of distal limb movements , particularly the upper limbs. It doesn't have a major role in posture and balance. D (Vestibulospinal tract): Contributes to balance by coordinating head and eye movements, but the reticulospinal tract is more involved in trunk and limb stability . Key Takeaways Reticulospinal tract is most responsible for postural control and proximal muscle tone in this scenario, differentiating it from pathways involved in fine motor skills. text: A 75-year-old male presents to the neurology clinic with complaints of a progressive tremor in his hands, which has worsened over the past year. He also reports increasing stiffness in his arms and legs, difficulty initiating movements (bradykinesia), and episodes of shuffling when he walks. His wife mentions that he seems less expressive and has developed a tendency to fall over the past few months. Based on the patient's symptoms, which part of the extrapyramidal nervous system is most likely affected, and what is the underlying mechanism?

options.A: Subthalamic nucleus; decreased inhibition of the thalamus
options.C: Globus pallidus interna; excessive excitation of the motor cortex
options.D: Substantia nigra; reduced dopamine release to the striatum

ansText: Substantia nigra; reduced dopamine release to the striatum
expl: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by: Resting tremors: Shaking that occurs when the muscles are at rest. Bradykinesia: Difficulty in initiating movements. Rigidity: Stiffness in the limbs and trunk. Postural instability: Tendency to fall, indicating balance issues. The pathophysiology of PD involves: Degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra . Dopamine deficiency leads to impaired communication within the basal ganglia, disrupting normal motor control. Clinical diagnosis is primarily based on: Neurological assessment and characteristic symptoms. Treatment options include: Medications like levodopa and dopamine agonists. Surgical interventions such as deep brain stimulation, for advanced cases. Why not the other options? A) Subthalamic nucleus; decreased inhibition of the thalamus: While the subthalamic nucleus plays a role in the basal ganglia circuitry, it is not primarily affected in Parkinson's disease; rather, it's the substantia nigra that shows degeneration. Damage to subthalamic nucleus causes intense flailing movement of proximal parts of limbs leading to hemiballismus B) Caudate nucleus; increased dopamine release: This is incorrect because, in Parkinson's disease, dopamine levels are reduced, not increased. Damage to caudate nucleus produces chorea that is rapid involuntary dancing like movement of distal parts of limb. C) Globus pallidus interna; excessive excitation of the motor cortex: While the globus pallidus is involved in the indirect pathway and can contribute to motor dysfunction, the primary issue in PD is the loss of dopamine from the substantia nigra affecting overall basal ganglia function. Key Takeaways: In Parkinson's disease , the substantia nigra is affected, leading to reduced dopamine release . This results in a disruption of motor control manifesting as tremors, stiffness, and bradykinesia. Understanding these mechanisms is crucial for effective diagnosis and treatment. Direct pathway in relation to dopamine (DA) DA stimulates D1 receptors on the striatum leads to inhibition of the globus pallidus internus (GPi) thalamus becomes disinhibited sends excitatory input into the cortex Indirect pathway in relation to dopamine DA stimulates D2 receptors on STN STN stimulates GP i Thalamus is inhibited No excitatory input into cortex. text: A 60-year-old man presents with tremors that occur when he is using her hands, such as when writing or drinking from a cup, or doing fine motor movements. Tremors do not occur on resting. Her mother had similar symptoms, and her condition improves with alcohol consumption. Neurological exam shows no signs of rigidity or bradykinesia. What is the most likely diagnosis and what part of the nervous system is primarily affected?
expl: Essential tremor is characterized by: Action tremors: These occur during voluntary movements, such as writing or holding objects, distinguishing them from resting tremors. Familial pattern: The presence of similar symptoms in the patient's mother suggests a genetic component. Improvement with alcohol: Essential tremor often temporarily improves with alcohol consumption, which is a classic feature. The pathophysiology involves: Cerebellar dysfunction: The cerebellum and its connections are primarily involved, affecting coordination and fine motor control. Why not the other options? A) Parkinson's disease; Substantia nigra: This condition is characterized by resting tremors, rigidity, and bradykinesia. The patient's action tremors and absence of resting tremors make this diagnosis unlikely. C) Dystonia; Putamen: Dystonia involves sustained muscle contractions causing abnormal postures or movements, which are not present in this patient. The lack of rigidity or abnormal posturing further rules this out. D) Huntington's disease; Caudate nucleus: Huntington's disease presents with chorea, cognitive decline, and psychiatric symptoms. The absence of these symptoms in this case makes this diagnosis inappropriate. Key Takeaways: The diagnosis of Essential tremor aligns with the presence of action tremors and familial history , with cerebellar involvement being key. Differentiating features like the absence of resting tremors and improvement with alcohol help clarify the condition. Understanding these nuances is essential for accurate diagnosis and management. text: A 60-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a fall resulting in a traumatic brain injury. Upon examination, he is found to have an abnormal posturing response. His arms are flexed at the elbows and wrists, and his legs are extended. The medical team notes that he does not respond appropriately to verbal commands but exhibits some spontaneous movements. The patient is found in below given position.
expl: Decorticate Rigidity: Characterization: Flexion of the arms at the elbows and wrists while the legs are extended. Indicates Damage: Suggests injury to the corticospinal tract , typically above the level of the red nucleus . Significance: Reflects loss of higher inhibitory control over spinal reflexes, leading to increased flexor tone . Involves overactivity of vestibulospinal and rubrospinal tracts. Why not the other options? A) Decerebrate Rigidity: (e-extended) Characterization: Extension of arms and legs, with arms adducted and extended at the elbows. The head may be extended backward. Indicates Damage: Suggests severe brainstem injury, especially in the upper brainstem or midbrain. Indicates disruption of both corticospinal and rubrospinal pathways, leading to unopposed extensor tone. C) Opisthotonos: Characterization: Spasm of back muscles leading to hyperextension of the back and neck, resulting in an arched body posture. Indicates Damage: Often suggests severe central nervous system irritation, such as meningitis or significant brain injury. D) Flaccid Posturing: Characterization: Lack of muscle tone, with limbs hanging loosely and without movement. Indicates Damage: Indicates severe neurological damage, often associated with conditions like brain death or extensive brain injury, where no motor responses are observed. Key Takeaways: Decorticate rigidity indicates damage to the corticospinal tract and reflects the brain's inability to exert inhibitory control over motor responses. Understanding these postures helps assess the level of neurological impairment and the location of brain injury. Tags: Inicet nov 2022 Reference: John. E. Hall, Michael .E. Hall/ Guyton and Hall Textbook of medical physiology, edition 14, page no. 720-727; Ganong's review of medical physiology 26 th edition, fig 12-12, pg no. 558

text: A 62-year-old patient is brought to the emergency department following a suspected stroke. On evaluation, he can speak fluently, but the words uttered lack coherent meaning and understanding. Which type of aphasia is most likely present in this patient?
expl: Explanation: As the patient speaks fluently but the speech is nonsensical, lacks meaningful content, and comprehension is poor, the findings are characteristic of Wernicke's aphasia . Aphasia Aphasias are disorders of language function that occur independently of visual, auditory, or motor deficits . They result from lesions in the dominant (categorical) cerebral hemisphere , most commonly due to embolism or thrombosis of a cerebral artery . Based on speech characteristics, aphasias are broadly classified into nonfluent , fluent , conduction and anomic types.

text: A 55-year-old man presents with gradually worsening weakness and spasticity in his right leg. On examination, there is increased muscle tone, hyperreflexia, and a positive Babinski sign, all confined to the right lower limb. His left leg and both upper limbs show no abnormalities. An MRI of the brain shows a lesion affecting the left motor cortex. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The patient's symptoms- progressive weakness , spasticity , increased muscle tone , hyperreflexia , and a positive Babinski sign in the right leg -are classic indicators of an upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion . These signs are typical of damage to motor pathways above the level of the spinal cord. The MRI reveals a lesion in the left motor cortex , which is responsible for controlling voluntary movement on the contralateral (right) side of the body due to the decussation (crossing over) of motor fibers in the medulla. This correlates well with the patient's right-sided motor findings and confirms the presence of a left-sided UMN lesion . Explanation for other options: Parkinson's disease (Option A): This condition primarily involves the basal ganglia and is characterized by bradykinesia , resting tremor , and rigidity- not by spasticity, hyperreflexia , or a Babinski sign . It does not typically present with isolated UMN signs. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) (Option B): ALS affects both upper and lower motor neurons . While UMN signs can be seen, patients usually also show lower motor neuron features such as muscle atrophy , fasciculations , and flaccid weakness -none of which are present in this case. Thus, isolated UMN involvement makes ALS less likely . Multiple sclerosis (MS) (Option C): MS commonly presents with relapsing-remitting neurological deficits and multiple demyelinating lesions throughout the central nervous system. The patient's symptoms are progressive and localized , with imaging showing a focal cortical lesion , which is not typical for MS. Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK537305/

text: A 62-year-old man presents with progressive involuntary movements, dementia, aggression, cognitive decline, He has a family history of a similar condition that affected his father at age of 68. Upon examination, you observe jerky, rapid, and irregular movements of the limbs (chorea). No history of substance abuse. What is the primary underlying mechanism leading to the symptoms in this patient?

options.A: Overstimulation of the cerebral cortex due to loss of GABAergic neurons in the basal ganglia
options.B: Degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra
options.C: Accumulation of misfolded tau protein in the neurons

ansText: Overstimulation of the cerebral cortex due to loss of GABAergic neurons in the basal ganglia
expl: Huntington's Disease (HD): Primary Mechanism: In HD, there is degeneration of GABAergic neurons (inhibitory neurons) in the basal ganglia, especially affecting the striatum (caudate nucleus and putamen). Outcome: This loss of inhibitory control leads to overstimulation of the cerebral cortex, resulting in the characteristic hyperkinetic movements , particularly chorea (involuntary, jerky movements). Additional Symptoms: Cognitive decline and psychiatric symptoms like aggression are also linked to the disruption of basal ganglia circuits. Why not the other options? B) Degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra: This is typical of Parkinson's disease , where loss of dopamine leads to bradykinesia, rigidity, and resting tremor, not chorea. C) Accumulation of misfolded tau protein in the neurons: This is associated with tauopathies , such as Alzheimer's disease and does not explain the hyperkinetic movements seen in HD. D) Demyelination of neurons: Demyelination is characteristic of conditions like multiple sclerosis , leading to varied neurological symptoms, but not specifically the involuntary movements seen in Huntington's disease. Key Takeaways: In Huntington's disease, the loss of GABAergic neurons leads to cerebral cortex overstimulation , causing chorea and associated cognitive and psychiatric symptoms. Differentiating the mechanisms behind neurodegenerative disorders is critical for accurate diagnosis and management. Tags: Fmge jan 2023 Reference: John. E. Hall, Michael .E. Hall/Guyton and Hall Textbook for physiology, edition 14, page no. 727; Ganong's review of medical physiology, 26 th edition, pg no. 563-56

text: A 45-year-old woman presents with involuntary, jerky movements of her limbs and face, which have progressively worsened over the past year. She also reports mood changes and memory difficulties. Her father had similar symptoms in his mid-40s. A brain MRI is performed, revealing atrophy of the nucleus in the basal ganglia, resulting in enlarged lateral ventricles. Which brain structure is most likely to be atrophied in this patient?
expl: Caudate Nucleus: Primary Affection: Atrophy of the caudate nucleus is characteristic of Huntington's disease . Imaging Findings: This atrophy leads to enlargement of the lateral ventricles , known as hydrocephalus ex vacuo. Function: The caudate nucleus is crucial for movement control , and its degeneration results in the choreiform movements seen in this condition. Why not the other options? B) Putamen: Explanation: While the putamen is involved in basal ganglia circuits , it is not the primary site of degeneration in Huntington's disease. It is more associated with conditions like dystonia or Parkinson's disease . C) Substantia Nigra: Explanation: This structure is predominantly affected in Parkinson's disease , leading to loss of dopaminergic neurons and symptoms such as resting tremor and bradykinesia . It is not primarily involved in Huntington's disease. D) Hippocampus: Explanation: The hippocampus is critical for memory formation and is primarily affected in Alzheimer's disease . Although cognitive decline occurs in Huntington's disease, the hippocampus is not the main area of atrophy; the caudate nucleus is. Key Takeaways: Atrophy of the caudate nucleus is a hallmark of Huntington's disease , leading to characteristic movement disorders and cognitive changes. Understanding the specific brain structures affected in different movement disorders aids in accurate diagnosis and management. Tags: Fmge jan 2023 Reference: John. E. Hall, Michael. E. text: A 42-year-old man presented with complaints of abnormal, sudden involuntary writhing movements (shown in the figure). What is the probable diagnosis and loss of which of the following is responsible for the hyperkinetic features seen in this case scenario?

options.B: Rheumatic chorea, Glutamate and cholinergic pathway

expl: Option A: Huntington's disease is a neurodegenerative disorder that primarily affects the intrastriatal GABAergic pathway . This pathway involves gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) neurons within the striatum. The loss of GABAergic pathway to the globus pallidus external segment releases inhibition, permitting the hyperkinetic features of the disease to develop. Option B: Rheumatic chorea, Glutamate and cholinergic pathway : Rheumatic chorea is linked to streptococcal infection, not Huntington's. The pathophysiology of rheumatic chorea involves immune-mediated inflammation in the basal ganglia , particularly affecting the glutamate and cholinergic neurotransmitter pathways. Option C: Huntington's disease, Nigrostriatal dopaminergic pathway : Dopaminergic pathways are more relevant to Parkinson's, not Huntington's. There is degeneration of the dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, leading to hypokinetic symptoms Option D: Rheumatic chorea, Intrastriatal cholinergic pathway : · Rheumatic chorea is associated with disruption of various neurotransmitter systems in the basal ganglia, including the intrastriatal cholinergic pathway . Huntington's disease involves GABAergic loss, not cholinergic. Key takeaways : Huntington's disease characterized by involuntary movements (chorea). This is due to the loss of the intrastriatal GABAergic pathway which leads to hyperkinetic symptoms. Tags: Good to know Reference: Ganong’s Review of Medical Physiology 26 th Edition Page no. 566

text: A 32-year-old male is brought to the emergency department after a road traffic accident. Following the accident, he exhibits significant behavioral changes, including increased appetite and overeating. Neurological examination reveals that he has difficulty regulating his body weight, and he reports feeling excessively hungry. MRI scans show's lesion in which part of hypothalamus?
expl: The patient’s symptoms of increased appetite and overeating indicate a dysfunction in the hypothalamus, specifically in the ventromedial nucleus (VMN) . Function of the VMN : Known as the satiety center , the VMN inhibits hunger and regulates energy balance. Lesions in this nucleus lead to hyperphagia (increased eating) and obesity due to the loss of inhibitory signals for hunger, consistent with the patient's condition. Mechanism : The VMN receives input from various hormonal signals (like leptin) that inform the body about energy reserves. When functioning properly, it signals the cessation of eating. However, lesions disrupt this signaling pathway, resulting in uncontrolled eating. Behavioral Changes : The patient’s difficulty regulating body weight and excessive hunger post-accident may reflect both the direct effects of the lesion and possible compensatory mechanisms activated in response to perceived energy deficiency. Why Not Other Options A (Lateral hypothalamic area) : Known as the "hunger center," lesions here typically cause decreased appetite and weight loss, contradicting the patient’s increased appetite. C (Paraventricular nucleus) : While involved in hormone production, lesions here do not primarily lead to increased appetite or hyperphagia. D (Suprachiasmatic nucleus) : Responsible for regulating circadian rhythms, it does not influence appetite or eating behaviors. Key Takeaways The ventromedial nucleus (VMN) lesion leads to hyperphagia and obesity due to the loss of inhibitory signals for hunger. Recognizing the specific roles of different hypothalamic nuclei can aid in effective diagnosis and treatment of eating disorders and obesity-related conditions! Understanding these mechanisms is crucial for managing behavioral changes following hypothalamic injuries. HYPOTHALAMIC NUCLEI Lateral-hunger Ventromedial-satiety Anterior-cooling in response to heat Posterior-heating in response to cold Suprachiasmatic-circadian rhythm Supraoptic-ADH(SAD) Paraventricular-oxytocin(POX) Preoptic-sexual response, determines GNRH release. Lateral and posterior nucleus controls sympathetic system. Preoptic nucleus controls parasympathetic system. Tags: NEET 2022 Reference: John. E. Hall/ GUTON AND HALL Textbook of medical physiology/14 th edition/page no:595-597

text: A 22-year-old male suffers a head injury in a road traffic accident. Following the injury, his family reports: 1.Excessive curiosity and hyperorality (constantly touching and putting objects in his mouth, including plates) 2.Hypersexual behavior (squeezing his genitals) 3.Rapid forgetfulness and impaired memory Which brain structure is most likely affected in this patient?

options.A: Gray matter around the aqueduct of Sylvius

expl: Explanation: The described symptoms are characteristic of Klüver-Bucy syndrome , which results from bilateral lesions of the amygdala . Key features of Klüver-Bucy syndrome: Hyperorality: putting objects in the mouth Hypersexuality: inappropriate sexual behaviors Hyperphagia: excessive eating Visual agnosia : inability to recognize objects Emotional changes: placidity or decreased fear responses The amygdala , located in the temporal lobe beneath the uncus , is critical for emotion regulation, fear response, memory, and social behavior . Damage → loss of fear, inappropriate emotional responses, and behavioral disinhibition. Bilateral temporal lobe damage (trauma, herpes encephalitis) → classic Klüver-Bucy syndrome Unilateral lesions may produce milder behavioral changes Amygdala Anatomy & Function Almond-shaped structure in the temporal lobe Composed of ~13 nuclei grouped into: Basolateral nuclei : emotion processing, learning Cortical-like nuclei : olfactory integration Central nuclei : autonomic and endocrine regulation Other nuclei & extended amygdala : behavior modulation Functionally connected to hippocampus, hypothalamus, thalamus, and prefrontal cortex Explanation of Other Options: Gray matter around the aqueduct of Sylvius (Option A): Involved in periaqueductal gray functions like pain modulation and autonomic responses. Not responsible for hyperorality or hypersexuality. Lateral nuclei of the hypothalamus (Option B): Regulate hunger and satiety . Lesions may cause anorexia or adipsia, but not Klüver-Bucy behavioral changes. Anterior cingulate gyri (Option D): Involved in emotion, attention, and autonomic regulation . Lesions → apathy, abulia, or impaired motivation, but not hyperorality or hypersexuality. Key Takeaway Points: Klüver-Bucy Syndrome Features

text: A 35-year-old man involved in a road traffic accident develops behavioral changes. On examination, he shows hyperphagia (increased appetite), hypersexuality, excessive anger, and loss of fear response. MRI reveals a focal lesion in a structure regulating autonomic, endocrine, and emotional behaviors. Which brain structure is most likely injured?
expl: Explanation of Correct Answer: The hypothalamus integrates autonomic, endocrine, and limbic functions. It regulates hunger, thirst, sexual behavior, aggression, circadian rhythms, and emotional responses . Damage to specific hypothalamic regions can lead to: Hyperphagia → lesion in ventromedial nucleus (satiety center). Hypersexuality and anger → dysregulation of hypothalamic-limbic circuits. Loss of fear → disruption of connections with the amygdala. Collectively, these features are consistent with hypothalamic injury . Explanation of Other Options: Amygdala (Option A) : Bilateral lesion causes Klüver-Bucy syndrome (hypersexuality, hyperorality, docility, visual agnosia). Fearlessness may occur, but marked hyperphagia is better explained by hypothalamic damage . Thalamus (Option B) : Relay station for sensory/motor signals. Lesions → sensory disturbances, pain syndromes, altered consciousness; not appetite/sexual behavior changes. Cingulate gyrus (Option C) : Part of limbic cortex; involved in emotion, learning, memory, and pain perception. Does not directly control feeding or sexual drive. Key Take Away Points: Hypothalamic Nuclei and Functions Distinction Between Hypothalamus and Amygdala Lesions Clinical Pearl: Hypothalamic lesions = metabolic + endocrine + behavioral changes . Amygdala lesions = emotional + behavioral changes (Klüver–Bucy syndrome) .

text: A 22-year-old male presents with symptoms of extreme fatigue, low libido, and decreased muscle mass. He has noticed a decrease in body hair and is concerned about his physical appearance. Blood tests reveal low testosterone and low luteinizing hormone (LH) levels.
expl: The arcuate nucleus plays a critical role in the hypothalamic regulation of reproductive hormones by producing gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) . GnRH stimulates the anterior pituitary to release luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) , essential for testosterone production and overall reproductive function. Clinical Significance : In this patient, a lesion or dysfunction in the arcuate nucleus could lead to decreased GnRH secretion, resulting in low levels of LH and testosterone. Symptoms such as fatigue, low libido, decreased muscle mass , and reduced body hair can all be attributed to low testosterone levels, highlighting the importance of the arcuate nucleus in maintaining hormonal balance. Comparison with Other Hypothalamic Nuclei : A (Ventromedial nucleus - VMN) : Known as the "satiety center," it regulates appetite and energy homeostasis, unrelated to reproductive hormone control. C (Lateral hypothalamic area - LHA) : Acts as the "hunger center," promoting appetite and food intake, again not directly involved in reproductive hormone regulation. D (Suprachiasmatic nucleus - SCN) : Functions as the body's master circadian clock, managing daily rhythms and not involved in the direct regulation of LH or testosterone. Why Not Other Options A (Ventromedial nucleus - VMN) : Its function is unrelated to the secretion of GnRH or reproductive hormones; thus, this option is incorrect. C (Lateral hypothalamic area - LHA) : While it regulates hunger and feeding behavior, it does not influence reproductive hormone levels, making it an incorrect option. D (Suprachiasmatic nucleus - SCN) : Focuses on circadian rhythms rather than hormonal regulation related to testosterone and LH levels, thus this option is incorrect. A dysfunction in the arcuate nucleus can lead to symptoms of hormonal imbalance, including fatigue and decreased libido . Understanding hypothalamic nuclei functions is vital for diagnosing hormonal disorders in young men. Tags: INICET nov 2022 Reference: John. E. text: A 27-year-old man develops adult respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) after near-drowning. Conventional mechanical ventilation on 100% O2 together with inhaled nitric oxide do not provide sufficient oxygenation. Porcine surfactant is instilled via fiberoptic bronchoscope, and the PaCO2, fraction of inspired oxygen (FIO2), and shunting improve impressively. The improvements in respiratory function occurred because surfactant increased which of the following?

options.B: The pressure gradient needed to inflate the alveoli

expl: Pulmonary surfactant increases lung compliance by lowering alveolar surface tension. As a result, the pressure gradient needed to inflate the alveoli decreases, as does the work of breathing. text: A 6 feet 3 inches tall, 140-lb, 20-year-old male was watching television when he felt pain in his shoulder blades, shortness of breath, and fatigue. His father noticed how pale he was and took him to the Emergency Department, where a chest X-ray revealed a 55% pneumothorax of the right lung due to rupture of a bleb on the surface of the lung. Which of the following is true?

options.A: The intrapleural pressure in the affected area is equal to atmospheric pressure
options.B: The chest wall on the affected side recoils inward
options.C: There is hyperinflation of the affected lung
options.D: The V/Q ratio on the affected side is higher than normal

ansText: The intrapleural pressure in the affected area is equal to atmospheric pressure
expl: When air enters the pleural space due to interruption of the pleural surface through either the rupture of the lung or a hole in the chest wall, the pressure in the pleural space becomes atmospheric, the lung on the affected side collapses because of the lung's tendency to recoil inward, and the chest wall on the affected side recoils outward. Because the intrapleural pressure is atmospheric, the mediastinum shifts farther to the normal side with each inspiration. With collapse of the lung, the V / Q ratio on the affected side decreases. Reference: Ganong, p 688. Kasper et al., p 1568. Levitzky, pp 12, 116-Stead et al., pp 273-274.

text: A 48-year-old coal miner complains of shortness of breath and a productive cough. The history reveals that he has smoked 1 to 2 packs of cigarettes per day since he was 16 years old. Pulmonary function studies are ordered including an esophageal balloon study to measure intrapleural pressures. Normally, intrapleural pressure is negative throughout a tidal inspiration and expiration because of which of the following?

options.A: The lungs have the tendency to recoil outward throughout a tidal breath
options.B: The chest wall has the tendency to recoil inward throughout a tidal breath
options.C: The intact pleura causes the lungs and chest wall to recoil away from each other throughout a tidal breath
options.D: The intact pleura causes the lungs and chest wall to recoil in the same direction throughout a tidal breath

ansText: The intact pleura causes the lungs and chest wall to recoil away from each other throughout a tidal breath
expl: When the pleura, and hence the lung-chest wall system, are intact, the inward elastic recoil of the lung opposing the outward elastic recoil of the chest wall results in a subatmospheric (negative) pressure with the pleural space. When one reaches lung volumes in excess of ~70% of the total lung capacity, the chest wall recoil is also inward. Reference: Ganong, pp 665-655. Levitzky, pp 17-23, 29-31.

text: A patient complains of paroxysmal episodes of not being able to catch her breath. When no abnormalities are detected with conventional pulmonary function screening, the pulmonologist orders a methacholine challenge test. Which of the following will increase as a result of stimulating cholinergic receptors on the bronchial smooth muscle?
expl: Methacholine is a cholinergic agonist, which causes constriction of bronchial smooth muscle. Bronchoconstriction reduces airway radius, which increases airway resistance, and thus the resistive work of breathing. Methacholine-induced bronchoconstriction decreases the anatomic deadspace but has no significant effect on the lung compliance, and thus does not affect the elastic work of breathing. Reference: Ganong, pp 649-650, 654, 657-659. Levitzky, pp 34-36, 49-50.

text: A patient with right lower lobar pneumonia exhibits increasing respiratory distress. The patient is intubated, placed on a mechanical ventilator, and positioned on his left side. The dependent lung has a lower:

options.A: Rate of alveolar ventilation per unit volume

expl: Even in normal individuals, the dependent lung has a greater ventilation per unit volume and a greater pulmonary blood flow, but because the effects of gravity (hydrostatic pressure) are greater for blood than air because blood is more dense, the increase in perfusion exceeds the increase in ventilation, and the V/Q ratio decreases. An area with a lower V/Q has less gas exchange, and thus Paco2 increases and PaO2 decreases. These changes are exacerbated in pneumonia, which causes an increase in the number of low V/Q areas in the lung. The greater hydrostatic pressure in the dependent lung causes an increased (less negative) intrapleural pressure, which decreases lung volume, and places the pressure-volume curve of the lung on a steeper slope (increased compliance). In patients with unilateral pneumonia, simply positioning the unaffected lung downward may result in improved ventilation-perfusion matching and an increase in PaO2 of 10-15 mmHg. Reference: Ganong, pp 662-663. Kasper et al., p 1537. Levitzky, pp 125-127.

text: A 68-year-old woman convalescing from surgery developed a fever, hypoxemia, and shortness of breath. She was given 100% O2 for 30 minutes, and the lab results were as follows: PaO2 = 95 mmHg PaCO2 = 33 mmHg pH = 7.46 [HCO3 -] = 22 mEq/L [Hb] = 15 g% SaO2 = 95% The response to 100% O2 reveals that the patient has which of the following?

options.C: V/Q inequality with low V/Q units

expl: The classification of the causes of hypoxemia (low PaO2) are Reduced PAO2 (alveolar hypoventilation or reduced PIo2 found at high altitude or with breathing low concentrations of oxygen), Diffusion impairment, Ventilation/perfusion inequality, and Right-to-left shunting (venous admixture). Left-to-right shunting does not cause hypoxemia. Administration of 100% O2 corrects the hypoxemia caused by alveolar hypoventilation, diffusion impairment, or ventilation/perfusion inequality, but not that due to right-to-left shunting (venous admixture). Alveolar hypoventilation would have an increased PaCO2. In carbon monoxide poisoning, the SaO2 would be lower than normal. On 100% O2, the PaO2 should be 1500 mmHg and the A-a PO2 difference should be "100 mmHg". This patient's Pao2 is only 95 mmHg on 100% O2, indicating the presence of right-to-left shunting, that is, areas of the lung that are perfused but not ventilated ( V / Q ratio = 0). Post-op complications such as pneumonia, pulmonary edema, and atelectasis are all causes of intrapulmonary right-to-left shunts. Reference: Ganong, pp 683-691. Levitzky, pp 180-183.

text: A 36-year-old man with a history of AIDS and Pneumocystis infection presents to the Emergency Department with severe respiratory distress. The patient is placed on a ventilator at a rate of 16, tidal volume of 600 mL, and FIO2 of 1.0. An arterial blood sample taken 20 minutes later reveals a Po2 of 350 mmHg, a Pco2 of 36 mmHg, and a pH of 7.32. At a barometric pressure of 757 mmHg, and assuming a normal respiratory exchange ratio (R) of 0.8, the patient's alveolar oxygen tension is approximately which of the following?
expl: The alveolar air equation is used to calculate the PAO2. PAO2 = PIO2 - (PaCO2/ R ) Given the barometric pressure of 757 mmHg, FIO2 = 1.0 (100% O2), PaCO2 = 36 mmHg, and R = 0.8, then PAO2 = (1.0)(757 - 47) - (36/0.8) = 710 - 45 = 665 mmHg Pneumocystis is an opportunistic fungal pulmonary pathogen that is an important cause of pneumonia (pneumocystosis) in immunocompromised hosts. HIV patients with a CD4 + cell count below 200/μL have an increased risk of developing Pneumocystis pneumonia. According to new, and still evolving nomenclature, Pneumocystis carinii is the name of the organism derived from rats, and Pneumocystis jiroveci is the name of the organism derived from humans. Reference: Ganong, p 660. Kasper et al., pp 1194-1196, 1583, 1592-1595. Levitzky, p 75. Stead et al., pp 202-204.

text: A 68-year-old man who has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) presents to his pulmonologist with fatigue, dyspnea at rest, and peripheral edema. His blood gases on room air are PaO2 = 60 mmHg, PaCO2 = 60 mmHg, and pH = 7.36. His alveolar-arterial (A-a) O2 gradient, at a barometric pressure of 760 mmHg and a respiratory exchange ratio (R) of 0.8, is approximately what?
expl: The A-a O2 gradient is the partial pressure difference between the alveolar gas and arterial blood. The PaO2 has been measured. The alveolar oxygen tension must be calculated using the modified alveolar gas equation PAO2 = PIO2 - PaCO2/ R PAO2 = [0.21 x (760 - 47 mmHg)] - 60 mmHg/0.8 PAO2 = 150 mmHg - 75 mmHg = 75 mmHg (A-a) O2 gradient = 75 mmHg - 60 mmHg = 15 mmHg The patient's low arterial oxygen tension (hypoxemia; hypoxic hypoxia) results from a low PAO2 due to hypoventilation (as evidenced by the elevated PaCO2), and thus the (A-a) O2 gradient is within the normal range. Reference: Levitzky, pp 75, 180-181, 262.

text: A hospitalized patient is found semicomatose. Arterial blood gases reveal hypercapnia. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the high arterial PCO2?
expl: Profound hypoxia depresses the central nervous system, including the medullary respiratory centers. As a result, alveolar ventilation may decrease, resulting in an increased PaCO2. A decrease in metabolic activity would decrease the rate of production of carbon dioxide (VCO2), which would decrease PaCO2, assuming that alveolar ventilation does not change. If an alveolar capillary block is severe, retention of CO2 could briefly occur, but the coexistent hypoxemia would cause reflex hyperventilation with a decrease in PaCO2. At a constant tidal volume and respiratory rate, a decrease in the deadspace volume would increase alveolar ventilation, and thus lower the PaCO2. Reference: Kasper et al. pp 209-210, 1624-1637. Levitzky, pp 66, 73-74, 136-138.

text: A patient with Wegener's glomerulonephritis presents with sinusitis and hemoptysis. His chest radiograph shows several large cavitary pulmonary nodules, consistent with ventilation- perfusion imbalance with low V'/Q' units. Which of the following will be greater than normal in a patient with a low V'/Q' ratio?
expl: Areas with low V/Q ratios produce hypoxemia or a decreased PaO2, which leads to A decrease in the dissolved oxygen content of the blood and A decrease in PaCO2, due to stimulation of the peripheral chemoreceptors. At lower PaO2 levels, arterial oxygen saturation is decreased, which decreases the oxyhemoglobin content. Because the mixed alveolar PO2 is normal and the arterial PO2 is less than normal, the A-a gradient is greater than normal. Reference: Levitzky, pp 113-116, 122-123.

text: A 24-year-old woman collapsed in a New York City subway station. An autopsy showed that a blood clot had travelled to her lung and caused her death. The medical examiner ultimately ruled that the blood clot was caused by the use of a birth control patch. Which of the following occurs if the blood flow to an alveolus is totally obstructed by a pulmonary thromboembolism?

options.A: The V/Q ratio of the alveolus equals zero
options.B: The PO2 of the alveolus will be equal to that in the inspired air
options.C: The PO2 of the alveolus will be equal to the mixed venous PO2
options.D: There will be an increase in shunting (venous admixture) in the lung

ansText: The PO2 of the alveolus will be equal to that in the inspired air
expl: A pulmonary thromboembolism results in areas of the lung that are ventilated, but not perfused, yielding V/Q ratios of infinity and an increase in alveolar deadspace. When the V/Q ratio equals infinite, the PAO2 of the affected alveoli will be the same as that in the humidified inspired air because atmospheric air enters the alveoli via the process of ventilation but no gas exchange takes place because the alveoli are not perfused. Areas of the lung that are perfused but not ventilated constitute areas of shunting (venous admixture), characterized as a V/Q ratio equal to 0, and having PAO2 values that equilibrate with the mixed venous blood. Reference: Kasper et al., pp 282, 1561. Levitzky, pp 114-117. Stead, pp 272-273.

text: A 75-year-old presented with increasing loss of memory. On histopathological examination, neurofibrillary tangles and amyloid plaque were seen. The probable diagnosis is Alzheimer's disease. There will be deficiency of which of the following neurotransmitter?
expl: Option B: Alzheimer’s disease is deficiency of acetylcholine in the subcortical area especially in the nucleus basalis of Meynert. It is is the most common age-related neurodegenerative disorder. Memory decline initially manifests as a loss of episodic memory, which impedes recollection of recent events, later on followed by general loss of cognitive and other brain functions, agitation, depression, the need for constant care, and, eventually, death. Option A: Glutamate: Increased in Alzheimer's, not decreased. Option C: Dopamine: Mainly associated with Parkinson's, not memory loss. Option D: Serotonin: Involved in mood regulation, not the primary neurotransmitter affected in Alzheimer's. Key takeaways: In Alzheimer's disease, there is a deficiency of acetylcholine which is critical for memory and cognitive function. Tags: AIIMS 2020 Reference: Ganong’s Review of Medical Physiology 26 th Edition Page no. 661

text: An 18-year-old college student living in a dormitory contracts meningitis, which causes a centrally mediated increase in his respiratory rate. The basic respiratory rhythm is generated in which of the following regions of the brain?
expl: The main components of the respiratory control pattern generator for the automatic control of breathing are located in the medulla. The basic respiratory rhythm is initiated by a small group of synaptically coupled pacemaker cells in the pre-Botzinger complex on either side of the medulla between the nucleus ambiguus and the lateral reticular nucleus. This basic rhythm can be modified by many factors, including higher centers in the cerebral cortex and hypothalamus and input from the reticular activating system and pontine respiratory centers, including the pneumotaxic center in the nucleus parabrachialis. Reference: Ganong, pp 192-193, 671-673. Levitzky, pp 188-194, 200.
