text: A female comes with a year old history of contact lens present with eye pain ,irritation and foreign body sensation. spot the diagnosis?
expl: Giant papillary conjunctivitis (GPC) is when the inside of your eyelid gets red, swollen, and irritated. Without GPC, the inside of your eyelid is very smooth. People who wear contact lenses (especially soft lenses) have the greatest chance of getting GPC. GPC can happen at any time, even after wearing contacts for many years. People who do not wear contact lenses can also get GPC. But this is rare, mostly affecting those who have an artificial eye or stitches. In giant papillary conjunctivitis, large bumps appear on the underside of the eyelid. GPC Causes GPC seems to be caused by the following: An allergy, either to contact lenses or the chemicals used to clean them. Contact lens wearers with asthma, hay fever, or other allergies are more likely to get GPC. A contact lens, artificial eye, or exposed stitches rubbing against the eyelid Deposits of proteins or other substances on the contact lenses Chronic eye allergies Incorrect Options Explanation: (A) Trachoma: Caused by Chlamydia trachomatis ; presents with follicles, Herbert’s pits, and Arlt’s line , but is not associated with contact lens wear. (C) Spring Catarrh (Vernal Keratoconjunctivitis): Seasonal allergic conjunctivitis in children with itching, mucoid discharge, and cobblestone papillae , but not related to contact lens use . (D) Acute Follicular Conjunctivitis: Caused by viral or chlamydial infections , presents with follicles , watery discharge, and lymphadenopathy, but lacks giant papillae on the eyelid. Key Takeaway: GPC is a chronic allergic reaction due to contact lens wear, presenting with eye irritation and giant papillae on the tarsal conjunctiva. Proper lens hygiene and switching to daily disposables can help prevent it.

text: An 18-year-old was brought to the emergency department by her friends as she had turned blue. She was well otherwise. On examination she has central cyanosis; all other parameters are normal. What is the most likely cause?
expl: The question deals with cyanosis in an otherwise well patient. Cyanosis is seen in hypoxia. But the patient with hypoxia will be dyspnoeic. Here the patient is otherwise normal. Rare cause of cyanosis is due to abnormal hemoglobins like methemoglobin or Sulfhemoglobin. The causes of methemoglobinemia includes: Nitrates, nitric oxide or nitrobenzene Aniline dyes Propanil(a herbicide) Dapsone Pyridium So the accurate among the options are drinking water contaminated with nitrates. Lead poisoning will not lead to cyanosis but bluish lines in the gums. Carbon monoxide poisoning will cause cherry red discolouration. Anorexia nervosa is a disease of distorted perception of body image, where the patient restricts food intake and will be malnourished. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch:459 Pg 3593

text: Which of the following parameters is not useful in analysing Light's criteria for pleural effusion?
expl: Exudative pleural effusions meet at ≥1 of the following criteria, whereas transudative pleural effusions meet none: Pleural fluid protein/serum protein >0.5 Pleural fluid LDH/serum LDH >0.6 Pleural fluid LDH more than two-thirds the normal upper limit for serum. These criteria misidentify ~25% of transudates as exudates. If one or more of the exudative criteria are met and the patient is clinically thought to have a condition producing a transudative effusion, the difference between the protein levels in the serum and the pleural fluid should be measured. If this gradient is >31 g/L (3.1 g/dL ), the exudative categorization by these criteria can be ignored because almost all such patients have a transudative pleural effusion. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch: 294 Pg 2197

text: A 58-year-old man presented to hospital with fever, intermittent rigors, and worsening fatigue. He had returned from a business trip to West Africa six months previously. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: The Duffy blood group on the red blood cells acts as a receptor for P. vivax. West Africans lack the Duffy blood group and therefore P. ovale replaces P. vivax in this region. Both P. vivax and P. ovale have a liver hypnozoite stage which can cause repeated relapses. falciparum typically presents within the first three months of return. Visceral leishmaniasis is not endemic in West Africa. Brucellosis is a zoonosis transmitted through contaminated and untreated milk and by direct contact with infected animals. The incubation period of brucellosis is usually one to three weeks, but sometimes may be several months. It may have either a sudden or insidious onset and is accompanied by continued, intermittent, or irregular fever. Typhoid fever presents within one to three weeks from return from an endemic area. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 224, Pg: 1723-1731

text: Myelophthisis is due to I. Marrow replaced by fibrous tissue by granulomatous process II. Marrow replaced by fibrous tissue by primary hematological process III. Marrow replaced by fibrous tissue by secondary to tumour

text: A 16-year-old girl presents with primary amenorrhoea. General physical examination reveals no abnormality. Breast development appear to be normal with scanty pubic hair growth. On karyotyping, she is found to have XY genotype. What is the most probable cause for her condition?
expl: This girl has testicular feminisation, wherein testosterone is being produced in adequate amounts by the testes located in the abdomen. The majority of cases occur due to a mutation in androgen receptor rendering them non-functional to testosterone and dihydrotestosterone (DHT). DHT is formed from testosterone by 5a-reductase and is responsible for the development of male secondary sex characteristics. In the absence of androgen receptors, the cells are more receptive to estradiol, which is also produced from testosterone by the enzyme aromatase. Thus, although the genotype is XY, these girls will have well-developed feminine secondary sex characteristics. Primary amenorrhoea is often the only symptom that brings these girls to medical attention. These children also would have absent mullerian structures due to normal MIS production from testes during intrauterine period. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 3003

However, it is believed that human papillomavirus infection may occur even before the woman starts taking the pill, and that there is no actual increase in the risk of acquiring infection. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 20 th edition Chapter:389 P page number :2814-15

text: A 46 year woman is admitted due to a single episode of haematemesis after taking a tablet of ibuprofen 6 hours previously. On examination, she had a blood pressure of 120/75 mmHg (lying) and 95/60 mmHg (standing). Her haemoglobin concentration is 7.5 g/dL. What is the likely cause of the haemetemesis?
expl: The likely answer is gastric erosions because the bleeding occurred after only one dose of Ibuprofen. There is no previous history of dyspepsia or upper GI bleeding. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs ( NSAIDs ) such as aspirin, ibuprofen, and naproxen cause gastric erosions via - Can be direct irritants of gastric mucosa Prostaglandins have a protective role in maintaining mucosal integrity. NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin production . Because of gravity, the irritants lie on the greater curvature of the stomach, and therefore, gastritis and ulcers are seen distally on or near the greater curvature of the stomach . Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 48, Pg: 312

text: Which is not correct regarding RA?

options.A: The incidence of RA increases between 25 and 55 years of age, after which it plateaus until the age of 75 and then decreases
options.B: The most common pattern of joint involvement is symmetrical and polyarticular.
options.C: Flexor tendon tenosynovitis is a frequent hallmark of RA
options.D: Macrocytic anemia is the most common hematologic abnormality in RA

ansText: Macrocytic anemia is the most common hematologic abnormality in RA
expl: A normochromic, normocytic anemia often develops in patients with RA and is the most common hematologic abnormality. Macrocytic anemia may occur in RA due to Methotrexate toxicity. Flexor tenosynovitis can occur in RA. It causes trigger fingers. The most common tendon involved is Flexor Pollicis Longus. The age of onset of RA is between 25 to 55 years of age, after which it plateaus until the age of 75 , after which it decreases. The most common pattern of involvement is symmetrical, polyarthritis. DIP is usually not involved, but if so, it is often due to OA. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Ch:358 Pg:2753

text: Which of the following statements is true? 1. In the context of a decreased GFR, autoregulatory mechanisms lead to prostacyclin mediated dialation of afferent arteriole and ACE mediated efferent arteriolar vasoconstriction. 2. NSAIDS cause inhibition of afferent arteriolar vasodilation and a decrease in GFR 3. NSAIDS cause inhibition of efferent arteriolar vasoconstriction and a decrease in GFR. 4. NSAIDS cause inhibition of efferent arteriolar vasodilation and a decrease in GFR.
expl: This question deals with renal autoregulatory mechanism. Under circumstances of reduced perfusion pressure, within the autoregulatory range, the GFR is maintained by the dialation of the afferent arteriole and constriction of the efferent arteriole . The former is mediated by prostaglandins and the latter by Angiotensin II. So drugs that inhibit the production of vasodilatory prostaglandins, eg NSAIDS, will reduce the GFR by inhibiting prostaglandin mediated afferent arteriolar vasodilation. ACEI or ARBs reduce the GFR by inhibiting Angiotensin II mediated efferent arteriolar vasoconstriction. Hence statements 1 and 2 are correct. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st ed, Chap 310 Pg. 2298

text: An 86-year-old woman presented with her first episode of urinary tract infection. Urine examination confirmed blood and proteinuria and E. coli was grown on culture. What is the next step in management after treating her with antibiotics?

options.D: Re-testing of urine with cytological examination after antibiotics

ansText: Re-testing of urine with cytological examination after antibiotics
expl: Urinary tract infection is common in females between the age of 20-40 years owing to their sexual activity. But UTI occurring in elderly females is usually due to anatomical factors. Urothelial malignancies present with hematuria and may be mistaken for UTI. Hence further work up is always needed. A concurrent UTI, if suspected, should be treated and urine should be re tested for persistent hematuria . If confirmeb, she should first be subjected to bladder cystoscopy. Along with this the kidneys and upper urinary tract should be visualized with CT Urogram. Retrograde pyelography is not routinely used, as CT urograms use very minimal contrast agents Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch:86, 135, Pg:677, 1071.

text: Which of the following denotes normal cardiac axis?
expl: The cardiac axis represents the overall direction of electrical activity as it spreads through the cardiac conduction system The normal cardiac axis is directed downward and slightly to the left. It falls within the range of -30° to +90°. Left Axis Deviation (LAD): When the QRS axis is less than -30°. Right Axis Deviation (RAD): When the QRS axis is greater than +90°. Extreme Axis Deviation: Occurs when the QRS axis lies between -90° and 180° ("Northwest Axis") Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 1870

text: Which of the following is not true regarding Ranolazine?

options.C: Administered at a dose of 500-1000 mg/day

text: Which of the following is caused by a lesion of the occipital lobe?
expl: Lesions of the frontal lobe include difficulties with task sequencing and executive skills: Expressive aphasia (receptive aphasias a temporal lobe lesion) Primitive reflexes Perseveration (repeatedly asking the same question or performing the same task) Anosmia Changes in personality. Lesions of the parietal lobe include : Apraxias Neglect Astereognosis (unable to recognise an object by feeling it) Visual field defects (typically homonymous inferior quadrantanopia). They may also cause acalculia (inability to perform mental arithmetic). Lesions of the temporal lobe cause: Visual field defects (typically homonymous superior quadrantanopia) Wernicke's (receptive) aphasia Auditory agnosia Memory impairment. Occipital lobe lesions include: Cortical blindness (blindness due to damage to the visual cortex and may present as Anton syndrome where there is blindness but the patient is unaware or denies blindness) Homonymous hemianopia Visual agnosia (seeing but not perceiving objects - it is different from neglect, since in agnosia the objects are seen and followed but cannot be named). Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 426, Pg: 3328

text: All of the following are effective osmoles, except?
expl: The solute or particle concentration of a fluid is known as its osmolality, expressed as milliosmoles per kilogram of water (mOsm/kg). Water easily diffuses across most cell membranes to achieve osmotic equilibrium (ECF osmolality = ICF osmolality). Notably, the extracellular and intracellular solute compositions differ considerably owing to the activity of various transporters, channels, and ATP-driven membrane pumps. The major ECF particles are Na+ and its accompany anions Cl- and HCO3 - , whereas K+ and organic phosphate esters (ATP, creatine phosphate, and phospholipids) are the predominant ICF osmoles. Solutes that are restricted to the ECF or the ICF determine the 'tonicity' or effective osmolality of that compartment. Certain solutes, particularly urea , do not contribute to water shifts across most membranes and are thus known as ineffective osmoles. Reference: Harrisons Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:53 Pg: 338

text: The major androgen secreted by adrenal gland is?

text: Most specific test for C.difficile is

text: Which of the following is not a cause of metabolic alkalosis?
expl: The various causes of metabolic alkalosis are summarized in the Table below. In attempting to establish the cause of metabolic alkalosis, one must assess the clinical circumstance (e.g., diuretics, vomiting) and the status of the ECF volume, blood pressure, serum K+ concentration, and in some cases the renin-aldosterone system. Urine electrolyte determinations and urine screening for diuretics are helpful diagnostic tools. Acetaminophen-induced high-AG metabolic acidosis is uncommon but is being recognized more often in either patients with acetaminophen overdose or malnourished or critically ill patients receiving acetaminophen in typical dosage. 5-Oxoproline accumulation after acetaminophen should be suspected in the setting of an unexplained high-AG acidosis without elevation of the osmolar gap in patients receiving acetaminophen. text: An 18 year-old female is admitted with a depression of her conscious level. Arterial blood gas analysis revealed: pH 7.26 pO2 90 mmhg pC02 29.25 mmhg standard bicarbonate 14.7 mmol/L Which one of the following would account for these results?
expl: The provided arterial blood gas results show: pH 7.26 (lower than the normal range of 7.35-7.45) pO2 90 mmHg (within the normal range) pCO2 29.25 mmHg (slightly elevated) Standard bicarbonate 14.7 mmol/L (lower than the normal range) These results suggest a primary metabolic acidosis. The low pH and low standard bicarbonate are indicative of an acidotic state. The elevated pCO2 indicates that there may be partial respiratory compensation occurring, which is the body's attempt to raise the pH by retaining carbon dioxide (which is acidic when dissolved in the blood). So, the correct answer is: B) Metabolic acidosis This is a physiological condition characterized by a decrease in blood pH due to an accumulation of acid or a loss of bicarbonate. In this case, the low standard bicarbonate indicates a loss of bicarbonate, contributing to the acidosis. The underlying cause of the metabolic acidosis would need further investigation, but it's not due to analytical error, respiratory acidosis, or persistent vomiting based on the information provided. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition, Ch: 55, Pg-359

text: Which of the following parameters in ABG analysis is a derived or calculated value rather than directly measured?
expl: Explanation: Bicarbonate concentration is a calculated value in arterial blood gas analysis, derived using the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation based on measured PCO₂ and pH values. The equation demonstrates how bicarbonate is formed when carbon dioxide dissolves in water to form carbonic acid, which then dissociates into hydrogen ions and bicarbonate: PCO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO 3 ⇌ H⁺ + HCO 3 - Understanding bicarbonate levels is crucial for assessing acid-base disorders: Elevated HCO 3 - occurs in metabolic alkalosis or as compensation in respiratory acidosis Decreased HCO 3 - occurs in metabolic acidosis or as compensation in respiratory alkalosis Arterial blood gas (ABG) analysis

text: A 45-year-old female presents to the emergency department. An arterial blood gas (ABG) reveals: pH 7.55, PaCO₂ 40 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 32 mEq/L. Which of the following conditions is most likely responsible for these findings?
expl: Explanation: This ABG demonstrates a primary metabolic alkalosis. The diagnosis is made through a systematic approach: Step 1: Analyze the pH The pH is 55 , which is > 7.45 . This indicates a primary alkalemia . Step 2: Determine the Primary Disorder The bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) is elevated at 32 mEq/L (normal ~24 mEq/L). This indicates a primary metabolic The PaCO₂ is normal at 40 mmHg . In a simple metabolic alkalosis, a compensatory rise in PaCO₂ (due to hypoventilation) is expected. A normal PaCO₂ here suggests the compensation is incomplete or the disorder is acute, but the primary driver is the elevated bicarbonate. The combination of alkalemia (high pH) and an elevated bicarbonate confirms a primary Metabolic Alkalosis . Common Causes of Metabolic Alkalosis This disorder often results from a loss of acid (H⁺ ions) or a gain of bicarbonate. Common causes include: Vomiting or nasogastric suction: Loss of gastric acid. Diuretic use: (especially loop and thiazide diuretics). Contraction alkalosis: From volume depletion. Hypokalemia Mineralocorticoid excess (e.g., hyperaldosteronism). Explanation of other options: Metabolic acidosis (Option A): This would present with a low pH and a low bicarbonate level. Respiratory acidosis (Option C): This would present with a low pH and a high PaCO₂ . Respiratory alkalosis (Option D): This would present with a high pH and a low PaCO₂ . Key Takeaways: High pH + High HCO₃⁻ = Metabolic Alkalosis. Use a stepwise approach: 1) pH to determine acidemia/alkalemia, 2) PaCO₂ and HCO₃⁻ to identify the primary disorder.

text: A patient presents to the casualty with multiple contusions on the chest. He is hypotensive. Arterial blood gas shows: pH 7.3, PCO2 44 mmHg, HCO3- 16 mEq/L, base excess -12, Na+ 130 mEq/L, Cl- 84 mEq/L. Which of the following explains the underlying abnormality?

options.A: Partially compensated respiratory acidosis with an anion gap of 12
options.B: Chronic respiratory acidosis with anion gap 30
options.D: Acute metabolic acidosis with anion gap 16

expl: Explanation: This patient's labs show acidemia (pH 7.3), low bicarbonate (16), and a normal PCO2 (44), suggesting that the primary abnormality is metabolic acidosis (not compensated by respiratory alkalosis/hyperventilation). The anion gap is: Na+ - (Cl- + HCO3-) = 130 - (84 + 16) = 130 - 100 = 30 This is a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. The findings are consistent with acute severe tissue hypoperfusion (due to shock or trauma), leading to lactic acidosis. Explanation of Incorrect Options: Partially compensated respiratory acidosis with an anion gap of 12 (Option A): PCO2 is not elevated, and the anion gap is much higher than 12. Chronic respiratory acidosis with anion gap 30 (Option B): The primary problem is metabolic, not respiratory, as PCO2 is not high but HCO3- is low. Acute metabolic acidosis with anion gap 16 (Option D): The actual anion gap is 30, not 16.

text: A 28-year-old male presents to the emergency department after ingesting a large quantity of salicylic acid tablets. Arterial blood gas (ABG) analysis reveals: pH = 7.30 pCO2 = 16 mmHg HCO2- = 6.3 mmol/L Na+ = 135 mmol/L K+ = 4.5 mmol/L Cl- = 113.7 mmol/L Lactate = Normal Which of the following best describes the acid-base abnormality in this patient?

options.A: Metabolic acidosis with partially compensated respiratory alkalosis with a high anion gap
options.B: Respiratory acidosis with compensatory metabolic alkalosis
options.C: Metabolic acidosis with uncompensated respiratory alkalosis

ansText: Metabolic acidosis with partially compensated respiratory alkalosis with a high anion gap
expl: Explanation of answer: The patient's ABG shows a high anion gap metabolic acidosis with evidence of partial respiratory alkalosis, commonly seen in salicylate poisoning. This question revolves around interpreting an ABG in the context of salicylate poisoning, which characteristically causes a mixed acid-base disorder. Here's a stepwise interpretation: Step 1: Check pH pH = 7.30 → Indicates acidemia Step 2: Identify the primary disorder HCO3- = 6.3 mmol/L (Low) → Suggests primary metabolic acidosis pCO2 = 16 mmHg (Low) → Normally, this would compensate for metabolic acidosis, but the level is lower than expected, hinting at a respiratory alkalosis component as well. Step 3: Calculate the anion gap Anion gap = Na+ - (Cl- + HCO3-) = 135 - (113.7 + 6.3) = 15 mEq/L Normal AG = 6-12 mEq/L → Thus, elevated anion gap Step 4: Assess respiratory compensation using Winter's formula Expected pCO2 = (1.5 × HCO3-) + 8 ± 2 = (1.5 × 6.3) + 8 = 17.45 ± 2 → Range: 15.5-19.5 mmHg Actual pCO2 = 16 mmHg → Within range → Compensatory respiratory alkalosis However, in salicylate poisoning, respiratory alkalosis may precede metabolic acidosis, creating a true mixed disorder. So, the acid-base status is: Primary high anion gap metabolic acidosis With superimposed respiratory alkalosis → mixed picture This pattern is characteristic of salicylate (aspirin) toxicity due to direct stimulation of the respiratory center and resulting hyperventilation. Explanation of other options: Respiratory acidosis with compensatory metabolic alkalosis (Option B): Incorrect. The pCO2 is low, not high, and HCO3- is also low, ruling out both respiratory acidosis and metabolic alkalosis. Metabolic acidosis with uncompensated respiratory alkalosis (Option C): Incorrect. The respiratory system has partially compensated for the metabolic acidosis, as pCO2 is within the Winter's predicted range. Respiratory acidosis with metabolic alkalosis (Option D): Incorrect. This pattern would show high pCO2 and high HCO3-, opposite to the findings here.

text: In some individuals, peptic ulcers do not develop despite the presence of Helicobacter pylori. This is most likely due to:

options.A: NSAIDs causing ulceration independent of H. pylori
options.B: Variation in host and bacterial virulence factors
options.C: Colonization limited to the antrum in asymptomatic individuals
options.D: All strains of H. pylori being non-ulcerogenic in certain hosts

ansText: Variation in host and bacterial virulence factors
expl: Explanation: The development of peptic ulcer disease in a person infected with Helicobacter pylori is not inevitable; it reflects a complex interaction between the bacterium's properties, the host's response, and environmental cofactors. Some H. pylori strains carry virulence determinants (for example, the cag pathogenicity island including cagA , cytotoxin-associated vacA genotypes, adhesins such as babA ) that provoke a stronger inflammatory response, more mucosal damage and a higher risk of ulcers. At the same time, host factors - including genetic polymorphisms in cytokine genes (e.g., IL-1β , TNF-α, IL-10), patterns of gastric acid secretion, and the effectiveness of mucosal defence (mucus, bicarbonate, prostaglandins) - alter how much damage a given bacterial insult produces. Thus, an infected person with a less virulent strain and/or a host genetic profile that limits inflammation or preserves mucosal defence may remain asymptomatic and ulcer-free, whereas another with a virulent strain and a pro-inflammatory host genotype may develop ulcers. Explanation for other Options: NSAIDs causing ulceration independent of H. pylori (Option A): This is true as a separate statement: NSAIDs can produce ulcers by inhibiting cyclooxygenase and lowering mucosal prostaglandins, so they can cause ulcers regardless of H. pylori status. However, this statement does not explain why some H. pylori-infected people do not develop ulcers; it only describes an alternate cause of ulcers. Colonization limited to the antrum in asymptomatic individuals (Option C): Antral infection can actually increase acid secretion and ulcer risk, so location alone is not protective. All strains of H. pylori being non-ulcerogenic in certain hosts (Option D): Many strains carry virulence genes; it is the interaction between host factors and bacterial virulence, not a universal lack of pathogenicity, that explains differing outcomes.

it reflects a complex interaction between the bacterium's properties, the host's response, and environmental cofactors. some h. pylori strains carry virulence determinants (for example, the cag pathogenicity island including caga , cytotoxin-associated vaca genotypes, adhesins such as baba ) that provoke a stronger inflammatory response, more mucosal damage and a higher risk of ulcers. at the same time, host factors - including genetic polymorphisms in cytokine genes (e.g., il-1β , tnf-α, il-10), patterns of gastric acid secretion, and the effectiveness of mucosal defence (mucus, bicarbonate, prostaglandins) - alter how much damage a given bacterial insult produces. thus, an infected person with a less virulent strain and/or a host genetic profile that limits inflammation or preserves mucosal defence may remain asymptomatic and ulcer-free, whereas another with a virulent strain and a pro-inflammatory host genotype may develop ulcers. explanation for other options: nsaids causing ulceration independent of h. pylori (option a): this is true as a separate statement: nsaids can produce ulcers by inhibiting cyclooxygenase and lowering mucosal prostaglandins, so they can cause ulcers regardless of h. pylori status. however, this statement does not explain why some h. pylori-infected people do not develop ulcers; text: What is the specific amino acid substitution responsible for sickle cell anemia?
expl: Explanation: Sickle cell anemia results from a missense point mutation in the β-globin gene (HBB) located on chromosome 11 . This mutation substitutes valine (a non-polar amino acid) for glutamic acid (a polar amino acid) at the 6th position of the β-globin chain This single base substitution (GAG → GTG in DNA) causes the synthesis of abnormal hemoglobin S (HbS) . Under deoxygenated conditions, HbS tends to polymerize , leading to distortion of red blood cells into a sickle shape. Pathophysiology of Sickle cell anemia: a. HbS Polymerisation: A single-nucleotide polymorphism in the β-globin gene results in the substitution of valine for glutamic acid at the sixth position in the β-globin chain. This mutation leads to the formation of mutated hemoglobin (HbS). After deoxygenation, HbS molecules polymerize to form bundles. These polymer bundles cause erythrocytes to adopt a sickle shape and also promote hemolysis of erythrocyte, releasing cell-free Hb into circulation. b. Vaso-occlusion: Sickled erythrocytes impair blood flow and aggregate with neutrophils, platelets, and endothelial cells, causing stasis. Leads to ischemia-reperfusion (I-R) injury. c. Endothelial Dysfunction: Oxygenated Hb (Fe²⁺) depletes endothelial nitric oxide (NO), forming nitrate (NOࠣ⁻) and methemoglobin (Fe³⁺). Free radicals are generated by NADPH oxidase, xanthine oxidase (XO), and uncoupled endothelial NO synthase (eNOS) contribute to endothelial damage and dysfunction. Methemoglobin (Fe³⁺) breaks down, releasing cell-free heme, which is a major erythrocyte damage-associated molecular pattern (DAMP). d. Sterile Inflammation: Cell-free heme or ischemia-reperfusion injury triggers sterile inflammation by: Generating reactive oxygen species (ROS). Activating Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4). Inducing neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs). Releasing DAMPs, DNA, and other unidentified factors. This activates the inflammasome pathway, releasing IL-1β. Sterile inflammation enhances the adhesiveness of neutrophils, platelets, and endothelial cells. This creates a cycle that promotes further vaso-occlusion. text: A 49-year-old man presents with repeated bouts of watery diarrhea, dehydration, low potassium levels, and lack of stomach acid. Which neuroendocrine tumor is most likely responsible for this presentation?
expl: Explanation: The patient's symptoms are consistent with a VIPoma , a rare neuroendocrine tumor that produces vasoactive intestinal peptide and leads to WDHA syndrome which is characterized by watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, and achlorhydria. This disorder results in secretory diarrhea caused by overproduction of VIP, which leads to significant fluid and electrolyte depletion. It manifests as severe watery diarrhea (often reaching 3 liters daily), causing dehydration, marked electrolyte disturbances such as hypokalemia , and reduced gastric acid secretion (achlorhydria). The symptoms arise directly from the actions of excess VIP on intestinal and gastric secretory functions. Explanations of other options: Insulinoma (Option A) : Insulinomas typically manifest with hypoglycemic symptoms such as tiredness, weakness, sweating, palpitations, confusion, and even seizures. They cause low blood sugar due to excess insulin production, but unlike this case, they do not result in severe diarrhea or significant electrolyte imbalances. Somatostatinoma (Option B) : Somatostatinomas usually present with features such as diabetes, gallstones, diarrhea, and fatty stools because somatostatin suppresses digestive enzyme release. Although diarrhea may be present, these tumors do not produce the full WDHA syndrome. Glucagonoma (Option D) : Glucagonomas typically manifest with necrolytic migratory erythema, diabetes, weight reduction, and anemia, but they are not usually associated with the marked secretory diarrhea and electrolyte imbalances observed in this patient.

text: All the below are features of Conn's syndrome except?
expl: Explanation: Metabolic acidosis is not a feature of Conn's syndrome. Conn's syndrome Conn's syndrome, also known as primary hyperaldosteronism , is characterized by autonomous aldosterone production from the adrenal glands. Epidemiology Most common cause of secondary hypertension (6-20% of adult hypertensive patients) Higher prevalence in resistant hypertension (up to 30%) More common in women Causes: Aldosterone-producing adenoma (50-60%) Bilateral idiopathic adrenal hyperplasia Aldosterone-producing adrenal carcinoma (1%) Familial hyperaldosteronism (Types 1-3) The pathophysiology involves excess aldosterone stimulating the ENaC channel , resulting in increased sodium and water reabsorption while promoting urinary loss of potassium and hydrogen ions. Clinical Features Resistant hypertension Muscle weakness/cramping: D ue to hypokalemia, leading to muscle weakness, fatigue, and cramping. Fatigue Headaches Polydipsia/polyuria Lab Findings ↓ K+ (can be normal in up to 38%) ↑ Na+ Metabolic alkalosis: Due to increased urinary loss of hydrogen ions and bicarbonate retention. ↑ Urinary K+ excretion (>30 mmol/day) Suppressed plasma renin ↑ Aldosterone-to-renin ratio (ARR) Diagnosis The accepted screening test is concurrent measurement of plasma renin and aldosterone with subsequent calculation of the aldosterone-renin ratio (ARR). ARR screening is positive if the ratio is >750 pmol/L per ng/mL per hour, with a concurrently high normal or increased aldoster Confirmatory tests: Saline infusion test Involves the IV administration of 2 L of physiologic saline over a 4-h period. Failure of aldosterone to suppress Alternative tests: Oral sodiumloading test Fludrocortisone suppression test Captopril suppression test

text: What is the immediate next step in managing a diabetic patient who presents with vomiting, abdominal pain, hyperventilation, fruity odor of breath, hypotension, blood glucose of 320 mg/dL, and urine positive for ketones?
expl: Explanation: The first step in diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) management is IV fluid resuscitation to correct dehydration and restore perfusion, along with checking serum potassium levels before insulin therapy. This prevents insulin-induced worsening of hypokalemia. Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA): Acute, potentially fatal complication, seen mostly in type 1 diabetes but may also occur in type 2 under stress. Precipitating Factors: Missed or inadequate insulin therapy Infections Infarctions Pancreatitis Pregnancy Drugs (e.g., cocaine, glucocorticoids) Pathophysiology: Insulin deficiency → ↓ glucose uptake, ↑ glucagon → hyperglycemia + lipolysis Ketogenesis → fatty acid oxidation produces ketone bodies (β-hydroxybutyrate, acetoacetate) → ketosis Metabolic acidosis → accumulation of ketone bodies → high anion gap acidosis Dehydration → osmotic diuresis due to hyperglycemia → volume depletion + electrolyte imbalance Investigations: Blood glucose: 250-600 mg/dL Serum ketones: β-hydroxybutyrate preferred ABG: pH 6.8-7.3, HCO 3 - 2 20-30 mmHg Electrolytes: ↓ total body potassium (despite normal/high serum at presentation), dilutional hyponatremia, ↑ anion gap Renal function: ↑ BUN, creatinine Management (ISPAD 2022): Fluids: Start with isotonic saline (0.9%), later switch to 0.45% if hypernatremia; add 5% dextrose when BG Insulin: IV regular insulin, 0.1 U/kg bolus, then 0.1 U/kg/hr infusion. Continue until acidosis resolves. Potassium: If K + + before insulin. Maintain K + between 3.5-5.0 mEq/L. Bicarbonate: Reserved for pH Explanation of other options: IV insulin drip (Option A): Should not be started before fluids and potassium correction, as it worsens hypokalemia and may precipitate arrhythmias. IV sodium bicarbonate (Option B): Not routinely indicated; used only if severe acidosis (pH Check blood ketone levels (Option C): Important for diagnosis but not the immediate step in acute stabilization. Key Takeaways: Initial management of DKA is fluids and potassium, not insulin. Potassium status must always be checked before insulin infusion. Bicarbonate is rarely indicated.

text: Which of the following electrolyte abnormalities is associated with metabolic alkalosis?
expl: Metabolic alkalosis is established by an elevated arterial pH, an increase in the serum [HCO3 -], and an increase in Paco2 as a result of compensatory alveolar hypoventilation. text: A patient's ABG reveals: pH = 7.12, pCO 2 = 50 mmHg, HCO 3 - = 28 mEq/L. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
expl: Explanation: pH 7.12 → Indicates acidosis (normal: 7.35-7.45). pCO 2 50 mmHg → Elevated CO 2 confirms respiratory acidosis due to hypoventilation. HCO 3 - 28 mEq/L → Elevated bicarbonate indicates renal compensation by bicarbonate retention. Thus, this is respiratory acidosis with renal metabolic compensation . Anion Gap Formula: Anion Gap = [(Na + ) - (Cl - + HCO 3 - )] Na + = Sodium concentration (mEq/L) Cl - = Chloride concentration (mEq/L) HCO 3 - = Bicarbonate concentration (mEq/L) Normal AG: 8-12 mEq/L. AG > 12 indicates high anion gap metabolic acidosis. A high anion gap may indicate metabolic acidosis due to conditions like diabetic ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, or renal failure. A low anion gap can be seen in hypoalbuminemia or the presence of abnormal proteins. Winter's formula It is used to estimate the expected compensatory bicarbonate (HCO 3 - ) level in metabolic acidosis with a high anion gap (HAGMA). (Expected bicarbonate (HCO 3 - ) = 24 + (1.5 × anion gap) - 8) Explanation of other options: Metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation (Option B): Metabolic acidosis presents with low HCO 3 - , not elevated as in this case. Respiratory alkalosis with metabolic compensation (Option C): Respiratory alkalosis is characterized by low pCO 2 . Metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation (Option D): Metabolic alkalosis shows elevated HCO 3 - with alkalemic pH , not acidemia. Key Takeaways: High pCO 2 with low pH → respiratory acidosis. Elevated HCO 3 - → compensatory renal mechanism.

text: A 69-year-old man presents with severe dyspnea and increasing amounts of clear sputum. ABG reveals pH 7.2, PCO2 66 mmHg, PaO2 44 mmHg, and bicarbonate 26 mEq/L. His SpO2 is 77%. Which of the following is the underlying abnormality?
expl: Explanation: This patient's ABG shows a low pH (acidemia), elevated PCO2 (hypercapnia), and a slightly increased bicarbonate (renal compensation), which is consistent with respiratory acidosis. Low pH, high pCO2, and HCO3 indicate that the primary acid-base disorder is acute respiratory acidosis. The elevated PCO2 indicates hypoventilation or respiratory failure, while low PaO2 and SpO2 demonstrate hypoxemia. The clinical scenario suggests a likely acute exacerbation of a chronic pulmonary disease (e.g., COPD). Explanation of Incorrect Options: Metabolic acidosis (Option A): Would be characterized by low pH and low bicarbonate, not high PCO2. Metabolic alkalosis (Option B): Would show high pH and high bicarbonate. Respiratory alkalosis (Option D): Would show high pH with low PCO2.

text: A male patient reports to the emergency room with the following arterial blood gas (ABG) results: pH: 7.2 pCO₂: 81 mmHg HCO₃⁻: 40 mEq/L What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The ABG findings are consistent with respiratory acidosis , which is identified by: Low pH ( Indicates acidemia. Raised pCO₂ (>45 mmHg): Suggests a respiratory etiology for acidosis. Elevated HCO₃⁻: Points toward partial renal (metabolic) compensation. Interpretation: Primary disorder: Low pH with high pCO₂ confirms primary respiratory acidosis. Compensatory mechanism: The increased HCO₃⁻level suggests renal adjustment, where kidneys retain bicarbonate to counter acidosis. Causes of Respiratory Acidosis: Acute: Severe asthma, COPD exacerbation, airway obstruction (foreign body, anaphylaxis), neuromuscular disorders (Guillain-Barré), central respiratory depression (opioids, sedatives). Chronic: COPD, obesity hypoventilation syndrome, sleep apnea. ABG Analysis Explanation of Other Options: Respiratory alkalosis (Option A): Incorrect, as it is defined by elevated pH and low PaCO₂ due to hyperventilation. In this case, the patient has low pH with high PaCO₂. Metabolic acidosis (Option B): Not correct, since it is typically marked by low HCO₃⁻ and compensatory low PaCO₂. Here, HCO₃⁻is elevated, not reduced. Metabolic alkalosis (Option D): Ruled out because this condition features high pH and elevated HCO₃⁻ , unlike the low pH present in this scenario. Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK536919/ https://www.thoracic.org/professionals/clinical-resources/critical-care/clinical-education/abgs.php

text: A 45-year-old patient is admitted with a decreased conscious level. She is oliguric and hyperventilating. Her investigations show: sodium 125 meq/l, potassium 6.0 meq/l, chloride 92 (95-107), Urea 15 mmol/l, creatinine 2.2 mg/dl, arterial blood gas pH 7.2, bicarbonate 16 meq/l. What is the anion gap?
expl: The anion gap is calculated with the formula (Na + K) -(Cl+HCO3). Normally itself, there is an anion excess in our body. Anion gap signifies the unmeasured anions in the plasma, which includes, albumin, phosphate, sulfate and organic anions. The normal anion gap is 8-16mEq/L Anion gap throws light into the cause of metabolic acidosis. In this case it is 125 + 6 - 92 - 16 = 23. This example indicates a high anion gap, possibly due to lactic acidosis or an overdose of a substance. Causes of HAGMA: Mnemonic for anion gap metabolic acidosis differential: CAT MUDPILES C: Cyanide and carbon monoxide poisoning A: Arsenic T: Toluene M: Methanol, Metformin U: Uremia D: DKA P: Paraldehyde I: Iron, INH L: Lactate E: Ethylene glycol S: Salicylates Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 55, Pg: 360

text: 650 mg of sodium bicarbonate tablets contain how much MEQ of HC03-?
expl: Because of the association of metabolic acidosis in advanced CKD with muscle catabolism, bone disease and more rapid progression of CKD, both the 'uremic acidosis' of ESRD and the non-AG metabolic acidosis of stages 3 and 4 CKD require oral alkali replacement to maintain the [HCO3 −] to approximately the normal value (25 mmol/L). text: All of the following are causes of high anion gap metabolic acidosis (HAGMA), except:
expl: Explanation: Diarrhea is associated with normal anion gap metabolic acidosis (NAGMA) , not high anion gap acidosis. This occurs due to loss of bicarbonate (HCO₋⁻) from the gastrointestinal tract without a compensatory increase in unmeasured anions. In contrast, DKA , AKI , and inborn errors of metabolism cause HAGMA , where there is accumulation of organic or metabolic acids (e.g., ketones, lactate, uremic acids) that increase the unmeasured anion concentration in plasma. Mnemonic for HAGMA: MUDPILES M - Methanol U - Uremia (AKI/CKD) (Option C ruled out) D - DKA (Option A ruled out) P - Propylene glycol I - Iron, INH, Inborn Errors of Metabolism (Option D ruled out) L - Lactic acidosis E - Ethylene glycol S - Salicylates ABG Analysis: Key Takeaway Points: Anion Gap Formula: Anion Gap = [(Na⁺) - (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻)] Na⁺ = Sodium concentration (mEq/L) Cl⁻ = Chloride concentration (mEq/L) HCO₃⁻ = Bicarbonate concentration (mEq/L) Normal AG: 8-12 mEq/L. AG > 12 indicates high anion gap metabolic acidosis. A high anion gap may indicate metabolic acidosis due to conditions like diabetic ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, or renal failure. A low anion gap can be seen in hypoalbuminemia or the presence of abnormal proteins. Winter's formula It is used to estimate the expected compensatory bicarbonate (HCO₋⁻) level in metabolic acidosis with a high anion gap (HAGMA). (Expected bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) = 24 + (1.5 × anion gap) - 8]

text: A 30-year-old female with tiredness and anemia has: Hb 9.8 g/dL, MCV 160 fL, elevated serum homocysteine, and normal methylmalonic acid (MMA) levels. Which therapy is indicated?
expl: Explanation: The findings point to a macrocytic anemia (high MCV)( Option B ruled out) . The critical differentiator between B12 and folate deficiency is the methylmalonic acid (MMA) level. Elevated Homocysteine: Seen in both Vitamin B12 and Folic acid deficiency. Normal Methylmalonic Acid (MMA): This is the key finding. MMA is elevated only in Vitamin B12 deficiency because B12 is a cofactor for the methylmalonyl-CoA mutase enzyme. A normal MMA effectively rules out significant B12 deficiency. (Option A ruled out) Therefore, the isolated elevation of homocysteine with a normal MMA is diagnostic of Folic Acid Deficiency . Common causes of folate deficiency include decreased intake due to inadequate diet, alcoholism, or infancy Impaired absorption from malabsorption syndromes, intrinsic intestinal disease, or use of anticonvulsants and oral contraceptives Increased loss such as with hemodialysis Increased requirement during pregnancy, infancy, disseminated cancer, or markedly increased hematopoiesis Impaired utilization caused by folic acid antagonists like methotrexate. Explanation of other options: Iron (Option B): Iron deficiency causes microcytic anemia (low MCV), not macrocytic. Vitamin C (Option C): Vitamin C deficiency (scurvy) can cause anemia, but it is not typically macrocytic and is not related to homocysteine metabolism. text: A 73-year-old man is admitted hypothermic and unconscious, having been found collapsed on his kitchen floor. Biochemistry reveals a significant metabolic acidosis(bicarbonate 8 mmol/l), sodium 139 mmol/l, potassium 4.5 mmol/l, chloride 97 mmol/l and glucose 5.6 mmol/l. What is the likely biochemical diagnosis?
expl: This patient is having metabolic acidosis. Once metabolic acidosis is diagnosed, the next step is to find out its cause by measuring the anion gap. Anion gap is the indicator of unmeasured anions in the plasma The anion gap is calculated with the formula (Na+K)-(Cl+HCO3). Normally itself, there is an anion excess in our body. Anion gap signifies the unmeasured anions in the plasma, which includes, albumin, phosphate, sulfate and organic anions. The normal anion gap is 8-16mEq/L Here the anion gap is (139+4.5)-(97+8) = 38.5 Anion gap throws light as to the cause of metabolic acidosis. So from the options, RTA can be ruled out. The blood glucose is given to be 6mmol/dL. Multiply it with 18 to get value in mg. which is 108mg/dL. Since the blood sugars are normal, DKA is unlikely. There is no history of alcohol intake given, hence we cant consider alcoholic ketoacidosis too. The best possible answer is lactic acidosis. What could be the cause of lactic acidosis? Our elderly patient was found unresponsive, which could be a cardiovascular event, which can lead to hypotension and lactic acidosis. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 55, Pg: 360.

text: Sustained metabolic alkalosis is always due to:

options.A: Impaired renal excretion of excess bicarbonate

ansText: Impaired renal excretion of excess bicarbonate
expl: While metabolic alkalosis is caused by a variety of factors, including chloride depletion, potassium depletion or increased secretion of mineralocorticoids, the end result is always impaired renal excretion of excess bicarbonate. Normally, excess bicarbonate is rapidly excreted by the kidney by: An increased filtered load, allowing additional bicarbonate to be delivered to the distal nephron; Chloride-dependent secretion of bicarbonate by pendrin, in the cortical collecting duct Down-regulation of H+ secretion in the cortical and medullary collecting duct. Metabolic alkalosis occurs when abnormal H+ loss or bicarbonate administration is coupled with: A reduced filtered load of bicarbonate (e.g., hypoperfusion of the kidney, advanced kidney disease); Enhanced bicarbonate reabsorption along the tubule (e.g., effects of angiotensin II, aldosterone, hypokalemia); Continued stimulation of H+ secretion by the α-intercalated cells in the collecting duct (e.g., primary hyperaldosteronism, chloride depletion) Impaired bicarbonate secretion by pendrin (e.g., chloride depletion; advanced kidney disease). Reference: Harrisons Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:55 Pg: 365

text: Which of the following drugs can cause non-anion gap acidosis?
expl: A non-anion gap metabolic acidosis can result from either renal or extrarenal causes. Renal causes of metabolic acidosis occur when renal bicarbonate generation, which results from net acid excretion, does not balance the loss of bicarbonate and other alkali buffers consumed in the buffering of normal endogenous acid production. This failure of net acid excretion is termed renal tubular acidosis (RTA). Extrarenal causes occur when exogenous acid loads, endogenous acid production, or endogenous bicarbonate losses are elevated and exceed renal net acid excretion. The most common extrarenal cause of non-anion gap metabolic acidosis is chronic diarrhea. Reference: Harrison's Principles Of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 55, Pg: 364

text: Ph 7.2, bicarbonate-10, PC02-32, uncompensated metabolic acidosis is probably due to?
expl: Metabolic acidosis is characterized by an increase in the hydrogen ion concentration in the systemic circulation, resulting in a serum HCO3 less than 24 mEq/L. Uncompensated Metabolic Acidosis : This occurs when there is a decrease in the HCO3 level without a resultant alteration (decrease) of the PaCO2 value. Non-gap metabolic acidosis: is primarily due to the loss of bicarbonate, and the main causes of this condition are diarrhea and renal tubular acidosis. Additional and rarer etiologies include Addison's disease, ureterosigmoid or pancreatic fistulas, acetazolamide use, and hyperalimentation through TPN initiation. GI and renal losses of bicarbonate can be distinguished via urine anion gap analysis: Urine AG = Urine Na + Urine K - Urine Cl In your provided scenario with arterial blood gas values: pH 7.2: Indicates acidemia, as it's lower than the normal reference range of arterial blood pH (7.35-7.45). Bicarbonate (HCO3-) 10: This value is below the normal reference range (22-28 mEq/L), indicating a decrease in bicarbonate. PCO2 32: Within the normal reference range (35-45 mm Hg), showing a compensatory response by the respiratory system. These values are indicative of uncompensated metabolic acidosis, with the primary issue being a decrease in bicarbonate (HCO3-). This condition is likely due to the kidneys' loss of bicarbonate (HCO3-) into the urine, resulting in an accumulation of hydrogen ions (H+), contributing to the metabolic acidosis. In uncompensated metabolic acidosis, the primary problem is not effectively compensated by the respiratory system, and the pH remains outside the normal range.

text: A 15 year old boy is being investigated for growth retardation. He has had no previous medical problems. He mentions that he had symptoms of worsening muscle weakness and fatigue. He also has polyuria. Investigations revealed: urea 48 mg/dl (NR:17 - 43 mg/dL) serum creatinine 1.3 mg/dl (NR: 0.6-1.4 mg/dL) potassium 2.8 mmol/l (NR: 3.5-4 mmol/L) sodium 133 mmol/l (NR:135-145 mmol/L) chloride 79 mmol/l (NR: 95-107 mmol/l) calcium 9.2 mg/dl (NR: 8.8 - 10 mg/dL) phosphate 2.66 mg/dl (3.0-4.5 mg/dL) magnesium 2.18 mg/dl (N.R:1.7 to 2.2 mg/dL) pH 7.58 (NR: 7.35 - 7.45) HCO3 40 mmol/l (NR: 18-22 mmol/l) What is the likely diagnosis?
expl: You will have to answer questions related to potassium abnormalities with acid base disturbance in your exam. It can occur in one of the several combinations. Hypokalemia with metabolic acidosis. Hypokalemia with metabolic alkalosis Hyperkalemia with metabolic acidosis We will discuss and describe each of these with examples So this is a young boy with hypokalemia. The associated acid base abnormality is a metabolic alkalosis, as evidenced by a pH of 7.58 and bicarbonate of 40. So such a combination occurs with disorders of renal channels that deal with sodium and potassium reabsorption and alkalosis occurs secondary to loss of potassium. When reabsorption of sodium is impaired in the proximal kidneys due to mutation of transporters , the distal delivery of sodium will be increased. This will stimulate the JG apparatus, which will increase the renin angiotensin aldosterone system, leading to distal absorption of sodium and secretion of potassium and H+ ions to maintain the elctroneutrality. So there will be hypokalemia, alkalosis and increased renin, angiotensin and aldosterone, causing sodium reabsorption. Eg: Barter and Gitleman Syndrome. Hypokalemia with alkalosis can also occur when there is activation of Sodium channels in the distal nephron ENaC. This sodium channel is under the influence of aldosterone. Sodium will be absorbed, potassium and H+ is secreted to maintain electrical neutrality. Such activation can occur when there is increased aldosterone(Conn's Syndrome), increased Renin(Renin secreting tumors, renal artery stenosis) or activating mutations of the ENaC, causing low renin and aldosterone(Liddle Syndrome). So this is the basic thing that you have to remember. There will be additional features favoring each disease which we will discuss with appropriate questions. Coming back to this question, this child has hypokalemia with metabolic alkalosis and among the options, the most appropriate answer is Bartter's Syndrome since there is growth retardation. Loop diuretic abuse is a close DD, but it is not associated with growth retardation. Diabetes insipidus does not cause hypokalemia. Congenital adrenal hyperplasia occurs due to defect of various enzymes in the steroidogenic pathway. The 21 Hydroxylases is involved in synthesis of cortisol and aldosterone and hence can present with salt wasting and hyperkalemia The basic defect is in the Na-K-2Cl transporter in the TAL of loop of henle. This leads to There are 4 types of Bartter's Syndrome depending upon the cause of the Na-K-2Cl transporter dysfunction. Type 1 is due to mutation of NA-K-2Cl transporter mutation. Type 2 is due to mutation of ROMK potassium channel. Type 3 is due to mutation of ClCk chloride channels. Type 4 is due to Barttin gene mutation. Type 1 and 2 presents antenatally itself characterized by polyhydramnios and pre term labor. Type 3 is called classic Bartter's Syndrome, presents with the typical features given in the flow chart above. Type 4 is associated with sensorineural deafness. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st edition, Ch: 53, Pg: 350.

text: A 27 year old man is admitted with pains radiating from his right loin to the groin. He also has haematuria. He gives a history of previous urinary tract infections. Clinical examination is unremarkable. Investigations are as follows: Serum Sodium 139 mmol/L, Potassium 2.8 mmol/L, Urea 39 mg/dl, Creatinine 1.18 mg/dl, Chloride 116 mmol/l, pH: 7.30, Bicarbonate 15 mol/L. Which of the following would help treat the condition?
expl: With this question we come to the next type of potassium and acid base anomaly, which is, hypokalemia with metabolic acidosis . In this group we have two disorders, the Type I and Type II Renal Tubular Acidosis. Another type of RTA, type IV is associated with hyperkalemia and is discussed else where. We know that RTA belongs to the class of normal anion gap metabolic acidosis. Here the anion gap is maintained by reabsorption of chloride ions from the kidneys. So lets see what type I RTA is. It is otherwise called the distal RTA. Here the acidosis occurs due to failure of the distal tubule to secrete H+ ions. In exchange of H+ ions sodium will be lost through urine, resulting in hypovolemia and stimulation of RAS. So there will be reabsorption of sodium distally and excretion of potassium resulting in hypokalemia. Chronic acidosis leads to consumption of bicarbonate in serum Chronic acidosis leads to mobilization of calcium from bone and decreased reabsorption from kidneys. Acidosis causes increased reabsorption of citrate causing hypocitraturia. Citrate is an important inhibitor of stone formation, so distal RTA is associated with renal stones. Manifests as failure to thrive, polyuria, nephrocalcinosis. Bicarbonate supplementation will improve systemic acidosis and electrolyte abnormality. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 21 st ed, Ch: 55, Pg: 364.

text: A young man trekking at 5000 meters develops headache, dizziness, dyspnea, and blurred vision. Which acid-base disturbance occurs at high altitude?
expl: Explanation: Hypoxia at altitude stimulates hyperventilation, causing excessive CO 2 washout, low PaCO 2 , and respiratory alkalosis. Explanation of Other Options: Metabolic alkalosis (Option A): Metabolic alkalosis → due to vomiting/antacids. Respiratory acidosis (Option C): Respiratory acidosis → due to hypoventilation (COPD, obstruction). Metabolic acidosis (Option D): Metabolic acidosis → due to DKA, lactic acidosis, renal failure.

text: Antidote for overdose of fibrinolytic drugs is?
expl: Fibrinolytics are drugs used to lyse a fibrin clot. Examples are Streptokinase, Urokinase, Alteplase, Tenecteplase etc. So the drugs that are used for treating fibrinolytic overdose should be antifibrinolytics. Both tranexamic acid and EACA are anti fibrinolytics. The antidote for fibrinolytic over dose is EACA. EACA should not be given unless the bleeding is life threatening, as EACA can cause widespread thrombosis and ischemia and can worsen DIC or HIT.

text: Which of the following statements is false about Pneumocystis jiroveci infection?

options.A: Most patients have CD4 <200 cells/mm3 at time of diagnosis
options.B: Most patients will have elevated Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)
options.C: Arterial blood gas (ABG) frequently reveals respiratory alkalosis and widened alveolar arterial oxygen tension difference.
options.D: A normal chest radiograph rules out the diagnosis

ansText: A normal chest radiograph rules out the diagnosis
expl: Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP) is caused by the fungus P. jirovecii and was once the hallmark of AIDS. The most common finding on chest x-ray is either a normal film, if the disease is suspected early, or a faint bilateral interstitial infiltrate. The classic finding of a dense perihilar infiltrate is unusual in patients with AIDS. In patients with PCP who have been receiving aerosolized pentamidine for prophylaxis, one may see an x-ray picture of upper lobe cavitary disease, reminiscent of TB. text: A 50 year old patient has a 2 year history of weight loss and diarrhea. He also gives a history of episodes of flushing. VIP syndrome is considered by the admitting physician. Which one of the following is a feature of VIPoma syndrome?

options.C: Induction of VIP release by somatostatin

expl: VIPomas [vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) originate in amine precursor uptake and decarboxylation (APUD) cells of the gastroenteropancreatic endocrine system and in adrenal or extra-adrenal neurogenic sites. Features of VIP syndrome include watery diarrhea (100%), hypochlorhydria (70% in adults), hyperglycemia (20-50% in adults), hypercalcemia (20-50% in adults), flushing (20% in adults) and hypokalemia due to diarrhea. text: A 48-year-old woman who works in a pharmacy presents with episodes of tiredness and lethargy. Her blood pressure is 115/75mmHg. Her bloods reveal hypokalaemia and a raised serum bicarbonate level. Urine collection reveals hypercalciuria. Otherwise the findings are unremarkable. What is the likely diagnosis?
expl: This picture could fit Bartter's syndrome , although Bartter's syndrome is rare (1 per million), has an autosomal-recessive pattern of inheritance and commonly presents below the age of 5 years. Features of Bartter's syndrome include volume depletion, tetany and muscle weakness. This woman's occupation is the clue, which unfortunately makes furosemide abuse very much more likely. Conn's syndrome is associated with hypertension and is due to aldosterone excess. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 350

text: All of the following are the cause of metabolic alkalosis, except?
expl: Barter, Gitelman and Liddle syndrome cause hypokalemia and alkalosis. Liddle syndrome causes hypertenstion, where as Bartter and Gitelman are characterized by normo or hypotension. Mutations in genes encoding WNK kinases, WNK-1 and WNK-4, cause pseudohypoaldosteronism type II (Gordon syndrome) characterized by familial hypertension with hyperkalemia and acidosis. WNK kinases influence the activity of several tubular ion transporters. Mutations in this disorder lead to overactivity of the apical Na+/Cl- cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule as the primary stimulus for increased salt reabsorption, extracellular volume expansion, and hypertension. Reference: Harrison's Principles Of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:53, Pg: 351 Reference: Textbook of Harrison 20 th edition page 321

text: An 18-year-old girl presents with intermittent weakness and feelings of tiredness. Her family physician requested some blood tests and found her to have a potassium level of 2.8 mmol/l and a bicarbonate of 32 mmol/l. She is normotensive. You arrange a renin and aldosterone level, and both are elevated. Urinary calcium excretion is elevated. Urinary diuretic screen is negative. Which diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
expl: The patient has increased urinary calcium excretion, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis and raised renin and angiotensin levels suggestive of Bartter syndrome. This is not Conn's syndrome because the patient is normotensive and both her renin and angiotensin levels are raised. Bartter's syndrome is due to a mutation in the Na+-K+-2Cl- co-transporter, the ATP-regulated potassium channel, or the kidney-specific basolateral chloride channel. This impairs sodium and chloride reabsorption, and causes an increase in the production of renal prostaglandin E2. Hyperplasia of the juxtaglomerular apparatus is seen on renal biopsy. Gitelman's syndrome is due to a different mutation, and produces a clinical picture similar to that seen with chronic thiazide administration. It also has hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis in the absence of hypercalciuria. Liddle's syndrome is characterised by potassium wasting and hypertension with suppresssed renin and aldosterone levels. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 350

text: An 18-year-old woman was referred for investigation of progressive generalised muscle weakness and lethargy. She was taking no regular medications. Examination was unremarkable. Her blood pressure was 108/60 mmHg. Her body mass index was 20.Investigations: Serum potassium 2.8mmol/L (3.5-4.9) serum bicarbonate 33 mmol/L (20-28) Serum creatinine 77 -mol/L (60-110) eGFR >90 ml/min Serum magnesium 0.61 mmol/L (0.75-1.05) Serum chloride 85 mmol/L (95-107) Urinary chloride 61 mmol/L (NR: 25 to 40 mmol/L ) Urinary sodium 57 mmol/L (NR:~20 mmol/L) 24-hour urinary calcium 1.6 mmol (2.5-7.5) What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: This patient has Hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with normal BP Low Potassium + High Bicarbonate and Normal Blood Pressure Consider Bartter's syndrome: mode of presentation & severity varies; autosomal recessive disorder. At least 6 subtypes now detected. All shared impaired Na reabsorption in the thick ascending limb of loop of henle giving a clinical picture of salt wasting and hypokalaemic alkalosis. On Biopsy Hyperplasia and hypertophy of the juxtaglomerular apparatus is seen. It's often present in childhood with polyuria (nocturia), Failure to thrive, muscle weakness; can be associated with nephrocalcinosis; can cause ESRD. Treatment: Oral potassium supplementation Spironolactone and NSAID Adjuvant use of ACEi has also been successful. Gitelman's: Autosomal recessive disorder; due to mutation in gene encoding the thiazide sensitive NaCl cotransporter in Distal convoluted tubule. Patients may complain of fatigue, muscle cramps, tetany. Associated with chondrocalcinosis. Distinguished from Bartter's by hypomagnesaemia and hypocalciuria . Treatment Oral potassium supplementation, Amiloride 5-40 mg od. NSAID are not helpful. Liddle syndrome Very rare Mutation in ENaC (epithelial sodium channel expressed on the apical surface of collecting duct cells). Autosomal dominant inheritance, young onset Hypertension with +ve family history salt retention ↓ K+ decrease renin and aldosterone Treatment: Low salt diet, Response to amiloride / triamterene (which directly inhibit ENaC) Reference: Harrisons Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:53 Pg: 351

text: A 48-year-old man presents to the clinic complaining of a lump in the neck which becomes particularly more prominent when she swallows. On examination there is a thyroid nodule at the base of the neck. Leukocyte screening of two other family members who suffered thyroid carcinoma has revealed the ret proto-oncogene. Which type of thyroid carcinoma is linked to the ret-proto-oncogene?
expl: The ret proto-oncogene encodes for a receptor tyrosine kinase. In medullary thyroid carcinoma the mutation is associated with hyperfunction. Ret is associated with familial cases of medullary thyroid carcinoma and the MEN-2 syndrome. text: A comatose elderly patient (weight ~70 kg) is brought to the emergency department. Investigations reveal serum glucose of 500 mg/dL, arterial pH of 7.30, elevated plasma ketones, and normal serum potassium. Which of the following should be added to the initial saline solution for treatment?
expl: Explanation: The patient is in Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA) , characterized by the triad of hyperglycemia, metabolic acidosis (pH intravenous insulin . Signs of DKA: Kussmaul breathing Fruity odor on the patients breath Tachycardia Dehydration Hypotension Management of Diabetic Ketoacidosis (ISPAD 2022) Rationale for Insulin Primary Action: Insulin inhibits lipolysis and ketogenesis, reversing the underlying metabolic acidosis. It also promotes cellular glucose uptake, correcting hyperglycemia. Timing: Insulin infusion should be initiated immediately after starting IV fluid resuscitation (0.9% saline), provided serum potassium is ≥ 3.3 mEq/L (as it is in this case). Dosing: The standard regimen is a continuous IV infusion (e.g., 0.1 units/kg/hour) after an optional initial bolus. The specific dose in Option D is incorrect because insulin dosing is weight-based and administered as an infusion, not a single static IV dose. Explanation of other options: Bicarbonate (Option B): Bicarbonate therapy is not routinely recommended. It is reserved for severe acidosis (pH Potassium (Option C): Although potassium levels will fall rapidly once insulin is started, the serum level is currently normal. Therefore, potassium is added to IV fluids after insulin initiation and upon confirmation of adequate urine output, not at the very start. 14 units of regular insulin intravenously (Option D): While insulin is correct, this specific fixed dose is not appropriate. Insulin therapy in DKA requires a weight-based calculation and must be administered as a continuous infusion for precise control. Key Takeaways: Immediate IV insulin is the definitive treatment for DKA.

text: A 22-year-old young woman with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus presents with a temperature, dehydration and altered consciousness. Her initial biochemistry shows sodium 130 mmol/l, potassium 4.5 mmol/l, bicarbonate 6 mmol/l, urea 50 mg/dl, creatinine 1.2 mg/dl and hydrogen ion 80. What is the most important immediate treatment?
expl: The patient has diabetic ketoacidosis , a condition still associated with mortality in patients with type-1 diabetes mellitus. There is a total body deficit of fluid and electrolytes. The most important initial treatment is intravenous saline as the hypovolaemia is the factor most likely to cause the patient to die. Intravenous insulin is required at an early stage; and, although it is normal, the potassium level will rapidly fall with fluid and insulin treatment and the patient will require potassium replacement. Intravenous bicarbonate should not be used immediately as it can cause massive fluid shifts and precipitate cerebral oedema. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Pg:3115

text: What is the enzyme deficiency in Pompe's disease?
expl: Explanation: Pompe disease, also known as Glycogen Storage Disease Type II, is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme acid alpha-1,4-glucosidase (acid maltase). This enzymatic defect leads to the abnormal accumulation of glycogen within lysosomes, predominantly affecting cardiac, skeletal, and smooth muscle cells. The disease manifests in two primary forms: the severe infantile-onset Pompe disease (IPD) and the less severe late-onset Pompe disease (LOPD). IPD presents with profound hypotonia, muscle weakness, feeding difficulties, hepatomegaly, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. In contrast, LOPD is characterized by progressive proximal limb-girdle muscle weakness, respiratory insufficiency, and potential cardiac rhythm abnormalities. Common laboratory findings include elevated serum levels of creatine kinase (CK), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), alanine aminotransferase (ALT), and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH). Radiographic studies in the infantile form often reveal cardiomegaly, while electrocardiogram (ECG) may show a shortened PR interval and tall QRS complexes. Management centers on enzyme replacement therapy with alglucosidase alfa, and a high-protein diet may provide additional support for patients with LOPD. Explanation of other options: Glucose-6-Phosphatase (Option B): This enzyme plays a critical role in both gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis. A deficiency is associated with von Gierke's disease (Glycogen Storage Disease Type I), not Pompe disease. This condition impairs the liver's ability to release glucose into the bloodstream, leading to severe hypoglycemia. Muscle Phosphorylase (Option C): Also referred to as myophosphorylase, this enzyme is essential for glycogen breakdown within muscle tissue. Its deficiency causes McArdle's disease (Glycogen Storage Disease Type V), which is clinically characterized by exercise intolerance, muscle pain, and cramps due to impaired energy production during physical activity. Phosphofructokinase (Option D): A key regulatory enzyme in the glycolytic pathway, phosphofructokinase facilitates the conversion of fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate. A deficiency results in Tarui's disease (Glycogen Storage Disease Type VII), presenting with symptoms such as exercise-induced muscle weakness, cramps, and hemolysis due to blocked glycolysis.

text: A software engineer presents with fatigue. He is having a sedentary life, mostly sitting in front of a computer for 12-14 hours. He takes junk food, and is not eating vegetables and fruits. Hb 9, MCV 120. What is the most likely etiology
expl: Our patient is having a macrocytic anemia, which easily rules out options c and d. Macrocytic anemia can be seen in either Folate or Vit B12 deficiency. The chief source of Vitamin B12 is animal and dairy products. Folic acid however is ubiquitous and is seen in most of the foods, but is easily destroyed by cooking. So in a person who eats junk food and does not consume fruits or vegetables, the most likely cause of macrocytic anemia is folate deficiency. B12 Deficiency (Option A): Vitamin B12 deficiency can cause macrocytic anemia. However, B12 deficiency is less likely in this scenario because it typically presents with additional neurological symptoms (e.g., tingling, numbness, balance issues). Folate Deficiency (Option B) : Folate deficiency is a common cause of macrocytic anemia. Folate (vitamin B9) is essential for RBC production and DNA synthesis. Poor dietary intake (especially lacking vegetables and fruits) can lead to folate deficiency. Given the sedentary lifestyle and junk food consumption, folate deficiency is a plausible explanation. Acute Blood Loss (Option C) : Acute blood loss can cause anemia, but it typically results in normocytic or microcytic anemia. The elevated MCV (macrocytosis) doesn't align with acute blood loss. Sideroblastic Anemia (Option D): Sideroblastic anemia is characterized by abnormal iron metabolism within RBC precursors. It usually presents with microcytic or normocytic anemia. Sideroblastic anemia is less likely based on the given information. In summary, considering the elevated MCV and the lifestyle factors, folate deficiency is the most likely cause of macrocytic anemia in this case Following tables depict the causes of B12 and folate deficiency:

text: A 72-year-old man presents with an acute onset of severe pain and swelling of the left elbow. He mentions that he had a chest infection 3 weeks ago. On examination, he had a temperature of 38°C and the left elbow was erythematous, swollen and tender. What is the most appropriate investigation?
expl: The differential diagnosis of acute monoarthritis includes- septic arthritis, crystal induced arthritis and hemarthrosis. The management of acute monoarthritis is always joint aspiration followed by appropriate therapy. In the context of an elderly male presenting with monoarthritis after a recent history of pneumonia should make us raise suspicion of a septic arthritis. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 370, Pg: 2852 20th edition Ch:355 Pg:2570

text: A child is brought to the emergency department with a history of ingesting 10-20 ferrous sulfate tablets. Arterial blood gas analysis shows acidosis. Which of the following agents can be used in the management of this condition?
expl: Explanation: The presentation is consistent with acute iron poisoning , typically seen after ingestion of large amounts of ferrous sulfate. Clinical consequences include gastrointestinal upset (vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain), metabolic acidosis , and in severe cases, multi-organ failure and death. Deferoxamine (Desferrioxamine): Drug of choice for iron toxicity. Chelates free circulating iron to form ferrioxamine, which is then eliminated via urine. Administered IM or IV in severe cases. Side effects: Skin rash, urticaria, pruritus, wheals, and in rare situations, anaphylaxis. The urine may become reddish-brown due to ferrioxamine excretion. Explanation of Other Options: Activated Charcoal (Option B): While useful in binding many drugs/toxins (e.g., carbamazepine, dapsone, barbiturates, quinine), it does not bind iron effectively , and therefore has no role in iron poisoning . Dimercaprol (Option C): A chelating agent effective against arsenic, mercury, gold, and lead . It has no efficacy in iron overdose . Penicillamine (Option D): Used as a chelator in copper poisoning (e.g., Wilson's disease) and in some cases of lead or mercury toxicity , but ineffective for iron . Key Takeaways: Deferoxamine is the definitive antidote for severe iron poisoning. Activated charcoal is ineffective in iron toxicity. Dimercaprol and penicillamine are chelators for other heavy metals but not for iron . Early recognition and treatment are critical to prevent multi-organ failure .

text: A 52 year old lady complains of epigastric burning pains due to stress. She finally undergoes an UGI endoscopy which shows gastro-oesophageal reflux. Which medication is the most effective for her condition?
expl: The main pharmacological therapy for GERD is inhibition of gastric acid suppression . Proton pump inhibitors such as omeprazole, lansoprazole and pantoprazole are more effective than H2 receptor blockers such as ranitidine, cimetidine or nizatidine. Healing in oesophagitis is better with a PPI. Bismuth is a mucosal protective agent used in the treatment of peptic ulcer disease. Magnesium hydroxide is an antacid. It is not as effective as PPI for GERD. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st ed, Ch: 323, Pg: 2429-2431

text: A patient with no comorbidities presents with serum K+ of 3.0 mmol/L and a normal ECG. What is the preferred treatment?
expl: Explanation: The patient has moderate, asymptomatic hypokalemia (K+ 3.0 mmol/L) with a normal ECG , indicating no immediate life-threatening conduction abnormalities. Oral potassium replacement (e.g., Potassium Chloride solution/powder) is safer than intravenous (IV) administration, carrying no risk of phlebitis or sudden hyperkalemia from infusion error. It is highly effective for correcting chronic deficits when the patient is stable and can tolerate oral intake. Standard management protocols recommend oral repletion for stable patients with moderate hypokalemia and no warning signs (e.g., ECG changes, muscle weakness, arrhythmias). Explanation of other options: Calcium gluconate (Option A): This is a cardioprotective agent used in the emergency treatment of severe hyperkalemia with ECG changes, to stabilize the cardiac membrane. It is contraindicated here. Sodium bicarbonate (Option B): This is used to correct metabolic acidosis and can also be used to shift potassium intracellularly in the treatment of hyperkalemia . Insulin with dextrose (Option D): This combination is used to drive potassium into cells as a temporizing measure for severe hyperkalemia . Key Takeaways: Oral potassium chloride is the first-line treatment for stable, asymptomatic hypokalemia. IV potassium is reserved for severe hypokalemia ( References: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK482465/

text: A patient presents with fatigue and a blood smear showing macrocytic anemia. Despite normal methylmalonic acid levels, homocystinuria is present, and serum vitamin B12 levels are normal. What is the recommended management strategy for this condition?
expl: Explanation: The appropriate management for this patient with macrocytic anemia is to treat folate deficiency. Causes of Macrocytic Anemia include: Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency Myelodysplastic syndromes Liver disease Alcohol use Hypothyroidism Certain medications (such as zidovudine, trimethoprim, phenytoin, methotrexate, hydroxycarbamide) Reticulocytosis, which involves an increase in larger, immature red blood cells, can also contribute and is typically seen in conditions like: Hemolysis Increased red blood cell production in response to anemia Folate Deficiency: Treatment of Folate Deficiency: Acute Treatment: Oral folic acid at a dose of 5 mg daily for 3 weeks is used to correct the deficiency, followed by a maintenance dose of 5 mg once weekly. Prophylaxis: Folate supplementation is recommended during pregnancy to prevent megaloblastic anemia and lower the risk of neural tube defects. Additional Uses: Folate is also given prophylactically in chronic hematological conditions such as hemolytic anemia, and to reduce homocysteine levels, which may help decrease the risk of coronary and cerebrovascular diseases. Fortification: To prevent folate deficiency and its complications, the US FDA requires folic acid to be added to common foods like bread, flour, and rice. Options A, B, and C are incorrect.

text: A patient presents with salt wasting, craving, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, and skin pigmentation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: Addison's disease, or primary adrenal insufficiency, causes a deficiency of both glucocorticoids and mineralocorticoids . This leads to salt wasting, hyperkalemia (due to decreased aldosterone), metabolic acidosis , and characteristic skin/mucosal hyperpigmentation (due to elevated ACTH). Addison's Disease Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison’s disease) results in a deficiency of both glucocorticoids and mineralocorticoids. In Addison's disease, the destruction of the adrenal cortex results in electrolyte disturbances-hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and metabolic acidosis. Aldosterone deficiency → increased Na+ and water loss, leading to hypovolemia , hypotension , and Cortisol deficiency → decreased gluconeogenesis, hypoglycemia , and decreased protein/lipid metabolism. Features of glucocorticoid deficiency include fatigue, weight loss, and poor stress tolerance. Salt craving is also a classic symptom due to the body's attempt to compensate for sodium loss Hyperpigmentation may also occur due to increased ACTH secretion in primary adrenal insufficiency. Explanation of Incorrect Options: Conn's disease (Option B): Causes sodium retention and hypokalemia, not hyperkalemia or hyperpigmentation. Pheochromocytoma (Option C): Presents with episodic hypertension, palpitations, and headaches, not salt wasting or skin pigmentation. Cushing's syndrome (Option D): Involves glucocorticoid excess with features like hypertension and striae, but does not cause hyperkalemia or pigmentation seen in Addison's disease.
