text: Which of the following drugs is employed in the management of tumour lysis syndrome (TLS)?
expl: Explanation: Tumor lysis syndrome occurs due to massive breakdown of malignant cells during chemotherapy, radiotherapy, or immunotherapy. This leads to release of potassium, phosphate, and uric acid into circulation. High uric acid precipitates in the renal tubules causing renal failure . Rasburicase is a recombinant urate oxidase enzyme that rapidly converts uric acid into the more soluble allantoin , easily excreted by kidneys, thereby preventing uric acid crystal deposition. Hence, it is the drug of choice in TLS management. Explanation of other options: Rituximab (Option B): Anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody used in B-cell malignancies, not for TLS. Gemtuzumab (Option C): Anti-CD33 monoclonal antibody used in acute myeloid leukemia, not indicated in TLS. Alemtuzumab (Option D): Anti-CD52 monoclonal antibody for CLL and lymphomas, not effective in TLS. Key Takeaways: TLS is life-threatening due to renal complications. Rasburicase is the drug of choice in preventing uric acid nephropathy in TLS.

text: A 63-year-old woman presents a 5 day history of progressive shortness of breath. Her family brought her in because she was increasingly sleepy during the last 24 hours. She was diagnosed with Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease 3 years ago and has a FEV1 less than 50% of predicted. She has an oxygen concentrator at home. Examination revealed depressed consciousness and a respiratory rate of 24 with shallow breaths. There were decreased breath sounds with minimal air movement. If an arterial blood gas on room air were to be performed, which of the following results would you expect?

options.A: pH 7.16; paCO2 70 mm; paO2 50 mm; HCO3 24 mmol/L
options.B: pH 7.24; paCO2 80 mm; paO2 55 mm; HCO3 30 mmol/L
options.C: pH 7.32; paCO2 60 mm; paO2 70 mm; HCO3 30 mmol/L
options.D: pH 7.41; paCO2 40 mm; paO2 50 mm; HCO3 24 mmol/L

ansText: pH 7.24; paCO2 80 mm; paO2 55 mm; HCO3 30 mmol/L
expl: This patient's presentation suggests that she has developed acute carbon dioxide retention and would be expected to have a low pH, low pO2, high pCO2 and a high HCO3 because she has long-standing COPD. Consequently the last two options really do not fit. The first option has a pretty much normal bicarbonate and this would be expected to be much higher in chronic COPD (as there would be metabolic alkalosis to compensate for the respiratory acidosis). Therefore this leaves the best fit as option B. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition, Ch: 55, Pg-367

text: Which of the following is found in subjects acclimatised to life at high altitudes?
expl: This question deals with a person who is already acclimatized to a high altitude. There are two responses to high altitude A normal initial “struggle response” to such an ascent includes increased ventilation—the cornerstone of acclimatization—mediated by the carotid bodies. Hyperventilation may cause respiratory alkalosis and dehydration. Respiratory alkalosis may be extreme, with an arterial blood pH of >7.7 (e.g., at the summit of Everest). Alkalosis may depress the ventilatory drive during sleep, with consequent periodic breathing and hypoxemia. So periodic breathing occurs in people who are yet to acclimatize. Once the individual gets acclimatized there will be increased sympathetic tone; increased erythropoietin levels, leading to increased hemoglobin levels and red blood cell mass; increased tissue capillary density and mitochondrial numbers; and higher levels of 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate, enhancing oxygen utilization, increased cardiac output and pulmonary artery pressure. Reference: Harrison’s principles Of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch:462, pg: 3617

text: Which of the following is the functional effect of Hypokalemia on kidney function?
expl: The functional effects of hypokalemia on the kidney can include Na+-Cl- and HCO3 - retention, polyuria, phosphaturia, hypocitraturia, and an activation of renal ammoniagenesis. Bicarbonate retention and other acid-base effects of hypokalemia can contribute to the generation of metabolic alkalosis. Hypokalemic polyuria is due to a combination of central polydipsia and an AVP-resistant renal concentrating defect. Structural changes in the kidney due to hypokalemia include a relatively specific vacuolizing injury to proximal tubular cells, interstitial nephritis, and renal cysts. Hypokalemia also predisposes to acute kidney injury and can lead to end-stage renal disease (ESRD) in patients with long-standing hypokalemia due to eating disorders and/or laxative abuse. Reference: Harrisons Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:53 Pg: 350

text: A patient taking antidepressants presents with hypotension. ECG reveals a wide QRS complex and right axis deviation. What is the most appropriate management in this case?
expl: Explanation: The presentation is consistent with tricyclic antidepressant (TCA) toxicity , which is characterized by: Hypotension Wide QRS complexes Right axis deviation QT prolongation on ECG TCAs block sodium channels in the myocardium, leading to arrhythmias and conduction abnormalities . Side effects of tricyclic antidepressants: Management of TCA Toxicity: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate : Mechanism: Alkalinizes serum, reversing sodium channel blockade and stabilizing myocardial membranes. Indication: QRS widening >100 ms, hypotension, or arrhythmias due to TCA overdose. Dose: 50-100 mEq bolus, repeated as needed until QRS narrows. Activated charcoal : Useful if ingestion is within 2 hours to reduce absorption. Seizures : Treat with benzodiazepines. Polymorphic VT (torsades de pointes) : Manage with IV magnesium sulfate. Explanation of other options: Antiarrhythmics (Option A): Class IA, IC, and III (e.g., quinidine, flecainide, amiodarone) worsen sodium channel blockade and are contraindicated. Propranolol (Option C): Ineffective in TCA-induced arrhythmias; may worsen hypotension and bradycardia. Phenytoin (Option D): Not indicated in TCA toxicity; can displace TCAs from protein binding, worsening toxicity. Key Takeaways: Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK557791/ https://www.uptodate.com/contents/tricyclic-antidepressant-poisoning https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15728327/ https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK430931/

text: A 30-year-old man initially develops paralysis in both legs, which then progresses to involve both upper limbs. Over time, he shows slight recovery in the upper limbs but persistent weakness in the lower trunk and legs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The clinical manifestations indicate diplegia , a condition characterized by symmetric paralysis that predominantly affects the lower body while sparing or minimally affecting the upper limbs. The patient's clinical course shows an initial widespread paralysis that improved to primarily affect the lower trunk and legs, and only slight involvement of upper limbs, which is characteristic of diplegia. Explanation of other options: Quadriplegia (Option B): Refers to paralysis of all four limbs and typically includes the torso. While the patient initially experienced widespread involvement, the final clinical picture with predominant lower body involvement does not correlate with quadriplegia. Paraplegia (Option C): Paraplegia involves paralysis of the lower half of the body, including both legs, but spares the arms. Monoplegia (Option D): Monoplegia refers to paralysis affecting only one limb. Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK132431/table/introduction.t1/

text: An adult patient collapses in the emergency room, and you are performing CPR alongside your medical team. What is the recommended ratio of chest compressions to rescue breaths?
expl: Explanation: In adults during CPR, a 30:2 ratio of chest compressions to rescue breaths is given to ensure adequate circulation and ventilation. CPR is a lifesaving procedure performed during cardiac arrest to maintain blood flow and oxygen delivery to vital organs. Chest compressions should be initiated by placing the hands on the lower half of the sternum. Compression rate: 100-120 per minute. Compression depth: At least 2 inches (5 cm) in adults. Allow full chest recoil after each compression. Minimize interruptions to maintain perfusion. Compression-to-ventilation ratio: Adults: 30:2 (single or two rescuers) Children and infants: 30:2 (single rescuer), 15:2 (two rescuers) Reference: https://www.redcross.org/take-a-class/cpr/performing-cpr/cpr-steps

text: Macula densa is formed by all except?
expl: At the point where the afferent arteriole enters the glomerulus and the efferent arteriole leaves, the tubule of the nephron touches the arterioles of the glomerulus from which it arose. This point marks the beginning of the DCT. There is a modified epithelium in the DCT here and is known as the macula densa. The media of the afferent arteriole contains the JG cells which contain membrane bound secretory granules. These along with the Lacis cells (agranular cells) which are found in the junction between the afferent and efferent arteriole, produce renin. text: Pigment producing atypical mycobacteria ?
expl: Ans. is 'c' i.e., M. gordonae and M. szulgai Non-tubercular mycobacteria (also called atypical mycobacteria) have been classified into four groups by Runyon based on pigment production and rate of growth. 1) Group I (photochromogens) :- These produce pigmented colonies (yellow-orange) only when exposed to light, but not in dark. Examples of photochromogens are M. asiaticum, M. kansasii, M. marinum, and M. simiae. 2) Group II (scotochromogens) :- These always produce pigmented colonies (yellow-orange-red), i.e. in dark as well as in light. Scotochromogens are M. flovescens, M. gordonae, M. scrofulaceum and M. szulgi. 3) Group HI (Nonchromogens) :- These do not produce pigment. Nonchromogens are M. avium complex (MAC), M. haemophilum, M. gastri, M. ulcerans, M. xenopi and M. nonchromogenicum. 4) Group IV (rapid growers) :- This is heterogeneous group of mycobacteria capable of rapid growth, colonies appearing within 7 days of incubation. Within the group, photochromogenic, scotochromogenic and nonchromogenic species occur. Chromogenic (pigment producing) rapid growers are mostly saprophytic, e.g. M. phlei and M. smegmetis. M. fortuitum and M. chelonei do not produce any pigment. Other rapid growers are M. abscessus, M. vaccae, M. genevense, M. confluentis, and M. intermedium.

text: A 23-year-old man who lives with his male partner consults you for an opinion. He has suffered anal discharge and pruritus for the past 3 days. There are also some symptoms of dysuria. A urethral smear reveals intracellular diplococci. What is the most likely infectious agent to fit with this clinical picture?
expl: Gonorrhea, a sexually transmitted bacterial infection, may manifest with urethritis, cervicitis, salpingitis or anorectal symptoms. Symptoms in men may be severe and include purulent discharge from the anterior urethra and dysuria, with rectal discharge where anal intercourse has taken place. Symptoms in women are often mild, with urethritis and cervicitis occurring a few days after exposure. In around 20% of cases, uterine invasion may occur with signs and symptoms of endometritis or salpingitis. Inflamed Bartholin's glands may occur. The cause is the Gram-negative intracellular diplococci Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Their presence is diagnostic in male urethral smears, although there is a false-negative rate of 60- 70% in samples from women. Patients should of course also receive screening for other sexually transmitted diseases. Gonorrhoeae should be treated with ceftriaxone 500 mg in a single IM dose plus treatment for chlamydia if infection has not been excluded. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 156 Pg: 1234-1240

text: Which of the following is an action of IGF-I?
expl: The growth promoting effects of GH is largely mediated via IGF1. The metabolic actions of GH like hyperglycaemia, hyperlipidemia, hypertriglyceridemia, nitrogen retention and lipolysis is independent of IGF1. GH impairs glucose tolerance by antagonizing insulin action. IGF-1 apart from binding to its own receptor, can also act on insulin receptor which is responsible for the hypoglycemic episodes. While, injected IGF-I induces hypoglycemia, and lower doses improve insulin sensitivity in patients with severe insulin resistance and diabetes. text: A 15-year-old boy who is 155 cm tall is worried that he may have stopped growing. Which hormone is chiefly responsible for epiphyseal fusion and cessation of growth?
expl: The growth spurt at puberty is brought about by the secretion of androgens in the male and estrogens in the female. However, it is estrogens that ultimately terminate growth by causing the epiphyses in the long bones to fuse. Thus, estrogens rather than androgens are responsible for skeletal maturation, epiphyseal fusion and cessation of growth in males and females. Growth hormone, thyroxine and insulin are involved in growth alone. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 2912

text: A 42-year-old woman who has been prescribed metoclopramide complains of galactorrhoea and amenorrhoea. What is the main mechanism of action of metoclopramide in this case?

options.A: Stimulates dopamine release by the hypothalamus
options.B: Direct stimulatory effect on pituitary lactotrophs
options.C: Binds to D2-receptors on pituitary lactotrophs

ansText: Binds to D2-receptors on pituitary lactotrophs
expl: This patient has developed hyperprolactinemia due to metoclopramide therapy. Dopamine secreted from the hypothalamus is the most important negative regulator of prolactin production from pituitary. Metoclopramide is a dopamine antagonist that binds to D2-receptors on pituitary lactotrophs. This stimulates the release of prolactin by the anterior pituitary thereby resulting in galactorrhoea. Prolactin inhibits gonadotropin-releasing hormone and gonadotropin secretion per se, and hence oligomenorrhoea or amenorrhoea may occur. text: The presence of galactorrhoea is MOST suggestive of which one of the following conditions?
expl: Galactorrhoea is a nonpuerperal expression of milk. Hyperprolactinemia causes galactorrhoea and amenorrhoea, which may result from a prolactin secreting pituitary tumour or hyperplasia. Hypothyroidism is a cause of raised prolactin levels. Primary hypothyroidism would result in low T3 and T4 with increase in TSH and TRH from pituitary and hypothalamus respectively. TRH has a stimulatory effect on lactotrophs of pituitary gland. Acromegaly is also associated with hyperprolactinemia in one-thirds of cases. Bromocriptine is a dopaminergic agent that has an inhibitory effect on prolactin and is frequently used to treat hyperprolactinemia. Sheehan's syndrome is a primary hypopituitarism due to ischemic necrosis of the pituitary gland caused by postpartum hemorrhage; it is characterized by failure of postpartum lactation due to hypoprolactinemia and failure to resume normal cyclic menstruation. Turner's syndrome (ovarian dysgenesis) causes primary amenorrhoea with poor development of the breast. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 2909

text: You review a 28-year-old girl who has been referred with amenorrhoea. She is noted on routine screening to have a raised prolactin level. Patient is keen to know about prolactin physiology. Thinking of hormones in general, which of the following hormones is under continuous inhibition?
expl: Prolactin is under predominantly inhibitory control , by levels of dopamine. Prolactin levels are known to rise during pregnancy, lactation, severe stress, sleep and coitus. Mildly increased prolactin levels in the range of 400-600 mU/litre may be physiological, but higher levels require a diagnosis. Levels above 1000 imply the possibility of microprolactinoma, and levels above 5000 imply the presence of macroprolactinoma. Drug causes of Hyperprolactinaemia are, not surprisingly, the dopamine antagonists, which include metoclopramide, domperidone and the phenothiazines. Features of Hyperprolactinaemia in women include amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, loss of libido, subfertility and features of androgen deficiency. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 20 th edition Chapter:371, Page number:2660-61

text: A 29-year-old man presents with coarse facial features and progressive enlargement of his hands and feet over the past 10 years. Acromegaly is confirmed by raised IGF-1 levels and failure of growth hormone suppression after a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test. Which medication is advised for his treatment?
expl: Explanation: The presentation is consistent with acromegaly, and lanreotide , a somatostatin analogue, is effective in suppressing GH and IGF-1 levels while offering the benefit of prolonged action. Lanreotide , given as a long-acting depot injection , is the preferred first-line medical treatment for acromegaly, acting by binding to somatostatin receptors on the pituitary tumour to suppress GH release and restore IGF-1 levels to normal. Explanation of other options: Terlipressin (Option B): Terlipressin, a synthetic analogue of vasopressin , is mainly used in managing hepatorenal syndrome and oesophageal variceal bleeding . It is not useful in acromegaly since it does not influence growth hormone secretion or activity. Ketoconazole (Option C): Ketoconazole is an antifungal drug that, although sometimes used off-label for endocrine issues like adrenal hypercortisolism, is not used in treating acromegaly since it has no impact on GH or IGF-1 levels. Leuprolide (Option D) : Leuprolide, a gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonist, is mainly prescribed for conditions like prostate cancer and endometriosis, but since it does not influence GH secretion, it is not useful in managing acromegaly.

text: A 12-year-old girl presents with short stature, webbed neck and primary amenorrhoea.Given the likely clinical diagnosis, which hormone would be most appropriate to treat this condition?
expl: This girl most probably has Turner's syndrome , which is most commonly associated with absence of one X chromosome (XO pattern). Characteristic features in this condition include streak ovaries and absent internal genitalia. Estrogen administration will develop female secondary sex characters and life-long therapy will be required. Growth hormone may be useful for a limited period to increase her height. As the ovaries are absent, pulsatile GnRH and luteinising hormone would be of no use. Progesterone would be useful for inducing withdrawal bleed in females sufficiently treated with estrogen. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 3000

text: You review a 28-year-old girl who has been referred with amenorrhoea. She is noted on routine screening to have a raised prolactin level. Patient is keen to know about prolactin physiology. Which of the following is the primary physiological regulator of prolactin production?
expl: Prolactin is under predominantly inhibitory control , by levels of dopamine. Prolactin levels are known to rise during pregnancy, lactation, severe stress, sleep and coitus. Drug causes of Hyperprolactinaemia include dopamine antagonists like metoclopramide, domperidone antipsychotics, proton pump inhibitors, H2 receptor blockers, Levosulprode etc. Features of Hyperprolactinaemia in women include amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, loss of libido, subfertility and features of androgen deficiency in males Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 2893

text: A 23-year-old student presents for review. She is distressed by the fact that she is overweight and is embarrassed of excessive facial hair. She also notices that she appears to have more generalized body hair than other women. On further history, she can sometimes miss a couple of menses, but pregnancy testing is consistently negative. Her mother apparently had similar problems in her youth, took a while to conceive and now has type-2 diabetes. Testosterone is just above the upper limit of normal range, her LH:FSH ratio is increased and prolactin is normal. Which diagnosis fits best with this woman's clinical picture?
expl: PCOS is said to occur in 3% of adult women. Symptoms usually begin around the time of menarche and the diagnosis is often made in adolescence. Obesity is present in around 40% of sufferers and there is an increased association with type-2 diabetes due to insulin resistance. Biochemical abnormalities characteristically include a mildly raised testosterone level and an increased LH: FSH ratio. The cornerstone of management is life style modifications to achieve weigh reduction. The use of OCPs can reduce the androgen levels and help achieve regular menstrual cycles. The anovulation associated with PCOS is treated with ovulation induction agents like Clomiphene citrate and Letrozole Hyperprolactinemia is unlikely as her prolactin is normal. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 3036

text: A 51-year-old woman presents with increasing lower back pain for the last six months. The pain is increased by working as a floor-layer, and is worse in the evening. There is no weight loss, night pain, or fever. Her back is stiff for 15 minutes in morning. Over the last few months she has developed firm to hard swelling on several distal and proximal interphalangeal joints, and has anterior knee pain worsened by climbing stairs. A full blood count, ESR, and CRP done by the GP have been normal. What is the diagnosis?
expl: This patient has generalised osteoarthritis (GOA), as there are OA related symptoms in at least three joint areas, namely Bony swellings at distal and proximal IPJs termed Heberden's and Bouchard's nodes respectively Anterior knee pain, worse on climbing stairs, suggesting patella-femoral joint OA, and Low back pain, suggesting spinal degenerative changes. Ankylosing spondylitis typically occurs in young men, and associates with pronounced early morning stiffness and buttock pain. Osteoporosis is not symptomatic, unless accompanied by a spinal fracture. Osteoporotic spinal fractures present with acute pain which improves over a period of few weeks to a couple of months. There are no red-flag symptoms to raise the possibility of discitis or malignancy. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 371 Pg: 2858-2859

text: A 56-year-old man with a history of smoking and hypertension presents to the emergency room with central crushing chest pain, nausea and sweating. On examination his BP is 104/70 mmHg, his pulse 105/min regular and he looks pale, grey and sweaty. ECG: ST elevation V1-V4, ST depression II, III and aVL Which of the following is the most likely finding on angiography?

options.B: 70% stenosis of left anterior descending artery
options.C: Total occlusion of left anterior descending artery

ansText: Total occlusion of left anterior descending artery
expl: This man is suffering from an ST elevation anterior myocardial infarction and most likely has an occlusion of his left anterior descending artery due to plaque rupture. Left circumflex or right coronary artery occlusions would be expected to result in either lateral or inferior ECG changes. Management of choice is primary PCI, as early as possible after the onset of chest pain. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 21 st edition Page 2044

text: A 62-year-old smoker is admitted with nausea, sweating and central crushing chest pain. A 12 lead ECG reveals ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF. Which coronary artery is most likely to have been affected in this case?
expl: Right coronary artery supplies the right ventricle, the posterior third of the interventricular septum, the inferior wall of the left ventricle and a portion of the posterior wall of the left ventricle. (leads II, III, aVF corresponds to inferior wall) Occasionally the posterior interventricular septum may be supplied by a branch of the of the left circumflex artery, called left dominant circulation. The left anterior descending and left circumflex coronary arteries arise at the left main coronary artery bifurcation and supply the anterior left ventricle, the bulk of the interventricular septum (anterior two thirds), the apex, and the lateral and posterior left ventricular walls. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page no: 2035

text: A 52-year-old man presents with central crushing chest pain. Examination is normal. The 12-lead ECG shows ST segment elevation in leads II, III, aVF, and ST depression in V1, V2 and V3. Which coronary artery is occluded?
expl: The ECG describes an inferior-posterior myocardial infarction (MI). This territory is supplied by a dominant right coronary artery . The concept of coronary dominance refers to which coronary artery supplies the posterior descending coronary artery. In the case of approximately 85% of patients this is the right coronary artery with about 15% of patients having a dominant left circumflex. The territories supplied by the arteries are as follows: Circumflex: Lateral Left anterior descending: Anterior and septum Left main stem: Branches into the left anterior descending artery and circumflex and supplies most of the left ventricle. Complete left main stem occlusion is invariably fatal Obtuse marginal: One of the branches of the circumflex and supplies the 'high lateral' region of the left ventricle (ECG leads I and aVL). Basic understanding of coronary anatomy is important as this is predictive of problems following MI. Right coronary artery supplies the AV node, so heart block following inferior MI is common. However, heart block following anterior MI is a grave prognostic marker as this indicates a large anterior wall infarct. The right coronary system also supplies the right ventricle, hence problems relating to a right ventricular infarct are commonly associated with an inferior MI. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page no: 2058

text: What is the diagnosis if the axis is on the mark '?'from the diagram shown below?
expl: Explanation: The QRS axis falls within the range of +90° to +180° , which is diagnostic for Right Axis Deviation (RAD) . This is determined using the hexaxial reference system, where the quadrant between +90° and +180° represents RAD. QRS Axis Interpretation: Normal: -30° to +100°, positive QRS in leads I and aVF. (Option B ruled out) Left Axis Deviation ( Tall R in I, deep S in III, biphasic RS in II; causes → LVH, left anterior fascicular block, inferior MI, normal variant. (Option C ruled out) Right Axis Deviation (> +90° to +100°): Tall R in III > II, deep S in I, tall R in II/III/aVF; causes → RV overload, lateral MI, left posterior fascicular block, dextrocardia, left pneumothorax, electrode misplacement, normal in children/young adults. text: A 48-year-old man presents with persistent headaches and progressive visual disturbance. On examination, he has prominent frontal bossing, thickened palms and soles, spaced central incisors, and coarse facial features. He is hypertensive and diabetic. What is the most appropriate screening test to evaluate his condition?

options.A: GH levels <0.4 µg/L after 1 hour of 75 g oral glucose load
options.B: Single early morning fasting GH level to establish the diagnosis
options.C: Age-specific IGF-1 levels are useful for screening
options.D: GH levels are used to assess disease severity

ansText: Age-specific IGF-1 levels are useful for screening
expl: Explanation of answer: Serum IGF-1, which reflects integrated GH secretion, is the most sensitive and reliable screening test for acromegaly. The patient's features-frontal bossing, acral enlargement, coarse facies, visual symptoms, and associated hypertension and diabetes-are classical signs of acromegaly, a disorder resulting from chronic growth hormone (GH) excess, usually due to a GH-secreting pituitary macroadenoma. The first-line screening test is serum Insulin-like Growth Factor 1 (IGF-1), measured against age-specific reference ranges. IGF-1 is more stable and reflects long-term GH exposure, unlike GH which has pulsatile secretion and fluctuating levels throughout the day. Acromegaly - Summary and Clinical Essentials Acromegaly is primarily due to excess growth hormone (GH) secretion, most commonly from a pituitary somatotroph macroadenoma (>1 cm). Cause: Mixed mammosomatotroph tumors (secreting GH and PRL) Acidophilic stem cell adenomas (PRL co-secretion → hypogonadism, galactorrhea) Ectopic GH/GHRH secretion from carcinoid tumors, pancreas, lungs, or ovaries Clinical Features Acral Changes: Frontal bossing, enlarged hands and feet Mandibular overgrowth (prognathism), interdental spacing Soft Tissue Features: Coarse facial features, macroglossia Increased heel pad (>25 mm), larger ring/shoe/glove size Visceromegaly: Cardiomegaly, thyroid enlargement Other Signs: Hyperhidrosis, oily skin, deep voice Arthropathy, kyphosis, carpal tunnel syndrome Acanthosis nigricans, skin tags, muscle weakness Complications Metabolic: Diabetes mellitus, hypertension Cardiac/Respiratory: Cardiomyopathy, sleep apnea Neoplastic: Colon polyps and malignancy Mass effect: Visual disturbances, hypopituitarism Investigations Screening test: Age-adjusted serum IGF-1 levels (stable marker of GH excess) Diagnostic test: 75 g Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT) GH suppression to 20% may show paradoxical GH rise GH levels: Not reliable for diagnosis or severity due to pulsatile secretion MRI Brain with contrast: Investigation of choice for tumor localization Other labs: Elevated PRL (25% cases), assess other pituitary hormones Management First-line: Transsphenoidal surgery (especially for GH-secreting adenomas) Medical therapy: Somatostatin receptor ligands (SRLs): Octreotide, Lanreotide GH receptor antagonist: Pegvisomant (normalizes IGF-1 in ~70%) Dopamine agonists: High-dose cabergoline (modest effect) Radiotherapy: For non-responders or surgical failures Explanation of other options: GH levels This is a confirmatory test, not a screening test. It is used after IGF-1 is found to be elevated. Single early morning fasting GH level to establish the diagnosis (Option B): Incorrect. GH secretion is pulsatile and highly variable, making a single random or fasting level unreliable for diagnosis. GH levels are used to assess disease severity (Option D): Incorrect. GH levels may correlate poorly with clinical severity due to fluctuations. IGF-1 is more reliable for both screening and monitoring. Reference: https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1155/2024/5085905

text: A 52-year-old patient who has had chemotherapy for metastatic breast cancer 6 months earlier comes to the clinic complaining of shortness of breath on exertion. Her BP is 125/78 mmHg, her pulse is 94/min and her apex beat is displaced to the anterior axillary line. CXR - Cardiomegaly, increased shadowing consistent with mild pulmonary oedema at both bases Which chemotherapeutic agent is most likely to be responsible for this patient's symptoms?
expl: Doxorubicin can be associated with cardiac failure, reduced left ventricular ejection fraction and tachyarrhythmias. Platinum based chemotherapies are associated with peripheral neuropathy, and bleomycin with interstitial pneumonitis and a specific skin lesion called 'flagellate dermatitis'. Drugs causing dilated cardiomyopathy Doxorubicin (Adriamycin) Trastuzumab (Herceptin) Tacrolimus Zidovudine Drugs like NSAIDs, Thiazolidinediones can cause fluid retention and thus worsen heart failure in patients with underlying disease. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 737,1964

text: A study reveals an immediate rise in blood pressure following infusion of a hormone in normal volunteers. Which of the following is the most likely hormone used in this study?
expl: Angiotensin II when infused intravenously produces an immediate rise in blood pressure being a potent vasoconstrictor . Both BNF and ANF result in natriuresis and lowering of blood pressure. Prolactin has no specific effect. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Principles, 20 th edition, ch:271 pg:1892,1893

text: A 52-year-old man suffers an extensive anterior myocardial infarction but recovers well in hospital. His pre-discharge ECHO shows him to have an ejection fraction 35%. He is otherwise asymptomatic. His medications on discharge should include which of the following?

options.A: Aspirin, metoprolol, ramipril and a statin
options.B: Aspirin, atenolol, ramipril, furosemide and a statin
options.C: Aspirin, isosorbide mononitrate, ramipril and a statin
options.D: Aspirin, nitrate, losartan and a statin

ansText: Aspirin, metoprolol, ramipril and a statin
expl: Following a myocardial infarction, patients with LV dysfunction benefit from taking β-Blockers and RAAS blockers. There is strong evidence supporting the use of aspirin and a statin post-MI. In the absence of anginal pain, prophylactic use of nitrates is not mandatory. Diuretics is indicated for patients with symptomatic heart failure and those with fluid overload. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page no: 2048-50

text: A 44 year old man presents to the ophthalmologist and was found to have anterior uveitis. Upon enquiry, he has mouth ulcers and a rash on his leg. What is the likely diagnosis?
expl: Among the given options Behcet is the disease causing uveitis. The typical lesion is a panuveitis. Behcet's disease may cause anterior or posterior uveitis, corneal ulceration,conjunctivitis, papillitis, SVC and IVC thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, erythema nodosum, pustular lesions, acneiform nodules, pathergy and oral ulceration. Anterior Uveitis in Behcet's disease HLA B27 associated arthritis usually cause acute Anterior uveitis. Psoriatic arthritis produces bilateral chronic posterior uveitis Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 364, Pg: 2818

text: A 52 year old lady complains of gradual onset of blurred vision in her left eye. Examination reveals a left sided relative afferent pupillary defect. Fundoscopy reveals left sided optic atrophy. Visual fields show a left sided central scotoma and an upper quadrantic visual field defect in the right eye. Where is the lesion?
expl: Lesions of the anterior chiasma (junction of optic nerve and chiasma) will produce an ipsilateral central scotoma and a contralateral superior quadrantanopia. text: A 52 year old man has subjectively diminished light touch and pinprick sensation in the left hand extending to above the elbow. Joint position sense is intact. He has difficulty distinguishing a cigarette from a pen using the right hand with his eyes closed. His two-point discrimination is 11 mm. Where is the lesion?
expl: The sensory signs described here are indicative of a lesion of the anterior parietal cortex (mid postcentral gyrus). The cingulate gyrus is part of the limbic system (mood and emotions). Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 426, Pg: 3326-3327

text: A 43- year-old gentleman develops chest pain 7 minutes after fibreoptic bronchoscopy. The procedure had been performed without sedation following an intratracheal injection of 5 ml 2.5% cocaine solution and xylocaine spray to the pharynx for topical anaesthesia. ECG showed an evolving anterior myocardial infarction. Which of the following would you prefer for his management?
expl: The underlying mechanism here is vasoconstriction, not thrombosis. Cocaine is cardiotoxic and its use has been linked to coronary artery spasm, angina, myocardial infarction, arrhythmias, sudden cardiac death, and myocardial contraction bands, which might act as a substrate for arrhythmias. It is important to avoid β-blockers in treating cocaine induced chest pains or acute myocardial infarctions as this may result in unopposed α1 adrenergic action with worsening coronary spasm. Calcium channel antagonists or nitrates should be administered as early as possible. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Principles, 20 th edition, ch:447 pg:3289,3290

text: A 19-year-old man is referred to the endocrine clinic by his GP because he had poorly developed secondary sexual characteristics. He describes anosmia. On examination, he has lack of axillary or pubertal hair, small sexual organs (testicular volumes of approximately 5 ml). Investigations reveal: Testosterone 3.5 nmol/L (10-30) Prolactin 350 mU/L (<450) FSH 2.2 iu/L (1-7) LH 1.8 iu/L (1-10) What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: X-linked Kallmann's syndrome (KS) is a genetic disease characterized by anosmia and hypogonadism due to impairment in the development of olfactory axons and in the migration of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH)-producing neurons. 50% of the patients also have unilateral renal agenesis. Abnormalities of the sexual organs, mainly cryptorchidism and testicular atrophy are common. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 20 th edition Chapter:372 Page number:2664-65

text: A 24-year-old woman visits her doctor complaining of feeling tired all the time for the last few months. She has amenorrhea for 6 months, and has been feeling dizzy while getting up in the morning. Which of the following clinical signs would the family doctor most likely find if the diagnosis was thought to be Addison's disease?

options.D: Hypertension in supine position with postural hypotension

expl: Hypoadrenalism has many causes including Addison's disease, granulomatous disorders, TB, tumour (particularly lung) or infections (meningococcal septicaemia). Secondary hypoadrenalism is caused by hypopituitarism or hypothalamic disorders. Pallor is present in hypopituitarism due to normochromic, normocytic anemia and a lack of melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH; cleaved from the precursor of ACTH). Secondary AI differs from Addison disease in that it lacks the hyperpigmentation, and aldosterone production is spared as it is regulated by RAAS rather than ACTH. Buccal pigmentation is also associated with glucocorticoid deficiency, most commonly from Addison's disease. ACTH is elevated in Addison's disease and results in higher levels of MSH, which causes the skin and buccal pigmentation found in this condition. Lack of body hair and amenorrhoea are features of hypogonadism in hypopituitarism. Postural hypotension is related to glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid deficiency and is more common in primary than secondary AI. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Edition, Page Number-2971.

text: A 70-year-old female is being reviewed in a clinic after having had an anterior wall MI. Her Echocardiogram showed an EF of 36%. Patient is already on diuretics, ramipril, aspirin and rosuvastatin. Which of the following beta blockers should be avoided in this patient?
expl: Sotalol may prolong the QT interval and leads to an increased risk of ventricular arrhythmias. This risk is increased in individuals with hypokalemia, which can occur due to co-administration of diuretics Conversely, beta blockers are the main stay of medical management in patients with congenital long QT syndrome to reduce ventricular arrythmias. Nadolol and Propranolol are the preferred agents for prophylaxis. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 1925

text: What is the name of the device shown in the image below?
expl: Explanation: The device shown in the x-ray is a cardiac pacemaker . Cardiac Conduction Devices (CCDs) Implantable Cardioverter Defibrillators (ICDs) Purpose: ICDs are designed to detect and correct life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias by delivering electrical shocks to restore normal sinus rhythm. Types of ICDs: Transvenous ICD (T-ICD): Leads are inserted via veins and positioned at the junction of the brachiocephalic vein/superior vena cava and the right ventricle (RV) . May be combined with biventricular pacemakers in Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy (CRT) . Subcutaneous ICD (S-ICD): No transvenous leads are used. The pulse generator is placed beneath the skin, and a subcutaneous lead is positioned along the left parasternal border to deliver shocks Main Components of CCDs: Pulse Generator: Produces electrical impulses to regulate heart rhythm. Electrodes: Conduct impulses directly to heart tissue. Lead Wires: Connect the pulse generator to the heart; may have different fixation mechanisms: Active Fixation: Uses helical (screw-like) tips to anchor directly into the myocardium. Passive Fixation: Relies on fibrosis to secure the lead within the trabeculae of the heart. Chest X-Ray in CCD Assessment Preferred modality for evaluating: Device placement Lead positioning Detection of complications (e.g., lead fracture, dislodgement) Two Standard Radiographic Views: Posterior-Anterior (PA) View: Useful for assessing lead continuity and device placement. Lateral (LAT) View: Crucial for identifying lead tip location and distinguishing between right and left ventricular lead positions. Explanation for other options: Chemoport Device (Option B): Implantable ports also known as chemoports, Port-A-Caths, or totally implantable venous access devices (TIVADs) are a type of central venous catheter specifically designed for patients who require long-term intravenous access. These ports offer a durable and reliable option for extended venous access, commonly used in patients undergoing chemotherapy. Compared to peripherally inserted central catheters (PICCs), chemoports provide several benefits, including a lower risk of infection and improved patient comfort over prolonged use. Options C and D are incorrect . Reference: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4286824/ https://radiopaedia.org/articles/implantable-port

text: What is the probable diagnosis for an overweight elderly man who arrived at the emergency department with intense chest pain lasting for two hours? He also experienced excessive sweating, pain in the left arm, nausea, and one instance of vomiting. During examination, his pulse rate was recorded as 58 beats per minute and his blood pressure was 90/60 mm of Hg. An electrocardiogram (ECG) was conducted and revealed the following results. Additionally, the patient's cardiac biomarkers indicated increased troponin levels.
expl: Explanation: The clinical presentation is classic for an acute Inferior Wall Myocardial Infarction (MI) . Key indicators include: Symptoms: Typical ischemic chest pain with autonomic features (sweating, nausea, vomiting). ECG: ST-segment elevation in the inferior leads (II, III, and aVF) . Hemodynamics: Bradycardia and hypotension can occur due to vagal stimulation or right ventricular involvement, which is common in inferior MIs. Biomarkers: Elevated troponin confirms myocardial necrosis. Explanation of other options: Anterior wall MI (Option A): Presents with ST-elevation in precordial leads V1-V4. Posterior wall MI (Option C): Typically shows ST-depression in V1-V4 with a tall R wave; it is often associated with an inferior or lateral MI. Pericarditis (Option D): Causes diffuse ST-elevation (often concave up) in multiple leads not following a vascular territory, and PR segment depression is common. Key Takeaways: ST-elevation in leads II, III, and aVF is diagnostic for an inferior wall MI. Inferior wall MIs are most commonly due to occlusion of the Right Coronary Artery (RCA).

text: A 33-year-old man is brought to ER in a collapsed state having sustained a precordial stab wound.Which of the following cardiac valves is most likely to have been injured?
expl: The tricuspid valve is the most anterior valve of the human heart and is the commonest to be injured during a stabbing attack. Penetrating injuries may cause lacerations to any of the heart chambers or great vessels, and death may result from haemorrhage or cardiac tamponade. Late complications include infective pericarditis, valve damage or intracardiac shunts.. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 2029

text: Which of the following anatomical considerations is correct?

options.A: Optic chiasm lesions characteristically produce a bitemporal hemianopia
options.B: The physiological blind spot is unaffected by papilloedema
options.C: In cortical blindness pupillary reactions are abnormal
options.D: Optic tract lesions produce an ipsilateral homonymous hemianopia

ansText: Optic chiasm lesions characteristically produce a bitemporal hemianopia
expl: B.The physiological blind spot is enlarged in papilloedema as peripapillary photo receptors are displaced. C.In cortical blindness, pupillary reflexes, eye movements and fundoscopy are all normal. D.Optic tract lesions produce an contralateral homonymous hemianopia. text: A patient presented with bitemporal hemianopia. On imaging it is found that an artery aneurysm is pressing on optic chiasma .What is the likely artery involved?

text: What is the likely diagnosis for a 53-year-old woman presenting with dysphagia, burning tongue, worsening exertional dyspnoea, palpitations, and mucosal webs in the upper third of the oesophagus on barium swallow?
expl: Explanation Plummer-Vinson Syndrome (PVS) is classically seen in middle-aged women and is associated with iron deficiency anaemia . It is characterized by the triad : Dysphagia → due to esophageal webs (typically in the upper oesophagus). Iron deficiency anaemia → manifests as fatigue, exertional dyspnoea, palpitations. Glossitis & angular cheilitis → cause burning tongue and oral discomfort. Barium swallow in PVS demonstrates thin mucosal webs in the proximal esophagus , consistent with the finding in this patient. Explanation of Incorrect Options Achalasia (Option B): Involves failure of relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter due to loss of ganglion cells in the myenteric plexus. Presents with progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids , regurgitation, and weight loss. Barium swallow shows bird-beak appearance in the distal esophagus, not mucosal webs in the upper esophagus. Esophageal adenocarcinoma (Option C): Usually arises in the lower third of the esophagus , commonly associated with Barrett's esophagus (longstanding GERD). Symptoms include progressive dysphagia (first solids, then liquids), weight loss, anemia . Barium swallow would reveal an irregular mass/narrowing , not thin mucosal webs. Zenker diverticulum (Option D): A pharyngoesophageal false diverticulum, located just above the upper esophageal sphincter (Killian's triangle). Presents with regurgitation of undigested food, halitosis, gurgling in neck, chronic cough , and sometimes aspiration. Barium swallow shows an outpouching , not mucosal webs.

text: A patient presents to the OPD with a history of diarrhoea after consuming a salad. What is the most likely organism responsible for this illness?
expl: Explanation: Staphylococcus aureus causes food poisoning due to ingestion of preformed enterotoxin , often found in improperly stored salads, dairy products, and bakery foods . The illness is characterised by a rapid onset (1-6 hours) of vomiting, abdominal cramps, and sometimes diarrhoea . Because the toxin is preformed, antibiotics are not useful; management is supportive. Explanation of other options: Bacillus cereus (Option B): Classically linked to reheated rice ("fried rice syndrome"), not fresh salads. Vibrio cholerae (Option C): Causes profuse watery diarrhoea (rice-water stools) due to contaminated water/seafood, not typically linked to salads. Salmonella enteritidis (Option D): Causes invasive gastroenteritis with fever, abdominal cramps, and diarrhoea after contaminated poultry/eggs; onset is slower (12-72 hours).

text: Which of the following investigations is most useful for the diagnosis of carcinoid tumors?
expl: Explanation: The most useful diagnostic test for carcinoid tumors is a 24-hour urinary 5-HIAA measurement. These tumors are neuroendocrine in origin and secrete serotonin, which is metabolized to 5-HIAA and excreted in urine. Carcinoid Syndrome Results from hormone secretion (mainly serotonin) from neuroendocrine tumors (NETs), usually in the small intestine or appendix . Syndrome occurs when tumors metastasize to the liver or retroperitoneum , allowing hormones to reach systemic circulation. Histamine and tachykinins (e.g., substance P) may also contribute. Clinical features Flushing: Sudden, intense red/purple color on face, neck, upper body, often with warmth. Diarrhea: Frequent watery stools (>10/day), affecting quality of life. Wheezing/asthma-like symptoms Cognitive impairment (advanced cases) Pellagra-like skin lesions (niacin deficiency due to tryptophan diversion to serotonin) Diagnosis of Carcinoid Syndrome Management: Somatostatin analogues: First-line therapy; inhibit hormone secretion. ~90% of NETs express somatostatin receptors. Telotristat ethyl: Inhibits serotonin synthesis; adjunct for refractory diarrhea. Surgery: For localized tumors; often not feasible in metastatic disease. Explanation of other options: 24-hour urinary catecholamines (Option A): 24-hour urinary catecholamines is used to diagnose pheochromocytoma and other catecholamine-secreting tumors, not carcinoid tumors. Serum calcitonin levels (Option B): Calcitonin levels are used in the diagnosis of medullary thyroid carcinoma, a type of neuroendocrine tumour. Calcitonin is unlikely to be elevated in carcinoid syndrome.

text: With respect to gastric carcinoma, which of the following statements is true?

options.D: Helicobacter pylori infection is not associated with gastric carcinoma

ansText: Endoscopic ultrasonography is superior to conventional CT scanning for local tumour staging
expl: Incidence of distal stomach tumors is actually decreasing while the incidence of tumors in the proximal stomach is increasing. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) use is associated with decreased risk of certain gastric tumors. pylori infection has been associated in a number of studies with increased risk of gastric carcinoma. Screening for gastric carcinoma in Japan detects up to 40% of gastric carcinomas at an early stage and in skilled hands five year survival can be upwards of 90%. Computed tomography (CT) with gastric dilatation is a useful complementary investigation in the staging of gastric carcinoma, but endoscopic ultrasonography is superior to conventional CT scanning as it is able to assess depth of infiltration and lymphatic dissemination of tumor. text: A patient is diagnosed with an ileal tumor, with elevated urinary 5-HIAA levels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: Carcinoid tumors arise from enterochromaffin (neuroendocrine) cells of the GI tract. They produce serotonin, metabolized to 5-HIAA in urine. Elevated urinary 5-HIAA is a diagnostic marker. Common sites: GI tract (small intestine, appendix, rectum), lungs. Clinical features: Local symptoms: obstruction, bleeding. Carcinoid syndrome (with metastasis): flushing, diarrhea, bronchospasm, right-sided valvular heart disease. Diagnosis: Urinary 5-HIAA, chromogranin A, imaging with PET/Octreoscan, histopathology (synaptophysin+, chromogranin+). Management: Surgery; medical control with somatostatin analogs (octreotide). Liver metastasis → embolization, RFA. Explanation of other options: Neuroblastoma (Option B): Pediatric tumor, presents with abdominal mass and systemic features. Leiomyoma (Option C): Benign smooth muscle tumor, no 5-HIAA secretion. Chromaffinoma (Option D): Pheochromocytoma, secretes catecholamines, not serotonin. Key Takeaways: Carcinoid tumors → serotonin → urinary 5-HIAA. Classic carcinoid syndrome occurs after hepatic metastasis .

text: A patient comes to you with history of head ache for the last one week. It is a dull aching occipitofrontal head ache. He has noticed that it becomes worse after he gets up and is relieved when he lies down for a while. What will be the imaging finding most likely to be seen in this patient?

options.A: Diffuse meningeal enhancement after Gd contrast
options.C: Space occupying lesion in the brain parenchyma
options.D: Blood in the sub arachnoid space

ansText: Diffuse meningeal enhancement after Gd contrast
expl: The question deals with a low CSF volume headache. It is due to CSF leak either spontaneous or associated a Lumbar puncture. The characteristic feature is head ache that worsens on assuming an upright posture and improves on lying down. The characteristic imaging finding is a diffuse meningeal enhancement. The site of CSF leak can be visualised by a spinal MRI. The main treatment is bed rest. If a leak is identified, it can be closed by a blood patch. IV Caffeine is often curative in patients with persistent pain. Empty sella is seen in head ache due to Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension. Blood in the sub arachnoid space is seen in SAH, which presents with thunderclap head ache. We should remember that meningeal enhancement can be seen in head ache due to meningitis as well, but here the history will be typical, with systemic symptoms . Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 16, Pg:115-116

text: A patient presents with headache and confusion and is diagnosed with a brain tumor. Family history reveals the presence of both brain and kidney tumors in close relatives. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation of answer: The combination of brain tumors, kidney tumors, and a positive family history strongly suggests Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) syndrome. VHL syndrome is a rare, inherited autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in the VHL tumor suppressor gene, predisposing affected individuals to a variety of benign and malignant tumors across multiple organ systems. This includes brain and kidney tumors, which are central to the case described. Common manifestations include: CNS hemangioblastomas: especially in the cerebellum, leading to headache, ataxia, and vomiting. Retinal hemangioblastomas: which may impair vision and may be an early sign. Renal cell carcinoma (clear cell type): Occurs in ~70% of patients and is a leading cause of mortality in VHL. Pheochromocytomas: Can cause hypertension, palpitations, and sweating. Pancreatic cysts and neuroendocrine tumors Endolymphatic sac tumors: May lead to hearing loss. Diagnostic criteria (Dutch and Danish): With a family history: One VHL-associated tumor and a first-degree relative with VHL. Without family history: At least two distinct VHL-related manifestations (e.g., cerebellar hemangioblastoma and renal cell carcinoma). Genetic testing confirming a pathogenic variant in the VHL gene is definitive. Management is multidisciplinary: Surgical removal of CNS hemangioblastomas, retinal tumors, pheochromocytomas, and renal tumors. Targeted therapies such as Pazopanib for advanced renal cancers and Belzutifan for VHL-associated tumors. Kidney transplant may be needed after bilateral nephrectomy in cases with extensive renal involvement. Explanation of other options: Neurofibromatosis (Option A): NF1 and NF2 can involve brain tumors (optic gliomas or vestibular schwannomas), but kidney tumors are not typical features. Li-Fraumeni syndrome (Option B): Associated with brain tumors, breast cancer, sarcomas, and adrenocortical carcinomas, but not classically with kidney tumors. Churg-Strauss syndrome (Option D): A vasculitic disorder with asthma and eosinophilia; tumors are not part of its clinical spectrum, ruling it out in this context. Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK1463/# https://www.cancer.gov/publications/dictionaries/cancer-terms/def/von-hippel-lindau-syndrome

text: Which of the following is caused by a lesion of the parietal lobe?
expl: Lesions of the frontal lobe include: Difficulties with task sequencing and executive skills Expressive aphasia (receptive aphasia, a temporal lobe lesion) Primitive reflexes Perseveration (repeatedly asking the same question or performing the same task) Anosmia Changes in personality. Lesions of the parietal lobe include Apraxias Neglect Astereognosis (unable to recognise an object by feeling it) Visual field defects (typically homonymous inferior quadrantanopia). They may also cause acalculia (inability to perform mental arithmetic). Lesions of the temporal lobe cause Visual field defects (typically homonymous superior quadrantanopia) Wernicke's (receptive) aphasia Auditory agnosia Memory impairment. text: Hamman crunch sign is seen in?
expl: The three main causes are Alveolar rupture with dissection of air into the mediastinum; Perforation or rupture of the esophagus, trachea, or main bronchi; and Dissection of air from the neck or the abdomen into the mediastinum. There is severe substernal chest pain with or without radiation into the neck and arms. The physical examination usually reveals subcutaneous emphysema in the suprasternal notch and Hamman's sign, which is a crunching or clicking noise synchronous with the heartbeat and is best heard in the left lateral decubitus position. The diagnosis is confirmed with the chest radiograph. Usually no treatment is required, but the mediastinal air will be absorbed faster if the patient inspires high concentrations of oxygen. If mediastinal structures are compressed, the compression can be relieved with needle aspiration.

text: What is the most probable diagnosis in an adult presenting with a pulsatile swelling in the neck, located below the angle of the jaw, showing an outward expansile impulse on examination, as confirmed by MRI angiography findings?
expl: Explanation: In this case, the presence of a pulsatile neck swelling along with the MRI angiography finding of Lyre's sign-which is the splaying of the internal and external carotid arteries-is diagnostic of a carotid body tumor. Carotid Body Tumor (CBT): Also known as paraganglioma or chemodectoma, CBT is a rare benign tumor arising from neural crest cells located in the adventitia at the bifurcation of the common carotid artery. CBTs typically grow slowly, have a low malignancy rate, and show no strong predilection for age or sex, although some studies suggest a slight female predominance. The exact cause is unclear but has been linked to chronic hypoxia and mutations in mitochondrial oxygen-sensing genes. Diagnosis: B-mode Ultrasonography: Reveals solid, hypoechoic masses adjacent to blood vessels. Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA): Demonstrates the tumor's blood supply and arterial displacement with nearly 100% diagnostic accuracy. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI): Shows a mass at the carotid artery bifurcation compressing and displacing the arteries. Tumors typically appear round or oval with heterogeneous or high signal intensity on T2-weighted images. The classic Lyre sign, representing the arterial splaying, is commonly seen on angiographic studies and can also be identified on CT angiography. Treatment: Surgical Removal: The primary and most effective treatment for carotid body tumors. Other Options: Radiotherapy, embolization, or a combination of therapies may be considered depending on the case. Explanation for other options: Grave's disease (Option A): is a hyperthyroid disorder characterized by protruding eyes, but the neck swelling in this condition is not pulsatile. Branchial cysts (Option B): are small, fluid-filled sacs that appear as lumps on the side of the neck and are more frequently seen in children than in adults. A thymic cyst (Option C): is a benign condition affecting the mediastinum and typically presents with symptoms such as shortness of breath, chest pain, cough, hoarseness, and difficulty swallowing. Reference: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8748146/ https://radiopaedia.org/articles/lyre-sign-carotid-artery

text: A 45-year-old chronic smoker with a 15-year history presents with hemoptysis. Imaging reveals a 3 cm mass in the upper lobe near the lung apex. What should be the next appropriate step in management?
expl: Explanation: The presentation suggests a potentially malignant lung lesion that necessitates histological confirmation. Since the mass is peripheral and located near the lung apex, the best next step is a CT-guided biopsy. In a CT-guided biopsy, a radiologist employs CT imaging to precisely direct a needle into the lung lesion to collect a tissue sample. This method yields reliable histopathological details about the mass, helping determine if it is malignant or benign, an essential step in a patient with a notable smoking history and hemoptysis. Explanations of other options: Bronchoscopy (Option A): Although bronchoscopy is valuable for assessing central or endobronchial tumors, it is less effective for peripheral lung lesions, particularly those situated near the lung apex. Sputum cytology (Option C): Sputum cytology is a low-cost, noninvasive test, but its sensitivity is lower than that of a biopsy, particularly when imaging already suggests a lung mass. It is most effective in detecting larger, centrally located tumors such as squamous cell carcinoma and small-cell carcinoma. Sputum for AFB (Option D): Although tuberculosis may present with hemoptysis, a 3 cm apical mass in the upper lobe on chest X-ray is not the usual finding for TB and instead suggests a possible malignancy, making tissue diagnosis a priority.

text: A patient presents with a five-day history of nausea and vomiting and watery diarrhea after eating crabs. He appears ill and is orthostatic. Serum Na is 129 mmol/L. Which of the following statements is true?

options.A: Urine Na will be less than 20 mEq/U
options.D: Serum osmolality is likely to be high

ansText: Urine Na will be less than 20 mEq/U
expl: This patient has developed hypovolemia from fluid losses from vomiting and diarrhea. There is no evidence that other osmotically active compounds have been ingested, thus serum osmolality is likely to be low. Because of hypovolemia, ADH (and aldosterone) will be stimulated, and serum ADH levels will be high. The kidney will be resorbing water and Na, and urine Na concentration will be low. Intravenous volume repletion with normal saline is advisable. Reference: Harrisons Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:53 Pg: 342

text: A 19-year-old woman sustains severe head injuries in a road traffic accident. The following day her investigations show: Sodium 160 mmol/l (137-144) Potassium 3.7 mmol/l (3.5-4.9) Chloride 120 mmol/l (95-107) Urea and Creatinine are Normal Which one of the following statements is correct?

options.A: Rapid rehydration with 5% dextrose is indicated
options.B: She should be treated with sodium restriction
options.C: She has the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH)

expl: There is a marked hypernatremia with elevated chloride but normal potassium and urea in a patient with severe head injuries. The likely cause of this presentation is diabetes insipidus. Urine osmolality is therefore likely to be low. You cannot say that she has a hyperchloraemic acidosis as you do not have her bicarbonate concentration but if you assume that the anion gap would be normal, that is 10-12, then this would suggest that the bicarbonate is elevated, suggesting either a metabolic alkalosis or respiratory acidosis with compensation. Although restoration of normal volume and osmolality is required, giving 5% dextrose may exacerbate any cerebral oedema and so correction should be gradual. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 53, Pg: 345

text: A patient has marked dizziness and unsteadiness during walking. On examination, he has a left sided Horner's syndrome and left sided ataxia. There is loss of sensation to pinprick on the right side. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.B: Right posterior inferior cerebellar artery occlusion

expl: The question describes the typical presentation of Lateral Medullary Syndrome Embolic occlusion or thrombosis of a V4 segment causes ischemia of the lateral medulla. The constellation of vertigo, numbness of the ipsilateral face and contralateral limbs, diplopia, hoarseness, dysarthria, dysphagia, and ipsilateral Horner's syndrome is called the lateral medullary (or Wallenberg's) syndrome. Ipsilateral upper motor neuron facial weakness can also occur. Most cases result from ipsilateral vertebral artery occlusion; in the remainder, PICA occlusion is responsible. Occlusion of the medullary penetrating branches of the vertebral artery or PICA results in partial syndromes. Hemiparesis is not a typical feature of vertebral artery occlusion; however, quadriparesis may result from occlusion of the anterior spinal artery. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 426, Pg: 3330

text: Infarctions secondary to low flow in the "watershed" between the distal PCA and MCA territories, as occurs after cardiac arrest is seen in which of the following?
expl: Bilateral visual association area lesions may result in Balint’s syndrome, a disorder of the orderly visual scanning of the environment, usually resulting from infarctions secondary to low flow in the “watershed” between the distal PCA and MCA territories, as occurs after cardiac arrest. Patients may experience persistence of a visual image for several minutes despite gazing at another scene (palinopsia) or an inability to synthesize the whole of an image (asimultagnosia). Anton’s syndrome occurs due to bilateral occlusion of distal posterior cerebral arteries. It produces cortical blindness (blindness with preserved pupillary light reaction). The patient is often unaware of the blindness or may even deny it. Wallenberg’s syndrome is lateral medullary syndrome which occurs due to occlusion of vertebral arteries. It results in acute onset ataxia, dizziness, Horner's syndrome and contralateral sensory loss. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Chapter:426 page number:3329

text: A 22-year-old is noted to have persistent polyuria in excess of 6 liters per day. She mentions recently being involved in an accident and sustained head injury which she thinks she has recovered from. Investigations reveal: potassium 4.2 mmol/l calcium 8.6 mg/dl glucose 106 mg/dl Serum osmolality : 290 mOsm/kg (280-295) Urine osmolality : 192 mOsm/kg Which one of the following is the best way of confirming the diagnosis?

options.D: Therapeutic trial of low dose DDAVP

expl: The diagnosis is likely to be diabetes insipidus . The causes for polyuria in a patient include primary polydipsia, central DI and Nephrogenic DI Diagnosis of DI in a patient with polyuria (urine output more than 50 ml/kg) is suggested by high plasma osmolality (>295 mOsm/kg) in a patient passing dilute urine ( urine osmolality If the diagnostic thresholds of DI are not met, DI can be confirmed by a water deprivation test where failure of urine concentration would be expected. During this test a patient is not allowed to drink and plasma ADH, plasma osmolality and urine osmolality are measured. A therapeutic trial of DDAVP is only appropriate if a diagnosis of DI is confirmed (On the water deprivation test) and helps to differentiate between cranial or nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. text: A 33-year-old woman is evaluated in the endocrinology clinic for increased urine output. She weighs 60 kg and has a 24-hour urine output of 3500 ml. Her basal urine osmolality is 210 mOsm/kg. She undergoes a fluid deprivation test and her urine osmolality after fluid deprivation (loss of weight 3 kg) is 350 mOsm/kg. A subsequent injection of subcutaneous DDAVP (desmopressin acetate) did not result in a further significant rise of urine osmolality after 2 hours (355 mOsm/kg). Which of the following is the likely diagnosis?
expl: Diabetes insipidus (DI) is suspected when the urine output is > 50 ml/kg per day . If the basal urine osmolality is > 300 mOsm/kg, it suggests an osmotic diuresis (due to glucose / mannitol). If fluid deprivation causes a urine osmolality > 300 mOsm/kg, it suggests psychogenic (primary) polydipsia as in this patient. If not, it is either pituitary or nephrogenic DI. These are differentiated by the administration of subcutaneous DDAVP which causes an increased urine osmolality > 300 mOsm/kg in pituitary DI. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 2921-22

text: A 28-year-old woman presenting with polyuria is found to have diabetes insipidus. Which part of the nephron is most affected in this condition?
expl: Fine-tuning of salt and water balance is achieved in the distal and collecting tubules under the influence of aldosterone and antidiuretic hormone (ADH). ADH, however, plays a central role in urinary concentration by increasing the water permeability of the normally impermeable cortical and medullary collecting tubules. In the absence of ADH, little water is reabsorbed in the collecting tubules and dilute urine is excreted. ADH mediated water reabsorption from the collecting tubules is facilitated via aquaporin 2 channels on the luminal surface. Around 15-20% of renal water reabsorption is ADH mediated. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 2919

text: A patient presented with nystagmus, ataxia and dysdiadokinesia. Identify the artery involved
expl: The symptoms of nystagmus, ataxia, and dysdiadochokinesia suggest involvement of the cerebellum or its connections. The blood supply to the cerebellum is primarily from the branches of the vertebrobasilar system, which includes the posterior cerebral artery (PCA) and branches from the basilar artery, such as the superior cerebellar artery (SCA), anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA), and posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA). Among the options given, the posterior cerebral artery (PCA) is part of this system and can be involved in cerebellar pathology.

text: Which of the following is seen in encephalitic rabies?
expl: Rabies encephalitis is distinguished by early brainstem involvement, which results in the classic features of hydrophobia (involuntary, painful contraction of the diaphragm and accessory respiratory, laryngeal, and pharyngeal muscles in response to swallowing liquids) and aerophobia (the same features causedby stimulation from a draft of air). These symptoms are probably due to dysfunction of infected brainstem neurons that normally inhibit inspiratory neurons near the nucleus ambiguus, resulting in exaggerated defense reflexes that protect the respiratory tract. The combination of hypersalivation and pharyngeal dysfunction is also responsible for the classic appearance of "foaming at the mouth". Brainstem dysfunction progresses rapidly, and coma-followed within days by death-is the rule unless the course is prolonged by supportive measures. With such measures, late complications can include cardiac and/or respiratory failure, disturbances of water balance (syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion or diabetes insipidus), noncardiogenic pulmonary edema, and gastrointestinal hemorrhage. Cardiac arrhythmias may be due to dysfunction affecting vital centers in the brainstem or to myocarditis. Multiple-organ failure is common in patients treated aggressively in critical care units. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 208, Pg: 1621

text: A patient came to medical OPD with complaints of polyuria. He has a history of undergoing total hypophysectomy. His Na+ levels were found to be 155 mEq/L, and his urine osmolarity was 200 mOsm/L. What is the definitive management in this patient?

options.A: DDAVP for 2 weeks and then discontinue
options.C: Upsetting of receptors, so no treatment required

expl: Explanation: Lifelong desmopressin (DDAVP) is the definitive treatment for central diabetes insipidus following total hypophysectomy. This patient has central diabetes insipidus (DI), a condition resulting from decreased vasopressin (ADH) secretion due to complete removal of the pituitary gland. Clinical features include polyuria, hypernatremia (Na⁺ = 155 mEq/L), and low urine osmolality (200 mOsm/kg), all indicating impaired water reabsorption. The definitive treatment is lifelong DDAVP (desmopressin), a synthetic ADH analog that restores water retention and corrects electrolyte imbalance. Explanation of other options: DDAVP for 2 weeks and then discontinue (Option A): Inappropriate, as hypophysectomy causes permanent ADH deficiency. Upsetting of receptors, so no treatment required (Option C): Incorrect; central DI involves hormone deficiency, not receptor issues. Thiazides for 2 weeks (Option D): Used in nephrogenic DI, not effective in central DI where ADH is lacking. Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK470458/

There are 4 types of DI Central DI: Due to primary deficiency of vasopressin secretion by the neurohypopysis. Primary polydipsia: Excessive water drinking leads to suppression of vasopressin. Gestational diabetes insipidus: Due to the excessive degradation of vasopressin by an aminopeptidase produced by the placenta. Nephrogenic DI: is due to the renal insensitivity to the action to AVP. It can be either acquired, due to drugs like LI or due to inherited mutations in the V2 genes. The most common type is inherited as a semi recessive X linked manner. There are AD and AR forms too.

text: Which of the following is the vasopressor of choice in patients with septic shock?
expl: In patients with distributive shock, the primary action used to mitigate the shock is to increase the systemic vascular resistance. Norepinephrine is the first choice vasopressor. It has potent action at alpha1 and beta1 adrenergic receptors. The alpha1 causes vasoconstriction while beta1 has positive inotropic and chronotropic effects. Option B: At high doses, epinephrine has a similar profile (at lower doses the β effects predominate), but is associated with tachyarrhythmia , myocardial ischemia , decreased splanchnic blood flow, pulmonary hypertension, and acidosis. Option C: Vasopressin is safe and has a role as a second agent for hypotension in septic shock. Option D: Dopamine does not have a role as a first line agent in distributive shock. Reference: Harrison 20 th chap 296 pg. 2044

text: Which of the following best explains the development of hyponatremia in a hypovolemic patient with diarrhea?

options.A: Decreased reabsorption of sodium from kidney
options.D: Decreased sodium absorption from the intestine

expl: Explanation: In a hypovolemic patient with diarrhea , significant loss of sodium and water occurs through the gastrointestinal tract. To maintain blood pressure and perfusion, the body triggers a non-osmotic release of ADH , which causes the kidneys to retain free water . This dilutes the serum sodium , leading to hyponatremia . The key mechanism here is water retention without equivalent sodium , resulting from volume depletion rather than hypo-osmolality . Mechanism of Hyponatremia in Hypovolemia Explanation for other Options: Decreased reabsorption of sodium from kidney (Option A): volume depletion stimulates sodium reabsorption in the kidneys via activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) . The kidneys conserve sodium, not waste it, in hypovolemia. Decreased secretion of aldosterone (Option B): Hypovolemia causes increased aldosterone secretion , which enhances sodium and water reabsorption in the distal nephron to restore intravascular volume. Decreased sodium absorption from the intestine (Option D): While diarrhea causes sodium loss , the resulting hyponatremia is not due to impaired absorption , but due to free water retention via ADH . Sodium loss alone does not explain the drop in serum sodium concentration unless accompanied by water retention . Key takeaway: Summary of Stimuli affecting Vasopressin Secretion

text: Below image shows Vasopressin and the regulation of water permeability in the renal collecting duct. AT which receptor vasopressin act?
expl: Vasopressin binds to the type 2 vasopressin receptor (V2R) on the basolateral membrane of principal cells, activates adenylyl cyclase (AC), increases intracellular cyclic adenosine monophosphatase (cAMP), and stimulates protein kinase A (PKA) activity. Cytoplasmic vesicles carrying aquaporin-2 (AQP) water channel proteins are inserted into the luminal membrane in response to vasopressin, thereby increasing the water permeability of this membrane. When vasopressin stimulation ends, water channels are retrieved by an endocytic process and water permeability returns to its low basal rate. The AQP3 and AQP4 water channels are expressed on the basolateral membrane and complete the transcellular pathway for water reabsorption. pAQP2, phosphorylated aquaporin-2. Reference: Harrisons Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:53 Pg: 339

text: A patient presented with acute chest pain radiating to the left shoulder. An ECG was performed which showed ST elevations in leads II, III, and aVF. What is the probable diagnosis?
expl: Explanation ST elevation in leads II, III, and aVF is diagnostic of an Inferior wall Myocardial Infarction . These leads correspond to the inferior wall of the left ventricle , which is usually supplied by the right coronary artery (RCA) (occasionally the left circumflex artery). Clinical features often include chest pain , radiation to left shoulder/jaw , bradyarrhythmias , or hypotension due to RCA involvement affecting the SA/AV nodes. Explanation of Incorrect Options Lateral wall MI (Option B): ST elevation occurs in leads I, aVL, V5, and V6 , not in II, III, aVF. Usually supplied by the left circumflex artery . Anterior wall MI (Option C): ST elevation is seen in precordial leads V1-V4 , indicating LAD artery involvement. Not the pattern described in this case. Posterior wall MI (Option D): Characterized by ST depression in V1-V3 with tall R waves, or reciprocal ST elevation in posterior leads V7-V9 . Not consistent with ST elevation in II, III, aVF.

text: A 54 year old man presents with speech difficulty. He has difficulty with word identification and repetition. He is able to pick out correct objects when instructed to do so and is not confused. Where is the lesion?
expl: This patient is definitely having an aphasia, since he has difficulty in word identification(anomia). his comprehension is normal hence is Wenicke’s area is normal. So he is likely suffering from Broca’s Aphasia. A patient with Wernicke’s Aphasia may look confused to the examiner because of the neologisms and increased word output. Repetition will be lost in all aphasias except, transcortical motor aphasia, transcortical sensory aphasia, pure anomia and pure alexia. Broca's Area (Inferior frontal lobe) damage causes impaired fluency, intact comprehension, impaired repetition [expressive dysphasia]. Wernicke's Area (posterior, superior temporal lobe) damage causes normal fluency, impaired comprehension, impaired repetition [receptive dysphasia]. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Chapter: 30, page number:196
