text: All of the following are the cause of NDI (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus), except?
expl: Hypercalcemia can also cause polyuria and NDI; calcium signals directly through the calcium-sensing receptor to downregulate Na+, K+, and Cl– transport by the TALH and water transport in principal cells, thus reducing renal concentrating ability in hypercalcemia. Another common acquired cause of NDI is hypokalemia, which inhibits the renal response to AVP and downregulates aquaporin-2 expression. Several drugs can cause acquired NDI, in particular lithium, Ifosfamide , and several antiviral agents. Lithium causes NDI by multiple mechanisms, including direct inhibition of renal glycogen synthase kinase-3 (GSK3), a kinase thought to be the pharmacologic target of lithium in bipolar disease; GSK3 is required for the response of principal cells to AVP Thiazides may reduce polyuria due to NDI, ostensibly by inducing hypovolemia and increasing proximal tubular water reabsorption. Occasionally, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) have been used to treat polyuria associated with NDI, reducing the negative effect of intrarenal prostaglandins on urinary concentrating mechanisms; however, this assumes the risks of NSAID-associated gastric and/or renal toxicity. Reference: Harrisons Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:381 Pg: 2920

expl: The presence of low back ache with morning stiffness in indicative of an inflammatory low back ache. The features of inflammatory back ache includes: Age of onset Morning stiffness of > 30 minutes Improvement with exercise No improvement with rest Pain during the second half of night which improves up on awakening Alternating buttock pain Axial spondyloarthritis are a common cause of inflammatory back ache in young patients and among the given options the test used in diagnosing an axial spondyloarthritis is Sacroiliac tenderness. Others include stretching of the Sacroiliac joint- FABER (Flexion abduction and external rotation) test or the Patrick test. Tenderness in the posterior spinous process of the vertebrae. text: A 25 year old man was noted by ophthalmologists to have a posterior uveitis requiring high dose immunosuppression. He has a history of recurrent mouth ulcers and painful ulcers on the scrotum.What is the likely diagnosis?
expl: Behcet's syndrome is classically characterized as a triad of symptoms that include recurring crops of mouth ulcers (called apthous ulcers), genital ulcers, and uveitis. The ulcers are usually painful. Typical eye involvement is bilateral pan uveitis. In addition, iritis, retinal vessel occlusions and optic neuritis can be found. Hypopyon uveitis is a rare manifestation. The arthritis of Behcet's disease is usually intermittent, self-limited, not deforming and localized to the knees and ankles. Oral ulceration in Behcet's disease Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Ch:364 Pg:2817

text: A 58-year-old diabetic man presents with septic shock. He is febrile, tachycardic, and has a blood pressure of 80/50 mmHg, despite adequate fluid resuscitation with crystalloids. His urine output is low and he is drowsy. What is the next best step in management?
expl: Explanation: Norepinephrine is the preferred first-line vasopressor for treating hypotension in septic shock , and should be initiated after fluid resuscitation if blood pressure remains low. Sepsis is defined as a life-threatening condition caused by a dysregulated immune response to infection , resulting in organ dysfunction .It is clinically diagnosed when there is suspected or confirmed infection along with an increase of 2 or more points in the SOFA (Sequential Organ Failure Assessment) score . Septic shock is a more severe subset, characterized by: The need for vasopressors to maintain a mean arterial pressure (MAP) ≥ 65 mmHg A serum lactate level > 2 mmol/L , despite adequate fluid resuscitation Initial Management Approach: Antibiotic Therapy: Broad-spectrum antibiotics should be administered within the first hour of recognition. Blood cultures must be obtained prior to antibiotic administration , if possible, but treatment should not be delayed. Fluid Resuscitation: Crystalloids (e.g., normal saline or lactated Ringer’s) should be administered at a dose of 30 mL/kg within the first 3 hours . The goal is to restore tissue perfusion and prevent progression of organ dysfunction. Vasopressors: If hypotension persists despite fluids, norepinephrine is the vasopressor of choice . The target MAP is 65 mmHg , and arterial line monitoring is recommended for accurate pressure measurement. Additional Considerations in Sepsis Management: Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS): In sepsis-associated ARDS, mechanical ventilation with low tidal volume (6 mL/kg) and high PEEP settings is advised to minimize ventilator-induced lung injury. Supportive Care Measures: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis unless contraindicated Stress ulcer prevention using proton pump inhibitors or H2 blockers Tight glucose control to avoid both hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia Renal replacement therapy (RRT) when indicated in patients with acute kidney injury (AKI) Dopamine is no longer preferred in the management of septic shock because it has a higher risk of causing arrhythmias and provides less consistent effects on blood pressure compared to norepinephrine. It may be considered in rare cases with bradycardia , but it is not the best choice for this patient. Explanations for other Options: Administer dopamine (Option A): Dopamine is no longer preferred in the management of septic shock because it has a higher risk of causing arrhythmias and provides less consistent effects on blood pressure compared to norepinephrine. It may be considered in rare cases with bradycardia , but it is not the best choice for this patient. Administer hydrocortisone (Option C): Hydrocortisone is used only in patients with septic shock who do not respond to both fluids and vasopressors , i.e., refractory shock . Since this patient has not yet received vasopressors , starting hydrocortisone at this point would be premature. Administer vasopressin (Option D): Vasopressin is used as a second-line vasopressor and is usually added to norepinephrine when blood pressure is still not maintained with norepinephrine alone. It is not recommended as an initial vasopressor , so it is not the next best step in this case. Key takeaway: SOFA SCORE

ansText: High ADH, high aldosterone, high renin
expl: In the setting of long-standing urinary tract obstruction, as evidenced by the severity of uraemia and thin cortices, the ability of the kidney to concentrate urine becomes severely impaired, resulting in partial nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Much of the polyuria that occurs after urinary tract obstruction is relieved is an appropriate attempt by the kidneys to deal with salt and water overload. However, a rise in serum osmolality to > 300 mOsm/l, as in this case, in the presence of a low urine osmolality indicates that the polyuria is pathological. The ability of the kidney to conserve Na+ is also impaired, as the patient becomes clinically volume-depleted. Therefore, one can infer that there is severe distal tubular damage with effective unresponsiveness to both ADH and aldosterone. Hypovolaemia is a potent stimulus for renin production from the juxtaglomerular apparatus and hypernatraemia is a potent stimulus for ADH production from the posterior pituitary. As there is nothing in this case to suggest adrenal disease, secondary hyperaldosteronism would be present. Obviously, this situation should never be allowed to occur in practice. A reasonable approach in postobstructive diuresis is to replace half the volume of urine with 0.45% saline or alternating dextrose 5% and normal saline, with frequent assessment of fluid status. Replacing urine ml for ml or even 'output minus 30 ml/h', prolongs the duration of diuresis. Reference: Harrison's principles of internal medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 319, Pg: 2376.

text: In a hypothyroid patient becoming pregnant, dose of levothyroxine should be?
expl: The dose of levothyroxine may need to be increased by 30-45% during pregnancy and returned to previous levels after delivery Five factors alter thyroid function in pregnancy : The transient increase in hCG during the first trimester, which weakly stimulates the TSH-R; The estrogen-induced rise in TBG during the first trimester, which is sustained during pregnancy Alterations in the immune system, leading to the onset, exacerbation, or amelioration of an underlying autoimmune thyroid disease; Increased thyroid hormone metabolism by the placental type III deiodinase; and Increased urinary iodide excretion, which can cause impaired thyroidhormone production in areas of marginal iodine sufficiency. The World Health Organizationrecommends a daily iodine intake of 250 μg during pregnancy and lactation, and prenatal vitamins should contain 150 μg per tablet. text: Calcitonin is a marker of which of the following malignancies?
expl: Explanation: Medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) originates from parafollicular C-cells of the thyroid, and calcitonin produced by these cells serves as a precise tumour marker for its diagnosis and follow-up. Explanations of other options: Papillary thyroid cancer (Option A): Papillary thyroid carcinoma develops from the thyroid's follicular epithelial cells rather than the parafollicular C-cells, and its follow-up is generally done with thyroglobulin measurement instead of calcitonin levels. Follicular thyroid cancer (Option B): Like papillary thyroid carcinoma, follicular thyroid carcinoma originates from the thyroid follicular cells and typically does not cause raised calcitonin levels. Thyroglobulin serves as the preferred tumour marker for its follow-up. Anaplastic thyroid cancer (Option D): Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma is a rare, highly aggressive thyroid malignancy that does not cause an increase in calcitonin levels. It develops from thyroid follicular cells, much like papillary and follicular thyroid cancers.

text: E cadherin gene deficiency is seen in -
expl: The majority of gastric cancers are not hereditary, the mutations identified in familial gastric cancer have provided important insights into mechanism of carcinogenesis in sporadic cancers. Germline mutations in CDHI, which encodes E cadherin, a protein that contributes to epithelial intercellular adhesion are associated with familial gastric cancers, which are usually of diffuse type. Mutations in CDH 1 are present in about 50% of sporadic cases of diffuse gastric cancers, while E cadherin expression is drastically decreased in the rest, often by methylation of the CDH I promotor. Lobular carcinoma of breast which also tends to infilterate as single cells, & individuals with BRCA2 mutations are at increased risk of developing diffuse gastric cancers.

text: An 18-week pregnant woman presents to hospital with failure to gain weight, hyperemesis and persistent tachycardia. She is found to be thyrotoxic. Which of the following is the best management step?
expl: The aim of treatment of thyrotoxicosis in pregnancy is the alleviation of symptoms and normalisation of tests in the shortest time. Both propylthiouracil and carbimazole are effective in controlling disease in pregnancy. The use of radioiodine is contraindicated in pregnancy. Surgery is rarely performed during pregnancy and is reserved for patients who do not respond to antithyroid drugs. A block and replace regime should not be used as this will result in fetal hypothyroidism. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 20 th edition Ch:377 Pg:2706-07

text: What would be the most suitable course of action for managing a 65-year-old male who presented with symptoms of weakness, lethargy, excessive cold intolerance, and slow ankle jerk? His thyroid function test (TFT) revealed a TSH level of 16 Mu/L (normal range: 0.4 - 4.0 mu / l), T4 level of 0.3 ng/dl (normal range: 0.6 - 1.6 ng / dl), and T3 level of 70 pg /dl.

options.A: Start levothyroxine at 100 micrograms and decrease the dose gradually
options.B: Start levothyroxine at 25 micrograms and increase the dose gradually
options.C: Start levothyroxine at 25 micrograms and decrease the dose gradually
options.D: Give T3 and T4 drugs simultaneously

ansText: Start levothyroxine at 25 micrograms and increase the dose gradually
expl: Explanation: The patient has overt primary hypothyroidism (high TSH, low T4/T3). In an older adult , it is crucial to start with a low dose of levothyroxine (e.g., 25 mcg/day) and titrate upwards gradually every 4-6 weeks based on TSH levels. This cautious approach prevents precipitating adverse cardiac effects like angina or arrhythmias, which can occur with rapid hormone replacement. Thyroid Function Test : TSH (Thyroid Stimulating Hormone) Normal range: 0.4-4.0 mIU/L Interpretation of Results: Treatment of hypothyroidism: Levothyroxine -6 µg/kg to be started Available as 25 µg / 50 µg / 88 µg / 100 µg If the dose is >100µg, it increases O2 consumption resulting in angina. Hence, careful titration of dose increments should be done. Explanation of other options: Start levothyroxine at 100 micrograms and decrease the dose gradually (Option A): A full replacement dose is too aggressive for initial therapy in an elderly patient and carries a high risk of cardiac complications. Start levothyroxine at 25 micrograms and decrease the dose gradually (Option C): The dose should be increased, not decreased, to reach a euthyroid state. Give T3 and T4 drugs simultaneously (Option D): Combination therapy is not first-line and is generally reserved for special circumstances under specialist care. Key Takeaways: Levothyroxine is the treatment for hypothyroidism. In elderly patients or those with known cardiac disease, "start low and go slow" is the guiding principle for initiation and titration.

text: T4 to T3 conversion may be impaired by?

text: A 37-year-old woman comes to you for consultation . She has experienced cold intolerance, weakness and constipation for 3 months. Her menses are regular but scanty. Her history is significant for hypertension and peptic ulcer disease. The patient is married but has never been pregnant and takes cimetidine 400 mg at bedtime, sustained-release nifedipine 60 mg daily and docusate sodium 100 mg three times a day. Her pulse is 58 beats/minute with a blood pressure of 135/90 mm Hg; Labs show a normal CBC, free thyroxine (T4) is 6.4 pmol/l (normal range, 10-22 pmol/l) and thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) is 1.5 mIU (normal range, 0.3-5.0 mIU). Which of the following is most likely to confirm the underlying cause?
expl: This patient has central hypothyroidism and should be evaluated for pituitary and end organ function as well as the presence of a pituitary tumor. The prolactin level should be measured and the pituitary adrenal, gonadal and growth hormone axes assessed. It is important to note that TSH may be either normal or low in central hypothyroidism The presence of a pituitary tumor can be determined by imaging the pituitary gland with MRI or computed tomography (CT) scan. Presence of pituitary tumor should also prompt evaluation for other anterior pituitary hormone status. Where appropriate, this should be followed by evaluation of the visual fields. Treatment of choice for most pituitary adenomas is trans sphenoidal resection, although microprolactinoma may be managed successfully with dopamine agonist therapy. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 2898

text: A 32-year-old woman presents to her GP with a history of amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea. She is keen to become pregnant and has been trying for 12 months to conceive without success. She is of normal weight and has no other constitutional symptoms. Which of the following is most likely to be the reason for her symptoms?
expl: Her symptoms are consistent with hyper-prolactinaemia . Raised prolactin has many causes including pituitary tumors (micro- and macroadenomas), drug treatment (some antidepressants like tricyclic antidepressants, antiemetics and cimetidine), pregnancy, stress, hypothyroidism (because thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) stimulates TSH and prolactin in primary hypothyroidism) and renal failure (prolactin accumulates in renal failure but not in hepatic impairment). While hyperprolactinemia can be present in hypothyroidism, it is usually associated with menorrhagia rather than amenorrhoea. Polycystic ovarian syndrome may be associated with amenorrhea and mildly raised prolactin levels, but unlikely to result in galactorrhea. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 2909

text: A 55-year-old man presents to the Emergency department with altered consciousness, his blood pressure is 80/50 mmHg, his skin is pigmented and he has a past history of Hashimoto's thyroiditis. His family say he has been tired for several months and has been losing weight and complaining of abdominal pain. Which of the following results is most likely to be found on investigation?
expl: The clinical picture is suggestive of Addison's disease with hypotension, pigmentation and a prodromal period with symptoms in keeping with glucocorticoid deficiency in a man with a history of another autoimmune endocrine disorder. Addison's disease refers to adrenal insufficiency due to an adrenal ethology (primary adrenal insufficiency) The most common cause for Addison disease worldwide is autoimmune adrenalitis while Tuberculosis is the most likely cause in India. Hypoglycemia, hyponatraemia, hyperkalemia, hypotension and an elevated urea are all present during a hypoadrenal crisis due to steroid deficiency and subsequent salt and water loss. Lymphocytosis along with eosinophilia are seen in acute adrenal insufficiency. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 2972

text: A person living in an iodine deficient area developed hyperthyroidism after taking iodine supplementation. Which phenomenon explains this?
expl: Explanation: The Jod-Basedow phenomenon describes the occurrence of iodine-induced hyperthyroidism , particularly in individuals with preexisting thyroid abnormalities such as multinodular goitre . When a person who has been iodine-deficient is suddenly exposed to high levels of iodine -either through dietary supplements or iodinated contrast media -the thyroid may begin producing excessive amounts of hormones, leading to thyrotoxicosis . This happens because autonomous thyroid tissue or nodules in these individuals function independently of pituitary feedback regulation . In contrast, individuals with a healthy thyroid typically do not experience this effect. Explanations for other Options: Wolff-Chaikoff effect (Option A): The Wolff-Chaikoff effect is the opposite of the Jod-Basedow effect. It describes a temporary suppression of thyroid hormone production in response to excess iodine . This is a protective autoregulatory mechanism to prevent hyperthyroidism, especially in people with a normal thyroid. However, this effect can "escape" after a few days, allowing hormone synthesis to resume. Goitre (Option C): A goitre is an enlargement of the thyroid gland , commonly caused by iodine deficiency , autoimmune disease, or nodular disease. While goitre can be seen in iodine deficiency, it does not explain the development of hyperthyroidism after iodine supplementation . It is more of a structural change , not a functional effect like the Jod-Basedow phenomenon. Medullary thyroid cancer (Option D): Medullary thyroid cancer (MTC) is a neuroendocrine tumor arising from parafollicular C cells of the thyroid that produce calcitonin , not thyroid hormones. It does not cause hyperthyroidism , and it is not related to iodine intake .

text: A patient presents with lethargy, increased sleep, and weight gain. Lab values show low plasma TSH, low T3, and low T4. After TRH administration, TSH levels increase. Which condition is likely?

options.A: Hyperthyroidism due to disease in the pituitary
options.B: Hypothyroidism due to disease in the pituitary
options.C: Hypothyroidism due to disease in the hypothalamus
options.D: Hyperthyroidism due to disease in the hypothalamus

ansText: Hypothyroidism due to disease in the hypothalamus
expl: Explanation: The lab profile (low T3, T4) confirms hypothyroidism (Option A and D ruled out) . The key to localization is the TSH response to TRH. Low TSH with Low T4: Indicates a problem at the pituitary or hypothalamus (secondary/tertiary hypothyroidism), not the thyroid itself (which would have high TSH). Positive TRH Stimulation Test (Increase in TSH): This demonstrates that the pituitary gland is intact and capable of producing TSH when stimulated. Therefore, the defect lies "upstream" in the hypothalamus , which is failing to produce adequate TRH to stimulate the pituitary under normal conditions. This pattern is diagnostic of Tertiary Hypothyroidism due to hypothalamic disease. Clinical Features of Hypothyroidism: Fatigue, weakness and increased sleep Cold intolerance, Weight gain Dry, coarse skin, Hair loss Constipation Depression and cognitive impairment Menstrual irregularities and infertility Bradycardia Myxedema Hoarse voice Carpal tunnel syndrome, Slow reflexes Goiter, Anemia, Hypercholesterolemia Primary hypothyroidism is due to thyroid gland dysfunction causing low thyroid hormones, commonly from Hashimoto's thyroiditis, surgery, radiation, iodine deficiency, medications, or infiltrative diseases. Secondary hypothyroidism results from pituitary or hypothalamic dysfunction leading to insufficient TSH, caused by tumors, surgery, Sheehan's syndrome, trauma, or genetic/hypothalamic defects. Labs show high TSH in primary and low/normal TSH in secondary, with low free T3/T4 in both. (Option B ruled out) Clinically, both present with fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, dry skin, hair loss, bradycardia, constipation, and myxedema, while secondary may have other pituitary hormone deficiencies. Treatment is levothyroxine, guided by TSH in primary and by free T4 in secondary hypothyroidism. Interpretation of thyroid function tests: Key Takeaways: Low T4 + Low/Normal TSH + Positive TRH test = Hypothalamic (Tertiary) Hypothyroidism. Low T4 + Low/Normal TSH + Blunted TRH test = Pituitary (Secondary) Hypothyroidism.

text: Titration of doses of anti-thyroid drugs is best based on?
expl: Thyroid function tests and clinical manifestations are reviewed 4-6 weeks after starting treatment, and the dose is titrated based on unbound T4 levels. Most patients do not achieve euthyroidism until 6-8 weeks after treatment is initiated. TSH levels often remain suppressed for several months and therefore do not provide a sensitive index of treatment response. When TSH suppression is alleviated, TSH levels can also be used to monitor therapy. Though total T3 and T4 can also be used, free hormones would be the better option. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page:2931

text: You are asked to review a 58-year-old woman who presents with a slowly enlarging hard mass in the anterior neck. Thyroid ultrasound reveals infiltration of the mass to adjacent structures,and biopsy reveal dense fibrous change and no atypical cells. Free T4 is low and her TSH is markedly raised, consistent with hypothyroidism. Thyroid autoantibodies are negative. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis given this clinical picture?
expl: By the nature of its presentation, Riedel's thyroiditis is often confused with thyroid carcinoma especially the anaplastic variant. It is characterised by marked fibrous infiltration of the thyroid gland, the aetiology of this being as yet unidentified. Treatment is with thyroxine replacement. Hashimoto's thyroiditis is autoimmune in aetiology and is characterised by lymphocytic infiltration and the presence of antimicrosomal antibodies(anti TPO). Grave's disease is associated with thyroid-stimulating autoantibodies and hyperthyroidism. Thyroid ultrasound reveals infiltration but no discrete mass is identified, and biopsy reveal dense fibrous infiltration of the gland. If the patient presents with severe compressive symptoms like dysphagia and dyspnea, then glucocorticoid therapy is useful. Other immunomodulators like mycophenolate and tamoxifen have also been tried. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page:2944

text: A 44-year-old woman presents to the Emergency department with palpitations and shortness of breath. Recent thyroid function tests on the hospital computer reveal thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) of Which of the following findings would be most consistent with Grave's disease?

text: A 26-year-old woman is referred by her family doctor. She is 10 week's pregnant and complaining of anxiety and an inability to sleep. Total thyroxine (T4) is noted to be 160 nmol/l (normal 70-140) Free T4 is noted to be 27 pmol/l (normal 9-25) thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) 0.4 mU/l. Which of the following is the management of choice in this patient?

options.C: Observe and repeat thyroid function tests in 1 month
options.D: Start high dose carbimazole and thyroxine concomitantly

ansText: Observe and repeat thyroid function tests in 1 month
expl: Suppression of TSH is seen in the first trimester in around 10% women, small but transient rises in T3 and T4 are also seen, this is physiological and due to the thyroid-stimulating action of b-human chorionic gonadotrophin (b-HCG). Total T4 rises due to increases in thyroid-binding globulin and again is physiological. A 10-20% increase in thyroid mass also occurs. Physiological suppression of TSH is also seen in 4-5% of women in the second trimester. Maternal hyperthyroidism has an incidence of 0.2%, in women who are in remission from Grave's disease, exacerbation occurs most commonly in the first trimester. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page:2940

text: Which of the following statements about TPP (thyrotoxic periodic paralysis) is true?

options.A: It is caused by missense mutations of voltage sensor domains within the α1 subunit of L- type potassium channels
options.B: B TPP develops more frequently in patients of Asian or Hispanic origin
options.C: TPP typically present with weakness of the respiratory muscles with paralytic episodes that occur most frequently between 1 and 6 p.m
options.D: Hypokalemia is usually accompanied by hyperphosphatemia and hypermagnesemia

ansText: B TPP develops more frequently in patients of Asian or Hispanic origin
expl: Redistributive hypokalemia can also occur in the setting of hyperthyroidism, with periodic attacks of hypokalemic paralysis (thyrotoxic periodic paralysis [TPP]). Similar episodes of hypokalemic weakness in the absence of thyroid abnormalities occur in familial hypokalemic periodic paralysis , usually caused by missense mutations of voltage sensor domains within the α1 subunit of L-type calcium channels or the skeletal Na+ channel; these mutations generate an abnormal gating pore current activated by hyperpolarization. Thyrotoxic Periodic Paralysis Develops more frequently in patients of Asian or Hispanic origin linked to genetic variation in 6 , a muscle-specific, thyroid hormone-responsive K+ channel. Patients typically present with weakness of the extremities and limb girdles, with paralytic episodes that occur most frequently between 1 and 6 a.m. Signs and symptoms of hyperthyroidism are not invariably present. Hypokalemia is usually profound and almost invariably accompanied by hypophosphatemia and hypomagnesemia . The hypokalemia in TPP is also attributed to both direct and indirect activation of the Na+/K+-ATPase, resulting in increased uptake of K+ by muscle and other tissues. Increases in β-adrenergic activity play an important role in that high-dose propranolol (3 mg/kg) rapidly reverses the associated hypokalemia, hypophosphatemia, and paralysis. References: Harrisons Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:53 Pg: 348

text: Which is the antibody associated with Hashimoto's thyroiditis?
expl: Explanation: Hashimoto's thyroiditis is an autoimmune thyroid disease characterized by marked lymphocytic infiltration of the thyroid, follicular atrophy, and fibrosis . The disease is primarily mediated by T-cell-induced thyroid cell destruction , but autoantibodies serve as important clinical markers . The most relevant antibodies in Hashimoto's thyroiditis are: Anti-thyroid peroxidase (Anti-TPO) antibodies → most commonly present, clinically useful for diagnosis. Anti-thyroglobulin (Tg) antibodies → also present in many cases. (vs Option C) TSH-receptor blocking antibodies → seen in some patients, especially in thyroid atrophy, but less common. text: What would be the most appropriate next step in managing a 40-year-old female patient who is experiencing cold intolerance, dry skin, constipation, and has a slow ankle jerk on examination, with a TSH level of 15 IU/L and low T3 and T4 levels?

options.C: Order a thyroid radionuclide uptake and scan

expl: Explanation: The patient has a classic clinical presentation of hypothyroidism with confirmatory biochemical evidence: elevated TSH with low T3 and T4 . This confirms the diagnosis of primary hypothyroidism . The definitive and most appropriate next step is to initiate hormone replacement therapy with levothyroxine (LT4) . Clinical features of hypothyroidism include fatigue, weakness, and somnolence , along with cold intolerance, weight gain, dry coarse skin, hair loss, constipation, and depression or cognitive slowing . Patients may develop menstrual irregularities, infertility, bradycardia, hoarseness, and myxedema . Other findings include carpal tunnel syndrome, delayed reflexes, goiter, anemia, and hypercholesterolemia . Treatment of hypothyroidism Levothyroxine - 1.6 µg/kg to be started Available as 25 µg / 50 µg / 88 µg / 100 µg If the dose is >100µg, it increases O2 consumption resulting in angina. Hence, careful titration of dose increments should be done. Explanation of other options: Measure thyroxine binding globulin (TBG) (Option B): It is not indicated, as the free hormone levels are the relevant measurement, and the diagnosis is already clear. Order a thyroid radionuclide uptake and scan (Option C): Used to differentiate causes of hyperthyroidism (e.g., Graves' vs. thyroiditis), not hypothyroidism. Order thyroid ultrasonography (Option D): Useful for evaluating a palpable thyroid nodule or goiter, but it is not necessary to initiate treatment in a straightforward case of primary hypothyroidism. Key Takeaways: Primary hypothyroidism is diagnosed by an elevated TSH with low free T4. Levothyroxine is the standard treatment.

text: A 40-year-old woman presents with fatigue and weight gain. On examination, a diffuse, non-tender goiter is noted. Her blood test results are shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: This is a classic presentation of Hashimoto's thyroiditis , and all the provided data points support this diagnosis. Clinical Presentation: The symptoms of fatigue and weight gain, along with a non-tender goiter , are typical for hypothyroidism. Thyroid Function Tests: The lab results show a high TSH and a low Free T4 , which is the biochemical pattern for primary hypothyroidism . Autoantibodies: The positive Anti-thyroid peroxidase (Anti-TPO) antibodies are the hallmark of Hashimoto's thyroiditis, confirming an autoimmune etiology where the body is attacking its own thyroid gland. Explanation of Other Options: Pituitary failure (Option A): Pituitary failure causing hypothyroidism (secondary hypothyroidism) would present with a low or inappropriately normal TSH in the setting of a low Free T4, which is the opposite of what is shown. Graves' disease (Option B): Graves' disease is the most common cause of hyperthyroidism. It would show a suppressed (low) TSH and a high Free T4. Furthermore, the Anti-TSH receptor stimulating antibodies would be positive. De Quervain's thyroiditis (Option C): While De Quervain's (subacute) thyroiditis can have a hypothyroid phase, it is classically characterized by a painful, tender goiter and a markedly elevated ESR. The patient's goiter is non-tender and her ESR is normal. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Edition, Page Number-2933.

text: A 35-year-old female is referred to the endocrine clinic for review. She has been suffering intermittent tachycardias and panic attacks. There is no significant past medical history. She takes a number of vitamin and mineral supplements, including kelp (a source of Iodine). On examination there are no eye signs and no goitre. TSH is What is the most likely cause of her thyrotoxicosis?
expl: Kelp is a very rich source of iodine. In patients with pre-existing thyroid hyperplasia or adenoma, the ingestion of large amounts of iodine (Jod-Besedow phenomenon) may precipitate thyrotoxicosis. Treatment is withdrawal of the kelp with monitoring of thyroid function. Thyrotoxicosis affects 2% of women and 0.2% of men in their lifetimes. Grave's disease is responsible for around 80% of cases of thyrotoxicosis, toxic multinodular goitre is the next commonest cause. In this patient, TSH receptor antibodies are negative ruling out Grave's disease. Patients with Grave's disease may be offered radioiodine, if suitable, or a period of medical therapy with antithyroid drugs . Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page:2945

text: An 11-week pregnant woman presents to hospital with hyperemesis, tremors and persistent tachycardia. Her investigation reports are as follows: TSH: 0.01 mIU/L (0.5-4.5) T4: 19 mcg/dl (5-12) TSH receptor antibodies: positive. Which of the following is the best management step?
expl: The two major causes for thyrotoxicosis during pregnancy are Gestational thyrotoxicosis and Graves disease. Gestational thyrotoxicosis is due to the action of HCG on TSH receptor to increase thyroid hormone production. Excessive HCG elevation occur during hyperemesis, twin pregnancy and vesicular mole. It is usually self limiting and is managed conservatively without anti thyroid drugs. Grave's disease during pregnancy should be managed with anti thyroid drugs. During the first 16 weeks of pregnancy, propylthiouracil is the preferred ATD due to lesser risk of teratogeniciTy. After 16 weeks, therapy is switched to carbimaxole/Methimazole. The use of radioiodine is contraindicated in pregnancy. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition page 2940-42

expl: The combination of low thyroglobulin, decreased uptake on scintigraphy and raised T4 is suggestive of thyrotoxicosis factitia. text: A 54-year-old woman complaining of a 4-kg weight gain, dry hair and skin, she feels slow and always has the heating up high. She has a small diffuse goitre. Her TSH level is 20 mU/l . Thyroid peroxidase antibody is positive at high titres. She has two sisters who have had thyroid disease. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Hashimoto's thyroiditis is an autoimmune thyroid disorder found more often in women than men. It is associated with positive thyroid antibodies and there may be a goitre that tends to be diffuse rather than multinodular. The classical antibodies include anti thyroid peroxidase and anti thyroglobulin antibodies. The gland is infiltrated with lymphocytes and patients can become hypothyroid. DeQuervain's thyroiditis is not associated with positive antibodies and tends to present with painful goitre and thyrotoxicosis. Grave's disease is also an autoimmune thyroid disorder but patients have hyperthyroidism and not hypothyroidism. Follicular carcinoma can present with a thyroid swelling but not hypothyroidism. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Pg:2935

text: An 81-year-old woman is referred to the thyroid clinic with increasing size of a pre-existing goitre. She has had long-standing hypothyroidism due to Hashimotos thyroiditis and has been on a dose of thyroxine of 100 mg daily for many years. Which of the following primary thyroid cancers is she most likely to have?
expl: Primary thyroid lymphoma is strongly associated with lymphocytic thyroiditis (Hashimoto's disease), which is present in 80% of cases. It is predominantly a disease of elderly women. Up to 30% of patients have a history of goitre and may be taking thyroxine. Anaplastic thyroid cancer is commonly found in elderly patients and usually presents with a thyroid mass. It is usually rapidly progressive and has the worst prognosis of the thyroid cancers. Medullary thyroid cancer arises from within the ‘C' cells of the thyroid, cells which produce calcitonin. It is commonly associated with multiple endocrine neoplasia type-2 (MEN2). Follicular thyroid cancer is typically found in middle-aged to older individuals and usually presents as a solitary asymptomatic thyroid nodule. Eventually 20% of patients will develop distant metastases. Papillary thyroid cancer is most commonly found in the 30-50 age group but can occur at any age. It most commonly metastasise to the local lymph nodes within the neck. Prognosis is better than the other thyroid cancers. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition page 2952

text: A 66-year-old man presents with lethargy and weight loss. This has gradually occurred over the last 6 months. On examination, a small goitre is palpable. There is no evidence of eye signs or pretibial myxedema. Investigations reveal: Free T4 - 21.1 (9.8-23) pmol/l T3 - 5.3 (3.3-5.5) pmol/l TSH - 0.05 (0.1-5) mU/l Thyroid autoantibody titres are all negative A thyroid uptake scan showed focal uptake of radioisotope with suppressed uptake in rest of thyroid. What is the diagnosis?
expl: This patient has subclinical hyperthyroidism .(suppressed TSH with normal T3 and T4). Grave's disease is unlikely due to negative antithyroid antibodies. This is because the T4 and T3 levels are normal. However, the TSH is reduced, so the hyperthyroidism is subclinical. Toxic multinodular goiter or toxic nodule is more common in the elderly. Very recently, activating point mutations in the TSH receptor, which result in continuous thyroid stimulation, have been described in the solitary nodule. It can cause hyperthyroidism or subclinical hyperthyroidism. In patients with toxic multinodular goitre, the thyroid uptake scan (with radioactive iodine) usually reveal patchy uptake, with areas of both increased and decreased uptake. Patients with Grave's disease usually have homogeneous diffuse uptake. Patients with subacute thyroiditis have low uptake in thyroid scintiography. Sick Euthyroid syndrome is usually associated with critically ill patients. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page:2948

text: A 25-year-old male patient came with complaints of palpitations, sweating, and restlessness. He has a complaint of sweaty palms. Clinical findings are depicted in the image given below. What is the diagnostic finding seen in this patient?
expl: Explanation: Thyroid receptor antibodies (TRAb), especially thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI), are diagnostic of Graves' disease, which this patient exhibits. The patient's symptoms-palpitations, sweating, restlessness, and sweaty palms-are classic for hyperthyroidism. The most likely diagnosis is Graves' disease , an autoimmune disorder in which thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI) bind to and activate TSH receptors on the thyroid gland. This leads to increased production of T3 and T4, causing hyperthyroid symptoms. In Graves' ophthalmopathy , characteristic signs include: Dalrymple's sign: Upper lid retraction due to Muller's muscle contraction (most common presenting sign) Von Graefe's sign: Lid lag on downward gaze and stare due to poor blinking, often earliest sign Enroth's sign: Lower eyelid fullness/edema Mobius sign: Weak convergence Griffith's sign: Lower lid lag on upward gaze Stellwag's sign: Infrequent/incomplete blinking Joffroy's sign: Absent forehead wrinkling on upward gaze Gellineck's sign: Hyperpigmentation of the eyelids Diagnosis is confirmed by: Elevated TSI or TRAb levels Thyroid function tests showing elevated T3/T4 and suppressed TSH Radioactive iodine uptake (RAIU): Increased in Graves' Management includes: Antithyroid drugs (Methimazole or PTU) Radioactive iodine ablation Surgery for large goiters or resistant cases Graves' ophthalmopathy: Corticosteroids, radiotherapy, or orbital decompression in severe cases Explanation of other options: Anti-thyroglobulin antibody (Option A): Commonly elevated in autoimmune hypothyroidism like Hashimoto's, not specific for Graves'. Anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody (Option B): Typically seen in Hashimoto's thyroiditis. Elevated ultrasensitive thyrotropin (TSH) levels (Option D): TSH is suppressed in hyperthyroid states like Graves'- disease due to negative feedback. Reference: Pubmed https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK582134/table/article-142674.table0/ https://eyewiki.org/Thyroid_Eye_Disease#:~:text=Eyelid%20retraction%20(Dalrymple's%20sign)%20is,bilateral%20axial%20proptosis%20(exophthalmos)

expl: Thyroid hormones stimulate gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis in liver. It can enhance the glucose uptake into the muscle. It will also enhance the clearance of insulin from circulation. text: All of the following are causes of Hypokalemia, except?
expl: Insulin, β2 -adrenergic activity, thyroid hormone, and alkalosis promote Na+/K+-ATPase-mediated cellular uptake of K+, leading to hypokalemia. Inhibition of the passive efflux of K+ can also cause hypokalemia, albeit rarely; this typically occurs in the setting of systemic inhibition of K+ channels by toxic barium ions. Exogenous insulin can cause iatrogenic hypokalemia, particularly during the management of K+-deficient states such as diabetic ketoacidosis. Alternatively, the stimulation of endogenous insulin can provoke hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and/or hypophosphatemia in malnourished patients given a carbohydrate load. Alterations in the activity of the endogenous sympathetic nervous system can cause hypokalemia in several settings, including alcohol withdrawal, hyperthyroidism, acute myocardial infarction, and severe head injury. β2 agonists, including both bronchodilators and tocolytics (ritodrine), are powerful activators of cellular K+ uptake; 'hidden' sympathomimetics, such as pseudoephedrine and ephedrine in cough syrup or dieting agents, may also cause unexpected hypokalemia. Finally, xanthine dependent activation of cAMP-dependent signaling, downstream of the β2 receptor, can lead to hypokalemia, usually in the setting of overdose (theophylline) or marked over ingestion (dietary caffeine). Trimethoprim leads to hyperkalemia by inhibition of ENaC epithelial sodium channel. Reference: Harrisons Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:53 Pg: 348

text: A 36-year-old man with Grave's disease is being considered for subtotal thyroidectomy. What is the most common postoperative complication following this operation?
expl: Hypothyroidism occurs in about 10% of such patients within 1 year of surgery. This percentage increases with time and a high proportion of patients become hypothyroid in the long term. Laryngeal nerve palsy occurs in 1% of cases. Transient hypocalcaemia occurs in up to 10% of patients, but permanent hypoparathyroidism is seen in less than 1% of patients. Recurrent hyperthyroidism occurs in 1-3% of cases within 1 year and 1% per year thereafter. Early postoperative bleeding may cause tracheal compression. This is a rare complication. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page:2940-43

text: A 66 year old man is investigated for lower back pain. He also complains of weight loss and fevers. On reviewing his history, he has been told before that he has ankylosing spondylitis. expl: The symptoms of fevers, weight loss and lower back pain are classical for retroperitoneal fibrosis. text: A patient who has had a subtotal thyroidectomy for hyperthyroidism is on thyroxine replacement. She has a normal thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), normal tri-iodothyronine (T3) and low free thyroxine (T4) levels. What is the most likely reason for those results?

options.C: The patient's results are as expected - no change in treatment is required

ansText: The patient's results are as expected - no change in treatment is required
expl: Once on a full replacement dose, thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) levels should be checked at intervals of 1-3 years, depending on their stability. Fluctuating or elevated TSH levels in a previously stable patient, or thyroxine requirements in excess of 200 mg/day, usually indicate compliance problems. It is important to rule out malabsorption or abnormal thyroxine kinetics caused by drugs: cholestyramine, ferrous sulphate, lovastatin, aluminium hydroxide, rifampicin, amiodarone, carbamazepine, and phenytoin all alter the absorption or clearance of thyroxine. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 20 th edition Ch:377 Pg:2705-07

text: A 34-year-old man comes to the clinic complaining of tiredness, lethargy and an increasingly hoarse voice. He also tells you that he has been losing his hair over the past few months and has noticed fullness in his neck; he has gained 7kg in the past 3 months. On examination he has a puffy face and periorbital oedema and there is a firm, rubbery goitre. His pulse is 48/min and regular, his BP 142/73 mmHg. Investigations; TSH 70.1 U/l Total cholesterol 320 mg/dl Triglycerides 290 mg/dl LDL 150 mg/dl FNA thyroid Diffuse lymphocytic and plasma cell infiltration Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: The features seen here are typical of Hashimoto's thyroiditis. Hashimoto's thyroiditis is autoimmune in aetiology and is characterised by lymphocytic infiltration and the presence of antimicrosomal (TPO) antibodies. De Quervain's thyroiditis is a self-limiting inflammatory disease of the thyroid gland that presents with pain and sore throat. It is not associated with positive antibodies and tends to present with painful swelling in the neck. Atrophic hypothyroidism is an organ-specific autoimmune disease with thyroid autoantibodies, functional hypothyroidism and absence of goiter. Usually seen in elderly women between 40-60 age groups. Grave's disease is associated with thyroid-stimulating autoantibodies and hyperthyroidism. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition page 2935

text: A 32-year-old woman with relapsed Grave's disease. TSH is less than 0.05 mU/l, with a Free T4 of 32.5 pmol/l(9-20). She has severe bilateral thyroid eye disease with marked orbital oedema and proptosis. You are considering radiotherapy as she has failed drug treatment. Which of the following statements best fits the management of her thyroid eye disease?

options.A: Systemic steroids are of no value in managing the eye disease
options.B: Orbital irradiation is commonly used to treat thyroid eye disease
options.C: Corrective eye muscle surgery should now be considered
options.D: Her thyroid eye disease may be worsened by radioiodine treatment

ansText: Her thyroid eye disease may be worsened by radioiodine treatment
expl: Exacerbation of thyroid eye disease is more common after radioiodine treatment IV glucocorticoids are the mainstay in patients with severe inflammatory changes. Orbital irradiation should be reserved only for those not responding to steroids and other second line therapies. Corrective eye muscle surgery should be delayed until thyroid eye disease has been stable for at least 6 months, but may be of value in improving diplopia. text: A 60-year-old man presents with progressive numbness in both lower limbs. On examination: 1. Positive Romberg sign 2. Broad-based gait 3. Loss of proprioception in lower limbs He also reports low blood pressure, has a history of hypothyroidism, and underwent a gastrectomy for gastric carcinoma one year ago. Which nutritional deficiency most likely explains his current neurological findings?
expl: Explanation: This patient's presents with: Numbness Loss of vibration and proprioception Positive Romberg's test Broad-based (sensory) gait is characteristic of subacute combined degeneration (SACD) of the spinal cord, a neurological manifestation of Vitamin B12 deficiency . After total or partial gastrectomy, intrinsic factor (from parietal cells) is lost → impaired absorption of Vitamin B12 in the terminal ileum → progressive neurological and hematological dysfunction . Explanation of Other Options: Folic acid deficiency (Option B) can lead to megaloblastic anaemia Found in alcoholism, malnutrition, or drug therapy (methotrexate, phenytoin). Key difference: Folate deficiency → anemia only; no neuropathy . Thiamine deficiency (Option C) causes Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome Features: Confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and confabulation (memory loss). Common in chronic alcoholics or malnutrition, not post-gastrectomy . No sensory loss or Romberg's sign. Transferrin deficiency (Option D) would result in iron deficiency anaemia Presents with pallor, fatigue, and microcytosis. No neurological involvement or proprioceptive loss. text: In adrenal insufficiency, during fever, the dose of hydrocortisone should be?
expl: During periods of intercurrent illness (fever), the dose of hydrocortisone should be doubled. Dose may have to be tripled in severe fever and illness. Acute Adrenal Insufficiency treatment Acute adrenal insufficiency requires immediate initiation of rehydration , usually carried out by saline infusion at initial rates of 1 L/h with continuous cardiac monitoring . Glucocorticoid replacement should be initiated by bolus injection of 100 mg hydrocortisone, followed by the administration of 200 mg hydrocortisone over 24 h, preferably by continuous infusion or alternatively by bolus IV or IM injections. Mineralocorticoid replacement can be initiated once the daily hydrocortisone dose has been reduced to because at higher doses hydrocortisone provides sufficient stimulation of MRs. Glucocorticoid replacement for the treatment of chronic adrenal insufficiency should be administered at a dose that replaces the physiologic daily cortisol production, which is usually achieved by the oral administration of 15-25 mg hydrocortisone in two to three divided doses . Pregnancy may require an increase in hydrocortisone dose by 50% during the last trimester . In all patients, at least one-half of the daily dose should be administered in the morning. Mineralocorticoid replacement in primary adrenal insufficiency should be initiated at a dose of 100-150 μg fludrocortisone. The adequacy of treatment can be evaluated by measuring blood pressure, sitting and standing, to detect a postural drop indicative of hypovolemia. In addition, serum sodium, potassium, and plasma renin should be measured regularly. Renin levels should be kept in the upper normal reference range. In patients living or traveling in areas with hot or tropical weather conditions, the fludrocortisone dose should be increased by 50 100 μg during the summer. Mineralocorticoid dose may also need to be adjusted during pregnancy due to the antimineralocorticoid activity of progesterone Adrenal androgen replacement is an option in patients with lack of energy, despite optimized glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement, women with features of androgen deficiency Adrenal androgen replacement can be achieved by once-daily administration of 25-50 mg DHEA. Treatment is monitored by measurement of DHEAS, androstenedione, testosterone, and sexhormone binding globulin (SHBG) 24 h after the last DHEA dose. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 2972

text: Which of the following antihypertensive agents will not affect the aldosterone-renin ratio?

text: A 36-year-old woman presents with a 4-month history of anorexia and weight loss, excess pigmentation and dizziness on standing. Initial investigations reveal hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia.Which of the following tests will be most useful to confirm the diagnosis?

text: A patient with Addison's disease presents with an acute onset of diarrhea and vomiting. He currently takes fludrocortisone and hydrocortisone. What is the most appropriate management?
expl: Patients receiving glucocorticoid replacement therapy should be advised to double the dose in the event of intercurrent febrile illness, accident, or mental stress such as an important examination. If the patient is vomiting and cannot take by mouth, parenteral hydrocortisone must be given urgently, as indicated above. There is no need to increase fludrocortisone dose during stress / inter current illness For minor surgery, 50-100 mg of hydrocortisone IV is given with the premedication. text: A 26-year-old student has been recovering at home after a period of intensive care and general medical admission for meningococcal septicemia. 4 days after discharge from hospital she visits her treating doctor complaining of dizziness on standing and profound tiredness. On examination she looks tired and has postural hypotension. Blood testing reveals a sodium concentration of 121 mmol/l, potassium of 6.7 mmol/l and urea of 78 mg/dl and normal urinary sodium. She has mild normochromic, normocytic anemia. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
expl: Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome is bilateral adrenal hemorrhage occurring due to massive septicemia, often associated with severe, life-threatening meningococcal disease. It may present as in this patient with tiredness, lethargy and postural hypotension a short period after discharge from the precipitating illness. Classically, laboratory findings associated with adrenal insufficiency are hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, elevated urea, anemia, elevated ESR, eosinophilia and mild hypercalcaemia. The commonest cause of primary adrenal insufficiency in the western world is autoimmune disease (70%) TB is a common association in the developing world Emergency treatment of adrenal insufficiency involves fluid replacement, iv hydrocortisone and glucose supplementation, often even prior to determining the underlying cause. SIADH is less relevant as there is normal urine sodium and no relevant H/O trauma, underlying cause for SIADH. Infections causing primary adrenal insufficiency: Tuberculosis HIV CMV cryptococcosis histoplasmosis coccidioidomycosis Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 2971

text: A patient presents with complaints of easy fatiguability, anemia, hyperpigmentation over the knuckles, oral mucosa, palms, and hands, along with tachycardia. Blood pressure is recorded at 80/60 mmHg, and serum sodium is 130 mEq/L. What is the most probable diagnosis?
expl: Explanation of answer: The constellation of fatigue, anemia, hyperpigmentation, hypotension, and hyponatremia is typical of Addison's disease ( primary adrenal insufficiency ). Primary adrenal insufficiency , also known as Addison's disease , results from destruction or dysfunction of the adrenal cortex, leading to decreased production of glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids, and androgens. The most common causes include autoimmune adrenalitis (most common worldwide), tuberculosis (most common in India), fungal infections, HIV/AIDS, metastatic malignancies, or bilateral adrenalectomy. The clinical features stem from hormone deficiencies: Glucocorticoid deficiency causes: fatigue, weight loss, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea or constipation, postural hypotension, and hyponatremia (dilutional). Mineralocorticoid deficiency leads to hypotension, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia. Excess ACTH (due to lack of cortisol feedback) results in hyperpigmentation of sun-exposed areas, skin creases, and mucosa. Androgen deficiency in females may cause reduced body hair and libido. Investigations: Random cortisol: >500 nmol/L rules out adrenal insufficiency. Short ACTH stimulation test: If cortisol remains Plasma renin and aldosterone levels help detect mineralocorticoid deficiency. Autoimmune adrenal antibodies may be checked if autoimmune cause is suspected; CT/MRI may be used in antibody-negative cases. Treatment: Glucocorticoid replacement: Oral hydrocortisone is first-line; prednisolone or dexamethasone are alternatives. Mineralocorticoid replacement: Fludrocortisone corrects aldosterone deficiency. Explanation of other options: Conn's syndrome (Option A): Characterized by hyperaldosteronism, leading to hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis. Hyperpigmentation and hypotension are not features. Vitamin B12 deficiency (Option C): May present with fatigue and anemia, but does not explain hyperpigmentation, hypotension, or hyponatremia. Neurological symptoms like paresthesias and gait disturbances would typically be present. Cushing syndrome (Option D): Features include central obesity, moon face, purple striae, and hypertension due to cortisol excess. Hypotension and hyperpigmentation are generally not observed, making it unlikely here.

text: Addison's disease is characterized by all of the following symptoms except?
expl: Explanation: Addison's disease (primary adrenal insufficiency) is characterized by a deficiency of both cortisol and aldosterone. The symptoms listed are consequences of these hormonal deficits, making Hyperglycemia the exception . Pathophysiology of Symptoms Cortisol Deficiency: Leads to hypoglycemia (due to impaired gluconeogenesis), not hyperglycemia. It also contributes to weakness, weight loss, and hypotension. Aldosterone Deficiency: Causes renal sodium wasting ( hyponatremia ) and potassium retention ( hyperkalemia ). (Oprion B and D ruled out) Combined Effect: The loss of both hormones' permissive effects on vascular tone and volume contributes to hypotension . (Option D ruled out) ACTH excess causes Pigmentation Adrenal androgen insufficiency results in Decreased body hair and loss of libido, especially in females Key Takeaways: Addison's disease typically presents with hypoglycemia , hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hypotension. Hyperglycemia is suggestive of diabetes or Cushing's syndrome (cortisol excess).

text: A 44-year-old with a history of travel presented with fever, mild bloody diarrhea which had lasted for two weeks. He had lost 2.5 kg in weight, had occasional lower abdominal cramping discomfort and a painful swelling of his left knee. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Campylobacter infection is one of the commonest causes of inflammatory diarrhea. Abdominal pain is often a prominent feature of the illness frequently localizing to the right iliac fossa. Diarrhea may be mild or very severe often with passage of blood. Symptoms may last a week or longer. Reactive arthritis and Reiter's syndrome can develop following infection with a number of enteric pathogens including Shigella, Salmonella, Campylobacter and Yersinia. Amoebiasis : presents with a gradual onset of lower abdominal pain and mild diarrhea is followed by malaise, weight loss, and diffuse lower abdominal or back pain. Cecal involvement may mimic acute appendicitis. Patients with full-blown dysentery may pass 10-12 stools per day. The stools contain little fecal material and consist mainly of blood and mucus. In contrast to those with bacterial diarrhea, fewer than 40% of patients with amebic dysentery are febrile. Virtually all patients have heme-positive stools. Crohn's disease is a cause of chronic diarrhea which is in contrast to the case given Gonococcal sepsis will cause prominent constitutional features with a maculopapular rash and may complicate to cause adrenal insufficiency. text: In treatment of Cushing's disease, which of the following drugs is useful?
expl: In Cushing's disease, steroidogenic inhibitors are used in combination with pituitary irradiation to block the adrenal effects of persistently high ACTH levels. expl: Cushing syndrome is characterised by obesity with features of protein catabolism like abdominal striae, proximal myopathy, facial plethora and easy bruins ability The overnight dexamethasone suppression test is one of the preferred investigations to confirm the diagnosis of Cushing's syndrome Cushing's syndrome: investigations Investigations are divided into confirming Cushing's syndrome, labelling them as ACTH dependant and independent, followed by distinguishing the causes if ACTH dependent . Hypokalemic alkalosis is seen in severe cases of Cushing syndrome due to action of cortisol on mineralocorticoid receptor in renal tubules. text: In a 60-year-old man, what is the most common underlying cause of Cushing's disease?
expl: Explanation: In a 60-year-old man, Cushing's disease is usually the result of a pituitary microadenoma . Cushing's disease is defined by a benign pituitary tumor that secretes ACTH, causing hypercortisolism due to excess ACTH release. This overproduction drives the adrenal glands to secrete elevated amounts of cortisol, producing the typical manifestations of Cushing's syndrome. Explanations of other options: Small-cell lung cancer (Option A): Small cell lung carcinoma may secrete ACTH or ACTH-like peptides, leading to paraneoplastic Cushing's syndrome. However, it is not the usual cause of Cushing's disease in older individuals. This cancer often presents with respiratory complaints and a faster development of hypercortisolism signs. Adrenal tumor (Option B): Adrenal tumors, whether adenomas or carcinomas, may lead to Cushing's syndrome by producing cortisol independently. Unlike pituitary microadenomas, which cause high ACTH levels, these adrenal tumors bypass the pituitary-adrenal axis and usually result in suppressed ACTH. Ectopic ACTH syndrome (Option C): Ectopic ACTH syndrome arises when tumors outside the pituitary, such as those in the lung, pancreas, or thymus, secrete ACTH. Although it can lead to Cushing's syndrome, it is less frequent than pituitary microadenomas as the main cause of Cushing's disease in elderly patients. This form usually presents with a faster onset and more pronounced metabolic disturbances.

text: In comparison to a normal healthy person in the evening time. Which of these will not have an elevated cortisol?

options.A: Normal healthy person in the morning

ansText: Normal healthy person in the morning
expl: Normal circadian rhythm of ACTH starts to rise early in the morning prior to awakening, reaches a peak in the morning and levels will fall by evening. Reduction in ACTH pulse occurs between 6PM and midnight. Cortisol secretion increases in response to stress like hypotension, hypoglycemia, exercise, fever, surgery and burns. In cushing's disease, the ACTH pulse frequency and amplitude is increased and hence the cortisol response and hence the circadian rhythm is lost.

text: A 44-year-old man presents with a six month history of diarrhea and abdominal cramps. On further questioning it appears he has also noticed facial flushing. On examination there is wheeze on auscultation of his chest and abdominal examination reveals hepatomegaly. Which of the following investigations would confirm the likely diagnosis?
expl: This patient has carcinoid syndrome . The diagnosis is made by 24-hour urine collection for 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) -excretion is greater than 0.3 mmol. Forty five per cent of carcinoid tumors arise in the appendix, 30% arise in the small bowel and 20% in the rectum. Most patients with carcinoid syndrome have liver metastases. 5-HT, kinins, prostaglandins and other vasoactive substances are secreted. Clinical features of carcinoid syndrome include diarrhea and abdominal cramps in the majority of patients.Flushing, which is often provoked by alcohol, bronchoconstriction and cardiac involvement with tricuspid or pulmonary incompetence are also features. Diagnosis also includes chest x ray, abdominal ultrasound scan, small bowel radiology and echocardiography to establish the extent of disease. Surgical resection of the primary tumor is possible in some cases; octreotide is the treatment of choice. In the majority of cases of Wilson's disease 24-hour urinary copper is greater than 3 micromol . In Cushing's syndrome 24-hour urinary free cortisol is elevated. Nephrotic syndrome is defined as proteinuria greater than 3.5 g/1.75 m2 of body surface per 24 hours, hypoalbuminemia and oedema. Screening for pheochromocytoma can be performed by 24-hour urine collection for 4-OH-3-methoxymandelate (HMMA, VMA). Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st Ed, Ch: 84, Pg:669

text: In hepatitis B vaccine the following subunit is most vital?
expl: The main component of Hepatitis B vaccine is the surface antigen. Current regimens use recombinant vaccines containing the surface antigen. Another recombinant hepatitis B vaccine with a novel adjuvant that activates Toll-like 9 receptors was approved for adults aged 18 or older. In a series of prospective trials, compared to three Engerix-B injections, two IM doses a month apart yielded higher proportions with protective levels of anti-HBs (≥10 mIU/mL): 95% of adults aged 18-55 or 18-70 (vs 81% for Engerix-B), 90% of older adults aged 40-70 (vs 71% for Engerix-B), and 90% of adults aged 18-70 with type 2 diabetes (vs 65% for Engerix-B). This two-injection regimen may be useful for revaccination of persons who failed to respond to the original vaccines. Another novel recombinant vaccine (PreHevbrio, VBI Vaccines) containing of all three hepatitis B surface antigens, S, pre-S1, and pre-S2, has been shown in clinical trials (three IM doses at 0, 1, and 6 months) to achieve higher proportions with protective anti-HBs and higher antibody levels than Engerix-B (which contains S antigen only), including in older persons (≥45 years), persons with diabetes, and overweight persons (body mass index >30)

text: A 54-year-old female with type 2 diabetes is admitted with diarrhea and vomiting. She has noticed small amounts of blood in her stools. The vomiting had commenced one day after having a non-vegetarian diet. The patient's type 2 diabetes is treated with diet alone. Stool cultures taken by the GP reveal Campylobacter jejuni.Which of the following is the most appropriate therapy?
expl: Campylobacter is a leading cause of diarrhoeal illness, often caused by ingestion of undercooked meat harboring the pathogen. It is also a major cause of traveller's diarrhea . The use of antibiotic therapy for the management of Campylobacter infection in adults is controversial. Antibiotic of choice in this infection is erythromycin, though ciprofloxacin and tetracycline may also be appropriate. However, appropriate fluid replacement and anti-emetics are initially indicated - most units advocate no antibiotic treatment. Antibiotics are not recommended in patients with nontyphoid Salmonella, Campylobacter, STEC, Aeromonas, or Yersinia, except in severe disease, because they do not hasten recovery or reduce the period of fecal bacterial excretion Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 133, Pg: 1065

text: Which of the following tests is the best for assessing long-term control of diabetes mellitus?
expl: Explanation: Glycosylated hemoglobin (HbA1c) is the gold standard for assessing long-term glycemic control in diabetic patients. Reflects average blood glucose over the past 2-3 months, which corresponds to the lifespan of red blood cells. Unlike daily glucose measurements, HbA1c is not affected by short-term fluctuations and does not require fasting. It measures the percentage of haemoglobin molecules bound to glucose, providing a stable and accurate assessment of overall glycemic control. A value of ≥48 mmol/mol (6.5%) is used for diagnosis, making HbA1c especially useful for early detection in individuals with risk factors such as obesity or a family history of diabetes. HbA1c interpretation: 7% - 6.5% : Pre-diabetic > 6.5% : Diabetic Explanation of other options: Glycated Albumin (Option B): Glycated albumin reflects average blood glucose over the preceding 2-3 weeks, due to the shorter half-life of albumin (~20 days). While useful for short-term glycemic monitoring, it does not provide the long-term assessment that HbA1c offers. Serum fructosamine (Option C): Serum fructosamine testing, like glycated albumin, reflects average blood glucose over the past 2-3 weeks by measuring glycated plasma proteins. It is particularly useful when HbA1c may be unreliable, such as in patients with hemoglobinopathies. Urine Sugar (Option D): Urine glucose testing is not reliable for assessing long-term glycemic control because it is influenced by factors such as the renal threshold, hydration status, and concurrent medications. Glucose appears in the urine only when blood levels exceed the renal threshold, making it an inadequate measure of overall blood glucose control.

text: Which of the following is not true for mucormycosis?

options.A: DKA increases risk of rhinocerebral mucormycosis.
options.B: A high index of suspicion of mucormycosis must be maintained, even in the absence of a known history of diabetes, if hyperglycemia is present.
options.C: Hyperglycemia enhances expression of mucorale specific protein mediating cell invasion.
options.D: Patients receiving antifungal prophylaxis with either itraconazole or voriconazole may not be at increased risk of mucormycosis.

ansText: Patients receiving antifungal prophylaxis with either itraconazole or voriconazole may not be at increased risk of mucormycosis.
expl: Mucormycosis typically occurs in patients with diabetes mellitus, solid-organ transplantation or hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT), prolonged neutropenia or corticosteroid use, or malignancy. Mucormycosis may be the first clinical recognition of hyperglycemia. So a high index of suspicion is needed. Use of iron chelators cause availability of iron to the fungus and promote their intake into the cells. Acidosis also causes availability of iron to the fungus. Though acidosis is told to be risk factor, most of the patients are not acidotic at the time of presentation. Patients receiving antifungal prophylaxis with either itraconazole or voriconazole may be at increased risk of mucormycosis. These patients typically present with disseminated mucormycosis, the most lethal form of disease. Breakthrough mucormycosis also has been described in patients receiving posaconazole, isavuconazole, or echinocandin prophylaxis. Mucormycosis has also emerged as an important superinfection in COVID-19 patients. This may be attributed to glucocorticoid use in COVID. But even during COVID 19 most of the cases of Mucor in India was unrelated to COVID 19 indicating the high base line cases. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch: 218, Pg 1682

text: What is the association of Rhino-cerebral Mucor mycosis?
expl: Explanation: Rhino-cerebral mucormycosis is a life-threatening fungal infection strongly associated with uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, particularly Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA) . The acidic, high-glucose environment in DKA impairs neutrophil function and promotes iron availability, which facilitates the growth of the angioinvasive Mucorales fungi in the nasal passages, sinuses, and brain. Agent: Rhizopus oryzae; common in uncontrolled diabetes and DKA. Pathophysiology: Starts in nasal turbinates → invades vessels → thrombosis, tissue necrosis. Clinical Features: Fever, facial pain/swelling, nasal discharge, necrotic eschar. Diagnosis: Imaging + histopathology (broad, non-septate hyphae). Treatment: Prompt IV amphotericin B + aggressive surgical debridement; correct underlying DKA/DM. Explanation of other options: Pregnancy (Option B): Not a specific risk factor for mucormycosis. Antibiotics (Option C): Broad-spectrum antibiotic use is a risk factor for candidiasis, not typically for mucormycosis. Inhaled steroids (Option D): A risk factor for oropharyngeal candidiasis, not mucormycosis. Key Takeaways: Rhino-cerebral mucormycosis is a medical emergency often seen in patients with DKA. It is characterized by black, necrotic eschar in the nasal cavity or palate and requires urgent surgical debridement and antifungal therapy. Reference: https://insightsimaging.springeropen.com/articles/10.1186/s13244-021-01109-z https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK557429/

text: A 29-year-old woman came to the diabetes clinic with her two children. This is her third pregnancy and although not normally diabetic, she was diagnosed with gestational diabetes mellitus. Recent fasting plasma glucose levels have been in the range of 80-90 mg/dl and she is taking BD mixed insulins. Later that evening she collapses while shopping and is brought to the Emergency Department with blood glucose of 56 mg/dl. Which of the following represents the most appropriate management in this patient?

options.A: Reduce her dose of BD mixed insulin by 50%
options.B: Reduce her dose of BD mixed insulin by 20%
options.C: Check a random cortisol to rule out Addison's disease
options.D: Change her to a basal bolus regime

ansText: Change her to a basal bolus regime
expl: This lady's fasting plasma glucose levels are appropriate, but taking a BD mixed insulin regime is probably not appropriate to her lifestyle where her mealtimes and portion sizes may be slightly irregular given the fact that she has two other children to manage. A basal bolus regime would give her more flexibility in varying insulin dose. The coexistence of Addison's is unlikely and increasing the size of her meals would only promote more excess weight gain and worsening insulin resistance. Reference: ADA Standards of Diabetes Care - 2023

text: A 60-year-old farmer who has long-standing type-1 diabetes is brought to the clinic by his wife. He has been limping for a while and his wife noticed that his ankle was rather abnormally shaped after he stepped out of the shower. Examination of his right ankle reveals a painless joint that is warm and swollen. There is crepitus and what appears to be palpable bone debris. X-ray reveals gross joint destruction and apparent dislocation. His CRP and white count are normal, the joint aspiration fluid shows no microbes and historical review of HBA1c reveals that it has rarely been below 9%. What is the most likely diagnosis in this case?
expl: Diabetic Charcot Neuropathy is a chronic and progressive disease that occurs as a result of loss of protective sensation which leads to the destruction of foot and ankle joints and surrounding bony structures. Diagnosis can be made clinically with a warm and erythematous foot with erythema that decreases with foot elevation. Radiographs often reveal obliteration of joint space and fragmentation of both articular surfaces of a joint leading to subluxation or dislocation. Treatment is a trial of total contact casting for acute Charcot deformities without skin breakdown. Operative management is indicated for recurrent infections, deformities, and severe skin breakdown. Charcot's joint is said to occur in 1 in every 750 patients with diabetes mellitus, although this is increased to 5 in every 100 in those with proven neuropathy. However, a Charcot's joint does not just occur in those with diabetes but may occur in 20-40% of patients with syringomyelia and 5-10% of those with long-standing syphilis (although this condition is now very rare). Management in diabetes includes tight control of blood glucose, appropriate orthotic intervention, and there is evidence that bisphosphonates may slow the pace of joint destruction. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page:3124

text: Which of the following statements is correct concerning the relationship between type 2 diabetes and colonic cancer?

options.A: Increased concentrations of C peptide are a marker of increased colorectal cancer risk
options.B: Insulin treatment increases recurrence free survival after treatment of colonic cancer
options.C: The increased risk of colorectal cancer in diabetes is related to BMI
options.D: The increased risk of colorectal cancer in diabetes is related to total cholesterol

ansText: Increased concentrations of C peptide are a marker of increased colorectal cancer risk
expl: Type 2 diabetes is associated with a 40-60% increase in the risk of cancer of the large bowel. This increase is linked to changes in HbA1c. Type 2 diabetes is associated with significantly higher rates of overall mortality and reduced disease free and recurrence free survival after chemotherapy/radiotherapy, and insulin has not been shown to have any effects on mortality. No association has been found between colonic malignancy and type 1 diabetes, nor gestational diabetes. A number of studies have independently linked high circulating concentrations of C Peptide, as a marker of insulin production, with increased colorectal cancer risk. The molecular basis has not been proven, but it may be reasonable to extrapolate that it is linked to the growth stimulation effects of insulin. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 81 Pg: 637

text: What is the expected finding in a patient with the following CXR?
expl: Explanation of answer: Flail chest causes paradoxical breathing due to a free-floating chest wall segment that moves opposite to normal during respiration. Flail chest is a traumatic condition resulting from fractures of three or more consecutive ribs in at least two places, creating a flail segment that becomes mechanically independent from the rest of the thoracic cage. This segment moves inward during inspiration (when negative pressure draws air in) and outward during expiration, which is the opposite of normal chest wall motion-this is termed paradoxical breathing. This paradoxical motion leads to: Impaired ventilation (due to ineffective pressure generation) Increased dead space and hypoventilation Risk of pulmonary contusion, edema, and atelectasis Clinical features like chest pain, respiratory distress, and tachypnea Diagnosis is suspected clinically and confirmed with imaging: Chest X-ray shows rib fractures CT scan with 3D reconstruction is more sensitive and specific Management includes: Pain control (nerve blocks, epidural) Oxygen supplementation Non-invasive or mechanical ventilation in severe cases Surgical rib fixation in select patients Explanation of other options: Kussmaul breathing (Option A): Deep, rapid breathing due to metabolic acidosis (e.g., diabetic ketoacidosis); unrelated to trauma or chest wall mechanics. Apneustic breathing (Option C): Abnormal breathing pattern with prolonged inspiration seen in pons lesions; not associated with rib fractures. Bronchial breathing (Option D): High-pitched breath sounds heard over areas of lung consolidation (e.g., pneumonia); not related to chest wall trauma. Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK534090/

text: Kussmaul's sign is classically described in:
expl: Answer is C (Constrictive pericarditis) Kussmaul's sign is classically described in association with Constrictive Pericarditis. Kussmaul's sign refers to paradoxical elevation of JVP/CVP during inspiration (In healthy persons venous pressure falls during inspiration because pressures in the right heart decrease as intrathoracic pressures fall) The Kussmaul's sign is classically described in association with Constrictive pericarditis. Kussmaul's sign is however also seen in association with Right Ventricular Infarction, Restrictive Cardiomyopathy, Pulmonary Embolism and Advanced Systolic Severe Heart Failure
