text: Amyloidosis is most commonly seen in ?
expl: Ans. is 'c' i.e., Type II DM The two best examples of localized amyloidosis are Alzheimer's disease and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Localized amyloid deposition results from the production of a unique polypeptide, which contains an amyloidogenic sequence and is capable of forming a beta-pleated sheet structure necessary for these deposits to aggregate. In type 2 diabetes it is the islet amyloid polypeptide (IAPP) also known as amylin. In Alzheimer's the unique peptide is the beta-amyloid protein (A beta).

text: Which of the following blood glucose readings is diagnostic of gestational diabetes according to IADPSG criteria?
expl: The screening for Diabetes mellitus should be performed in women at the first prenatal visit First trimester screening is performed for high risk women according to ADA while ACOG advocates universal screening for all women The diagnosis of Gestational Diabetes mellitus is made if either one of the following is satisfied: Fasting blood glucose > 92 mg/dl 1 hr post OGTT > 180 mg/dl 2 hr post OGTT > 153 mg/dl If fasting blood glucose is more than 126 mg/dl or 2-hour post glucose load value is > 200 mg/dl, the diagnosis of overt diabetes mellitus is made Reference: ADA Standards of Medical Care in Diabetes 2023

text: In glucagonoma the MOST likely associated skin lesion is?
expl: Glucagonoma syndrome (diabetes mellitus, weight loss and anaemia) is associated with a characteristic skin rash (necrolytic migratory erythema) in 75% of cases. The lesion starts as an indurated erythema at the perineum, face and nose. Within a few days blisters will cover the surface of the skin which then crust and heal leaving hyperpigmented skin. This process takes 7-14 days with lesions developing in one area while others are resolving. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 20 th edition Pg:597,599,609,2749

text: What is the standard amount of glucose used for testing when diagnosing diabetes mellitus?
expl: Explanation: In adults, the standard OGTT for diagnosing diabetes mellitus uses 75 grams of anhydrous glucose dissolved in water, administered orally after an overnight fast. Blood glucose levels are measured fasting and 2 hours after ingestion to assess glucose tolerance. In pregnancy, Gestational DM is screened with a 50 g glucose challenge test and diagnosed with a 100 g OGTT .

text: A 57-year-old man, newly diagnosed with type-2 diabetes mellitus, presents to the clinic for his first assessment. He is found to have changes in his eyes on fundoscopy. Which of the following is most likely to need immediate referral to the ophthalmologist?

options.A: A few dot and blot haemorrhages
options.B: Some hard exudates > 1 disc diameter from the fovea

expl: Background diabetic retinopathy consists of dot and blot haemorrhages and hard exudates. Patients do not need to be referred to the ophthalmologist unless these are within 1 disc diameter of the fovea. This can be monitored annually at the routine clinic. Cataracts appear about 10 years earlier in type-2 diabetes than in non-diabetic patients. If the vision is significantly affected the patients warrant routine and not urgent referral to the ophthalmologist. Soft exudates suggest retinal ischaemia, which would require routine referral to the ophthalmologist. New vessels anywhere in the fundus are a feature of proliferative retinopathy and, as new vessels have a risk of haemorrhage and can threaten sight, they should be referred urgently to the ophthalmologist. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 20 th edition Ch:398 Pg:2877

text: A 25-year-old woman with type-1 diabetes mellitus came for her routine review and says she is keen on becoming pregnant. Which of the following is the factor most likely to make you ask her to defer pregnancy at this stage?

options.C: She hasn't been taking folic acid
options.D: Microalbumin level of 6-mg excretion in 24 hours

expl: Pregnancy in type-1 diabetes is still associated with a two- to threefold increase in congenital abnormalities when compared with the background population. It is also associated with higher neonatal morbidity and mortality and higher operative delivery rates. Prepregnancy counselling with the aim of bringing the Hb A1c to near-normal levels are associated with better pregnancy outcomes. Diabetic retinopathy can progress during pregnancy and the eyes must be checked at least once each trimester; if there is progression that is sight-threatening then the patient should be referred to an ophthalmologist. Background retinopathy would not be a contraindication to pregnancy. The microalbumin level is within normal limits. Nephropathy can also progress during pregnancy, but microalbuminuria would not be a contraindication to pregnancy and nor would sensory neuropathy. It is important that patients with diabetes take 5 mg folic acid daily prepregnancy (this reduces neural tube defects) and this can be started when the patient starts trying to conceive, although it should ideally be taken for 3 months before hand. The most important thing this woman can do is to improve her glycaemic control before trying to conceive. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition page 3096

text: A 64-year-old man presents to the diabetes clinic for review. He complains of difficulty in maintaining penile erection despite having normal libido. Which of the following is true regarding his condition?

options.A: Diabetes mellitus is less likely to cause these conditions
options.B: Penile pain is a common association
options.C: Autonomic neuropathy is unlikely to be present
options.D: β-blockers and thiazide diuretics may exacerbate the problem

ansText: β-blockers and thiazide diuretics may exacerbate the problem
expl: Libido is rarely affected, which makes the condition all the more frustrating for affected men. Between 30 and 50% of men with diabetes of more than 6 years' duration are affected. There is an association with other autonomic neuropathies such as postural hypotension and gastroparesis. The condition is not usually associated with pain, and may be exacerbated by both β-blockers and thiazide diuretics. PDE-5 inhibitors are available as oral therapies for impotence, but these are often required at high dose. Alprostadil and vacuum devices are alternative methods. Estimates put successful treatment at only around 70%. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 3058

text: In a patient with type 1 diabetes with 3rd stage of beta cell damage, which of the following situations is associated with the same?
expl: Explanation of answer: Stage 2 of type 1 diabetes is defined by the presence of islet autoimmunity along with dysglycemia but without overt symptoms. Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (T1DM) is an autoimmune disease characterized by T-cell-mediated destruction of pancreatic β-cells, leading to absolute insulin deficiency. It progresses through three defined stages before becoming symptomatic. Stages of T1DM Development: Stage 1: Positive for ≥2 islet autoantibodies (e.g., GAD65, IA-2, ZnT8, ICA) Normoglycemia on glucose testing (Option A ruled out) Clinically asymptomatic Stage 2: Positive islet autoantibodies (same as stage 1) Dysglycemia (abnormal glucose tolerance, elevated fasting glucose or postprandial glucose) Still asymptomatic Stage 3: Islet autoantibody positive Hyperglycemia exceeding diagnostic threshold for diabetes Clinically symptomatic (e.g., polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, possible DKA) The patient is autoantibody positive and has dysglycemia but no overt symptoms yet, making this Stage 2 of T1DM. This staging allows for early identification of individuals at risk for T1DM, which is especially important for clinical trials and preventive strategies. Explanation of other options: Autoimmune negative with normoglycemia (Option C): This individual does not have autoimmune T1DM and shows no biochemical evidence of dysglycemia-unlikely to progress. Autoimmune negative with dysglycemia (Option D): May suggest Type 2 diabetes or another form of non-autoimmune dysglycemia, not T1DM.

text: A 43 year old man is being investigated for a 3 year history of arthralgia. On examination, his skin color was normal and there was no evidence of jaundice or hepatomegaly. He has the following results: Alanine aminotransferase 35 U/L Aspartate aminotransferase 40 U/L Fasting plasma glucose 126 mg/dl Ferritin 500 ug/L, (15-300) Which one of the following is an appropriate investigation?
expl: In hemochromatosis, the serum Fe is elevated (> 300 mg/dL). The serum transferrin saturation is a sensitive parameter of increased Fe and merits evaluation when > 50%. The serum ferritin is increased. Urinary Fe excretion is markedly increased (> 2 mg/24 h) by the chelating drug deferoxamine (500 to 1000 mg IM based on the size of the patient), and this has been used as a diagnostic test. In addition, when the Fe content in the liver is significantly increased, an MRI may reflect this change. Liver biopsy had been the gold standard in diagnosis; it now serves only to provide evidence of fibrosis (cirrhosis). It is considered only when genetic testing is negative along with ferritin >1000 μg/L or abnormal LFT Gene assay (Homozygosity C282Y mutations) is also an excellent diagnostic test. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st Ed, Ch: 414, Pg: 3232-3234

text: A 70-year-old male with a 5-year history of type II diabetes mellitus presents for annual review with a blood pressure of 188/88 mmHg. Clinical examination was normal. An ECG reveals evidence of left ventricular hypertrophy. Which one of the following drugs is the most appropriate treatment for this patient's hypertension?
expl: This elderly male diabetic has isolated systolic hypertension associated with left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH being defined as a complication of hypertension). Evidence would support the use of a calcium channel blocker and/or ACE inhibitor as first line. In a diabetic patient with evidence of nephropathy or any patient with LVH there is compelling evidence to suggest that ACE inhibitor or angiotensin II receptor blockers should be first line treatment for hypertension. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Principles, 20 th edition, ch:271 pg:1901,1902

text: A 65 year old woman has a diagnosis of insulin dependent diabetes mellitus (poorly controlled) for 25 years. She complains of repeated episodes of abdominal pain following meals. These episodes have become more frequent over the past 3 months. There is no abdominal tenderness on palpation. Which of the following is the likely diagnosis?
expl: Abdominal angina is postprandial pain that occurs in mesenteric vascular occlusive disease when blood flow to the colon is unable to meet visceral demands. Atherosclerotic disease is the most common cause of abdominal angina. It frequently involves ostia of the mesenteric vessels. In most people, it is occlusion of the superior mesenteric artery that is responsible for the abdominal symptoms. Diabetes, especially Type 2 diabetes, is associated with macrovascular disease. text: Which of the following is seen in a patient with Right ventricular myocardial infarction?

options.A: ST-segment elevation in leads II, III and aVF
options.B: Occlusion of the left circumflex artery

ansText: ST-segment elevation in leads II, III and aVF
expl: Right ventricular myocardial infarction (RVMI) usually occurs in association with an inferior-wall left ventricular infarction, as revealed by the ECG. In ECG, along with ST elevation in leads II, III, aVF which suggests an inferior wall MI, a patient with RVMI may also have ST elevation in V1 and in right sided chest leads V3R-V6R. The typical clinical findings in RVMI include bradycardia (due to AV node involvement), hypotension, raised JVP with positive Kussmaul sign (inspiratory rise of JVP). Hypotension is typically treated with IV fluids (0.9% saline) There is usually a right coronary occlusion. Characteristic clinical features include a low cardiac output syndrome with jugular venous distension but no pulmonary vascular congestion. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page no: 2062

expl: The common peroneal nerve is involved. Nerve roots L5 and S1 supply the nerve for foot eversion. text: A 30 year old man has a blood pressure of 200/90. His serum potassium is 2.8 mmol/l, creatinine is 0.9 mg/dl. Urine dipstick shows protein trace. Which of the following diagnoses is likely?
expl: This patient is having hypertension with hypokalemia. The answer is Conn's syndrome. Another associated finding would be metabolic alkalosis. Other conditions that can present with the same findings will be Liddle Syndrome, Apparent Mineralocorticoid Excess, Cushing syndrome, renal artery stenosis and renin secreting tumors. They can be distinguished by the Renin and aldosterone levels. Option B: Pheochromocytoma presents with episodic headache, sweating and palpitations. Hypokalemia is not an associated feature Option C: Diabetic nephropathy will cause a rise in serum creatinine and hyperkalemia. Proteinuria is a cardinal feature. Option D: Hypertensive nephropathy will cause a rise of serum creatinine with hyperkalemia. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 53, Pg: 354.

text: A 77-year-old male presented with a quadrantic hemianopia. Which of the following conditions is most likely to cause such a presentation?

options.B: A lesion of the optic chiasma

expl: Superior quadrantanopia is seen in temporal lobe lesion . inferior quadrantanopia is seen in parietal lobe lesion. Unilateral occipital lobe lesions (left or right) cause contralateral hemianopia or quadrantanopia, visual agnosia, visual illusions and elementary visual hallucinations. Left occipital lobe lesions cause these symptoms and alexia and colour agnosia. Right occipital lobe lesions cause impaired visual orientation and topographical memory in addition. Bioccipital lesions are rare, but cause cortical blindness, altitudinal hemianopia, impaired colour perception, Anton syndrome and prosopagnosia. A lesion of the optic chiasm would cause a Bitemporal hemianopia. Diabetic retinopathy can rarely cause an 'apparent quadrantic hemianopia' because the distribution of the retinal changes may just correspond to quadrantic hemianopia - but this is not the most likely. Tobacco amblyopia causes symmetric central or centrocecal scotomas. Chloroquine poisoning causes symmetric bilateral scotomas. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st ed, Ch: 32, Pg: 219

text: What is the most reliable method to confirm that a central line is correctly placed in the jugular vein?
expl: Explanation: Role of Chest X-ray in Central Line Placement Initial Assessment: A chest X-ray should be obtained immediately after placing a central line in the internal jugular or subclavian vein to confirm proper catheter position and to exclude complications such as iatrogenic pneumothorax. Post-Procedure Verification: It is essential to verify the catheter's placement and ensure there are no complications like pneumothorax following the procedure. Ipsilateral Side Approach: If insertion into the internal jugular vein fails, the next step is to attempt placement in the ipsilateral subclavian vein. Before attempting catheterization on the opposite side, a chest X-ray or ultrasound must be performed to avoid the risk of bilateral pneumothoraces. Options B, C, and D are incorrect. text: A 58-year-old man with type-2 diabetes presents with background diabetic retinopathy. His HB A1c has been consistently above 9% for the past 5 years. Which of the following factors may impact most negatively on the prognosis for his retinopathy?

options.A: Rapid improvement in blood glucose levels

ansText: Rapid improvement in blood glucose levels
expl: Rapid improvement in blood glucose levels may be associated with worsening of diabetic eye disease. Both the Diabetes Control and Complications Trial (DCCT) in type-1 diabetes and the UKPDS (United Kingdom Prospective Diabetes Study) in type-2 diabetes have demonstrated the long-term benefits of reducing blood sugar levels in controlling future microvascular complications. All diabetic patients should be offered yearly eye screening, preferably with a digital retinal camera. Rapidly deteriorating visual acuity, hard exudates encroaching on the macula, preproliferative changes or new-vessel formation are all reasons for early referral to an ophthalmologist. Diabetic retinopathy has been known for many years to be the leading cause of blindness in people of working age. Smoking has no effect on the prognosis of retinopathy. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 20 th edition Ch:398 Pg:2877

text: A 56-year-old woman, diagnosed with type-2 diabetes mellitus and losing weight, is referred for an opinion; her doctor is thinking about insulin therapy. A normochromic, normocytic anemia is noted. On examination she has angular stomatitis and a well-demarcated erythematous rash in her groin, which extends to her lower limbs, buttocks and perineum. What is the next step in her management?

options.C: Observe and see again in 6 months

expl: There is a suggestion that this patient has a glucagonoma , 90% of which are associated with the characteristic skin rash - necrolytic migratory erythema. The annual incidence of glucagonoma is estimated at 1 in 20 million. Over 70% of glucagonomas are malignant, but, because of their indolent presentation, the diagnosis is often overlooked for many years. Due to insulin antagonism over 90% are associated with impaired glucose tolerance, and eventually weight loss due to protein catabolism. Surgical cure rate is as low as 5%, due to metastases many years prior to presentation. Octreotide improves the skin rash but may have a detrimental effect on glucose control; combination chemotherapy with streptazocin and 5-fluoruracil (5-FU) gives good palliative results, as does hepatic embolisation. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page:384,665

text: A 56-year-old man came to the clinic following a myocardial infarction one year previously. During his admission he was found to be hypertensive and diabetic. He complains that he has put on 5kg in weight in the past 6 months. Which of his medications may be contributing to his weight gain?
expl: Sulfonylureas Sulfonylureas are oral hypoglycaemic drugs used in the management of type 2 diabetes mellitus. They work by increasing pancreatic insulin secretion and hence are only effective if functional B-cells are present. text: A 60-year-old type 2 diabetes patient who is fasting for religious rituals. He has background diabetic retinopathy, and currently takes metformin 500mg TDS as well as ramipril 10mg and aspirin 75mg. Investigations Hb 12.1 g/dl WCC 5.0 x 10^9/L PLT 212 x 10^9/L Na+ 139 mmol/l K+ 4.9 mmol/l Creatinine 1.0 mg/dl HbA1c 7.8% What advice would you give him regarding his medication while fasting?

options.B: Give short acting insulin for the evening meal
options.D: Give metformin 500mg in morning, 1000mg in evening

ansText: Give metformin 500mg in morning, 1000mg in evening
expl: Metformin is not associated with hypoglycaemia when used as monotherapy. It reduces hepatic glucose output and has its predominant effects on fasting plasma glucose. Even so, it would seem sensible to divide the dose with the larger portion taken in the evening after the fast is broken. Giving short acting insulin or switching to insulin is likely to increase the risk of hypoglycaemia. Whilst diabetes patients are exempted from the need to fast, if this patient wishes to do so in this case it would seem unfair to prevent him fasting, as metformin should not preclude it altogether. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 20 th edition Ch:397 Pg:2865-66,2868-69

expl: The drugs that should be avoided in renal failure are Metformin, Mepiridin, NSAIDs and OHAs that are eliminated by the kidneys. Sulfonyl ureas should be avoided only in advanced renal failure. text: A 54-year-old diabetic man presents with malaise and loss of libido. On examination there is evidence of hepatomegaly. Blood tests show Hb 14.1 g/dl (13-18), fasting glucose 144 mg/dl, serum iron 45 mmol/l (14-29) and serum ferritin 250,000 mmol/l (15-200). What would be the most appropriate treatment for his symptoms?
expl: This patient most probably has hereditary haemochromatosis which causes hypo gonadotrophic hypogonadism or rarely hyper gonadotropin hypogonadism due to iron deposition in pituitary and testis respectively. Although venesection is the treatment of choice for reducing the iron load, this will not correct testicular atrophy or hypopituitarism, either or both of which may contribute to a loss of libido. Testosterone replacement is used for improvement of symptoms in these patients. Desferrioxamine is indicated in rare cases who cannot tolerate venesection (because of severe cardiac disease or anemia). Insulin therapy would not be helpful in restoring libido. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 20 th edition Chapter:407 Page number:2890-82

text: A 45-year-old diabetic gentleman had a renal biopsy during investigation of worsening renal failure. Which of the following is typical of diabetic nephropathy?

options.D: Basement membrane thickening and mesangial widening

ansText: Basement membrane thickening and mesangial widening
expl: The earliest morphologic abnormality in diabetic nephropathy is the thickening of the glomerular basement membrane(GBM) and expansion of the mesangium due to accumulation of extracellular matrix. Light microscopy findings show an increase in the solid spaces of the tuft material(diffuse diabetic glomerulopathy). Large acellular accumulations also may be observed within these areas. These are circular sections and are known as the Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules which are PAS positive, eosinophilic material . Immunofluorescence microscopy may reveal deposition of immunoglobulin G along the GBM in a linear pattern, but this is not diagnostic. In advanced disease, the mesangial regions occupy a large proportion of the tuft, with prominent matrix content. Further, the basement membrane in the capillary walls(i.e., the peripheral basement membrane) is thicker than normal. Diabetic glomerulopathy of Kimmelstiel-Wilson disease Option A: Hyaline changes in blood vessel is seen in hypertension and is non specific. Option B:Mesangeal hypercellularity is seen in glomerular diseases like Ig A nephropathy, Lupus Nephritis, post streptococcal glomerulonephritis etc. Option C: Basement membrane spikes are seen in membranous nephropathy. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st edition, Ch: 314, Pg: 2344.

text: A 78-year-old man with type-2 diabetes and a creatinine level of 1.85 mg/dl presents to radiology for a contrast angiography. He has had a mild episode of gastroenteritis but is keen to go ahead with the investigation. He is discharged the following morning but presents to ER 48 h later feeling acutely unwell. His serum creatinine level is now 2.85 mg/dl.What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
expl: In patients who have impaired renal function, the use of iodine-containing contrast media may be directly nephrotoxic. Contrast nephropathy mechanisms include: Hypoxia in the renal outer medulla due to perturbations in renal microcirculation and occlusion of small vessels Cytotoxic damage to the tubules directly or via the generation of oxygen-free radicals, especially because the concentration of the agent within the tubule is markedly increased Transient tubule obstruction with precipitated contrast material. The toxic effects appear to be dose-dependent and therefore where large amounts of contrast are used, such as in angiography, there is an increased incidence of contrast nephropathy. The most common clinical course of contrast nephropathy is characterized by a rise in S.Cr beginning 24-48 h following exposure, peaking within 3-5 days, and resolving within 1 week. Dialysis requiring renal impairement is seen in the setting of severe pre existing renal failure, congestive cardiac failure etc. Risk factors for Contrast induced Nephropathy: Diabetic nephropathy Coexistent hypovolaemia Multiple myeloma Pre-existing CKD Low fractional excretion of sodium (FeNa) and relatively benign urinary sediment without features of tubular necrosis (see below) are common findings Prehydration with normal saline and acetylcysteine may reduce the incidence of contrast nephropathy, although care must be taken not to precipitate volume overload. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st edition, chp:310, pg: 2300

expl: An elderly man with atherosclerotic risk factors with asymmetric kidneys point to atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis. text: A 39-year-old woman presents to the clinic with difficult to treat hypertension. She is on two anti-hypertensives and currently has a BP of 155/95 mmHg. She has noted that her face has become more rounded over the years and she is having increasing trouble with both acne and hirsutism. Fasting blood glucose testing has revealed impaired glucose tolerance. There has also been increasing trouble with abdominal obesity and she has noticed some purple stretch marks appearing around her abdomen. What is the most likely diagnosis
expl: Cushing's syndrome is associated with a round, plethoric, facial appearance and weight gain - in particular truncal obesity, buffalo hump and supraclavicular fat pads, skin fragility, proximal muscle weakness, mood disturbance, menstrual disturbance and reduced libido. Hypertension is present in more than 50% of patients, impaired glucose tolerance in 30%. Osteopenia and osteoporosis, and premature vascular disease are an inevitable consequence in untreated Cushing's. Phaeochromocytoma presents with episodic headaches, sweating and palpitation along with refractory hypertension. Primary aldosteronism is characterised by resistant hypertension with hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 2961

text: What condition is illustrated in the image provided below?
expl: Explanation: The image displays characteristic features of Cushing's syndrome, a condition caused by prolonged exposure to elevated levels of glucocorticoids. Cushing's Syndrome Overview Cushing's syndrome refers to a group of clinical signs and symptoms resulting from chronic glucocorticoid excess. When the cause is specifically a pituitary adenoma producing ACTH, the condition is termed Cushing's disease. Though rare, subtle or early forms of the syndrome may be more common, especially in patients presenting with central obesity, type 2 diabetes, or osteoporosis. Clinical Features of Cushing's Syndrome Physical Appearance Weight gain with central (truncal) obesity Moon face: Rounded, full face Buffalo hump: Fat pad over the upper back/neck Skin changes: Thin, fragile skin prone to easy bruising Wide, purple striae (stretch marks), especially on the abdomen Acne and hirsutism Musculoskeletal Osteoporosis, especially spinal fractures (see Option B) Proximal muscle weakness, particularly in the thighs and upper arms Reduced deep tendon reflexes Metabolic Hyperglycemia or overt type 2 diabetes Dyslipidemia (elevated cholesterol/triglycerides) Cardiovascular Hypertension Hypokalemia Peripheral edema Reproductive & Hormonal Amenorrhea and reduced libido Menstrual irregularities in women, often due to gonadotropin suppression Neuropsychiatric Mood disturbances: Irritability, depression, emotional lability Cognitive issues, sometimes progressing to psychosis in severe cases Immune & Hematologic Immunosuppression: Higher risk of infections Elevated WBC count, eosinopenia Hypercoagulable state: Risk of DVT or pulmonary embolism Explanation for other options: Acromegaly (option A): incorrect because Features include enlarged hands/feet, coarse facial features, jaw protrusion are not seen here. PCOS (Polycystic Ovary Syndrome) (option B): Typically presents with menstrual irregularities, acne, and hirsutism, but lacks the specific Cushingoid features like striae and buffalo hump. Advanced Obesity (option D): While obesity is present, the hallmark signs of glucocorticoid excess (e.g., moon face, striae, muscle wasting) differentiate it from simple obesity.

text: A 35 year old male presents with history of weakness of both the lower limbs of insidious onset, for the past 2 years. He has mild difficulty in swallowing liquids too. There are no sensory symptoms. On examination, he has fasciculations and areflexia. You also notice gynecomastia. He is also undergoing investigation for infertility. What is the likely molecular abnormality be seen in this patient?
expl: The given patient has an LMN type of weakness without any sensory symptoms and with associated androgen insensitivity as evidenced by the gynecomastia and the sub fertility. text: A 26-year-old overweight woman presents with hirsutism and oligomenorrhoea. She has been unable to conceive for 18 months. The adrenals appear normal on ultrasound scanning, but an ovarian ultrasound scan reveals numerous small follicles in both ovaries. Which of the following is likely to fit best with her diagnosis?

options.A: The LH/FSH ratio is likely to be normal
options.B: Sex hormone-binding globulin is low in 50% of sufferers with this condition
options.D: Fertility is usually unaffected by this condition

ansText: Sex hormone-binding globulin is low in 50% of sufferers with this condition
expl: This is polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS). Oligo/amenorrhoea is present in 70%, hirsutism in 60%, obesity in 35% and infertility in 30%. LH is usually markedly raised, as is the LH/FSH ratio. Sex hormone-binding globulin is low in 50% of sufferers primarily due to hyperinsulinaemia. Testosterone and DHEAS (dehydroepiandrosterone) levels are also usually raised. Up to 40% of women with PCOS may have impaired glucose tolerance, and up to 10% frank type-2 diabetes mellitus. The insulin-resistant state is also associated with dyslipidemia. Management is usually with weight loss and lifestyle advice. Metformin is a useful treatment for insulin resistance and may help restore fertility, although clomiphene may also be required for ovulation induction. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 3035

text: A 43-year-old lady has increasing hirsutism. Her voice is becoming deeper. Ultrasound of the pelvis was unremarkable. Her serum testosterone was 2.1 ng/ml (normal-0.6 ng/ml) and serum DHEAS was 982 mcg/dl (normal: 35-200). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Rapid development of hirsutism with or without signs of virilisation can be caused by adrenal or ovarian tumours. Elevated testosterone can be present in both adrenal and ovarian tumours, however, elevated DHEAS level is characteristic of an adrenal tumour. A normal USG pelvis does not totally rule out ovarian tumours and may require further imaging, including MRI. A CAH is unlikely to present at this age. All forms of virilising CAH are characterised by elevated 17 hydroxyprogesterone levels. PCOS would have ovaries full of multiple cysts along with features of hyperandrogenism and insulin resistance. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Edition, Page Number-2968.

text: What is the likely diagnosis for a tall male who has no pubic or axillary hair, underdeveloped genitalia, high levels of LH and FSH, and an XXY karyotype?
expl: Explanation: The combination of male phenotype, tall stature, hypogonadism (underdeveloped genitalia, absent secondary sexual characteristics), hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (high LH/FSH), and a confirmed 47,XXY karyotype is diagnostic of Klinefelter syndrome. Pathophysiology The extra X chromosome leads to abnormal testicular development, resulting in: Primary Testicular Failure: This causes low testosterone (leading to undervirilization) and elevated gonadotropins (LH/FSH) due to lack of negative feedback. Infertility: Due to azospermia. Tall Stature: Disproportionately long legs. Explanation of other options: Vanishing testis syndrome (Option A): This would present with hypergonadotropic hypogonadism but in a patient with a normal 46,XY karyotype and unilateral or bilateral absence of testes. Noonan syndrome (Option C): This is characterized by short stature, congenital heart defects (e.g., pulmonic stenosis), and typical facial features, not tall stature and an XXY karyotype. Adrenal hyperplasia (Option D): This can cause virilization or salt-wasting in infants, but not this specific phenotype and karyotype. Key Takeaways: Klinefelter Syndrome = 47,XXY + Male Hypogonadism + Hypergonadotropic Hypogonadism. The classic triad is small firm testes, gynecomastia, and infertility .

text: A 29-year-old female with Turner syndrome is referred by the GP concerned about her blood pressure which he has found to be persistently elevated at between 140-160/90 mmHg. On examination she is noted to have a blood pressure of 148/92 mmHg, with no radio-femoral delay and no murmur audible. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her hypertension?
expl: Hypertension is quite common in Turner syndrome (10%) and is typically idiopathic i.e. essential hypertension. In a small proportion of cases, causes can include coarctation of the aorta and renal dysfunction due to horse-shoe kidney. In this case, the absence of specific features of coarctation would make essential hypertension the most appropriate option. text: A 44-year-old man attends a fertility clinic. On examination, he is tall, slim and has bilateral gynaecomastia. Investigations show high levels of plasma gonadotropins. What is the likely diagnosis?
expl: Klinefelter's syndrome is the most common cause of male hypogonadism with an incidence of 1 in 1000 male births. Usually, the karyotype is 47, XXY. Accelerated atrophy of germ cells before puberty results in sterility with small, firm testes . Many patients are tall with relatively long legs. Behavioral disorders and delayed speech development are common. Testosterone therapy may be used to improve the development of secondary sexual characteristics. Kallmann syndrome is characterised by hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (low LH, FSH) with anosmia. Testicular feminization syndrome( aka complete androgen insensitivity) is characterized by testosterone resistance.It presents as female phenotype, normal breast development (due to aromatization of testosterone), a short vagina but no uterus (because MIS / AMH production is normal), scanty pubic and axillary hair with a karyotype of 46 XY; Noonan syndrome (NS) is a clinically and genetically heterogeneous autosomal-dominant disorder. The classical features include short stature and congenital heart disease Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 3016

text: All of the following tests are done for screening in patients with Turner's syndrome, except?
expl: Explanation: Turner syndrome is a genetic condition caused by the complete or partial absence of one X chromosome. Individuals with Turner syndrome require lifelong, multidisciplinary care to monitor and manage associated health complications. The ANA test is not typically performed as part of Turner mosaic screening. ANA testing is primarily used to help diagnose autoimmune conditions such as systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) or other connective tissue diseases. Explanation of other options: Audiometry (Option B): This test is a standard and recurring part of care. Individuals with Turner syndrome have a very high prevalence of hearing issues, including conductive hearing loss from frequent otitis media and sensorineural hearing loss . Therefore, serial audiology evaluations are mandated throughout their lifespan. Echocardiography (Option C): This is a critical and mandatory screening tool, not an exception. Cardiovascular anomalies are among the most serious complications of Turner syndrome. An echocardiogram is required to diagnose and monitor conditions like bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation of the aorta, and aortic dilation/ dissection , which are significant causes of morbidity and require ongoing surveillance. Fasting Blood Glucose (Option D): Screening for metabolic disorders is a standard practice. Due to an increased risk of insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes , regular assessment of fasting glucose (and often hemoglobin A1c) is a core part of the annual health evaluation for adolescents and adults with Turner syndrome. Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK554621/

text: A 47-year-old woman presents complaining of fatigue and weight loss. She was successfully treated medically for a prolactinoma 3 years ago, and it is suspected that she might now have MEN-1. Which of the following underlying conditions is she most likely to have?
expl: Parathyroid hyperplasia is seen in the vast majority of patients with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN-1), and hypercalcaemia is the most common presenting feature of the condition. Hypercalcaemia may be discovered incidentally or because it is symptomatic, but the symptoms are often non-specific. Most common GEP-NET in MEN1 syndrome is gastrinoma and non-functional pancreatic NET Pituitary tumors occur in about 30% of patients: over a half are prolactinomas. Medullary-cell carcinomas of the thyroid and pheochromocytomas occur in MEN-2 but not in MEN-1. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 20 th edition Chapter:381 Page number:2746-48

text: Which of the following is not a feature of MEN-1?

text: Which of the following is associated with MEN-1 syndrome?

Parathyroid involvement is typically the first and most frequent manifestation of this syndrome. MEN-1 MEN-1 syndrome, also known as Wermer syndrome , results from a mutation in the MEN-1 gene located on chromosome 11q13 . The gene mutation leads to uncontrolled mitosis in endocrine glands. Triad of MEN-1 Parathyroid adenoma Presents as primary hyperparathyroidism (↑ PTH and ↑ Ca) Most common manifestation. Treatment of choice is total or subtotal parathyroid resection Pancreatic adenoma Commonly presents as Gastrinoma or Zollinger-Ellison syndrome Manifests as peptic ulcer disease in the duodenum, which is the leading cause of death in this type. Pituitary adenoma Presents as prolactinoma, causing amenorrhea and Infertility.

text: Which of the following is not a feature of MEN 2B syndrome?
expl: Explanation: Parathyroid adenomas are typically associated with MEN 1 and MEN 2A , but they are not a feature of MEN 2B . MEN 2B (also referred to as MEN 3) is an uncommon inherited disorder resulting from gain-of-function mutations in the RET proto-oncogene on chromosome 10q11.2. Key Features of MEN 2B: Medullary Thyroid Carcinoma (MTC): Most common; aggressive, often presenting at a young age. Pheochromocytoma: Usually bilateral, presenting with palpitations, headache, and sweating. Mucosal Neuromas (Option C ruled out): Seen as thickened lips, tongue, and eyelid nodules. Marfanoid Habitus (Option D ruled out): Tall stature, long limbs, arachnodactyly, hypermobile joints. Megacolon (Option A ruled out): Due to autonomic ganglion dysfunction of the intestine. Additional findings: Thickened corneal nerve fibers, delayed puberty. Comparison of MEN Syndromes

text: A 40-year-old male presents with recurrent urinary stones. His urine analysis showed crystals as shown below. What advice should be given to him?

options.A: Dietary calcium intake should be reduced to reduce the incidence of this stone.
options.B: Calcium supplements should be given to reduce the incidence of this stones.
options.C: DASH diet is an appropriate and readily available option to reduce the incidence of this stone.
options.D: Sodium bicarbonate can be an efficient agent to alkalinize the urine in this condition.

ansText: DASH diet is an appropriate and readily available option to reduce the incidence of this stone.
expl: So this question basically deals with identification of the specific stone type and its prevention strategies. Figure shows bipyramidal shaped crystals which indicate oxalate dihydrate crystals and hence the most likely stone is Calcium oxalate. So we have to understand the strategies to prevent Calcium oxalate stone formation. Oxalate monohydrate crystals are dump-bell shaped. Calcium and Oxalate in urine increases stone formation and citrate in urine decreases stone formation. STRATEGIES TO REDUCE URINE CALCIUM: Dietary calcium should not be lowered to reduce urinary calcium excretion. Lowering of dietary calcium increases the risk of oxalate absorption and also reduced bone health. Supplemental calcium increases stone formation , may be due to the timing of intake or net increase in total calcium intake. Sodium and sucrose intake should be reduced , since sodium will increase calcium excretion independent of calcium intake. Animal proteins also increase calcium levels in urine. Potassium supplements decrease calcium excretion and enhance the citrate excretion in urine. Urine alkalinization, to increase citrate excretion, using potassium citrate or bicarbonate is preferred. Sodium salts are not used because of the direct effect of sodium on calcium excretion. Dietary citrate should be increased by eating fruits and vegetables. STRATEGIES TO REDUCE URINARY OXALATE: Diet rich in oxalate like spinach, rhubarb, almonds and potatoes should be avoided. Adequate calcium intake must be ensured to reduce oxalate absorption. Citrate in diet or supplemented as potassium citrate is useful A practical approach is DASH diet. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 318, Pg: 2370-2372.

text: A 46-year-old woman has attended the emergency on a number of occasions this year because of renal tract stones. She has also suffered depression during the past year or two. She is found to have a serum calcium of 13 mg/dl, creatinine of 1.3 mg/dl and albumin of 4.0 g/dl. What is her most likely underlying diagnosis?
expl: This woman most likely has hyperparathyroidism. Hyperparathyroidism is the most common cause for hypercalcemia in an outpatient. Malignancy related causes form a major share of hypercalcemia etiology in an inpatient Hyperparathyroidism is a feature in 95% of patients with MEN-1 (multiple endocrine neoplasia - type 1) and may coexist with prolactin- or growth hormone-producing pituitary adenomas, pancreatic islet cell tumors, non-functioning adrenal adenomas or thyroid adenomas. As part of the MEN-2 syndrome, there is an association with phaeochromocytoma, Cushing's syndrome and medullary carcinoma of the thyroid. Short metacarpals (usually the fourth or fifth) are associated with pseudohypoparathyroidism, which, in turn, is associated with hypocalcaemia due to an abnormality of the G-protein receptor for parathyroid hormone. In the case of parathyroid hyperplasia or parathyroid adenoma, a surgical solution is the best option where symptoms such as renal stones have begun to appear. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 3173-74

text: A 45-year-old woman presents with a 6-month history of galactorrhoea. She also complains of a 5-year history of dyspepsia and persistent use of PPIs. Examination reveals a BMI of 23.5 kg/m2 and galactorrhoea was noticed. Slight neck enlargement was noticed during examination. Investigations show: prolactin: 980 mU/l (50-500 mU/l) estradiol: 85 pmol/l (130-500) LH of 3.1 mU/l (3.5-8) FSH of 2.8 mU/l (3-8) Serum calcium : 11.2 mg/dl (8.5-10.5) Ultrasonography revealed a parathyroid enlargement and a 99mTcO4/MIBI scan showed two hyperplastic lesions. What is the likely diagnosis?
expl: The biochemical picture suggests a diagnosis of a microprolactinoma. The patient is also likely to have a parathyroid tumour. In the presence of dyspepsia, a gastrinoma should be considered to form an overall diagnosis of MEN 1 [pituitary tumour, parathyroid tumor, pancreatic tumour]. Hyperparathyroidism is the most common manifestation of MEN 1, caused by hyperplasia of multiple parathyroid glands. Pancreatic islet cell tumors represent the second most common manifestation of MEN 1 and occur in 80% of patients. Gastrinoma, insulinomas or glucagonomas are all pancreatic tumors which may occur. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 20 th edition Chapter:381 Page number:2746-48 https://www.grepmed.com/images/7926/endocrine-men1-men2b-multiple-syndromes

text: A 74 year old man has significant bony pains which have been occuring for 3 years. He presents to the clinic for assessment and the investigations results were obtained below: Corrected calcium 9.6 mg/dl ESR 20 mm/1st hr Alkaline phosphatase 625 iu/L (50 - 100) gamma GT 42 iu/L (10-50) Prostate specific antigen 7.4 pg/L (0-6) What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: In Paget's disease, onset of symptoms is usually insidious, with pain, stiffness, bone deformity, headaches, decreasing auditory acuity, and increasing skull size. Signs may be bitemporal skull enlargement with frontal "bossing," dilated scalp veins, nerve deafness in one or both ears, angioid streaks in the fundus of the eye, and anterolateral bowing of the thigh or leg with warmth and periosteal tenderness. Pagetic lesions are metabolically active and highly vascular and may lead to high-output heart failure. Deformities may develop from bowing of the long bones or osteoarthritis of adjacent joints. Pathologic fractures may be the presenting finding. Characteristic x-ray findings include increased bone density, abnormal architecture, cortical thickening, bowing, and overgrowth. Biochemistry includes elevated serum alkaline phosphatase (or bone-specific alkaline phosphatase) and increased urinary excretion of pyridinoline cross-links. Serum calcium and phosphorus levels usually are normal, but serum calcium may increase during bed rest. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 412 Pg: 3211

text: A 58-year-old woman is referred by the Ortho department after attending with a vertebral fracture, the second in the last 3 years. She underwent a total hysterectomy with oophorectomy at the age of 38 for carcinoma. Bone densitometry confirms osteoporosis. The calcium and parathyroid hormone assays are normal. Which of the following is the most likely concerning her underlying pathophysiology?

options.A: She has suffered predominantly cortical bone loss
options.B: She has probably suffered an equal mix of cortical and trabecular bone loss
options.C: She has probably suffered predominantly trabecular bone loss

ansText: She has probably suffered predominantly trabecular bone loss
expl: Hypo-estrogenization, as in this case, is usually characterized by predominantly trabecular bone loss. Involutional bone loss of old age is characterized by a mixed picture of trabecular and cortical bone loss. In the presence of normal calcium and parathyroid hormone levels, parathyroid disease is ruled out. Hormone replacement therapy was formerly the mainstay of treatment, but this has fallen out of favor due to increased thromboembolic disease and the risk of breast carcinoma. The current line of therapy for osteoporosis include either anti-resorption agents like bisphosphonates and denosumab or anabolic agents like Teriparatide. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 3192-93

text: Which of the following statements is true regarding parathyroid hormone (PTH)?

options.C: The effect of magnesium on secretion is the same as that of calcium
options.D: Secretion is stimulated by low 1,25-hydroxyvitamin D and inhibited by high levels of 1,25-hydroxyvitamin D

ansText: Secretion is stimulated by low 1,25-hydroxyvitamin D and inhibited by high levels of 1,25-hydroxyvitamin D
expl: PTH, an 84-amino-acid peptide synthesized and secreted by the parathyroid gland, is a potent regulator of the serum calcium level. Hypocalcemia is the most potent stimulator of PTH secretion. Hypocalcemia stimulates the secretion of PTH acutely (with increased PTH synthesis and parathyroid cell hypertrophy and hyperplasia after chronic hypocalcemia), whereas hypercalcemia leads to decreased secretion of PTH. Hypomagnesemia inhibits PTH secretion. Elevated 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D affects PTH synthesis and secretion by directly inhibiting the parathyroid gland and indirectly via hypercalcemia. Low levels of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D have the opposite effect. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 3170

text: You got a reference from the Surgical dept to see a 36-year-old woman on the surgical ward who is 2 days' post-thyroidectomy. She is complaining of tingling around her mouth and in her hands and has developed a spasm of her hands. What immediate treatment can you give that is most likely to resolve her symptoms?

expl: Postoperative complications of thyroidectomy include recurrent laryngeal damage, hemorrhage and inadvertent removal of the parathyroid glands, although actually less than 1% of patients suffer permanent hypocalcemia. text: Which one of the following statements is true for the actions of parathyroid hormone (PTH)?

options.A: Acts directly on renal, bone, and intestinal cells
options.B: Acts directly on renal cells and indirectly on bone and intestinal cells
options.C: Acts directly on renal and bone cells and indirectly on intestinal cells
options.D: Has no direct actions on renal, bone, and intestinal cells

ansText: Acts directly on renal and bone cells and indirectly on intestinal cells
expl: PTH shares a receptor with PTH-related peptide (PTHrP), and this receptor is a member of the G protein–coupled receptor (GPCR) family. PTH/PTHrP receptors are expressed by kidney and bone cells, and PTH acts directly on renal and bone cells. PTH acts indirectly on intestinal cells to enhance calcium absorption as follows: PTH stimulates renal 1α-hydroxylase activity to promote synthesis of the active form of vitamin D (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D), which then acts on the intestine to enhance calcium absorption. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition, page number 3171

text: A 65-year-old man, who has been on haemodialysis for 12 years, presents with gradually increasing bone pain. He underwent subtotal parathyroidectomy 4 years ago. Current medications include alfacalcidol 1 m g/day and calcium carbonate 500 mg three times daily. His serum calcium concentration is 10.6 mg/dl, phosphate is 2.8 mg/dl. What is the most probable cause of his symptoms?
expl: Bone pain in patient with renal impairment points towards metabolic bone disease. It can be of 3 types: Secondary hyperparathyroidism: this is very rare these days due to the treatment of secondary hyperparathyroidism. It is characterized by hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia and high PTH Adynamic bone disease: Occurs due to over enthusiastic treatment of secondary hyperparathyroidism with vitamin D and calcium. It results in hypercalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, suppressed PTH and metastatic calcification. Tertiary hyperparathyroidism and Osteitis fibrosa Cystica, where untreated secondary hyperparathyroidism leads to autonomy and enlargement of one parathyroid gland leading to high calcium, low phosphorus and high PTH. Despite his previous parathyroidectomy, this patient clearly has hypercalcaemia and hypophosphatemia. This indicates tertiary hyperparathyroidism due to hyperplasia of retained parathyroid tissue. Indeed, even after total parathyroidectomy in end-stage renal failure, only 10% of patients have a total lack of parathyroid activity postoperatively. Residual parathyroid tissue may be detected using technetium-99 sestamibi scanning. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21 st edition, Ch:410, Pg:3181, 3182.

text: A 27-year-old woman is in end-stage renal disease. She has been started on regular haemodialysis. She complains of pain in her fingers. An X-ray shows digital subperiosteal erosions. What is the primary metabolic cause for her bony condition?
expl: Digital sub periosteal resorption is classical of Osteitis fibrosa cystica of hyperparathyroidism. In CKD secondary hyperparathyroidism may progress to tertiary hyperparathyroidism. The series of events that happen in CKD is: Declining GFR leads to reduced excretion of phosphate and thus, phosphate retention The retained phosphate stimulates increased synthesis of both FGF-23 by osteocytes and of PTH and also stimulates growth of parathyroid gland mass PTH production is stimulated by decreased levels of ionized calcium, which in turn, result from decreased levels of renal calcitriol production with reduced kidney mass and suppression of calcitriol production due to phosphate retention and elevated levels of FGF-23, which also increases degradation of calcitriol. text: Which of the following mechanisms is responsible for Glucocorticoid induced osteoporosis?

options.C: Decreased calcium absorption from the gastrointestinal (GI) tract

expl: The incidence of steroid-induced osteoporosis is unknown, but it appears to be related to the duration of treatment, half-life of the steroid and its dose . Risk factors associated with increased bone loss include age, body mass index and duration of use. Steroid-induced osteoporosis proceeds rapidly in the first 6 months of steroid use and slows thereafter. Trabecular bone and the cortical rim of the vertebral body are most susceptible to the effects of steroids. Glucocorticoids induce bone loss by several mechanisms. Inhibit calcium absorption in the GIT while enhancing calcium loss in the kidneys. These effects induce secondary hyperparathyroidism, which leads to increased bone resorption. Lower sex hormone levels through an effect on the gonadotropin levels and a direct effect at the gonadal level, as well as by decreasing adrenal sex steroid synthesis by inhibiting ACTH release. Direct inhibitory effect on osteoblast proliferation, activity and half-life, leading to decreased bone formation. Induce proximal muscle weakness. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 3195

text: Which of the following is not a cause of hypocalcemia?
expl: Acute adrenal insufficiency is associated with hypercalcemia, not hypocalcemia. Hypocalcemia typically occurs in patients with secondary hyperparathyroidism and in those with vitamin D–resistance disorders. In addition, autoimmune destruction of the parathyroids, resulting in hypoparathyroidism, or autoantibodies to the calcium-sensing receptor may be associated with hypocalcemia. Endocrinological causes of hypercalcemia: Primary hyperparathyroidism (adenoma, hyperplasia, rarely carcinoma) Tertiary hyperparathyroidism (long-term stimulation of PTH secretion in renal insufficiency) Ectopic PTH secretion (very rare) Adrenal insufficiency Pheochromocytoma Thyrotoxicosis Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 3186

expl: MEN-1 is associated with Pituitary adenoma, Parathyroid hyperplasia and Pancreatic tumours. text: A 30-year-old woman presents with bone pain and abdominal cramps, and her family mentions a history of unusual behaviour. Based on these clinical features, the doctor suspects a diagnosis. Which investigation would be the most suitable to confirm it?
expl: Explanation: The clinical features of bone pain due to excessive bone resorption, abdominal discomfort from elevated calcium levels, and neuropsychiatric manifestations such as behavioural changes point toward primary hyperparathyroidism , for which the preferred imaging modality is a sestamibi scan . Explanation of other options: MRI (Option A): Although MRI can detect soft tissue lesions, it is not the preferred initial imaging technique for identifying parathyroid adenomas, as it is costlier, takes longer, and provides no clear benefit compared to sestamibi scanning in parathyroid evaluation. Ultrasonogram (Option B): Ultrasound can help visualise parathyroid enlargement, but its accuracy is limited by operator skill and difficulty in detecting ectopic glands. It is often used as an adjunctive test rather than the most reliable first-line diagnostic method. CT scan (Option D) : CT scan offers precise anatomical detail but does not provide the functional assessment available with sestamibi scans. Although helpful in preoperative planning, it is not considered the primary imaging method for diagnosing parathyroid adenomas.

text: First line drug for post-menopausal osteoporosis
expl: Postmenopausal women are susceptible to primary osteoporosis since osteoporosis is closely related to estrogen deficiency. During the menopausal transition period, the drop of estrogen leads to more bone resorption than formation, resulting in osteoporosis. Bisphosphonates are the first line agent for postmenopausal osteoporosis. ANTIRESORPTIVE AGENTS: Bisphosphonates are the first line agent for postmenopausal osteoporosis. Calcitonin : nasal and subcutaneous are approved for treatment of postmenopausal osteoporosis, but not as the first line agent. Strontium is used in patients not responding to other agents Denosumab is the first human monoclonal antibody approved for treatment and prevention of osteoporosis. Estrogens have fallen out of choice because of their side effects like DVT and risk of breast and endometrial malignancy. Odanacatib, a cathepsin K inhibitor, inhibits the osteoclast collagenase enzyme, preventing bone resorption but not affecting osteoclast viability ANABOLIC AGENTS: Parathormone: Intermittent Teriparatide is indicated in moderate to severe osteoporosis. Abaloparatide is a synthetic analogue of human PTHrP, which has significant homology to PTH and also binds the PTH type 1 receptor. Romosozumab is a humanized antibody that blocks the osteocyte production of sclerostin, resulting in an increase in bone formation and decline in bone resorption.

text: Which of the following foods is not included in the DASH diet?
expl: Explanation: The DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) diet specifically emphasizes limiting sodium intake . It is designed to be low in sodium while being rich in potassium, calcium, magnesium, and fiber to help lower blood pressure. Developed in 1990s (NIH); lowers systolic BP by 6-11 mmHg. Focuses on fruits, vegetables, whole grains, lean protein, low-fat dairy, and low sodium (~1500 mg/day). Key Nutrients: Carbs: Whole grains, legumes, greens Fats: Healthy oils, nuts, omega-3 fish; avoid trans fats Proteins: Plant-based preferred, lean meats, low-fat dairy Electrolytes: Potassium (bananas, spinach, beans) - lowers BP Sodium restriction (~1500 mg/day)- reduces HTN risk Calcium (dairy, greens) - bone/muscle health Magnesium (whole grains, nuts, seeds) - vessel relaxation, BP control Clinical Benefits: Lowers BP, glucose, LDL, triglycerides, and insulin resistance; beneficial in metabolic syndrome, diabetes, and HF. Reduces risk of colorectal cancer, liver disease, celiac disease, and improves HF outcomes. Explanation of other options: Rich in potassium ,Rich in calcium and Rich in magnesium (Option A,B and D): The DASH diet encourages the consumption of foods rich in these minerals, such as fruits, vegetables, low-fat dairy, and nuts, which are integral to its blood pressure-lowering effects. Key Takeaways: The DASH diet is a low-sodium, high-potassium, high-calcium, and high-magnesium eating plan. Its primary goal is the prevention and management of hypertension.

text: A 57 year old man with diabetic nephropathy has a plasma creatinine of 4.3 mg/dl(NR 0.6-1.4 mg/dl), potassium 5.2 mmol/l, calcium 8.8 mg/dl, albumin 4.2 g/dl, phosphate 4.4 mg/dl and PTH 1.6 pmol/l(NR 1.4-6.8). Which of the following should be commenced?
expl: This question basically deals with Ca and phosphate metabolism in CKD. There are certain key points to be understood in CKD. The basic problem in CKD is phosphate retention due to decreased GFR and decreased Vitamin D activation due to 1α hydroxylase deficiency which leads to hypocalcemia, both lead to increased PTH production and secondary hyperparathyroidism. Uncontrolled secondary hyperparathyroidism leads to osteitis fibrosa cystica. So treatment of Secondary hyperparathyroidism is essential to prevent bone changes. The first step is to restrict dietary phosphorus The next step is phosphate binders. Calcium acetate and calcium carbonate are phosphate binders. Non calcium containing phosphate binders are Aluminium containing antacids, ferric citrate, sucroferric oxohydroxide and magnesium. Phosphate binding resins include Sevelamer and Lanthanum. Calcium levels should be measured and corrected. Vitamin D levels should be measured and corrected. Calcitriol and 1α hydroxylated vitamin D are given to treat secondary hyperparathyroidism after correcting phosphate levels and monitoring of 25 hydroxy vit d levels. So this patient should be treated with dietary phosphate deficiency, calcium supplements and phosphate binder. Since Calcium carbonate can act as a phosphate binder and source of calcium, it can be given. Alfacalcidol could be considered for prophylaxis against renal bone disease and progressive hyperparathyroidism. However, the patient's phosphate level is already elevated and vitamin D supplementation may increase this further. Vitamin D supplements should not be started without correcting phosphate levels. Aluminium-containing phosphate binders carry the risk of aluminium accumulation and CNS effects. Calcium acetate or calcium carbonate can be used. It should be taken with(or just before) meals and may offer advantages over calcium carbonate. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal medicine, 21 st edition, Ch:311, Pg:2314-2315

expl: So this patient already is on treatment to retard secondary hyperparathyroidism. From the previous question, we know what are the agents used for treatment of Ca and PO 4 homeostasis. So what will be the adverse effects of over enthusiastic correction of secondary hyperparathyroidism? Calcium containing phosphate binders will lead to hypercalcemia. Over enthusiastic treatment with vitamin D will lead to hyperphosphatemia, hypercalcemia and soft tissue calcification. Calcium and vitamin D supplementation will lead to excessive suppression of PTH and impaired bone remodelling. All these together constitute ADYNAMIC BONE DISEASE. If we look at the values, our patient is also suffering from adynamic bone disease. The intake of calcium, vitamin D supplements should be avoided and dialysate calcium should be reduced. Decrease in dietary phosphorous will be helpful too. But there will not be much use in adynamic bone disease by increasing the dialysis frequency. text: The anti-arrhythmic effect of amiodarone is mostly attributed to blockade of which of the following?
expl: Amiodarone is a class III antiarrhythmic used in many supra and ventricular arrhythmias. Its antiarrhythmic effects are due mostly to the inhibition of the rapid component of the delayed potassium rectifier IKr channel (as with sotalol) but also an effect on the slow component. It can also block the inactivated Na channels during Phase 0 of cardiac action potential. It has milder calcium channel and beta receptor blocking action as well. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 1914

text: A 50 year old man who presents with dizziness has broad complexes on the ECG. His blood gas reveals that his K is 8 mmol/l. Which of the following is the best medical therapy?
expl: Urgent management of hyperkalemia constitutes a 12-lead ECG, admission to the hospital, continuous electrocardiographic monitoring, and immediate treatment. The treatment of hyperkalemia is generally divided into three categories: (1) antagonism of the cardiac effects of hyperkalemia; (2) rapid reduction in K+ by redistribution into cells; and (3) removal of K+ from the body. Intravenous calcium is the first-line drug in the emergency management of hyperkalemia, even in patients with normal calcium levels. The mutually antagonistic effects of calcium and K+ on the myocardium and the protective role of Ca 2+ in hyperkalemia have long been known. The first line therapy for cardio-protection is calcium gluconate. Following this, insulin and dextrose should be given. Reference: Harrisons Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:53 Pg: 355

text: A 54-year-old chronic smoker presents with polyuria, polydipsia and altered sensorium for the past 2 days. He is known to be suffering from squamous-cell carcinoma of the lung. On examination he is lethargic and confused. ECG shows a narrowed QT interval. What is the most probable metabolic abnormality?
expl: Paraneoplastic syndromes in bronchogenic carcinoma can cause several electrolytes abnormalities. The features in this case are suggestive of hypercalcaemia. This occurs due to parathyroid hormone-related peptide (PTHrP) production. Important complications of hypercalcemia include encephalopathy, dehydration and risk of pre renal AKI, acute pancreatitis and shortened QT interval. expl: Explanation: Hypothermia ( J waves (Osborn waves) on ECG. They may resemble a "camel hump" appearance. The ECG presented here demonstrates these characteristic findings, which are strongly indicative of hypothermia. text: A 52-year-old man has effort-related angina. His total cholesterol is 212 mg/dl. He has no other cardiac risk factors and no other relevant medical history. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
expl: The choice of first-line treatment for the prophylaxis of effort-related angina in someone without contraindications is a β-Blocker . β-Blockers also remain the choice in someone who has suffered a previous myocardial infarction. Calcium-channel blockers - especially diltiazem and verapamil can be used, although they should be avoided in the presence of significant left ventricular dysfunction. Nitrates are of good value, but they come after β-Blockers. Care should be taken before combining a β-Blocker and non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker, especially if there is evidence of conduction disturbance or LV dysfunction . The Scandinavian Simvastatin Survival Study showed that a statin given to patients with angina pectoris and a cholesterol level of 212-308 mg/dl significantly reduced the risk of MI. Aspirin would also of course be recommended for secondary prevention of ischaemic events and nitrates could be used for symptom relief. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page no: 2041

text: All of the following are ECG changes of hypercalcemia, except?
expl: Mild hypercalcemia (up to 11-11.5 mg/dL) is usually asymptomatic and recognized only on routine calcium measurements. Some patients may complain of vague neuropsychiatric symptoms, including trouble concentrating, personality changes, or depression. Other presenting symptoms may include peptic ulcer disease or nephrolithiasis, and fracture risk may be increased. More severe hypercalcemia (>12-13 mg/dL), particularly if it develops acutely, may result in lethargy, stupor, or coma, as well as gastrointestinal symptoms (nausea, anorexia, constipation, or pancreatitis). Hypercalcemia decreases renal concentrating ability, which may cause polyuria and polydipsia. With long-standing hyperparathyroidism, patients may present with bone pain or pathologic fractures. Finally, hypercalcemia can result in significant electrocardiographic changes, including bradycardia, AV block, and short QT interval; changes in serum calcium can be monitored by following the QT interval. Osborn waves in severe hypercalcaemia Reference: Harrisons Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:54 Pg: 357

text: A 32-year-old woman with a 10-year history of chronic renal insufficiency secondary to bilateral obstructive hydronephrosis presented for evaluation of pain in the right hip. She had undergone bilateral ureterostomies, but her creatinine level remained chronically elevated. An X ray revealed a fracture of the right femoral neck necessitating internal fixation. X-ray hand also showed resorption of middle phalanx of fingers. What is the likely diagnosis?
expl: In this patient, hyperparathyroidism is secondary to renal osteodystrophy. The hip fracture and the typical radiographic findings in hand X-ray are consistent with hyperparathyroidism. The factors contributing to hyperparathyroidism in renal failure include impaired phosphate excretion, decreased 1 alpha hydroxylase activity leading to hypocalcemia and renal resistance to PTH. Osteoporosis, a condition characterized by decreased bone strength which predominantly affects post menopausal women and presents as vertebral and hip fractures. Osteopetrosis refers to a group of disorders caused by severe impairment of osteoclast-mediated bone resorption. Severe forms present as cranial nerve palsies, pancytopenia, hypersplenism, hypocalcaemia Pseudohypoparathyroidism refers to a group of distinct inherited disorders which present with hypocalcaemia with or without skeletal deformities due to deficient downstream signaling of parathyroid hormone Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 3173

text: A 65-year-old man presents with bony pain that has been present for some months, particularly affecting his left femur, pelvis and lower back. Blood testing reveals a normal serum calcium and phosphorous level, but a raised alkaline phosphatase. X-rays of the femur and pelvis reveal mixed lytic and sclerotic change, with accentuated trabecular markings. Chest X-ray is normal. What is the likely diagnosis?
expl: Paget's disease is thought to be present in 2% of the population above 55 years of age, with 90% being asymptomatic. It is more common in Caucasian populations and rarer in populations of African descent. There are said to be three phases associated with the time course of radiological changes seen in Paget's disease. primarily lytic mixed lytic and sclerotic changes primarily sclerotic change with increasing bony thickening. The typical named X-ray signs associated with Paget's disease include 'flame sign/blade of grass sign' in long bones, 'ivory vertebra', 'cotton wool skull' and 'Mickey Mouse pelvis' Goals of treatment are to normalize bone turnover, maintain the alkaline phosphatase level within the normal range, minimize symptoms and prevent long-term complications. Bisphosphonates (IV zoledronic acid) is the treatment of choice. Long-term complications include deafness (in up to 50% of patients with skull-base Paget's disease), high output cardiac failure, fractures and very rarely osteogenic sarcoma. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 3210

text: A 46 year old man has had a 5 year history of severe sharp, epigastric pains and diarrhoea. He gets 2-3 episodes of these symptoms a day. His GP has prescribed proton pump inhibitors which has helped partly, but he still complains that the symptoms are severe. Which one of the following might confirm the diagnosis?
expl: Severe epigastric pain with only partial response to PPI indicates a peptic ulcer secondary to Gastrinoma, which is supported by the symptom of diarrhoea. The diagnosis is likely to be Zollinger Ellison syndrome. Gastrin levels are significantly elevated. The secretin test can help to confirm the diagnosis. There is increased gastrin elevation (greater than 200 pg/mL) in a positive test after secretin is given intravenously . The most common presentation is abdominal pain (gastric acid hypersecretion causes ulceration) followed by diarrhea (due to malabsorption, pancreatic enzyme inactivation by acid) There is an association with the MEN 1 syndrome , so calcium levels should be checked (to screen for a parathyroid adenoma). text: A 75-year-old woman was brought to the hospital following a fall. Her neighbour thinks that she was on the floor for about 4 days. Her blood results show: sodium 132 mEq/l, potassium 6.5 mEq/l, urea 110 mg/dl, creatinine 7.3 mg/dl, calcium 7.6 mg/dl, phosphate 7.5 mg/dl.(Ref values: s. creatinine: 0.6-1.4 mg/dl; S. urea: 17 - 43 mg/dL; s. sodium: 135-145 mEq/L; S. potassium: 3.5-5 mEq/L; S. calcium: 8.8 - 10 mg/dl; S. phosphate: 3.0-4.5 mg/dL)Which of the following investigations is most likely to reveal the diagnosis?
expl: The question deals with renal impairment, probably acute, in an elderly woman, who was found unresponsive and who is suspected to have fallen at least 4 days back. Muscle compression due to prolonged immobilization, as in this case will result in release of myoglobin. It is toxic to the renal tubules and will result in AKI. The most likely diagnosis is rhabdomyolysis and acute renal failure. The history is suggestive along with hyperkalemia, hypocalcaemia, and hyperphosphatemia. Serum creatine kinase and myoglobin will be elevated. Other causes of rhabdomyolysis are: Traumatic crush injuries Muscle ischemia during vascular or orthopedic surgery Compression during coma or immobilization Prolonged seizure activity Excessive exercise Heat stroke Malignant hyperthermia Infections Metabolic disorders (e.g., hypophosphatemia, severe hypothyroidism) Myopathies (drug-induced, metabolic, or inflammatory). Urine dipstick will be positive for blood (myoglobinuria) but microscopy will not show red cells. A renal biopsy may also reveal the diagnosis. Treatment is with hydration (normal saline) and alkalinisation of urine with sodium bicarbonate infusion. Option A: Ultrasound is useful only to distinguish obstructive Etiologies and cystic kidney diseases Option B: MRA is useful to assess for renal vascular diseases Option C: A DMSA scan is a radionuclide scan that uses dimercaptosuccinic acid (DMSA) in assessing renal morphology, structure and function Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st Ed, Ch: 310 Pg: 2301

text: A 30-year-old man has returned from a trip to India recently. He presents with bloody diarrhoea which started three weeks ago. He now has malaise and swelling of his legs. He has poor urine output. Blood tests show: Hb 8 g/dL WBC: 14,000/ µL Neutrophils: 9000/ µL Platelets: 20,000/ µLPT 13s, APTT 33sFibrinogen 4 g/dL, sodium 136 mmol/ L, potassium 6.1 mmol/L, urea 420 mg/dl creatinine 7.8 mg/dl albumin 3 g/dL. Urine dipstick: blood ++, protein +. (Ref values: Hb: 1B-14 g/dl; WBC: 4000-10000/ µL; Platelets: 1.5 to 4.5 lakh/µL; s. creatinine: 0.6-1.4 mg/dl; S. urea: 17 - 43 mg/dL; s. sodium: 135-145 mEq/L; S. potassium: 3.5-5 mEq /L; S. calcium: 8.8 - 10 mg/dl; S. phosphate: 3.0-4.5 mg/dL; S. albumin: 3.5 -5 g/dl) What is the next best investigation to confirm the likely diagnosis?
expl: The patient gives history of a diarrhoeal illness, following which he develops renal impairement. In addition to renal failure, he has anemia, thrombocytopenia. All these favor the diagnosis of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia and thrombotic microangiopathy following an infection. The diagnosis is haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS) . The typical presentation is with a triad of acute renal failure, Microangiopathic haemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia. Most commonly the cause is E coli O157:H7 (verotoxin producing E coli), hence stool cultures would be the best investigation to confirm the diagnosis in this case. Other diagnostic measure will be the demonstration of Shiga toxin in the stool specimen. Other causes are shigella, cyclosporine and connective tissue diseases. The thrombocytopenia is thought to be a consequence of platelet consumption at sites of endothelial injury. Despite this blood clotting times (prothrombin time, kaolin clotting time) are normal. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch:317, Pg:2364.

text: A 68-year-old man has a new-patient screen carried out by his GP. He is noted to have microscopic haematuria. His GP also notes a raised ESR and a calcium concentration of 12.4 mg/dl. On examination he appears to have a varicocele. What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
expl: Elderly male with microscopic hematuria and varicocoele with hypercalcemia best fits into the diagnosis of renal cell carcinoma. Renal-cell adenocarcinoma makes up 3% of all adult malignancies, with peak incidence being 50-70 years. There is a male to female preponderance of 2:1. Haematuria is the presenting feature in 50-60% of cases, raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate(ESR) in 50-60% and abdominal mass a presenting feature in 25-45%. Varicocele, resulting from obstruction of venous drainage, is found in 2-3% of cases. Hypercalcaemia occurs due to raised parathyroid-related protein in around 3% of cases. Erythrocytosis, non-metastatic hepatic dysfunction(Stauffer's Syndrome) and dysfibrinogenemia are other paraneoplastic syndromes associated. Anemia occurs in advanced cases. Genetic causes of RCC include Tuberous Sclerosis and Von Hippel Lindau syndrome Imaging studies to detect renal-cell adenocarcinoma include ultrasound scan, intravenous pyelography(IVP), abdominal CT with contrast and MRI. Commonest sites of metastases are lung(50-60%) and bone(30-40%). Treatment of choice is nephrectomy in localized disease. Metastatic RCC is resistant to cytotoxic chemotherapy. They are treated with TKI and mTOR inhibitors. Immune check point inhibitor Nivolumab is the second line agent. Prognosis is related to tumour staging: the 5-year survival rate is around 80-100% in those with TNM stage-1 lesions, but this falls to 5-10% in those with stage-4 lesions. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 85, Pg: 673-676.

text: Identify false statement?

options.A: Primary hyperoxaluria predisposes to calcium oxalate stones, renal parenchymal calcification and renal failure.
options.B: Male calcium oxalate stone formers should be advised not to take vitamin C.
options.C: Avoidance of purine rich diet is beneficial in preventing all types of stones.
options.D: Struvite stones does not require removal in most cases

ansText: Struvite stones does not require removal in most cases
expl: Struvite stones occur due to infection with urease producing bacteria, Klebsiella, Proteus, Pseudomonas and Providencia. Coffin lid shaped. Form rapidly growing stag horn calculi and usually requires removal. Acetohydroxamic acid which inhibits urease is not used because of side effects. Avoidance of purine rich diet is helpful in preventing stones because purine in diet causes metabolic acidosis and acidosis leads to hypocitraturia. Citrate in urine inhibits stone formation. Vitamin C supplementation increases oxalate excretion in males and hence should be avoided in oxalate stone formers. Primary hyperoxaluria is an AR disease, associated with excessive oxalate production, stone formation and renal failure. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 318, Pg: 2369-2373.
