text: CFTR gene mutation involves which ion and which mutation?

options.A: Chloride ion and deletion of phenylalanine at 508 positions
options.B: Chloride ion and deletion of tryptophan at 508 positions
options.C: Chloride ion and deletion of phenylalanine at 708 positions
options.D: Chloride ion and deletion of tryptophan at 708 positions

ansText: Chloride ion and deletion of phenylalanine at 508 positions
expl: The gene product responsible for CF is CFTR, which serves as an anion channel in the luminal surfaces of epithelial cells, where it regulates the volume and consistency of exocrine secretions. CFTR mutations lead to abnormally thick secretions. In the lung it leads to recurrent infections. In the pancreas, it leads to the obstruction of the pancreatic duct leading to malabsorption and steatorrhoea . Obstruction of intrahepatic bile duct leads to cirrhosis, in males it leads to involution of vas deferens and infertility. CFTR mutations: Class I mutation: Absence of synthesis of CFTR. CFTR nonsense mutations like G542X, R553X, or W1282X are examples. Class II mutation: Defective protein maturation and premature degradation. F508 deletion. Most common mutation. Lumacaftor and Tezacaftor repair CFTR misfolding and promote cell surface localization of F508 CFTR. Elexacaftor, is a third generation molecule effective for F508 as well as a variety of other CFTR mutations. Class III: Disordered gating, ATP binding or hydrolysis. G551D, leads to inability to transport Cl or HCO3. Ivacaftor overcomes the defect. Approved for 96 other variants apart from G551D. Class IV: Defective conductance through the pore. Class V: A reduced number of CFTR transcripts. Class VI: Accelerated turnover from the cell surface. Ivacaftor tezacaftor and Elixacaftor are approved as triple combination therapy for CF. it benefits >90% cases with the disease . Improvements in FEV1, fewer infections, improvement in QOL and diminished sweat chloride levels. Designated as Highly Effective Modulator Treatment.

text: A 65 year old male patient visited the ER for chest pain and his BP was measured as SBP 190 mmHg, DBP 70 mmHg, Pulse pressure 90 mmHg. Which of the following parameters should decrease for the high pulse pressure?
expl: Pulse pressure = Systolic BP-Diastolic BP The diastolic BP is determined by the arterial compliance. The diastolic BP falls as the arterial compliance decreases as in old age. The systolic BP is dependent on the stroke volume. So for pulse pressure to increase, either the stroke volume has to increase or the arterial compliance has to decrease.

text: A patient with chronic liver disease presents to the emergency department with the acute onset of fever after ingestion of oysters. The physical examination reveals a patient in shock with multiple erythematous lesions on the extremities. The most likely pathogen involved is:
expl: Vibrio vulnificus is the most likely pathogen. It causes severe sepsis with soft tissue involvement in patients with chronic liver disease. Infections in humans typically occur in coastal states between May and October and most commonly affect men >40 years of age. V. vulnificus has been linked to two distinct syndromes: primary sepsis, which usually occurs in patients with underlying liver disease primary wound infection, which generally affects people without underlying disease. The organism's virulence is considerably increased under conditions of iron overload; this observation is consistent with the propensity of V. vulnificus to infect patients who have hemochromatosis. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 168 Pg: 1310

text: A 30-year-old woman presents with symptoms of an unsteady gait, memory loss, and mood swings. During the neurological examination, the findings shown in the image below are observed. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The image displays fine pigmented, granular deposits characteristic of Kayser-Fleischer rings, which result from copper buildup in the Descemet's membrane of the cornea. This finding is highly suggestive of Wilson's disease. Wilson's Disease Also called hepatolenticular degeneration, Wilson's disease is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by abnormal copper accumulation in the liver, brain, eyes, and other organs. This leads to elevated free copper levels, increased copper in the liver and urine, and decreased serum ceruloplasmin. Genetic Cause: The disease is caused by mutations in the ATP7B gene on chromosome 13. This gene encodes a copper-transporting ATPase responsible for removing copper from the liver into bile. Pathogenesis: Mutation in the ATP7B gene Impaired biliary copper excretion Copper accumulates in liver cells (hepatocytes) Excess copper causes oxidative damage, promoting inflammation and fibrosis in the liver When liver storage capacity is exceeded, copper is released into the bloodstream Copper then accumulates in other tissues: Brain: Particularly basal ganglia, causing neurological symptoms Cornea: Forms Kayser-Fleischer rings Kidneys: Can lead to renal dysfunction Joints: Causes arthritic changes Copper accumulation causes tissue damage through oxidative stress, lipid peroxidation, and enzyme inhibition Explanation of Other Options: Neurofibromatosis 2 (Option A): typically presents with juvenile cataracts in children, retinal hamartomas, and similar features. Neurofibromatosis 1 (Option C): is characterized by Lisch nodules, which are small, raised brown spots on the iris. Cataracts (Option D): usually appear as wedge-shaped opacities (cortical cataracts) or darkened lenses (nuclear cataracts) with distinct clinical signs. The scenario described here does not align with cataract presentations. Reference: https://tinyurl.com/3ek9r4ym

text: Congo red positivity and apple green bifringence is seen in which among the conditions?
expl: Explanation: The diagnostic hallmark of amyloidosis is the detection of amyloid protein deposits in tissues. The most widely used method is Congo red staining , which shows apple-green birefringence under polarized light microscopy . Amyloid is formed from misfolded proteins that aggregate into β-pleated sheet structures , giving them a unique staining pattern. On routine histology, amyloid appears as amorphous, eosinophilic deposits . When stained with Congo red dye , these deposits display apple-green birefringence under polarized light - a pathognomonic feature of amyloidosis. This is in contrast to other protein deposits such as collagen, which appear white under polarized light. The deposits can be detected in tissues like abdominal fat (via fat pad biopsy), kidney, heart, liver, rectal mucosa, or gingiva. Multiple myeloma (Option A): While AL amyloidosis can occur secondary to multiple myeloma, the staining pattern itself is not a feature of myeloma but specifically of amyloid. Sarcoidosis (Option B): Characterized by non-caseating granulomas , not amyloid deposits, and does not show Congo red positivity. Hemochromatosis (Option C): Involves iron overload in tissues, demonstrated by Prussian blue staining , not Congo red.

text: The KF ring is associated with which of the following conditions?
expl: Explanation: The Kayser-Fleischer (KF) ring is due to copper deposition in Descemet's membrane of the cornea . It is a hallmark feature of Wilson's disease , an autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism characterised by hepatic, neurological, and psychiatric manifestations . Slit-lamp examination is the best method to visualise KF rings. Explanation of other options: Hemochromatosis (Option A): Characterised by iron overload affecting the liver, pancreas, heart, and skin ("bronze diabetes"), but no KF ring is seen. Alzheimer's disease (Option C): A neurodegenerative disorder with memory loss and amyloid plaques, not associated with copper deposition. Huntington's disease (Option D): A genetic movement disorder due to CAG repeats, with chorea and psychiatric features, but no ocular signs like KF rings.

text: You are asked to review a 56-year-old psychiatric patient by his family doctor. This patient has been diagnosed with impaired glucose tolerance. He also has a history of hypertension, for which he takes Ramipril. Which of the following drug classes is most well known as a cause of impaired glucose tolerance?
expl: Older atypical antipsychotic agents have been implicated as a cause of impaired glucose tolerance, and are thought to put those taking them at increased risk of type-2 diabetes. Thiazides and β-blockers may also impact negatively on the incidence of new diabetes, and this combination of antihypertensives is no longer a first choice for patients with a high type-2 diabetes risk. Ramipril was shown in the HOPE (Healthcare Options Plan Entitlement) study to reduce progression to type-2 diabetes; this is thought to be mediated by a reduction in insulin resistance. The LIFE (Longitudinal Interval Follow-up Evaluation) study using losartan has demonstrated that angiotensin-receptor blockers also probably reduce the incidence of new cases of type-2 diabetes. Thiazolidinediones and biguanides work by primarily reducing insulin resistance, sulphonylureas stimulate insulin release; all three are used as treatments for type-2 diabetes. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Pg:3095

text: All of the following increase risk of Alzheimer's disease except?
expl: A history of head trauma with concussion increases the risk for AD. AD is more common in groups with low educational attainment, but education influences test-taking ability, and it is clear that AD can affect persons of all intellectual levels. Diabetes increases the risk of AD threefold. Elevated homocysteine and cholesterol levels; hypertension; diminished serum levels of folic acid; low dietary intake of fruits, vegetables, and red wine; and low levels of exercise are all being explored as potential risk factors for AD. Several retrospective studies suggest that nonsteroidal antiinflammatory agents and 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A (HMG-CoA) reductase inhibitors (statins) may have a protective effect on dementia if used prior to the onset of disease but do not influence clinically symptomatic AD. text: A 30-year-old woman presents with vomiting, malaise and weakness 5 weeks after delivering a healthy male infant. The pregnancy had been uncomplicated with no hypertension evident. Her blood pressure is now 210/110 mmHg, plasma creatinine is 5.5 mg/dl and potassium: 6.9 mmol/l. Haemoglobin: 7.6 g/dl, platelet count of 65000/&microl, reticulocytes of 7%, normal clotting indices and lactate dehydrogenase levels of 800 IU/l. Which of the following most accurately describes the pathological process?
expl: The history is typical of postpartum haemolytic-uraemic syndrome(HUS) , which usually occurs 4-6 week's postpartum and is characterised by microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, severe irreversible renal failure and hypertension. Schistocytes are evident on the blood film but the clotting indices are normal, the latter helping to distinguish it from the DIC. The differential diagnosis of acute renal failure in the setting of pregnancy includes postpartum HUS, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura(which occurs invariably antepartum and usually before 24 weeks and is associated with relatively mild renal failure) and the HELLP syndrome(which is usually preceded by a history of pre-eclampsia and is characterised by evidence of disseminated intravascular coagulation). All may be complicated by acute cortical necrosis, resulting in oliguria, haematuria and flank pain. In cases of postpartum HUS, it is important to consider the possibility of retained products of conception. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 314, Pg: 2348.

text: A patient who is a known case of hypertension on multiple antihypertensive medications came to the OPD. His ECG finding is given below. Which of the following drugs is responsible for the ECG finding?
expl: Explanation: Spironolactone can cause hyperkalemia, which presents on ECG as tall, peaked T waves. The ECG finding of tall, peaked T waves is a classic sign of hyperkalemia. Among the given options, spironolactone is the most likely culprit because it is a potassium-sparing diuretic. It acts by blocking aldosterone receptors in the distal tubule and collecting duct, thereby inhibiting sodium reabsorption and reducing potassium excretion. This leads to potassium retention, raising serum potassium levels and causing hyperkalemia. ECG changes in hyperkalemia progress with severity: Explanation of other options: Prazosin (Option A): Alpha-1 blocker used in hypertension; not associated with hyperkalemia. Metoprolol (Option B): Beta-blocker; does not usually cause hyperkalemia, though rare cases exist in renal dysfunction. Hydrochlorothiazide (Option C): Thiazide diuretic that promotes potassium loss, leading to hypokalemia rather than hyperkalemia. Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6205312/

text: 'Obstruction of Inferior vena cava' presents :
expl: :B A. Paraumbilicus vein dilation and B i.e. Thoraco-epigastric dilation The thoracoepigastric vein is unique in that it drains to both the Superior Vena Cava (SVC) and to the Inferior Vena Cava (IVC). Hence, it serves as an anastomotic caval-caval link between the two. Furthermore, the thoracoepigastric vein is connected to the portal vein via the paraumbilical vein and thereby serves as a portocaval anastomosis as well. When a patient experiences portal hypertension, there can be congestion (backup) of blood that enters into the caval system via the thoracoepigastric vein. When this occurs, there can be an externally visible dilation of the paraumbilical (and perhaps even the thoracoepigastric veins) which leads to the appearance of "Caput Medusae"

text: A patient with uncontrolled hypertension on amlodipine losartan and hydrochlorothiazide medications taken regularly. What is the next best step for the management of hypertension
expl: Explanation: The next best step in this patient, already on a CCB (amlodipine), an ARB (losartan), and a thiazide diuretic (HCTZ), is spironolactone . Spironolactone is highly effective because resistant hypertension is often driven by excess aldosterone activity. When a patient remains hypertensive despite being on three antihypertensive agents (including a diuretic) , the condition is termed resistant hypertension . In resistant hypertension, the first step is to rule out pseudo-resistance (improper BP measurement, white coat effect, poor adherence) and secondary causes (OSA, renal artery stenosis, drugs raising BP, etc.). Once true resistant hypertension is confirmed, guidelines recommend adding a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (MRA) such as spironolactone as the fourth-line therapy. Increase dose of Losartan (Option B): Simply increasing ARB dose rarely controls resistant hypertension and is less effective than adding a new class (MRA). Start Clonidine (Option C): Centrally acting drugs like clonidine are not the first choice due to side effects (sedation, rebound HTN). Used only in refractory cases. Add Atenolol (Option D): Beta-blockers are not preferred unless there is a compelling indication (e.g., CAD, HF). They are not first choice in resistant hypertension.

text: A 66-year-old patient with a history of chronic hypertension presents to the emergency room with altered mental status and severely elevated blood pressure of 210/110 mm Hg. A brain CT scan reveals bleeding within the brain tissue. What is the most common site of such hemorrhage in similar cases?
expl: Explanation: The clinical presentation indicates intraparenchymal hemorrhage caused by hypertension, which typically occurs in the deep regions of the brain, with the putamen being the most common site. A sudden spike in blood pressure can overwhelm cerebral autoregulation, most often affecting the small penetrating arteries known as lenticulostriate arteries. Common causes of intracerebral hemorrhage include: Hypertension (the most frequent cause, affecting areas such as the basal ganglia, thalamus, pons, and cerebellum) Drug use (e.g., cocaine, methamphetamine), especially in younger patients Cerebral amyloid angiopathy (usually in the elderly, causing lobar hemorrhages) Coagulopathies Vascular malformations Head trauma Hemorrhagic transformation of ischemic stroke Regarding vessel wall damage: Chronic cocaine use can lead to endothelial dysfunction and vessel damage, but acute hemorrhage is mainly caused by pressure effects rather than direct injury. Vasculitis, sometimes linked to chronic cocaine use, usually affects multiple vascular territories, often causing ischemic events rather than acute hemorrhage, and develops over time. Amyloid deposition: Seen mainly in elderly patients (over 60 years) Associated with lobar hemorrhages Results from β-amyloid buildup in vessel walls Although intraparenchymal hemorrhage can also affect other brain areas like the thalamus (Option B) , pons (Option C) , or cerebellum (Option D) , the putamen remains the most frequently involved site in hemorrhages related to chronic hypertension.

text: Which of the following diseases presents with Thrombotic microangiopathy without Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia?
expl: Thrombotic microangiopathy(TMA) is a pathological lesion characterized by the presence of endothelial injury in the terminal arteriole and capillaries of organs, causing hyaline platelet thrombi, resulting in partial or complete occlusion of vessels. In kidneys it leads to a membranoproliferative pattern in glomerulus. Usually TMA is associated with Micro angiopathic hemolytic anemia(MAHA) characterized by schistocytes and thrombocytopenia. Typical examples of TMA include: Hemolytic uremic syndrome Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura Malignant hypertension Scleroderma renal crisis APLa syndrome HELLP syndrome HIV infection Radiation nephropathy TMA without MAHA is seen in POEMS Syndrome TMA associated with Myeloproliferative neoplasias Reference: Harrison's Principles of internal medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 217, Pg: 2364.

text: Which one of the following features is characteristic of Bartter's syndrome?

options.B: Reduced urinary excretion of potassium and chloride

expl: Bartter's syndrome is a childhood disease inherited as an autosomal recessive trait. Pathophysiology impaired loop sodium NaK2Cl reabsorption leads to increased renin and aldosterone secretion with juxtaglomerular hyperplasia. Enhanced sodium-chloride delivery to the collecting duct stimulates potassium secretion leading to hypokalemia . It also causes hydrogen ion secretion resulting in metabolic alkalosis . Accelerated kinin and prostaglandins secretion may account for the vascular unresponsiveness to the pressor effect. This explains the absence of increase in blood pressure and oedema despite the elevated levels of renin and aldosterone. Indomethacin inhibits prostaglandin and restores normal physiological vascular response. Hypokalemia with hypertension is seen with disorders that are related to the ENaC Conn's Syndrome, Liddle syndrome. Bartter's syndrome is associated with increased urinary excretion of potassium and chloride. IN Bartter's syndrome, the addition of Spironolactone, Amiloride or ACE inhibitors improves hypokalemia, but worsens the hypovolemia. NSAIDS may be useful in Bartter's syndrome, as they inhibit the tubuloglomerular feedback. Potassium supplementation and liberal salt intake should be given. Gitelman syndrome also should be treated similarly, but NSAIDS have no role. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st edition, Ch: 53, Pg:353.

text: Graham steel murmur is seen in?
expl: Explanation for answer: Graham Steell Murmur Definition : High-pitched, decrescendo diastolic murmur heard along the left sternal border. Cause : Pulmonary regurgitation (PR) due to pulmonary valve ring dilation from long-standing severe pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). Mechanism : Backflow of blood from pulmonary artery (PA) to right ventricle (RV) during diastole. Pathophysiology of Pulmonary Regurgitation (PR) RV Changes : Causes RV chamber enlargement and eccentric hypertrophy (similar to aortic regurgitation). Hemodynamics : ↑ Preload and afterload. Reverse pressure gradient (PA → RV) in diastole → decrescendo murmur. Murmur duration shortens as RV diastolic pressure rises. Cardiac Output : Initially maintained; declines with progression, especially on exertion. Symptoms of PR Mild to Moderate PR : Often asymptomatic. Severe PR/RV Dysfunction : Fatigue Exertional dyspnea Abdominal fullness Lower extremity edema Physical Findings Graham Steell Murmur : Louder with inspiration; may mimic aortic regurgitation. Additional Signs : Loud/palpable P2 Right ventricular lift → suggests significant PAH Laboratory & Imaging Evaluation ECG : RV hypertrophy (RVH), right atrial (RA) enlargement. Chest X-ray : RV and RA enlargement. Echocardiography : Primary tool for assessing pulmonary valve and RV systolic pressure (via tricuspid regurgitation jet). Cardiac MRI (CMR) : Detailed valve anatomy; accurate RV volume/function assessment. Cardiac Catheterization : Used when planning transcatheter pulmonary valve procedures. Explanation of other options: Pulmonary Hypertension (Option A): Pulmonary hypertension is a cause of Graham Steell murmur but not the murmur itself . The murmur results from pulmonary regurgitation secondary to PAH . Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD) (Option C): VSD causes a holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border , not a diastolic murmur . Large VSDs can lead to pulmonary hypertension , but the Graham Steell murmur is specifically due to PR. Pulmonary Stenosis (PS) (Option D): Pulmonary stenosis produces a harsh, systolic ejection murmur , typically heard best at the left upper sternal border with an ejection click. It does not cause a diastolic murmur . Key Takeaways: Graham Steell murmur is a high-pitched, early diastolic murmur caused by pulmonary regurgitation, most commonly due to pulmonary hypertension. It is best heard at the left upper sternal border and intensifies with inspiration.

text: A 1 year old boy presents with renal insufficiency. Upon evaluation he has evidence of portal hypertension and dilation of intra hepatic bile ducts. Which protein mutation is he likely suffering from?
expl: The history of renal insufficiency in a young infant with portal hypertension and dilation of intrahepatic bile duct points towards the diagnosis of Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease. The gene responsible is PKHD1 gene on chromosome 6, which encodes for protein Fibrocystin/polyductin. The classical form presents with fetal oligamnios and pulmonary hypoplasia with neonatal death due to pulmonary insufficiency(not renal). The older forms is seen in infants in association with congenital hepatic fibrosis and intra hepatic bile duct dilation(Caroli's Disease). Renal impairment is slowly progressive and is due to fibrosis rather than formation of cysts. Polycystin gene is mutated in ADPKD Hamartin and tuberin are the proteins involved in Tuberous sclerosis. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 315, Pg: 2353-2354.

text: A 44-year-old man presents with haematemesis and melaena. He admits to high alcohol intake. On examination, his heart rate is 110 beats per minute and blood pressure is 92/74 mmHg. There is evidence of leukonychia and abdominal examination reveals tenderness in the epigastrium. What is the most likely underlying cause of the gastrointestinal haemorrhage?
expl: Peptic ulceration is the most common cause of acute upper gastrointestinal (GI) haemorrhage. Epigastric tenderness also points towards peptic ulcer disease. The history of high alcohol intake can be misleading the candidate towards varices. In this case the answer is the most common cause of an acute upper GI bleed which is peptic ulceration. Gastric antral vascular ectasia is a relatively uncommon condition. It typically presents as a cause of iron-deficiency anaemia as a result of chronic GI blood loss. Overt symptoms of upper GI haemorrhage may be precipitated by administration of anti-platelet agents or anti-coagulants. The mean age of diagnosis is around 70 and there is an association with scleroderma. Portal hypertensive gastropathy is a poorly understood complication of portal hypertension (usually as a result of chronic liver disease). There is a typical mosaic or snake skin like appearance to the gastric mucosa. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 48 Pg: 331

text: What is the most probable diagnosis for a 45-year-old man presenting with chest pain and shortness of breath that worsen when lying down but improve when sitting up, along with muffled heart sounds on examination?
expl: Explanation: The symptoms of breathlessness worsening when lying down and improving when sitting up, along with the enlarged cardiac silhouette seen on the X-ray, strongly suggest a diagnosis of pericardial effusion. Pericardial effusion: This condition involves the accumulation of fluid in the pericardial sac, which can lead to cardiac tamponade if the fluid builds up rapidly. Clinical signs include muffled or faint heart sounds and an enlarged cardiac silhouette on chest X-ray. Chest X-ray showing waterbottle configuration in Pericardial effusion Electrical alternans is a classic ECG feature seen in pericardial effusion, especially when it progresses to cardiac tamponade. It appears as a beat-to-beat variation in the QRS complex amplitude, caused by the swinging motion of the heart within the fluid-filled pericardial sac. This finding indicates a substantial buildup of fluid and increased pressure inside the pericardium, which hinders proper heart filling during diastole. ECG showing Electrical alternans Explanation for other options: Tetralogy of Fallot (Option B): typically presents with a boot-shaped heart on an X-ray. Transposition of the great arteries (Option C): is characterized by an egg-on-string appearance on the X-ray. Pulmonary hypertension (Option D): displays a pruned tree appearance of the pulmonary vasculature on imaging.

text: A young male presents to the clinic with a persistent high-grade fever lasting 5 days. On examination, he has painless lesions on his hands and a newly detected regurgitant heart murmur. Echocardiography reveals a mass on the mitral valve. Considering these findings, which of the following abdominal signs is most likely to be observed in this patient?
expl: Explanation: The combination of persistent high-grade fever, painless lesions on the hands (likely Janeway lesions), and a newly developed regurgitant heart murmur is strongly indicative of infective endocarditis. In such cases, splenomegaly is a common abdominal finding due to immune system activation and potential embolic phenomena. Acute Bacterial Endocarditis Course : Rapid and more severe than subacute endocarditis. Common Pathogens : Staphylococcus aureus (most frequent, including MRSA), Streptococcus pneumoniae, Listeria monocytogenes, Haemophilus species, and group A, B, or G streptococci. Risk Factors : Underlying conditions such as cancer, diabetes, intravenous drug use, or chronic alcohol use. Clinical Presentation : Rapid onset of symptoms, typically within 2 weeks. Fever, general fatigue, and malaise. New or changing heart murmur; possible progression to heart failure. Physical Findings : Janeway lesions (painless hemorrhagic spots on palms and soles) Petechiae Roth's spots (retinal hemorrhages) Splinter hemorrhages (under fingernails) Splenomegaly may occasionally be present ( Option B ) Options A, C, and D are incorrect. Reference: Subacute SBE Peripheral signs

text: What is the most common presentation of visceral leishmaniasis?
expl: The most common presentation of visceral leishmaniasis (VL) is an abrupt onset of moderate to high-grade fever associated with rigor and chills. Fever may continue for several weeks with decreasing intensity, and the patient may become febrile for a short period before experiencing another bout of fever. Other features: Splenomegaly may be palpable by the second week of illness (may be massive) Hepatomegaly (usually moderate in degree) soon follows. Lymphadenopathy; common in most endemic regions of the world except the Indian subcontinent, where it is rare. Weight loss Skin hyperpigmentation that is most easily seen in brown-skinned individuals. In advanced illness, hypoalbuminemia may manifest as pedal edema and ascites. Anemia appears early and may become severe enough to cause congestive heart failure. Epistaxis, retinal hemorrhages, and gastrointestinal bleeding are associated with thrombocytopenia. Secondary infections such as measles, pneumonia, tuberculosis, bacillary or amebic dysentery, and gastroenteritis are common. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch: 226Pg 1744

text: A 65-year-old man with a known history of hypertension presents with ankle oedema after taking an antihypertensive prescribed by his General Practitioner. He is now found to have a Blood Pressure of 160/100 mmHg. Which of the following would be the preferred drug for this patient?
expl: The patient has ankle oedema which is usually due to vasodilatation by calcium channel blockers . text: Which of the following is not true regarding the cardiac biomarkers in myocardial infarction?

options.A: Myoglobin is the earliest to rise following MI
options.B: CK-MB is useful in assessment of reinfarction as it returns to baseline following 48-72 hours
options.C: Troponins are more specific for MI diagnosis than Creatine kinase
options.D: The order of rise of biomarkers is CK-MB, LDH followed by troponins

ansText: The order of rise of biomarkers is CK-MB, LDH followed by troponins
expl: The order of rise of cardiac biomarkers is Myoglobin (2-3 hours) → CK-MB (3-6 hours) → Troponins (3-12 hours) → LDH (24 hours) CK-MB levels rise by 3-6 hours, reaches its peak by 12-24 hours and return to baseline by 48-72 hours. Hence it is useful for evaluation of a suspected reinfarction. In myocardial infarction, levels of LDH 1 > 2 in plasma which is called 'flipped LDH' pattern. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page no: 2055

text: A 45 year old male who presented with sudden onset severe chest pain was detected to have bradycardia and hypotension on evaluation. What is the most probable diagnosis?
expl: Inferior wall MI can lead to bradycardia and hypotension by 2 mechanisms: Ischemia of the AV node: The AV nodal artery, which arises from the right coronary artery (RCA) 80% of the time, supplies blood to the AV node. In an inferior wall MI, if the RCA is occluded, it can lead to ischemia of the AV node, resulting in significant bradycardia. Bezold-Jarisch reflex: This reflex is characterized by increased vagal tone secondary to ischemia. The heightened vagal activity can slow the heart rate and cause vasodilation, leading to hypotension Anterior wall MI may be associated with features of sympathetic overactivity like tachycardia and hypertension, while extensive anterior wall MI can lead to reduced cardiac output and hypotension. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page no: 2054

text: A 40 year old man has symptoms of lethargy, joint pains and jaundice which have occurred over the past 8 months. Four years later he became diabetic and was referred to our hospital clinic. text: A 42 year old man has worsening jaundice and has deranged liver function tests which have worsened over the last 3 months. He has positive IgG to hepatitis C. Which of the following investigations is most useful for management of the condition?
expl: Liver biopsy is useful to determine the severity of the disease and for monitory progression when treatment with ribavirin and interferon is instigated. text: Vitamin K is given to a patient of jaundice but PT remains unchanged. The probable cause is?
expl: Vitamin K requires biliary excretion for its subsequent absorption; thus, in patients with chronic cholestatic syndromes, vitamin K absorption is frequently diminished. Intravenous or intramuscular vitamin K can quickly correct this abnormality. More commonly, the synthesis of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors is diminished because of a decrease in hepatic mass, and, under these circumstances, administration of parenteral vitamin K does not improve the clotting factors or the prothrombin time. Marked prolongation of the prothrombin time, >5 s above control and not corrected by parenteral vitamin K administration , is a poor prognostic sign in acute viral hepatitis and other acute and chronic liver diseases Reference : Harrison's Principles of internal medicine 21st ed chap 337 pg. 2556

text: Which of the following investigations is not useful in assessment of acute liver injury?
expl: Serum albumin has a long half-life: 18-20 days, with ~4% degraded per day. Because of this slow turnover, the serum albumin is not a good indicator of acute or mild hepatic dysfunction; only minimal changes in the serum albumin are seen in acute liver conditions such as viral hepatitis, drug-related hepatotoxicity, and obstructive jaundice. Hypoalbuminemia is more common in chronic liver disorders such as cirrhosis and usually reflects severe liver damage and decreased albumin synthesis. Option A: The aminotransferases (transaminases) are sensitive indicators of liver cell injury and are most helpful in recognizing acute hepatocellular diseases such as hepatitis. They include aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT). AST is found in the liver, cardiac muscle, skeletal muscle, kidneys, brain, pancreas, lungs, leukocytes, and erythrocytes in decreasing order of concentration. ALT is found primarily in the liver and is therefore a more specific indicator of liver injury Option B: The prothrombin time may be elevated in hepatitis and cirrhosis as well as in disorders that lead to vitamin K deficiency such as obstructive jaundice or fat malabsorption . Option C: The activities of three enzymes-alkaline phosphatase, 5′-nucleotidase, and γ-glutamyl transpeptidase (GGT)-are usually elevated in cholestasis. Alkaline phosphatase and 5′-nucleotidase are found in or near the bile canalicular membrane of hepatocytes, whereas GGT is located in the endoplasmic reticulum and in bile duct epithelial cells. Reflecting its more diffuse localization in the liver, GGT elevation in serum is less specific for cholestasis than are elevations of alkaline phosphatase or 5′nucleotidase. Reference : Harrison's Principles of internal medicine 21st ed chap 337 pg. 2555

text: A patient is being evaluated for jaundice and liver fibrosis. His AST-57 and ALT-81 IU/mL serological tests are given below. Which of the following is the next step in the diagnosis?
expl: The serological status of this patient shows HCV infection since anti-HCV antibody is reactive. Hepatitis B surface antigen is negative and IgG Anti- HBcAg is reactive indicating remote infection with hepatitis B. Recovery is the rule in hepatitis B. In contrast hepatitis C results in development of cirrhosis. Even if transaminases are normal. hepatitis C results in long term damage to the liver. Hence the reason for elevated liver enzymes with development of liver fibrosis points to HCV being the culprit. The next step shall be to perform a PCR-HCV RNA and initiate treatment based on prevalent genotype in the area. Approximately one-third of patients with chronic hepatitis C have normal or near-normal aminotransferase activity; although one-third to one-half of these patients have chronic hepatitis on liver biopsy Liver biopsy is ruled out as the question says the patient is already having fibrosis. Standard indications of therapy in Standard Indications for Therapy in HCV All patients with chronic HCV infection ( detectable HCV RNA, with or without elevated ALT) except for those with short life expectancies owing to comorbid conditions. Any stage of fibrosis; pretreatment biopsy is no longer embraced and has been supplanted by noninvasive measures of fibrosis, e.g., imaging to determine liver elasticity. Responsiveness in groups previously refractory to interferon-based therapy (HIV-HCV co-infection, renal insufficiency, African-American and Latino ethnicity, IL28B non-C haplotype, obesity, insulin resistance, hepatic decompensation, etc.) is not diminished to contemporary direct-acting oral combination regimens. Reference : Harrison's Principles of internal medicine 21st ed chap 341 pg. 2604, 2608

text: A young man had a history of jaundice and raised HBsAg levels a year back. On follow-up now, he has normal levels of liver enzymes. His current profile is shown in the image. What is the diagnosis for his current condition?

options.A: Chronic Hepatitis B with HBeAg negative
options.C: Chronic Hepatitis B with HBeAg positive

ansText: Chronic Hepatitis B with HBeAg positive
expl: Explanation of answer: Persistent HBsAg positivity >6 months, HBeAg positivity, and anti-HBc IgG indicate chronic active Hepatitis B with ongoing viral replication. The key diagnostic criteria for chronic Hepatitis B infection are: Persistence of HBsAg for >6 months Presence of anti-HBc IgG Absence of anti-HBs In this case, the patient continues to have HBsAg positivity after 1 year, indicating chronic infection. The presence of HBeAg implies active viral replication and high infectivity. Since anti-HBc IgG is positive and IgM is negative, the acute phase is over, confirming the chronic stage. There are two main types of chronic Hepatitis B: HBeAg-positive chronic hepatitis B: High infectivity, active replication HBeAg-negative chronic hepatitis B (precore mutant): Lower replication, often inactive phase or fluctuating activity The current serology fits the HBeAg-positive type, with active replication and potential for liver damage even if enzymes are temporarily normal. text: A patient comes with fever, jaundice, and malaise. Based on the following serology findings, what is the most likely diagnosis? Serology Reports: 1. HBsAg: Positive 2. Anti-HBc: Positive 3. Anti-HCV: Negative
expl: Explanation: The combination of clinical presentation (fever, jaundice, malaise) along with the serological profile is most consistent with acute hepatitis B . HBsAg (Hepatitis B surface antigen): Its positivity indicates an ongoing hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection, essential for diagnosing both acute and chronic HBV. Anti-HBc (IgM anti-Hepatitis B core antibody): The detection of IgM anti-HBc denotes a recent exposure and acute infection with HBV, as IgM antibodies are produced in the early phase. Anti-HCV: Negative result excludes hepatitis C, thereby ruling out acute or chronic hepatitis C ( Option D excluded ). Table: Clinical Phases of HBV Infection and Serology Additional Diagrams: Acute HBV infection with recovery Chronic HBV infection Explanation of Other Options: Acute hepatitis D (Option A): Hepatitis D virus requires the presence of hepatitis B infection to replicate. In this case, although anti-HBc is positive, no additional hepatitis D markers (e.g., HDV RNA) are present, hence this option is not correct. Chronic hepatitis B (Option C): Chronic infection would typically show persistent HBsAg for >6 months, with anti-HBc usually being IgG rather than IgM . Since IgM anti-HBc is positive here, chronic HBV is excluded. Chronic hepatitis C (Option D): Ruled out due to negative anti-HCV in the serology profile. Reference: Hepatitis B Vaccines - ResearchGate

text: A 56-year-old man presents with a history of abdominal discomfort that is relieved by passing stool. In the past month his stools have been looser in nature and he has had a feeling of urgency and incomplete evacuation. His symptoms seem to be worse with eating. He has also noticed that he has passed mucus per rectum. He is overweight with a BMI of 28 kg/m2. His weight has fallen. He says that he has adjusted his diet in the last six months. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnosis?
expl: Weight loss, tenesmus and a recent change in bowel habit all point towards an underlying diagnosis of colorectal cancer. Onset of symptoms in later life and a relatively short duration (that is, weeks rather than years) also point towards a 'biological' cause rather than irritable bowel syndrome. The passage of mucus per rectum is a normal physiological function and not indicative of underlying pathology. The symptoms are not suggestive of malabsorption. Diverticulitis and inflammatory bowel disease are both potential diagnoses but given the duration of symptoms less likely than a colonic neoplasm. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, CH: 81, Pg: 639

text: What is the differentiating feature between IBS and organic GI disease?
expl: Irritable bowel syndrome is a functional bowel disorder which is non inflammatory. The unifying feature of inflammatory diarrhea due to any cause is the presence of leukocytes or leukocyte derived protein Calprotectin in stools. Another inflammatory marker in stool is Fecal Lactoferrin, which is also present in activated neutrophils. Both of them can be used in diagnosis of relapses of inflammatory bowel disease from IBS or bacterial overgrowth. Fecal calprotectin is also having the advantage of being a sensitive marker of Colonic or ileocolonic inflammation rather than isolated ileal inflammation. Abdominal pain, diarrhea and presence of mucous in stools can be seen in IBS as well as inflammatory diarrhea. Blood in stools, nocturnal symptoms and weight loss is uncommon in IBS.

text: A 42 year old man presented with a 5 day history of bloody diarrhea. On examination, he was apyrexial, jaundiced and pale. There was no organomegaly but there was mild lower abdominal tenderness.Investigations reveal: Hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL White cell count 17500/μL Platelets 70000/μL urea 54 mg/dl creatinine 2.0 mg/dl aspartate aminotransferase 110 IU/L Prothrombin time 12s (11.5-15.5) Blood film shows fragmented red cells What is the likely diagnosis?
expl: The combination of haemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia in the setting of a normal coagulation profile is consistent with haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS - TTP). The fragmented cells are schistocytes which are a consequence of small vessel thrombosis which cause intravascular hemolysis The most likely cause of diarrhea is E coli O157. Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) is characterized by the triad of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute renal failure. Diarrhea and upper respiratory infection are the most common precipitating factors. Other bacterial agents include Shigella, Salmonella, Yersinia, and Campylobacter species. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st ed, Ch: 317 Pg: 2365

text: A 43 year old man has recurrent episodes of bloody diarrhea and lower abdominal cramping. expl: 75% of patients with primary sclerosing cholangitis have inflammatory bowel disease, especially ulcerative colitis. text: A 42-year-old man with a history of ulcerative colitis (UC) comes to the gastroenterology clinic. He currently takes mesalazine and has quiescent disease. text: A male patient presents with recurrent oral ulcers and painful ulcers in the anal canal. He is diagnosed with Behçet's disease. Which of the following findings is not characteristic of this condition?

options.A: Ulcer over the dorsum of the penis
options.B: It is more similar to Crohn's disease than ulcerative colitis
options.D: Pathergy test positive is a criterion of ISG diagnostic criteria

ansText: Ulcer over the dorsum of the penis
expl: Explanation: Ulcers on the dorsum of the penis are not typical of Behçet's disease . In males, genital ulcers in Behçet's disease most commonly occur on the scrotum or glans penis and usually heal with scarring . In contrast, ulcers on the dorsal aspect of the penis are atypical and should prompt evaluation for other causes such as sexually transmitted infections (STIs) or traumatic ulcers . text: A 24 year old man presents with a 10 month history of weight loss, oral ulceration and diarrhoea. A flexible sigmoidoscopy is performed and a colonic biopsy was taken. Which of the following histological features would favour a diagnosis of Crohn's disease over ulcerative colitis?
expl: Crohn's disease is characterized by transmural inflammation (inflammation of all layers of the gut), fissures, preservation of crypt architecture and non caseating granulomata. text: A 19-year-old woman returns from her gap year travels with chronic low grade fever, intermittent abdominal pain and diarrhoea. text: A 36 year old woman presents with abdominal pain, weight loss, diarrhoea and mouth ulcers. Full blood count reveals normocytic normochromic anaemia, inflammatory markers are raised, and biochemical investigation reveals a raised alkaline phosphatase. Barium follow through shows terminal ileal inflammatory disease. Long term remission may be maintained by the use of which of the following drugs?
expl: This is a case of Crohn’s disease . Remission of Crohn's disease may be achieved by the use of steroids, elemental diet, surgery or infliximab. Mesalazine may maintain remission if induction has been achieved by surgery and if an 8-week course of metronidazole is administered. It has many side effects. text: A patient with known ulcerative colitis (UC) who has failed to respond to anti-TNF-α therapy requires an alternative drug for moderate to severe disease. Which of the following Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors is most appropriate in this setting?
expl: Explanation: Tofacitinib is an orally active JAK inhibitor approved for the management of moderate to severe ulcerative colitis , particularly in patients who are refractory or intolerant to anti-TNF-α therapy . It acts by inhibiting Janus kinases (JAK1 and JAK3) , thereby blocking the JAK-STAT intracellular signaling pathway , which mediates the action of multiple proinflammatory cytokines such as interleukin (IL)-2, IL-4, IL-6, IL-7, IL-9, IL-15, IL-21 , and interferons . This suppression of cytokine-driven immune activation helps reduce intestinal inflammation, promote mucosal healing, and maintain remission in ulcerative colitis. Mechanism of Action Normal Pathway: Cytokine → JAK receptor activation → STAT phosphorylation → Gene transcription → Inflammation Tofacitinib action: Inhibits JAK1 and JAK3 → prevents STAT activation → reduces transcription of proinflammatory cytokines → controls mucosal inflammation Side effects include an increased risk of infections, venous thromboembolism, and lipid elevation, requiring careful patient selection and monitoring. Explanation of Other Options: Vedolizumab (Option A): Class: Gut-selective anti-integrin monoclonal antibody. Mechanism of Action: Targets α4β7 integrin , a cell adhesion molecule present on the surface of gut-homing T lymphocytes. Prevents these activated T cells from binding to MAdCAM-1 (mucosal addressin cell adhesion molecule-1) on intestinal endothelial cells. This selectively blocks lymphocyte trafficking into the gastrointestinal mucosa , thereby reducing inflammation in the colon. Acts primarily in the gut , with minimal systemic immunosuppression. Clinical Use: Approved for moderate to severe ulcerative colitis (UC) and Crohn's disease , especially when conventional therapies (steroids, azathioprine, 5-ASA) or anti-TNF agents fail. Effective for induction and maintenance of remission . Often preferred in patients who are at higher risk of systemic infections , given its gut-selective mechanism. Adverse Effects: Infusion reactions (headache, arthralgia, nausea). Risk of upper respiratory tract infections. Rarely, hypersensitivity reactions. No association with progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML), unlike natalizumab. Ozanimod (Option C): Class: Sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) receptor modulator . Mechanism of Action: Selectively binds to S1P1 and S1P5 receptors on lymphocytes. Causes functional sequestration of lymphocytes in lymph nodes → prevents them from entering systemic circulation and reaching inflamed intestinal tissue. Reduces local intestinal inflammation by decreasing immune cell infiltration. Clinical Use: Approved by the FDA (2021) for moderate to severe ulcerative colitis . Also indicated for multiple sclerosis (MS) . Used when patients are refractory to anti-TNF agents or cannot tolerate JAK inhibitors. Dosing and Route: Oral, once daily - convenient compared to injectable biologics. Dose titration is required initially to minimize cardiac side effects. Adverse Effects: Cardiac: Bradycardia and atrioventricular (AV) block, especially with the first dose (due to S1P1 receptor modulation on cardiac tissue). Hepatic: Elevated liver enzymes. Respiratory: Mild reduction in FEV��� in some patients. Infectious: Risk of reactivation of viral infections such as VZV. Ophthalmologic: Rare macular edema (requires baseline eye exam). Leflunomide (Option D): Class: Disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD) ; pyrimidine synthesis inhibitor. Mechanism of Action: Inhibits dihydroorotate dehydrogenase , an enzyme essential for de novo pyrimidine synthesis in rapidly dividing lymphocytes. Decreases proliferation and activation of T and B cells → immunomodulatory effect. Clinical Use: Primarily used in rheumatoid arthritis and psoriatic arthritis . Sometimes used as an alternative to methotrexate in patients with intolerance or contraindications. Not used in ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease. Adverse Effects: Hepatotoxicity (requires regular liver function monitoring). Teratogenicity - contraindicated in pregnancy. Gastrointestinal upset, diarrhea. Hypertension, weight loss, rash, and alopecia. Key Takeaway Points: Reference: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6535722/

text: A patient with a known history of inflammatory bowel disease presents with the skin lesion shown below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The clinical presentation and image suggest Pyoderma gangrenosum, a condition more frequently seen in ulcerative colitis, a type of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Pyoderma gangrenosum is a rare inflammatory skin disorder characterized by painful, ulcerative lesions, often affecting the lower limbs. These ulcers typically have undermined edges and may appear necrotic or purulent. Extraintestinal manifestations of IBD include: Erythema nodosum (Option A ruled out): Painful red nodules usually on the shins Ankylosing spondylitis (spinal arthritis) Pancreatitis Uveitis (inflammation of the uveal tract of the eye) Osteoporosis and osteonecrosis are among the most common extraintestinal complications of IBD. Pyoderma gangrenosum and primary sclerosing cholangitis are especially common in ulcerative colitis, while renal calculi are more typical in Crohn's disease. Explanation for other options: Diabetic ulcer (Option C): is not linked to inflammatory bowel disease; it typically occurs as a complication of uncontrolled diabetes mellitus. Venous ulcer (Option D): generally, results from chronic conditions such as long-standing varicose veins and is commonly found around the ankles.

text: Which of the following interleukins chiefly drive PsA?
expl: The chief interleukins that drive PsA are IL17 and IL 23. The biologics that are used in treatment of PsA act by antagonizing these cytokines. They include: Anti IL 17: secukinumab and ixekizumab Anti IL-23/IL-12p40 : ustekinumab, a monoclonal antibody to the shared subunit. Anti IL-23 (p19 subunit)-guselkumab, risankizumab, and tildrakizumab Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 362, Pg: 2800

text: Swimmer's ear is caused by
expl: P. aeruginosa infections of the ears vary from mild swimmer's ear to serious life-threatening infections with neurologic sequelae. Swimmer's ear is common among children and results from infection of moist macerated skin of the external ear canal. Most cases resolve with treatment, but some patients develop chronic drainage. Swimmer's ear is managed with topical antibiotic agents (otic solutions). There is narrowing of the ear channel, with a small amount of exudate and swelling of the outer ear. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 164 Pg: 1289

text: A 57 year old man is suspected of having a duodenal ulcer recurrence despite being on omeprazole. Which of the following is the most sensitive test in detecting ongoing infection with Helicobacter pylori?

options.B: The urease test on a gastric biopsy

expl: The urea breath test is expensive but has up to 98% sensitivity . It requires stringent test conditions like fasting and may not be convenient as serology. It can be used for detecting response to treatment. Serology is simple and convenient and is not affected by the use of PPI or antibiotic use. So in this patient who is already on PPI this may be the most convenient investigation. The gastric biopsy culture has high specificity but sensitivity of 90%. Histology of gastric biopsy (not listed above) has both high sensitivity and specificity . Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, ch: 163, Pg: 1281

text: A 62 year old man with history of colorectal polyps presents with low grade fever, weight loss and night sweats. ECHO showed vegetations on the aortic valve. Which is the most likely organism to be grown in blood culture?
expl: Streptococcus bovis bacteremia and endocarditis have been strongly associated with colorectal neoplasia. Patient identified to have S. bovis endocarditis should be evaluated for the presence of colorectal polyps or cancer. Penicillin G is the treatment of choice for S. bovis endocarditis typically given for 4 weeks. Staphylococcus aureus is the most commonly isolated organism from endocarditis occurring in IV drug abusers, which preferentially affects the tricuspid valve. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 1023-25

text: A 10-year-old boy is brought to the clinic with complaints of fever for 1 week. He also has cracked lips, which are painful. On examination, his eyes are red and he has a lymph node in the cervical region. Kawasaki syndrome is suspected. Which of the following is the best treatment choice?
expl: This is a case of Kawasaki's syndrome, which is also known as mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome and occurs mainly in children under 10 years of age. It is a form of vasculitis, which affects coronary arteries and is associated with the development of coronary aneurysms. Aspirin and IV immunoglobulin at high doses is the treatment of choice. Corticosteroids used to be contraindicated, but recently trials have shown that it reduced the risk of heart damage caused by coronary vessel vasculitis. Infliximab is also being used in trials. Warfarin is used if coronary aneurysms develop as a complication. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Ch: 363 Pg: 2816

text: A 64-year-old man presents with palpitations and syncope. He has a history of an inferior-wall myocardial infarction one year ago. A 24-hour Holter study was performed, and the ECG strip obtained is given below. What is the long-term treatment for this condition?
expl: Explanation: The clinical presentation of syncope and palpitations in a patient with a prior MI, combined with a Holter monitor showing sinus pauses or arrests , is diagnostic of sick sinus syndrome (sinus node dysfunction) . Rationale for Permanent Pacemaker Symptomatic Bradycardia: The syncope is directly attributable to the arrhythmia, making it a Class I indication for permanent pacing. The goal is to prevent life-threatening pauses and alleviate symptoms. Irreversible Cause: Sinus node dysfunction following a myocardial infarction is often permanent due to irreversible damage to the heart's conduction system. Pharmacological agents like atropine or isoproterenol are only temporary measures. Standard of Care: According to ACC/AHA/HRS guidelines, permanent pacemaker implantation is the definitive long-term therapy for symptomatic sinus node dysfunction. Sick Sinus Syndrome This syndrome encompasses various sinus node abnormalities, including severe sinus bradycardia, sinus pauses >3 seconds, and sinoatrial exit block . The history of inferior MI is highly relevant, as the sinus node artery often originates from the right coronary artery, which is commonly involved in inferior wall infarctions. In hemodynamically unstable patients, bradycardia is managed with intravenous atropine 0.5 mg every 3-5 minutes to a maximum dose of 3 mg, and if there is no improvement, a temporary pacemaker should be considered. In stable patients, long-term management involves treating underlying causes, withdrawing bradycardia-inducing medications, and inserting a permanent pacemaker when indicated. Explanation of other options: Amiodarone (Option A): This is a Class III antiarrhythmic drug. It can itself cause or exacerbate bradycardia and is contraindicated in this scenario. It is used for tachyarrhythmias, not symptomatic bradycardia. Atropine only (Option B): Atropine is an anticholinergic agent used for acute, hemodynamically unstable bradycardia in an emergency setting. It is not a sustainable or appropriate long-term treatment. Atropine and isoproterenol (Option D): Isoproterenol is a beta-agonist used as a temporary chronotropic agent. Combining these drugs is a short-term bridge to pacing in an acute care setting and is not a long-term solution. Key Takeaways: Symptomatic bradycardia due to sick sinus syndrome requires a permanent pacemaker. Drugs like atropine are for acute management only. A history of myocardial infarction, especially inferior, is a common cause of acquired sinus node dysfunction.

text: A patient arrives at the emergency department after consuming ten paracetamol tablets. He now has oliguria, and his liver function tests are abnormal. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
expl: Explanation: The patient's presentation with a history of paracetamol overdose, oliguria, and deranged liver function strongly suggests paracetamol-induced hepatotoxicity . The specific antidote in this situation is N-acetylcysteine (NAC) . Acetaminophen (Paracetamol) Toxicity: Most common cause of acute liver failure worldwide. Toxic dose: Ingesting ≥25 g may be fatal. Clinical features: Oliguria, elevated liver enzymes, signs of hepatic injury. Mechanism of Toxicity: Normally, paracetamol is metabolized in the liver. A fraction is converted via CYP2E1 into a toxic metabolite, NAPQI (N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone-imine) . In overdose, glutathione stores become depleted , leading to accumulation of NAPQI, which causes hepatocellular necrosis. Management: Antidote: N-acetylcysteine (NAC). Mechanism: Restores glutathione reserves, thereby detoxifying NAPQI. Timing: Most effective when administered within 8 hours of overdose; benefit persists up to 36 hours. Severe cases: Liver transplantation may be required if fulminant hepatic failure develops despite NAC therapy. Explanation of other options: Dopamine (Option B): Used in cardiogenic or septic shock; has no role in paracetamol toxicity. Ursodeoxycholic acid (Option C): Utilized in cholestatic liver diseases such as primary biliary cholangitis, not in drug-induced hepatic injury. Furosemide (Option D): A loop diuretic for fluid overload; does not treat paracetamol-induced hepatotoxicity. Key Takeaways: N-acetylcysteine is the drug of choice in paracetamol overdose. Works best within 8 hours but still beneficial later. In refractory cases, liver transplantation is the definitive treatment. References: https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/full/10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.107.728840

text: A 45 year old man presents with acute, profuse, watery diarrhea some days after returning from a holiday. Which one of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
expl: The most likely cause of travellers diarrhoea is E. coli. Ciprofloxacin would cover for this as well as shigella, salmonella and campylobacter. However, if giardiasis was cultured in the stool then metronidazole is recommended. Most secretory forms of traveler's diarrhea (usually due to enterotoxigenic or enteroaggregative E. coli or to Campylobacter) can be treated effectively with rehydration, bismuth subsalicylate, or antiperistaltic agents. Antimicrobial agents can shorten the duration of illness from 3-4 days to 24-36 h but may be associated with the acquisition of multidrug-resistant organisms; their use should therefore be reserved for severe cases Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 133, Pg: 1065

text: Which of the following is not a first line therapy drug for treatment of acute uncomplicated cystitis?
expl: Traditionally, TMP-SMX has been recommended as first-line treatment for acute cystitis The generally accepted explanation is that β-lactams fail to eradicate uropathogens from the vaginal reservoir. Most fluoroquinolones are highly effective as short-course therapy for cystitis when the causative organism is susceptible to them; the exception is moxifloxacin, Guidelines also recommend fosfomycin as a first-line agent to treat acute, uncomplicated cystitis in women. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 135, Pg: 1076

text: A 24 year old man has previously been well and there is no past medical history. He has a 5 day history of bloody diarrhea and has acute abdominal pains. On examination, he has a temperature of 38°C and a tender lower abdomen. What is the likely causative organism?
expl: Bloody diarrhoea is more likely to be caused by shigella. Cholera and giardial diarrhoea are not typically bloody. There is no history of immunocompromise to suggest cryptosporidium infection. Shigellosis Transmission : fecal-oral transmission. Other modes include ingestion of contaminated food or water, contact with a contaminated inanimate object, and sexual contact. Presentation: Sudden onset of severe abdominal cramping, high-grade fever, emesis, anorexia, and large-volume watery diarrhea are presenting features. Complications : Seizures, delirium and haemolytic uraemic syndrome Treatment: Cotrimoxazole and ampicillin are recommended treatments. Causes of bloody diarrhea: CHESSY C ampylobacter jejuni Entero h emorrhagic E Coli E ntamoeba histolytica S higella dysenteriae S almonella Y ersinia enterocolitis Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 133, Pg: 1061

text: Which of the following statements regarding von Willebrand disease is incorrect?

options.A: Type 2 von Willebrand disease is associated with a moderate bleeding tendency
options.B: Type 3 von Willebrand disease is associated with a complete absence of factor VIII
options.C: Type 1 von Willebrand disease presents with severe bleeding since childhood
options.D: Type 2 von Willebrand disease includes subtypes with varying defects in von Willebrand factor

ansText: Type 1 von Willebrand disease presents with severe bleeding since childhood
expl: Explanation of answer: Type 1 von Willebrand disease causes only mild to moderate bleeding symptoms and typically does not present with severe bleeding early in life. Von Willebrand Disease (vWD) is the most common inherited bleeding disorder, resulting from a quantitative or qualitative defect in von Willebrand factor (vWF), a glycoprotein critical for platelet adhesion and stabilization of factor VIII. Classification of vWD: Clinical Manifestations: Mild bleeding (Type 1): Easy bruising, epistaxis, prolonged bleeding after dental procedures, menorrhagia. Moderate bleeding (Type 2): Subtypes show qualitative dysfunction in vWF. Severe bleeding (Type 3): Presents like severe Hemophilia A due to virtual absence of both vWF and Factor VIII. Common symptoms: Mucocutaneous bleeding Post-surgical or dental procedure hemorrhage Prolonged bleeding time despite normal platelet count Treatment:

text: A 27 year old man presents with sudden onset left sided pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness. On examination he is distressed, tachypnoeic and has tracheal displacement to the right together with a hyper-resonant percussion note on the left side. There were no breath sounds on the left. Chest x ray shows a < 2 cm left sided pneumothorax. What is the best management procedure?
expl: The history of a young male without any prior lung disease with a pneumothorax suggests the possibility of a Primary Spontaneous Pneumothorax due to rupture of sub pleural blebs. Treatment of a pneumothorax of This is less painful, leads to a shorter duration of admission, reduces the need for pleurectomy. If the lung does not expand with aspiration or if the patient has a recurrent pneumothorax, thoracoscopy with stapling of blebs and pleural abrasion is indicated. Thoracoscopy or thoracotomy with pleural abrasion is almost 100% successful in preventing recurrences. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch: 294Pg 2200

text: A 18-year-old female is admitted with an oculogyric crisis. Which of the following statements concerning this case is correct?

options.A: She is likely to have been prescribed olanzapine
options.B: She should be observed without treatment
options.C: She should be treated with parenteral procyclidine
options.D: She should receive procyclidine as long term prophylaxis

ansText: She should be treated with parenteral procyclidine
expl: Oculogyric crisis is an acute dystonic reaction of the face/eyes and is usually a consequence of typical neuroleptic drugs such as haloperidol and chlorpromazine but is unusual with newer agents such as olanzapine and clozapine. The condition is often precipitated by re-introduction of the agent. The condition should be treated with procyclidine (usually IV or IM) or benztropine. Chronic treatment beyond a couple of days is not required. Reference: Harrison's principles of internal medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 436 Pg: 3403

text: A 50-year-old man is evaluated for hyperaldosteronism because of difficult to-control hypertension. He is otherwise healthy. Evaluation was done during treatment with agents that do not affect aldosterone or renin levels and include an aldosterone-to-renin ratio of more than 40 and lack of aldosterone suppression to oral salt loading. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the adrenal glands shows a 1-cm mass on the right with a density of 10 HU. What is the next best step?

options.D: Review of CT scan to exclude hyperplasia of the left adrenal gland

expl: Adrenal venous sampling should be performed to identify the source of excess aldosterone. It is possible that the visualized mass is a non functioning tumor. Adrenal venous sampling is the gold standard investigation for lateralisation of aldosterone excess. This man is a good surgical candidate, and laparoscopic adrenalectomy would be recommended if venous sampling is consistent with unilateral disease. The CT scan is not helpful in identifying bilateral disease. Treatment with eplerenone or spironolactone would be done if he were not a surgical candidate; eplerenone would be an appropriate treatment for bilateral disease. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 2966

text: A 15 year old female who is diagnosed with SLE has come to your OP for review. Which of the following statements is true? 1. Permanent remission is seen only in 2. Aim of treatment is disease remission on treatment or Low Lupus Disease Activity. 3. Anti ds DNA or C3 levels are used as markers of disease flare 4. SLEDAI 2k score of >3 indicates active disease.
expl: The question deals with treatment endpoints in SLE. Complete permanent remission(no disease activity without any treatment) is seen in Aim of treatment in SLE is disease remission on treatment or low level disease activity. Disease activity is measured using SLEDAI 2k score and a score of > 4 indicates an active disease. Anti ds DNA titres and C3 complement levels are used as markers of disease flare. From among the given options, SLEDAI2K score of > 3 does not indicate active disease. Hence it is wrong. So statements 1,2 and 3 are correct. Reference: Harrison's principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Ch : 356 Pg: 2740, 2746

text: A 58-year-old male presents with dysphagia, retrosternal discomfort and weight loss. Studies reveal achalasia. Which of the following is most definitive way to provide symptomatic relief?
expl: The only durable therapies for achalasia are pneumatic dilation and LES myotomy (Heller myotomy). The patient shows excellent symptom improvement. Reflux is the most common side effect and a concomitant anti-relfux procedure (Nissen's fundoplication) may be performed. Both calcium channel blockers (nifedipine) and nitrates relax the lower oesophageal sphincter. However the effect on symptoms is variable, short-lived and usually suboptimal. Use is frequently limited by adverse effects. Consequently medical therapy is typically limited to those patients too frail or unwilling to undergo definitive treatment or other therapies. Latest treatment is POEM. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 23,Pg: 2427-2428

text: Drug of choice for treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy is
expl: Nitrofurantoin, ampicillin, and cephalosporins are considered relatively safe in early pregnancy. One retrospective case-control study suggesting an association between nitrofurantoin and birth defects has not been confirmed. Sulfonamides should clearly be avoided both in the first trimester (because of possible teratogenic effects) and near term (because of a possible role in the development of kernicterus). Fluoroquinolones are avoided because of possible adverse effects on fetal cartilage Ampicillin and the cephalosporins have been used extensively in pregnancy and are the drugs of choice for the treatment of asymptomatic or symptomatic UTI in this group of patients. Generally, pregnant women with ASB are treated for 4-7 days in the absence of evidence to support single-dose therapy. For pregnant women with overt pyelonephritis, parenteral ß-lactam therapy with or without aminoglycosides is the standard of care. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 135, Pg: 1077

text: A 63-year-old diabetic woman presents with fever, flank pain, dysuria, and elevated WBC count. Imaging reveals mild hydronephrosis. Urinalysis shows pyuria and bacteriuria. She is diagnosed with a complicated urinary tract infection (UTI). Which of the following is the best initial treatment?
expl: Explanation: She is diagnosed with a complicated urinary tract infection (UTI) and hence the patient should be treated with Meropenem. Meropenem is the best initial treatment in this case because: The patient has a complicated UTI (due to diabetes, systemic signs, and possible urinary tract obstruction). There is a high risk of infection with resistant organisms , particularly ESBL-producing Gram-negative bacilli like E . coli . Meropenem , a carbapenem , offers broad-spectrum coverage including Gram-negative organisms , anaerobes , and ESBL producers . It is effective when oral agents or narrower-spectrum antibiotics are likely to fail or when systemic illness is present. Explanations for other Options: Ceftriaxone (Option A): Ceftriaxone is a third-generation cephalosporin that is commonly used for UTIs, but it may not be effective against ESBL-producing organisms , which are often found in complicated infections, especially in diabetic or hospitalized patients. While it can be used in some uncomplicated cases, it is not the preferred choice for severe or high-risk infections like the one described. Amoxicillin-clavulanate (Option C): Amoxicillin-clavulanate is an oral antibiotic with some activity against common urinary pathogens, but it has limited effectiveness against resistant Gram-negative bacteria , including ESBL-producing strains. It is not suitable for treating complicated UTIs , especially when there are systemic signs such as fever or flank pain, or imaging findings like hydronephrosis. Nitrofurantoin (Option D): Nitrofurantoin is only effective for lower urinary tract infections (cystitis) because it does not reach adequate concentrations in the renal tissue . Therefore, it is ineffective for pyelonephritis or complicated infections involving the kidneys or upper urinary tract, such as in this case with flank pain and hydronephrosis .

text: What is the drug of choice for Legionnaire's disease?
expl: Explanation: Azithromycin is the preferred agent for treating Legionnaire's disease due to its superior efficacy, better tolerability, and lower potential for drug interactions compared to erythromycin. Legionella Features: Thin, Gram-negative, non-capsulated bacilli. Poor Gram staining; best visualized by Direct Fluorescent Antibody (DFA) staining. Requires Buffered Charcoal Yeast Extract (BCYE) agar for growth. Mode of Infection: Microaspiration and aerosol inhalation; no human-to-human transmission. Epidemiology: Associated with air conditioners, showers, coolers; commonly seen in smokers, immunocompromised, and elderly patients. Treatment: First-line: Macrolides [Azithromycin preferred over Erythromycin], ciprofloxacin, tetracyclines. Severe cases: Rifampicin may be added. Ineffective: Beta-lactams and aminoglycosides. Explanation of other options: Vancomycin (Option A): Active against Gram-positive bacteria like Staphylococcus and Enterococcus; ineffective for Legionella. Streptomycin (Option C): Aminoglycoside used in TB and plague; lacks efficacy against Legionella. Erythromycin (Option D): Previously first-line, now replaced by Azithromycin due to better tolerability. References: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK7619/

text: What is the treatment of Grade I Meningioma?
expl: Explanation: The standard treatment for a symptomatic or growing Grade I (benign) meningioma is surgical excision . The goal is complete resection, which is often curative for this slow-growing tumor. Meningioma is the most common primary CNS tumor arising from the dura mater, usually slow-growing but with higher-grade variants being rare. It is linked to genetic mutations, radiation exposure (especially in childhood), neurofibromatosis type 2, and older age. Grading: Grade 1 (low grade): Most common, slow-growing, more frequent in females. Grade 2 (atypical): Higher recurrence risk; includes chordoid and clear cell types; may invade bone. Grade 3 (anaplastic/malignant): Aggressive, fast-growing; includes papillary and rhabdoid types; can spread to brain and other organs. Clinical features depend on location and may include seizures, morning headaches, vision or hearing loss, altered smell, and confusion. MRI typically shows an enhancing extra-axial mass, with Grade 2/3 lesions appearing brighter with contrast. Treatment: Grade 1 is managed primarily with surgical excision. Grades 2 and 3 require surgery followed by adjuvant radiotherapy, chemotherapy, or clinical trials (e.g., targeted or immunotherapy). Explanation of other options: Reassurance (Option A): Asymptomatic, small, incidentally discovered Grade I meningiomas may be managed with observation and serial imaging. Chemotherapy (Option C): Has a very limited role and is generally reserved for recurrent or higher-grade (Grade II/III) meningiomas that are not amenable to surgery or radiation. Radiotherapy (Option D): Used as adjuvant therapy for subtotally resected or higher-grade meningiomas, or as primary treatment for surgically inaccessible tumors. Key Takeaways: Grade I meningiomas are benign and surgical resection is the primary curative treatment. Management strategy depends on the tumor's size, location, associated symptoms, and growth rate. Reference: https://www.cancer.gov/rare-brain-spine-tumor/tumors/meningioma

text: The preferred test for confirming H. pylori eradication is:
expl: Answer is A (Urease Breath Test) The test of choice for documenting eradication is urease breath test. Assessment of success of Treatment with Eradication of H. Pylori should be done at least 4 weeks after completion of anti H. Pylori therapy. Non-invasive tests are typically preferred for assessment of Eradication. The test of choice for documenting eradication is urease breath test. Urease breath test detects H. pylori infection by 'bacterial urease activity' and remains positive till the bacteria has not been eradicated with treatment. Thus urease breath test becomes negative only aftereradication of organism following treatment and not with chronic infection.

text: A 50 year old man presents with a history of intermittent, but slowly progressive dysphagia for both solids and liquids. He has pain on swallowing and has regurgitation of food swallowed several hours earlier. He has not lost weight. Barium swallow demonstrates proximal dilatation of the oesophagus and failure of relaxation of the lower oesophageal sphincter. Which treatment option is best in the long term?
expl: The diagnosis is achalasia cardia . This is a functional obstruction at the lower oesophageal sphincter caused by a failure of relaxation. Heller's oesophageal myotomy (surgical division of the lower oesophageal sphincter) is the best treatment option. It can be done via an abdominal incision or laparoscopically. It is often combined with fundoplication for reflux. Pneumatic dilation is another procedure done for achalasia. Per Oral Esophageal Myotomy(POEM) is the latest treatment for Achalasia and is as effective as Heller's Myotomy with few complications and early recovery. Botulinum toxin injection can be used to treat achalasia. But it is a temporary measure. Sengstaken Blakemore tube is used in the management of esophageal varices via balloon tamponade. Amyl nitrite is an arterial vasodilator. It has no role in management of achalasia. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 23,Pg: 2427-2428

text: A 15-year-old girl presents with primary amenorrhoea. She represents her school in athletics and is now training for the national championships. Which of the following would be the most appropriate treatment for her?
expl: Menarche may be delayed in girls who are involved in strenuous physical activity. This is termed as"Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea" in which strenuous physical activity, caloric restriction and extreme stress can lead to reduced GnRH and gonadotropins production from hypothalamus and pituitary. Treatment with GnRH or gonadotropins are not required as the reversal of these risk factors would lead to resumption of normal menstrual cycles. Provision of an adequate diet and the relief of stress would be the most appropriate treatment in this case. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 3035

text: What is the treatment of a patient diagnosed with H.pylori?

options.A: A combination of a proton pump inhibitor and an antibiotic

ansText: A combination of a proton pump inhibitor and an antibiotic
expl: Explanation: The treatment regimen for a patient with H.pylori is a combination of a proton pump inhibitor and antibiotics. Although pylori is sensitive to many antibiotics in vitro, monotherapy is generally ineffective due to insufficient antibiotic delivery to its colonization site. The failure of single-drug therapy led to the development of multidrug regimens. At present, standard treatment consists of a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) combined with two or three antimicrobial agents for 10-14 days. Common Treatment Regimens for H.pylori
