text: A 25-year-old female presents with red crusted lesions around the mouth and finger pulps, three months after having had small bowel resection for Crohn's disease. What is the most likely cause of her skin condition?
expl: The features of this patient who had bowel resection suggest zinc deficiency . Zinc deficiency can lead to a condition called acrodermatitis enteropathica which presents with diarrhea, alopecia, muscle wasting, depression, irritability, and a rash involving the extremities, face (perioral), and perineum . The rash is characterized by vesicular and pustular crusting with scaling and erythema. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:333 Pg: 2532

text: A 67 year old man presents with dysphagia of solids for the past three months. There is a history of 10 kg weight loss in 4 months following loss of appetite. He has had symptoms of indigestion and heartburn for 10 years. He regularly takes Gaviscon and milk of magnesia. He is a heavy smoker. He undergoes endoscopy, which reveals a small tumour at the lower part of the oesophagus. What is the likely aetiological cause?
expl: The history is suggestive of gastro oesophageal reflux for the past 10 years. Continuous acid reflux causes metaplasia of the stratified squamous epithelium (which normally lines the distal oesophagus) to an abnormal columnar epithelium. This is known as Barrett's oesophagus . Barrett's oesophagus increases the risk of development of adenocarcinoma of the oesophagus . Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 323 Pg: 2430

text: A 45-year-old man presents with fatigue and hemoptysis. His hemoglobin has dropped from 12 g/dL to 8 g/dL in one week. Bronchoalveolar lavage reveals a reddish fluid, and his serum creatinine is elevated at 1.7 mg/dL. He tests ANCA-positive, and a renal biopsy shows pauci-immune glomerulonephritis without granulomatous inflammation. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation of answer: Microscopic polyangiitis presents with ANCA-positive pauci-immune glomerulonephritis and pulmonary-renal syndrome, without granulomas. Microscopic polyangiitis (MPA) is a pauci-immune small vessel vasculitis characterized by necrotizing glomerulonephritis and pulmonary capillaritis. The hallmark features include: Hemoptysis (due to alveolar hemorrhage) Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (causing a drop in hemoglobin, elevated creatinine) ANCA positivity - typically p-ANCA (anti-MPO antibodies) Pauci-immune pattern on renal biopsy (minimal immune complex deposition) Absence of granulomatous inflammation (unlike GPA or Churg-Strauss) This clinical presentation of pulmonary-renal syndrome, especially with no granulomas, strongly favors MPA. Microvascular Vasculitis: Explanation of other options: Systemic lupus erythematosus (Option C): SLE causes immune complex-mediated (not pauci-immune) nephritis and is typically ANA positive. It does not usually present with ANCA-positive vasculitis or isolated pulmonary-renal syndrome. Henoch-Schonlein purpura (Option D): HSP is an IgA-mediated vasculitis seen mainly in children, with purpura, arthralgia, abdominal pain, and renal involvement. Pulmonary hemorrhage and ANCA positivity are uncommon.

text: A 34-year-old man presented for a routine check-up from company. He was symptom free, but clinical examination suggested a small ventricular septal defect. Which one of the following findings was most likely to have been present?

options.B: A short systolic murmur at the right sternal edge
options.C: A systolic murmur maximal at the apex
options.D: A systolic murmur with thrill at the left sternal edge

ansText: A systolic murmur with thrill at the left sternal edge
expl: Typically, a small VSD generates a pansystolic murmur at the left sternal border(LSB) accompanied by a thrill. The murmur may be heard at the apex but is usually loudest at the LSB . Very small defects may generate an early/late systolic murmur. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 20 th edition, ch:234,264 pg:1673,1833

text: A 61-year-old male presents with a six month history of a gradually increasing burning sensation in his feet. Examination revealed normal cranial nerves and higher mental function. He has normal bulk, tone, power, light touch and pinprick sensation, co-ordination and reflexes in upper and lower limbs. With which of the following are these clinical findings consistent?
expl: The burning sensation described is typical of a small fibre sensory neuropathy. The small unmyelinated and thinly myelinated nerve fibres are affected. General neurological examination and reflexes are usually normal in this type of neuropathy. Treatment - Symptomatic therapy with local Lidoderm patch or oral amitriptyline, gabapentin or duloxetine. Conditions in which the small fibres are preferentially affected in the early stages include diabetes and amyloidosis . In the later stages however the neuropathy in these conditions also affects large fibres.The neuropathy associated with Sjogren's syndrome is a pure sensory neuropathy (ganglionopathy). Neuropathy affecting the large myelinated sensory fibres generally causes glove and socking sensory loss and loss of reflexes. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 446, Pg: 3482

text: A 15-year-old boy presents with a non-blanching rash over his shins and a swollen knee. He has noticed haematuria. Blood tests show a urea of 72 mg/dl and Creatinine 3 mg/dl. Urine dipstick shows: blood +++, protein +. What is the renal biopsy likely to show?
expl: The clinical presentation fits Henoch Schoenlein purpura renamed as IgA vasculitis. This is an autoimmune disorder which is related to multisystemic IgA deposition. It is usually a self-limited disease. It is the most common form of childhood vasculitis and results in Inflammatory changes in small vessels. Male:female = 1.5:1 It presents acutely with Headache Fever GI symptoms: loss of appetite, cramping abdominal pain Joint pain Red or purple spots typically appear on the skin(petechial purpura). Palpable purpurae is seen in almost all patients. Inflammatory changes associated with Henoch-Schönlein Purpura can also develop in the joints, kidneys, digestive system, and in rare cases, the brain and spinal cord. Mesangial Ig A deposits are typical features of HSP on the renal biopsy. IgA nephropathy is clinically similar to HSP, except that it lacks the systemic features, slightly older age of development, absence of abdominal pain and preceding infection. Serum complement levels are normal. Serum IgA levels May be elevated. Glucocorticoids have been proven to be beneficial in abdominal pain, arthralgias. Not in skin and renal disease, except in RPGN. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st edition, Ch: 363, Pg: 2813-2815.

text: A 50 year old asthmatic treated with a high dose of inhaled corticosteroids develops a skin rash. His routine blood tests show mild renal dysfunction and blood eosinophilia. His chest radiograph is normal. Which blood test should be done next?
expl: Skin rash and renal dysfunction in an asthmatic suggests Churg- Strauss syndrome. Churg-Strauss syndrome, or allergic granulomatous angiitis, is a rare syndrome that affects small- to medium-sized arteries. The presence of 4 or more criteria indicates a high likelihood of Churg-Strauss syndrome. These criteria are: asthma eosinophilia of more than 10% in peripheral blood paranasal sinusitis pulmonary infiltrates (may be transient) histological proof of vasculitis with extravascular eosinophils mononeuritis multiplex or polyneuropathy. Hypergammaglobulinemia, increased immunoglobulin E (IgE) levels, rheumatoid factor, and positive ANCA are usually present. Pulmonary Infiltrates in Churg Strauss Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:293 Pg: 2196

text: Which of the following statements regarding SSc is false?

options.A: ESR is usually normal in SSc, and an elevated ESR indicates coexisting myositis or malignancy
options.B: Sicca Syndrome can occur with SSC and is due to lymphocytic infiltration
options.C: Trigeminal neuropathy may occur with SSc
options.D: SSc may represent a paraneoplastic manifestation in those with malignancies of breast, lung or ovarian carcinoma and is associated with RNA polymerase III

ansText: Sicca Syndrome can occur with SSC and is due to lymphocytic infiltration
expl: Sicca symptoms are common in SSc, but unlike in Sjogren's Syndrome, it is due to fibrosis of the glands rather than lymphocytic infiltration. ESR is usually normal in SSc, since there is no active inflammation of vessel walls. A high ESR indicates myositis or malignancy. The CNS is usually spared in SSc, the only CNS manifestation could be unilateral or bilateral trigeminal neuropathy. Breast, lung, ovarian malignancy and lymphoma may occur in temporal association with SSc, where SSc may represent a paraneoplastic manifestation and is associated with antibodies to RNA polymerase III Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 360, Pg: 2783

text: A 21-year-old woman with no underlying health conditions presents with numbness and tingling in the fingers of both hands. The image below shows a characteristic finding. She reports that these episodes typically occur during periods of high stress or exposure to cold weather. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: This patient is most likely experiencing Primary Raynaud's phenomenon because: She is a young female (age 20-40 years; female-to-male ratio 5:1) There is no underlying disease Symptoms are symmetrical Episodes are triggered by cold Raynaud's Phenomenon Overview: Primary Raynaud's: Typically affects young women No associated underlying illness Normal nail fold capillaries with regular hairpin loops Accounts for over 50% of cases Has a better prognosis-improves in 15%, worsens in 30% Characterized by classic triphasic color changes (white, blue, red) Secondary Raynaud's (Option B ruled out): Commonly caused by connective tissue diseases, especially scleroderma (Option D ruled out) Other causes include arterial occlusive diseases, blood disorders, certain drugs (ergot, beta-blockers, bleomycin), and occupational exposures (vibrating tools) Clinical Features: Sequential color changes: White (ischemia) → Blue (deoxygenation) → Red (reperfusion) Triggered by cold or emotional stress Can involve fingers, toes, nose, ears May be accompanied by pain, numbness, or tingling Treatment: Conservative: Warm clothing, avoiding cold, smoking cessation Medications for severe cases: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, alpha-1 blockers (prazosin), phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors, topical nitroglycerin Digital sympathectomy for refractory cases Explanation of other options: Cold sores (Option C): are caused by the herpes virus and present as small fluid-filled blisters on the lips, mouth, nose, or cheeks, which does not fit this patient's symptoms or presentation.

text: A 26 year old patient who is a known case of SLE is coming to you with a positive UPT. She is on 5mg prednisolone and 200 mg HCQ daily and her disease is well controlled. What advice will you give her?

options.A: It is safe to continue both prednisolone and HCQs
options.B: Prednisolone has to be changed to Dexamethasone, HCQS is safe and may be continued
options.C: Prednisolone is safe and can be continued, but HCQS has to be stopped
options.D: No need to continue treatment as the disease is well controlled

ansText: It is safe to continue both prednisolone and HCQs
expl: SLE and Pregnancy: Rate of fetal loss is high in people with SLE than in general population and hence treatment has to be continued. So option D is incorrect. Risk of fetal loss in SLE is associated with high disease activity, APLA, Lupus nephritis and Hypertension. Prednisolone is the drug that can be given in pregnancy since 11β degydrogenase in placenta inactivates it and prevents fetal exposure. 11β dehydrogenase cant inactivate fluorinated glucocorticoids like dexamethasone and hence it is contraindicated in pregnecy, except for neonatal lupus. HCQS is also recommended by FDA for controlling disease activity in pregnancy. Drugs used in treatment of SLE in pregnancy First line agents: prednisone, prednisolone, HCQ Second line agents: Azathioprine. (May cause fetal harm) Breast feeding is contraindicated with immunosuppressants Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21th edition Ch:346 Pg:2747

text: What is the entry criteria in the new ACR/EULAR classification scheme for SLE?
expl: It is important to know that ANA is a highly sensitive test and thus a good screening test. In the new ACR/EULAR classification scheme, ANA positivity of more than 1:80 by ELISA is the entry criterion for classification to SLE. SLICC does not have such entry criteria. text: A 49 year old female is having history of Raynaud's phenomenon for the last 6 years. She has noticed skin tightening for the last one year. On examination, you pinched the skin of her chest and found that it was normal. Which of the following complication is she least likely to develop?

text: A 45-year-old woman presents with symptoms of dry mouth and eyes and tests positive for anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies. The image below demonstrates a positive test result, showing a score of less than 5 mm in 5 minutes without anesthesia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The presence of dry eyes and dry mouth, along with a Schirmer's test result of ≤5 mm in 5 minutes and positive anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies, strongly suggests a diagnosis of Sjogren syndrome. Sjogren Syndrome Pathogenesis: Sjogren syndrome is an autoimmune disease primarily targeting exocrine glands. It involves lymphocytic infiltration-mainly T and B cells-into the salivary and lacrimal glands. This immune attack is triggered by a combination of genetic susceptibility, environmental factors, and an abnormal immune response. Key features include: B-cell hyperactivity causing hypergammaglobulinemia and autoantibody production (anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB). Exocrine gland epithelial cells express autoantigens (Ro, La), secrete pro-inflammatory cytokines, and activate immune pathways via Toll-like receptors. Genetic predisposition, such as specific HLA alleles (e.g., HLA-DQA1*0501) and immune regulatory genes (IRF5, STAT4), increase susceptibility. Clinical Features: Xerostomia (dry mouth) and keratoconjunctivitis sicca (dry eyes) are hallmark symptoms. Oral symptoms: difficulty swallowing, increased dental caries, and parotid gland enlargement. Ocular symptoms: gritty sensation, burning, and decreased tear production. Systemic signs: fatigue, joint pain, Raynaud's phenomenon, and increased risk of lymphoma (especially marginal zone B-cell lymphoma). Diagnosis: Diagnosis is based on clinical presentation and supportive tests: Unstimulated whole saliva flow rate ≤0.1 mL/min. Schirmer's test ≤5 mm/5 min in at least one eye. Ocular staining score ≥5 or van Bijsterveld's score ≥4 in at least one eye. Presence of serum antibodies (anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB). Minor salivary gland biopsy showing lymphocytic infiltration with a focus score ≥1. Treatment: Management focuses on symptom relief and controlling systemic disease: For eye symptoms: artificial tears and topical cyclosporine for inflammation. For dry mouth: frequent sips of water, pilocarpine, or cevimeline to stimulate saliva production. For systemic involvement: hydroxychloroquine for mild symptoms, and immunosuppressants such as rituximab in severe cases. Explanation for other options: Scleroderma (Option A): is associated with anti-Scl-70 and anti-centromere antibodies, so it is unlikely to be the diagnosis in this case. Dehydration and lacrimal duct stones (Options B and C): are also unlikely, as the presence of anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies is characteristic of Sjogren syndrome.

text: An 18 year old female comes to you with history of arthritis for the past two months. She also gives history of hematuria. Her ESR is 140 and urine shows numerous crenated RBC with proteinuria. Suspecting SLE with nephritis you ordered for ANA test. Which of the following statements is true?

options.A: ANA is the specific investigation for SLE
options.B: ELISA is the gold standard method for detecting ANA
options.C: Specific patterns in IF are diagnostic of the type of ANA
options.D: The specific type of ANA is best detected by ELISA

ansText: The specific type of ANA is best detected by ELISA
expl: This question basically deals with the tests for detecting Antinuclear Antibodies. Antinuclear Antibodies are highly sensitive for diagnosing SLE, but not specific. Antinuclear antibodies is not a single entity, but consists of antibodies that are directed against several different components of a cell, nucleus in particular. Hence ELISA is not the method for detecting ANA. Immunofluorescence is the preferred method. 4 different patterns of fluorescence is identified. But they are not specific for a particular antibody. So the specific antibody is identified by ELISA, if ANA is positive. So the screening test is ANA by immunofluorescence and the test to identify the particular antibody is ELISA. Patterns of staining in IF Reference: Harrisons Principles Of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 356, Pg: 2738

text: Which of the following statements are true regarding the management of Lupus nephritis? 1. HCQS should be included as treatment for all classes since it reduces the accrual of tissue damage. 2. Management of class I and Class II should be guided by the extra renal manifestations. 3. Class III and IV requires aggressive immunosuppression. 4. Isolated Class V has got better prognosis than class IV. 5. Isolated class V without nephrotic range proteinuria requires only supportive management.
expl: The question deals with the management and prognosis of Lupus Nephritis. HCQ should be in the management of allclasses of lupus nephritis. Class I and II should be treated mainly based on the extra renal manifestations. Class III and IV are the proliferative and serious forms and require aggressive immunosuppression with high dose glucocorticoid with either MMF or Cyclophosphamide. Isolated Class V presents with proteinuria alone and has got better outcome than class IV. But class V often co exists with class III and IV. Class V with nephrotic range proteinuria should be treated with immunosuppression, usually steroid with calcinurin inhibitors. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Ch:356 Pg:2739-2747 KDIGO guidelines

text: A woman presents with fever, joint pains, oral ulcers, and fatigue for six months, now associated with hematuria. Urine analysis reveals red blood cell casts and proteinuria. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The presence of systemic features of SLE (fever, arthralgia, ulcers, fatigue) along with renal involvement (RBC casts, proteinuria, hematuria) strongly indicates lupus nephritis , a renal manifestation of systemic lupus erythematosus caused by immune complex deposition in the glomeruli. Lupus Nephritis: Pathophysiology: Immune complex-mediated glomerular injury involving anti-dsDNA antibodies. Clinical features: Proteinuria (may reach nephrotic levels) Hematuria with RBC casts Systemic SLE manifestations: fever, arthralgia, oral/nasal ulcers, photosensitivity, fatigue Risk of progression to hypertension and ESRD if untreated Diagnosis: Urinalysis: proteinuria, hematuria, RBC casts Serology: ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm positivity Renal biopsy: classification into six histological classes (I-VI) Management: Corticosteroids, cyclophosphamide, mycophenolate mofetil Hydroxychloroquine (for systemic SLE; safe in pregnancy) Explanation of other options: Acute interstitial nephritis (Option A): Typically drug-induced (e.g., NSAIDs, antibiotics) or due to infections. Presents with fever, rash, eosinophilia, and urine showing WBC casts-not RBC casts. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (Option B): Seen in children post-streptococcal infection; presents with hematuria, edema, and hypertension, but lacks systemic lupus features such as ulcers or arthritis. IgA nephropathy (Option D): Often presents with recurrent hematuria following an upper respiratory infection; shows mesangial IgA deposits on biopsy but does not include systemic SLE manifestations. Key Takeaways: RBC casts + systemic SLE features = lupus nephritis. Always confirm with serology and renal biopsy for classification and prognosis. Requires immunosuppressive therapy to prevent progression to renal failure.

text: A 35-year-old female patient with fever and malar rash was found to have vegetations on either side of the heart valves. What is the diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The presentation of fever, malar rash, and cardiac vegetations is classic for Libman-Sacks endocarditis , which is a non-infectious complication of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) . Key Diagnostic Features Malar Rash: A hallmark cutaneous manifestation of SLE. Vegetations: Libman-Sacks lesions are characterized by sterile, verrucous (wart-like) vegetations that are unique because they can occur on both sides of the valve leaflets (mitral and tricuspid are most common). Systemic Illness: Fever is a common systemic feature of active SLE. Explanation of other options: Infective endocarditis (Option A): This involves infective vegetations usually in a patient with predisposing factors (e.g., valvular disease, IV drug use). While fever is present, a malar rash is not a typical feature. Rheumatic Heart Disease (Option C): This results from untreated Group A streptococcal infection, leading to valvular damage (e.g., mitral stenosis). It does not cause a malar rash or the specific bilateral vegetations seen in Libman-Sacks endocarditis. Key Takeaways: Libman-Sacks endocarditis is a diagnostic feature of SLE. The vegetations are sterile and can be found on both sides of the valve leaflets . The presence of a malar rash strongly points toward an underlying autoimmune etiology.

text: A 30-year-old woman with known SLE presents with ankle swelling. Her blood pressure is 170/100 mmHg and she has marked lower limb oedema. Urine dipstick discloses +3 protein with no haematuria. Plasma creatinine concentration is 1.1 mg/dl, albumin is 1.2 g/dl and urinary protein excretion rate is 6.9 g/24 h. What is the cause of this presentation?
expl: This patient is a young female with SLE who presents with massive proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia and hypertension without hematuria. This is typical of Nephrotic syndrome. Amyloidosis is known to cause nephrotic syndrome. But the diseases that are known to be associated with AA amyloid are Rheumatoid Arthritis, Juvenile idiopathic arthritis, chronic infections and Familial Mediterranean Fever. And AL amyloidosis with monoclonal gammopathies. Class II Lupus Nephritis typically presents as Nephritic syndrome and not pure nephrotic syndrome. Class V Lupus nephritis is the one which may present as pure Nephrotic syndrome. The histology will be pure membranous nephropathy. It can precede the extra renal manifestations in SLE. Fibrillary glomerulopathy is characterized by the accumulation of congo red negative fibrils in the glomerulus. It is found to be associated with malignancies, autoimmune diseases, monoclonal gammopathies. It presents with proteinuria and hematuria. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21 st edition, Ch:314, Pg:2345, 2338

text: A 40-year-old woman is found to have absent ankle jerks and gait disturbance. Which of the following investigations is not indicated?
expl: Absent ankle jerks may occur in conditions associated with neuropathy (B12 deficiency, systemic lupus erythematosus [SLE], cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis) and dorsal root disease (tabes dorsalis). Gait disturbance may occur for a variety of reasons: Sensory ataxia in B12 deficiency and tabes dorsalis Pyramidal signs in B12 deficiency and SLE Cerebellar ataxia in cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis. Cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis is an inherited condition, associated with accumulation of cholesterol in tissues including brain, peripheral nerve and tendons which produces a clinical picture of: Early onset dementia Gait ataxia Loss of vibration sense Cataracts Large tendon xanthomata. It is eminently treatable by the oral administration of chenodeoxycholic acid. To clarify option 3, cholestanol is a derivative of cholesterol. In cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis there is a deficiency in sterol storage, and diagnosis is based on high serum (and tendon) cholestanol Serum cholesterol may be normal or low. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:442, Pg: 3454

text: A 30-year-old woman presents with seizures, hypertension and photosensitivity. Bloods show: Hb 11 g/dl, WCC 8000/μL, platelets 180000/μL, urea 98 mg/dl, creatinine 3.2 mg/dl, sodium 140 mmol/l, potassium 5 mmol/l, ESR 100 mm/hr, CRP 25 mg/l. Urine showing 3+ protein and hematuria. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: We have a young female with history of seizures, hypertension and photosensitivity rash, who has renal impairment with hematuria and proteinuria, high ESR points to the diagnosis of SLE with Lupus nephritis. Option A: Anti GBM disease is a cause of rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis which presents as an acute nephritic syndrome leading to renal failure and may also affect the lung causing diffuse alveolar haemorrhage which presents with hypoxemia and haemoptysis(known as Goodpasture syndrome) Option B: Myeloma causes renal impairment, but the patient profile will be an elderly patient with skeletal pains, hypercalcemia and renal impairment. Option D: Wegener's granulomatosis is a small vessel vasculitis which causes rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis(RPGN) along with pulmonary cavities & infiltrates and is characterized by cANCA positivity. text: A 30-year-old heroine addict was found dead in his room. He was last seen alive by his neighbours around 4 weeks ago and he was presumed to be unwell over the past 4 weeks. At autopsy, his kidneys had a flea bitten appearance and renal biopsy showed sub epithelial and sub endothelial deposits of Immunoglobulin and C3. What could be the possible cause of these findings?
expl: The patient is a IV drug abuser, who was presumed to be not well for the past few weeks. IV drug abuse increases the risk of Infective endocarditis. So the patient probably died of an untreated Infective endocarditis. The appearance of kidneys in IE is 'Flea Bitten' and microscopy shows immune complex deposition. It is more common in Sub Acute Bacterial endocarditis than Acute, since acute will be more symptomatic and the patient would have got treated. SLE presents with varying degrees of proliferation. Moreover, the history of drug abuse cant be ignored. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Pg: 2337.

text: A 44 year woman has Raynaud's phenomenon. She also has difficulty in swallowing and dyspnoea. Echocardiography shows right heart strain. Her BP was 150/100 and her renal functions were derranged. Which one of the following antibodies is specific to this lady's condition?
expl: This patient has esophageal dysmotility, dyspnoea and evidence of PAH. But this is not CREST syndrome seen with limited cutaneous disease, because she has derranged renal function. So this is progressive systemic sclerosis and hence the antibody associated is anti ScL-70 or Topoisomerase I. Anti RNA polymerase III will have rapidly progressive skin thickening and joint symptoms and renal crisis, like Scl-70, but instead of ILD, they are at risk of developing GAVE and contemporaneous cancers. Anti centromere antibody is seen in limited cutaneous variety and is found to be protective of renal involvement. Anti UIII RNP is positively associated with renal involvement in systemic sclerosis. They can have skin involvement of either diffuse or limited cutaneous type. Some patients with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis have antibodies directed against Th/T0 antigen and these patients develop both ILD and PAH Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Chapter:360 Page number :2776

text: Which of the following concerning congenital heart disease is correct?

options.A: ASD is the commonest cardiac malformation at birth

options.C: Ebstein's anomaly is associated with maternal exposure to lithium carbonate
options.D: Hypoplastic left heart syndrome is characterised by a large, dilated left ventricle

ansText: Ebstein's anomaly is associated with maternal exposure to lithium carbonate
expl: Ebstein's anomaly is associated with maternal exposure to lithium carbonate in the first trimester . It causes malformed tricuspid valve leading to tricuspid regurgitation. Option 1 - VSD is the most congenital heart disease. Option 2 - In the vast majority of cases of neonates with complete heart block the cause is unknown but in the minority it may be caused by autoimmune disease, particularly Anti-Ro antibodies, in the mother. text: A 55-year-old woman presents with a history of progressive difficulty in climbing stairs and rising from chairs. She also complains of difficulty in swallowing. She complains that her hands discolor and become cold easily. On examination she has purple discoloration of her eyelids and periorbital oedema. There is weakness of the muscles of her limb girdles. What is the likely cause of the dysphagia?
expl: The diagnosis is dermatomyositis. Characteristic features of DM: Symmetric, proximal greater than distal weakness Heliotrope rash (erythematous discoloration of eyelids with periorbital edema) Gottron sign (erythematous rash over the extensor surfaces of joints such as the knuckles, elbows, knees, and ankles) Gottron papules (raised erythematous rash over knuckles) V-sign (rash on the sun-exposed anterior neck and chest) Shawl sign over the back of the neck and shoulders Dysphagia in dermatomyositis is primarily due to weakness of the striated musculature of the posterior pharynx. Dysphagia may also result from cricopharyngeal obstruction secondary to inflammation or fibrosis of the cricopharyngeus muscles. text: A 50-year-old female reports trouble performing tasks such as climbing stairs, rising from a seated position, and combing her hair. On examination, a violaceous rash over the upper eyelids is observed. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: Proximal muscle weakness (problems climbing stairs, getting up from a chair, and combing hair) combined with the distinctive violaceous rash on the upper eyelids (heliotrope rash) points to a diagnosis of dermatomyositis. Explanations of other options: Inclusion body myositis (Option A): Inclusion body myositis mainly occurs in older individuals and is characterized by distal, often asymmetric muscle weakness. Unlike dermatomyositis, it lacks skin involvement and most commonly affects the quadriceps and finger flexors. Polymyositis (Option C): Polymyositis is an autoimmune condition marked by inflammatory muscle involvement, presenting as symmetric proximal muscle weakness. Unlike dermatomyositis, it does not feature the distinctive skin signs such as the heliotrope rash or Gottron's papules. Scleroderma (Option D): Scleroderma is a connective tissue disease that mainly involves the skin and internal organs. Although muscle weakness may occur, its defining features are skin thickening and fibrosis rather than the violaceous rash of dermatomyositis. It is also associated with Raynaud's phenomenon and multi-organ involvement.

text: What is the investigation of choice for detecting enteric fever in the first week?
expl: Explanation: Blood culture is the most sensitive diagnostic modality for early detection of enteric fever , as Salmonella typhi or Salmonella paratyphi are present in the bloodstream during the initial phase of infection. Enteric Fever: Diagnosis Definitive Diagnosis: Isolation of Typhi or S. Paratyphi from blood, bone marrow, sterile sites, rose spots, stool, or intestinal secretions. Blood Culture: ~60% sensitive; lower with small volume, prior antibiotics, or early illness ( Bone Marrow Culture: >80% sensitive; unaffected by up to 5 days of prior antibiotics. Intestinal Secretions: Positive even if bone marrow culture is negative; duodenal string test is preferred noninvasive method. Combined Cultures: Blood + bone marrow + intestinal secretions → >90% yield. Stool Culture: Often negative in the first week (60-70%), may become positive by the third week in untreated cases. Serology: Widal Test: Rapid, simple, but limited sensitivity/specificity; cannot distinguish active vs. prior infection or vaccination. IDL Tubex, Typhidot: More accurate but expensive, limiting use in low-resource settings. Molecular Methods: Nucleic acid-based tests not yet commercially available.

text: A 25-year-old female presented with a sudden onset of left sided head and neck pain. 24 hours later she presents with sudden onset of right hemiparesis, facial weakness and homonymous hemianopia and left Horner's syndrome. A CT brain showed a left middle cerebral artery territory infarction. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: The presence of neck pain on the left side, followed by a right sided weakness points to the diagnosis of carotid dissection. The two commonest causes of young onset stroke (less than 40 years) are cardio-embolism and carotid artery dissection. Carotid artery dissection is either spontaneous or traumatic. Facial/head/neck pain and Horner's syndrome are characteristic features. Migrainous stroke usually affects the posterior circulation (posterior cerebral artery territory is the commonest). Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 426, Pg: 3341

text: Presence of which of the following will help to determine HBV-HDV coinfection and exclude HBV-HDV superinfection
expl: When a patient presents with acute hepatitis and has HBsAg and anti-HDV in serum, determination of the class of anti-HBc is helpful in establishing the relationship between infection with HBV and HDV. Although IgM anti-HBc does not distinguish absolutely between acute and chronic HBV infection, its presence is a reliable indicator of recent infection and its absence a reliable indicator of infection in the remote past. In simultaneous acute HBV and HDV infections, IgM anti-HBc will be detectable, whereas in acute HDV infection superimposed on chronic HBV infection, anti-HBc will be of the IgG class.

text: A 38-year-old woman is referred to the gastroenterology clinic. The patient has persistent lethargy and blood results have demonstrated iron deficiency anemia. Which of the following statements regarding iron deficiency anemia is correct?

options.A: Endomysial antibody serology to investigate for coeliac disease should always be requested in addition to duodenal biopsies
options.B: Low serum iron with a low total iron-binding capacity confirms iron deficiency
options.C: Microcytosis may be absent where there is combined iron and folate deficiency
options.D: The presence of Howell-Jolly bodies on blood film would go against coeliac disease

ansText: Microcytosis may be absent where there is combined iron and folate deficiency
expl: Distal duodenal (D2) biopsies should be taken in any patient with iron deficiency anemia undergoing a gastroscopy as 2-3% of patients will have celiac disease. Endomysial antibody serology can be useful to confirm that subtotal villous atrophy found at histology is not due to another cause.Antibody titres help to determine whether or not the patient is adhering to a gluten free diet. In the investigation of iron deficiency anemia serology for coeliac disease would be performed prior to an OGD. Low serum iron ( high total iron-binding capacity (> 70 pmol/L) confirms iron deficiency. Howell-Jolly bodies on blood film indicate hyposplenism and are consistent with a diagnosis of coeliac disease. Thrombocytosis may occur in acute hemorrhage but is also found in a number of other situations such as inflammatory conditions. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st ed, Ch: 325, Pg: 2463

text: A 25-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes mellitus and hypothyroidism presents with chronic oral mucocutaneous candidiasis persisting for 5 years. She is diagnosed with Autoimmune Polyendocrinopathy Syndrome (APS) Type 1. Which of the following statements about this condition is incorrect?
expl: Explanation: Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) is strongly associated with APS Type 2 (Schmidt syndrome) but not typically seen in APS Type 1 . Autoimmune Polyendocrinopathy Syndrome Type 1 (APS-1) also known as APECED (Autoimmune Polyendocrinopathy, Candidiasis, and Ectodermal Dystrophy) is a rare, monogenic autoimmune disorder that primarily affects children. It results from a mutation in the AIRE gene (Autoimmune Regulator), leading to a breakdown of central immune tolerance and the formation of multiple autoantibodies against endocrine and non-endocrine tissues. APS Type 1 is more associated with conditions like hypoparathyroidism, adrenal insufficiency, and chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis. Autoimmune Polyendocrinopathy Syndrome (APS): Autoimmune Polyendocrinopathy Syndrome iis a group of autoimmune disorders characterized by the immune system mistakenly attacking multiple endocrine glands, leading to hormonal imbalances. It is classified into two main types. APECED: Autoimmune Polyendocrinopathy-Candidiasis-Ectodermal Dystrophy

text: A 33 year old lady presents with stiffness, pain and swelling of her hands and wrists. Investigations reveal a normocytic, normochromic anemia, elevated ESR and CRP. What antibody would you use if you wanted to do A test for detecting RA factor?
expl: IgM, IgG, and IgA isotypes of RF occur in sera from patients with RA, although the IgM isotype is the one most frequently measured by commercial laboratories. The sensitivity of RA is only 75%, therefore a negative test does not exclude the presence of the disease. False positive in other connective tissue diseases, such as primary Sjogren's syndrome, systemic lupus erythematosus, and type II mixed essential cryoglobulinemia, as well as chronic infections such as subacute bacterial endocarditis and hepatitis B and C. Serum RF may also be detected in 1-5% of the healthy population. Anti CCP has sensitivity almost similar to RA factor, but is almost 95% specific for RA. Anti CCP has a role in predicting the outcomes too, as it is associated with worse outcomes. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Ch:358 Pg:2759

text: A 42 year old man is referred to the renal physician due to symptoms of haemoptysis and haematuria. These symptoms have been going on for 6 months. expl: The patient has pulmonary renal syndrome, and among the given options, the diagnosis would fit Wegener's granulomatosis, which is commonly cANCA positive. text: A 40-year-old woman presents with left flank pain. On examination she was febrile, had livedo reticularis and a blood pressure of 190/100 mmHg. She has also had a history of a butterfly rash in the past. Investigations revealed: Hb 13.9 g/dL WBC 6.5 x 10^9/L Platelet count 110 x 10^9/L Serum Creatinine 0.9 mg/dL Urine dipstick analysis: blood ++, protein - Which one of the following tests is likely to be positive?
expl: The patient is an adult female with history of butterfly rash in the past, which points to the diagnosis of SLE. Causes of flank pain includes Acute pyelonephritis or Renal vein thrombosis. Urinalysis here is not favoring a pyelonephritis and hence can be ruled out. So the possibility here is renal vein thrombosis How can renal vein thrombosis be linked to SLE? Lupus Nephritis causing Nephrotic range proteinuria and renal vein thrombosis A secondary APS causing renal vein thrombosis. Hypertension can be seen in both lupus nephritis and APS with renal vein thrombosis. Thrombocytopenia can occur in both SLE and APS, but the presence of a clinical evidence of thrombosis despite thrombocytopenia points towards an underlying APS. So this patient is having a renal vein thrombosis due to Secondary APS with SLE. So the antibodies that should be tested are the Antiphospholipid antibodies. Among the given options it is the anti Cardiolipin. Anti Ro antibody is not a marker of thrombosis, but of cutaneous disease and neonatal lupus with CHB. Hence option A is ruled out Anti GBM antibody is seen in Goodpasture's syndrome. The disease has got a very different clinical presentation and is included under the pulmonary renal syndromes. It presents with hemoptysis and hematuria. ASOT is probably ASO titre which is seen in acute rheumatic fever and not APS Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Ch:357 Pg:2749

text: A 43-year-old woman presents with left flank pain. On examination she was febrile, had livedo reticularis and a blood pressure of 190/100 mmHg. She has also has history of a butterfly rash in the past. Investigations revealed: Hb 13.9 g/dL WBC 6.5 x 10^9/L Platelet count 110 x 10^9/L Serum Creatinine 0.9 mg/dL Urine dipstick analysis: blood ++, protein - Which one of the following tests is likely to be positive?
expl: The presence of acute onset flank pain plus uncontrolled hypertension would point us towards us a renal cause. We also have history that she had a butterfly rash in the past-> suggestive of SLE. The fact that she had haematuria without proteinuria and acute onset of symptoms-> would point us towards Renal vein thrombosis. This with livedo reticularis would likely be because of APLA secondary to SLE. Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) is a disorder characterized by recurrent venous or arterial thrombosis and/or fetal losses associated with typical laboratory abnormalities. These include persistently elevated levels of antibodies directed against membrane anionic phospholipids (ie, anticardiolipin [aCL] antibody, antiphosphatidylserine). Other features are nonthrombotic neurologic symptoms, such as migraine headaches, chorea, seizures, transverse myelitis, Guillain-Barre syndrome, thrombocytopenia or hemolytic anaemia, Livedo reticularis, Avascular necrosis of bone and Pulmonary hypertension. Aspirin or warfarin is recommended for patients with thrombotic syndromes. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Chapter:357 ,Page number :2749

text: A 35-year-old woman experiences skin thickening, muscle weakness, and pale peripheries upon cold exposure. Her creatine kinase is increased with positive ANA, and biopsy revealed scl-70 positivity and perifascicular infiltration. What is the antibody linked to this condition?
expl: Explanation: The simultaneous presentation of Raynaud's phenomenon and anti-Scl-70 positivity is indicative of systemic sclerosis, specifically the diffuse subtype. Peri-fascicular inflammation and elevated creatine kinase levels are characteristic of dermatomyositis or polymyositis. When these clinical and serological features coexist, an overlap syndrome most notably scleroderma-myositis overlap should be suspected. This particular overlap is strongly associated with the presence of anti-PM/Scl antibody. Overlap syndromes are defined by the co-occurrence of dermatomyositis or polymyositis with one or more additional connective tissue diseases, such as systemic sclerosis, mixed connective tissue disease, Sjögren's syndrome, systemic lupus erythematosus, or rheumatoid arthritis. The clinical presentation of systemic sclerosis can be broadly categorized into two main subtypes: diffuse and limited cutaneous disease. Histopathology and Pathogenesis of polymyositis Polymyositis exhibits diverse muscle changes, with inflammatory cell infiltration that is more prominent in the perimysium than in the endomysium. The predominant inflammatory cells are CD8+ T lymphocytes and macrophages, which are mainly located in the endomysial, perimysial, and perivascular areas. Autoantibodies in systemic sclerosis Explanation of other options: Anti-Jo-1 Antibody (Option B): This antibody is a marker for antisynthetase syndrome. The clinical presentation of this syndrome includes a combination of symptoms such as myositis, non-erosive arthritis, interstitial lung disease, Raynaud's phenomenon, mechanic's hands, and fever. Since these findings are not described in the provided scenario, this antibody is not the most specific answer. Anticentromere Antibody (Option C): This antibody is highly associated with the limited cutaneous form of systemic sclerosis, also known as CREST syndrome. The acronym CREST represents its key features: Calcinosis, Raynaud's phenomenon, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, and Telangiectasia. Anti-Nuclear Antibody (Option D): This antibody is a general screening test for autoimmunity and is positive in a wide range of autoimmune disorders, including systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). However, since the scenario already states that the ANA is positive, the question is asking for a more specific antibody that would confirm the diagnosis, making this option insufficient on its own.

text: A 57-year-old woman with longstanding well controlled seropositive Rheumatoid Arthritis, treated with methotrexate (20 mg/week) and folic acid 5 mg/day, presents with cough productive of green phlegm, fever (38.5°C), and severe sore throat. On examination, the BP is 110/70 mmHg, SaO2 is 98% on air. There is an occasional crackle at the right lung base. Chest x ray is normal. CBC, RFT, and LFTs are also normal. The CRP is 34 mg/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?

options.B: IV antibiotics, stop methotrexate, and give folinic acid rescue

expl: The most likely diagnosis in this scenario is a lower respiratory tract infection (because of the presence of productive cough). In the setting of acute infection , most DMARDs (except hydroxychloroquine) should be discontinued until the infectious process has resolved. Option 1 - Methotrexate should be stopped until the infection resolves. Option 2 - Taken in overdose , methotrexate can cause multiple organ damage. Folinic acid is indicated and should be given intravenously as soon as it is suspected to limit toxicity. There is no suggestion of methotrexate overdose in this patient, and therefore folinic acid is not indicated. Option 4 - Oral antibiotics can be used to control the infection but methotrexate should be stopped until the infection resolves. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition, Ch:358, Pg:2762

text: A 34 year old woman has generalized joint pains and muscle aches. She alsocomplains of gritty sensations in the eye in the mornings. Blood tests show Anti NuclearAntibody ++, Rheumatoid Factor ++. What is the diagnosis?
expl: This question deals with the manifestations of Sjogren's syndrome. Exocrine gland involvement is most common manifestation. The lacrimal and the salivary glands are most frequently involved. The characteristic symptoms are dry eyes (causing gritty sensation), dry mouth. Exocrine glands of the respiratory tree can lead to dry nose, throat and trachea. GI involvement can lead to atrophic gastritis. Genital involvement can cause dyspareunia. Extra glandular involvement is also seen in1/3 rd patients. Peri epithetlial involvement is characterized by accumulation of activated lymphocytes and hence is called autoimmune epithelitis. Sjogren's Syndrome predisposes to the development of MALTOMA. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st ed, Ch: 361, Pg: 2789

text: A 40 year old man has a history of long standing cough with sputum production. He also has recurrent episodes of chest infections and sinusitis. He is married but has been unsuccessful in having children. He also has hearing difficulty. Which one of the following is likely?

text: The image shown below depicts a specific physical finding (Palmar Erythema). Which of the following conditions is not associated with this finding?
expl: Explanation: Palmar erythema is associated with states of increased estrogen or vasodilation. The condition listed that is not associated with this finding is Menopause , which is characterized by low estrogen levels . Associations of Palmar Erythema Pregnancy (Option B ruled out): A classic physiologic cause due to high estrogen levels and increased cardiac output. Liver Cirrhosis (Option C ruled out): Impaired liver function leads to decreased metabolism of estrogen, causing relative hyperestrogenism. Rheumatoid Arthritis (Option A ruled out): An autoimmune cause, likely related to increased vascularity and chronic inflammation. Key Takeaways: Palmar erythema is a sign of hyperestrogenic states (pregnancy, cirrhosis) or chronic inflammatory diseases (RA). Menopause , with its low estrogen state, is not associated with this finding.

text: A 54 year old man presents with a 6 week history of lethargy and diffuse purpuric rash. He is noted to have a right foot drop and a left ulnar nerve palsy. Dipstick urinalysis shows blood ++. What is the likely diagnosis?
expl: A low C4 together with a strongly positive rheumatoid factor suggests cryoglobulinemia as a cause of mononeuritis multiplex and rash. Palpable purpura, arthralgia, hepatosplenomegaly, diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis, Raynaud's phenomenon and thrombosis may occur. Type I cryoglobulinemia may be associated with lymphoproliferative disorders, multiple myeloma, and monoclonal gammopathy of uncertain significance, and macroglobulinemia. Plasmapheresis may reduce the levels of cryoglobulin. Type II cryoglobulinemia (mixed monoclonal) is usually composed of a monoclonal component (usually IgG, IgM or IgA) and a polyclonal component (mainly IgG). Causes are connective tissue diseases, Hepatitis B and C infection, infectious mononucleosis and lymphoma. Reference: Harrison's Principles Of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Ch:363 Pg:2814

text: For the patient described in the question above, what will you give for long term management initially?
expl: The cornerstone in the management of RA are DMARDS. Conventional DMARDS are the first choice, Methotrexate is the DMARD of choice for RA. text: A 60 year old female, who is a known case of Rheumatoid Arthritis on Adalimumab for the past 1 year. She now presents with a not feeling well and feverishness of one month duration. She also has arthralgias. On examination, she is febrile with no organomegaly. Her chest X ray shows multiple cavitary lesions with prominent hilar lymph nodes. A biopsy from the nodes show necrotizing granulomas. Which of the following is the likely cause?
expl: This question deals with causes of granulomatous necrosis. A,B and D are causes of necrotizing granulomas. We have a patient with impaired immunity by virtue of use of Adalimumab for RA. She is prone to develop infections that can cause granulomatous inflammation. Among the options Histoplasmosis is the best answer. Wegener’s Granulomatosis does not cause significant mediastinal adenopathy. Sarcoidosis also causes granulomatous inflammation, but here there is a background of immunosuppression, making the possibility of infections more than sarcoidosis. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Ch:363 Pg:2807

text: Patient is on a single drug for Rheumatoid arthritis for years. Symptoms are controlled. Then he developed corneal opacity. Which of the following medications was the patient on?
expl: Chloroquine : Toxicity occurs in 6% of patients with a cumulative dose of 1000g over 5 years with continuing therapy. Early eye symptoms include blurring of vision or defective accommodation, which resolves. Retinal toxicity is the most feared one, described as bilateral Bulls eye maculopathy, with retinal pigment epithelial degeneration of the central macula with sparing of a small area in the fovea. It is more seen with chloroquine than hydroxychloroquine. Early diagnosis is possible by visual field analysis, even before fundal changes are evident. With advanced disease, the visual symptoms progress despite the stoppage of the drug due to long half life of the drug in retina. Corneal deposits are also common with CQ and HCQs which presents as halos around light and are reversible. Hydroxychloroquine can cause cardiomyopathy and bonemarrow suppression Methotrexate causes bone marrow suppression, hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, pulmonary fibrosis and pseudolymphoma. Leflunomide causes hepatotoxicity and myelosuppression. Sulfasalazine causes granulocytopenia and hemolytic anemia in G6PD deficiency.

What is the likely diagnosis?
expl: The presence of fever and weight loss for 20 days points towards a chronic etiology rather than an acute one. The presence of a pleural effusion is atypical of ILD. Since, the patient is giving a history of use of a TNF alpha inhibitor-> Opportunistic infection such as tuberculosis is more likely. text: A 33-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of arthralgia, painful mouth ulceration and eye irritation. On examination, he had some ulceration in the mouth, bilaterally swollen wrists and reduced range of movements of both knees. His investigations showed: white cell count 11 x 10^9/L, C reactive protein 100 mg/dl,Rheumatoid factor negative. What is the likely diagnosis?
expl: Recurrent oral ulcers, eye irritation which may suggest a uveitis and arthritis suggests the diagnosis of Behcet's Disease. Although Sjogren's Syndrome can cause dry eyes, painful mouth ulcers are not seen. Behcet's syndrome is a multisystem disorder characterized by recurrent oral genital ulceration, eye lesions (anterior and posterior uveitis or retinal vasculitis), skin lesions, (erythema nodosum, papulopustular lesions folliculitis) and a positive pathergy test. Following a needle prick or intradermal injection with saline or dilute histamine, the puncture site becomes inflamed and develops a small sterile pustule due to hyperactivity of the skin to any intracutaneous insult. Oral Ulceration in Behcet's disease Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Ch:364 Pg:2817

text: A 46 year old man has difficulty bending touching his toes when bending over. He has lower back pain, stiffness in the thoracic region and reduced chest expansion. His lower spine X-ray is shown above. He has negative rheumatoid factor, and a HLA-B27 genotype. What is the diagnosis?
expl: A young individual with inflammatory low back ache, reduced movements of the spine and chest with HLA B 27 positivity and a lumbar spine X-ray showing bridging osteophytes is suggestive of Ankylosing Spondylitis. The clinical features of AS includes: Inflammatory type of low back ache in the lumbar or gluteal region lasting for > 30 minutes, improving with activity and recurring after periods of rest. Pain becomes persistent once the disease progresses, becomes bilateral with nocturnal symptoms Enthesitis (Pain at the site of insertion of tendons, ligaments or joint capsules) can cause costochondral tenderness, iliac crest, greater trochanter etc Hip and shoulder joint arthritis occurs and is considered as a part of axial arthritis and not peripheral arthritis. HLA B27 is one of the single genes representing the inheritance of AS. HLA B 27 is seen in 85-90% of patients with AS. AS is found in 1-6% of adults having HLA B 27. There are around 115 other genetic alleles responsible for AS, apart from HLA B27. The radiological features of AS includes: Sacroiliitis : blurring of the cortical margins of the subchondral bone, followed by erosions and sclerosis. Progression of the erosions leads to "pseudowidening" of the joint space; followed by ankylosis and bony obliteration. MRI STIR sequence is required for demonstrating early sacroiliitis. In spine, it leads to marginal erosions at the anterior corners( Romano Lesions) followed by ossification, causing marginal syndesmophytes seen as bony ridges joining the vertebral bodies anteriorly and laterally. Bamboo Spine Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st ed, Ch: 362, Pg: 2790-2794

text: A 60-year man has been on haemodialysis for 15 years due to diabetic nephropathy. He now has joint pains in the shoulders and knees. expl: The history of joint pains and Carpal tunnel syndrome in a dialysis patient suggests Aβ2 microglobulin(Aβ2M) amyloidosis. Amyloid deposits are composed of β 2 - microglobulin Develop approximately > 12 years of dialysis. Carpal Tunnel syndrome is the first presentation. Joints involved are bilateral and symmetrical and large joints. Joint effusions are non inflammatory and contains β2 microglobulin on congo red. There will be visceral deposits of β2 microglobulin. expl: OCULAR MANIFESTATIONS OF CONNECTIVE TISSUE DISEASES: SLE: keratoconjunctivitis sicca is the commonest ocular manifestation . It occurs with or without secondary Sjogrens syndrome. SLE retinopathy can be detected on ophthalmoscopic examination as retinal hemorrhages, vasculitic appearing lesions, cotton wool spots and hard exudates. The pathology is either immune complex mediated vasculopathy or micro thrombotic events. Retinal abnormalities correlate with CNS lupus, lupus nephritis and APS. Episcleritis and scleritis occurs in SLE, but uveitis is extremely rare. Anterior or posterior uveitis, panuveitis bilateral, iridocyclitis, keratitis, episcleritis, vitritis, retinal vein occlusion and optic neuritis. Ankylosing spondylitis: Acute anterior uveitis or iridocyclitis is the most common ocular manifestation occurring in 25-30% cases. More seen with B27 positive patients than negative patients. Reactive arthritis: conjunctivitis, anterior uveitis(iritis). Rare: scleritis, pars palnitis, iridocyclitis IBD associated arthritis: Scleritis and episcleritis follows disease activity. text: A 27-year-old lady presents to the clinic with a one-year history of intermittently painful fingers. The pain occurs commonly in low ambient temperatures and there is commensurate skin colour change from white to blue to red. Each episode lasts approximately 15 - 20 minutes. She tells you that her mother suffered from rheumatoid arthritis and Raynaud's. Which bedside test could you perform that may indicate an underlying connective tissue disorder as the probable diagnosis?
expl: The presentation is typical of Raynaud's phenomenon. After recognizing this, we need to differentiate between primary and secondary Raynaud's phenomenon. Nailfold capillaroscopy is an important tool to differentiate primary Raynaud's from secondary. Nailfold capillaroscopy is performed by applying a drop of oil onto the periungual region of the nail and using an ophthalmoscope set to 40 diopter to examine. Raynaud's phenomenon: episodic vasoconstriction affecting the tops of fingers and toes and sometimes of the tip of nose and earlobes. Pallor(vasoconstriction), cyanosis( ischemia) and hyperemia(reperfusion). Primary Raynaud's phenomenon: Raynaud's disease. occurs in the absence of any underlying condition. exaggerated vasomotor response to cold. Secondary Raynauds phenomenon: Connective tissue diseases: Systemic sclerosis, Sjogren syndrome, PAN, Takayasu Arteritis, Antisynthetase syndrome, SLE, MCTD, APS. Systemic diseases: Hypothyroidism, acromegaly, progressive diaphyseal dysplasia, paraneoplastic, cold agglutinins, POEMS, Cryoglobulinemia, Hyperviscosity syndromes Drugs: beta blockers, cisplatin, bleiomycin, ergot alkaloids, bromocriptine, Clonidine, cocaine, Dextramphetamine, methylphenidate, phentermine, interferons Obstructive vascular disease: Atherosclerosis, TAO, Thoracic outlet syndrome, Cardioembolism Thermography can be a useful confirmatory test for Raynauds phenomenon. Dermoscopes are more accurate in finding the capillary changes. Finger systolic pressure and digital artery closing temperature are laboratory investigations for other potential secondary causes. Cold water challenge is a provocation test that is no longer recommended as responses are inconsistent even in those with established RP. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Ch:360 Pg:2778

text: A 31 year old man has a 6 month history of dry eyes and mouth. On examination, there was evidence of keratoconjunctivitis, parotid gland enlargement and a Schirmer's test is positive. His blood tests reveal a positive ANA, Ro and La, extra nuclear antigens are also positive. What is the diagnosis?
expl: The patient has Sjogren's syndrome. Sjogren’s syndrome is a chronic autoimmune disorder characterized by xerostomia (dry mouth), xerophthalmia (dry eyes), and lymphocytic infiltration of the exocrine glands. This triad is also known as the sicca complex. The Schirmer test is probably the only test available in the ED to strongly support or refute suspicion of Sjögren syndrome. A test strip of filter paper is placed near the lower conjunctival sac to measure tear formation. A positive test occurs when less than 5 mm of filter paper is wet after 5 minutes. It is characterized by B cell hyper activity. It leads to hypergammaglobulinemia and is responsible for the auto antibodies seen which includes Rheumatoid factor, ANA, Ro and La antigens . Approximately 10% of these patients can develop non-Hodgkin lymphoma (1% of all patients with Sjögren syndrome). Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Chapter:361 Page number :2787-2788

text: What immunological abnormality is observed due to the absence of CD40 in B cells?

options.C: Decreased IgG and increase in IgM
options.D: Inability of neutrophils to act against infections

ansText: Decreased IgG and increase in IgM
expl: Explanation: This immunological profile is the hallmark of a group of disorders known as Hyper IgM Syndromes . The interaction between the CD40 ligand (CD40L, primarily expressed on activated T cells) and the CD40 receptor (on B cells) is a critical signal in the immune response. This interaction is essential for initiating immunoglobulin (antibody) class switching. In the absence of functional CD40L signaling , B cells are unable to receive the necessary instructions to switch from producing IgM (the default antibody) to producing other isotypes like IgG, IgA, and IgE. Consequently, patients have: Normal or elevated levels of IgM Severely decreased levels of IgG, IgA, and IgE This failure in class switching results in a significant immunodeficiency. Despite having high IgM, patients are highly susceptible to recurrent infections, particularly opportunistic infections, due to the lack of a diverse and mature antibody repertoire. Hyper IgM syndrome A rare primary immunodeficiency disorder characterised by low or absent IgG, IgA, and IgE, with normal or increased IgM levels. Causes: Results from various X-linked or autosomal mutations. Clinical Manifestations: Pulmonary complications (e.g., infections) Gastrointestinal issues Autoimmune diseases Hematologic abnormalities Lymphoproliferation Increased risk of malignancies Diagnosis: Based on immunoglobulin levels and genetic testing. Management: Treatment varies depending on the genetic mutation and clinical presentation. Options may include immunoglobulin replacement therapy, antibiotics, and management of associated complications. Explanation of other options: Total lack of NK cells (Option A) : N atural killer deficiency is a rare genetic disorder that has a genetic mechanism causing it. This is not associated with hyper IgM syndrome. Lack of CD8-mediated cytotoxicity (Option B) : It can be as a result of many chronic autoimmune diseases (like multiple sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, SLE, etc). It can also be seen in healthy blood relatives of people with autoimmune disorders. However, it is not associated with increased IgM production. The inability of neutrophils to act against infections (Option D) : This describes defects in neutrophil function, such as in Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD) or Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency. Neutrophil activity is independent of the CD40-CD40L signaling pathway that is central to B-cell and T-cell communication. Reference: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30439505/

text: A 64-year-old man has a painful, swollen right knee and difficulty in walking for three days. He had two self-limiting episodes of severe pain and swelling in the right big toe last year. He drinks 26 cans of beer/week. On examination, his temperature is 36.8 C. The right knee is red, swollen, warm and tender and has restricted movement. The knee aspirate shows no organisms on Gram stain, plenty of leucocytes, and negatively birefringent crystals on polarised light microscopy. The results of recent blood tests are: Hb 12.3 g/dl(13.0 - 18.0 g/dL) WBC 14.3 x10^9/μl(4 - 11 x 10^9/L) Neutrophils 88%(40-75%) Platelet 340 x 10^9/L (150 - 400 x 10^9/L) Urea, electrolytes and creatinine: Normal ESR 79 mm/hr(0 - 15 mm/1st hr) Uric acid 11 mg/dl What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Monosodium urate crystals are needle shaped and are negatively birefringent. Therefore, this patient has acute gout. He has several risk factors for gout including Age more than 40 years Male gender High alcohol consumption (more than 21 units for men, more than 14 units for women). Pseudogout is caused by intra-articular shedding of calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPPD) crystals. CPPD crystals are rhomboid and show a weak positive birefringence on polarised light microscopy. Pseudogout is common at the knee but rarely leads to podagra. There is no history of recent infections to suggest reactive arthritis. Septic arthritis of the knee is less likely as the Gram stain is negative. Osteoarthritis of the knee usually presents as chronic mechanical joint pain. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 372, Pg: 2863

text: Which purine analog drug is most appropriate for the long-term management of gout after diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: Allopurinol, a purine analog is the first-line choice for gout management. Allopurinol Allopurinol works by directly inhibiting xanthine oxidase and by competing with phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate in the purine salvage pathway. Allopurinol is the first-line treatment for the prevention of gouty arthritis, particularly in patients who are overproducers of uric acid. The initial dose is typically 100 mg daily, with a target urate level of In patients with renal impairment, dose adjustments are essential. Adverse effects : Stevens-Johnson syndrome Toxic epidermal necrolysis Acute gout flare-up, which may occur due to rapid urate level reduction Pathogenesis and Pharmacotherapy in Gout Explanation of other options: Capecitabine (Option B): Capecitabine is a pyrimidine analog used in breast cancer treatment. Cytarabine (Option C): Both a cytosine arabinoside and pyrimidine analog used as a chemotherapeutic agent in various conditions like ALL, AML. Febuxostat (Option D): Febuxostat also a xanthine oxidase inhibitor used in managemnt of gout, but is not a purine analog.

text: A 24-year-old lady presents to the clinic with a painfully swollen hot right knee. She gives a 2-week history of migratory polyarthritis and urethritis. Clinical examination reveals a pustular skin rash, right Achilles tendinitis and left plantar fasciitis. She is HLA-B27 negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: The presence of arthritis, urethritis and enthesitis makes the possibility of Reactive arthritis as well as Gonococcal arthritis. 10-15% of reactive arthritis may be HLA B27 negative. But the point in favour of Gonococcal arthritis is the migratory arthritis. The arthritis in Reactive arthritis is additive. The rash in Gonococcal infection is pustular. Disseminated Gonococcal infection is a rare entity having a bacteremic phase, characterized by fever, migratory arthritis, enthesitis and rash, followed by a septic arthritic phase characterised by a monoarthritis. text: A patient presents with severe pain and swelling in his knee joint for 10 days. He also complains of pain and discomfort during urination. He says that he had diarrhea one month ago and he has been unwell since then. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation : This is a classic presentation of Reactive Arthritis (Reiter's Syndrome) , which is characterized by an asymmetric oligoarthritis (often affecting the knees) that develops 1-4 weeks after a genitourinary (e.g., Chlamydia) or gastrointestinal infection (e.g., Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter). Urethritis is a common extra-articular feature. Explanation of other options: Enteropathic arthritis (Option B): Associated with active Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) , not a preceding episode of infectious diarrhea. Rheumatoid arthritis (Option C): A symmetric polyarthritis of small joints, not typically triggered by infection or associated with urethritis. Psoriatic arthritis (Option D): Associated with psoriasis and can cause arthritis, dactylitis, and enthesitis, but not typically linked to a preceding GI or GU infection. Key Takeaways: Reactive arthritis is an autoimmune condition triggered by an infection at a distant site, often presenting with the classic triad of arthritis, conjunctivitis, and urethritis (can be incomplete).

text: Which of the following clinical feature cannot help in differentiating psoriatic arthritis from other forms of inflammatory arthritis?
expl: Explanation: Diarrhea is not a specific clinical marker for psoriatic arthritis (PsA). While some patients with PsA may have coexistent inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) , diarrhea is non-specific and can also occur in other arthritides such as reactive arthritis or enteropathic arthritis associated with IBD. In contrast, dactylitis (sausage digits) , enthesitis , and nail pitting are characteristic hallmarks that help distinguish PsA from other types like rheumatoid arthritis (RA) or osteoarthritis (OA) .

text: A patient presents with pain and swelling of the knee joint. Synovial fluid aspirate shows rhomboid-shaped crystals that are positively birefringent under polarized light microscopy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: This is a case of pseudogout (Calcium Pyrophosphate Deposition Disease – CPPD) characterized by acute monoarticular arthritis and synovial fluid analysis showing rhomboid-shaped crystals that are positively birefringent under polarized light. Key diagnostic clues: Joint: Most commonly involves the knee. Synovial fluid crystals: Positively birefringent under polarized light. Shape: Rhomboid or rod-shaped crystals (not needle-shaped). Contrast with Gout: Factors and Conditions Associated with Calcium Pyrophosphate Crystal Deposition Disease Aging Osteoarthritis Postmeniscectomy or joint trauma Familial-genetic Endocrine-metabolic conditions: Primary hyperparathyroidism Hemochromatosis Hypophosphatasia Hypomagnesemia Certain drugs: thiazides and loop diuretics, potentially proton pump inhibitors Malabsorption Gitelman's syndrome Gout X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia Explanation of Incorrect Options: Gout (Option A): Synovial fluid contains needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals. Septic arthritis (Option C): Joint fluid shows a high leukocyte count and bacteria, not crystals. Rheumatoid arthritis (Option D): Typically presents with chronic, symmetric joint pain but does not have diagnostic crystals in the synovial fluid.

text: A 70 year old female with long standing history of untreated RA comes to your OP with deformities. Which among the following represents Boutonniere deformity?
expl: All the 4 of the figures represent the joint deformities that we come across in RA. The first figure shows flexion of DIP and hyperextension of the PIP, known as Swan Neck deformity. The second figure shows the prominence of the ulnar styloid due to destruction of the ulnar collateral ligament. This causes floating of the ulnar head, causing “ Piano-Key” deformity. The third figure shows subluxation of the first MCP with hyperextension of the thumb, called the Z line deformity. The fourth figure shows the Boutonniere deformity, characterized by flexion of the PIP and extension at DIP Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 358, pg: 2752

text: A 48 year old lady has had long standing arthritis of her hands. Her has hand X-rays done. Which of the following X ray changes suggests rheumatoid arthritis ?
expl: Classically in RA, the initial radiographic finding is periarticular osteopenia. Periarticular erosions are most suggestive of rheumatoid arthritis. Other findings on plain radiographs include soft tissue swelling, symmetric joint space loss, and subchondral erosions. It frequently involves the wrists and hands (MCPs and PIPs) and the feet (MTPs). In the feet, the lateral aspect of the fifth MTP is often targeted first. Osteophytes and asymmetric loss of joint space is seen in osteoarthritis. Periarticular erosions Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Ch:358 Pg:2759

text: A 41-year-old woman has a three month history of progressive pain, swelling and stiffness in both wrists, and the majority of her metacarpophalangeal joints (MCPJs). The symptoms are worse in the morning and it takes an hour to loosen up her joints. There has been no recent illness and there is no personal or family history of chronic skin conditions. She drinks alcohol occasionally. On examination there is synovitis in both wrists, and MCPJs. Examination of skin, nails and other joints is normal. These are results of recent blood tests: Haemoglobin 13.1gm/dl (11.5 - 16.5 g/L) WBC 8.2 x 10^9/L (4 - 11 x 10^9/L) Neutrophils 5.1 x 10^9/L (1.5 - 7 x 10^9/L) Platelets 280 x 10^9/L (150 - 400 x 10^9/L)ESR 48 mm/hr (0 - 20 mm/1st hr) Rheumatoid factor: positive (1:256)( Which among the following will provide immediate symptomatic relief?
expl: The symptoms, signs and blood results described above suggest a diagnosis of Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) . Diagnosis of RA should be made as early as possible , on the basis of persistent joint inflammation affecting at least three joints with early morning stiffness of at least 30 minutes. The first step in management should be symptomatic relief from pain and inflammation. NSAIDS and Steroids are used for this purpose as they are rapid in the onset of action, as opposed to DMARDS, which takes weeks for its onset of action. The duration of therapy should be maintained to the minimum possible to reduce the incidence of side effects. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Ch:358 Pg:2761

text: Identify the deformity depicted in the image.
expl: Explanation: The image depicts a Boutonniere deformity , a classic finding in rheumatoid arthritis. The deformity is characterized by a specific imbalance of the extensor tendon apparatus at the finger: Flexion at the Proximal Interphalangeal (PIP) joint. Hyperextension at the Distal Interphalangeal (DIP) joint. Pathophysiology The primary defect is the rupture or stretching of the central slip of the extensor tendon at its insertion on the middle phalanx. This allows the lateral bands of the tendon to slip volarly, acting as flexors of the PIP joint and extensors of the DIP joint. In rheumatoid arthritis, autoimmune inflammation leads to pannus formation that erodes articular cartilage and bone, typically involving the MCP, PIP, and wrist joints. Common deformities include: Swan neck deformity (Option A ruled out) , characterized by extension at the PIP and flexion at the DIP due to tendon tension (the DIP itself is not directly involved) Boutonniere deformity , with flexion at the PIP and extension at the DIP Z-line deformity (Option C ruled out) , involving subluxation of the first MCP joint with hyperextension of the interphalangeal joint. Swan neck and boutonniere deformities may occur in different fingers of the same hand. Explanation of other options: Mallet finger deformity (Option D): This results from an injury to the extensor tendon at the DIP joint, causing flexion at the DIP joint without primary PIP joint involvement. Key Takeaways: Boutonniere Deformity = PIP Flexion + DIP Hyperextension. It is caused by a disruption of the central slip of the extensor tendon. Swan Neck Deformity = PIP Hyperextension + DIP Flexion.

text: A 44 year old man presents with a painful swollen knee. He feels generally unwell and has a fever. He has recently had a flu like illness, an erythematous rash on the trunk followed by a self-limiting episode of diarrhoea. A diagnosis of reactive arthritis is made by the rheumatologist. How should the patient be managed?

options.C: Arthroscopy and washout of the joint
options.D: If the symptoms becomes chronic, sulphasalazine may be useful

ansText: If the symptoms becomes chronic, sulphasalazine may be useful
expl: The diagnosis is likely to be reactive arthritis following an infectious illness. Although joint aspiration may be useful, there is no need for arthroscopy at present. NSAIDs may be used for symptoms control now. If the symptoms persist, sulfasalazine or methotrexate may be useful. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st ed, Ch: 362, Pg: 2798

text: A 32 year old woman has a 3 month history of arthralgia joint pain and early morning stiffness. There is swelling of the distal interphalangeal joints of the ring fingers of the hand. The wrist on the right and ankles are swollen as well. Onycholysis was noted on the nails. Her serum inflammatory markers are raised.Which of the following is the likely diagnosis?
expl: The presence of joint pains and early morning stiffness points towards an inflammatory arthritis. The patient in the given question is suffering from an asymmetric oligoarthritis, with involvement of DIP, which rules out RA. The sparing of large proximal joints and the age of the patient speaks against a Polymyalgia rheumatica. There are no other indicators to suggest a chronic gout, like tophi. An asymmetric oligoarthritis with onycholysis points to the diagnosis of Psoriatic Arthritis. Wright and Moll described five patterns of Psoriatic Arthritis: arthritis of the DIP joints asymmetric oligoarthritis symmetric polyarthritis similar to RA axial involvement (spine and sacroiliac joints) arthritis mutilans, a highly destructive form of the disease. A simpler scheme in recent use contains three patterns: oligoarthritis, polyarthritis, and axial arthritis. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st ed, Ch: 362, Pg: 2799

text: A 64 year old man presents has recently developed an acutely painful right knee. On examination, he had a temperature of 37.2°C a hot and swollen right knee. expl: The clinical picture is typical of pseudogout. Calcification of the articular cartilage would be consistent and the culture results excludes septic arthritis.
