text: A 55-year-old male presents with symmetric polyarthritis involving the small joints of hands excluding the DIP, along with both wrist joints of 3 months duration. Which of the following statements favours the diagnosis of Psoriatic arthritis in this patient?

options.A: Psoriatic skin lesions are universally present in all patients with Psoriatic arthritis
options.B: Presence of axial spondylitis involving the Thoracolumbar spine favors the diagnosis of Psoriatic Arthritis
options.C: Presence of acute anterior uveitis favours the diagnosis of Psoriatic arthritis
options.D: The presence of nail changes favours the diagnosis of Psoriatic arthritis

ansText: The presence of nail changes favours the diagnosis of Psoriatic arthritis
expl: The usual presentation of Psoriatic Arthritis (PsA) is arthritis involving the DIP. When it is symmetrical and sparing the DIP it may be mistaken for RA. However, it can be distinguished from RA by the presence of typical Psoriatic skin lesions. But skin disease occurs only in 70% of patients. In 15% cases, skin disease and arthritis occur within one year of onset of each other. In 15% cases, the skin lesions occur after the onset of arthritis. So it is possible that PsA can present even without skin lesions. In such cases, the clinician should search for psoriatic lesions in areas like scalp, behind the ears, umbilicus and in the gluteal region. Or, the clinician should look for nail changes. The nail changes will be seen in most of the patients with PsA. The nail changes include pitting, horizontal ridges, yellowish discolouration of nails, dystrophic hyperkeratosis and onycholysis. PsA is a spondyloarthritis, making other like AS DDs. But what makes it different from AS is that PsA involves the cervical spine more where as AS involves the thoracic spine and will not have the nail changes of psoriasis. Also the uveitis in AS is acute anterior uveitis, where as in PsA is insidious onset bilateral chronic posterior uveitis. So among the options, the answer is nail changes. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 362. Pg: 2799

text: A chronic alcoholic patient presents with acute pain and swelling of the left great toe. There is no history of trauma. Synovial fluid analysis shows raised leukocytes. Lab investigations show normal serum uric acid levels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: Acute gout is the most likely diagnosis due to the classic presentation of podagra, even with normal serum uric acid levels during an acute flare. This patient presents with acute monoarthritis of the first metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint (known as podagra), which is highly characteristic of acute gout-a condition caused by the deposition of monosodium urate (MSU) crystals in joints. Although serum uric acid is often elevated in gout, normal uric acid levels do not rule out gout during an acute attack. Gout Gout is an inflammatory arthritis caused by MSU crystal deposition in joints and soft tissues due to hyperuricemia. However, the uric acid levels may be normal during flares due to crystal precipitation into the joint. Etiology of Gout: Primary Gout: Genetic defects in purine metabolism Decreased renal excretion of uric acid Secondary Gout: Chronic kidney disease, malignancy, or increased cell turnover (e.g., tumor lysis) Medications: Diuretics, low-dose aspirin Diet: Alcohol, red meat, seafood-especially relevant here as the patient is a chronic alcoholic Pathophysiology: Hyperuricemia leads to precipitation of MSU crystals in joints. These crystals trigger activation of NLRP3 inflammasome in macrophages → release of IL-1β, causing intense inflammation. Clinical Features of Gout: Asymptomatic hyperuricemia may be present without symptoms. Acute Gout Attack: Sudden onset of joint pain, swelling, erythema, and warmth; especially at night. Most commonly affects the first MTP joint (podagra). Intercritical gout: Symptom-free intervals between flares Chronic tophaceous gout: Formation of tophi, chalky urate deposits in joints and soft tissues. Diagnosis of Gout: Synovial Fluid Analysis: Gold standard for diagnosis Presence of needle-shaped, negatively birefringent MSU crystals under polarized light microscopy Serum Uric Acid: Often >6.8 mg/dL, but may be normal during an acute attack. Imaging Findings: X-ray: Punched-out erosions in chronic gout Ultrasound: Double-contour sign Dual-energy CT: Detects urate deposits Martel sign: Erosions with sclerotic margins and overhanging edges Management of Gout: Acute Attack: Colchicine: 0.6 mg TID (adjust in renal impairment) NSAIDs: Indomethacin, naproxen (avoid in CKD) Glucocorticoids: Used if NSAIDs/colchicine contraindicated Canakinumab: IL-1β inhibitor in resistant cases Ice therapy: Adjunctive anti-inflammatory Post-Attack Management: Goal: Serum uric acid Allopurinol: First-line xanthine oxidase inhibitor Febuxostat: Alternative when allopurinol is contraindicated Probenecid/Sulfinpyrazone: Uricosuric agents (avoid in renal dysfunction) Pegloticase: Refractory cases Lifestyle: Avoid alcohol, red meat, seafood Explanation of other options: Pseudogout (Option A): Caused by calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPPD) crystal deposition, typically affects knee, wrist, elbow, and shoulder rather than the big toe. Crystals are rhomboid-shaped and positively birefringent under polarized light. Reactive Arthritis (Option C): A post-infectious arthritis typically following GI or GU infections, and classically presents with the triad: arthritis, urethritis, and conjunctivitis. It does not fit this monoarticular toe presentation. Septic Arthritis (Option D): Usually involves larger joints like knee or hip, not typically the toe. Synovial fluid would show very high WBCs, purulent fluid, and may grow bacteria on culture. Fever is commonly present, which is absent here. Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK546606/ Anakinra - LiverTox - NCBI Bookshelf Colchicine - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf

text: A haemodialysis patient has recurrent knee and ankle swelling and pains. Aspiration of the knee synovial fluid reveals negatively birefringent crystals. Which one of the following treatments is the least effective either acutely or in the chronic situation?
expl: Negative birefringence with polarised light demonstrates urate crystals, making the diagnosis consistent with gout. The treatment of acute gout is NSAIDS, Colchicine and steroids. NSAIDS should not be used in CKD. Colchicine requires dose reduction in CKD. Steroids are safe in CKD. Urate lowering agents: Allopurinol is a xanthene oxidase inhibitor and can be used in CKD with dose reduction. Febuxostat is another xanthene oxidase inhibitor and requires no dose reduction in moderate to severe renal impairment too. Uricosuric drugs: Probenecid and Benzbromarone are the drugs. Probenecid is not effective in renal impairment, Cr >2mg/dl. Benzbromarone is useful in renal impairment. Haemodialysis will also ease urate clearance. Intracellular monosodium urate crystal viewed under a polarized light microscope(right) andconventional light microscope(left). Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st edition, Ch: 372, Pg:2865

text: A 59 year old man presents with pain in his left foot. He mentions that he has had poor mobility. General examination reveals a swollen ankle. Neurological examination reveals absent ankle jerk and weak foot flexion/extension on the left. His ESR is 30 mm/hr, CRP is <5mg/l. Joint x ray reveals subchondral fractures, soft tissue swelling and a narrowed joint space. The likely diagnosis is:
expl: An absent ankle jerk with weak joint, predisposes the joint to neuropathic joint. OA rarely affects the ankle joint. Gout presents with acute painful joint in a predisposed individual. There is nothing to suggest a juvenile chronic arthritis too. Charcot joint or neuropathic joint disease can be caused by diabetic neuropathy, syphillis, syringomyelia or leprosy. The X ray changes are reduced joint space with periarticular destruction, subchondral bodies, loose bodies and occasionally joint dislocation. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:374 Pg: 2873

text: A 54-year-old woman on treatment for longstanding rheumatoid arthritis has recently become short of breath on mild exertion and developed a dry cough.Oxygen saturation was found to be 87% on air, and chest x ray showed a diffuse bilateral interstitial infiltrate. An extensive infection screen was negative and her symptoms were thought to be drug-induced. Which drug is most likely to have caused this adverse effect?
expl: Methotrexate is widely used in the management of rheumatoid arthritis . Pneumonitis is a potentially fatal hypersensitivity reaction associated with methotrexate. Symptoms are non-specific à progressive dyspnoea, cough, fever, hypoxia, tachypnea, crackles on chest auscultation. Chest radiographs reveal interstitial or alveolar infiltrate , concentrated within the lower lung fields. Spirometry demonstrates a restrictive pattern with reduced diffusion capacity . Lung biopsy reveals cellular interstitial infiltrates, granulomas or a diffuse alveolar damage pattern accompanied by perivascular inflammation. If suspected, methotrexate should be stopped , other causes investigated and supportive measures initiated. Additional adverse effects associated with methotrexate include hepatic toxicity and neutropenia . Regular blood tests are done to monitor them. Methotrexate is a folic acid antagonist . Folic acid should be given daily to reduce the incidence of side effects in patients treated with methotrexate. Side effects of cytotoxic agents include: Azathioprine : commonly associated with mild bone marrow suppression. Should be used with caution in patients receiving allopurinol due to the risk of life-threatening bone marrow failure. Cyclosporine : common side effects include hirsutism, liver dysfunction, gum hypertrophy and hypertension. Hydroxycholoroquine : may cause hair loss and 'bull's eye maculopathy'. Visual acuity should be monitored every 6 to 12 months. Sulphasalazine : associated with pancytopenia. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Ch:358 Pg:2762-2763

azathioprine cyclosporine hydroxychloroquine methotrexate  methotrexate is widely used in the management of rheumatoid arthritis . pneumonitis is a potentially fatal hypersensitivity reaction associated with methotrexate. symptoms are non-specific à progressive dyspnoea, cough, fever, hypoxia, tachypnea, crackles on chest auscultation. chest radiographs reveal interstitial or alveolar infiltrate , concentrated within the lower lung fields. spirometry demonstrates a restrictive pattern with reduced diffusion capacity . lung biopsy reveals cellular interstitial infiltrates, granulomas or a diffuse alveolar damage pattern accompanied by perivascular inflammation. if suspected, methotrexate should be stopped , other causes investigated and supportive measures initiated. additional adverse effects associated with methotrexate include hepatic toxicity and neutropenia . regular blood tests are done to monitor them. methotrexate is a folic acid antagonist . folic acid should be given daily to reduce the incidence of side effects in patients treated with methotrexate. side effects of cytotoxic agents include: azathioprine : commonly associated with mild bone marrow suppression. should be used with caution in patients receiving allopurinol due to the risk of life-threatening bone marrow failure. cyclosporine : common side effects include hirsutism, liver dysfunction, gum hypertrophy and hypertension. hydroxycholoroquine : may cause hair loss and 'bull's eye maculopathy'. visual acuity should be monitored every 6 to 12 months. sulphasalazine : associated with pancytopenia. reference: harrison’s principles of internal medicine 21 st edition ch:358 pg:2762-2763

text: A 54-year-old homeless man presents with a six month history of periodic knee pains and aching legs. These have been occurring monthly and episodes last up to two weeks. He has noticed a 'bumpy' rash to his lower legs and complains of feeling more tired than usual. He has no significant past medical history. He is currently reporting to a pharmacy daily for methadone. Clinical examination demonstrated; pulse 88 (regular), normal heart sounds and chest sounds, painful but full active range of knee motion and palpable purpura to the lower extremities. Blood tests revealed; Hb 11.9 g/dL(1C-18)MCV 93fL(80 - 96)WCC 9.8 x 109/L (4 - 11)ALT 150 iu/L(5 - 35)AST 90 iu/L(1 - 31)Complement C4 64 mg/dL(75-135) Which test is most likely to assist you in the management of this man's illness?
expl: The background of a destitute male who is on methadone currently indicates possibility of an IV opioid abuser who is currently on deaddiction. IV drug abuse predisposes the patient to blood borne infections like chronic Hepatitis and HIV. Apart from that, now the patient has arthralgia, rash and hypocomplementemia. He has transaminase elevation as well. This points to the possibility of a Hepatitis C associated Cryoglobulinemic vasculitis. Learning points: Presentation of mixed cryoglobulinemia (MCG), Risk factors for (MCG) and Haematological profile of MCG. Mixed cryoglobulinemia manifests as Purpura Cutaneous ulcers Polyneuropathy Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis and non-erosive polyarthralgia is associated with hepatitis C. Laboratory investigations show positive rheumatoid factor, low C4, active urine sediments, and type II or III serum cryoglobulins. There may be axonal polyneuropathy. Active urinary sediment suggests the presence of membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis. Type II (mixed essential) cryoglobulinemia is closely associated with persistent hepatic infection (transaminitis, inferred IVDU) most commonly hepatitis C and to a lesser extent hepatitis B. Management involves treating the underlying cause in the absence of any immediate life, organ or limb threatening complications. In this case with pegylated interferon alpha and ribavirin. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Ch:363 Pg:2586

text: A 54 year old female has been on long-term steroids for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. She complains of pain in her right groin radiating down the anteromedial thigh. She has an antalgic gait. On examination of the hip, there is decreased range of movement especially flexion, abduction and internal rotation. What is the likely diagnosis?

options.D: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head

ansText: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
expl: In a patient on long term steroids presenting with groin pains radiating to the thigh associated with an antalgic gait and decreased range of movement of the hip, the most likely diagnosis is avascular necrosis of the femoral head. In this condition, MRI is the most sensitive and specific technique and is useful for early diagnosis before collapse of bone occurs. CT scan and X-ray are useful to rule out advanced disease if duration is not clear. Bone scanning is more sensitive than X-ray but is non-specific. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 370, Pg: 2847

text: A 21-year-old lady has a swinging fever, significant weight loss over 2 months, generalised myalgia, polyarthralgia affecting wrists, knees, ankles, elbows metacarpophalangeal joints and a sore throat. Investigations show : Hb 9.5g/l, MCV 85 fl, ESR 92 mm in first hour, CRP 45 g/l, serum ferritin 1600 mg/dl, RF negative, ANA negative, ENA negative, ASO titre What is the likely diagnosis?
expl: The most appropriate answer from among the option is C. Adult Onset Still's Disease (AOSD) is an acute febrile illness in young adults. It usually affects multiple organs, but is a diagnosis of exclusion. The presence of high ferritin and negative serological markers of other autoimmune diseases makes the possibility of Adult Onset Still's Disease. Clinical features include a high fever, arthralgia and arthritis, phayngitis, typical rash (evanescent salmon-colored, macular or maculopapular eruption), lymphadenopathy, and serositis. Chronic arthritis and constitutional symptoms are common. The triad of fever, rash, and arthralgia are often absent during the first month of the illness. The usual joints affected are wrists, knees, and ankles in descending order. Two thirds of cases experience polyarticular arthritis and one third have monoarticular symptoms. Approximately 1/3 of patients have chronic persistent disease with progressive joint damage. Reference : Harrison's Principles Of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed Ch: 19, Pg: 135

text: A 68 year old woman with ischaemic heart disease and rheumatoid arthritis presents with worsening angina. Bloods show: hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL; MCV: 80 fl; MCH: 29 pg; WBC: 7000/μL; platelets 300000/μL; S. Iron: 37 μg/dL (NR: 50-150 μg/dL) Transferrin saturation 12% (NR: 15-50%) Total iron-binding capacity 200μg/dL (NR: 240-450 μg/dL) Vitamin B12 400 ng/L (NR: 160-950 ng/L) folate 8 ng/mL (NR: 3-10 ng/mL) What is the most likely cause of her anemia?
expl: She has a normochromic, normocytic anemia with low iron, iron-binding capacity and transferrin saturation in keeping with anemia of chronic disease. Anemia of chronic disease results from impaired iron handling. In iron deficiency anemia, the patient is iron depleted, leading to a raised iron-binding capacity in the context of low iron and transferrin saturation. Folate deficiency, myelodysplasia and autoimmune haemolysis are associated with an elevated MCV. Reference: Harrison's Principles of internal medicine 21st ed chap 97 pg. 752-753

text: A 74 year old woman with longstanding Rheumatoid arthritis has great difficulty walking and comments that both her legs are stiff and 'jumpy'. What is the most likely cause of the presentation?
expl: Stiff and jumpy legs suggest-> spasticity-> suggestive of Upper motor neuron disorder. The problem can be at the level of the brain or spinal cord. Now, we need to think about where RA affects the spinal cord. RA affects the cervical spine. Unlike Spondyloarthropathy it does not affect the thoracic or lumbar spine. Cervical cord compression due to atlanto-axial instability at C1/C2 is the most likely cause of UMN nerve weakness. The laminations of the pyramidal tract in the spinal cord is in such a way that the sacral fibres are lateral and the cervical fibres are medial. Hence, in a long standing upper cervical cord compression, as in the case of an atlanto axial instability, the symptoms will first begin in the lower limbs and then involve the upper limbs and may be asymmetrical too. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Ch:358 Pg:3752

text: Patients well controlled on theophylline should not be given which antibiotic?
expl: Macrolides increase the level of theophylline by inhibiting Cyp450 and causes theophylline toxicity. Hence co administration should be avoided. Agents which enhance theophylline metabolism primarily by inducing CYP1A2 lower its plasma level: dose has to be increased by the factor given in parenthesis. Smoking, phenytoin, rifampicin, phenobarbitone, charcoal broiled meat meal. Drugs which inhibit theophylline metabolism and increase its plasma level are-erythromycin, ciprofloxacin, cimetidine, oral contraceptives, allopurinol; dose should be reduced to 2/3.

text: In which of the following conditions is pneumomediastinum commonly found?
expl: Explanation: Pneumomediastinum is one of the complication associated with Boerhaave syndrome. Boerhaave syndrome It is a spontaneous esophageal rupture caused by a sudden increase in intraesophageal pressure. Results from forceful vomiting against a closed glottis, leading to a left-sided oesophageal perforation , which allows gastric contents to spill into the pleural cavity, leading to a left pleural effusion and subcutaneous emphysema. Clinical features Manifests as Mackler's triad Vomiting Chest pain Subcutaneous emphysema Other symptoms include fever, tachycardia, and tachypnea in the presence of sepsis. Physical examination reveals Hamman's sign Crunching sound on auscultation due to surgical emphysema. Commonly affects the lower third of the oesophagus and results in a direct communication between the esophageal lumen and mediastinal space. The rupture allows oesophagal contents to spill into the mediastinum, which can occasionally lead to complications such as: Pneumomediastinum Chemical mediastinitis . Pneumothorax Sepsis Explanation of other options: Pulsion diverticulum (Option A): Pulsion diverticulum occurs due to increased intraluminal pressure in the esophagus, forming an outpouching of the esophageal wall. While it can cause symptoms like dysphagia and regurgitation, it does not typically result in pneumomediastinum as the esophageal wall remains intact. Mallory-Weiss syndrome (Option C): Mallory-Weiss syndrome involves longitudinal mucosal tears at the gastroesophageal junction, typically following forceful vomiting. While it can cause hematemesis, the tear is superficial and does not extend through the full thickness of the oesophageal wall, thus not causing pneumomediastinum. ; Pericarditis (Option D): Pericarditis is the inflammation of the pericardium, the fibrous sac surrounding the heart, and causes chest pain and other symptoms related to inflammation.

text: Which of the following is not a characteristic finding of Gaisbock syndrome?
expl: Explanation: Hypotension is not a characteristic finding of Gaisbock syndrome . Gaisbock syndrome , commonly linked with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), involves secondary polycythemia caused by long-standing hypoxemia. In response to low oxygen levels, the body increases erythropoietin production, resulting in erythrocytosis. Patients usually present with high blood pressure rather than low blood pressure, due to the underlying lung condition and greater blood viscosity.

text: A hypertensive patient who is non-compliant with his medications presents with sudden-onset severe breathlessness. Chest X-ray findings are consistent with pulmonary edema. What is the most appropriate immediate management for this patient?
expl: Explanation: The presentation indicates acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema (ACPE) , a medical emergency often precipitated by severe hypertension, myocardial infarction, or medication non-compliance. Intravenous nitroglycerin is the drug of choice as it provides rapid relief by reducing preload and afterload via venodilation , thereby decreasing pulmonary venous pressure. Clinical Features of ACPE: Symptoms: Sudden dyspnea, pink frothy sputum, cyanosis, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. Signs: Tachypnea, rales and rhonchi on auscultation, raised jugular venous pressure, gallop rhythm. Chest X-ray findings: Interstitial edema, alveolar edema in "butterfly pattern," cardiomegaly. Management of Cardiogenic Pulmonary Edema: IV Nitroglycerin: First-line agent; start sublingual, escalate to IV if required. Rapid symptom relief without hypotension. Oxygen therapy: Maintain SpO 2 >92%; non-invasive ventilation (NIPPV) or intubation if severe. Diuretics (e.g., furosemide): Used after stabilization to remove excess fluid. Morphine: Reduces anxiety and provides venodilation; use cautiously due to risk of respiratory depression. Positioning: Upright posture with legs dependent reduces venous return. Explanation of other options: Intravenous salbutamol (Option A): Salbutamol is a β 2 -agonist used in asthma and hyperkalemia, not in pulmonary edema. Nebulization with salbutamol (Option C): Similar to Option A; appropriate in obstructive airway disease, not ACPE. Oxygen and antibiotics (Option D): Oxygen is beneficial, but antibiotics are unnecessary unless infection (e.g., pneumonia) coexists. Key Takeaways: Intravenous nitroglycerin is the first-line drug in ACPE. Oxygen and diuretics are supportive measures after stabilization. Antibiotics are not part of routine management unless secondary infection is present. References: https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/full/10.1161/JAHA.119.013441 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31587602/

text: A 52-year-old man enquired about the advisability of vaccination prior to a holiday abroad. He had been treated for asthma with long-term steroids and regularly required doses of Prednisolone in excess of 30mg daily to control acute exacerbations. Which one of the following vaccinations would be contra-indicated in this man?
expl: Some individuals, particularly those that are immunosuppressed, are at risk if they are given live vaccines. Inactivated vaccines are generally not dangerous but may be ineffective. They are also at risk of severe manifestations to vaccines such as disseminated infection with BCG. Those patients who receive prednisolone 40mg/day for more than a week or who are on lower doses for more prolonged periods should be considered to be immunosuppressed. Asthma alone is not a contra-indication to vaccination even if patients are taking inhaled corticosteroids. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch:123, Pg: 981-989

text: A 35 year old man has significant wheezing and breathlessness. Recordings of peak flows show diurnal variation. He was prescribed salbutamol but continues to have frequent wheezy episodes. What is the next step in management?
expl: Diurnal PEFR variation points towards a diagnosis of asthma. GINA does not recommend SABA only treatment for asthma in adults and adolescents and does not recommend the scheduled day use of SABAs. Although SABA is effective as a quick relief medication, patients who are treated with SABA are at increased risk for asthma-related death even if their symptoms are controlled. Increased use (more than one cannister a month) indicates diminished asthma control and the need for adding long term therapy. Leukotriene antagonists are less effective than inhaled corticosteroids for exacerbation reduction but may be considered as alternatives in patients with asthma who are unable to take inhaled corticosteroids or who experience undesirable steroid side effects. text: An asthmatic patient on salbutamol and ipratropium continues to have nocturnal exacerbations. Which of the following is the next best step?

options.B: Add long-acting beta agonist + inhaled corticosteroid

ansText: Add long-acting beta agonist + inhaled corticosteroid
expl: Explanation: For a patient with uncontrolled asthma despite use of a short-acting beta agonist (salbutamol) and an anticholinergic (ipratropium), the next recommended step is to add an inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) and a long-acting beta agonist (LABA). This combination addresses airway inflammation (ICS) and provides prolonged bronchodilation (LABA), improving symptom control and reducing nocturnal exacerbations. Bronchial asthma management depends on the severity and frequency of symptoms, as well as objective measures of lung function, such as forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) . Patients with intermittent asthma , who experience symptoms less than twice a week and have normal FEV1 (>80%) , usually require only as-needed inhaled β2-agonists (e.g., albuterol). However, if: Symptoms occur more than twice per week , Nocturnal symptoms are present more than twice a month , or FEV1 , Then, additional maintenance therapy is warranted. The first-line controller medication is a low-dose inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) . Alternatives include leukotriene receptor antagonists (LTRAs) or mast cell stabilizers like cromolyn . Theophylline is now rarely used due to its narrow therapeutic window and side effect profile and is typically reserved for cases unresponsive to standard therapies. Explanation of Incorrect Options: Add oral corticosteroids (Option A): Reserved for severe exacerbations and not for routine long-term control due to side effects. Increase frequency of salbutamol (Option C): Can cause side effects and does not address the underlying inflammation. Add montelukast (Option D): Used as an add-on in mild-to-moderate asthma, but evidence is stronger for ICS+LABA at this stage.

text: For which of the following groups is pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine not routinely recommended?

options.A: Otherwise healthy adults aged 50 to 65 years
options.B: Adults aged 19 to 65 years who have immunocompromising conditions

ansText: Otherwise healthy adults aged 50 to 65 years
expl: Pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine is not recommended for otherwise healthy adults aged 50 to 65 years. This vaccine is, however recommended for persons who have immunocompromising conditions or lung disease (such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or asthma) and for persons who are cigarette smokers and heavy consumers of alcohol. Post splenectomy or hyposplenism is another indication There are 2 types of pneumococcal vaccine pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23) and a protein conjugate pneumococcal vaccine (PCV13) Routine use of PCV13 is recommended among adults aged 65 and older . Individuals 65 years of age or older who have never received a pneumococcal vaccine should first receive PCV13 followed by a dose of PPSV23 6-12 months later . Individuals who have received more than one dose of PPSV23 should receive a dose of PCV13 more than 1 year after the last dose of PPSV23 was administered. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 146, Pg: 1177

text: A 13 year old male has recent onset breathlessness. He has a history of wheezing particularly during the summer when the pollen count is high.Which of these tests would help to confirm the diagnosis?
expl: The history of wheezing during pollen exposure suggests asthma. The best diagnostic test for asthma would be demonstration of variable airways obstruction with Bronchodilator reversibility and serial peak flow measurements. Reversibility is defined as a ≥12% increase in the FEV1 and an absolute increase of ≥200 mL at least 15 min after administration of a β2 -agonist or after several weeks of corticosteroid therapy. text: A patient has presented with features of cardiac tamponade. Which of the following is correct regarding this condition?

options.D: Jugular veins column is visibly distended without pulsations

ansText: Jugular veins column is visibly distended without pulsations
expl: Explanation: In cardiac tamponade, the pericardial effusion causes elevated and equalized pressures throughout the heart. This leads to elevated jugular venous pressure (JVP) . A key finding is the loss of the y descent in the JVP waveform due to impaired early diastolic filling, making the veins appear distended but quiet , without the normal visible pulsations. In cardiac tamponade the Compression of cardiac chambers by pericardial effusion, limiting cardiac inflow; can occur with 200 ml-2 L of fluid. Beck's Triad: Jugular venous distension (↑ CVP, prominent x, absent y descent) Hypotension (↓ cardiac output) Muffled heart sounds (fluid dampens sounds) Other Feature: Pulsus paradoxus (>10 mmHg fall in systolic BP on inspiration). Causes of Pulsus Paradoxus: Lung: Acute asthma, COPD, tension pneumothorax, pleural effusion, PE Heart: Cardiac tamponade, constrictive pericarditis JVP Waveform in Cardiac tamponade Explanation of other options: Pulsus Paradoxus is always present (Option A): While a highly specific sign, it may be absent in patients with pre-existing conditions like aortic regurgitation, atrial septal defect, or severe hypotension. Kussmaul sign is always present (Option B): Kussmaul sign (a rise in JVP on inspiration) is characteristic of constrictive pericarditis , not cardiac tamponade. Tall A wave is present (Option C): Tall A waves are seen in conditions causing reduced right ventricular compliance (e.g., pulmonary hypertension, pulmonic stenosis), not in tamponade where the waveform is dampened. Key Takeaways: Cardiac tamponade is a clinical diagnosis characterized by Beck's triad: hypotension, JVD, and muffled heart sounds. The JVP is elevated with a prominent x descent and an absent y descent.

text: A 25 year old male with a 5 year long history of bronchial asthma, presented with worsening of asthma and fever of 20 days duration. expl: ABPA usually occurs in association with asthma, but can occur in cystic fibrosis. Peripheral Eosinophilia and high IgE levels>1000 It is treated with either oral or inhaled steroids. text: A patient who has undergone cardiac surgery suddenly develops low blood pressure, elevated central venous pressure, and pulsus paradoxus four hours after the operation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The symptoms observed in the postoperative cardiac surgery patient strongly suggest cardiac tamponade. This is a medical emergency caused by the buildup of fluid or blood within the pericardial sac, which compresses the heart and disrupts its normal function. Cardiac Tamponade Definition: A condition in which the heart chambers are compressed by a tense pericardial effusion, restricting the heart’s ability to fill properly. Fluid accumulation ranging from as little as 200 ml to over 2 liters can cause cardiac tamponade. Clinical Features: Beck's Triad: Jugular Venous Distension: Due to increased central venous pressure, with a prominent x descent and absent y descent. Hypotension: Caused by reduced cardiac output. Muffled Heart Sounds: Fluid in the pericardial space dampens the heart sounds. Other Features: Pulsus Paradoxus: A drop in systolic blood pressure of more than 10 mm Hg during inspiration. Causes of Pulsus Paradoxus: Lung-related: Acute asthma, COPD, tension pneumothorax, pleural effusion, pulmonary embolism. Heart-related: Cardiac tamponade, constrictive pericarditis. Low-Pressure Cardiac Tamponade Definition: A form of tamponade occurring when pericardial pressure is relatively low, often seen in cases of intravascular volume depletion such as hypovolemia. Features: Jugular venous distension is often absent. Pulsus paradoxus is rare. Diagnosis requires a high index of suspicion since classic signs like jugular venous distension and pulsus paradoxus may be missing. Explanation for other options: Ventricular dysfunction (Option A): can lead to hypotension and cardiac symptoms, but it usually does not cause raised central venous pressure or pulsus paradoxus. Moreover, the sudden onset of symptoms in this case indicates an acute condition like cardiac tamponade rather than a chronic ventricular dysfunction. Congestive heart failure (CHF) (Option C): may result in fluid retention, causing increased venous pressure and symptoms such as shortness of breath and edema. However, it rarely presents with sudden hypotension, elevated central venous pressure, or pulsus paradoxus. Excessive mediastinal effusion (Option D): can compress the heart and produce symptoms similar to cardiac tamponade. Still, the presence of raised central venous pressure and pulsus paradoxus more specifically suggests cardiac tamponade as the most probable diagnosis. Reference: Low-Pressure Cardiac Tamponade | Circulation Fluid amount Pulsus paradoxus

text: A 40-year-old worker presents with wheezing and breathlessness which seem to improve over weekends and holiday periods when he is not working. What is he most likely to be exposed to at work?
expl: Disinfectants and preservatives including glutaraldehyde, chlorhexidine and formaldehyde can cause occupational asthma. Metals causing occupational asthma include isocyanates cobalt, aluminium, chrome, manganese, nickel, zinc, and platinum. Exposure to Actinomyces (farmer's lung, mushroom workers' lung), avian bloom (bird fanciers' lung) and aspergillus clavatus (malt worker's lung) cause extrinsic allergic alveolitis. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch:288 Pg 2160

text: A 40 year old woman has been breathless and is undergoing investigations for the cause. She has a previous history of being a smoker and has a dry cough as well. Her ABGs show a pO2 of 67 mmHg and pCO2 of 37 mm Hg. Lung function tests show reduced vital capacity, reduced TLCO but increased KCO. What is the likely diagnosis?
expl: In this scenario, the lung function indicates that the surface area for exchange are inadequate (low TLCO) hence suggesting that lung expansion is reduced. However, cardiac output is increased to compensate, and hence KCO is increased. Kyphoscoliosis would restrict lung expansion, or a neuromuscular disorder (e.g. spina bifida) could cause this. K CO = Transfer coefficient = DL CO /volume of air in alveoli Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch: 285Pg 2138

expl: The patient has the clinical features of limited cutaneous scleroderma ( formerly CREST syndrome). Anticentromere antibodies occur in 70-80% of these patients. text: A 60-year-old male patient comes to your clinic with an 8-month history of shortness of breath and non-productive cough. He has smoked half a pack of cigarettes for the past 30 years. On physical examination, clubbing is seen and fine crackles are heard on both sides during inspiration. You perform pulmonary function tests and it shows an FEV1/FVC ratio of 92%. The CT scan of the chest is shown below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The presentation is classic for a restrictive lung disease , specifically Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF) . Key indicators include: Symptoms: Progressive dyspnea, dry cough. Examination: Clubbing, bilateral inspiratory crackles ("Velcro" crackles). PFTs: Normal or high FEV1/FVC ratio (ruling out obstructive disease like COPD) indicating a restrictive pattern. Imaging: The CT image shows the presence of honeycombing (black arrows), traction bronchiectasis (white arrow), and a reticular pattern (black dotted arrows). B ronchiectasis in a subpleural and basal distribution. Explanation of other options: Bronchial asthma and Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) (Option A and D): These are obstructive diseases, characterized by a low FEV1/FVC ratio on PFTs. Pulmonary tuberculosis (Option C): Typically causes upper lobe infiltrates, cavitation, or lymphadenopathy on imaging, not the classic subpleural honeycombing of IPF. Key Takeaways: IPF is a restrictive lung disease with a characteristic HRCT pattern of usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP).

text: Patient presents with fever, nocturnal cough, breathlessness and wheezing for 4 weeks. Absolute eosinophil count >5000. X-ray shows a military pattern. Diagnosis?
expl: The given history and lab findings suggestive of tropical pulmonary Eosinophilia. TROPICAL PULMONARY EOSINOPHILIA Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia (TPE) is a distinct syndrome that develops in some individuals infected with the lymphatic- dwelling filarial species. The majority of cases have been reported from India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Brazil, Guyana, and Southeast Asia; the decreasing incidence of TPE in last decade probably reflects global MDA efforts. CLINICAL FEATURES The main features include a history of residence in filaria-endemic regions, paroxysmal cough and wheezing (usually nocturnal probably related to the nocturnal periodicity of microfilariae), weight loss, low-grade fever, lymphadenopathy, and pronounced blood eosin- ophilia (>3000 eosinophils/µL). Chest x-rays or CT scans may be normal, but generally show increased bronchovascular markings. Diffuse miliary lesions or mottled opacities may be present in the middle and lower lung fields. Tests of pulmonary function show restrictive abnor- malities in most cases and obstructive defects in half. Characteristically, total serum IgE levels (4-40 KIU/mL) and anti filarial antibody levels are markedly elevated.

text: A 71-year-old man presents with difficulty speaking. He has a history of diabetes, hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. He is currently on aspirin, simvastatin, amlodipine and hydrochlorothiazide. On examination the patient is awake, his blood pressure is 150/70 mmHg. His pulse is irregularly irregular. He has 4/5 strength in the right arm and leg and 5/5 strength on the left. When asked to point to the window he does this correctly. When told to raise his arms and place his hands out he is seen to have a pronator drift on the right. He is shown a pen and asked what it is. He responds fluently but makes some paraphasic errors. He is asked to use it appropriately and begins to write on a piece of paper. When asked to repeat 'Today is a sunny day', he is unable to do so. Which of the following terms best describes these signs?
expl: In Broca's or nonfluent or expressive aphasia the patient is unable to name objects with poor comprehension and repetition. It localises to the Broca's area in the left posterior inferior frontal gyrus. In transcortical motor aphasia, which localises to the anterior superior frontal lobe, the patient is has good comprehension and repetition but has halting, effortful speech. Patients also have impaired writing skills. Transcortical sensory aphasia is characterised by impaired auditory comprehension with intact repetition and fluent speech, and is caused by damage to the temporal lobes. It differs from Wernicke's aphasia in that patients still have intact repetition, and exhibit echolalia (the compulsive repetition of words). Improvement may be seen with speech therapy. Anomic aphasia (also known as nominal aphasia) results in word finding difficulties. On closer examination there may also be repetition problems and comprehension problems but these are typically mild compared to other aphasia syndromes. This scenario describes conduction aphasia. It is characterised by frequent speech errors, impaired repetition, reduced phonological short-term memory and naming difficulties. In contrast to other forms of dysphasia, speech output is otherwise fluent and grammatically correct. Comprehension is intact. It is thought to be caused by left temporo-parietal region damage. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st ed, Ch: 30, Pg: 196

text: A 65-year-old man presents with a five day history of lower abdominal pain and diarrhea.He has a history of chronic obstructive airways disease (COAD) and has had numerous acute infective exacerbations over the last three months.On examination he was dehydrated, with a temperature of 38.6°C, a blood pressure of 102/72 mmHg and has a distended, tender abdomen.Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation for this patient?
expl: This is pseudomembranous colitis due to Clostridium difficile secondary to antibiotic usage for his COPD. Plain AXR is useful for diagnosing toxic dilatation and would be the investigation of choice here due to his abdominal distension, so toxic dilatation should be excluded prior to sigmoidoscopy. However it does not establish the diagnosis.Stool microscopy has no value but stool toxin assay is useful. A patient with diarrhea normally has involvement of the distal colon and rectum, and sigmoidoscopy with biopsy is helpful for rapid diagnosis but should not be performed if toxic dilatation is suspected.Patients with involvement of right colon usually have little or no diarrhoea. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 138, Pg: 1069

text: A 74-year-old man presents with difficulty speaking. He has a history of diabetes, hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. He is currently on aspirin, simvastatin, amlodipine and hydrochlorothiazide. On examination the patient is awake, his blood pressure is 150/70 mmHg. His pulse is irregularly irregular. He has 4/5 strength on the right arm and leg and 5/5 strength on the left.When asked to point to the window he appears unable to do so. When told to raise his arms and place his hands out he does not. When visually shown the same action he is able to perform it. expl: In Broca's or non-fluent or expressive aphasia the patient is unable to name objects with poor comprehension and repetition. It localises to the Broca's area in the left posterior inferior frontal gyrus. In Wernicke's or fluent or receptive aphasia the patient is able to form correct grammatical sentences but language content is incorrect. It localises to the dominant superior temporal gyrus. There is poor comprehension and repetition but verbal output is fluent. In transcortical motor aphasia, which localises to the anterior superior frontal lobe, the patient has good comprehension and repetition but has halting, effortful speech. Patients also have impaired writing skills. Global aphasia results in an almost mute patient: there is poor verbal output, comprehension, repetition and understanding. Transcortical sensory aphasia is what is described in this case. It is characterised by impaired auditory comprehension with intact repetition and fluent speech, and is caused by damage to the temporal lobes. It differs from Wernicke's aphasia in that patients still have intact repetition, and exhibit cholalia (the compulsive repetition of words). Improvement may be seen with speech therapy. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 30, Pg: 196

expl: In Broca's or non-fluent or expressive aphasia the patient is unable to name objects with poor comprehension and repetition. text: A patient came with the complaints of fatigue and difficulty breathing. On examination, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds were found. X-ray is shown below. Identify the condition.
expl: Explanation: The chest X-ray shows a normal-sized heart with a thickened, fibrosed/calcified pericardium, producing the classic 'egg-in-cup' appearance. Along with the clinical triad of dyspnea, distended neck veins (reflecting elevated JVP), and muffled heart sounds, these findings are characteristic of constrictive pericarditis. Constrictive Pericarditis: Constrictive pericarditis is characterised by the progressive thickening, fibrosis, and calcification of the pericardium, restricting heart filling. Calcification can extend into the myocardium, impairing myocardial contraction. Restricted ventricular filling leads to elevated atrial pressures, causing: Atrial hypertrophy Atrial dilation Atrial fibrillation (common). Primarily manifests as systemic venous congestion (lung congestion is rare). Shows"Egg in cup appearance" on Xray Examination Findings : Explanation of other options: Acute pericarditis (Option A): The most common symptom of acute pericarditis is pleuritic chest pain. It worsens on lying supine and improves on sitting up or leaning forward. While causes like TB, uremia, post-irradiation, and neoplasia may be painless, the CXR is usually normal in uncomplicated pericarditis, showing cardiomegaly only if effusion is present. Bronchial asthma (Option B): Bronchial asthma in chest xray shows pulmonary hyperinflation with bronchial wall thickening. Atrial myxoma (Option D): T ypically presents with cardiomegaly, left atrial enlargement, and vascular redistribution.

text: A 40-year-old woman presents with chest pain and shortness of breath. She reported a viral illness one week prior. Her chest X-ray is given below. What is not true about this condition?

options.D: ECHO showing diastolic collapse of RA and RV walls during inspiration

expl: Explanation: The patient's presentation of chest pain, dyspnea, and a water-bottle configuration of the cardiac shadow on X-ray following a viral infection strongly suggests pericardial effusion , which may progress to cardiac tamponade . In this setting, heart sounds are muffled , not loud, due to the insulating layer of fluid around the heart. Therefore, a loud S1 is not characteristic of pericardial effusion.

text: Patient is scheduled for an elective splenectomy. At least how long before the operation should pneumovax be given?
expl: All patients undergoing an elective splenectomy should be immunised with polyvalent pneumococcal vaccine (Pneumovax), which currently gives variable protection against 23 strains of Streptococcus pneumoniae. Where possible, it should be given at least 2 weeks and preferably at least 4 weeks prior to splenectomy to allow immunoglobulin G (gG) antibody production. text: A 30 year old lady is referred for investigation of abnormal liver function tests. She has been taking several drugs to treat tuberculosis for a long period of time.Her albumin is 3.0 g/dl, bilirubin 5 mg/dl, ALP is 250 U/l and ALT is 300 U/l.She has a liver biopsy which shows histological evidence of liver necrosis eroding the portal zone and extending into the liver lobule. expl: Periportal necrosis, portal inflammation, bridging necrosis and interface hepatitis are features of active liver inflammation. Inflammatory conditions (e.g Wilson's disease) and drugs such as methyldopa and isoniazid can precipitate chronic active hepatitis. text: Which criterion helps differentiate exudative from transudative pleural effusion?
expl: Explanation: High protein content in pleural fluid is a key criterion in Light's Criteria for distinguishing exudative from transudative pleural effusions. An exudative pleural effusion occurs due to inflammation or infections such as bacterial pneumonia, malignancy, or viral infection, while a transudative pleural effusion results from an imbalance between hydrostatic and osmotic pressures. Lights Criteria Helps to differentiate transudative from exudative pleural effusions based on LDH and protein levels in pleural fluid. Exudative pleural effusions meet at least one of the following criteria, whereas transudative pleural effusions meet none: Pleural fluid protein/serum protein > 0.5 Pleural fluid LDH/serum LDH > 0.6 Pleural fluid LDH exceeds two-thirds of the normal upper limit for serum. ~25% of transudates may be misidentified as exudates. If exudative criteria are met but a transudative condition is suspected, measure protein difference; if >31 g/L (3.1 g/dL), likely transudative. A transudative pleural effusion occurs when systemic factors that influence the formation and absorption of pleural fluid are altered. The leading causes of transudative pleural effusions in the United States are left ventricular failure and cirrhosis. An exudative pleural effusion occurs when local factors that influence the formation and absorption of pleural fluid are altered. The leading causes of exudative pleural effusions are bacterial pneumonia, malignancy, viral infection, and pulmonary embolism.

text: A patient with Parkinson's disease had aspiration pneumonitis. How will you manage this patient?
expl: Explanation: PEG gastrostomy tube insertion is the best appropriate step for long-term prevention of recurrent aspiration pneumonia. Chronic neurological illnesses such as Parkinson's disease or amyotrophic lateral sclerosis often cause oropharyngeal dysphagia , creating a high risk of recurrent aspiration. Nasogastric feeding can provide temporary nutrition but does not prevent aspiration of saliva or refluxed gastric contents. For long-term support, a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) is frequently chosen to deliver food directly into the stomach and reduce episodes of aspiration pneumonia. A PEG tube offers several advantages: it avoids nasal irritation, is less prone to accidental displacement, and allows more reliable feeding. After placement, a fibrous tract typically matures in about 10 days . If the tube is removed or dislodged before this tract is established, gastric contents can leak into the peritoneal cavity, posing a significant risk of peritonitis . Explanation for other Options: High frequency chest oscillation (Option A): This airway-clearance technique is used in conditions with thick secretions (e.g., cystic fibrosis, bronchiectasis). It does not address the root cause of aspiration in Parkinson's disease and will not prevent further aspiration episodes. Macrolides (Option B): Antibiotics such as azithromycin are indicated for bacterial pneumonia , not for chemical aspiration pneumonitis , which is an inflammatory injury from gastric/oral contents.They do not prevent future aspiration. N-acetylcysteine (Option C): Functions as a mucolytic or an antidote for acetaminophen toxicity . It has no established role in treating or preventing aspiration pneumonitis.

text: A young man came to the medical OPD with complaints of early morning backache and stiffness, which improves on exercise, and persistent red eyes. On examination, lung expansion was less than 3 cm. X-ray is shown in the image given below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The classic triad of inflammatory back pain, reduced chest expansion, and uveitis strongly suggests ankylosing spondylitis, supported by the “bamboo spine” seen on X-ray. Ankylosing Spondylitis (AS) is a chronic inflammatory seronegative spondyloarthropathy that primarily affects the spine and sacroiliac joints. The hallmark feature is inflammatory back pain, which is worse in the morning or after periods of inactivity, and improves with exercise. Reduced lung expansion ( The patient also has persistent red eyes, suggesting anterior uveitis, the most common extra-articular manifestation of AS. Characteristic radiological features of AS seen in this case: Sacroiliitis: bilateral and symmetrical involvement with erosion, sclerosis, and eventual fusion. Syndesmophyte formation leads to bamboo spine appearance on X-ray. Dagger sign: a radiodense line due to ossification of interspinous and supraspinous ligaments. Other clinical features include: Enthesitis (especially at Achilles tendon, plantar fascia) Peripheral large joint arthritis (hip, shoulder) Postural changes: forward stooping due to thoracic kyphosis Fatigue, anemia of chronic disease, and rarely cardiac/aortic involvement Investigations: HLA-B27 positive in >90% of patients Elevated ESR, CRP MRI is more sensitive than X-ray in early disease Explanation of other options: Paget's Disease (Option B): Characterized by abnormal bone remodeling with cortical thickening and lytic-sclerotic lesions, not vertebral fusion or syndesmophytes. Does not cause morning stiffness or uveitis. Healed Tuberculosis (Option C): Pott's spine may cause vertebral collapse or gibbus deformity, but not the bamboo spine appearance. Uveitis and reduced lung expansion are uncommon. Osteopetrosis (Option D): A genetic disorder with diffuse bone sclerosis due to defective osteoclast function. X-rays show dense bones, but there is no inflammatory back pain, uveitis, or vertebral fusion.

text: A 28-year-old woman is referred with intermittent diarrhoea present for a couple of years. She states that her weight has been steady but describes watery motions up to six stools per day and has also noted abdominal discomfort with bloating. She has not been aware of any blood in the motions or melaena. She describes no other medical history and denies taking any medication. Investigations show: Complete blood count : Normal Urea and electrolytes : Normal Albumin 3.9 g/dL(3.7-4.9) Corrected Calcium 8.6 mg/dl Alkaline phosphatase 94 U/L(45-105) C-reactive protein 6 mg/L ( Prothrombin time 12 s(11.5-15.5) What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: The normal albumin and C-reactive protein levels count against a diagnosis of inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's or ulcerative colitis) or an infectious pathology such as intestinal tuberculosis. Whilst small bowel bacterial overgrowth does not typically produce a raised C-reactive protein level it is very unusual in patients without risk factors for the condition (previous bowel surgery, Crohn's disease, motility disorders such as scleroderma). This leaves laxative abuse as the most likely diagnosis. Laxative abuse, where not a function of chronic constipation, is usually closely linked to eating disorders (Bulimia and Anorexia) and as such is typically over-represented in young, female patients. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 46 Pg: 303

text: A 20 year old Armenian man presents with pain and swelling of the left knee. He also gives a history of recurrent episodes of fever, pleuritic pains in the chest,and generalised rash. These episodes typically last for 2-3 days. Examination reveals splenomegaly, swollen knees and ankles.Urine dipstick reveals 2+ proteinuria. What is the likely diagnosis ?
expl: A young male presenting with history of recurrent fevers, arthritis and serositis especially in a person belonging to the Armenian descent points to the possibility of an autoinflammatory syndrome. Among the given options, Familial Mediterranean fever is the autoinflammatory syndrome seen in Armenians. Autoinflammatory syndromes are characterized by recurrent fevers, serosal, synovial and cutaneous inflammation and the eventual development of AA amyloidosis. They are called so because of the relative infrequency of autoantibodies or antigen specific T cells. The diseases included in this disease are: Familial Mediterranean Fever. TNF receptor associated periodic syndrome Hyperimmunoglobulinemia D with periodic fever syndrome NLRP 3 associated autoinflammatory disease. FMF occurs predominantly in Armenians, Arabs and Non Ashkenazi Jews. Hyperimmunoglobulin D with periodic fever is seen predominantly in Dutch and northern European. The rest of the autoinflammatory syndromes don't show any ethnic propensity. Familial Mediterranean fever: AR mainly, can be AD too. Fever lasting for 24-72 hours. Associated with abdominal pain in 90% cases. Unilateral pleurisy. Monoarticular arthritis, non erosive, without warmth or erythema. Skin rash resembling erysipelas. Exercise induced myalgia. Mutations in PYRIN gene, which is involved in host defense, where the threshold of activation of pyrin is reduced. Treatment is Cochicine or anti IL1β( Canakinumab) Rash seen in familial mediterranean fever Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Ch:369 Pg:2841-2842

text: A 30-year-old man with a history of tuberculosis now complains of abdominal distension and pedal edema. On examination, his neck veins are prominent. His chest x-ray is given below. Which of the following findings will be likely seen in this patient?
expl: Explanation: The chest X-ray shows an increased cardiothoracic ratio , and clinically the patient presents with distended neck veins (elevated JVP), abdominal distension, and pedal edema, consistent with cardiac tamponade . Given the patient's history of tuberculosis, the most likely underlying cause is tuberculous pericarditis leading to tamponade. In cardiac tamponade, there is typically a significant drop in systolic blood pressure during inspiration (pulsus paradoxus), which in this case is represented by the fall in SBP from 80mmHg to 60mmHg (>10mmHg drop). Cardiac tamponade A condition where the cardiac chambers are compressed by a tense pericardial effusion, limiting cardiac inflow. Fluid accumulation of as little as 200 ml to upwards of 2L may lead to cardiac tamponade development. Clinical features Beck's triad Jugular Venous Distension : Due to increased central venous pressure. Prominent x descent and an absent y descent. Hypotension : Resulting from impaired cardiac output. Muffled Heart Sounds : Caused by fluid accumulation in the pericardial space, dampening heart sounds. Pulsus Paradoxus : A hallmark finding. A drop in systolic BP during inspiration, greater than 10 mm Hg. Causes of Pulsus paradoxus: Lung Conditions: Acute asthma, COPD, tension pneumothorax, pleural effusion, pulmonary embolism. Heart Conditions: Cardiac tamponade, constrictive pericarditis. Explanation of other options: Pulsus bisferiens (Option A): Pulsus bisferiens is a double-peaked pulse typically seen in aortic regurgitation and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Kussmaul breathing (Option B): Kussmaul breathing refers to deep and laboured breathing seen in metabolic acidosis, particularly diabetic ketoacidosis; not a characteristic finding in cardiac tamponade. Fine crepitations (Option D): Fine crepitations are typically heard in pulmonary edema or pneumonia.

text: A 42-year-old male presents with a six hour history of profuse vomiting and over the last two hours had developed left-sided chest pain and dyspnoea. On examination he had a pulse of 110 beats per minute regular and a blood pressure of 168/90 mmHg. On palpation, he had crepitus over the left supraclavicular region and neck, reduced heart sounds and left basal sided crackles, plus some dullness to percussion over the right base of the chest. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: This man has a history of vomiting which then progressed to chest pain. The most relevant finding on examination is the crepitus over the chest, indicating surgical emphysema. The most probable cause is therefore spontaneous rupture of the oesophagus, secondary to forceful vomiting, called the Boerhaave's Syndrome . Mackler's triad (vomiting, chest pain and surgical emphysema) is classical but absent in almost half the cases. The chest x ray (CXR) may reveal the surgical emphysema and a gastrografin swallow is diagnostic . A CT scan should be performed if a gastrografin swallow is not possible or negative. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 323, Pg: 2433

text: Following type of pulmonary TB is most likely to be associated with AFB sputum positivity:
expl: Cavitary pulmonary tuberculosis is more likely to be associated with Acid-Fast Bacilli (AFB) sputum positivity . In cavitary TB, cavities or cavitations (hollow spaces or gaps) form within the lung tissue as a result of the disease process. These cavities often contain a high concentration of mycobacteria, making it more likely for AFB to be present in the sputum of affected individuals. Sputum from cavitary TB lesions is more infectious and has a higher likelihood of yielding positive AFB smear results compared to other forms of pulmonary TB. Cavities represent necrosis of tissue resulting in communication of the infected material with the airways. The bacteria are thus discharged in the bronchial tree from where they can be coughed out with sputum. The infected material can cause tubercular bronchopneumonia in the host by spreading to other parts of lungs or gastro-intestinal tuberculosis by means of swallowed secretions. The risk of spreading to other individuals is very high with cavitary tuberculosis. Other options Primary complex: This is usually associated with the initial infection and may not always yield AFB-positive sputum. Fibro nodular: While fibro nodular lesions can be seen in tuberculosis, they are not typically associated with the highest likelihood of AFB sputum positivity. Pleural effusion: Tuberculous pleural effusion can occur, but it involves fluid in the pleural space rather than cavities within lung tissue. The presence of AFB in pleural effusion is less common compared to cavitary TB. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch:178 Pg:1362-1364

text: Nucleic acid amplification (NAA) tests for the diagnosis of TB

options.A: Are not approved by the FDA.
options.B: Require more than one month for results.
options.C: May not be used with smear-positive specimens.
options.D: Are able to differentiate between different species of M. tuberculosis.

ansText: Are able to differentiate between different species of M. tuberculosis.
expl: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved three commercially available nucleic acid amplification (NAA) tests for use in confirming tuberculosis in procured specimens. The first is the Amplicor Test, which is based on the polymerase chain reaction. It amplifies a specific portion of the RNA from the TB organisms and measures the results with a photometer. The findings of this test are usually available within six to seven hours. The FDA has approved the Amplicor Test only for smear-positive specimens. The second approved probe is the amplified tuberculosis direct (Amplified MTD) test, which uses transcription-mediated amplification in order to identify and magnify the RNA target. Results are generally available within three to four hours. This test is approved for the detection of tuberculosis in both smear-positive and smear-negative cultures. The third NAA test is the Xpert MTB/RIF Assay, which is able to detect the presence of tuberculosis organisms as well as resistance to rifampicin. This automated, cartridge-based system requires a sputum sample and results are available within two hours. Non-FDA approved NAA tests (often called "in-house" tests) may be used to diagnose TB and to test for drug-resistant TB. These tests are also able to differentiate the DNA of different species of tuberculosis , also called DNA fingerprinting or genotyping. Because most strains of bacteria share patterns, it has been difficult to follow the person-to-person transmission of certain strains. Using genotyping, researchers have shown that each strain has a distinct DNA fingerprint and that all samples sharing the same DNA fingerprint were isolated from people who live together. This will help track the path of transmission and aid public health researchers to pinpoint patterns of infection, which in turn helps to plan prevention programs that target the areas of heightened infection rates. Truenat MTB and MTC Plus are two newly introduced rapid molecular tests with a sensitivity of 83% and 89%, respectively, if compared to bacteriological culture. They were developed in India. Loop Mediated Isothermal Amplification, is another method using the DNA amplification and can be substituted for microscopy Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 178, Pg: 1369

text: Which of the following is not common in primary pulmonary tuberculosis?
expl: Because most inspired air is distributed to the middle and lower lung zones, these areas are most commonly involved in primary TB. In the majority of cases, the lesion heals spontaneously and becomes evident only as a small calcified nodule. Pleural reaction overlying a subpleural focus is also common. The Ghon focus, with or without overlying pleural reaction, thickening, and regional lymphadenopathy, is referred to as the Ghon complex. text: In the stage of Grey hepatization -
expl: Ans. is 'd' i.e., Accumulation of fibrin Pathological changes of bacterial pneumonia A.Lobar pneumonia Large confluent area of the lung or entire lobes are consolidated. The lower lobes are affected most commonly. There are four stages of the inflammatory response (Laennec's stages) ? Stage of congestion (initial phase) The affected lobe is enlarged, heavy, dark red and congested. Cut surface exudes blood-stained frothy fluid. There is dilatation and congestion of alveolar capillaries. There are few neutrophils and numerous bacteria in the alveolar fluid. Stage of red hepatization (early consolidation) The term hepatization refers to liver-like consistency of the affected lobe on cut section. o The affected lobe is red and firm. The edema fluid of preceding stage is replaced by strands of fibrin. There is marked cellular exudate of neutrophils with extravasation of red cells. Stage of gray hepatization (late consolidation) The affected lobe is grayish brown, firm and dry. The fibrin strand are dense and more numerous. There is progressive disintigration of red cells and neutrophils. The macrophages begin to appear in the exudate. The organisms are less numerous and appear as degenerated forms. Resolution The previously solid and fibrinous constituent is liquefied by enzymatic action. Granular and fragmented strands of fibrin in the alveolar spaces are seen due to progressive enzymatic digestion. There is progressive removal of fluid content as well as cellular exudate from the air spaces, resulting in restoration of normal lung parenchyma with areation. B.Bronchopneumonia Patchy areas of red or grey consolidation, more often multilobar and frequently bilateral and basal (lower zones) because of tendency of secretions to gravitate into lower lobes. There is suppurative exudate, consisting chiefly neutrophils, filling bronchi, bronchioles and adjacent alveolar spaces. Alveolar septa thicken due to congested capillaries and leucocytic infiltration.

text: Most common complication of pneumococcal pneumonia?
expl: Empyema is the most common focal complication of pneumococcal pneumonia, occurring in When fluid in the pleural space is accompanied by fever and leukocytosis (even low-grade) after 4-5 days of appropriate antibiotic treatment for pneumococcal pneumonia, empyema should be considered. text: Multidrug-resistant (MDR) tuberculosis is characterized by resistance to which of the following anti-tubercular drugs?
expl: Explanation: MDR-TB is specifically defined as resistance to both isoniazid and rifampicin , the two most powerful first-line anti-tubercular medications. This form of TB poses major therapeutic challenges as these drugs form the backbone of standard treatment regimens. Drug-Sensitive Tuberculosis (DSTB): Refers to tuberculosis that responds to the main first-line drugs such as isoniazid and rifampicin . Drug-Resistant Tuberculosis (DR-TB): Defined as TB caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains resistant to at least one first-line anti-TB drug . Multidrug-Resistant Tuberculosis (MDR-TB): TB caused by strains resistant to both isoniazid and rifampicin . Extensively Drug-Resistant Tuberculosis (XDR-TB): A severe subset of MDR-TB where the bacilli are resistant to isoniazid, rifampicin, any fluoroquinolone, and at least one second-line injectable drug (such as amikacin, kanamycin, or capreomycin). Explanation of Other Options: Immediately (Option A): Incorrect, as MDR-TB does not require resistance to fluoroquinolones. This definition corresponds to XDR-TB. Fluoroquinolones (Option B): Wrong, since resistance to only fluoroquinolones defines neither MDR-TB nor XDR-TB by itself. Isoniazid, rifampicin, and kanamycin (Option D): Incorrect, as this again falls under the definition of XDR-TB rather than MDR-TB. References: NCBI Bookshelf - Tuberculosis MDR Overview PMC - Multidrug-Resistant Tuberculosis Review

text: A 40-year-old man with pneumonia is being examined. Which one of the following positive auscultatory signs is diagnostic of bronchial breathing?
expl: Whispering pectoriloquy is a diagnostic sign for bronchial breathing. Refers to an increased loudness of whispering on auscultation. In areas of consolidation of the lungs, these whispered spoken sounds by the patient will be heard clearly through the stethoscope. This increase in sound occurs because sound travels through solid or liquid medium versus gaseous (air in the lung) media. It is usually performed in cases of consolidation or mass. Reference: “Bates Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking” 11 th edition, 314-5

text: Hospital acquired pneumonia can be labelled if it develops after __ hours after hospital admission.
expl: Hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP) occurs more than 48 hours after admission to the hospital or other health care facility and excludes any infection present at the time of admission. If it develops within 48 hours it is considered as community acquired pneumonia (CAP) Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) develops more than 48 hours following endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation. It presents as At least two of the following: fever, leucocytosis, purulent sputum OR a new or progressive parenchymal opacities on chest radiograph. Reference: CMDT 2020 page number 285

text: A 30-year-old man came with complaints of fever and cough for 3 days. On examination, creatinine is 1.5 and BUN is 45. Chest-x ray shows infiltrates in the right lung and patchy infiltrates in the left lung. A nasopharyngeal swab shows only Rhinovirus. The patient is shifted to the ICU. Which antibiotics are suitable for this patient?
expl: Explanation: In this case, the patient presents with fever, cough, and chest X-ray findings of patchy infiltrates, which most likely indicate pneumonia. Since the condition qualifies as severe pneumonia requiring ICU admission, the preferred treatment is a combination of a beta-lactam and a macrolide, such as ceftriaxone with azithromycin. The treatment protocol in an inpatient with pneumonia would be chosen based on the severity of the disease. CURB-65 Score: Used to stratify patients with the following factors: Hospitalisation Criteria: CURB-65 score 0: Outpatient treatment Score 1 or 2: Indicates hospitalization Score ≥3: Indicates ICU admission and more intensive therapy. In non-severe case a B-lactam with a macrolide or a respiratory fluoroquinolone is used and in a severe pneumonia case a B-lactam with a macrolide (ceftrioxone+azithromycin) or a B-lactam+ respiratory fluoroquinolone is used. Explanation of other options: Amoxicillin with clavulinic acid (Option A): Inadequate for this patient due to the severity of his illness and the risk of resistant organisms. Monotherapy with amoxicillin does not provide sufficient coverage for his condition, especially considering the possibility of Pseudomonas and MRSA. Azithromycin (Option B): Not appropriate for this patient due to the severity of his condition, indicating he requires more intensive treatment. Azithromycin is preferred for outpatient therapy, suitable for lower-risk patients without significant comorbidities. Piptaz + ciprofloxacin (Option D): Piptaz (piperacillin/tazobactam) is a beta-lactam antibiotic combination, while ciprofloxacin belongs to the fluoroquinolone class. However, in this patient's case, these options alone are not appropriate, as the management of severe pneumonia requires the addition of a macrolide along with either a fluoroquinolone or a beta-lactam.

text: Which of the following statements is NOT true of primary pulmonary tuberculosis:

options.B: Miliary spread is commoner in a younger age group
options.C: pleural effusion occurs before tuberculin skin testing is positive
options.D: A positive tuberculin skin test develops within two weeks of infection

ansText: A positive tuberculin skin test develops within two weeks of infection
expl: Primary TB is usually asymptomatic, with miliary TB most likely to occur in young children. The Ghon focus is the area of consolidation from cellular infiltration and response to uptake of organisms by macrophages, which transform into epithelioid cells and group into granulomata. Bacilli are transported via lymphatics early in the disease process to regional lymph nodes to cause marked lymphadenopathy. Positive tuberculin test occurs between 3 weeks to 3 months after primary infection. Pleural and pericardial infections occur at or shortly after primary infection. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 178, Pg: 1362

text: Urinary antigen is a useful test to detect which of the following organisms causing pneumonia?
expl: Two commercially available tests detect pneumococcal and Legionella antigen in urine. The test for Legionella pneumophila detects only serogroup 1 , but this serogroup accounts for most community-acquired cases of Legionnaires’ disease in the United States. The sensitivity and specificity of the Legionella urine antigen test are as high as 70% and 99%, respectively. The pneumococcal urine antigen test is also quite sensitive and specific (70% and >90%, respectively). Although false-positive results can be obtained with samples from pneumococcus-colonized children, the test is generally reliable. Both tests can detect antigen even after the initiation of appropriate antibiotic therapy C&S: Culture & Sensitivity PCR: Polymerase Chain Reaction Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21 st ed, ch:126 Pg: 1012

text: A patient has been diagnosed with chlamydia pneumonia. What is the most appropriate antibiotic therapy?
expl: Macrolide antibiotics (erythromycin and clarithromycin) are the treatment of choice for chlamydia and other atypical pneumonias. The diagnosis of chlamydia pneumonia is difficult. The organism is cultivated like a virus using tissue cultures, but few laboratories offer this test. Serology is difficult to interpret; the usual titres for IgM or serial changes with acute and convalescent sera are arbitrary. Like mycoplasma, this is an organism that is often suspected, infrequently proven, but easily treated empirically Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 189 Pg: 1447

text: Most common organism causing overwhelming infection in post-splenectomy patients is:
expl: Splenic individuals are at increased risk of overwhelming post-splenectomy infections (OPSI). Patients without spleen are 58 times more likely to succumb to sepsis than the general population. text: Antibiotic of choice for Legionella pneumonia is
expl: Because Legionella is an intracellular pathogen , antibiotics that reach high intracellular concentrations are more likely to be effective. The macrolides (especially azithromycin ) and the quinolones (especially levofloxacin or ciprofloxacin) are the antibiotics of choice and are effective as monotherapy. Compared With erythromycin, the newer macrolides have superior in vitro activity, display greater intracellular activity, reach higher concentrations in respiratory secretions and lung tissue, and have fewer adverse effects. Quinolones are the preferred antibiotics for transplant recipients because both macrolides and rifampin interact pharmacologically with cyclosporine and tacrolimus. Reference : Harrison's principles of internal medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:159 Pg: 1256

text: Urinary antigen test is used for diagnosis of pneumonia caused by
expl: Two commercially available tests detect pneumococcal and Legionella antigen in urine. The test for Legionella pneumophila detects only serogroup 1, but this serogroup accounts for most community- acquired cases of Legionnaires' disease in the United States. The sensitivity and specificity of the Legionella urine antigen test are as high as 70% and 99%, respectively. The pneumococcal urine antigen test is also quite sensitive and specific (70% and >90%, respectively). Although false-positive results can be obtained with samples from pneumococcus-colonized children, the test is generally reliable. Both tests can detect antigen even after the initiation of appropriate antibiotic therapy Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 126, Pg: 1012

expl: The question depicts a patient with Pneumonia. The severity of pneumonia is calculated based on two scores- CURB 65 or the PSI. The CURB-65 criteria include five variables: confusion (C) Blood urea Nitrogen >7 mmol/L (U)(>19 mg/dL)(Blood Urea of >40 mg/dl) respiratory rate ≥30/min (R) blood pressure— systolic ≤90 mmHg or diastolic ≤60 mmHg (B) an age of ≥65 years. Patients with a score of 0 (a 30-day mortality rate of 1.5%) can be treated as outpatients. With a score of 1 or 2, the patient should be hospitalized unless the score is entirely or in part attributable to an age of ≥65 years; in such cases, hospitalization may not be necessary.
