text: A 56-year-old man presents with fever, chills, and a productive cough. His vital signs reveal a BP of 150/88 mmHg, pulse rate of 110 bpm, respiratory rate of 18/min, and SpO2 of 88% on room air. A chest X-ray was performed and is shown below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
expl: Explanation of answer: The combination of fever, cough with sputum, hypoxia, and lobar consolidation on chest X-ray is most consistent with community-acquired pneumonia (CAP). This clinical scenario strongly indicates community-acquired pneumonia (CAP), which presents acutely with systemic and respiratory symptoms and radiographic signs of consolidation. Etiology: Typical pathogens: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Staphylococcus aureus Atypical pathogens: Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae, Legionella, influenza virus Clinical Features: Symptoms: Fever, chills, productive cough, dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain Signs: Increased respiratory rate, hypoxia, dullness to percussion, increased tactile fremitus, bronchial breath sounds, crepitations Radiographic Findings: Chest X-ray in CAP shows: New lobar infiltrates/consolidation May involve cavitation or multilobar disease in severe cases Diagnosis: Clinical + Radiographic correlation is key Supportive tests: CBC, CRP, procalcitonin, blood cultures, sputum Gram stain and culture, urine antigen for Legionella and S. pneumoniae Severity Assessment - CURB-65 Criteria: Criteria - Points Confusion - 1 Urea >7 mmol/L - 1 Respiratory rate >30 - 1 BP Age ≥ 65 years. - 1 Score 0: Treat outpatient Score 1-2: Hospital admission Score ≥3: ICU care Treatment: Score Recommended Regimen 0 Amoxicillin + macrolide/doxycycline, or monotherapy with either 1-2 β-lactam + macrolide, or respiratory fluoroquinolone ≥3 β-lactam + macrolide or β-lactam + fluoroquinolone (IV) Explanation of other options: Tubercular pleural effusion (Option A): Usually presents with pleuritic chest pain, dullness, and decreased breath sounds. Imaging shows blunted costophrenic angle or meniscus sign, not lobar consolidation. Coal worker pneumoconiosis (Option C): Chronic occupational disease with small upper lobe opacities. No acute presentation with fever or lobar consolidation. Silicosis (Option D): Due to silica exposure, it shows multiple small upper lobe nodules with possible eggshell calcification of lymph nodes. No acute systemic symptoms or lobar involvement.

text: A patient on a ventilator presents with cough and breathlessness. Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) is diagnosed. What is the role of procalcitonin?
expl: Explanation: The role of procalcitonin is to decide the duration of antibiotics . Procalcitonin is a biomarker that increases in response to bacterial infections , especially in systemic bacterial infections such as pneumonia. In the management of VAP , procalcitonin is not used to diagnose the infection or choose initial therapy, but it can help guide the duration of antibiotic treatment . Serial procalcitonin levels can be used to support early discontinuation of antibiotics when levels fall, helping to avoid unnecessary prolonged antibiotic use. This approach can reduce antibiotic resistance and side effects . Explanations for other Options: Choosing empirical antibiotics (Option B): Procalcitonin does not guide the selection of empirical antibiotics. The choice of initial antibiotics in VAP is based on clinical factors like hospital stay duration, previous antibiotic use, and local resistance patterns , not on procalcitonin levels. Confirmation of VAP (Option C): Procalcitonin is not used to confirm the diagnosis of VAP. Diagnosis relies on clinical signs , such as fever, purulent secretions, and imaging findings, as well as microbiological culture results , not solely on biomarkers like procalcitonin. Differentiate fungal and bacterial etiology (Option D): Procalcitonin cannot reliably distinguish between bacterial and fungal infections. Although it typically rises in bacterial infections, it does not provide specific information about the type of pathogen involved, so it cannot differentiate fungal from bacterial causes.

text: An 82-year-old man came to the clinic complaining of feeling generally unwell for about the last 3-4 months and of losing about 9.5 kg weight during this period. On further enquiry he said he had been having night sweats for the last month. He also has a past history of angina and arthritis and was on medication. On examination he did not look well. He was pyrexic and without lymphadenopathy. Bibasal crepitus on the lower zone was heard on chest auscultation. He had hepatosplenomegaly and clubbing. Investigations showed WBC 12300/µl (neutrophils 52%, lymphocytes 39%), Hb 9.1 g/dl, with all other routine investigations being normal. A chest X-ray showed 1-2 cm diameter miliary shadows all over the lung field. The Mantoux test was negative. No bacteria growth on culture. His X-ray is following What is the probable cause of the illness and the X-ray finding?
expl: We have an elderly male with weight loss and night sweats. He is immunocompromised owing to his age and prior illness of arthritis for which he might be on DMARDS. On examination he is febrile with anemia and clubbing. He has hepatosplenomegaly too. The clinical possibilities in this context are either a chronic infection or malignancy. The most common chronic infection in our country is tuberculosis. The chest x-ray here is showing small miliary shadows. Hence the most probable answer is miliary TB. There is organomegaly because of the extrapulmonary infection. Mantoux may be negative because of the age and dissemination of the pathogen. Miliary tuberculosis, is caused by a diffuse disseminated spread of tubercle bacilli via the bloodstream. In older patients it is difficult to diagnose. It presents with a gradual onset of vague ill health, loss of weight and then fever. It can also present as tubercular meningitis. Hepatosplenomegaly is seen in advanced disease. Initially, a chest X-ray may be normal. Later, chest X-ray reveals the presence of small 1-2 cm lesions. CT scanning may show a lung parenchymal abnormality at an early stage. The Mantoux test may be negative in up to half of the patients with severe disease. A transbronchial biopsy is positive at an early stage. If untreated miliary tuberculosis is universally fatal. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 178, Pg: 1366

text: Tree in bud appearance is seen in CT chest of pneumonia caused by
expl: Tree-in-bud sign or pattern describes the CT appearance of multiple areas of centrilobular nodules with a linear branching pattern. The pattern can manifest because of the following disease processes, often in combination: Airway-centered : bronchioles filled with pus or inflammatory exudate e.g. pulmonary tuberculosis, aspiration bronchopneumonia, MAC infection bronchiolitis: thickening of bronchiolar walls and bronchovascular bundle e.g. cytomegalovirus pneumonitis, obliterative bronchiolitis bronchiectasis/bronchiolectasis with mucus plugging e.g. cystic fibrosis bronchovascular interstitial infiltration e.g. sarcoidosis, lymphoma, leukemia Vascular-centered: tumor emboli to centrilobular arteries (or carcinomatous endarteritis) e.g. breast cancer, stomach cancer granulomatous response to excipient material in intravenous drug abusers Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 180 Pg: 1395

text: A 50-year-old meat factory worker has been unwell with fever, cough, sweats and lethargy. On examination, he had a purpuric rash and hepatosplenomegaly. What is the likely diagnosis?
expl: Q fever is a zoonosis and is transmitted by the infected animal and is acquired by aerosol route. Veterinarians, abbatoir workers etc are at risk. Q fever is due to Coxiella Brunetti and is acquired via animal contact. It can occur in outbreaks in farming communities and in abattoirs. Treatment is with prolonged courses of tetracyclines. Rarely infection can be persistent leading to chronic symptoms including fatigue, malaise and sweats. Hepatitis, hepatosplenomegaly, maculopapular rash and endocarditis are associated. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 187, Pg: 1439

text: A 40-year-old man presented with a history of recurrent haemoptysis. He has previously been treated for tuberculosis. Chest x ray showed rounded soft tissue masses seen within a cavity in the right upper lobe with an air crescent. What is the diagnosis?
expl: Aspergillomas are masses of fungal mycelia that grow in pre-existing lung cavities. Haemoptysis is a common symptom. They may require treatment with either antifungals or excision surgery if large. They are not associated with bronchiectasis (unlike allergic Bronchopulmonary aspergillosis). text: A 65-year-old man with persistent fever and long-standing respiratory distress that did not improve with standard therapy was diagnosed with cryptic tuberculosis. Which of the following statements correctly applies to this condition?

options.A: Positive skin tuberculin test and negative chest X-ray
options.B: Positive skin tuberculin test and positive chest X-ray
options.C: Negative skin tuberculin test and negative chest X-ray
options.D: Negative skin tuberculin test and positive chest X-ray

ansText: Negative skin tuberculin test and negative chest X-ray
expl: Explanation: Cryptic tuberculosis is an uncommon, atypical form of TB in which both the tuberculin skin test and chest X-ray appear negative, even though Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection is present. In cryptic tuberculosis , the usual diagnostic methods such as the tuberculin skin test (which assesses delayed hypersensitivity to M. tuberculosis*antigens) and chest X-ray (which typically shows parenchymal infiltrates)-may fail to reveal the infection. In its severe variant, called cryptic miliary TB , the disease may cause pancytopenia and widespread hematogenous spread, with autopsy findings showing multiple necrotic, non-granulomatous lesions . Explanations of other options: Positive skin tuberculin test and negative chest X-ray (Option A): This reflects an immune hypersensitivity reaction to *M. tuberculosis* in the absence of radiological signs of active disease, which is characteristic of latent tuberculosis infection. Positive skin tuberculin test and positive chest X-ray (Option B): This is the typical picture of active pulmonary tuberculosis, where both immune reactivity and radiological abnormalities are present. In contrast, cryptic tuberculosis lacks both of these findings. Negative skin tuberculin test and positive chest X-ray (Option D): This pattern indicates active lung disease without a detectable immune reaction, often observed in immunocompromised patients. Although it may be seen in certain types of TB, it is not cryptic tuberculosis, which is defined by both tests being negative.

text: A 60-year-old patient presents with complaints of chest pain and dyspnea. Pleural fluid analysis reveals a pleural fluid protein to serum protein ratio >0.5 and a pleural fluid LDH to serum LDH ratio >0.4. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation of answer: The pleural fluid profile is consistent with exudative pleural effusion, and among the options given, tuberculosis is the most likely cause. The provided pleural fluid analysis shows a pleural protein/serum protein ratio > 0.5 and a pleural LDH/serum LDH ratio > 0.4, which are indicative of exudative pleural effusion, as per Light's criteria . Light's Criteria for Exudative Effusion: Pleural fluid is considered exudative if any one of the following is true: Pleural fluid protein / serum protein > 0.5 Pleural fluid LDH / serum LDH > 0.6 Pleural fluid LDH > 2/3 the upper limit of normal serum LDH The presence of an exudative effusion narrows down the differential diagnosis to conditions causing pleural inflammation, such as: Tuberculosis Malignancy Pneumonia (parapneumonic effusion) Pulmonary embolism Autoimmune diseases (e.g., RA, SLE) Tuberculous Pleuritis: A common cause of exudative pleural effusion, especially in endemic regions. Typically presented with lymphocyte-predominant fluid, elevated adenosine deaminase (ADA >40 IU/L), and interferon gamma (>140 pg/mL). May also have low glucose and high protein levels. text: A 35-year-old lady has a headache, cough and myalgia. On examination, she has a pyrexia and scattered crackles bilaterally on auscultation of the chest. Rapid cold agglutinins were positive. What is the likely diagnosis?
expl: Mycoplasma pneumonia is the commonest atypical pneumonia. Approximately 15% of pneumonias in adults are due to Mycoplasma pneumoniae. Transmission occurs from person to person by infected droplets. The incubation period is 9-21 days. The incidence is higher during the winter months. Fever, chills, cough and headache are early symptoms. Dyspnoea, chest pain and haemoptysis are rare. Small pleural effusions may occur but are rare. Cold agglutinins are usually present in a titre greater than 1:32. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch:188, Pg: 1441-1442

text: A 35-year-old woman presents with fever, shortness of breath, and productive cough with expectoration. A CT chest scan was performed (shown below). What is the most probable diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The combination of fever, dyspnea, and expectoration , along with CT findings of consolidation accompanied by an air bronchogram , is highly suggestive of lobar pneumonia leading to pneumonic consolidation . Clinical manifestations of Lobar Pneumonia Common Symptoms: Fever Cough Mucopurulent sputum production Pleuritic chest pain (localized, sharp pain - especially in lobar disease) Constitutional Symptoms: Fatigue, headache, myalgia, arthralgia Severe Cases: Dyspnea Confusion, sepsis, multi-organ dysfunction Clinical Signs Respiratory signs: Tachypnea (↑ respiratory rate) Increased vocal fremitus Egophony (E-to-A changes) Dullness on percussion Crackles/rales and bronchial breath sounds (tubular type) Investigations & Findings Initial Evaluation: Based on history and clinical exam Chest Radiography: Most important initial test for pneumonia Detects pulmonary infiltrates (lobar, interstitial, unilateral, or bilateral) Cannot reliably separate bacterial vs. non-bacterial causes CT Scan: More sensitive than chest X-ray Dense opacification of an entire lobe with sparing of major airways May show ground-glass opacities and lobar/segmental pattern of involvement Image finding: Left upper lobe consolidation of heterogeneous density with multiple air bronchograms and a small pleural effusion Laboratory Tests: CBC: Leukocytosis (left shift) → infection marker; leukopenia → poor prognosis Inflammatory markers: ESR, acute phase reactants Sputum Analysis: Gram stain and culture critical in suspected lobar pneumonia Culture = most specific diagnostic test Influenza Testing: Recommended in winter due to co-infection risk Risk Stratification: CURB-65 / Pneumonia Severity Index → hospitalization decisions Other Diagnostic Measures: Blood cultures, urine antigen tests (before antibiotics) Thoracocentesis, bronchoscopy, pleural biopsy/culture (rare) Open lung biopsy = gold standard diagnostic test Explanation of Other Options Mediastinal Mass (Option B): Causes chest pain, cough, dyspnea, but not classical pneumonia features (fever, productive cough). Appears as a well-defined localized lesion with mass effect in mediastinum. Pleural Effusion (Option C): Appears on CT as fluid collection in pleural cavity. Leads to breathlessness, but not consolidation with air bronchograms. Typical finding = homogeneous pleural opacity. Diaphragmatic Hernia (Option D): On CT shows abdominal organs (stomach/bowel) in thoracic cavity . Not associated with fever, expectoration, or pulmonary consolidation. Key Takeaways Air bronchogram within consolidation is a hallmark of lobar pneumonia. Diagnosis requires clinical-radiological correlation. CT is more sensitive, but X-ray remains the first-line test . Always confirm etiology with sputum culture when possible. Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK534295/ https://radiopaedia.org/articles/lobar-pneumonia

text: A 46-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus presents with fever, malaise, and a productive cough. Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding the radiological findings and their interpretation?

options.A: Patchy infiltrates as seen in pyogenic pneumonia
options.B: Interstitial infiltrates as seen in Mycoplasma pneumonia
options.C: Hilar lymphadenopathy with infiltrates as seen in malignancy
options.D: Aspiration pneumonia is more common in the upper segment of the lower lobe and posterior segment of the upper lobe

ansText: Hilar lymphadenopathy with infiltrates as seen in malignancy
expl: Explanation: Pyogenic (bacterial) pneumonia , such as that caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae or Klebsiella pneumoniae, classically produces lobar consolidation rather than patchy infiltrates . Patchy or diffuse infiltrates are more typical of atypical pneumonia , which is commonly caused by organisms like Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, or viruses. Explanation of Other Options: Interstitial infiltrates in Mycoplasma pneumonia (Option B): Common pathogens: Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Legionella pneumophila, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, viruses (e.g., influenza, RSV). CXR findings: Bilateral, patchy or reticulonodular interstitial infiltrates , mainly in the perihilar regions. Absence of lobar consolidation. Clinical features: Gradual onset with low-grade fever, dry cough, malaise, headache, myalgia. Mild symptoms compared to X-ray findings ("walking pneumonia"). → Therefore, patchy interstitial infiltrates suggest an atypical pattern rather than pyogenic pneumonia. Hilar lymphadenopathy with infiltrates in malignancy (Option C): Typical of: Malignancy: Bronchogenic carcinoma, lymphoma, metastatic disease. Granulomatous infections: Tuberculosis, sarcoidosis. CXR appearance: Enlarged hilar nodes with adjacent parenchymal opacity ("mass-like" or mixed pattern). Clinical note: In acute pneumonia, lymphadenopathy is less common and usually mild Hence, this finding would point toward an alternate diagnosis if present. Aspiration pneumonia distribution (Option D): Etiology: Aspiration of oropharyngeal or gastric contents into the lower respiratory tract, especially in: Alcoholics, stroke patients, unconscious or intubated individuals, or those with impaired gag reflex. Causative organisms: Anaerobes (Bacteroides, Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus), mixed flora, and Klebsiella. Commonly affected sites: Supine position: Posterior segment of the upper lobe and superior segment of the lower lobe (especially right lung). Upright position: Basal segments of lower lobes. CXR findings: Patchy, segmental consolidations in dependent areas. Complications: Abscess formation, empyema, necrotizing pneumonia.

text: A patient with HIV presents with a CD4 count of 180 cells/mm³ and a 2-week history of dry cough, exertional dyspnea, and fever. Microbiological staining shows organisms with a "crushed ping-pong ball" appearance. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) is an important AIDS-defining illness , typically occurring in patients with CD4 counts . It presents with a subacute onset of dry cough, progressive dyspnea, and fever , often with hypoxemia out of proportion to chest X-ray findings. Microscopically, silver staining of bronchoalveolar lavage specimens shows the classic "crushed ping-pong ball" or "cup-shaped cyst" appearance . Explanation of other options: CMV pneumoniax (CMV pneumonia) (Option A): Seen in severely immunocompromised patients but presents with retinitis or systemic involvement ; histology shows owl's eye inclusion bodies , not "ping-pong ball" cysts. Cryptococcal pneumonia (Option B): Caused by Cryptococcus neoformans, usually associated with meningitis ; diagnosed by India ink stain showing encapsulated yeast , not crushed cysts. Bacterial pneumonia (Option D): Presents with a productive cough and lobar consolidation ; it does not occur with this classic cyst morphology.

text: A 30-year-old man comes to the clinic with a productive cough. Sputum is smear-positive for tuberculosis. What does this mean?

options.A: He needs treatment for tuberculosis and his close contacts need screening, but he is not infectious to casual contacts
options.B: He needs treatment for tuberculosis, his close contacts need screening and he needs to be isolated from casual contacts
options.C: He needs treatment for tuberculosis, but he is not infectious to close or casual contacts

ansText: He needs treatment for tuberculosis, his close contacts need screening and he needs to be isolated from casual contacts
expl: He needs treatment for tuberculosis, his close contacts need screening and he needs to be isolated from casual contacts. Smear-positive tuberculosis means the patient is highly infectious to both close contacts (More than 8 hours together per day) and casual contacts, such as other patients on the ward and healthcare workers. He therefore needs isolating in a negative-pressure room and contacts should wear particulate masks until he has received antituberculous therapy for 2 weeks. The sputum may remain positive after this time, but the organisms will be dead. Culture-positive tuberculosis means the immediate smear is negative, but prolonged culture has shown tuberculosis. Smear-positive TB does not necessarily indicate drug resistance or associated HIV infection. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 178 Pg: 1369-1379

text: A 45-year-old HIV-positive male came with complaints of persistent cough and weight loss. He has skin lesions that appear as umbilicated papules and nodules predominantly on the face, trunk, and upper extremities. Chest x-ray showed multiple bilateral nodular infiltrates. His sputum CBNAAT for tuberculosis was negative and he has a low CD4 count. What is the probable diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: Disseminated histoplasmosis commonly presents with systemic symptoms, pulmonary infiltrates, and skin lesions in immunocompromised individuals, particularly those with HIV and low CD4 counts. Histoplasma capsulatum , a dimorphic fungus, causes disseminated histoplasmosis in immunocompromised patients, especially those with CD4+ counts Infection is acquired via inhalation of microconidia from bird or bat droppings. In such patients, the yeast forms multiply within macrophages and spread systemically. Clinical features of progressive disseminated histoplasmosis (PDH) include fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia, diffuse interstitial or reticulonodular pulmonary infiltrates, and characteristic skin lesions (papules, plaques, ulcers, sometimes umbilicated in ~10% cases). Diagnosis involves urine or serum antigen testing, fungal cultures, and histopathological identification of yeast within macrophages. Treatment: Liposomal amphotericin B is used for induction in severe cases, followed by oral itraconazole maintenance for ≥12 months. Explanation of other options: HIV with disseminated cryptococcosis (Option B): Cryptococcosis usually presents with meningeal involvement; the absence of neurological signs and predominant lung and skin involvement makes this less likely. HIV with molluscum contagiosum (Option C): While the patient has umbilicated papules, molluscum contagiosum does not explain systemic symptoms or lung infiltrates. HIV with tuberculosis (Option D): Although TB is common in HIV, a negative sputum CBNAAT and bilateral nodular infiltrates without typical granulomatous findings reduce its likelihood. hiv with disseminated histoplasmosis hiv with disseminated cryptococcosis hiv with molluscum contagiosum hiv with tuberculosis  explanation: disseminated histoplasmosis commonly presents with systemic symptoms, pulmonary infiltrates, and skin lesions in immunocompromised individuals, particularly those with hiv and low cd4 counts. histoplasma capsulatum , a dimorphic fungus, causes disseminated histoplasmosis in immunocompromised patients, especially those with cd4+ counts infection is acquired via inhalation of microconidia from bird or bat droppings. in such patients, the yeast forms multiply within macrophages and spread systemically. clinical features of progressive disseminated histoplasmosis (pdh) include fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia, diffuse interstitial or reticulonodular pulmonary infiltrates, and characteristic skin lesions (papules, plaques, ulcers, sometimes umbilicated in ~10% cases). diagnosis involves urine or serum antigen testing, fungal cultures, and histopathological identification of yeast within macrophages. treatment: liposomal amphotericin b is used for induction in severe cases, followed by oral itraconazole maintenance for ≥12 months. explanation of other options: hiv with disseminated cryptococcosis (option b): cryptococcosis usually presents with meningeal involvement; the absence of neurological signs and predominant lung and skin involvement makes this less likely. hiv with molluscum contagiosum (option c): while the patient has umbilicated papules, molluscum contagiosum does not explain systemic symptoms or lung infiltrates. hiv with tuberculosis (option d): although tb is common in hiv, a negative sputum cbnaat and bilateral nodular infiltrates without typical granulomatous findings reduce its likelihood. reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/pmc3687172/ https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/pmc3969680/

text: A 60-year-old miner has been in the occupation for 20 years. He presents with a cough and breathlessness. Chest XR shows diffuse interstitial shadowing. A sputum sample is positive for acid fast bacilli. Which of the following dusts is most likely to have predisposed the patient to tuberculosis?
expl: Slate workers, stonemasons and miners are exposed to silica dust. mining; stonecutting; sand blasting; glass and cement manufacturing; foundry work; packing of silica flour; and quarrying, particularly of granite are other occupational sources of silica exposure. text: A 30-year-old female presents with a history of weightloss, mediastinal lymphadenopathy, and pleural effusion. HRCT shows a “tree-in-bud" appearance with lung consolidation and effusion. Pleural fluid analysis reveals low ADA levels and lymphocytic predominance. What is the most likely finding on a biopsy from the lymph node?

options.C: C) Fungal Hyphae surrounded by lymphocytes

ansText: C) Fungal Hyphae surrounded by lymphocytes
expl: Explanation: The combination of: Weight loss and mediastinal lymphadenopathy Tree-in-bud pattern (suggestive of endobronchial spread of infection) Lymphocytic pleural effusion all point toward tuberculosis (especially pulmonary or lymph node TB). Even though ADA is low , this can occur in: Healed/fibrotic TB lesions , or Immunocompromised individuals (where cellular response is suppressed). Explanation of Other Options: Reactive Hyperplasia (Option A): Represents non-specific immune response of lymph nodes to infections or inflammation. Histology: Prominent germinal centers with active mitotic figures . Polyclonal B-cell proliferation. No necrosis or granuloma formation. Seen in: Viral infections (e.g., EBV, CMV) Autoimmune conditions Chronic inflammatory states Fungal Hyphae Surrounded by Lymphocytes (Option C): The "tree-in-bud" appearance and low ADA are not characteristic of fungal infections. Indicates fungal lymphadenitis (e.g., Histoplasmosis , Aspergillosis , Coccidioidomycosis ). Histology: Fungal hyphae or yeast forms within granulomas or necrotic tissue. PAS or GMS stains highlight fungal elements. Clinical features: Usually occurs in immunocompromised or HIV-positive May present with high ADA levels and neutrophilic effusion , not lymphocytic. Anthracosis Pigment (Option D): Benign finding , not associated with lymphocytic effusion, weight loss, or tree-in-bud appearance. Refers to carbon deposition in the lungs and lymph nodes from inhaled pollutants or smoke. Histology: Black carbon pigment seen within macrophages . No necrosis or granulomatous reaction. Seen in: Urban dwellers Smokers Coal workers (anthracotic lymph nodes)

text: A 72-year-old man presented with weight loss, decreased appetite, and iron deficiency anemia. Chest x-ray was done and given below. What is the diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The radiographic description of multiple, large, rounded, well-circumscribed pulmonary nodules is characteristic of "cannonball" metastases . This pattern is typical of hematogenous spread from extrapulmonary primary malignancies. The accompanying constitutional symptoms (weight loss, anorexia) and iron deficiency anemia (which could be a clue to a primary GI malignancy) support this diagnosis. The most common primary malignancies known to cause cannonball metastases in the lungs include: Mnemonic: CRESP C: Choriocarcinoma/colorectal carcinoma R: Renal cell carcinoma E: Endometrial carcinoma S: Synovial sarcoma P: Prostate carcinoma Explanation of other options: Bronchogenic carcinoma (Option B): It presents as a single dominant mass or nodule, not multiple bilateral cannonball lesions. Miliary tuberculosis (Option C): It appears as innumerable, tiny (1-2 mm) nodules distributed throughout the lungs, giving a "millet seed" appearance, not large cannonball opacities. Mesothelioma (Option D): Typically associated with pleural effusion and pleural thickening, not multiple discrete intraparenchymal nodules. Key Takeaways: "Cannonball" metastases on chest X-ray indicate hematogenous spread from an extrapulmonary primary cancer. Reference: https://radiopaedia.org/articles/cannonball-metastasis-mnemonic-1 https://radiopaedia.org/articles/cannonball-metastases-lungs

text: A 44 year old renal transplant recipient has been on prednisolone and azathioprine for several months. He has suddenly developed a cough and fevers. On investigation, he was found to have a Hb of 9 g/dl and a WCC of 3000/mm3 What is the most likely cause?
expl: Cytopenias in a renal transplant recipient is most likely due to antimetabolites used to prevent graft rejection. Azathioprine is a prodrug belonging to the class of antimetabolites, which is inactivated by Thiopurine S Methyl Transferase(TPMT). Those with two non functional TPMT will experience life threatening myelosuppression while on Azathioprine. Hence it is replaced by more effective agents. Mycofenolate mofetil is a drug which has similar mechanism of action as Azathioprine and has lesser myelosuppression. The other groups of drugs used in transplant recepients are Calcineurin Inhibitors and mTOR inhibitors. Steroids generally cause lymphocytopenia and leukocytosis. Low EPO causes low Hb, but not low total count. Pneumonia is a consequence of low count. Other ADR of Azathioprine: Hepatotoxicity Pancreatitis Alopecia GI symptoms Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 313, Pg: 2328.

text: A 46-year-old Asian woman complains of dysuria and flank discomfort. Her blood pressure is 200/100 mmHg despite taking three medications. Urine microscopy showed leukocytes and red cells, but there is no significant bacterial growth. Renal ultrasound shows two 9-cm kidneys with medullary calcification and mild hydronephrosis on the left. What is the most likely cause of this presentation?
expl: The combination of sterile pyuria, haematuria, dysuria and renal tract calcification is highly suggestive of renal TB. Glomerular granulomas develop at the time of primary infection due to haematogenous seeding. These usually heal without consequence, but may remain for many years, eventually caseating and rupturing into the tubular lumen. Granulomas then form in the renal medulla, the ureters(resulting in ureteric stricture), bladder(bladder contraction) and vas deferens. Many patients have refractory hypertension, which is renin-mediated and presumably due to segmental renal ischaemia. Reflux nephropathy refers to the scarring that develops following childhood renal infection occurring in the setting of vesicoureteric reflux. It presents in adulthood with proteinuria, hypertension and progressive renal impairment. Acute pyelonephritis presents with an acute history of high fever, rigors, nausea, vomiting and flank and/or loin pain. Urine RM shows plenty of pus cells with red blood cells and ultrasound shows edematous changes with areas of collection. Aristolochic acid has been identified as the causative agent in Chinese herb nephropathy, a condition characterised by anaemia out of proportion to the degree of renal impairment, rapid renal atrophy and fibrosis, bland urine sediment and a high incidence of GU cancer. The histological appearance and clinical course are very similar to Balkan nephropathy. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 178, Pg: 1365.

text: A 63 year old man complains of a 6 month history of lethargy, fever, weight loss, arthralgia and diarrhoea. Jejunal biopsy reveals flattened mucosa with evidence of periodic acid Schiff (PAS) positive macrophages. What is the diagnosis?
expl: The presence of PAS positive inclusions in the macrophages in a patient with chronic malnutrition, with arthralgia and fever may be either Tuberculosis or Whipple's Disease. Both of them cause PAS positive macrophages. But Mycobacterium tuberculosis is acid-fast, where as Trophyrema whipplei is non acid fast. Since the question does not mention anything about the acid fastness, we assume it to be negative. Moreover, Tuberculosis mainly affects the ileum, here jejunum is involved. This is a case of Whipple's disease . It is a chronic, multiorgan disease caused by Tropheryma whipplei - gram-positive, non-acid-fast bacillus. Most commonly occurs in middle-aged men. Classically presents with arthralgias, weight loss, diarrhea, and abdominal pain. Central nervous system and cardiac involvement is common and occur later in the disease. The intestinal lesion is also characterized by PAS-positive macrophages , that fills the lamina propria. Figure showing H and E staining of the jejunum, where the lamina propria is replaced by foamy macrophages. The PAS staining will be positive in the macrophages as shown below: Treatment is with a prolonged course of antibiotics, optimal regimen is uncertain. Penicillin + streptomycin for 2 weeks, followed by 1 year of trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st ed, Ch: 325, Pg: 2464

text: Which of the following Is the most common site of Nocardia?
expl: The most common site of dissemination is the brain. Other common sites include the skin and supporting structures, kidneys, bones, muscles, and eyes, but almost any organ can be involved. Peritonitis has been reported in patients undergoing peritoneal dialysis. Nocardiae have been recovered from blood in a few cases of pneumonia, disseminated disease, or central venous catheter infection. Nocardial endocarditis occurs rarely and can affect either native or prosthetic valves. Reference : Harrison's Principles of internal medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:174 Pg: 1337

text: Which of the following statements is false?

options.A: Neurological involvement in HUS is as common as in TTP
options.B: TTP is more common in adults and HUS in children.
options.C: Atypical HUS occurs due to dysregulation of classical complement pathway

ansText: Atypical HUS occurs due to dysregulation of classical complement pathway
expl: Atypical HUS is due to dysregulation of alternate complement pathway. Let us see the salient features of HUS: MAHA and renal impairment. Two varieties: Typical and Atypical Typical HUS: Common in children Occurs following a bloody diarrhoes. Most common causative agent is Shiga toxin producing enterohemorrhagic E.coli O157:H7. Other agent is Shigella dystentriae. Toxin binds to glycolipid surface receptor in renal microvascular endothelium and enters the endothelial cells and activates inflammatory cytokines and causes platelet activation. MAHA occurs within 1 week of bloody diarrhoea. Neurological symptoms are as common as in TTP. Fever is typically absent. Streptococcus pneumonia produce neuraminidase that cleaves Thompson Friedenreich Antigen on platelets and endothelium. This is a cryptic antigen, which is recognized by IgM and causes MAHA. Atypical HUS : Occurs due to defect in alternate complement pathway. Factor H deficiency is the most common cause-inherited. Factor H inhibits the activation of Alternate pathway C3 convertase, in the absence of factor H, there will be dysregulated activation of the alternate complement pathway. C3 will be low and C4 will be normal. Autoantibody to factor H results in a specific type of atypical HUS called DEAP HUS. It is very severe and causes ESRD. Reference: Harrisons Principles of Internal medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 317, Pg:2364-2365.

text: A 22-year-old lady recently returned from a holiday in Malta was admitted with a 3 day history of fever, generalised lymphadenopathy and a macular rash over the trunk and legs. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis.
expl: Among the given options the most likely diagnosis is IMN, considering the age and the travel history. Familial Mediterranean fever should have recurrent history of fever. Tuberculosis is a chronic infection with a more prolonged course. There is nothing to suggest a sarcoidosis like mediatinal adenopathy and the duration is short. Infectious Mononucleosis occurs most commonly in adolescents and young adults. Clinical features occur after a 2-5 week incubation period and include fever, malaise, pharyngitis, and lymphadenopathy. text: Which of the following statements regarding the lung manifestation of SSc is false?

options.A: Pulmonary complications account for the most important cause of death in patients with SSc
options.B: New onset ILD can occur in patients with long standing ILD
options.C: Esophageal dilation with severe efflux is an important risk factor governing the development and progression of ILD
options.D: The incidence of lung cancer is high in patients with SSc

ansText: New onset ILD can occur in patients with long standing ILD
expl: ILD and other organ involvement occurs within the first few years of diagnosing SSc, especially during the edematous phase of skin disease. Skin involvement reaches a plateau after around 4 years of onset of symptoms, even after which, visceral involvement can progress. New onset ILD, occurring late in the course is very rare. Pulmonary complications are major cause of mortality in patients with SSc. Esophageal dialation with sever reflux is an important risk factor for developing ILD. The incidence of lung cancer is high in patients with SSc. Mycofenolate mofetil and Cyclophosphamide are used in the treatment of ILD. Reference : Harrison's principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 361, Pg:2780-2786

text: A 55 year old farmer has had progressive breathlessness over the past 2 years. He presents with a severe episode of dyspnea and productive cough which occurred 6 hours after he started working. He mentions that these episodes are typical but today is more severe. On admission, his O2 saturations are 94% on air. CXR shows bilateral interstitial shadowing in upper zones. Which of the following is the most useful test?
expl: This patient is likely to have extrinsic allergic alveolitis. The classic presentation of farmer's lung results from inhalational exposure to thermophilic Actinomyces species. Patients with extrinsic allergic alveolitis may present acutely with a flulike illness with cough. They can also present sub acutely with recurrent pneumonia or chronically with exertional dyspnoea, productive cough, and weight loss. The onset of symptoms after acute exposure is usually between 4 and 12 hours . Some antigens provoke symptoms after repeated exposure; these include bio aerosols of microbial or animal antigens and a few reactive chemicals. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 288, Pg: 2161

text: A 40 year male presents with a 6 month history of intermittent haemoptysis. He describes episodes of cutaneous flushing, which typically affects the head and neck. The episodes are often associated with an unpleasant warm feeling, itching feeling. They last for half an hour. He is slightly breathless but has had no evidence of leg swelling or chest pain. He smokes 10 cigarettes a day. He has lost 3 kg of weight in the past two months and has been experiencing night sweats. A Chest x ray shows sail sign in the left lower lobe, but no visible consolidation. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: A sail sign on the CXR indicates collapse of the left lower lobe. The likely diagnosis is a carcinoid tumour, which is associated with smoking. An early and frequent (94%) symptom of carcinoid tumours is cutaneous flushing, which typically affects the head and neck. Episodes are often associated with an unpleasant warm feeling, itching, palpitation, upper-body erythema and edema, salivation, diaphoresis, lacrimation, and diarrhea. Exercise, stress, or certain foods (eg, cheese) may trigger an attack. Initial attacks are short, lasting only a few minutes. With time, the duration increases to hours. Flushes are reported to be longest in association with bronchial carcinoids. Carcinoid tumours are neuroendocrine tumours arising from Kulchitsky cells. They can be central or peripheral, and are classified as typical or atypical depending on their histology. They are slow growing tumours of the lung with a peak incidence around age 40. Bronchial obstruction is common. Diagnosis is by bronchoscopy and biopsy. Treatment is usually with lobectomy. Sail sign (straight line around the heart border) Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch: 84 Pg 669

text: A physician is evaluating a patient for an occupational disease and finds that a coproporphyrin test has been performed. Which of the following conditions is most likely suspected?
expl: Explanation of answer: Lead poisoning disrupts heme biosynthesis, resulting in elevated urinary coproporphyrin , making it a key diagnostic clue. Lead poisoning, particularly from occupational exposure, interferes with heme synthesis by inhibiting several key enzymes such as δ-aminolevulinic acid dehydratase (ALAD) and ferrochelatase, leading to accumulation of heme precursors including coproporphyrin and δ-ALA (aminolevulinic acid) in the urine. Investigations in Lead Poisoning: Blood Findings: Microcytic hypochromic anemia Basophilic stippling of RBCs Cabot rings ↑ Zinc protoporphyrin (ZnPP) ↑ Free erythrocyte protoporphyrin (FEP) ↑ Blood lead levels (>5 µg/dL is significant; >40 µg/dL may show symptoms) Urine Findings: ↑ Urinary ALA (>5 µg/L) ↑ Urinary coproporphyrin (>150 µg/L) ↑ Urinary lead (>0.25 mg/L) Radiological Findings (especially in children): "Lead lines" (dense metaphyseal bands) seen at long bone metaphyses due to inhibited osteoclastic activity. Special Tests: Calcium disodium EDTA mobilization test (especially in children) to assess response to chelation therapy. Pathophysiology of Coproporphyrin Elevation: Lead inhibits the enzymes involved in the conversion of porphyrin precursors to heme, including: δ-ALA dehydratase Ferrochelatase This leads to an accumulation of porphyrin intermediates like coproporphyrin and ALA, which are excreted in urine and used diagnostically. Explanation of other options: Berylliosis (Option B): Occupational granulomatous lung disease due to beryllium exposure. Diagnosed via imaging and lung biopsy, not associated with porphyrin abnormalities. Silicosis (Option C): Caused by inhalation of silica dust leading to nodular pulmonary fibrosis. Diagnosis is based on chest imaging and history of exposure, not urinary porphyrin tests. Asbestosis (Option D): Chronic interstitial lung disease from asbestos exposure. Diagnosed via imaging (e.g., pleural plaques on X-ray/CT), not via heme biosynthesis markers.

expl: The painful red lesions that are not responding to antibiotics may indicate Erythema nodosum. text: A group of friends went to a bar and consumed alcohol. Later, they were involved in a physical altercation, during which one individual was punched in the chest. After dinner, he developed difficulty breathing. On examination, there are absent breath sounds on one side and hyperresonance to percussion. A chest X-ray shows tracheal deviation. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The most likely diagnosis in this case, where a person was punched in the chest, presented with difficulty breathing, and shows physical findings of absent breath sounds on one side, hyperresonance on percussion, and tracheal deviation on a chest X-ray, Tension pneumothorax . Tension pneumothorax occurs when air enters the pleural space and cannot escape, leading to increased pressure in the chest. This pressure pushes on the lung, causing it to collapse, and can also shift the trachea and other mediastinal structures to the opposite side (tracheal deviation), which is life-threatening due to impaired venous return to the heart and decreased cardiac output. Key Indicators for Tension Pneumothorax : Absent breath sounds and hyperresonance : Indicates air in the pleural space with no lung sounds in the affected area. Tracheal deviation : Suggests significant pressure buildup that is shifting mediastinal structures. Acute onset after trauma : The history of being punched in the chest directly relates to the likelihood of a traumatic pneumothorax that progressed to tension pneumothorax. Explanation of other options: Traumatic Pneumothorax (Option A): Traumatic pneumothorax presents with absent breath sounds and hyperresonance but does not cause tracheal deviation or hemodynamic instability. The presence of tracheal deviation indicates progression to tension pneumothorax, making it the better answer. Hemothorax (Option C): Dullness to percussion (due to blood in pleural space) is seen in hemothorax, whereas this patient has hyperresonance. Hemothorax is also associated with hypovolemia and shock due to blood loss. Pulmonary Contusion (Option D): Pulmonary contusion results in alveolar hemorrhage and presents with crackles, not absent breath sounds. Chest X-ray would show patchy lung opacities instead of hyperresonance or tracheal deviation. Key Takeaways: Tension pneumothorax is a life-threatening emergency caused by progressive air trapping in the pleural space, leading to tracheal deviation, absent breath sounds, and hyperresonance. Immediate needle decompression is required.

text: A 40 year old woman presents with breathlessness, cough and fever. On examination, she has basal crackles in the lung fields. Circulating precipitins to Micropolyspora faeni are positive. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Farmer's lung is the most common type of hypersensitivity pneumonitis. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis, also known as extrinsic allergic alveolitis, is associated with intense or repeated exposure to inhaled biologic dusts. The classic presentation of farmer's lung results from inhalational exposure to thermophilic Actinomyces species and occasionally from exposure to various Aspergillus species. Acute farmer's lung develops after large exposure to mouldy hay or contaminated compost. Symptoms often spontaneously resolve within 12 hours to days if antigen exposure is eliminated or avoided. It manifests as new onset of fever, chills, non-productive cough, chest tightness, dyspnoea, headache, and malaise. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition, Ch:288, Pg-2160

text: An 18-year-old male has had a 5-year history of renal failure. On examination, he had, maculopapular rashes, erythema nodosum, arthritis, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly. Chest X-ray shows hilar adenopathy. A renal biopsy specimen revealed tubulointerstitial nephritis and non-caseating granulomatous lesions. What is the diagnosis?
expl: The question deals with multi system involvement with non caseating or naked granulomas, which is classical of Sarcoidosis. Sarcoidosis is a chronic, multi-system granulomatous disorder of unknown etiology characterized by non-caseating granulomas. The most commonly affected organ is the lung, other organs include the lymph nodes, skin, eyes, parotid glands, bones, joints, liver and kidney. Patients mostly present with respiratory symptoms or joint and skin manifestations. Renal involvement and presentation with renal failure are relatively rare in sarcoidosis. Renal sarcoidosis is reported to have three categories: Renal changes by abnormal calcium metabolism(Most common cause of renal impairment in Sarcoidosis), Interstitial nephritis or granulomatous nephritis or granulomatous nephritis and Glomerulonephritis(mostly membranous). Option A: Wegener's granulomatosis also involves lungs in the form of pulmonary infiltrates or nodules along with upper respiratory involvement. Hilar adenopathy is not seen. Cutaneous nodules and arthritis can also be seen, but hepatosplenomegaly has not been desribed. But the biopsy reveals necrotizing granulomas. Option B: lupus nephritis may cause an overlap of nephrotic and nephritic syndrome and may have a maculopapular rash esp. on the face(butterfly distribution) Option C: Renal tuberculosis can occur as a late complication to primary TB and thus have hilar adenopathy, but causes caseating granulomas. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal medicine, 21 st edition, Ch:367 Pg:2833

text: Which of the following is elevated in liver abscess except
expl: Diagnostic studies of the abdomen, especially the right upper quadrant, should be a part of any workup for fever of unknown origin. The single most reliable laboratory finding is an elevated serum concentration of alkaline phosphatase , which is documented in 70% of patients with liver abscesses. 50% of patients have elevated serum levels of bilirubin , and 48% have elevated concentrations of aspartate aminotransferase . Concomitant bacteremia is found in one-third to one-half of patients. text: Which of the following is a recognised treatment for complications of cystic fibrosis?

options.A: DNAase to assist in reinflating collapsed lung segments.
options.B: Rectal pull-through and anastamosis for rectal prolapse.
options.D: Nebulised tobramycin for pseudomonas colonisation of the lower respiratory tract.

ansText: Nebulised tobramycin for pseudomonas colonisation of the lower respiratory tract.
expl: Outpatient regimens for cystic fibrosis management include: Exogenous pancreatic enzymes taken with meals Nutritional supplementation Anti-inflammatory medication Bronchodilators Chronic or periodic administration of oral or aerosolized antibiotics (e.g., as maintenance therapy for patients with p. Aeruginosa). Recombinant dnase aerosols (degrade dna strands that contribute to mucus viscosity) and nebulized hypertonic saline (serves to augment pcl depth, activate mucociliary clearance, and mobilize inspissated airway secretions) are administered routinely. Chest physiotherapy several times each day is a standard means to promote clearance of airway mucus. Among adults with cf, malabsorption, chronic inflammation, and endocrine abnormalities can lead to poor bone mineralization, requiring treatment with vitamin d, calcium, and other measures Rectal prolapse is usually idiopathic, occurring between 1 and 5 years. Intestinal parasites, malnutrition, acute diarrhoea, ulcerative colitis, pertussis, Ehlers Danlos Syndrome, meningocele, cystic fibrosis, and chronic constipation can also predispose to it. Following defecation the prolapse usually resolves spontaneously, or through manual reinsertion by the patient or parent. text: A 26 year old woman with cystic fibrosis presents with abdominal pain. The abdominal pain is colicky and localized in the lower abdomen. On examination, she has pyrexia and tachycardia. Her abdomen was distended. There was guarding and bowel sounds were present. Which of the following is likely to be the cause?
expl: Meconium Ileus is the earliest clinical manifestation of cystic fibrosis (CF) and occurs in approximately 16% of patients with CF. Contents of the intestinal lumen are often difficult to excrete, leading to meconium ileus (a presentation in 10–20% of newborns with CF) or distal intestinal obstructive syndrome in older individual. Signs of peritonitis include tenderness, abdominal wall edema, distension, and clinical evidence of sepsis. A palpable mass may indicate pseudocyst formation. Surgical exploration is indicated for patients with progressive distension, signs of peritonitis, or clinical deterioration. Complicated Meconium Ileus requires resection more often than simple cases and always requires temporary stomas. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:291 Pg: 2176

text: A 63 year old woman has recently been treated with amoxycillin for a tooth abscess. Since then, she has developed diarrhea up to 15 times a day. There is blood in the stools.Her Hb is 13 g/dl, WCC 13 x 10^9/l, platelets 500 x 10^9/L. Her CRP is 80 mg/l. What is the likely infective organism?
expl: In a patient who has recently had antibiotics, Clostridium difficile is the most likely infective organism. Clindamycin, ampicillin, and cephalosporins are the implicated drugs. Discontinuation of the offending antibiotic is important (not always easy if an infection such as a dental abscess persists). Oral administration of fidaxomicin or vancomycin is the treatment. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 134, Pg: 1068

expl: The lesion given in the figure depicts a boggy swelling of the scalp with pustules and scarring alopecia, characteristic of Kerion. They are usually found on the face, neck, or trunk and are slow-growing and painless. They may have a blackhead plugging the central opening and can leak a thick, cheesy substance if ruptured or removed. They don't typically require treatment unless they become painful or infected. Abscess : An abscess is a painful, red, swollen infection filled with pus. It can form on the skin or inside the body. Abscesses are usually caused by bacteria and can cause symptoms elsewhere in the body. Unlike cysts, which grow slowly, an abscess can appear quickly and is often accompanied by fever or other systemic symptoms2. Folliculitis : This is the inflammation of hair follicles on the skin. It appears as small, red bumps that may have a white, pus-filled tip. Folliculitis can be itchy or irritating and is often caused by bacterial infection, although it can also result from fungal infections, irritation, or physical injury to the hair follicles.

text: Which of the typhoidal salmonella is most likely to cause pyogenic abscess formation during enteric fever?
expl: Explanation: Among the typhoidal Salmonellae, Salmonella Paratyphi C (also known as Salmonella Hirschfeld ) is the serotype most likely to cause pyogenic abscess formation . While S. Typhi , S. Paratyphi A , and S. Paratyphi B classically present with enteric fever (systemic febrile illness with gastrointestinal symptoms), S. Paratyphi C often presents as a septicemia with a high tendency for suppurative complications (metastatic abscesses in organs like the liver, spleen, or bones). In this regard, it behaves clinically more like the invasive non-typhoidal Salmonellae (e.g., S. Choleraesuis ) than the other typhoidal strains. Explanation of Other Options: (A), (B), (C): S. Typhi, S. Paratyphi A, and S. Paratyphi B are the primary agents of classic Enteric Fever. While they can rarely cause abscesses (usually in patients with pre-existing structural abnormalities like cholelithiasis or tumors), it is not their defining clinical characteristic compared to S. Paratyphi C .

text: Which membrane channel is mainly affected in Cystic fibrosis?
expl: Explanation: Cystic fibrosis is caused by a defect in the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) protein, which functions as a chloride and bicarbonate channel located in apical plasma membranes. (Option A,B and D) The most common mutation, F508del, involves the deletion of a phenylalanine residue. This defect leads to depleted airway surface liquid and impaired mucociliary clearance, resulting in the accumulation of thick mucus. These airway changes create an environment prone to chronic bacterial colonization, particularly by pathogens such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Staphylococcus aureus. The persistent infection and inflammation drive progressive bronchiectasis and recurrent pneumonia, causing ongoing lung damage and necessitating aggressive antibiotic therapy.

ansText: Suspected bacteremia is not a contraindication to LP.
expl: It is contraindicated in patients with a suspected spinal epidural abscess. Suspected bacteremia is NOT a contraindication to LP. text: Human to human transmission of nontuberculous mycobacteria infection occurs almost exclusively in patients with:
expl: NTM are ubiquitous in soil and water. Specific organisms have recurring niches, such as M. simiae in certain aquifers, M. fortuitum in pedicure baths, and M. immunogenum in metalworking fluids. text: Hemoglobinopathies are
expl: Hemoglobinopathies are autosomal codominant traits-thus, compound heterozygotes who inherit a different abnormal mutant allele from each parent exhibit composite features of each. For example, patients inheriting sickle β thalassemia exhibit features of β thalassemia and sickle cell anemia. The α chain is present in HbA, HbA2 and HbF; α-chain mutations thus cause abnormalities in all three. The α-globin hemoglobinopathies are symptomatic in utero and after birth because normal function of the α-globin gene is required throughout gestation and adult life. In contrast, infants with β-globin hemoglobinopathies tend to be asymptomatic until 3-9 months of age, when HbA has largely replaced HbF. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 98, Pg: 755

text: Which of the following is the most preferred modality for assessing myocardial viability?

ansText: Stunning is a state of depressed myocardial function due to chronic hypoperfusion
expl: Myocardial stunning represents prolonged myocardial dysfunction that follows a brief episode of severe ischemia , with gradual return of contractile activity. Conversely, Myocardial hibernation is the term applied to myocardial dysfunction resulting from chronic hypoperfusion . Myocardial stunning affects both systolic and diastolic function and may occur in globally as well as regionally ischemic myocardium. Clinically, stunning is most frequently seen in patients recovering from ischemic arrest during cardiopulmonary bypass. 3 mechanisms of myocardial stunning: Generation of oxygen-derived free radicals, Calcium overload, and Reduced sensitivity of myofilaments to calcium. text: A 42-year-old smoker has the following pulmonary function test (PFT) results: FEV1/FVC: 0.62, FVC: 60% and RV/TLC: 142%. Which of the following best describes the underlying abnormality?
expl: Explanation: The given scenario of a patient with FEV1/FVC: 0.62, FVC: 60% and RV/TLC: 142% signifies Obstructive Lung Disease, which will lead to trapping of air with hyperinflation of lungs.Chronic smoking causes persistent airway inflammation and destruction of lung tissue, producing air trapping and progressive hyperinflation . These changes elevate residual volume (RV) and total lung capacity (TLC) , so the RV/TLC ratio rises . During ordinary breathing, the thorax remains hyperinflated; this actually helps maintain expiratory flow because the increased lung volume enhances elastic recoil and slightly widens the airways, lowering resistance. When lung volumes are measured: A maximal inhalation to total lung capacity , followed by a forceful, complete exhalation, provides the forced vital capacity (FVC) . The amount of air expelled in the first second of that maneuver is the forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV 1 ) . In obstructive diseases , both FEV 1 and FVC fall, but FEV 1 declines disproportionately , producing a reduced FEV 1 /FVC ratio . Abbreviations: FVC - Forced Vital Capacity FEV1 - Forced Expiratory Volume in 1 second FEF 25-75 - Forced Expiratory Flow at 25-75% vital capacity TLC - Total Lung Capacity RV - Residual Volume DLCO - Diffusion capacity of lung for Carbon Monoxide Explanation for other Options: Restrictive lung disease (Option A): Characterized by low TLC and normal or high FEV 1 /FVC ratio . Reduced lung compliance (Option B): Seen in interstitial lung disease or pulmonary fibrosis, which cause stiff lungs and a restrictive pattern (low TLC, normal/high ratio). Age-related change (Option D): Ageing causes a slight decline in FEV 1 and can mildly increase RV, but it does not reduce FEV 1 /FVC to 0.62 or raise RV/TLC to 142 % , which are clearly pathologic. text: A 32-year-old man is admitted to hospital with a history of breathlessness of 4-6 weeks duration. He initially had flu-like symptoms and was treated by his doctor with a 5-day course of amoxicillin. However, he then started coughing up blood, leading to urgent referral. expl: The clinical picture of pulmonary and renal involvement is typical of Good pasture’s syndrome. text: A 30 year old man is admitted with a history of haemoptysis, cough and dyspnoea. He has been previously fit and has smoked 25 cigarettes a day for the last 10 years. A chest XRay shows diffuse alveolar infiltrates. He has a microcytic, hypochromic anaemia, urine dipstick confirms haematuria and proteinuria. His lung function tests showed a normal spirometry and a DLCO of 125% predicted.What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Good pasture’s syndrome is characterised by diffuse alveolar haemorrhage and glomerulitis. Men are commonly affected with most cases occurring between the ages of 20-30 years. It is more likely to occur in smokers. The anti-glomerular basement antibody (Anti-GBM) is present in up to 90% of the patients. Renal histology usually shows a focal segmental necrotizing glomerulitis with crescent formation. The DLCO is increased during active bleeding and can be used to monitor disease activity. An increase above 30% of baseline is suggestive of an intra-alveolar bleed. Causes of increased DLCO: Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage (Eg, Goodpasture syndrome) Asthma Polycythemia Obesity Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch:285,314, Pg: 2139,2335

text: A 70 year old man presents with a chronic cough. He is a heavy smoker of over 40 cigarettes a day. CXR shows a peripheral right-sided lesion. A biopsy which was taken shows squamous cell carcinoma. No regional lymph nodes are involved. Lung function tests show a FEV1 of less than 1.5 litres. The recommended treatment is:
expl: Although surgical treatment is possible in non small cell lung carcinoma, a FEV1 of less than 1.5 litres contraindicates surgery. Hence, radiotherapy is recommended. Surgical resection, ideally by an experienced thoracic surgeon, is the treatment of choice for patients with clinical stage I and II NSCLC who are able to tolerate the procedure. In patients with stage I NSCLC, lobectomy is the preferred procedure. In patients with comorbidities, compromised pulmonary reserve, and small peripheral lesions, a limited resection, wedge resection, or segmentectomy (potentially by video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery) may be reasonable surgical options. Pneumonectomy is reserved for patients with central tumors and should be performed only in patients with excellent pulmonary reserve. Patients with a FEV1 > 2 L or > 80% of predicted can tolerate pneumonectomy those with an FEV1 > 1.5 L have adequate reserve for a lobectomy Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch:78 Pg 602

text: In restrictive lung disease due to respiratory muscle weakness, which of the following statements is true?

options.C: Low VC, low FEV1, normal TLC, low RV/TLC
options.D: Low VC, low TLC, high RV/TLC

ansText: Low VC, low TLC, high RV/TLC
expl: The lung itself can function normally yet muscle weakness will result in grossly low lung volumes including FEV1, FVC and TLC. However residual volume will be relatively high as a consequence of this weakness. Consequently, RV/TLC will be elevated. However the transfer of carbon monoxide (TCO) will be unaffected. text: Which ONE of the following is correct regarding severe bullous emphysema:

options.A: Helium dilution is more accurate than body plethysmography in measuring residual volume.
options.B: Hypoxaemia at rest will improve with exercise.
options.D: The carbon monoxide transfer factor is reduced.

ansText: The carbon monoxide transfer factor is reduced.
expl: Whole body plethysmography also measures trapped gas i.e. intrathoracic gas (including within bullae and other poorly ventilated areas) which barely communicates with the airway. Standard gas-dilution measures gas that communicates with the airway. Mixing in helium dilution is more difficult in airways obstruction requiring multi breath methods lasting 5 minutes rather than single breath test. Exertion will exacerbate breathlessness and hypoxia. The characteristic changes of severe emphysema are increase in static compliance and reduction in lung recoil pressure. Loss of lung recoil causes a reduction of alveolar pressure (elastic recoil pressure of lung + pleural pressure) leading to collapse of peripheral airways on expiration. Emphysematous patients purse their lips in expiration to increase airway pressure to prevent this collapse. CO transfer factor is reduced. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: Ch: 285 Pg:2139

text: A 40 year old man has a 2 year history of increasing shortness of breath. This is worse with exertion e.g. climbing the stairs at home and is even slightly so at rest. He is a non-smoker. On examination, his pulse is 95 beats/min and his blood pressure is 140/95 mmHg. He has finger clubbing and a crackling noise at the end of inspiration over the bases of the lungs. There was no ankle oedema Lung function tests show :FVC 2.5 L (predicted 3.2 )FEV1 2.1 L (predicted 2.4)FEV1 % 76% (predicted 75%)Diffusing Capacity: Gas Transfer Factor for carbon monoxide: DLCO 17 ml/min/mmHg (predicted:25 ml/min/mm Hg)Which one of the following diagnoses is likely?
expl: A reduced FVC, with normal FEV1, FEV1% and PEF usually indicates restriction of lung volume. KCO (transfer factor) is also reduced in fibrotic lung disease, as in this case. The additional findings of inspirational crackles and clubbing suggests the diagnosis of cryptogenic fibrosing alveolitis. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:285 Pg: 2138

text: A 22 year old female patient presents with a 5-day history of ascending muscle weakness in both hands and feet. EMGs confirm acute demyelinating sensory and motor neuropathy. What treatment should be started?
expl: The diagnosis is Guillain Barre syndrome . It is preceded by diarrhea (e.g. campylobacter) or chest infections (e.g. mycoplasma) in two thirds of cases. Autonomic dysfunction and hyporeflexia are associated. P rogressive symmetric ascending weakness is characteristic . Management: Plasma exchange (OR) IVIG (IV immunoglobulins) - 2 g/kg/day for 5 days. As effective as plasma exchange. Easier to administer and fewer side effects. No benefit in combining both treatments. Steroids and immunosuppressants have not been shown to be beneficial. Regular FVC (Forced vital capacity ) to monitor respiratory function and assess need for ventilation. ICU admission is recommended when FVC is less than 20 mL/kg and intubation is recommended in most cases when FVC is less than 15 mL/kg . Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 ST Ed, Ch: 447, Pg: 3503

text: Which of the following is preserved in locked in state?
expl: A “locked-in” state of preserved consciousness with quadriplegia and cranial nerve signs suggests complete pontine and lower midbrain infarction. It occurs secondary to basilar artery damage. Bilateral Corticospinal damage leads Quadriplegia Bilateral Corticobulbar damage to 3rd, 4th 6th and 7th nerves leads to loss of horizontal gaze, facial diplegia. Bilateral Corticobulbar damage to nerves leads to aphonia and tongue paralysis Brain stem damage leads to loss of respiratory function. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition, chapter 426 page number. 3332

text: Which of the following organ systems is used to define organ failure in acute pancreatitis
expl: Three organ systems should be assessed to define organ failure: respiratory, cardiovascular, and renal. Organ failure is defined as a score of 2 or more for one of these three organ systems using the modified Marshall scoring system. Persistent organ failure (>48 h) is the most important clinical finding regarding severity of the acute pancreatitis episode . Organ failure that affects more than one organ is considered multisystem organ failure CT imaging is usually not needed or recommended during the first 48 h of admission in acute pancreatitis. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine 21st ed chap 348, pg. 2661

text: A 2D.year-old female complaining of acute onset of palpitations. She is attached to a cardiac monitor and her pulse rate is 180 bpm. She is warm and well perfused, her BP is 135/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, oxygen saturation 100% on air and on auscultation her chest is clear with no evidence of cardiac failure. ECG shows a narrow complex tachycardia. Carotid massage and Valsalva manoeuvre have failed to attenuate the rhythm disturbance What is the appropriate initial management?
expl: This patient has a narrow complex supraventricular tachycardia. From history and examination she is not hemodynamically compromised and, therefore, initial management would be IV adenosine in the absence of contraindication (e.g. asthma) in order to create a transient conduction delay. This may terminate the tachycardia, or cause a slowing in rate to allow identification of the underlying rhythm, to guide optimal antiarrhythmic therapy. If the patient had chest pain, hypotension, SBP Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 20 th edition, chapter:244 page number:1742,1743; 21st Ed fig 249-6

text: A 40-year-old male presents with epigastric pain radiating to the back for the past 5 days. He gives a history of heavy alcohol consumption. Blood investigations reveal amylase and lipase levels elevated five times the upper limit of normal. He received 2 liters of intravenous saline in the last 24 hours. Chest X-ray is shown below: Based on the clinical and radiological findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation of answer: Chest X-ray shows diffuse bilateral lung opacities. Acute pancreatitis can lead to non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema (ARDS) due to systemic inflammation and capillary leakage, seen as bilateral diffuse infiltrates on chest X-ray. This patient has acute pancreatitis, likely alcohol-induced, with classical symptoms (epigastric pain radiating to the back) and elevated amylase/lipase. The chest X-ray shows diffuse bilateral opacities, which, in the setting of acute pancreatitis, are most consistent with non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema, specifically acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). Mechanism: Acute pancreatitis leads to systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS). Inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6, IL-8) increase capillary permeability in pulmonary vasculature. This leads to protein-rich alveolar edema, not caused by heart failure - hence non-cardiogenic. ARDS is a known complication of pancreatitis. Berlin Definition of ARDS: Timing: Within 1 week of a known insult (e.g., pancreatitis) Chest imaging: Bilateral opacities Origin: Not explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload Oxygenation: PaO2/FiO2 ratio used to classify severity Management: Supportive care with lung-protective ventilation Conservative fluid management Prone positioning, high PEEP in moderate/severe cases Avoid overhydration, which can worsen pulmonary edema Management according to grade of ARDS Explanation of other options: Aspiration pneumonia (Option A): Typically causes localized infiltrates (often in the right lower lobe) with a history of vomiting, altered sensorium, or seizures. It doesn't match the diffuse bilateral opacities seen here. Miliary tuberculosis (Option C): Presents with tiny, uniform nodules ("millet seed" pattern) and systemic features like fever, weight loss, night sweats. It's a chronic illness, not acute, and unrelated to acute pancreatitis. Bilateral pulmonary embolism (Option D): Presents with acute dyspnea, chest pain, hypoxia, and possibly clear chest X-ray (may show Westermark sign or Hampton's hump, rarely bilateral infiltrates). PE is not typically associated with pancreatitis or diffuse infiltrates. Reference: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7997862/

text: Which of the following is not an indication of Non-Invasive Ventilation?
expl: It has been observed that patient intolerance is the major limitation in widespread application of non-invasive ventilation because it can result in both physical and psychological discomfort. In addition, NIV has had limited success in patients with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure, for whom endotracheal intubation and conventional MV remain the ventilatory method of choice. The most common reasons for instituting MV are: acute respiratory failure with hypoxemia (acute respiratory distress syndrome, heart failure with pulmonary edema, pneumonia, sepsis, complications of surgery and trauma), which accounts for ~65% of all ventilated cases hypercarbic ventilatory failure—e.g., due to coma (15%), exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD; 13%), and neuromuscular diseases (5%) Reference: Harrison 20 th chap 295 pg. 2035

text: A 19-year-old girl is short in stature for her age. She has not shown any changes of puberty. She has a webbed neck. Her vital signs include - Temperature 36.6oC, Respiratory rate 18/min. Pulse 78 bpm and BP 160/86 mmHg. On physical examination, she has a continuous murmur heard over both the front of the chest as well as her back. Her lower extremities are cool with poor capillary filling. A chest radiograph reveals a prominent left heart border, no oedema or effusions, and rib notching. Which of the following pathologic lesions best explains these findings?

options.A: Constriction of the aorta past the ductus arteriosus
options.B: Lack of development of the spiral septum and partial absence of conus musculature
options.C: Shortening and thickening of chordae tendineae of the mitral valve

ansText: Constriction of the aorta past the ductus arteriosus
expl: This patient with Turner's syndrome has coarctation of the aorta , and the constriction is postductal , allowing prolonged survival. Turner's syndrome (45,X0) It is caused by either the presence of only one sex chromosome (X) or a deletion of the short arm of one of the X chromosomes. Features - Short stature Shield chest, widely spaced nipples Webbed neck Cardiac defects: bicuspid aortic valve (15%), coarctation of the aorta (5-10%) Primary amenorrhoea Associated absent uterus and streak ovaries Cystic hygroma (often diagnosed prenatally) High-arched palate Short fourth metacarpal Multiple pigmented naevi Keloid scars Lymphoedema in neonates (especially feet) Horseshoe kidney is strongly associated with Turner's syndrome. Associated conditions - Autoimmune diseases - Autoimmune thyroiditis (Hypothyroidism is much more common), Crohn's disease Hypertension is quite common and is typically idiopathic (essential hypertension). In a small proportion cause can include coarctation of the aorta and renal dysfunction due to horse-shoe kidney. Metabolic abnormalities (dyslipidaemia and glucose intolerance) Recurrent otitis media Diagnosis is made by karyotype identification of 45X0. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 20 th edition, ch:264,383 pg:1837,2763,2764

text: A 60 year old man has been a smoker of 20 a day for 30 years. He has a cough and difficulty in breathing for 3 days which has worsened and he presents to hospital. He has home nebulisers but not home oxygen. On examination, his oxygen saturations are 95%, blood pressure 110 / 60 mmHg and respiratory rate 32. He has diffuse wheezes and is using his respiratory muscles. Arterial blood gases done on 6 litres of oxygen show : pH 7.25 pO2 120 mmhgpCO2 61.5 mmhgWhat should be the next management step?
expl: This man with Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) has blood gases showing type II respiratory failure with acidosis. He has been placed on 6 litres of oxygen, which is too much for a patient with severe COPD as the history of home nebuliser use suggests. His respiratory drive is suppressed by too much oxygen inspired, which may explain the increase in pCO2 and hence reduction to a lower concentration (e.g. 1 - 2 litres) to maintain a pO2 above 65 mmhg is recommended Or spO2 >90%. If that does not improve the pCO2, Non Invasive Ventilation may be required in the absence of hemodynamic instability. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:292 Pg:2189

text: Insensible water loss per day is ?
expl: Ans. C. 700 ml Insensible water loss- There is continuous loss of water by evaporation from respiratory tract and diffusion through the skin, which together accounts 700 ml/day of water loss under normal conditions. The insensible water loss from skin (diffusion through skin) occurs independently of sweating and accounts 350 ml ofwater loss per day. So, in the absence of sweating, water loss from the skin is 350 ml/day

text: Which of the following is a cause of type 2 respiratory failure?
expl: Any pathological process which affects the gas exchange at the level of alveoli will cause type 1 respiratory failure. These include causes of acute respiratory distress syndrome like: Pneumonia Sepsis Multiple blood transfusions Near drowning Pancreatitis Aspiration pneumonitis Type 2 respiratory failure is caused by any process which impairs entry of air into lungs. This includes: Central causes: Cerebrovascular stroke causing brain stem injury drug overdose sleep-disordered breathing severe hypothyroidism. Peripheral causes Nerve: GBS, phrenic nerve injury Neuromuscular junction: myasthenic crisis Muscle: muscle dystrophies Pleural effusion Reference: Harrison's principles of internal medicine 20th Ed pg. 2026

text: Which of the following conditions leads to type 3 respiratory failure?
expl: Type 3 respiratory failure results from lung atelectasis. Because atelectasis occurs so commonly in the perioperative period, this form is also called perioperative respiratory failure . After general anesthesia, decreases in functional residual capacity lead to collapse of dependent lung units. Such atelectasis can be treated by frequent changes in position, chest physiotherapy, upright positioning, and control of incisional and/or abdominal pain. Noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation may also be used to reverse regional atelectasis. Option A: shock causes hypoperfusion of respiratory muscles which leads to type 4 respiratory failure Option B: ARDS causes type 1 respiratory failure Reference: Harrison's principles of internal medicine 20th Ed pg. 2026
