text: A 60-year old patient was involved in a car accident and sustained multiple fractures. He had been in the ICU and not long before, there was a suspicion of severe respiratory distress syndrome. Which of these would help to confirm the diagnosis?
expl: Respiratory distress syndrome can be caused by severe trauma, smoke inhalation, multiple blood transfusions, drowning and aspiration, and drugs such as salicylates and narcotics. A chest XR would show bilateral infiltrates, and the presentation mimics heart failure. Hence, the best test would be PCWP, which would be normal (4 to 12 mm hg). Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page Number-2226.

text: A critically ill patient with ARDS due to COVID-19 is admitted to the ICU and has PaO2/FiO2 of 100. Which among the following is the ideal ventilator setting?

options.A: High PEEP and high tidal volume
options.B: Low PEEP and low tidal volume
options.C: Low PEEP and high tidal volume
options.D: High PEEP and low tidal volume

ansText: High PEEP and low tidal volume
expl: Explanation: For severe ARDS (PaO2/FiO2 ≤100), lung-protective ventilation with low tidal volume (6ml/kg ideal body weight) and high PEEP is recommended. By increasing lung volume and improving alveolar recruitment, PEEP reduces the transpulmonary pressure required to inflate the lungs, hence reducing the work of breathing. High PEEP helps prevent alveolar collapse and improves oxygenation, while low tidal volume minimizes ventilator-induced lung injury by reducing volutrauma and barotrauma. PEEP increases FRC and reduces the work of breathing. This approach improves outcomes in patients with severe hypoxemia and is endorsed by current ARDS and COVID-19 critical care guidelines. Explanation of Incorrect Options: High PEEP and high tidal volume (Option A): Increases risk of ventilator-induced lung injury due to overdistension (volutrauma). Low PEEP and high tidal volume (Option C): Fails to prevent alveolar collapse and increases risk of lung injury.

text: A 26-year-old woman presents to the ER with fever, myalgia and shock after returning from a holiday in Korea. Her blood pressure is 78/50 mmHg, respiratory rate is 40/min, she is cyanosed but not jaundiced and has bilateral conjunctival haemorrhage with epistaxis and hemoptysis. She receives volume resuscitation but remains oliguric (5 ml/hour). Plasma creatinine is 4.60 mg/dl, urea is 182 mg/dl, Hb is 9.1 g/dl, platelet count is 34 x 1012/l and prothrombin time is 32 seconds. What is the diagnosis?

options.A: Acute interstitial nephritis to be replaced with Weger's granulomatosis

expl: The patient here has bleeding manifestations in the pulmonary haemorrhage, epistaxis and conjunctival congestion, along with thrombocytopenia and renal impairement. Everything occurred with fever that followed her return from Korea. So this is mostly an exotic infection that can cause hemorrhage and renal failure. So the most appropriate answer will be Hanta virus infection. Hantavirus causes a ‘haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome' and is endemic in Korea and other Asian countries, the Balkans (the recent war there was associated with a mini-epidemic of hantavirus), some parts of Scandinavia and some US cities. The clinical manifestations are very variable and there are numerous substrains with different rodent vectors. Far-eastern disease often has a more severe clinical course, as in this case. Leptospirosis is endemic in our country too. Given the travel history and absence of other epidemiological clues like contact with dirty water and absence of hepatic involvement, it need not be considered. Pulmonary hemorrhage with glomerulonephritis is also seen in diseases like small vessel vasculitis, Goodpasteur’s syndrome, SLE. But there will not be thrombocytopenia. HUS may present with renal failure and thrombocytopenia, but is associated with hypertension rather than shock and is not known to cause pulmonary hemorrhage. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch:209 Pg: 1642

text: A patient with on steroid therapy and having chronic urticaria now developed respiratory distress. Bronchoalveolar lavage was done and larva was seen. What is the likely parasite?
expl: Strongyloidiasis - caused by the nematode helminth, Strogyloides stercoralis The infective filariform larvae penetrate the human skin and complete their parasitic life cycle by migrating through the lungs and settling in the small intestine In uncomplicated strongyloidiasis, many patients are asymptomatic or have mild cutaneous and/or abdominal symptoms. Recurrent urticaria, often involving the buttocks and wrists, is thecom most common cutaneous manifestation. Migrating larvae can elicit a pathognomonic serpiginous eruption, larva currens ("running larva"). This pruritic, raised, erythematous lesion advances as rapidly as 10 cm/h along the course of larval migration Patients infected with Strongyloides can be asymptomatic, or present with abdominal pain, diarrhea, urticarial skin rashes, cough, shortness of breath, and even hemoptysis in hyperinfection or disseminated disease Subjects immunocompromised, or on steroids are susceptible to hyperinfection and dissemination In disseminated strongyloidiasis, filariform larvae should be sought in samples obtained from sites of potential larval migration, sputum, bronchoalveolar lavage fluid, or surgical drainage fluid.

text: A patient presented with resting tremors, bradykinesia, and postural instability. He eventually became bedridden and died due to respiratory failure. On brain biopsy, which of the following pathological findings is most likely?
expl: Explanation: The clinical presentation of resting tremors, bradykinesia, and postural instability is characteristic of Parkinson's disease. Lewy bodies are the pathological hallmark of this condition, representing eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions containing both neurofilaments and α-synuclein. The disease is characterized by degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta , leading to reduced striatal dopamine. These pathological changes manifest as the classic motor symptoms seen in this patient. Explanation of other options: Hirano bodies (Option B): Hirano bodies are inclusions typically observed in amyotropic lateral sclerosis and Parkinsonism-dementia complex, not in classic Parkinson's disease. Guarneri bodies (Option C): These are cytoplasmic inclusions found specifically in cells infected with smallpox or vaccinia virus. They have no association with movement disorders or neurological conditions like Parkinson's disease. Negri bodies (Option D) : Negri bodies are eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions found in neurons infected with rabies virus, containing viral proteins and RNA. They are diagnostic of rabies infection.

text: A 25-year-old woman is found dead in her apartment. Postmortem examination reveals cherry-red discoloration of the skin and mucosa, and bilateral bright red hypostasis. Which of the following poisons is most likely responsible?
expl: Explanation: Carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning leads to the formation of carboxyhemoglobin , which imparts a cherry-red coloration to the skin, mucosa, and hypostasis. CO has 200 -250 times more affinity for hemoglobin than oxygen, leading to tissue hypoxia despite normal oxygen partial pressures. CO poisoning can be accidental (e.g., in poorly ventilated rooms with gas heaters), homicidal, or suicidal. Explanation of Incorrect Options: Cyanide (Option A): Cyanide poisoning also causes bright red blood due to cellular hypoxia from inhibition of cytochrome oxidase , but cherry-red skin discoloration is less common , and there is typically a bitter almond smell noted during autopsy (though not perceived by all individuals). The rapidity of death is also more sudden. Methanol (Option C): Methanol poisoning leads to optic nerve damage , causing blindness , metabolic acidosis, and CNS depression. It does not cause cherry-red coloration . Postmortem findings include cerebral and optic nerve edema. Organophosphate (Option D): These compounds inhibit acetylcholinesterase , leading to cholinergic symptoms (salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, GI upset, miosis). There is no cherry-red discoloration , and cause of death is usually respiratory failure due to bronchorrhea and muscle paralysis.

text: A patient with lung cancer reports difficulty in breathing. On auscultation over the left infrascapular region, bronchial breath sounds are heard along with dullness on percussion. What is the likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: In patients with malignancy, pleural effusion is a frequent complication. The finding of dull percussion with bronchial breathing suggests underlying consolidation due to compression from effusion. In this context, malignant pleural effusion is the most probable cause. Etiologies: Transudates: CHF, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome. Exudates: TB, pneumonia, malignancy, connective tissue diseases, drugs. Clinical features: Dyspnea, cough, pleuritic pain. Dullness, decreased breath sounds, reduced fremitus. Egophony at fluid upper level. Radiology: X-ray shows blunting of costophrenic angle, homogeneous opacity, Ellis S-shaped curve. Ultrasound detects fluid more accurately. Pleural fluid analysis: Light's criteria differentiates transudates from exudates. Exudative effusions → protein-rich, high LDH. Management: Diagnostic/therapeutic thoracentesis, pleurodesis for recurrent malignant effusions. Explanation of other options: Cardiac tamponade (Option A): Causes Beck's triad (muffled sounds, hypotension, distended veins), not pleural effusion signs. Constrictive pericarditis (Option B): Produces right heart failure findings (ascites, hepatomegaly), no dullness or bronchial breathing. Pulmonary embolism (Option C): Presents with acute dyspnea and chest pain, not bronchial breathing with dullness. Key Takeaways: Malignant pleural effusion is a common cause of dyspnea in lung cancer. Diagnostic confirmation is by thoracentesis and pleural fluid analysis .

text: A 24-year-old man was found to have iron deficiency anemia when he went to donate blood. Generally, the patient was very well. He had a good appetite, his weight was steady and he ate a normal diet. He had a normal bowel habit and had never passed any blood, mucus or diarrhea in his stools. There is no history of any overt blood loss. His general practitioner got an open access endoscopy which was normal; duodenal biopsies were unremarkable. His father had died of what he thought was secondary liver and lung cancer but he was unsure. On general physical examination he was fit and athletic. The skin and mucosal membranes were unremarkable. Vitals were normal. Heart sounds were normal and the chest was clear. His abdomen was soft and nontender with no palpable masses or organs. Rectal examination was normal. On viewing the rectal mucosa through a rigid sigmoidoscope the colonic mucosa was covered in innumerable polyps. What specific genetic abnormality is responsible for this appearance?

options.A: Germline mutation of the STK11 gene on chromosome 19
options.B: Heterozygous mutation of the MYH gene
options.C: Loss of the APC gene on chromosome 5
options.D: Mutations in mismatch repair genes (for example, MSH2)

ansText: Loss of the APC gene on chromosome 5
expl: The patient will need a full colonoscopy and biopsy but the information presented is highly suggestive of familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) , caused by the loss of the APC gene on the short arm of chromosome 5. Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS) is an autosomal dominant inherited disorder caused by a germline mutation of the STK11 (serine threonine kinase 11) gene, usually located on the long arm of chromosome 19. Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is associated with intestinal hamartomatous polyps, but is usually (90%) associated with perioral pigmentation . Hereditary nonpolyposis colon cancer (HNPCC) and MYC polyposis do not cause multiple polyps as suggested in this case. InHNPCC, affected individuals inherit a mutation in one of several genes involved in DNA mismatch repair, including MSH2, MLH1, and PMS2. Homozygous mutations in the MYH gene have been associated with a phenotype of multiple colorectal adenomas with or without cancer. This accounts for a proportion of FAP patients without a pathogenic APC mutation. Mutations in the p53 tumor suppressor gene are found in many different cancers. While mutations in p53 are seen in cases of colon cancer, the question asks for the specific mutation associated with polyposis coli. The main differential in this question is between FAP and PJS but the lack of perioral pigmentation favors FAP as the diagnosis. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 81, Pg: 638

text: A lung cancer patient has hyperpigmentation of palmar and sole creases. Which of the following is responsible for this presentation?
expl: Explanation: The clinical features are suggestive of ectopic Cushing's syndrome, a paraneoplastic condition frequently linked to lung cancer. In this setting, tumour-derived proopiomelanocortin is cleaved into ACTH and melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH), resulting in hyperpigmentation. This represents one of the most common hormone-mediated paraneoplastic syndromes in small cell lung cancer (SCLC). Paraneoplastic Syndromes Caused by Ectopic Hormone Production Explanation of other options: C-peptide (Option B): C-peptide is a byproduct formed during the conversion of proinsulin to insulin. It has no role in the hyperpigmentation seen in paraneoplastic syndromes associated with lung cancer. Neuropeptide Y (Option C): Neuropeptiode C is involved in appetite regulation through hypothalamic signaling. This peptide does not contribute to the hyperpigmentation observed in paraneoplastic syndromes. Melanin (Option D) : Melanin is the end product of melanogenesis responsible for skin pigmentation. While it is the final pigment, the question asks about the hormone responsible for triggering the hyperpigmentation, which is MSH. Key Takeaway: Lung tumors and their associated paraneoplastic syndromes

text: A 50-year-old man receiving therapy for lung cancer reports breathlessness and dizziness. On examination, reduced breath sounds are detected over the left lower scapular area. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The symptoms point toward pleural effusion , a frequent complication in lung cancer, with dyspnea, dizziness, and the notable finding of decreased breath sounds over the left lower scapular area being typical indicators. Pleural effusion develops when cancer cells infiltrate the pleural cavity or trigger inflammation, leading to fluid accumulation. The malignancies most often associated include lung cancer (mesothelioma more than adenocarcinoma), breast cancer, ovarian cancer, and gastrointestinal cancers. Explanations of other options: Constrictive pericarditis (Option A): This disorder is marked by pericardial thickening and scarring, which restricts cardiac filling. Although shortness of breath may occur, it more often manifests with features of right-sided heart failure, such as jugular venous distension and a pericardial knock. Focal reduction in breath sounds is not usually seen. Cardiac tamponade (Option C): This condition is characterized by Beck's triad-low blood pressure, neck vein distension, and muffled heart sounds-along with pulsus paradoxus. Although breathlessness is common, it does not produce localized reduction in breath sounds, and the presentation is typically more sudden and severe than in this scenario. Pneumothorax (Option D): It is marked by abrupt chest pain, sudden shortness of breath, and a hyperresonant percussion note on the affected side. The presentation is usually more acute, with breath sounds being absent rather than merely reduced. Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK448189/# https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK559322/#

text: A 65 year old male presents with history of hemoptysis and is admitted in hospital. He has been a heavy smoker for 25 years. A chest X-ray shows a mass in the right upper lobe. Which is the best test to investigate at present?
expl: The initial evaluation of a patient with hemoptysis is a plain radiograph of the chest. In a low risk individual (age In individuals who are high risk for lung malignancy( age > 40 years or smokers), even if the initial chest xray is normal, they should undergo a contrast enhanced CT of the chest. If a lesion is visible on the CT it should be sampled for histopathology. If a sampling is not possible or a lesion is not visible, a bronchoscopy should be done. So our patient is at high risk for a bronchogenic carcinoma,and has a lesion visible on the chest xray. The next step will be a CT of the lung to characterize the lesion and to find the feasibility of a percutaneous biopsy. Sputum cytology has a very low yield. text: A chronic smoker presents with dysphagia. Which type of lung cancer is most likely?
expl: Explanation: SCC is centrally located, strongly associated with smoking, and can compress the esophagus, causing dysphagia. Types of Lung Cancer and Their Features Adenocarcinoma: Most common histologic subtype (~45% of lung cancers). Early spread, often to the CNS. Produces mucin; shows glandular differentiation. Location: Peripheral. Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC): Strongly linked to smoking (~90% cases). Histology: keratinization, intercellular bridges, central necrosis, cavitation. Location: Central. Large Cell Carcinoma: Aggressive tumor, poorly differentiated. Lacks defining histologic features. Tends to grow slowly but has high vascularity. Location: Peripheral. Small Cell Neuroendocrine Carcinoma: Very aggressive, with early nodal and distant metastasis. Arises from neuroendocrine cells. Location: Central. Typical/Atypical Carcinoid Tumors: Typical: Indolent course. Atypical: More aggressive behavior. Location: Variable. Pancoast's Tumor (Apical): Located at lung apex, invades brachial plexus. Causes severe local pain. Associated with Pancoast's syndrome . Clinical Features of Lung Cancer Cough: Common but non-specific. Hemoptysis: Present in Chest pain: Severe pain indicates chest wall or intercostal nerve involvement. Dyspnea: Due to reduced lung function, lymphatic spread, or pleural effusion. Dysphagia: From mediastinal node enlargement or upper lung involvement compressing the esophagus. Pleural fluid: Hemorrhagic fluid suggests pleural invasion. Clubbing/Hypertrophic osteoarthropathy: Sometimes present, may regress after tumor removal. Mediastinal invasion: May cause hoarseness (recurrent laryngeal nerve), dysphagia, or SVC obstruction. Pancoast's syndrome: Due to apical invasion with brachial plexus involvement. Explanation of other options: Adenocarcinoma (Option B): The most common lung cancer in non-smokers, usually arising in the lung periphery. It is less often associated with dysphagia compared to squamous cell carcinoma. Large Cell Carcinoma (Option C): A relatively uncommon lung cancer that often presents with vague, non-specific symptoms. Dysphagia is not typically seen with this type. Bronchogenic Carcinoma (Option D): A general term describing cancers originating from the bronchial epithelium, which includes subtypes such as squamous cell carcinoma and adenocarcinoma. However, it is not a precise diagnosis and therefore does not specifically address the question.

text: A 55 year old shipbuilding worker presents with dyspnea. He has been working in this industry for the past 25 years. Which is the most specific malignancy that we can expect in this patient?
expl: Explanation: A long-term history of occupational asbestos exposure (common in shipbuilding) is the primary risk factor for malignant mesothelioma , a cancer arising from the mesothelial cells of the pleura. While asbestos also increases the risk for bronchogenic carcinoma, mesothelioma is the most specific malignancy linked to this exposure. Pathology: Advanced pleural thickening/fibrosis makes the hemithorax rigid; mediastinal fixation may occur, but mediastinal shift is uncommon . Most common cytogenetic abnormality: 9p homozygous deletion (CDKN2A loss) . Clinical Features: Progressive dyspnea, chest pain, weight loss, chronic cough, hemoptysis; decreased breath sounds and dull percussion due to effusion or thickening. Diagnosis: CT scan: Pleural thickening, effusion, 'frozen hemithorax'(no mediastinal shift). Biopsy: Epithelioid: Tubules/nests/papillary structures, uniform nuclei, eosinophilic cytoplasm Sarcomatoid: Spindle cells, fibrosarcoma-like Biphasic: Mixed pattern Markers: Calretinin, epithelial membrane antigen (EMA), cytokeratin, mesothelin. Gross Findings: Lobulated pleural mass encasing lung, rib erosion, massive effusion, calcified pleural plaques (bilateral, prior asbestos exposure). Explanation of other options: Bronchogenic carcinoma ,Small cell carcinoma and Squamous cell carcinoma (Option A,C and D): These are types of lung cancer. Asbestos exposure is a risk factor, especially when combined with smoking, but they are not as specifically linked to asbestos as mesothelioma. Key Takeaways: Malignant mesothelioma is strongly and specifically associated with asbestos exposure. Shipbuilding, construction, and insulation work are high-risk occupations.

text: A 45-year-old male complains of daytime sleepiness and nighttime insomnia. His wife reports that he snores loudly. Which of the following statements about his condition is incorrect?

options.A: Increased tone of the pharyngeal muscle worsens obstruction
options.B: Fall of oxygen saturation triggers waking up at night
options.C: Episode of apnea increases stress on heart

ansText: Increased tone of the pharyngeal muscle worsens obstruction
expl: Explanation: The patient has Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA), a sleep disorder caused by repetitive upper airway collapse during sleep leading to intermittent hypoxia and sleep fragmentation . Pathophysiology: During sleep, pharyngeal muscle tone decreases , causing collapse of the upper airway . This leads to airflow obstruction despite continued respiratory effort → apnea episodes . The fall in oxygen saturation activates chemoreceptors , triggering brief arousals → fragmented sleep → daytime fatigue. It is decreased , not increased, tone of the pharyngeal muscles that worsens obstruction. Increased tone would actually help maintain airway patency. Clinical Features: Loud snoring Witnessed apnea episodes Excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS) Morning headaches Poor concentration, irritability Complications: Cardiovascular: Hypertension, arrhythmias, pulmonary hypertension, right heart failure Metabolic: Insulin resistance, metabolic syndrome Explanation of Other Options: Fall of oxygen saturation triggers waking up at night (Option B): True as hypoxia activates chemoreceptors → stimulates arousal reflex. Restores muscle tone and breathing effort. Leads to repeated micro-arousals → daytime sleepiness. Oxygen desaturation is a key diagnostic feature on polysomnography . Episode of apnea increases stress on heart (Option C): True as repeated hypoxia increases sympathetic activation . Raises heart rate and blood pressure transiently. Leads to arrhythmias, hypertension, and cardiac failure in chronic cases. Also increases risk of sudden cardiac death during sleep . Low oxygen stimulates respiratory effort (Option D): True as hypoxemia and hypercapnia stimulate medullary respiratory centers. Increased respiratory effort against obstruction causes chest retractions . Effort continues until arousal restores airflow. Seen as thoraco-abdominal asynchrony on sleep studies.

text: Which of the following is true regarding diagnosis of obstructive sleep apnoea?

options.A: Snoring along with 5 episodes of apnoea overnight fulfills the criteria
options.B: Lack of symptoms along with 15 episodes of apnea overnight fulfills the criteria
options.C: Each episode of apnoea or hypopnea lasts at least 10 seconds

ansText: Each episode of apnoea or hypopnea lasts at least 10 seconds
expl: options A and B are incorrect because the given number of episodes should occur per hour of night to satisfy the criteria Diagnosis of OSA requires the patient to have: (1) either symptoms of nocturnal breathing disturbances (snoring, snorting, gasping, or breathing pauses during sleep) or daytime sleepiness or fatigue that occurs despite sufficient opportunity to sleep and is unexplained by other medical problems; and (2) five or more episodes of obstructive apnoea or hypopnea per hour of sleep (the apnoea-hypopnea index [AHI], calculated as the number of episodes divided by the number of hours of sleep) documented during a sleep study. OSA also may be diagnosed in the absence of symptoms if the AHI is ≥15 episodes/h . Each episode of apnoea or hypopnea represents a reduction in breathing for at least 10 s and commonly results in a ≥3% drop in oxygen saturation or a brain cortical arousal Polysomnography is used for the diagnosis of OSA. Reference: Harrison's principles of internal medicine 21st Edition, chapter 297, page number.2205

text: A 33-year-old woman presents with a one-year history of daytime sleepiness and memory impairment. She has a BMI of 43 and blood pressure of 170/98 mmHg. Arterial blood gas analysis while awake shows pO 2 70 mmHg, pCO 2 53 mmHg, and HCO 3 - 33 mmol/L. What is the most probable diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The patient shows typical signs of Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome (OHS) , such as marked obesity (BMI 43), excessive daytime sleepiness, impaired memory, and high blood pressure. The hallmark of OHS diagnosis is arterial blood gas findings that reveal hypoxemia (pO2 70 mmHg) , hypercapnia (pCO2 53 mmHg), and increased bicarbonate (HCO3 33 mmol/L), consistent with chronic respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation , considered pathognomonic for OHS. It develops in individuals with severe obesity who demonstrate hypoventilation both while asleep and awake. Explanations of other options: Central Sleep Apnea (Option B): Although central sleep apnea may lead to daytime drowsiness, it stems from impaired central nervous system regulation of breathing during sleep. However, the ABG findings of chronic compensated respiratory acidosi s align more with obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS) than with a CNS-related disorder. Narcolepsy (Option C): Narcolepsy typically presents with excessive daytime sleepiness along with cataplexy, sleep paralysis , and hypnagogic hallucinations. Since these features are absent, and instead there is marked obesity with respiratory acidosis, this diagnosis is less probable. Obstructive Sleep Apnea (Option D): While OSA often coexists with OHS, the presence of daytime hypercapnia is not typical for isolated OSA. The chronic respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation is more characteristic of OHS.

text: A 40-year-old man presents with daytime sleepiness and impaired concentration and memory. On examination his BMI is 41 kg/m2, BP is 160/100 mm Hg. His awake ABG analysis is given: PaO₂= 66mm Hg PaCO₂= 50 mm Hg HCO₃= 28 mEq/L What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: Obesity Hypoventilation Syndrome (OHS) is a medical condition characterized by persistent daytime hypercapnia (elevated arterial carbon dioxide pressure) in individuals with obesity, after other potential causes of hypoventilation have been ruled out. Pathophysiology The syndrome arises primarily because severe obesity mechanically restricts lung expansion, leading to chronic hypoventilation. This is compounded by several factors: The increased work of breathing due to excess chest and abdominal weight. Respiratory muscle impairment from adipose tissue. A blunted ventilatory response to hypercapnia and hypoxemia. Frequently co-existing obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), which further disrupts normal gas exchange during sleep. Notably, the impaired ventilatory drive appears to be a consequence of the condition rather than its initial cause Diagnostic Criteria A diagnosis of OHS is confirmed when the following three criteria are met: Body Mass Index (BMI): A BMI ≥30 kg/m². Daytime Alveolar Hypoventilation: An awake arterial PaCO 2 ≥45 mmHg, without other explanations such as severe lung or neuromuscular disease. Sleep-Disordered Breathing: The presence of a disorder like obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). Risk Factors The primary risk factors for developing OHS are: Severe obesity (BMI >40 kg/m²) Severe obstructive sleep apnea (Apnea-Hypopnea Index, AHI >30 events per hour) Treatment : Explanation of other options: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) (Option A) : is a disorder that is characterized by obstructive apneas and hypopneas due to repetitive collapse of the upper airway during sleep. The clinical features against OSA include hypercapnia and hypoxemia in an awake individual . Narcolepsy (Option B): is characterized by excessive daytime sleepiness, sudden loss of muscle tone (cataplexy), and disrupted sleep patterns. While impaired concentration and memory can be seen in narcolepsy, the ABG is normal. Central sleep apnea (Option D): is a condition in which there is a lack of respiratory effort during sleep, leading to pauses in breathing. Impaired concentration and memory can occur in central sleep apnea.

text: What is the uppermost intercostal space used for hepatic biopsy :
expl: Answer is B 7th The right surface of the liver is in contact with the diaphragm opposite the 7th to 11th ribs. In needle biopsy of the liver through the intercostal route, the needle may be inserted through the 6th 7th, 8th, 9th or 10th right intercostal space in the mid-axillary line. The 8th and 9th intercostal spaces are most commonly used. Insertion in the 6th or 7th intercostal space may also be used but is associated with risk of injury to the Lung. Needle is typically inserted at the end of expiration (Attempted Apnoea).

text: What is observed in the case of an abnormal accumulation of misfolded protein?
expl: Explanation: The condition directly caused by the abnormal accumulation of misfolded proteins is Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) . This is a rare, fatal neurodegenerative disorder that rapidly impairs brain function. CJD is classified as a prion disease . Prions are infectious, misfolded proteins that cause normally folded proteins in the brain to also misfold. This leads to the accumulation of abnormal protein aggregates, resulting in progressive and severe damage to nerve cells, giving the brain a sponge-like (spongiform) appearance. Clinical Presentation The disease progresses rapidly and is characterized by: Severe mental deterioration (dementia) Involuntary muscle jerks (myoclonus) Lack of coordination and balance problems Behavioral changes , anxiety, and confusion Vision problems and unusual sensations As it advances, it leads to coma and ultimately death, often from secondary infections like pneumonia. Types of CJD Sporadic (sCJD): The most common form (85% of cases) with no known cause. Genetic (gCJD): Inherited through a gene mutation (10-15% of cases). Acquired (vCJD): The rare "variant" form, linked to consuming products from cattle with bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE or "mad cow disease"). Diagnosis and Management Diagnosis is supported by clinical signs, characteristic EEG patterns, MRI brain imaging, and detecting the 14-3-3 protein in cerebrospinal fluid. Definitive diagnosis often requires brain biopsy or postmortem examination. Treatment: There is no cure. Management focuses on palliative care to alleviate symptoms and provide comfort. Explanation of other options: Nephritic syndrome (Option B): It is primarily associated with immune-mediated damage and not the accumulation of misfolded proteins. Sickle cell anaemia (Option C): This is a genetic hemoglobinopathy caused by a mutation in the beta-globin gene, leading to abnormally shaped red blood cells. Megaloblastic anaemia (Option D): It is a type of anaemia characterized by the presence of large, immature red blood cells (megaloblasts) in the bone marrow. Megaloblastic anaemia does not involve the accumulation of misfolded proteins. Reference: https://www.ninds.nih.gov/health-information/disorders/creutzfeldt-jakob-disease

text: Which of the following diseases present mainly as Glomerulonephritis?
expl: Glomerular diseases can present in 2 ways- Nephritic Syndrome or Nephrotic Syndrome. Clinical distinction of both is required to identify the disease process and to plan investigations. NEPHRITIC SYNDROME: Hematuria. RBC cast. Hypertension. Proteinuria of the range 1-2g/day. Varying degrees of decline in GFR. Diseases that present predominantly as Nephritis are: Post streptococcal Glomerulonephritis, Sub acute bacterial endocarditis, Lupus Nephritis, IgA Nephropathy, Basement Membrane Disease, ANCA associated vasculitis, Membraneoproliferative glomerulonephritis. NEPHROTIC SYNDROME: Heavy proteinuria, >3gm/day Edema/anasarca Hypertension Hypercholesterolemia Hypoalbuminemia Hematuria, variable. Diseases that predominantly present as Nephrotic syndrome: Minimal change disease, Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, Membranous glomerulonephritis, diabetic nephropathy, Amyloidosis, Light chain deposition disease, Fabry’s Disease. There can be overlap between these two, eg: heavy proteinuria in Glomerulonephritis, known as Nephritic-nephrotic Syndrome. Reference: Harrison's principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 314, Pg: 2334.

text: Which one of the following is the commonest cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults?
expl: The incidence of FSGS is increasing, and it now represents up to one third of cases of nephrotic syndrome in adults and one-half of cases of nephrotic syndrome in African Americans. MCD causes 70–90% of nephrotic syndrome in childhood but only 10–15% of nephrotic syndrome in adults MGN, or membranous nephropathy as it is sometimes called, accounts for ~25% of cases of nephrotic syndrome in adults, with a peak incidence between the ages of 30 and 50 years and a male-to-female ratio of 2:1. IMN is rare in childhood and the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in the elderly. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Principles, 21 st edition, Ch: 314 Pg: 2341

text: Which of the following features are characteristic of glomerular hematuria? Statements: 1. Brown-colored urine 2. Dysuria absent 3. Crystals present 4. Edema rare
expl: Explanation: Glomerular hematuria occurs when damage to the glomerular filtration barrier allows red blood cells (RBCs) and plasma proteins to leak into the urinary space. It typically presents with cola-colored (brown) urine , absence of dysuria , and may be associated with edema when part of a nephritic syndrome . The presence of urinary crystals is not a feature of glomerular bleeding, it suggests a metabolic or post-renal cause such as stones or hyperuricosuria. Explanation of Other Statements: Brown-colored urine (Statement 1) - True The urine appears cola- or tea-colored due to oxidation of hemoglobin released from RBCs that have traversed damaged glomeruli. Indicates bleeding originating above the renal pelvis. Dysuria absent (Statement 2)- True Dysuria (painful micturition) suggests inflammation or infection of the lower urinary tract (urethra, bladder). Glomerular hematuria is non-irritative and painless. Crystals present (Statement 3) - False Crystalluria is associated with renal calculi or metabolic disorders (e.g., hyperuricemia, cystinuria), not glomerular diseases. Edema rare (Statement 4) - True in isolated glomerular hematuria Mild or no edema may be seen in isolated microscopic hematuria. However, when hematuria occurs as part of nephritic syndrome , edema can be marked.

text: A 45-year-old woman presents with dipstick positive haematuria. Her blood tests reveal a urea of 150 mg/dl and creatinine of 2.9 mg/dl. Which of the following most strongly suggests post streptococcal glomerulonephritis?
expl: Post streptococcal glomerulonephritis is caused by Group A beta haemolytic streptococci. A second episode is unusual in those who have previously had the disease because there is good immunity to the cell wall proteins of Group A strep. Acute Rheumatic Fever, which is also a disease caused by β hemolytic Sterptococci, is known for recurrences without secondary prophylaxis. Although features of hypertension with papilledema, complete anuria and nephrotic syndrome can occur, the strongest predictor is the clinical history of sore throat suggesting infection with streptococci leading to nephritic syndrome. PSGN due to skin infection develops after 2-6 weeks while that after a throat infection develops after 1-3 weeks. This glomerulus is hypercellular and capillary loops are poorly defined in post streptococcal glomerulonephritis. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 314, Pg: 2337.

text: A 17-year-old male presents with proteinuria >4g/day, edema, and hypoalbuminemia, consistent with nephrotic syndrome. What is the recommended management for this patient?
expl: Explanation: Management of Nephrotic Syndrome in a 17-Year-Old Male First-line Treatment : Steroids (Prednisone) Based on high remission rates in minimal change disease (MCD), the most common cause in children and adolescents. Leads to complete remission in 90 -95% of children , 80 -85% of adults . Given daily or on alternate days . Other immunosuppressants (cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil, mycophenolate mofetil) are used for frequent relapsers , steroid-dependent , or steroid-resistant Presentation & Epidemiology Features : Proteinuria >4 g/day , edema , hypoalbuminemia , hypercholesterolemia Minimal hematuria , possible hypertension Without treatment : Risk of progression to renal failure Therapeutic Overview Edema : Managed with diuretics Hypercholesterolemia : Treated with lipid-lowering agents Hypercoagulability : May need anticoagulants Proteinuria : May use RAAS inhibitors Minimal Change Disease (MCD) Prevalence : 70 -90% of pediatric cases 10 -15% of adult cases Histology : Normal on light microscopy , foot process effacement on electron microscopy Etiology : Linked to T-cell dysfunction ; triggered by infections , allergies , or medications Clinical Features of MCD Sudden onset of edema Classic nephrotic syndrome signs Hypertension and microscopic hematuria are uncommon Renal function usually returns to normal after remission Outcomes & Prognosis Relapses common, especially in children Long-term prognosis is poorer in cases of acute renal failure or steroid resistance Children : Remission typically within 8 weeks Adults : Remission may take 20 -24 weeks Explanation of other options: Steroids and Cyclophosphamide (Option B): Cyclophosphamide is NOT first-line for nephrotic syndrome. It is reserved for steroid-resistant or frequently relapsing cases . IV Albumin (Option C): Albumin infusion can be used temporarily for severe edema but does NOT treat the underlying disease. Main treatment is still steroids . Cyclophosphamide (Option D): Cyclophosphamide is used for steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome or frequent relapses, NOT as initial therapy. Key Takeaways: Nephrotic syndrome in adolescents is most commonly due to Minimal Change Disease, which responds well to corticosteroids. First-line treatment is prednisone.

text: Aldosterone synthesis is stimulated by which of the following?
expl: Mineralocorticoid secretion is stimulated by hypotension, hyperkalemia, angiotensin II, ACTH and hyponatremia, in reducing order of efficacy. Aldosterone secretion in response to hyperkalemia is the most important and forms the basis for renal regulation of body potassium balance. Stimulation of aldosterone by angiotensin II (through renin-angiotensin system) is important for the correction of hypovolemia and hypotension in conditions like salt depletion or renal ischemia. Stimulation of aldosterone secretion by ACTH results in diurnal variation of aldosterone secretion. However, ACTH is not an important physiological regulator for aldosterone secretion. Hyponatremia is a weak stimulator of aldosterone secretion. Factors stimulating release of aldosterone release: Hypotension Hyperkalemia Acidosis Angiotensin 2 Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 2958

text: A 65-year-old man is brought in with a sudden inability to speak coherently, producing nonsensical grammar despite speaking fluently and rapidly. He had normal communication ability before this event. Which type of defect does this patient have?
expl: Explanation: The given clinical scenario of quick speech, which does not make sense, is suggestive of fluent aphasia , also known as Wernicke's aphasia . Fuent aphasia, or Wernicke's aphasia, arises from injury to Wernicke's area in the brain. It is characterised by effortless and well-structured speech, but the content is nonsensical or filled with invented words. Patients usually retain normal rhythm and fluency yet produce meaningless language, and they are generally unaware of their communication difficulties. Explanation of other options: Motor aphasia (Option A): Motor aphasia, or Broca's aphasia, is marked by impaired speech production , including reduced vocabulary, slow and effortful speech, and poor grammar. Affected individuals find it hard to construct complete sentences and often become frustrated with their inability to communicate. Since the patient can speak smoothly and rapidly, this condition is unlikely. Anomic aphasia (Option B): Anomic aphasia involves difficulty retrieving words , causing pauses and the use of substitute terms, though grammar and speech fluency are usually preserved. Since the patient shows meaningless speech content rather than problems with word retrieval, this diagnosis is improbable. Conduction aphasia (Option D): Conduction aphasia arises from injury to the arcuate fasciculus , which links Broca's and Wernicke's areas. It is marked by impaired ability to repeat words or phrases , despite having relatively preserved comprehension and spontaneous speech. Because this patient's main problem lies in the meaning of their speech rather than repetition, this diagnosis is less likely.

text: Two weeks after an episode of infective diarrhoea, a 15-year-old child presents with fever, hypertension and haematuria. A possible diagnosis could be:
expl: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura(TTP) and hemolytic-uremic syndrome(HUS) represent a spectrum of thrombotic microangiopathies. TTP and HUS share the general features of idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura, hemolytic anemia, fever, renal failure and neurologic disturbances. When patients, particularly children, have more evidence of renal injury, their condition tends to be called HUS. In adults with neurologic disease, it is considered to be TTP. Childhood HUS is caused by a toxin released by Escherichia coli 0157:H7 and occasionally by Shigella dysenteriae . This shiga toxin(verotoxin) directly injures endothelial, enterocytes and renal cells, causing apoptosis, platelet clumping and intravascular hemolysis by binding to the glycolipid receptors(Gb3). Investigations reveal anemia with schistocytes; a normal bleeding profile and impaired renal function. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 314, Pg: 2348.

text: A 40-year-old woman has a history of Raynaud's phenomenon, stiffness in the hands, butterfly rash on her face and arthralgia. She has a blood pressure of 175/90 mmHg. options.A: Mesangial IgA staining and proliferative glomerulonephritis
options.B: Subendothelial deposits seen as humps with focal glomerulonephritis
options.C: Deposition of IgA, IgG, IgM and complements with proliferative glomerulonephritis
options.D: Focal or diffuse glomerular necrosis with crescents and liner IgG deposits along the basement membrane in IF.

ansText: Deposition of IgA, IgG, IgM and complements with proliferative glomerulonephritis
expl: So this question deals with a young woman with history suggestive of SLE. So we have to find out, from the options, the most likely finding in lupus nephritis. There are 6 classes of lupus nephritis. The histological pattern is membranoproliferative or mesangiocapillary glomerulonephritis, where you can see focal or diffuse, segmental or global endocapillary proliferation. The immune deposits are seen sub endothelially along the basement membrane. There will be variable degree of mesangial proliferation. All classes of immunoglobulins and complement will be seen(Full house staining) Sub endothelial deposits of immunoglobulins IgG, M and complements with endocapillary and mesangial proliferation and polymorphonuclear infiltration is seen in PSGN. There will be sub epithelial humps on electron microscopy. Focal necrosis of the glomeruli with linear IgG deposits along the basement membrane is seen in Anti GBM disease. There will not be any proliferation seen. Mesangial IgA staining with mesangial hypercellularity, known as mesangioproliferative glomerulonephritis is seen in IgA nephropathy. Here the immunoglobulin deposits are IgA class and there will be no staining of sub epithelium or sub endothelium of the basement membrane. Note: Sub endothelial deposits occur with pre formed immune complexes precipitating along the sub endothelial side. Immune complexes that are formed in situ will be seen along the sun epithelial side. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 21 st edition, Ch: 314, Pg: 2332-2343.

text: A 45-year-old patient with chronic hepatitis C has a creatinine of 1.5 mg/dl. His BP is 150/90. He has a urine dipstick showing blood ++, protein +++. Which of the following might be demonstrated in histology?
expl: This question deals with another cause of glomerulonephritis. Our patient is a chronic Hepatitis C infected individual who presents with Glomerulonephritis. The type of glomerulonephritis that we see in such a patient is Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis. Unlike the glomerulonephritis that we learned so far which is specific for a particular etiology, MPGN is a histology patten that is common for many diseases. In a simplified form, the causes of MPGN can be broadly divided into three: Type I: Immune complex or monoclonal antibody mediated: Hep B or Hep C, Malaria, Schsitosomiasis, Infective endocarditis, SLE, Sjogren's syndrome, Cryoglobulinemia, MGUS or myeloma. Type II: Dense deposit disease Type III: Idiopathic Hepatitis C infection as well as Cryuoglobulinemia associated with it can lead to glomerulonephritis and the MC histology will be MPGN Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st edition, Ch: 314, Pg: 2341.

text: A hepatitis B-positive patient presented to your OPD with massive proteinuria (>3.5 g/day). A renal biopsy was subsequently performed, as shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: This renal biopsy shows the condition membranous glomerulonephritis Investigations in Membranous Nephropathy/Glomerulonephritis: Kidney function tests: Elevated creatinine levels. Urine protein: Proteinuria exceeding 2 grams per gram of urinary creatinine. Renal biopsy findings: Light Microscopy: Shows uniform thickening of the glomerular basement membrane, especially along peripheral capillary loops. Immunofluorescence: Displays diffuse granular deposits of IgG and C3. Electron Microscopy: Reveals dense subepithelial deposits with a characteristic 'spike and dome' pattern. Autoantibody testing: Autoantibodies against M-type phospholipase A2 receptor (PLA2R) are found in about 70% of cases. Thrombospondin type-1 domain containing 7A (THSD7A) autoantibodies are seen in 3-10% of cases. Secondary membranous nephropathy usually lacks these autoantibodies. Management: Symptomatic treatment: Includes control of edema (using thiazide diuretics), dyslipidemia, and hypertension (using ACE inhibitors or ARBs). Immunosuppressive therapy: Considered for primary membranous nephropathy patients with persistent proteinuria above 3 g/day. Options include corticosteroids, cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil, mycophenolate mofetil, cyclosporine, and rituximab (an anti-CD20 antibody). Prophylactic anticoagulation: May be advised in patients with hypoalbuminemia due to an increased risk of thrombotic events. Complications: High risk of renal vein thrombosis. Other thrombotic complications such as deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism due to the hypercoagulable state associated with nephrotic syndrome. Prognosis: Approximately one-third of patients progress to advanced disease. One-third achieve spontaneous remission. One-third maintain stable disease without progression. Poorer outcomes are linked to male sex, older age, hypertension, and ongoing nephrotic-range proteinuria. Explanation of other options: Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) (Option A): involves scarring and sclerosis that affects some glomeruli (focal) and only portions of each affected glomerulus (segmental). Membranoproliferative Glomerulonephritis (MPGN) (Option C): is defined by a combination of basement membrane thickening and mesangial cell proliferation. Minimal Change Disease (Option D): is the leading cause of nephrotic syndrome in children, but it occurs less frequently in adults.

text: A 30-year-old lady has haematuria on the dipstick and was referred by the GP for further investigation. She eventually has a renal biopsy which shows mesangial hypercellularity with IgA deposition. What is the diagnosis?
expl: The diagnosis is IgA nephropathy. Epidemiology: IgA nephropathy is the commonest glomerulonephritis worldwide Males are more commonly affected; peak incidence affecting individuals in 2 nd & 3 rd decades Pathogenesis: Deposition of immune complexes in the mesangium; antibodies are formed against galactose deficient polymeric IgA1. Presentation: Recurrent gross hematuria during or immediately following an upper respiratory tract infection(unlike PSGN, where there will be a period of 1-3 weeks) Persistent microscopic hematuria ± proteinuria Biopsy shows mesangial IgA deposits, which is composed of polymeric IgA joined by J chain. Prognosis: Renal failure develops in 30% patients over 20-25 years. MEST C score is used for prognosis. Treatment: Conservative; ACE inhibitors in patients with proteinuria; steroids for patients with persistent proteinuria or presenting with Rapidly progressive Glomerulonephritis Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st edition, Ch: 314, Pg: 2339.

text: A 35-year-old man has been given some painkillers by his GP for pleuritic chest pains following a chest infection. 2 weeks later he presents again with ankle oedema. His blood pressure is 130/70 mmHg, and urine dipstick reveals protein +++ and no blood. Plasma creatinine is 1.4 mg/dl.What is the likely diagnosis?
expl: Here the patient has mild renal impairment with urine dipstick showing 3+ proteinuria. The very short history points against renal amyloidosis. Amyloidosis can cause heavy proteinuria with bland urinary sediments. But the patient lacks other features that may predispose to renal amyloidosis. FSGS and Membraneous nephropathy causes variable degree of hematuria along with proteinuria. So the most appropriate option is an acute interstitial nephritis. The point against an interstitial nephritis is the 3+ proteinuria. Tubulointerstitial diseases usually cause mild proteinuria The most frequent causes of acute interstitial nephritis can be found in one of three general categories: drug-induced (NSAID, anti TB drugs, sulphonamides) infection-associated (legionella, HIV, Hep C) immune or neoplastic disorders (SLE, Sjogrens, Wegeners). The clinical presentation can range from asymptomatic elevation in creatinine or blood urea or abnormal urinary sediment, to generalized hypersensitivity syndrome with fever, rash, eosinophilia, and oliguric renal failure.Proteinuria is much more common in NSAID-induced nephritis than other causes. Resolution of proteinuria should occur with discontinuation of NSAID drugs, although steroids can be used in cases of heavy proteinuria. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 310, Pg: 2302

text: Which of the following is/are novel biomarkers for acute kidney injury?
expl: Option A: Kidney injury molecule-1 (KIM-1) is a type 1 transmembrane protein that is abundantly expressed in proximal tubular cells injured by ischemia or multiple, distinct nephrotoxins, such as cisplatin. It can be detected after ischemic or nephrotoxic injury in the urine and plasma Option B: Neutrophil gelatinase associated lipocalin (NGAL, also known as lipocalin-2 or siderocalin) is another biomarker of AKI. NGAL was first discovered as a protein in granules of human neutrophils. It is highly upregulated after inflammation and kidney injury and can be detected in the plasma and urine within 2 h of cardiopulmonary bypass–associated AKI. Other biomarkers include: Plasma levels of soluble urokinase Plasminogen Activator Receptor(suPAR) Urinary concentration of two cell-cycle arrest biomarkers, insulin-like growth factor binding protein 7 ( IGFBP7 ) and tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinase-2 ( TIMP-2 ) (option C) - predictive biomarkers for higher risk of the development of moderate to severe AKI. Cystatin C Osteopontin β-D-glucosaminidase Clusterin Reference: Harrison's principles of internal medicine 21st ed, Chap 310 Pg. 2305

text: Which of the following statements is correct regarding prerenal acute kidney injury (AKI)?

options.A: Ultrasound (USG) of the kidneys typically shows significant kidney size differences
options.B: Creatinine clearance is usually significantly decreased in prerenal AKI
options.C: Fractional excretion of sodium (FeNa) is typically less than 1% in prerenal AKI
options.D: In prerenal AKI, the urine usually shows high sodium concentration due to impaired tubular function.

ansText: Fractional excretion of sodium (FeNa) is typically less than 1% in prerenal AKI
expl: Explanation: In prerenal acute kidney injury (AKI), the kidneys respond to decreased blood flow or volume by conserving sodium and water to maintain intravascular volume. The fractional excretion of sodium (FeNa) is a diagnostic tool used to evaluate the percentage of sodium filtered by the kidney that is excreted in the urine. In cases of prerenal AKI, where the renal tubules are functioning properly and effectively conserving sodium due to reduced renal perfusion, the FeNa is typically less than 1%. This indicates an efficient reabsorption of sodium by the tubules, suggestive of prerenal etiology rather than intrinsic kidney damage, where FeNa would generally be greater due to impaired tubular function. Prerenal Azotemia Characteristics: Low tubular flow rate and increased renal medullary recycling of urea often cause a disproportionate elevation of the BUN relative to creatinine. Causes of disproportionate BUN elevation include gastrointestinal bleeding, hyperalimentation, increased tissue catabolism, and glucocorticoid use. Fractional Excretion of Sodium (FeNa): FeNa is less than 1% in prerenal azotemia, indicating avid sodium reabsorption by the tubules. High FeNa (>1%) might still occur in conditions such as chronic kidney disease (CKD) or due to the effects of diuretics. Diagnostic Use of FeNa: While low FeNa is suggestive of effective intravascular volume depletion, it should not be used as the sole indicator for volume management. The diagnostic utility of FeNa can be affected by factors like diuretic use, which can elevate FeNa despite hypovolemia. Response to Fluids: The response of urine output to fluid administration (either crystalloid or colloid) can be diagnostic and therapeutic, helping to distinguish prerenal azotemia from intrinsic AKI. Urine Osmolality and Concentrating Ability: In prerenal azotemia, urine osmolality is often greater than 500 mOsm/kg, reflecting an intact ability to concentrate urine due to effective tubular function and elevated serum vasopressin levels. Loss of urine concentrating ability, indicated by urine osmolality less than 350 mOsm/kg, is common in AKI affecting tubules and interstitium but is not specific to prerenal conditions. Explanation of other options: Ultrasound (USG) of the kidneys typically shows significant kidney size differences (Option A): Prerenal AKI is caused by hypoperfusion , not structural kidney abnormalities. Renal ultrasound is usually normal in prerenal AKI. Kidney size differences are more commonly seen in chronic kidney disease (CKD) or congenital anomalies . Creatinine clearance is usually significantly decreased in prerenal AKI (Option B):Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is reduced due to low renal perfusion, but creatinine clearance improves rapidly with hydration . If persistent low clearance is observed despite fluid resuscitation, it suggests intrinsic renal damage (e.g., acute tubular necrosis) rather than prerenal AKI. In prerenal AKI, the urine usually shows high sodium concentration due to impaired tubular function (Option D): In prerenal AKI, urine sodium is low ( due to active sodium reabsorption . High urine sodium (>40 mEq/L) is seen in intrinsic AKI , where tubular dysfunctionprevents sodium reabsorption. Key Takeaway: Prerenal AKI is characterized by FeNa 20:1, high urine osmolality, and low urine sodium. It is reversible with fluid resuscitation, unlike intrinsic AKI.

text: The AKIN (Acute Kidney Injury Network) and RIFLE (Risk, Injury, Failure, Loss, End-stage kidney disease) criteria are used for the classification of which of the following conditions?
expl: Explanation: The RIFLE and AKIN criteria are internationally recognized, standardized classification systems specifically designed to define and stage the severity of Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) . Purpose and Utility These criteria provide a uniform language for clinicians and researchers to: Diagnose AKI Grade its severity (from mild to severe). Predict prognosis based on the stage. Guide management decisions , such as the need for renal replacement therapy (dialysis). Both systems use changes in Serum Creatinine (SCr) and Urine Output (UO) from baseline to categorize AKI into stages of increasing severity. The fundamental principle is assessing the rapid decline in kidney function over hours to days, which is the hallmark of AKI. This is distinct from chronic kidney disease (CKD), which develops over months to years. RIFLE Classification Table for Acute Kidney Injury (AKI): AKIN (Acute Kidney Injury Network) Classification Table for AKI: Explanation of other options: Chronic kidney failure (Option B): CKD is classified based on the persistent reduction in Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) over 3 months or more, typically using the KDIGO (Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes) CKD stages, not the RIFLE/AKIN criteria. Acute glomerulonephritis (Option C): While AGN can cause AKI, its diagnosis relies on specific findings like hematuria, proteinuria, and often a kidney biopsy. The RIFLE/AKIN criteria would only be used to grade the severity of the AKI resulting from the glomerulonephritis. Nephrotic syndrome (Option D): This is defined by heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, edema, and hyperlipidemia. It is a distinct clinical syndrome, not classified by AKI staging systems. Key Takeaways: RIFLE and AKIN are staging systems for Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) . They utilize Serum Creatinine and Urine Output to define stages of severity. The current standard is the KDIGO criteria , which integrated and refined the RIFLE and AKIN systems. References: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for Acute Kidney Injury.

text: A 45-year-old man feels unwell following a sore throat and cough. He has a blood pressure of 170/90 mm Hg. Dipstick of his urine reveals blood ++ and protein ++. His blood tests show:Hb 10.5 g/dl, MCV 85 fl, WBC 7000/mm3, platelets 200000/mm3, sodium 135 mmol/l, potassium 4.2 mmol/l, urea 50 mmol/l, creatinine 2.6 mg/dl, ALT 25 (5-35) U/l, AST 35 (A-35) U/l, ALP 75 (20-120) U/l, GGT 30 (D-35) U/l, Bilirubin 0.8 mg/dl, Albumin 3.8 (3.5-5) g/dl, calcium 8 mg/dl, phosphate 4.5 mg/dl. C3 - 0.5 g/L (0.8 - 1.6), C4 - 0.17 g/L (0.15 - 0.55). C3 nephritic factor is positive.Ultrasound scan of his kidneys reveal left kidney of 8.5 cm and right kidney of 9.3 cm. What is the diagnosis?
expl: The given patient has clinical features of glomerulonephritis. On blood examination he has low Serum C3, Normal C4 and C3 nephritic factor. If we refer above, we saw that the glomerulonephritis can be classified based on the status of immune activation and complement levels. Furthermore, if we look into the causes of MPGN in the previous question, we can see that all the diseases causing Type I MPGN will cause immune activation and complement consumption causing low C3 and C4. Type II MPGN needs mention here. It is now called Dense Deposit Disease and is included under the class of C3 Glomerulopathies. The other C3 Glomerulopathy is C3 Glomerulonephritis. Both have MPGN in renal biopsy. But DDD will have a dense deposit causing ribbon like appearance and is a disease of the young, where as C3 Glomerulopathy lacks it and occurs in elderly. Both are characterized by activation of alternate complement pathway either by genetic mutation or by presence of paraproteins. So the C3 levels will be low and C4 will be normal and C3 Nephritic factor will be present. Here IF will show only C3, but no immunoglobulin. So Type I will have low C3 and C4. But type II will have low C3, Normal C4 and C3 Nephritic factor and biopsy will not be showing any immunoglobulin deposited. In PSGN, C3 and C4 will be low, but C3 nephritic factor will be absent. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 314, Pg: 2341.

text: A 70-year-old man with no previous past medical history presents with a BP of 180/100 mm Hg, frothy urine and peripheral oedema. There is 1+ blood and 3+ protein on urinalysis. 24-hour protein loss is 5 grams. Plasma albumin is 2.5 g/dL. Plasma C3 is 0.1 (low). Plasma creatinine is 1.80 mg/dl. A renal biopsy is performed. ANA is negative. ESR is 110. Which of the following is most likely to be found on the biopsy?
expl: This is patient has low C3 levels. So we may tend to think of PSGN. But here, there is no history of sore throat or preceeding streptococcal illness. Another point against PSGN is the presence of nephrotic range proteinuria which is very rare in PSGN. So the answer is MPGN. We should know that mesangiocapillary glomerulonephritis and membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis are the same and is just a histologic diagnosis and noy etiologic. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 314, Pg: 2341.

text: A patient underwent renal biopsy for nephrotic syndrome. His biopsy showed collapsed glomerular capillary and scarring focally. What is he likely suffering from?
expl: This is the typical histology of FSGS. There are certain varients described. Endocapillary hypercellularity: Associated with heavy proteinuria. Collapsing glomerulopathy: Rapid decline in renal function Glomerular tip lesion: Associated with a good prognosis. Idiopathic membranous nephropathy is associated with uniform thickening of basement membrane with IgG and C 3 deposited, silver staining shows silver staining spikes and dense sub epithelial deposits on electron microscopy. Diabetic nephropathy is also associated with thickening of basement membrane. There will be measngial expansion and Kimmelstein Wilson nodules. Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis causes of nephritic syndrome or nephritic-nephrotic syndrome and is associated with mesangial and endocapillary proliferation. Reference: Harrison's principles of internal medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 314, Pg: 2332-2343.

text: An 18-year-old male is admitted with a history of haematuria and facial swelling. Two weeks ago he complained of a sore throat which was very bad and persistent. On examination there is facial and ankle oedema. His blood pressure is marginally elevated at 150/90. Investigations show haematuria and red cell casts. Blood urea is elevated. C3 and C4 levels are reduced. Abdominal ultrasound shows normal sized kidneys. What is the diagnosis?
expl: This patient has an antecedent sore throat followed by an acute nephritic syndrome, characterized by hematuria, proteinuria and hypertension. Among the options, Post streptococcal glomerulonephritis is the best answer. IgA Nephropathy is also a nephritic syndrome characterized by hematuria during or immediately after an upper respiratory infection. PSGN develops after a period of 1-3 weeks after pharyngitis. PSGN: Typical age group is 2-14 years of age. In developed countries it can affect elderly. Pharyngitic strains of streptococci predate the infection. The streptococcal antigens proposed to be responsible are Streptococcal Pyrogenic Exotoxin B(SPEB) and Nephritis Associated Plasmin Receptor(NPlR). Antibiotic treatment does not alter the development of PSGN. Sub clinical nephritis is 4-5 times more common and manifests as asymptomatic hematuria and low C3. Flank pain is a common symptom due to stretching of the renal capsule. Positivity for RA factor, ANCA, Cryoglobulins, low C3 etc.., can be seen. ASO titre, Anti DNAse B and Anti hyaluronidase help in diagnosis. Biopsy shows both sub epithelial humps and sub endothelial deposits and mesangial proliferation. Treatment is supportive. RPGN and ESRD are rare in children. Elderly patients up to 60% develop renal failure and ESRD. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st edition, Ch: 314, Pg: 2337.

text: A 10-year-old child presents with flank pain, fatigue, and red-colored urine. Investigations reveal more than 20 RBCs per high-power field, with microscopy showing dysmorphic RBCs. What is the most probable diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The presentation of flank pain, fatigue, hematuria with >20 dysmorphic RBCs/hpf on microscopy is consistent with Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis (PSGN). Dysmorphic RBCs on urine microscopy signify glomerular bleeding , a hallmark of PSGN. PSGN is an acute glomerulonephritis that develops after a streptococcal infection , caused by immune complex deposition in the glomeruli and the resulting inflammatory response. Explanations of other options: Minimal change disease (Option A): This type of nephrotic syndrome shows heavy proteinuria with only minimal alterations on light microscopy. It usually presents with proteinuria and oedema, with blood pressure being normal or mildly increased. Gross hematuria, flank pain, and dysmorphic RBCs are not typical features. UTI (Option C): Although a urinary tract infection may lead to hematuria, it usually does not show dysmorphic RBCs on urine microscopy. Moreover, UTIs are generally associated with symptoms like dysuria and increased frequency, which are not reported here. Bladder calculi (Option D): Bladder stones can produce hematuria, but they do not account for dysmorphic RBCs, which are a marker of glomerular disease. Furthermore, the pain from bladder stones is usually felt in the lower abdomen or suprapubic area rather than in the flanks.

text: A 15-year-old girl has nephrotic syndrome due to minimal change in glomerulonephritis. What is the likely long-term outcome?
expl: Minimal change disease usually responds well to medical treatment, with response to corticosteroids usually within the first month. 90-95% of children with minimal change disease achieve remission after 8 weeks of steroids. Relapse occurs in 70-75% children after 1 st remission 80-85% adults will achieve remission after 20-24 weeks of steroid therapy Relapses are less common in adults but less likely to respond to therapy Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 314, Pg: 2341.

text: A 35-year-old lady with SLE presents with significant proteinuria and hypoalbuminemia. A renal biopsy confirms diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis(WHO Class IV). Which of the following treatment regimes is recommended?
expl: Diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis is the commonest glomerulonephritis in SLE. There is mesangial and endothelial cell proliferation, polymorphonuclear cell infiltrate and granular subepithelial deposits of C3. It also carries the worst prognosis with progression towards renal failure. The currently recommended therapy is pulse intravenous corticosteroids in combination with pulse cyclophosphamide continued for at least 12 months after remission. Newer regimes include combinations of prednisolone and mycophenolate. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 314, Pg:2338.

text: Following a renal allograft transplantation, which of the following findings would be suggestive of graft rejection?

options.A: Rise of creatinine by more than 10% is suggestive of acute rejection.
options.B: Rise of creatinine by more than 5% is suggestive of acute rejection
options.C: Serum creatinine does not rise in acute renal allograft rejection.
options.D: Any rise in serum creatinine will be suggestive of acute renal allograft rejection.

ansText: Any rise in serum creatinine will be suggestive of acute renal allograft rejection.
expl: Explanation: In the post-renal transplant setting, serum creatinine is the earliest and most reliable marker of graft dysfunction. Even a slight, unexplained increase in serum creatinine from baseline should prompt immediate evaluation for rejection , unless an alternative cause (e.g., dehydration, drug toxicity, infection, obstruction) is clearly identified. This is because acute rejection reflects immune-mediated injury to the transplanted kidney, which impairs glomerular filtration long before symptoms appear. Acute Renal Allograft Rejection Definition: Acute renal allograft rejection occurs when the recipient's immune system recognizes the transplanted kidney as foreign. This triggers an immune response that causes inflammation and damage to the graft. The reaction can be mediated by T-lymphocytes (cellular rejection) or antibodies (antibody-mediated rejection). Clinical Presentation: Typically develops weeks to months after transplantation. Can occur later if immunosuppressive therapy is reduced or interrupted. Common clinical findings include: Decreased urine output. Tenderness or pain over the graft site. Fever, malaise, or general discomfort. Sometimes asymptomatic, with only a rise in serum creatinine indicating dysfunction. Any unexplained increase in serum creatinine should prompt evaluation for possible graft rejection. Types of Acute Rejection: Cellular (T-cell Mediated) Rejection Caused by activation of recipient T-lymphocytes against donor antigens. Leads to inflammation and injury of renal tubules and blood vessels. Histopathological findings include: Infiltration of lymphocytes. Tubulitis (lymphocytes within the tubular epithelium). Intimal arteritis (inflammation of arterial walls). Antibody-Mediated (Humoral) Rejection Mediated by recipient antibodies directed against donor endothelial antigens. Causes complement activation, endothelial injury, and microvascular thrombosis. Biopsy features include: Endothelial swelling and capillaritis. Fibrin deposition within small vessels. Positive C4d staining indicating complement activation. Diagnosis: The gold standard for diagnosis is renal biopsy. Biopsy findings help classify the type and severity of rejection: Cellular rejection shows T-cell infiltration and tubulitis. Antibody-mediated rejection shows vascular injury and C4d deposition. Laboratory findings: Rising serum creatinine. Decreased urine output. Other causes such as dehydration, obstruction, drug toxicity, or infection should be excluded. Treatment: Key Takeaway Points:

The important ones are: Adaptive response to loss of renal mass as post nephrectomy, in obesity and in hyperfiltration. text: A patient underwent renal biopsy for evaluation of hematuria and hypertension. His biopsy showed mesangial and endocapillary proliferation, with immunoglobulin deposits in the sub endothelium and duplication of basement membrane with a tram track appearance. What is he likely suffering from?

options.D: Excessive activation of alternate complement pathway activation

expl: This appearance is typical of type I MPGN. Type I MPGN occurs secondary to diseases like SLE, Infective Endocarditis etc. The histology of IgA and Anti GBM disease are described above. Defects in alternate complement pathway causes C 3 Glomerulopathy , which includes dense Deposit disease(previously called Type II MPGN) and C 3 Glomerulonephritis. It is histologically characterized by lobular appearance of glomeruli with Complement deposition. The difference between C 3 glomerulonephritis and Dense deposit disease is that the latter contains electron dense deposits along the glomerular basement membrane. C 3 glomerulopathies are characterized by abnormal activation of alternate complement pathway by a factor called C 3 nephritic factor which prevents the cleavage of alternate pathway C 3 convertase. So there will be persistent complement activation causing low S C 3 but normal C 4 Reference: Harrisons principles of internal medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 314, Pg: 2340.

text: A 15-year-old boy presents with dark discoloration of urine. There is a history of upper respiratory tract infection two weeks earlier. If untreated, he may go on to develop:

options.B: Immune deficiency with normal complement(C3) levels

expl: The given patient has a nephritic syndrome(indicated by the hematuria) following a sore throat. So the diagnosis is most likely PSGN. The outcome of PSGN is complete recovery in 90-97% cases by 3-6 weeks of onset of the PSGN. Acute renal failure is very rare. In 3-10% cases, there may be persistent non nephrtic range proteinuria, microscopic hematuria or hypertension. The main of treatment in PSGN is to treat Hypertension and fluid overload and also treatment of the streptococcal infection. Low complement levels are common during the first week, but recovers. So if left untreated, it can lead to complications like hypertensive encephalopathy, pulmonary edema etc. Hypertensive encephalopathy can present as seizures or stroke like episodes. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st edition, Ch: 314, Pg: 2337.

text: A 42-year-old man has generalised oedema. Urine dipstick shows protein +++, blood -ve. Which one of the following findings is suggestive of amyloidosis?

options.D: Large numbers of granular casts, fat bodies and red cells in the urine

expl: The presence of anasarca, proteinuria and absence of RBC in urine suggests diagnosis of Nephrotic syndrome. Amyloidosis is a known cause of nephrotic syndrome. Amyloidosis occurs due to the deposition of light chain of immunoglobulins. It occurs with myeloma, lymphoproliferative disorders, Waldenstrom's macroglobulinemia. Amyloidosis can also occur in MGUS and smouldering myeloma. The clonal plasma cells produce immunoglobulin, which will be fragmented by macrophages so that they can self aggregate and get deposited as AL amyloid. It is usually formed of the lambda light chain. 10% of patients with AL amyloid have overt myeloma. The paraprotein(Light chain or whole immunoglobulin) in Myeloma associated amyloidosis can be detected by SPEP or urine BJP. But if the quantity of immunoglobulin is not sufficient, SPEP will be negative and immunofixation electrophoresis or quantification of free light chains. AL Amyloidosis often has other manifestations like cardiomyopathy, neuropathy etc in addition to renal involvement. AA amyloidosis can also present as nephrotic syndrome. It is seen with chronic inflammatory diseases like Ankylosing Spondylitis, Rheumatoid Arthritis, Familial Mediterranean fever etc. Diagnosis of AL Amyloidosis can be done by biopsy of liver or kidney in 90% and abdominal fat pad in 70%. Serum light chain can be used for following up the disease. In AL amyloidosis renal impairment improves with treatment of myeloma. But in AA amyloidosis, it progresses to daialysis dependence in majority of cases. Abnormal liver function can cause anasarca, but here urine albumin will be negative. Cryoglobulinemia causes nephritis rather than nephrotic syndrome. Granular cast RBC in urine is a feature of nephritic syndrome. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st edition, Ch:112, Pg:880.

text: A patient undergoes investigation for chronic upper urinary tract obstruction with intravenous urography. The patient should be informed about which severe complication?
expl: Intravenous urography will usually demonstrate the site, cause and degree of obstruction and is much less operator dependent than ultrasound since the number of images checked by the clinician is equal to the number of images reported by the radiologist. Its major disadvantage is that the technique carries a mortality owing to contrast hypersensitivity reactions of perhaps 1 in 200 000. It also involves an intravenous injection, exposure to radiation(of particular concern in pregnant women and children), worsening of pain due to the diuretic effect of contrast medium when an upper tract(or tracts) is obstructed and the potential for contrast nephrotoxicity. Patients with impaired renal function, particularly those with diabetes and perhaps patients with myelomatosis, are at particular risk. Such risk is minimised by employment of low osmolality contrast medium and the avoidance of prior dehydration. These procedures do not carry risk of contrast-induced acute kidney injury in patients with renal insufficiency. Radionucleide scan is used for understanding differential function of kidneys. Voiding cystourethrography is used for reflux nephropathy and bladder and urethral obstruction. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st edition, Ch:319, Pg:2376.

text: A 30-year-old female with chronic urinary tract infections presents for investigations. Ultrasound scan reveals scarring over the renal calyces. Which one of the following is most likely?
expl: History of recurrent urinary tract infections with renal scarring over the renal calyces is typical of Reflux Nephropathy. It is a type of chronic interstitial nephritis. It is due to Vesico Ureteral reflux(VUR), from the bladder to one or both of the ureters due to incompetent vesicoureteral valve. VUR causes renal scarring, tubular dysfunction and secondary FSGS. Often associated with recurrent urinary tract infection. VUR is often asymptomatic and is common in females and diagnosed during pregnancy or other routine evaluation. Hypertension is common. Proteinuria may be moderate. Ultrasound shows focal scarring over areas of clayces with areas of compensatory hypertrophy. Confirmation is by DMSA scan, MRI or CT. Re implantation of ureters is indicated if renal scarring has not occurred and with high grade reflux. Maintenance of sterile urine with prophylactic antibiotics and ACEI or ARBs for proteinuria may retard the progression. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21 st edition, Ch:316, Pg:2361-2362
