text: A 30-year-old woman presented with a history of nephrotic syndrome diagnosed when she was 4 years old. There was no family history of renal disease. An initial renal biopsy performed showed minimal-change disease. She was treated with steroids and was determined to be steroid-dependent. Subsequent trials of cyclosporine and cyclophosphamide failed to improve her condition and she was referred for additional evaluation. She has a second renal biopsy. Light microscopic examination showed a patchy but striking vacuolar change in the renal tubular cells, with large nodular aggregates of foamy cells. Intracellular accumulation of several glycosphingolipids was suspected. Which one of the following is likely?
expl: Accumulation of vacuoles in tubular epithelial cells and proteinuria is seen in Fabry’s disease. Inheritance of Anderson Fabry disease is usually X linked recessive. A rare, inherited metabolic disease in which a glycolipid, ceramide trihexoside, accumulates in blood vessels, as well as in numerous tissues and organs. The excessive amounts present in the kidneys and other organs impairs their function. It is due to the absence of alpha galactosidase A. Patients present with the skin lesions(angiokeratoma corporis diffusum), small red spots seen on the lower abdomen, thighs and scrotum, corneal opacities, episodes of fever, primary paraesthesia of the extremities and peripheral oedema and renal failure. It is prevalent in males, who present with full-blown syndrome. Females are more likely to present with a partial form. The vacuoles appear as Zebra bodies under electron microscope. Urinalysis shows oval fat bodies and maltese cross response under polarization microscope. Angiokeratoma corporis diffusum Reference: Harrison's Principles of internal medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 314, Pg: 2345.

text: Which of the following is most likely to cause CKD?
expl: All the other conditions cause acute renal failure. Berger's disease(IgA nephropathy) is associated with chronic renal failure in up to 30% of adult cases. It is the commonest glomerular disease worldwide. It usually follows a viral upper respiratory tract infection. Heavy proteinuria, renal failure and hypertension indicate a poor prognosis. Option A: Leptospirosis, also called Weil's disease, is spread by contact with infected rat urine. Features include meningitis, myocarditis, acute renal failure and haemolytic anemia. Option B: Haemolytic uraemic syndrome is associated with acute damage and occlusion of small blood vessels(arterioles and capillaries) in the kidney. Thrombotic microangiopathy associated with Escherichia coli infection(especially O157 serotypes) is now the most common cause of acute renal failure in children in developed countries. Option C: Vancomycin is a bactericidal antibiotic. Indications are limited to serious infections such as endocarditis and septicaemia. It is nephrotoxic and can precipitate acute renal failure. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21 st edition, Ch:314, Pg:2339.

text: The mechanism of action of Patiromer?
expl: Novel intestinal potassium binders have recently become available for the management of hyperkalemia. These agents appear to lack the intestinal toxicity of SPS (Sodium Polystyrene Sulfonate). Patiromer is a nonabsorbed polymer provided as a powder for suspension, which binds K+ in exchange for Ca2+. In healthy adults, patiromer causes a decrease in urinary potassium, magnesium, and sodium excretion, suggesting the binding of the polymer to these cations in the intestine; notably, a side-effect of the medication is hypomagnesemia. ZS-9 is an inorganic, nonabsorbable crystalline compound that exchanges both Na+ and H+ ions in exchange for K+ and NH4 + in the intestine. These agents promise to revolutionize the management of both chronic and acute hyperkalemia. In particular, the availability of safe, well-tolerated potassium binders is expected to allow for greater intensity of RAAS inhibition in both renal and cardiac disease Reference: Harrisons Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:53 Pg: 355

text: A 40-year old woman from southern India has severe lymphedema of her right lower extremity and left breast. text: The work-up of a 25-year-old hotel worker shows the following profile: 1. HbsAg = Negative 2.Anti HBsAg= Negative 3.HBeAg = Negative 4.Anti Hbe = Negative 5.Total anti-HBc = IgG positive What is the diagnosis?

text: A patient who is a known case of CKD was presented to the OPD with bilateral oedema. On urine examination showed elevated albumin. His BP was on the higher side. What is the likely treatment for his hypertension?
expl: Explanation: Telmisartan (an ARB) is the best choice as it provides both blood pressure control and renal protection while avoiding ACEI-related cough. Hypertension is highly prevalent in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) , particularly in advanced stages where 80-85% are affected. The combination of increased vascular resistance, volume overload, and impaired autoregulation of glomerular pressure leads to further renal injury. A key feature in this patient is albuminuria , which reflects intraglomerular hypertension and glomerular damage. The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) plays a central role in CKD-related hypertension. ACE inhibitors (ACEIs) and angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) are the preferred agents because they: Cause efferent arteriolar dilation Reduce intraglomerular pressure Lower proteinuria (albuminuria) Slow progression of CKD Propranolol (Option A): Non-selective beta-blocker. While it lowers BP, it does not reduce albuminuria or protect the kidney. Metoprolol (Option B): Cardioselective beta-blocker, useful in heart disease but not first-line in CKD with proteinuria. Enalapril (Option C): An ACE inhibitor that is effective, but ARBs like Telmisartan are often preferred due to better tolerability (avoiding dry cough/angioedema).

text: A CKD patient undergoing pyeloplasty. What is the best suited post op analgesic?
expl: The best analgesic for a patient with CKD is acetaminophen among the given options. NSAIDS are contraindicated in renal impairment. The normal glomerular filtration pressure is maintained by dilation of the afferent arteriole by prostaglandins and constriction of the efferent arteriole by Angiotensin II, in case of reduced perfusion pressure within the autoregulatory range. If NSAIDS are used, loss of vasodilatory prostaglandins occur and the glomerular capillary pressure decreases and the GFR falls. ARBs or ACEI cause reduction in Angiotensin II and leads to loss of constriction of efferent arteriole and reduced glomerular capillary pressure and the GFR falls.

text: Which of the following statements is false regarding CKD?

options.A: CKD poses risk for bleeding as well as thrombosis.
options.B: Uremic peripheral neuropathy occurs in stage 4 CKD
options.C: Glucose metabolism is impaired in CKD.
options.D: Uremic pruritis improves dramatically with dialysis.

ansText: Uremic pruritis improves dramatically with dialysis.
expl: Dermatological manifestations in CKD include hyperpigmentation due to accumulation of Urochromes. Most of the cutaneous abnormalities improve with dialysis, but pruritis does not fully improve. Hyperphosphatemia can contribute to itch. Kappa opioid receptrs have shown to be promising in CKD pruritis. CKD increases the risk of bleeding by impairment of platelet aggregation, adhesion and impaired action of Platelet factor III and also prothrombin consumption. Thrombosis is common in conditions where there is nephrotic range proteinuria. Desmopressin may be used to gtemporarily improve bleeding. Optimal dialysis will improve bleeding time. Uremic neuromuscular diseases become prominent after stage 3 CKD. Insomnia, memory disturbance, hiccups, cramps, twitching are the early manifestations. Uremic peripheral neuropathy begins at stage 4 CKD, with sensory more than motor, distal more than proximal, lower limb more than upper limb. CKD causes mild glucose intolerance and does not require treatment. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 311, Pg: 2317, 2318.

MDRD for measuring eGFR 5.CKD EPI measurement of EGFR: MDRD and CKD EPI measure the e GFR, Cockcroft and Gault measures the CR Clearance. The Kidney Disease Improving Global Outcomes workgroup recommends estimated GFR(eGFR) formulae as the primary method for evaluating GFR. They recommend using the 2009 CKD-Epidemiology(EPI) Collaboration creatinine equation (https://www.kidney.org/content/ckd-epi-creatinineequation-2009). The creatinine clearance(CrCl) is approximately 100 mL/min/1.73 m 2 in healthy young women and 120 mL/min/1.73 m 2 in healthy young men. The creatinine clearance declines by an average of 0.8 mL/min/yr. after age 40 years as part of the aging process, but this is variable Option B: Creatinine clearance can also be estimated using the Modification of Diet in Renal Disease(MDRD) Study equation, but multiple studies across many populations show that the CKD-EPI equation is more accurate. Option C: Cockcroft Gault formula, is still commonly used to determine drug dosing, but it was developed before the standardization of creatinine assays currently in use today and thus, its use is not recommended. Option D: A Kidney Failure Risk(KFR) equation has been devised to predict the risk of progression to stage 5 dialysis-dependent kidney disease. It is therefore a prognostic score. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 311, Pg: 2311

text: Which of the following statements regarding CKD is wrong?

options.A: Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of mortality in CKD.
options.B: Heart failure can occur due to systolic or diastolic failure.
options.C: Pulmonary edema in CKD is always associated with high PCWP
options.D: Absence of hypertension in CKD is associated with adverse outcome and poor prognosis in CKD.

ansText: Pulmonary edema in CKD is always associated with high PCWP
expl: A special form of "low Pressure" pulmonary edema is seen in CKD patients. It manifests as exertional dyspnoea and is associated with bat wing in chest X-ray. It is associated with normal or mildly elevated PCWP. It is due to the excessive permeability of the alveolar membrane due to the uremia. It responds well to dialysis. CKD is associated with systolic dysfunction, diastolic dysfunction, left ventricular hypertrophy or cardiomyopathy. Hypertension develops early in the course of CKD. Absence of hypertension indicates left ventricular dysfunction and is associated with adverse outcome. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 311, Pg: 2315.

text: A 54-year-old man is admitted to the intensive therapy unit with left ventricular failure post- myocardial infarction. Despite prompt activity including angioplasty within a few minutes of the onset of chest pain, his systolic BP on admission to the unit was only 80 mmHg, with a pulse of 105/min. The team decide to insert an intra-aortic balloon pump timed to coincide with the dicrotic notch. What does the dicrotic notch refer to?
expl: The systolic part in the pulse wave is contributed by the percussion wave, the tidal wave and the end marked by the dicrotic notch. The dicrotic notch refers to a secondary upstroke in the downward part of the pulse wave which corresponds with closure of the aortic valve. Intra-aortic balloon pumps deflate during systole which then increases forward blood flow because of the reduction in afterload. The pump then re-inflates during diastole, increasing the blood flow to coronary arteries. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page

text: A 45-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her daughter because she saw something moving in her mother's eye. The patient is visiting from Africa where she lives in the rainforest. The patient reports some occasional eye swelling and redness. On examination, you find a worm in the subconjunctiva see Figure .Which of the following medications is indicated for therapy?
expl: This patient has loiasis caused by the African eye worm Loa loa. It is endemic to the rain forests of Central and West Africa. Microfilaria circulate periodically in blood with macrofilaria living in subcutaneous tissues including the subconjunctiva. Loiasis is often asymptomatic in indigenous regions with recognition, as in this case, only with visualized macrofilarial migration. Angioedema and swelling may occur in affected areas. Diethylcarbamazine (DEC) is effective treatment for the macro- filarial and microfilarial stages of disease. Multiple courses may be necessary. Albendazole and ivermectin are effective in reducing microfilarial loads but are not approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration. There are reports of deaths in patients with heavy loads of microfilaria receiving ivermectin. Terbinafine is the treatment for ringworm. Voriconazole is an antifungal with no activity against worms. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch: 233Pg 1783-1784

text: A 39-year-old healthy woman has a faint systolic murmur on physical examination. An echocardiogram is performed, and she is found to have a bicuspid aortic valve. In explaining the meaning of this finding to her, the most appropriate statement is that?

options.A: An aortic valve replacement is eventually likely to be required.
options.B: Other family members are not likely to have the same condition
options.C: She should be treated with a cholesterol-lowering agent
options.D: Down syndrome is a common association of this condition

ansText: An aortic valve replacement is eventually likely to be required.
expl: Bicuspid aortic valve is perhaps the most common form of congenital heart disease in adults (0.5-1.4% of population). Bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) tends to occur sporadically although it can also be inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. The prevalence of BAV disease among first-degree relatives of an affected individual is ~10%. Complications that can occur in BAV include aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation and increased risk of aortic dissection. Aortic aneurysm may also be coexistent with BAV. Bicuspid valves have a propensity to wear out and calcify with aging . So an aortic valve replacement is eventually likely to be required in the 5th and 6th decades of life. BAV is seen in association with turner's syndrome . Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 20 th edition, ch:256 pg:1803,1804,1807

text: Which among the following statements is false?

options.C: Immunosuppression is required lifelong for patients after transplant, except if donated by an identical twin or simultaneous kidney-bone marrow transplantation.
options.D: ATG and Alemtuzumab are used as depleting agents

ansText: In renal transplantation, Kidneys with high KDPI are allocated to those expected to have high post-transplant survival.
expl: Kidney Donor Profile Index(KDPI) is a score designed to estimate the risk of graft survival, ranging from 0-100%. Lower KDPI is associated with lesser chance of rejection. KDPI of Living donor transplants do well than deceased donor transplant. Immunosuppression is not required for identical twin and combined kidney-bone marrow transplant. Induction therapy will be done with depleting agents like ATG or Alemtuzumab or non-depleting agents directed against IL2 receptors to reduce the risk of acute rejection. Reference: Harrison's principles of internal medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 313, Pg: 2325-2328.

text: A patient received high-dose corticosteroid therapy. A few days later, he came with complaints of black discharge from the nose. On examination, he also had periorbital swelling and eschar formation on the nasal mucosa. What is the likely causative organism?
expl: Explanation: The given clinical features of black discharge from the nose along with periorbital swelling and eschar formation on the nasal mucosa in a patient receiving high-dose corticosteroid therapy, is suggestive of mucormycosis caused by fungi of the order Mucorales. Explanation of other options: Candida (Option A): Candidiasis presents in three main forms. Cutaneous and mucosal disease includes thrush, vulvovaginitis, diaper rash, intertriginous infections, and nail involvement such as onychomycosis and paronychia. Systemic candidiasis occurs in immunocompromised patients and can affect multiple organs, including the kidneys, heart, and CNS, often associated with biofilm formation on prosthetic devices. Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis is a rare condition characterised by persistent granulomatous lesions on mucosal and skin surfaces, linked to immune defects such as impaired Th17 responses. Aspergillus (Option C): Aspergillosis presents in three major forms. Allergic forms include allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, marked by asthma, recurrent infiltrates, eosinophilia, and hypersensitivity reactions. Aspergilloma and colonization occur in pre-existing cavities or sites such as sinuses, ears, or nails, producing cough, hemoptysis, or remaining asymptomatic. Invasive aspergillosis affects immunocompromised patients, causing fever, cough, dyspnea, hemoptysis, and vascular invasion with necrosis and dissemination to multiple organs, often carrying a poor prognosis. Histoplasma (Option D): Histoplasmosis most often presents as acute pulmonary disease , resembling a flu-like illness with fever, cough, chest pain, and hilar lymphadenopathy, which usually resolves on its own, leaving calcified nodules. In some cases, it progresses to chronic pulmonary histoplasmosis , especially in older men with lung damage, mimicking tuberculosis. A minority, particularly immunocompromised or very young/old patients, may develop disseminated disease , with fever, anemia, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and mucocutaneous ulcers, often fatal without treatment.

text: A 30-year-old male is found to be positive for HBsAg and HBeAg and is diagnosed with chronic hepatitis B. The viral load of the patient was 2 x 100,000, and SGPT is found to be doubled. What is the appropriate management in this patient?
expl: Explanation: Tenofovir is a first-line potent antiviral agent for chronic hepatitis B with high efficacy and low resistance, recommended for long-term therapy. The patient meets the criteria for chronic hepatitis B infection, confirmed by persistent HBsAg and HBeAg positivity, elevated viral load (2 × 100,000), and raised SGPT indicating active liver inflammation. The goal in managing chronic HBV is to suppress viral replication, reduce hepatic inflammation, and prevent progression to cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma. Tenofovir is a nucleotide analog and one of the first-line oral agents for treating chronic HBV. It has high potency, a favorable resistance profile, and effectively reduces HBV DNA, normalizes ALT, and improves liver histology. It is administered once daily and typically continued for more than 40 weeks (usually 48-52 weeks or longer depending on clinical response). Tenofovir also has a better side effect profile compared to older drugs, although monitoring for renal dysfunction and hypophosphatemia is advised. Key drugs used in chronic Hepatitis B treatment include: Interferons: Peginterferon alfa-2a, interferon alfa-2b Nucleoside analogs: Entecavir, lamivudine, telbivudine Nucleotide analogs: Adefovir, tenofovir First-line oral agents: Entecavir, Tenofovir Second-line agents (less preferred due to resistance): Lamivudine, adefovir, telbivudine Duration of therapy is generally 48-52 weeks, with long-term therapy depending on viral suppression and liver response. Lifestyle modification is also critical: avoid alcohol, hepatotoxic drugs, and unregulated herbal medications. Explanation of other options: Lamivudine for 30+ weeks (Option A): Lamivudine is an older nucleoside analog that suppresses HBV replication but has a high risk of resistance and is considered a second-line agent. Hence, not preferred over tenofovir. Pegylated interferon for 52 weeks (Option C): Although pegylated interferon is used for finite-duration treatment, it is less tolerated, requires subcutaneous administration, and is less effective than oral agents like tenofovir in most patients. Combined pegylated interferon with lamivudine (Option D): Combination therapy does not offer significant advantage over monotherapy and increases the risk of side effects, making it less preferred in standard management protocols. Reference: Hepatitis B - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf

text: You are called to a cardiac arrest in the Emergency Department where a patient who is known to the dialysis unit has been brought by ambulance. On reviewing her drugs, you note that she is taking a statin, three antihypertensive agents, aspirin and has been receiving erythropoietin injections. Unfortunately, resuscitation is unsuccessful. Which of the following is the commonest cause of death in renal dialysis patients?
expl: Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in patients with CKD at all the stages. Hypertension and dyslipidemia are the risk factors that accelerate atherosclerosis in CKD. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st edition, Ch:311, Pg:2315

text: A 28-year woman who is 20 weeks pregnant is seen in the outpatient clinic and noted to have a sustained blood pressure of 180/95 mmHg. What is the most appropriate antihypertensive therapy for this patient?
expl: Methyldopa is the safest agent to use in the first and second trimester of pregnancy. Beta blockers may cause intrauterine growth retardation. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Principles, 20 th edition, ch:466 pg:3440,3441

text: A 51 year old presents with tiredness and heavy periods. She is known to drink large amounts of alcohol. Her investigations reveal: Hemoglobin 7.3 g/dl MCV 72 fL white cell count 7500/μL platelet count 250000/μL serum ferritin 7 μg/L, (15-300) She was commenced on oral iron therapy one month later but her hemoglobin concentration was 7.8 g/dl. What is the likely cause of the failure of her hemoglobin to respond?
expl: The likely explanation for failure of an iron deficiency anemia to respond iron therapy in a patient with heavy periods is poor compliance. Folate deficiency will cause a Megaloblastic picture with MCV>100 fL Sideroblastic anemia would cause an increase in serum iron and ferritin. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:97 Pg:752

text: You are asked to recommend management for a 27-year-old woman with secondary syphilis who is midway through her second trimester of pregnancy. The patient has a well-documented history of penicillin allergy. The recommended therapy for this patient is:

options.A: Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 14 days
options.B: Azithromycin 2.0 g orally as a single dose
options.C: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM or IV once daily for 10 days
options.D: Penicillin desensitization followed by a single intramuscular injection of 2.4 million units of benzathine penicillin

ansText: Penicillin desensitization followed by a single intramuscular injection of 2.4 million units of benzathine penicillin
expl: For treatment of syphilis in pregnancy, there are no recommended alternatives to penicillin for therapy. Doxycycline could cause dental staining in her child, and neither doxycycline nor azithromycin has been studied in this situation. As a result, pregnant, penicillin-allergic patients should be desensitized and treated as recommended for the stage of disease they have. There is no evidence that pregnant patients need treatment with higher doses or prolonged therapy. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 182 Pg: 1412

text: A hypertensive patient presents to the ER with palpitations, dyspnoea, BP 220/140 mmHg, and encephalopathy. Which of the following is NOT used in management?
expl: Explanation: This is a hypertensive emergency with target organ damage. First-line therapy includes IV antihypertensives (nicardipine, nitroprusside, labetalol, esmolol). Mannitol is used for raised ICP, not BP control. Hypertensive Crisis: Urgency: Severe BP >180/120 without organ damage → oral agents. Emergency: Severe BP + organ damage → IV antihypertensives, reduce MAP ≤25% in first hour. Explanation of Other Options: IV Nicardipine (Option A): Nicardipine → IV CCB, effective in hypertensive emergency. IV Esmolol (Option C): Esmolol → IV short-acting β-blocker, useful in aortic dissection. IV Sodium Nitroprusside (Option D): Nitroprusside → potent IV vasodilator, rapid control. Key Takeaway: Hypertensive emergency requires IV antihypertensives. Mannitol has no role.

text: A 50-year-old man has end stage renal failure due to diabetes. He receives 4 hours of haemodialysis, 3x weekly. His pressure is 180/105 mmHg pre-dialysis and 160/90 mmHg post dialysis. Pre-dialysis bloods show: Hb 10 g/dL sodium 132 mmol/l potassium 6.5 mmol/L urea 270 mg/dl creatinine 12.7 mg/dl calcium 8.6 mg/dl (Ref values: s. creat: 0.6-1.4 mg/dl; S. urea: 17-43 mg/dL; s. sodium: 135-145 mEq/L; S. potassium: 3.5-5 mEq/L; S. calcium: 8.8-10 mg/dl; S. phosphate: 3.0-4.5 mg/dL) What is the best management step?
expl: The high urea and creatinine, as well as hypertension suggests there is more room for dialysis. Although EPO or vit D supplements are probably beneficial, longer dialysis sessions would help clear the fluid overload and reno-toxins. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21 st edition, Ch:312, Pg:2323

text: A 40-year-old man is referred with gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GERD).Which of the following concerning GERD is correct?

options.A: Acid suppressant therapy should not be given continuously
options.C: Esophageal pH monitoring is a good guide to therapy
options.D: Symptoms do not correlate with mucosal status at endoscopy

ansText: Symptoms do not correlate with mucosal status at endoscopy
expl: Symptoms of GERD do not correlate with the mucosal appearances at endoscopy. PPIs can be given continuously where the diagnosis has been satisfactorily proven and relapse of symptoms persist after withdrawal. Although endoscopy can be performed in cases that are not clear cut or do not respond to proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), it is not mandatory. The doubt of Barrett's oesophagus can only be clarified with biopsy. Monitoring of pH is not a good guide to therapy. Symptomatic improvement is a good guide to the efficacy of therapy. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st , Ch: 323, Pg: 2429-2431

text: At what GFR should a patient of chronic kidney disease be prepared for maintenance dialysis?
expl: KDIGO Classification of CKD. Patient education and preparation for dialysis should be commenced by stage 4 CKD GFR of 15-29 ml/min/1.73m 2 falls in the category of stage 4 CKD as per KDIGO staging and it is in this stage the patient of CKD is prepared for dialysis In stage 5 i.e., 2 , Dialysis is STARTED. Indications for maintenance hemodialysis includes: Presence of uremic symptoms Hyperkalemia despite medical management Edema despite medical therapy Acidosis refractory to medical therapy Bleeding diathesis GFR 2 Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed., Ch: 311, Pg: 2320, Ch:312, Pg: 2321.

text: A 55 year old man had a renal transplant 2 years ago. He is on cyclosporine, prednisolone and tacrolimus. He now has several symptoms. Which one of the following is a side effect of cyclosporine?
expl: Cyclosporine is a Calcineurin inhibitor used as maintenance therapy to prevent transplant rejection . Side effects of cyclosporine: 2N+5H Nephrotoxicity Neuropathy Hyperkalaemia Hirsutism Hypertension Headache Hypomagnesaemia Hyperlipidemia Gum hypertrophy Tremors Tacrolimus is another Calcineurin inhibitor and the side effect profile is almost same, except that it causes hair loss and does not cause hirsutism or gingival hyperplasia. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 th edition, Ch:313, Pg:2328.

text: For maximal absorption, oral iron preparations should be taken
expl: Typically, for iron replacement therapy, up to 200 mg of elemental iron per day is given, usually as three or four iron tablets (each containing 50-65 mg elemental iron) given over the course of the day. Ideally, oral iron preparations should be taken on an empty stomach, since food may inhibit iron absorption. But gastrointestinal distress is the most prominent side effect presenting with abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, or constipation, leading to noncompliance. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 97, Pg: 751-752

text: Which Among the following persists after Dialysis?
expl: Indications for starting RRT(Renal replacement therapy)in patients with renal impairment are- Anorexia and nausea not attributable to other causes Malnutrition Electrolyte imbalance Fluid overload Encephalopathy and pericarditis. Hence these symptoms will improve after dialysis. Dialysis has no effect on peripheral neuropathy.

text: Which of the following is false?

options.A: Anaphylactoid reactions are common during the first dialysis.
options.B: It is mainly due to the dialyzer used.
options.C: Type B reaction is life threatening
options.D: Type A reaction is life threatening.

ansText: Type B reaction is life threatening
expl: Anaphylactoid reaction is common during first dialysis. It is mainly directed against the dialyzer used, esp cellulosic containing bio incompatible membranes. Type A: Immediate hypersensitivity reation. Occurs soon after initiation of treatment. May progress to anaphylaxis. Type B: Occurs several minutes after dialysis run. Non specific back and chest pain. Due to complement activation. Resolves over time with continued dialysis. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, Ch: 312, Pg: 2323.

text: A 65-year-old man is being considered for dialysis. Which of the following suggests that the patient should be considered for continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis(CAPD) rather than haemodialysis?
expl: Severe cardiac failure often leads to circulatory compromise(hypotension) during haemodialysis, hence such a patient would be better dialysed by CAPD. Recent inguinal surgery is a relative contraindication. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st edition, Ch:312, Pg:2323.

text: A 72-year-old man who had a bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement three years ago is reviewed.What antithrombotic therapy is he likely to be taking?

text: What is the most common delayed side effect seen after radiation therapy to the head and neck?
expl: Explanation: The most frequently observed late complication following radiation therapy for head and neck cancers is xerostomia, or dry mouth. Explanation for other options: Myelopathy (Option C): involves spinal cord dysfunction and is not a typical delayed effect of radiation therapy to the head and neck. Dysgeusia (Option D): means a distorted or altered sense of taste. Although taste disturbances may happen after head and neck radiation, xerostomia is more frequently seen as a delayed symptom. Reference: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7533405/

text: A 55-year-old male with ischaemic heart disease is seen for review. He reports that he has developed some muscle aches and pains and you attribute this to a myalgia associated with simvastatin. His Creatinine kinase is within the normal range. However, his dyslipidaemia is still sub-optimal and you wish to add in a further agent. Which of the following agents would not be an appropriate additional therapy for this patient in view of his presentation?
expl: This patient presents with a probable statin induced myalgia which often improves with time. Sometimes stopping therapy briefly or reintroducing a different statin may resolve the myalgia. Statin induced myositis is relatively uncommon. But, the risk of myositis and the potentially fatal rhabdomyolysis is increased with Gemfibrozil , in susceptible subjects in combination with a statin and as such should be avoided. Additional agents this patient can be prescribed could include Omega-3 fatty acids and Ezetimibe. Nicotinic acid is less used due to problems with flushing though can be useful particularly in hypertriglyceridaemia. Cholestyramine can also be used. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Principles, 20 th edition, ch:400 pg:2899,2901

text: A 26-year-old man has returned a few days earlier from a Nile cruise. He has begun suffering from profuse bloody diarrhoea. He opens his bowels several times per day, and there is blood and mucus mixed in with the motion each time. He is also complaining of dull abdominal pain. There is no past medical history of note. On further questioning he admits to buying fruit from local stalls at the river side. On examination he is pyrexial 37.8°C, and has generalized lower abdominal tenderness.Investigations show: Haemoglobin 12.1 g/dl(13.5-8) White cell count 11.4 x 10^9/L (4-10) Platelets 204 x 10^9/L (150-400) Sodium 139 mmol/l (134-143) Potassium 3.9 mmol/l (3.5-5) Creatinine 1.2 mg/dl Stool Blood+ White cells ++ Trophozoites+ Which of the following is the most appropriate initial therapy?
expl: This man has amoebic dysentery which occurs around seven days after exposure to Entamoeba histolytica. Acute amoebic dysentery is managed with a course of oral metronidazole or tinidazole, to be followed by a ten day course of diloxanide to eradicate colonization of the gut. With appropriate diagnosis and treatment, mortality from amoebiasis is less than 1%. Amoebic liver abscess may appear at any time from eight weeks after infection, and presents with night sweats, anorexia and right upper quadrant pain. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 223, Pg:1718

text: A 32-year-old man has Lipoprotein lipase deficiency. Which one of the following features is most likely?
expl: Mutations in the LPL gene (lipoprotein lipase) result in Familial Chylomicronemia This will prevent lipoprotein lipase from breaking down chylomicrons effectively, leading to high triglyceride levels in the plasma. Inherited in autosomal recessive fashion Other causes of Familial chylomicronemia include ApoC2 deficiency, ApoA5 deficiency and Lipase maturation factor deficiency. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 20 th edition Chapter:400 Page number:2893

text: Investigation of choice for Acanthamoeba infection is
expl: Examination of the CSF for trophozoites may be diagnostically helpful, but lumbar puncture may be contraindicated because of increased intracerebral pressure. CT frequently reveals cortical and subcortical lesions of decreased density consistent with embolic infarcts. In other patients, multiple enhancing lesions with edema may mimic the CT appearance of toxoplasmosis. Demonstration of the trophozoites and cysts of Acanthamoeba on wet mounts or in biopsy specimens establishes the diagnosis. Culture on non-nutrient agar plates seeded with Escherichia coli also may be helpful. Fluorescein- labeled antiserum is available from the CDC for the detection of protozoa in biopsy specimens Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch: 223Pg 1719

text: A patient presents with seizures. His CT head reveals multiple parenchymal cysts. Which of the following is correct regarding management in this case?

options.B: Steroids followed by Anti Parasitic drug

ansText: Steroids followed by Anti Parasitic drug
expl: The arrow in the MRI shows viable cysts in the brain parenchyma . It is characteristic of neurocysticercosis. The arrow in the MRI shows viable cysts in the brain parenchyma. It is characteristic of neurocysticercosis. The clinical manifestations of neurocysticercosis is mainly seizures. It can cause obstructive hydrocephalus by blocking CSF flow. Patients can present with features of raised ICP like head ache and papilledema. They can also lodge in the sub arachnoid space causing chronic meningitis, arachnoiditis, communicating hydrocephalus, hemorrhages or strokes. TREATMENT: Intestinal disease is treated with a single dose Praziquantal or Niclosamide. Neurocysticercosis: Antiepileptics should be started. Albendazole 15mg/kg for 8-28 days with or without Praziquantal 50-100mg/kg/day for 15-30 days . Combination is preferred for people with more than 2 lesions. Lesions in the subarachnoid space need prolonged treatment and here Methotrexate or anti TNF agents can be used as steroid sparing agents. High dose steroids are needed since antiparasitic drugs will elicit an inflammatory response. Steroids will enhance the first pass effect of Praziquantal and it should be co administered with Cimetidine. For multiple lesions and diffuse cerebral edema, steroids are the initial mainstay and antiparasitic drugs should be avoided. Surgery is the main treatment for ocular disease. Spinal disease may worsen with antiparasitic lesions and may lead to irreversible damage. Either medical or surgical treatment can be used for spinal disease.

text: A 20-year-old male with history of recurrent fevers since childhood comes to you. In addition to fever, he has repeated attacks of migratory myalgia with conjunctival congestion. Which inherited fever syndromes will you suspect?
expl: The inherited autoinflammatory disease where there is migratory myalgia and conjunctival congestion is TNF receptor associated periodic syndrome. It is an AD disorder. It responds better to steroids than colchicine. Etanercept can be used, but monoclonal antibodies to TNF should not be used. Mevalonate Kinase Deficiency is an AR disorder, involved in the synthesis of cholesterol, which is involved in proper localization and activation of pyrin inflammasome. In addition to fever, there will be painful cervical adenopathy, oral ulcers, and maculopapular rash in the palms and soles. Pleurisy is rare. IgD may be elevated, but not associated with the disease activity. Canakinumab is the treatment. Muckle-Well syndrome, Familial Cold Autoinflammatory Syndrome and Neonatal onset multisystem inflammatory disease are the three disorders grouped under Cryopyriniopathy or NLRP associated autoinflammatory disease. They are mostly AD. It is associate with the activation of NLRP inflammasome. Canakinumab or rilonacept are approved treatments. Muckle well syndrome is associated with fever, arthritis conjunctivitis and sensorineural hearing loss Familial Cold Autoinflammatory Syndrome develop fever , arthritis and conjunctivitis on exposure to cold. Neonatal Onset multisystem inflammatory disease is the most severe of the Cryopyrinopathies. It is associated with aseptic meningitis. It is due to de novo mutations. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 369, Pg: 2843

text: A 30-year-old man had progressive deafness and hematuria from childhood and had undergone renal transplant eight years ago for chronic renal failure. Examination revealed perceptive high-tone deafness and anterior lenticonus in both eyes. What is the likely diagnosis?
expl: This patient had developed chronic kidney disease in his early life itself with involvement of eyes and ears, suggestive of an inherited disorder. Among the given options Alport’s syndrome causes all of the above Alport's syndrome Genetics: X-linked inheritance of mutations in the α5(IV) collagen chain Characterised by a triad of Progressive hematuric nephritis Progressive perceptive high-tone hearing loss Ocular signs(cataracts, spherophakia and anterior lenticonus, dot and fleck retinopathy) Renal Biopsy: Early features: thin basement membranes on renal biopsy which thicken over time into multilamellations surrounding lucent areas that often contain granules of varying density-the so-called split basement membrane. Advanced disease: Tubules drop out, glomeruli scar and the kidney eventually succumbs to interstitial fibrosis. ADPKD is associated with Intracranial aneurysms, hepatic cysts, mitral valve prolapse, abdominal wall hernias and colonic diverticulae. NF is associated with stenosis of renal vessels. Romanoward syndrome is a congenital long QT syndrome without deafness. Jervell’s Syndrome is another congenital long QT syndrome with deafness. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal medicine, 21 st edition, Ch:314, Pg:2346

text: A 35-year man has been referred for management of hypertension. On examination, he had palpable kidneys. This was confirmed by abdominal ultrasound which showed multiple cysts. Which of the following is likely to be associated?
expl: A young hypertensive with palpable kidneys and cysts on ultrasound points to the diagnosis of ADPKD (autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease). Polycystic kidney disease is associated with increased levels of EPO which lead to polycythemia. Associations of ADPKD: Cardiovascular: Intracranial aneurysm (5 times more common than general population), can rupture to cause subarachnoid hemorrhage. Diffuse arterial dolichoectasia of the anterior and posterior cerebral circulation → predisposed to arterial dissection and stroke. Mitral valve prolapse. Insufficiency of the mitral, aortic, and tricuspid valves. Gastrointestinal: Colonic diverticula Abdominal wall hernia Polycystic liver disease Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Edition, Page Number 2350-2354.

text: A 56-year-old man presents with flank pain and haematuria. His plasma creatinine concentration is 3.2 mg/dl and renal ultrasound reveals bilateral 1-cm kidneys with multiple cysts. There are also cysts scattered through the liver. What is the cause of this condition?

options.B: Genetic defect in the gene encoding polycystin
options.C: Genetic defect in the von Hippel-Landau gene
options.D: Genetic defect in the gene encoding type-IV collagen

ansText: Genetic defect in the gene encoding polycystin
expl: Cysts in the kidney and liver Two other genes are identified to be responsible for AD PKD, GANAB and DNAJB11 genes in a small number of families. Here kidneys are normal sized and cysts are smaller and liver cysts are absent. The von Hippel-Landau gene is a tumour-suppressor gene on chromosome 3, defects which result in von Hippel-Landau syndrome. It is an AD disorder characterized by retinal and cerebellar hemangioblastomas. It is also characterized by clear cell Renal cell carcinoma, cystadenoma of epididymis and broad ligament and renal and pancreatic cysts. Patients with Alport's syndrome(a condition not associated with renal cysts) have mutations in the a-5 chain of type-IV collagen. Bilateral VUR results in scarred kidneys. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st edition, Ch:315, Pg:2350

text: A 37-year-old woman presents with collapse. She works in an office environment and it has been a particularly hot day. On examination in casualty she looks a little dehydrated. BP is 110/70 mmHg. The following serum electrolyte results are obtained;Na+ 134mmol/lK+ 2.9mmol/l Mg++ 0.57 mmol/l (0.75-1.05)HCO3- 34mmol/l. The 24 hour urine calcium is also reduced. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Gitelman's syndrome is due to a mutation in the thiazide-sensitive Na-Cl transporter in the distal convoluted tubule. It is associated with hypokalemia, hypomagnesaemia and raised serum bicarbonate levels. There is also hypocalciuria. Treatment is with potassium and magnesium replacement with or without potassium-sparing diuretics. Differentiation between Gitelman and Bartter's syndromes is made by measuring the urinary excretion of magnesium (which is high in Gitelman syndrome and normal in Bartter syndrome) and calcium (which is high in Bartter syndrome and low in Gitelman syndrome). Bartter's syndrome presents earlier with hypokalemic alkalosis and hypercalciuria, due to a mutation in the frusemide-sensitive Na+-K+-2Cl-transporter. Treatment is with potassium replacement, NSAIDs and sometimes ACE inhibitors. Liddle's syndrome is due to an activating mutation in the epithelialsodium channel (ENaC) which remains activated irrespective of aldosterone stimulation, and is associated with hypokalaemic alkalosis and resistant hypertension with low renin and aldosterone levels Gordon's syndrome is the opposite of Gitelman syndrome, presenting with hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis and hypertension. Conn's syndrome refers to primary aldosteronism due to aldosterone producing adenoma. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 350

text: A 28-year-old woman presents to casualty with flank pain and a 48-h history of dysuria. Her past medical history includes polycystic ovarian syndrome. There is haematuria and proteinuria on urine dipstick testing. Examination reveals a pyrexia of 38.1°C and flank pain. What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
expl: Presence of fever and flank pain, preceded by history of cystitis favors the diagnosis of a pyelonephritis. Presence of fever in a patient with cystitis points to the development of pyelonephritis. Gram-negative bacilli such as Escherichia coli or Klebsiella species are responsible in more than 95% of cases. Unusual organisms may be responsible if there has been a history of urethral instrumentation. Staphylococcal urinary sepsis is usually indicative of haematological seeding of infection. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 135, Pg: 1075.

text: All of the following are cause of salt losing nephropathy, except?
expl: Salt-losing nephropathies may lead to hyponatremia when sodium intake is reduced, due to impaired renal tubular function; typical causes include: reflux nephropathy interstitial nephropathies post obstructive uropathy medullary cystic disease recovery phase of acute tubular necrosis. Thiazide diuretics cause hyponatremia via a number of mechanisms, including polydipsia and diuretic-induced volume depletion. Notably, thiazides do not inhibit the renal concentrating mechanism, such that circulating AVP retains a full effect on renal water retention. In contrast, loop diuretics , which are less frequently associated with hyponatremia, inhibit Na+-Cl- and K+ absorption by the TALH, blunting the countercurrent mechanism and reducing the ability to concentrate the urine. Increased excretion of an osmotically active non reabsorbable or poorly reabsorbable solute can also lead to volume depletion and hyponatremia; important causes include glycosuria, ketonuria (e.g., in starvation or in diabetic or alcoholic ketoacidosis), and bicarbonaturia (e.g., in renal tubular acidosis or metabolic alkalosis, where the associated bicarbonaturia leads to loss of Na+). References: Harrisons Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:53 Pg: 342

text: A 32-year-old woman complains of weakness and lethargy. Clinical examination is normal with a blood pressure of 96/70 mmHg and no oedema. Her plasma creatinine concentration is 0.70 mg/dl and her potassium is 2.8 mmol/l. A blood test 3 years ago demonstrated a potassium concentration of 2.7 mmol/l. A urinary screen fails to reveal any diuretics. Renal ultrasound shows bilateral nephrocalcinosis. What is the probable tubular defect?

options.C: Genetic defect of the Na+-K+-2Cl- co-transporter
options.D: Pharmacological inhibition of the Na+-K+-2Cl- co-transporter

ansText: Genetic defect of the Na+-K+-2Cl- co-transporter
expl: Hypokalemia with nephrocalcinosis is seen in Bartter's syndrome. The mechanism we have already discussed above. It is indistinguishable from loop diuretic use. But since it is given that diuretic screen is negative, Bartter syndrome is a possibility. It is due to a genetic defect in Na-K-2Cl transporter in Thick ascending limb of loop of henle. To summarize, Aquaporin channels are expressed in the cortical collecting ducts and are involved in water handling. Defects result in diabetes insipidus. Carbonic anhydrase is expressed in the proximal tubule and is inhibited by acetazolamide; this is manifested biochemically by normal anion-gap metabolic acidosis. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine 21 st edition, page no.350,2293

text: Which of the following conditions does not present with hypokalemia?
expl: Explanation: Among the given options, hypokalemia is seen in all except RTA 4 . Type 4 Renal Tubular Acidosis (RTA 4), also called hyperkalemic RTA, is distinct in that it presents with hyperkalemia rather than hypokalemia. It results from reduced aldosterone levels or resistance to its action, causing defective secretion of hydrogen and potassium ions in the distal tubules, which leads to potassium retention, hyperkalemia, and metabolic acidosis . Explanations of other options: RTA1 (Type 1) (Option A): Distal renal tubular acidosis is caused by defective hydrogen ion excretion in the distal tubules, which also reduces potassium reabsorption, ultimately leading to hypokalemia . RTA2 (Type 2) (Option B): In proximal renal tubular acidosis, defective bicarbonate reabsorption in the proximal tubules increases sodium delivery to the distal nephron, which enhances potassium excretion in urine and results in hypokalemia. Ureterosigmoidostomy (Option D): In this surgical procedure, where the ureters are attached to the sigmoid colon, hypokalemia occurs as a result of potassium loss through the colonic lining (secretion) as well as renal potassium wasting. The kidney-related loss is the more significant contributor, driven by acidosis, volume depletion, and stimulation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.

text: A person collapses following a road traffic accident (RTA). You initiate CPR, and soon the rescue team arrives. Which is the correct action among the given options?

options.A: Perform 5 cycles of CPR at 30:2 before applying AED
options.B: Continue CPR while the AED is being attached
options.C: Stop CPR to allow AED paddles to be applied
options.D: Hand over the patient and leave the scene

ansText: Continue CPR while the AED is being attached
expl: Explanation: CPR must be continued without interruption until the AED is ready for use. Pausing chest compressions decreases perfusion and lowers survival chances. AED application should not be delayed or prioritized over CPR. Explanation of Other Options: Perform 5 cycles of CPR at 30:2 before applying AED (Option A): Incorrect, as AED should be applied immediately once available, not delayed. Stop CPR to allow AED paddles to be applied (Option C): Wrong approach, since interrupting CPR during AED preparation reduces perfusion and lowers survival. Hand over the patient and leave the scene (Option D): Inappropriate, as leaving before confirming safe transfer to the emergency team is both unethical and unsafe. Key Takeaways: During cardiac arrest management, uninterrupted CPR is critical until the AED is functional and ready to deliver a shock.

text: A patient who was involved in a road traffic accident (RTA) underwent ileal resection. He now presents with fatigue. Which of the following is NOT expected in this patient?
expl: Explanation of answer: Microcytic hypochromic anemia is typically seen in iron deficiency , not in vitamin B12 deficiency , which occurs after ileal resection and causes macrocytic anemia . The terminal ileum is essential for vitamin B12 absorption, facilitated by intrinsic factor. Ileal resection impairs this process, leading to vitamin B12 deficiency, which results in: Macrocytic anemia Neurological symptoms due to subacute combined degeneration (SACD) Proprioceptive loss and Romberg's sign Cytoplasmic-nuclear dys-synchrony on bone marrow biopsy Key Features of Vitamin B12 Deficiency (Post-Ileal Resection): Anemia Type: Macrocytic, not microcytic Neurologic: Peripheral neuropathy, sensory ataxia, SACD Histology: Hypersegmented neutrophils, megaloblastic changes Bone Marrow: Cytoplasmic maturation continues, but nuclear maturation is delayed → cyto-nuclear dys-synchrony (Option A ruled out) Romberg's sign: Positive due to dorsal column involvement (Option C ruled out) Subacute Combined Degeneration: Posterior and lateral column demyelination (Option D ruled out) Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK441923/

text: A 30-year-old male suffered a road traffic accident (RTA). A few days later, he presents with exaggerated right-sided extensor plantar reflex and increased right knee jerk. Which of the following additional findings is most likely in this patient?

options.A: Ankle clonus in the right foot
options.B: Proprioception lost in the left leg
options.C: Pain and temperature were lost in the right leg

ansText: Ankle clonus in the right foot
expl: Explanation of answer: These findings are consistent with an upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion. Clonus is a classic sign of upper motor neuron lesions, typically seen along with hyperreflexia and extensor plantar response. The signs described-exaggerated deep tendon reflexes (knee jerk) and extensor plantar response (Babinski sign)-are characteristic of an upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion affecting the right side. UMN lesions commonly occur in: Spinal cord trauma Stroke Multiple sclerosis Cerebral palsy One of the hallmark features of UMN lesions is clonus-involuntary rhythmic contractions typically seen at the ankle or patella when the muscle is stretched. Ankle clonus, therefore, is a logical and expected associated finding in this patient with right-sided UMN signs. Comparison of UMN Vs LMN Explanation of other options: Proprioception lost in the left leg (Option B): Proprioception is carried by the dorsal column, which ascends ipsilaterally in the spinal cord and decussates in the medulla. A right-sided spinal cord lesion would impair right-sided proprioception, not left-sided. Pain and temperature lost in the right leg (Option C): Pain and temperature sensations travel in the spinothalamic tract, which crosses at the level of entry into the spinal cord. A right-sided lesion would affect left-sided pain and temperature sensation, not right. Fasciculations in the right foot (Option D): Fasciculations are a sign of a lower motor neuron (LMN) lesion, not UMN. LMN signs include flaccid paralysis, muscle atrophy, fasciculations, and reduced reflexes; none of which match this case. Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK537305/ https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/neuroscience/lower-motor-neuron-lesion https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK541082/#

text: A 64-year-old man presents to casualty with severe chest pain. ECG shows anterior ST-segment elevation and he receives prompt thrombolysis with reteplase with good resolution of changes. He is commenced on aspirin, a β-blocker, an ACE inhibitor and a statin. His initial progress is complicated by further pain, worse with inspiration and movement and relief by non-steroidal drugs. You are called to see him on day 5 post infarct when he complains of shortness of breath on walking to the bathroom. He looks unwell with a cool periphery and resting tachycardia. Blood pressure is reduced at 90/50 mmHg. Jugular venous pressure is elevated to around 8 cm and rises with inspiration. His ECG shows preserved anterior R waves and anterolateral T-wave inversion together with sinus tachycardia. Chest X-ray shows an increase in the cardiothoracic ratio but clear lung fields. What is the most likely complication to have developed to account for this deterioration?
expl: Devastating complications still do occur following acute myocardial infarction. Cardiogenic shock tends to occur early following a large infarct (or in the presence of already impaired left ventricular function), typically in the first 24-48 hours. The development of acute mitral regurgitation or VSD is associated with severe pulmonary oedema. While they would give rise to an elevation of jugular venous pressure, Kussmaul's sign would not be present (increase in JVP with inspiration). Although pericarditis is common following an MI, and in particular anterior MI, tamponade occurs relatively infrequently. Chest X-ray shows a large heart with normal pulmonary vasculature. Echocardiography is vital to assist in the management of such a patient and permits easy differentiation of the possible causes of haemodynamic collapse. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Principles, 20 th edition, ch:269 pg:1883,1884

text: What is the gene mutation associated with Marfan syndrome?
expl: Explanation: Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant connective tissue disorder caused by mutations in the FBN1 gene on chromosome 15, which encodes fibrillin-1 , an important component of elastic fibres. Defective fibrillin leads to abnormal connective tissue, causing skeletal (tall stature, long limbs), ocular (lens subluxation), and cardiovascular manifestations (aortic root dilation, dissection) . Explanation of other options: FGFR3 (Option B): Mutation causes achondroplasia , leading to short-limb dwarfism, not Marfan's tall stature. COL1A1 (Option C): Mutations cause osteogenesis imperfecta , characterised by brittle bones, blue sclera, and hearing loss. TSC1 (Option D): Mutation causes tuberous sclerosis , a neurocutaneous syndrome with cortical tubers, seizures, and skin lesions.

text: A 56-year-old man presents to the diabetes clinic for review. He has had type-1 diabetes for 30 years. Recently he has suffered a number of falls, which he describes as attacks where he feels 'faint' and loses his footing. He has suffered from impotence for a number of years and takes antireflux medication. On examination he has a postural drop of 35 mmHg in his blood pressure. Which diagnosis fits best with this history and examination?
expl: This man has a marked postural drop, features of GI tract neuropathy and impotence. Further assessment of his cardiovascular system is likely to reveal tachycardia and impaired cardiovascular response to the Valsalva manoeuvre. Other symptoms of GI tract involvement may include diarrhea and intractable vomiting. Bladder involvement may result in atonic bladder and problems with painless urinary retention and recurrent urinary tract infections. TIA is a brief episode of neurological dysfunction with a vascular cause, with clinical symptoms typically lasting less than one hour, and without evidence of infarction on imaging. Symptoms are so strongly suggestive of diabetic autonomic neuropathy such as impotence, gastropathy, postural hypotension, that arrythmia is not the preferred option from above. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page:3122

text: A 50-year-old woman with a history of hypertension presents with shortness of breath and exertional dyspnea lasting one week. On physical examination, she has elevated jugular venous pressure, lung crepitations, and a liver palpable 3 cm below the costal margin. The image of her legs is shown below. What is the name of the finding observed in her legs?
expl: Explanation: The image shows pedal edema, which, combined with the clinical signs, indicates the patient is likely suffering from congestive heart failure. Pitting pedal edema is swelling of the feet and ankles where applying pressure leaves a noticeable indentation or "pit" that remains for a while after releasing the pressure. This form of edema is commonly seen in cases of congestive cardiac failure. Explanation for other options: Superficial thrombophlebitis (Option A): is an inflammation of the superficial veins accompanied by blood clot formation. It most commonly affects the lower limbs, particularly the great and small (short) saphenous veins. Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) (Option B): occurs when a blood clot forms in a deep vein, usually in the legs, blocking normal venous blood flow. These clots often originate in the deep calf veins and may extend upward. Clubbing (Option C): is a physical sign characterized by the swelling and rounding of the tips of one or more fingers or toes. Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6676283/

text: A patient presents with muffled heart sounds and low blood pressure. What would you expect the jugular venous pressure (JVP) to show?
expl: Explanation: The clinical manifestations such as muffled heart sounds with low blood pressure indicate s cardiac tamponade. In cardiac tamponade, the characteristic finding is absent y descent and non-pulsatile elevated JVP due to impaired right ventricular filling during diastole. Cardiac Tamponade In cardac tamponade the cardiac chambers are compressed by a tense pericardial effusion, limiting cardiac inflow. Fluid accumulation of as little as 200 ml to upwards of 2L may lead to cardiac tamponade development. Clinical Features Beck's triad Jugular Venous Distension: Due to increased central venous pressure, resulting in prominent x descent and an absent y descent. text: A patient presents with an irregularly irregular pulse of 120/minute and a pulse deficit of 20. Which jugular venous pressure (JVP) finding is most likely seen in this patient?
expl: Explanation: This presentation is consistent with atrial fibrillation (AF) , characterized by chaotic atrial activity leading to ineffective atrial contraction. The absence of effective atrial systole causes the a wave in JVP to be absent , making it the classical venous finding in AF. The pulse deficit indicates irregular AV nodal conduction, with some atrial impulses not producing ventricular contractions. Key Features of Atrial Fibrillation: Mechanism: Abnormal atrial automaticity and multiple re-entry circuits. Pulse: Irregularly irregular. Symptoms: Palpitations, breathlessness, syncope; systemic embolism may occur even if asymptomatic. ECG Findings: QRS complexes: Normal but irregular. P waves: Absent, replaced by fibrillatory waves. Ventricular rate: Rapid (120-160/min at onset), slower in chronic AF due to AV nodal fatigue/therapy. JVP: Absent a wave. Management Overview: Paroxysmal AF: Beta-blockers (first-line in CAD, hypertension, heart failure). Class Ic (propafenone, flecainide) and Class III (amiodarone, dronedarone). Rate control: Digoxin, verapamil. Catheter ablation for drug-resistant cases. Persistent AF: Rhythm control with cardioversion (pharmacological/electrical). Anticoagulation if AF ≥48h. Rate control with digoxin, β-blockers, or calcium channel blockers. Thromboprophylaxis: Anticoagulation guided by CHA 2 DS 2 -VASc score . INR 2.0-3.0 for warfarin; DOACs (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, dabigatran) as alternatives. CHA 2 DS 2 -VASc Score for Stroke Risk in AF: Score 0 → no anticoagulation Score 1 → aspirin Score ≥2 → anticoagulation (warfarin/DOACs) Explanation of other options: Absent p wave (Option A): ECG hallmark of AF, but JVP finding is absent a wave, not absent p wave. Cannon a wave (Option C): Seen in AV dissociation (atrium contracting against closed tricuspid valve). Raised JVP with normal waveform (Option D): Occurs in CHF, RV infarction, or SVC obstruction-not typical of AF. References: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34506629/ https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34506629/

text: In JVP which of the following coincides with isovolumetric contraction phase of the heart?
expl: After the atrial systole, the atria starts to relax, indicated by the x descent in the JVP. Isovolumetric contraction occurs after that, where the AV valves are closed. The tricuspid valve bulges into the atria and causes the c wave. It correlates with S1 Isovolumetric contraction is followed by ventricular systole, where the pressure inside the ventricles exceed the Aortic and pulmonary pressure and the semilunar valves open and the ventricles contract. The AV valves remain closed. The atria continue to relax and get filled by the venous return. This results in v wave in JVP. Ventricular systole is followed by ventricular diastole. During isovolumetric relaxation, the pressure inside the great vessels start falling and to prevent back flow the semilunar valves close, the AV valves continue to remain closed. The pressure inside the ventricles continue to fall and the AV valves open and the ventricles start filling passively. After the passive filling, the atria contracts and ejects blood into the ventricles, which is represented by a wave in the JVP. It correlates with S4.

text: A 30-year-old patient presents with chest pain, shortness of breath, and pedal edema. Jugular venous pressure (JVP) shows a rapid Y descent. Auscultation reveals a high-pitched early diastolic sound. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.C: Rheumatic heart disease with mitral stenosis
options.D: Bicuspid aortic valve with Aortic regurgitation

expl: Explanation of answer: The presence of rapid Y descent on JVP along with a high-pitched diastolic sound suggests chronic constrictive pericarditis . Chronic constrictive pericarditis results from pericardial thickening, fibrosis, and sometimes calcification, which restricts diastolic filling of the heart. Over time, this condition impairs ventricular filling and elevates systemic venous pressures, causing signs of right heart failure such as pedal edema, hepatomegaly, and ascites. Key features include: Elevated JVP with rapid Y descent: Due to abrupt early diastolic filling before sudden pericardial restriction halts further expansion. High-pitched diastolic sound (" pericardial knock "): Heard early in diastole, representing sudden cessation of ventricular filling due to the stiff pericardium. Kussmaul's sign: Rise in JVP on inspiration. Fatigue, ascites, peripheral edema: Reflect systemic venous congestion. Atrial fibrillation: Common due to chronic atrial dilation and hypertrophy. Investigations: Chest X-ray and CT scan: May reveal pericardial calcification. Echocardiography: Shows thickened pericardium and characteristic Doppler flow patterns. Cardiac catheterization: Confirms equalization of diastolic pressures, helping differentiate from restrictive cardiomyopathy. Management: Medical therapy: Diuretics to manage symptoms. Definitive treatment: Pericardiectomy, which removes the thickened pericardium. Though curative in many, it carries a significant operative risk and variable outcomes. Explanation of other options: Cardiac tamponade (Option B): Presents with prominent X descent and absent Y descent on JVP, due to restriction of diastolic filling. The presence of rapid Y descent in this case argues against tamponade. RHD with mitral stenosis (Option C): Typically presents with a loud S1, opening snap, and low-pitched diastolic rumble, not a high-pitched knock or rapid Y descent. Bicuspid aortic valve with aortic regurgitation (Option D): Produces a high-pitched decrescendo diastolic murmur, best heard at the left sternal border, but does not explain the rapid Y descent or right-sided signs.

text: C wave in JVP is due to which of the following?

options.A: Ventricular diastole when the tricuspid valve is open
options.B: Ventricular diastole when the tricuspid valve is closed
options.C: Bulging of the tricuspid value into the right atrium

ansText: Bulging of the tricuspid value into the right atrium
expl: a wave represents atrial systole, occurs along with S4, preceeding theS1. a wave will be hence absent in atrial fibrillation. A prominent wave will be seen when the atria contracts against a non compliant right ventricle. Canon a wave occurs in AV dissociation, where the atria contracts against a closed ventricle, as in Ventricular tachycardia. X descent indicates a fall in the right atrial pressure, after the atrial systole. During this time, the tricuspid valves close and the valve is pushed into the atria, resulting in a small positive c wave, which interrupts the x descent. Hence it correlated with S1. Immediately after the closure of the tricuspid valve, the ventricular systole begins, during which time, the atria is relaxed and the atrial filling takes place. The atrial filling is represented by the v wave in JVP. When the filling of the atria is increased the v wave will be accentuated. In tricuspid regurgitation, the tricuspid valves fail to close properly hence the c wave will merge with the v wave to form a giant v wave or the v wave is ventricularized. They descent indicates the rapid filling of the ventricles. In tricuspid regurgitation, the y decent will be rapid. In conditions where the RV compliance is reduced or the tricuspid valve is stenosed, the y decent will be prolonged. KEY TAKE AWAY

text: A 68-year-old woman was admitted to hospital with severe acute dyspnoea. She denied having any chest pain but said that she had become progressively breathless over the past three months.On examination, her pulse was 120 beats per minute and regular. Her blood pressure was 95/55 mmHg and her jugular venous pressure was elevated to the angle of the jaw. Her heart sounds were normal. Auscultation of her chest revealed bilateral fine inspiratory crackles to the mid zones. She had hemorrhages in both fundi. Investigations revealed: The ECG showed the left bundle branch block, which had been documented previously. She is given 80 mg of intravenous furosemide which results in an excellent diuresis. Which of the following is the next most appropriate immediate step in her management?

options.C: Start intramuscular vitamin B12 and oral folic acid

expl: The clinical picture represents likely severe megaloblastic anemia with cardiac failure. The question asks about immediate management. Although the anemia has been developing slowly, she has become acutely hemodynamically compromised. In such circumstances, it would be most appropriate to transfuse the patient. This would need to be done very cautiously with diuretic cover. She will clearly need to start an intensive course of intramuscular vitamin B12 and oral folic acid as well, but this is less important in the hyperacute situation where there is a risk of the patient dying from anaemia. Giving oral folic acid without vitamin B12 would be hazardous and could precipitate subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 1942-44

text: A patient presents with shortness of breath and distended neck veins that become more prominent on inspiration, with no associated murmur. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The given clinical features of dyspnea and distended neck veins that increase on inspiration are suggestive of constrictive pericarditis . Constrictive pericarditis involves thickening and scarring of the pericardium, which restricts the heart’s ability to fill properly. It is suggested by the presence of Kussmaul's sign (a rise in jugular venous pressure with inspiration) and the absence of a murmur. During inspiration, the stiff pericardium limits normal ventricular expansion, leading to an abnormal increase in venous pressure. The underlying pathology is pericardial inflammation and fibrosis, which forms a rigid shell around the heart and restricts diastolic filling. Pathophysiology: Ongoing pericardial thickening, scarring, and calcification limit ventricular filling. In some cases, the calcification extends into the myocardium, reducing contractility. Impaired ventricular filling raises atrial pressures, resulting in: Atrial enlargement Atrial hypertrophy Frequent atrial fibrillation The condition mainly presents with systemic venous congestion, while pulmonary congestion is uncommon. Examination Findings: Explanations of other options: Aortic regurgitation (Option B): Aortic regurgitation usually presents with a distinct diastolic murmur , which is not observed here, and it is not associated with inspiratory elevation of jugular venous pressure. Tricuspid stenosis (Option C): Tricuspid stenosis is marked by raised jugular venous pressure along with a diastolic murmur, but it does not show Kussmaul's sign, as the jugular venous pressure typically stays the same or falls during inspiration. Pulmonary arterial hypertension (Option D): Pulmonary artery hypertension may lead to elevated jugular venous pressure and right-sided heart failure signs, but it does not produce Kussmaul's sign, as the typical inspiratory rise in neck vein distention is not seen in this condition.

text: A 64-year-old man presents to casualty with severe chest pain. ECG was suggestive of anterior wall ST elevation MI. He underwent thrombolysis with reteplase with good resolution of ECG changes. On day 3, he developed sharp chest pain, worse with inspiration and movement and improved with NSAIDs. On day 5, patient has progressive dyspnea. His heart rate was 110/min, BP was 90/50 mmHg with elevated JVP. What is the most likely complication that has occurred in this patient?
expl: The presence of typical sharp chest pain which increases on inspiration is suggestive of pericarditis. However, it would not per se lead to hypotension and raised JVP as seen in this patient. Cardiac tamponade can occur as a rare complication in post-MI patients. It is the rapid accumulation of fluid in pericardial sac under pressure. The typical clinical triad seen in tamponade is 'Beck's triad' (low BP, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds) The development of acute mitral regurgitation or VSD is associated with severe pulmonary oedema and less likely to be associated with chest pain. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page no: 2064

text: A 26-year-old male accident victim develops progressive breathing difficulty. On examination, his blood pressure is 80/40 mmHg, pulses are feeble, jugular venous pressure (JVP) is elevated with absent Y descent, and heart sounds are muffled. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The combination of hypotension (80/40 mmHg), weak pulses, raised JVP with absent Y descent, and muffled heart sounds indicates cardiac tamponade . Cardiac Tamponade Definition: Compression of cardiac chambers due to tense pericardial effusion, restricting cardiac filling. Clinical Features: Beck's Triad: Jugular venous distension (prominent x descent, absent y descent), hypotension from reduced cardiac output, muffled heart sounds from fluid damping. Pulsus paradoxus: Fall in systolic BP >10 mmHg during inspiration. Causes of Pulsus Paradoxus: Pulmonary causes: Acute asthma, COPD, tension pneumothorax, pleural effusion, pulmonary embolism. Cardiac causes: Cardiac tamponade, constrictive pericarditis. Investigations: Echocardiography (IOC): Shows pericardial effusion, right ventricular diastolic collapse, and inspiratory variation in transvalvular flow. ECG: Low QRS voltage, electrical alternans. Right heart catheterization: Equalization of diastolic pressures in all chambers. Pericardial fluid analysis: For etiology (cytology, cultures, PCR). Management: Emergency pericardiocentesis: Definitive, usually USG-guided. IV fluids: Temporarily to maintain preload. Catheter placement: For continuous drainage if fluid recurs. Surgical drainage (subxiphoid pericardiotomy): Indicated for recurrent, loculated effusions or failed pericardiocentesis. Explanation of Other Options: Constrictive pericarditis (Option A): Chronic process, develops gradually; though both conditions show elevated JVP, tamponade presents acutely. Acute pericarditis (Option C): Typically causes chest pain, fever, and pericardial rub. Absence of these features and presence of acute hemodynamic compromise rules it out. Cardiac failure (Option D): Can cause hypotension and dyspnea but does not present with the classic triad of tamponade. Key Takeaways: Classic Beck's triad = JVD, hypotension, muffled heart sounds. Absent y descent is specific for tamponade. Pulsus paradoxus is a key supportive finding.

text: A 21 year-old woman has a history of palpitations and light-headedness. ECG shows short PR interval and inferior Q waves with prolonged QRS duration. Her symptoms improve with atenolol 25 mg/day but she has had two short episodes of similar symptoms in the previous 24 hours. What is the long-term management of choice?
expl: The diagnosis is Wolff Parkinson white syndrome and the patient is likely atrial tachycardias (AVRT) which are not controlled by medical therapy. She should be referred to a cardiac physiologist for radiofrequency ablation of the accessory pathway. Procainamide is used to terminate acute attacks of AVRT due to WPW syndrome Drugs like beta blockers, verapamil and adenosine that block AV nodal conduction are contraindicated in AVRT due to WPW syndrome Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 1896

text: A 55-year-old female presents with complaints of palpitation and dizziness. ECG taken shown the below findings. What is the best treatment option?
expl: Explanation: The given ECG shows a narrow QRS complex tachycardia, suggesting paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia , most likely AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia (AVNRT) , which is best managed with adenosine. The most common cause of a regular narrow QRS tachycardia is Paroxysmal Supraventricular Tachycardia (PSVT), particularly AV Nodal Re-entrant Tachycardia (AVNRT). In PSVT/AVNRT, there is a re-entry circuit within or near the AV node, leading to sudden-onset rapid heart rate that can cause palpitations, dizziness, and sometimes syncope. In a typical AVNRT, the ECG will show a P wave buried or fused within the QRS; ventricular rate is 120-220 beats/min. Treatment of AVNRT If the patient is stable: First line management involves vagal manoeuvres like Valsalva, carotid sinus massage. Vagal manoeuvres increase vagal tone and slow AV nodal conduction. If ineffective, the drug of choice is IV Adenosine, which transiently blocks AV nodal conduction and usually terminates the arrhythmia. If patient unstable (hypotension, chest pain, altered sensorium): Immediate synchronized DC cardioversion.

text: Which of the following statements about Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome is accurate?
expl: Explanation: Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome is caused by an accessory pathway (bundle of Kent) between the atria and ventricles, producing characteristic ECG findings of a short PR interval ( wide QRS complex , and a delta wave. The delta wave produces an initial slurring of the QRS complex, making it look wider than usual. This broad QRS pattern occurs because the accessory pathway triggers early ventricular activation, leading to ventricular pre-excitation . Explanations of other options: Short PJ interval (Option A): In Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome, the typical ECG abnormality is a reduced PR interval, not a shortened PJ interval. The PR interval reflects the conduction time from the atria to the ventricles. Because WPW involves an accessory pathway that allows impulses to bypass part of the normal conduction route, the PR interval appears shortened on the ECG. Tall Tented T waves (Option C): Tall tented T waves are not characteristic of WPW syndrome; instead, they are commonly linked to conditions such as hyperkalemia. Prolonged PR interval (Option D): In WPW syndrome, the PR interval becomes shortened because the accessory pathway bypasses the normal conduction route, whereas a lengthened PR interval is more suggestive of conditions such as first-degree heart block. Reference: Wolff-Parkinson-White Syndrome - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf
