text: A patient is evaluated for recurrent seizures. EEG shows hypsarrhythmia. What is the preferred drug?
expl: Explanation Hypsarrhythmia on EEG is the classical finding in Infantile Spasms (West Syndrome) . ACTH (adrenocorticotropic hormone) is considered the first-line therapy for infantile spasms. It improves seizure control and may also help in neurodevelopmental outcomes. Alternative treatments include oral corticosteroids and vigabatrin (especially when spasms are due to tuberous sclerosis). Antiepileptic drug choice according to seizure type: Explanation of Incorrect Options Carbamazepine (Option A): Used for focal seizures and trigeminal neuralgia. Not effective for infantile spasms and may actually worsen generalized seizures . Lamotrigine (Option B): Effective in generalized tonic-clonic and absence seizures.Not preferred for hypsarrhythmia/infantile spasms. Vigabatrin (Option D): Can be used in infantile spasms due to tuberous sclerosis , but ACTH remains the preferred first-line drug in general cases.

text: Which of the following combinations of seizure and its corresponding medication is not accurate? 1. Generalized onset tonic-clonic seizures: Lamotrigine 2. Focal seizures: Levetiracetam 3. Typical absence seizures: Topiramate 4. Myoclonic seizures: Valproic acid
expl: Explanation: The incorrect pairing is Typical absence seizures: Topiramate . The first-line medications for typical absence seizures are Ethosuximide and Valproate . While topiramate has broad-spectrum activity, it is not a primary or preferred agent for absence seizures. Ethosuximide is used in children Explanation of other options: Generalized tonic-clonic seizures: Lamotrigine (Option A): Lamotrigine is a broad-spectrum antiepileptic effective for generalized seizures. Focal seizures: Levetiracetam (Option B): Levetiracetam is a first-line treatment for focal seizures. Myoclonic seizures: Valproic acid (Option D): Valproate is a first-line broad-spectrum drug, highly effective for myoclonic seizures (e.g., in Juvenile Myoclonic Epilepsy). Key Takeaways: Typical Absence Seizures: First-line = Ethosuximide or Valproate . Topiramate is a broad-spectrum drug used for various seizure types but is not a first-line choice for absence seizures.

text: A 18-year-old girl presents with recurrent episodes of loss of consciousness. Over the last two years she has had blackouts which last approximately 2 minutes. They typically occur when she is standing. These have occurred more frequently over the last week. The last episode was witnessed by her friend who noted that she collapsed without any abnormal movements. On coming round she was rather drowsy initially but generally fine and recovered relatively quickly. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: This young girl has features suggestive of vasovagal syncope . The story suggests that the episodes always occur when she is standing (whereas cardiac syncope could occur at any time but may be precipitated by exercise), that there are no abnormal movements (making epilepsy less likely) and that there is an almost full recovery (again making epilepsy less likely). Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Principles, 20 th edition, ch:253 pg:122,127-129

text: A 40-year female has several episodes of vomiting and loose stool. She was managed at the periphery by IV fluids and hyponatremia was corrected. She presented to ER with paralysis, dysarthria, dysphagia, loss of consciousness. What might be the cause?

options.D: Excessive infusion fluids leading to fluid overload

expl: Overly rapid correction of hyponatremia (>8-10 mM in 24 h or 18 mM in 48 h) causes Osmotic demyelination syndrome. Hypertonic stress in astrocytes within brain regions prone to ODS, leading to generalized protein ubiquitination and endoplasmic reticulum stress due to activation of the unfolded protein response; this is accompanied by apoptotic and autophagic cell death. Rapid correction of hyponatremia also causes a disruption in integrity of the blood-brain barrier, allowing the entry of immune mediators that may contribute to demyelination. The lesions of ODS classically affect the pons, a neuroanatomic structure wherein the delay in the reaccumulation of osmotic osmolytes is particularly pronounced; clinically, patients with central pontine myelinolysis can present 1 or more days after overcorrection of hyponatremia with paraparesis or quadriparesis, dysphagia, dysarthria, diplopia, a "locked-in syndrome" , and/or loss of consciousness. Other regions of the brain can also be involved in ODS, most commonly in association with lesions of the pons but occasionally in isolation; in order of frequency, the lesions of extrapontine myelinolysis can occur in the cerebellum, lateral geniculate body, thalamus, putamen, and cerebral cortex or subcortex. Clinical presentation of ODS can, therefore, vary as a function of the extent and localization of extrapontine myelinolysis, with the reported development of ataxia, mutism, parkinsonism, dystonia, and catatonia. However, even appropriately slow correction can be associated with ODS, particularly in patients with additional risk factors; these include alcoholism, malnutrition, hypokalemia, and liver transplantation.

text: A 73-year-old male presents with weakness and reduced mobility. On examination he has a slow gait with reduced arm swing and a tremor is noticed in the left arm. Which of the following is the typical frequency of the rest tremor in Parkinson's disease?
expl: The tremor of Parkinson's disease is a rest tremor with low to moderate frequency 3 to 6 HZ. Initially, the tremor is usually one-sided. As the disease progresses, the tremor becomes bilateral and increases in severity. Although the classical tremor of Parkinson's disease is a rest tremor, over time an action tremor may develop. Furthermore, it may increase in severity with levodopa. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 435, Pg: 3387

text: A patient presents with spastic quadriplegia. What is the most likely site of lesion?
expl: Explanation: Periventricular leukomalacia (PVL) refers to ischemic necrosis of the white matter adjacent to the lateral ventricles, typically seen in preterm infants due to hypoxic-ischemic injury . It affects the descending corticospinal tracts → spasticity and motor deficits . If extensive, both upper and lower limbs are affected → spastic quadriplegia . Pathogenesis: Hypoxia → ischemia of watershed zones near ventricles → demyelination and necrosis → cystic cavitations in periventricular white matter. Explanation of Other Options: Basal ganglia calcification (Option B): Seen in hypoparathyroidism or Fahr's disease . Produces extrapyramidal symptoms (rigidity, tremor, dystonia). Does not cause spasticity or pyramidal signs. Usually bilateral and symmetric on CT scan. Cerebellar degeneration (Option C): Causes ataxia , dysmetria, intention tremor, and hypotonia. Gait becomes wide-based and unsteady . No hyperreflexia or spastic quadriplegia. Seen in chronic alcoholism , paraneoplastic syndromes , or vitamin E deficiency . Cystic encephalomalacia (Option D): Post-hypoxic destruction of brain parenchyma forming cystic cavities . Causes focal neurological deficits depending on area affected. Usually results in seizures or cognitive delay , not pure spasticity. Common sequel of severe hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy.

text: A 78-year-old woman presents with a progressive decline in daily activity. She gives a history of convulsions and visual hallucinations. She does not talk to anyone and keeps looking at the sky. Pathological examination shows the presence of Lewy bodies within the neurons. What is the most probable diagnosis?
expl: Explanation of answer: Lewy bodies in neurons along with progressive motor and cognitive decline are hallmark features of Parkinson's disease . Parkinson's disease is a neurodegenerative disorder marked by the loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra. A key pathological feature is the presence of Lewy bodies- eosinophilic, intracytoplasmic inclusions primarily composed of alpha-synuclein. Patients typically present with motor symptoms like bradykinesia, rigidity, resting tremor, and postural instability. In later stages, non-motor symptoms such as cognitive decline, visual hallucinations, sleep disturbances, and behavioral changes can occur-consistent with this patient's clinical presentation. Convulsions are rare but can be seen in late-stage disease or in Parkinson's disease dementia. Management involves dopaminergic therapies like levodopa/carbidopa, dopamine agonists, and MAO-B inhibitors. Reference: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5771416/ https://www.nia.nih.gov/health/alzheimers-and-dementia/understanding-different-types-dementia

text: Which part of the brain is most commonly involved due to rapid correction of sodium in extrapontine myelinolysis?
expl: Overly rapid correction of hyponatremia (>8-10 mM in 24 h or 18 mM in 48 h) is also associated with a disruption in integrity of the blood brain barrier, allowing the entry of immune mediators that may contribute to demyelination. The lesions of ODS classically affect the pons, a neuroanatomic structure wherein the delay in the re accumulation of osmotic osmolytes is particularly pronounced; clinically, patients with central pontine myelinolysis can present 1 or more days after overcorrection of hyponatremia with paraparesis or quadriparesis, dysphagia, dysarthria, diplopia, a 'locked-in syndrome,' and/or loss 301 of consciousness. Other regions of the brain can also be involved in ODS, most commonly in association with lesions of the pons but occasionally in isolation; in order of frequency, the lesions of extrapontine myelinolysis can occur in the cerebellum, lateral geniculate body, thalamus, putamen, and cerebral cortex or subcortex . Clinical presentation of ODS can, therefore, vary as a function of the extent and localization of extrapontine myelinolysis, with the reported development of ataxia, mutism, parkinsonism, dystonia, and catatonia. Relowering of plasma Na+ concentration after overly rapid correction can prevent or attenuate ODS. Reference: Harrisons Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:53 Pg: 344

text: A patient is unable to perform the heel-to-shin test properly and repeatedly misses during the finger-to-nose test. What is the most likely site of the lesion?
expl: Explanation: Inability to perform the heel-to-shin and finger-to-nose tests is indicative of a cerebellar lesion , reflecting impaired coordination and dysmetria. Cerebellar Lesion: Key Clinical Signs Cerebellar ataxia: Uncoordinated voluntary movements, producing a drunken gait . Dysmetria: Inability to accurately reach a target; finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin tests are impaired . Dysdiadochokinesia: Difficulty performing rapid alternating movements . Nystagmus: Involuntary oscillation of the eyes. Intention tremor: Tremor during voluntary movement , worsening near the target (different from Parkinson's resting tremor). Pendular knee jerk: Leg swings like a pendulum due to hypotonia . Rebound phenomenon: Inability to stop a movement suddenly , causing exaggerated response. Explanation of other options: Caudate (Option B): The caudate nucleus , a component of the corpus striatum , when affected, can cause chorea , which consists of involuntary, purposeless, jerky, dancing movements. Globus pallidus (Option C): Lesions of globus pallidus can cause athetosis, characterized by slow, writhing, purposeless, involuntary movements that are often described as snake-like. Subthalamic nucleus (Option D): A lesion of the subthalamic nucleus causes hemiballismus, characterised by involuntary, purposeless, flailing movements of the extremities. Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK562317/

text: Cytogenetic abnormalities seen in myelodysplastic syndromes include all except
expl: Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) is a clonal hematopoietic stem cell disorder characterized by disordered cell proliferation, impaired differentiation, and aberrant hematopoiesis, resulting in cytopenias and risk of progression to leukemia . Both chromosomal and genetic instability have been implicated; both are aging-related . Cytogenetic abnormalities are found in approximately one-half of patients. Aneuploidy (chromosome loss or gain) is more frequent than translocations . Loss of all or part of chromosomes 5, 7, and 20, and trisomy of 8 may be related to etiology ( 11q23 following topoisomerase II inhibitors ). The type and number of cytogenetic abnormalities strongly correlate with the probability of leukemic transformation and survival. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 102, Pg: 801

text: Which of the following findings are typical of an upper motor neuron lesion (UMNL)? 1. Rigidity 2. Exaggerated reflexes 3. Fasciculations 4. Severe muscular atrophy 5. Spasticity
expl: Explanation: Upper motor neuron (UMN) lesions result from damage to the descending corticospinal or corticobulbar tracts, which normally exert inhibitory control over lower motor neurons. When this control is lost, characteristic motor signs emerge due to unopposed reflex activity and altered muscle tone regulation . Key clinical features of UMNL: Spasticity: A velocity-dependent increase in muscle tone, classically described as "clasp-knife rigidity", where resistance to passive movement is initially high but then suddenly gives way. Hyperreflexia: Deep tendon reflexes become exaggerated as inhibitory supraspinal modulation is lost. Positive Babinski sign: Upgoing plantar response due to corticospinal tract involvement. Minimal muscle atrophy: Only from disuse, not denervation. Absence of fasciculations: Because the lower motor neuron remains intact. UMN vs LMN lesion: Key Takeaway Points: Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK537305/ https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/neuroscience/lower-motor-neuron-lesion

text: A 77-year-old man comes to the clinic with his wife. He has been suffering from increasingly frequent falls and now has marked problems with his mobility. Past history of note includes an inferior MI and TIA a few years earlier. He has also suffered from two episodes of urinary retention and now has an indwelling catheter. On examination his BP is 142/72 mmHg, with a postural drop of 30 mmHg on standing. He has a quiet ejection systolic murmur, his chest is clear, and abdominal examination is unremarkable. Neurological examination reveals cogwheel rigidity and bradykinesia. He has a mild tremor only. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: The particular features of autonomic dysfunction seen here, with postural hypotension and urinary retention and parkinsonism point towards a diagnosis of multi-system atrophy. As here, whilst the motor symptoms are parkinsonian in nature, the tremor is often less pronounced than in a patient with idiopathic Parkinson's. The Parkinson's symptoms associated with multi-system atrophy usually respond poorly to dopamine agonists or L-dopa, in contrast to idiopathic Parkinson's. Urinary retention can be managed with an indwelling catheter if required, and postural hypotension managed with support stockings plus mineralocorticoids if required. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st Ed Ch: 435, Pg: 3388

text: Which of the following conditions leads to the development of a wing-beating tremor?
expl: Explanation: A wing-beating tremor is a highly characteristic, low-frequency, high-amplitude tremor that is provoked when the patient's arms are extended and is a classic neurologic manifestation of Wilson's disease . Pathophysiology Wilson's disease is an autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism, leading to copper accumulation in the liver, cornea, and brain-particularly the basal ganglia . This toxic accumulation disrupts neural circuits controlling movement, producing tremors, dystonia, and parkinsonism. The "wing-beating" quality is distinctive. Wilson's disease presents with hepatic involvement such as chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis with portal hypertension, or acute liver failure. Neurological features include tremors, dystonia, ataxia, dysarthria, and parkinsonism-like symptoms, along with psychiatric changes like depression and cognitive decline. Ocular signs include Kayser-Fleischer rings and, rarely, sunflower cataracts. Renal manifestations include Fanconi syndrome, hematologic involvement is hemolytic anemia, and skeletal features include osteopenia, osteoporosis, and arthropathy. Differentiation from Other Movement Disorders Huntington's chorea and Sydenham's chorea (Option B and D ruled out): These conditions present with chorea (brief, irregular, dancelike movements), not a rhythmic, postural tremor. Parkinsonism (Option D ruled out) : The classic tremor is a pill-rolling tremor at rest, which is finer and disappears with voluntary movement, unlike the large, flapping tremor of Wilson's. Key Takeaways: The wing-beating tremor is a pathognomonic sign of Wilson's disease . Other key features include Kayser-Fleischer rings, neuropsychiatric symptoms, and liver disease. It is a treatable condition, making early recognition critical.

text: Patient presents to the neurology clinic with complaints of difficulty switching from one movement to another. He also reports having uncontrolled hand movements when trying to perform rapid alternating movements, particularly when asked to tap his fingers. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: Dysdiadochokinesia is a medical term used to describe a difficulty in performing rapid, alternating movements . It is often considered a sign of cerebellar dysfunction . The cerebellum is a part of the brain that plays a crucial role in motor control and coordination . When there is damage or dysfunction in the cerebellum, it can lead to impaired ability to coordinate these movements, manifesting as dysdiadochokinesis . Patients with dysdiadochokinesis will have trouble performing tasks that require quick and alternating movements, such as tapping their foot quickly or rapidly alternating hand movements , like the finger-tapping task described. The symptoms are typically due to the inability of the cerebellum to correctly time muscle contractions needed for smooth execution of these movements. Clinical Presentation: Difficulty with rapid alternating movements : This includes tasks like quickly switching the position of the hands or feet. Uncoordinated movement : Movements may appear clumsy or jerky. Other associated cerebellar signs : These might include ataxia, nystagmus, or a wide-based gait. Explanation of other options: Ataxia (Option B): Ataxia refers to a broad lack of coordination in voluntary movements, including gait instability, limb incoordination, and speech issues. While dysdiadochokinesia is a specific sign of cerebellar dysfunction , ataxia is a more general term encompassing various coordination deficits. Tremors (Option C): Tremors are involuntary rhythmic movements , often seen at rest (e.g., Parkinson's disease) or during movement (e.g., essential tremor). The patient's main issue is difficulty switching movements , not rhythmic oscillations. Bradykinesia (Option D): Bradykinesia (seen in Parkinson's disease) is slowness of movement with difficulty initiating motion. Unlike dysdiadochokinesis, it is not primarily a coordination problem but rather a movement initiation and execution issue due to basal ganglia dysfunction. Key Takeaways: Dysdiadochokinesia is a hallmark of cerebellar dysfunction, characterized by difficulty performing rapid alternating movements, as seen in this patient's inability to switch movements smoothly.

text: A 41 year old man presented with double vision and was found to have normal vertical eye movements. On left lateral gaze, there was absence of adduction of the right eye, and nystagmus in the abducting left eye. This eye movement disorder can be explained by a lesion in the:
expl: The diagnosis is right internuclear ophthalmoplegia due to a lesion in the right medial longitudinal fasciculus. The likely underlying pathology is multiple sclerosis, other causes of INO include a glioma or vascular lesion. INO Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) is a disorder of conjugate lateral gazein which the affected eye shows impairment of adduction. When an attempt is made to gaze contralaterally (relative to the affected eye), the affected eye adducts minimally, if at all. The contralateral eye abducts, however with nystagmus. Additionally, the divergence of the eyes leads to horizontal diplopia . That is if the right eye is affected the patient will "see double" when looking to the left, seeing two images side-by-side. Convergence is generally preserved. Schematic Explanation Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st ed, Ch: 32, Pg: 230

text: A 77-year-old man comes to the clinic with his wife. He has been suffering from increasingly frequent falls and now has marked problems with his mobility. Past history of note includes an inferior MI and TIA a few years earlier. He has also suffered from two episodes of urinary retention and now has an indwelling catheter. On examination his BP is 142/72 mmHg, with a postural drop of 30 mmHg on standing. He has a quiet ejection systolic murmur, his chest is clear, and abdominal examination is unremarkable. Neurological examination reveals loss of upward gaze, cogwheel rigidity and bradykinesia. He has a mild tremor only. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: The particular features of autonomic dysfunction seen here, with postural hypotension and urinary retention, coupled with the loss of upward gaze and parkinsonism point towards a diagnosis of multi-system atrophy. As here, whilst the motor symptoms are parkinsonian in nature, the tremor is often less pronounced than in a patient with idiopathic Parkinson's. The Parkinson's symptoms associated with multi-system atrophy usually respond poorly to dopamine agonists or L-dopa, in contrast to idiopathic Parkinson's. Urinary retention can be managed with an indwelling catheter if required, and postural hypotension managed with support stockings plus mineralocorticoids if required. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st Ed Ch: 435, Pg: 3388

text: A patient presented with hyponatremic encephalopathy with Na 126 meq/L. She was administered 3% NS over the next 24 hours. Following this, the patient deteriorated and developed quadriparesis. What is the next best step in management?
expl: Explanation: Overly rapid correction of hyponatremia, particularly with hypertonic (3%) saline, can result in central pontine myelinolysis (osmotic demyelination syndrome) , presenting with new neurological deficits including quadriparesis. The next best diagnostic step is MRI brain , which can detect characteristic demyelinating lesions (especially in the pons) and confirm the diagnosis. Overly rapid correction of hyponatremia (>8-10 mM in 24 h or 18 mM in 48 h) is also associated with a disruption in the integrity of the blood-brain barrier, allowing the entry of immune mediators that may contribute to demyelination. Extrapontine Myelinosis: Extrapontine myelinolysis (EPM) is a form of osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS) that occurs outside the pons. It is often associated with the rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia. Other regions of the brain can also be involved in ODS, most commonly in association with lesions of the pons but occasionally in isolation. In order of frequency, the lesions of extrapontine myelinolysis can occur in the cerebellum, lateral geniculate body, thalamus, putamen, and cerebral cortex or subcortex. (Other options ruled out) Clinical presentation of ODS can, therefore, vary as a function of the extent and localisation of extrapontine myelinolysis, with the reported development of ataxia, mutism, Parkinsonism, dystonia, and catatonia. Relowering of plasma Na+ concentration after overly rapid correction can prevent or attenuate ODS. Central Pontine Myelinolysis Explanation of Incorrect Options: Brainstem evoked potential (Option A): Not used for diagnosis of osmotic demyelination, but may be used for brainstem function in other contexts. Electroencephalogram (EEG) (Option B): Detects electrical activity, useful for seizures or encephalopathy but not for demyelinating lesions. Nerve conduction study (Option D): Evaluates peripheral nerves, not central demyelination.

text: A 50-year-old man presents with hand tremors and movement abnormalities, along with emerging cognitive and emotional disturbances. Which of the following conditions is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The presence of choreiform movements, progressive cognitive impairment, and psychiatric symptoms is characteristic of Huntington's disease , an autosomal dominant neurodegenerative condition resulting from a mutation in the HTT gene. Huntington's disease typically presents in middle adulthood between ages 30-50 and involves a trinucleotide repeat expansion (CAG repeats) in the HTT gene, leading to the accumulation of abnormal protein in the brain. Explanations of other options: Parkinson's disease (Option A): Parkinson's disease usually affects people over the age of 60 and is marked by movement issues, most notably a resting tremor , which differs from the involuntary choreiform movements of Huntington's disease. Although cognitive and emotional symptoms may arise, they tend to appear later in the illness or alongside related conditions such as Lewy body dementia. Friedreich's ataxia (Option B): Friedreich's ataxia is an inherited condition that mainly impacts the nervous system, leading to progressive damage of the spinal cord and peripheral nerves. It usually begins in childhood or adolescence and presents with ataxia rather than chorea, while cognitive and emotional disturbances are not key features of the disease. Alzheimer's disease (Option C): Alzheimer's disease mainly impairs memory, cognition, and behaviour, with its defining feature being gradual memory decline . Although psychiatric symptoms can occur, movement abnormalities such as tremors or chorea are not typical, and the condition usually presents at an older age. Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK559166/

text: A 41 year old man complains of pain in the right eye, which has worsened over the last few days. On examination, he had a ptosis of the right eye. He also had a weakness of superior upgaze of the right eye and loss of accommodation reflex, with a dilated pupil. Which of the following is likely?
expl: Complete Ptosis of the right eye with loss of accommodation reflex indicates a 3 rd nerve palsy. Patients with painful, isolated third nerve palsy with pupillary involvement is most likely due to a posterior communicating artery aneurysm. Other causes of mononeuritis multiplex (diabetes, vasculitis, syphilis), can also cause a third nerve palsy, but seldom are painful. Arteriogram - Lateral view showing a posterior communicating artery aneurysm. Option A: Myasthenia gravis would cause diurnal symptoms of ptosis and diplopia which would occur a few hours after waking up. Option B: Neurosyphilis would cause an Argyll Robertson Pupil which is characterized by absent pupillary reflex with a preserved accommodation reflex. It occurs due to lesion in the pretectal region Option C: Multiple sclerosis would cause an internuclear ophthalmoplegia which causes a loss of adduction of ipsilateral eye on abduction of contralateral eye. It occurs due to lesion in medial longitudinal fasciculus Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 429, Pg: 3355

text: A 33-year-old banker presents for to the clinic. Apart from a past history of reflux symptoms, her previous medical history is unremarkable. She gives a history of increasing fatigue, being sometimes unable to leave her bedroom; She feels unable to concentrate, has headaches, intermittent sore throats and feels that when she is able to sleep, she awakes unrefreshed. Full blood count, viscosity, urea and electrolytes, liver function testing, thyroid function testing and a Synacthen test have all been normal. On examination in the clinic there are no abnormal physical findings in this normal weight, normal height young woman. What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
expl: The prevalence of chronic fatigue syndrome is estimated at 1-3 per 1000 individuals. The predominant age at presentation is young adulthood to middle age, and there is a slight female preponderance. Sufferers often report a short flu-like illness at the point of onset and some scientists believe that an initial viral trigger may be responsible. Conventional investigation and physical examination prove normal. EBV infection was thought to be a trigger but there’s no definitive evidence Education, counselling and goal setting have proved useful in stimulating recovery, and trials have demonstrated improvements with amitriptyline use, but many patients take years to return to normal life. Physical exam is normal. Myasthenia Gravis is an autoimmune disorder of NMJ causing skeletal muscle weakness commonly those of eyes, face and swallowing. It can cause diplopia, ptosis, difficult in talking and walking. Often associated with thymoma. Hypothyroidism is excluded as thyroid function tests are normal. Addison's is less likely as Synecthen test (ACTH stimulation test) is normal. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 20 th edition Chapter:442 Page number:3254-56

text: A 20-year-old student is brought to emergency after he had been playing that afternoon, and while resting (after having had a pasta meal), complained of generalized weakness. He was unable to stand and had to be carried in by his friends. His potassium level was noted to be 2.1 mmol/l. Urine screen for diabetic and laxative abuse was normal. Apparently, he has had similar attacks since his early teenage years. Symptoms were aborted by potassium chloride. What type of mutation best fits the underlying pathology of this autosomal-dominant condition involving intermittent paralysis?

options.A: Mutation of a muscle voltage-gated sodium channel
options.B: Mutation in a muscle voltage-gated potassium channel
options.C: Mutation in a renal potassium channel
options.D: Mutation in a muscle voltage-gated calcium channel

ansText: Mutation in a muscle voltage-gated calcium channel
expl: Hypokalaemic periodic paralysis is related to a muscle calcium-channel mutation (CAClN1A3). It is an autosomal-dominant condition; attacks usually begin in the teenage years and may remit after around 35 years of age. Potassium is normally below 3 mmol/l during an attack and symptoms resolve with the administration of potassium chloride. Attacks appear to be precipitated either by a high carbohydrate meal or by a period of rest after extreme exercise. Loss of function of muscles concerning speech, bulbar or generalized weakness may occur and attacks can last for several hours. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 20 th edition Page number:304, 305, 3251

text: A 42-year-old man has weakness in the extensors of the upper limb and flexors of the lower limb muscles. His speech has a nasal quality. There is tongue fasciculation. What is the likely diagnosis?
expl: The patient has only motor symptoms like weakness of muscles of the upper and lower limbs and possibly of the palate, causing the nasal twang. There is fasciculation too. So among the given options the diseases that presents with pure motor weakness are MND and Myasthenia gravis. But fasciculation is seen in diseases of the neurons and not the neuromuscular junction. So the best possible answer is Motor Neuron Disease. Motor neuron disease presents with muscle weakness with either UMN features, or LMN features or both. In motor neuron disease, UMN signs include muscle spasticity, slowed recruitment of voluntary muscle strength, weakness especially in the extensors of the upper limb and flexors of the lower limb muscles and hyperreflexia with extensor plantar. LMN features include muscle wasting and fasciculation, depressed reflexes and bulbar palsy. Onset of the disease is usually in mid to late adult life with the incidence increasing with advancing age. Wilson's Disease presents with extrapyramidal features and neuropsychiatric manifestations. Creutzfeldt Jacob disease presents with rapidly progressive dementia and death. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 437, Pg: 3410-3415

text: A 52 year old man presents with a history of slowly progressive, abnormal movements of his body. On examination there are jerky, semi-purposive movements involving the entire body and abnormal tongue movements. What is the likely diagnosis?
expl: Huntington's disease is a genetic disorder characterized by abnormal, involuntary movements known as chorea. These movements can involve the entire body and often affect the face, resulting in abnormal tongue movements. The condition typically progresses slowly and is associated with neurological and cognitive symptoms. It is an autosomal dominant genetic disorder caused by a mutation in the HTT gene. There are many causes of chorea. Inherited- Ataxia-telangiectasia, Huntington disease, Wilson disease. Drugs - Anticonvulsants (eg, phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital), Antidopaminergic agents (eg, phenothiazines, haloperidol, metoclopramide) Behcet disease, antiphospholipid antibody syndrome, Bacterial endocarditis, Herpes simplex encephalitis, Lyme disease. The other options can be ruled out as follows: A) Parkinson's disease: Parkinson's disease primarily presents with symptoms such as resting tremors, bradykinesia (slowness of movement), rigidity, and postural instability, which are different from the choreiform (chorea-like) movements seen in Huntington's disease. B) Motor neuron disease: Motor neuron disease, such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), typically presents with muscle weakness, muscle atrophy, and spasticity rather than the choreiform movements seen in this case. C) Frontal lobe tumor: Frontal lobe tumors may present with various neurological symptoms, but the combination of jerky, semi-purposive movements affecting the entire body and abnormal tongue movements is not characteristic of frontal lobe tumors. text: Gas gangrene is caused by which organism?
expl: Explanation: Gas gangrene (clostridial myonecrosis) is most commonly caused by Clostridium perfringens , an anaerobic, spore-forming, gram-positive bacillus. The organism produces the potent alpha-toxin (lecithinase), which destroys muscle tissue, causes hemolysis, and produces gas within tissues. It is a rapidly progressive, life-threatening infection requiring urgent surgical debridement with high-dose penicillin and clindamycin , and sometimes hyperbaric oxygen therapy. Explanation of other options: Clostridium difficile (Option A): Causes pseudomembranous colitis due to toxins A and B after broad-spectrum antibiotic use, not gas gangrene. Clostridium tetani (Option C): Produces tetanospasmin , leading to spastic paralysis, risus sardonicus, and opisthotonus, but not muscle necrosis with gas. Clostridium botulinum (Option D): Produces botulinum toxin , causing flaccid paralysis and foodborne botulism, not gas gangrene.

text: In Myasthenia gravis, antibodies are targeted at the NMJ on receptor:
expl: Explanation Myasthenia gravis (MG) is an autoimmune disorder of the neuromuscular junction. Autoantibodies are directed against the postsynaptic acetylcholine (ACh) receptors . This prevents normal neuromuscular transmission, leading to fluctuating muscle weakness that worsens with activity (fatigability). Common symptoms: ptosis, diplopia, dysphagia, proximal limb weakness . Associated with thymic hyperplasia or thymoma . Myasthenia Gravis Explanation of Incorrect Options Presynaptic Ach receptors (Option A): The presynaptic terminal releases acetylcholine; however, MG antibodies do not target presynaptic receptors.Presynaptic pathology is instead seen in botulism and Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome (LEMS) (where calcium channels are affected). Voltage gated calcium channels (Option C): These are the antibody targets in Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome (LEMS) , not MG.In LEMS, impaired calcium influx leads to reduced ACh release. Motor end plate (Option D): The motor end plate is the anatomical site where the NMJ exists, but MG specifically targets the postsynaptic ACh receptors , not the entire motor end plate structure.

text: A 30-year-old woman presents with unilateral ptosis that worsens by evening and is diagnosed with myasthenia gravis. What is the drug of choice for her management?
expl: Explanation: The goals of treatment in myasthenia gravis are to maximize acetylcholine activity at remaining neuromuscular junction receptors and limit or abolish the immune attack on motor end plates. The duration of acetylcholine action is prolonged by acetylcholinesterase inhibition, with pyridostigmine being the most commonly used drug. Myasthenia gravis: Management Anticholinesterase medication Anticholinesterase medications produce at least partial improvement in most myasthenic patients, although complete recovery is uncommon. Patients with anti-MuSK myasthenia generally benefit less from these agents and may even worsen. Pyridostigmine , the most widely used anticholinesterase, is started at 30-60 mg three to four times daily. Immunological treatment includes: Acute treatments Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG): Rapidly reduces antibody levels and weakness. Plasmapheresis: P roduces a short-term reduction in anti-AChR antibodies , leading to temporary improvement in myasthenic symptoms. IVIG and plasmapheresis are reserved for myasthenic crisis or preoperative preparation . (Option D ruled out) Long-term treatments Glucocorticoids: Glucocorticoids effectively improve myasthenic weakness in most patients. To minimise adverse effects, prednisone should be given as a single daily dose rather than in divided doses. (Option B ruled out) In patients with more severe weakness or those already hospitalized , starting at a high dose is reasonable to achieve a faster therapeutic effect. Pharmacological immunosuppression: Azathioprine 5 mg/kg daily reduces steroid requirements and may allow withdrawal, though effects are delayed for months. Mycophenolate mofetil is widely used in myasthenia gravis due to its presumed effectiveness and relatively favourable side-effect profile. Calcineurin inhibitors such as cyclosporine and tacrolimus and monoclonal antibodies like Rituximab and Eculizumab are also currently used. (Option C ruled out) Thymectomy: Indicated in antibody-positive patients under 45 years with generalized symptoms, or in patients with thymoma ; less effective if disease duration exceeds 7 years or symptoms are confined to extraocular muscles.

text: Which type of hypersensitivity reaction is seen in myasthenia gravis?
expl: Explanation: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune condition caused by IgG autoantibodies against acetylcholine receptors (AChR) at the neuromuscular junction. This leads to complement-mediated cytotoxicity and receptor destruction , producing fatigable muscle weakness. Since the disease mechanism involves antibody-mediated cellular damage, it is classified under Type II hypersensitivity reaction . Explanation of Other Options: Type 1 hypersensitivity reaction (Option A): IgE-mediated immediate reaction (e.g., anaphylaxis, asthma). Not applicable in MG. Type 3 hypersensitivity reaction (Option C): Immune complex-mediated (e.g., SLE, RA). Different from antibody cytotoxicity. Type 4 hypersensitivity reaction (Option D): T-cell mediated delayed hypersensitivity (e.g., contact dermatitis, Mantoux). Not relevant here.

text: A 16-year-old girl presents with generalized muscle weakness and ptosis that worsens as the day progresses. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The clinical manifestations of muscle weakness and fatigability, especially worsening as the day progresses, are highly suggestive of myasthenia gravis. Myasthenia Gravis Myasthenia Gravis (MG) is a neuromuscular junction disorder characterized by skeletal muscle weakness and fatigability. The underlying mechanism is a reduction in available acetylcholine receptors (AChRs) at the neuromuscular junction due to antibody-mediated autoimmune destruction. Clinical Features of Myasthenia Gravis: Fatigable muscle weakness : Muscle strength decreases with continued use , especially: Later in the day as day progresses After exercise No sensory or CNS involvement , distinguishing it from other neurological disorders. Common initial symptoms Ptosis (drooping eyelid) Diplopia (double vision) Weakness can spread to: Chewing, swallowing, and speaking muscles Limb muscles Muscle Weakness Patterns: Diagnosis Anti-AChR Ab: + in 85% generalized, 50% ocular; confirms diagnosis if positive; AChR-negative: 40% MuSK+, 2% LRP-4+. Repetitive Nerve Stimulation: >10% decrement → probable MG. SFEMG: Jitter/blocking; confirmatory, not specific. Edrophonium Test: Positive → probable MG. Ice-Pack Test: Improves ptosis; highly sensitive. CT/MRI: Exclude intracranial lesions in ocular/cranial MG. Explanation of other options: Fibromyalgia (Option B): This chronic condition is characterized by widespread musculoskeletal pain, fatigue, and tender points rather than true muscle weakness. It does not present with ptosis or demonstrate diurnal variation in symptoms. Myotonic Dystrophy (Option C): A genetic disorder causes progressive muscle weakness with myotonia (delayed muscle relaxation) and primarily affects distal muscles. The absence of myotonia and the presence of generalized muscular weakness points away from this diagnosis. Guillain-Barré Syndrome (Option D): Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) is an acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy. GBS typically presents with acute-onset symmetric flaccid limb weakness that begins in the lower extremities and progresses upward.

text: A 30-year-old woman presents with ptosis, diplopia, and generalised fatigable muscle weakness, along with difficulty chewing and swallowing, which worsens later in the day. A Tensilon test is positive. Which investigation is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The patient's symptoms of ptosis, diplopia, fatigable muscle weakness, and diurnal variation strongly suggest Myasthenia Gravis (MG) . A positive Tensilon test supports this clinical suspicion. The most sensitive confirmatory investigation is Single Fiber Electromyography (SFEMG) , with sensitivity up to 99%. While SFEMG is the most sensitive, Repetitive Nerve Stimulation (RNS) is more commonly performed as a confirmatory test in clinical practice. Myasthenia Gravis Myasthenia Gravis (MG) is an autoimmune disorder of the neuromuscular junction characterized by skeletal muscle weakness and fatigability . The underlying mechanism involves antibody-mediated destruction of acetylcholine receptors (AChRs) at the neuromuscular junction. Clinical Features: Fatigable muscle weakness: Strength worsens with continued use, especially later in the day or after exercise . No sensory or central nervous system involvement , distinguishing MG from other neurological disorders. Common initial symptoms include ptosis and diplopia. Evaluation and Diagnosis Diagnosis involves a comprehensive approach integrating clinical evaluation and specific diagnostic tests. Explanation of other options: MRI of the brain (Option D): MRI may be useful in ruling out other neurological conditions that can present with similar symptoms, such as multiple sclerosis or brainstem lesions. However, it does not provide specific diagnostic information for MG and is primarily used to exclude other conditions.

text: A 64-year-old man develops swallowing difficulties and complains of difficulty walking up stairs. On examination, there is weakness and wasting of the distal muscles of the arms. There are visible fasciculations. Reflexes are brisk and the plantars are up going. There are no sensory abnormalities. Speech and language assessment suggests the presence of pharyngeal muscle weakness.What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: This patient presents with pure motor weakness, with UMN features like hyper-reflexia and extensor plantar and LMN features like fasciculations. This is a classical presentation of motor neuron disease. There is a pseudobulbar palsy in association with fasciculations of the muscles and a mixture of upper and lower motor neuron signs. GBS is less likely as it is not acute onset, no preceding infection. Moreover, fasciculation and muscle wasting are the classic features found in MND and not in GBS. This features also differentiates it from Myasthenia gravis. As sensory is normal, CIDP is less likely. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 437, Pg: 3410

text: A middle aged man comes to the ER with altered sensorium of insidious onset. ansText: Microcytic hypochromic anemia with Basophilic stippling of RBC on peripheral smear
expl: A pure motor neuropathy with encephalopathy points to toxicity with lead. text: A 75-year-old patient with long-standing diabetes presents with loss of ankle reflex. Which of the following patterns describes neuropathy most commonly seen in diabetes?
expl: Explanation: The most common type of diabetic neuropathy is distal symmetric polyneuropathy. It primarily affects the sensory and motor nerves in a “stocking and glove” distribution, starting distally in the feet and progressing proximally. Diabetic distal Sensory and Sensorimotor Polyneuropathy (DSPN) is the most common form of diabetic neuropathy and manifests as sensory loss beginning in the toes that gradually progresses over time up the legs and into the fingers and arms. Loss of ankle reflex is a hallmark sign. Symptoms may include numbness, tingling, burning pain, and sometimes weakness. This neuropathy develops gradually and is the typical neuropathic pattern seen in long-standing diabetes. The most common cranial nerve involvement in Diabetes mellitus is the Oculomotor nerve, followed by the abducens and facial nerves. Explanation of Incorrect Options: Mononeuritis multiplex (Option B): Involves asymmetric involvement of individual nerves, often in an acute or subacute fashion, not the typical pattern in diabetes. Proximal neuropathy (Option C): Also called diabetic amyotrophy; less common and usually involves the thigh and hip muscles with pain and weakness. Amyotrophy (Option D): Refers to muscle wasting and weakness, often associated with proximal neuropathy, not the classic diabetic sensory polyneuropathy.

text: A 21-year-old female, who was 32 weeks pregnant is brought to the ER, with 1 week history of fever. She had been complaining of sever fatigue, decreased urine output and high coloured urine. This morning she developed two episodes of seizures and is unconscious. There were no focal deficits and both the plantar were extensor. Her investigations showed Hb: 6g/dL, Total Count of 20,000 cells/μL, Platelet of 10,000/μL, S. Cr was 4.5mg/dL. Her peripheral smear showed shistocytes. Her Prothrombin time and activated thromboplastin time were normal. Which of the following statements is false?

options.A: HELLP Syndrome can be a possible differential diagnosis.
options.B: TTP can be triggered by pregnancy
options.C: Renal impairment is life threatening in HELLP
options.D: ADAMTS 13 activity can be decreased in HELLP syndrome also.

ansText: Renal impairment is life threatening in HELLP
expl: Renal failure is a common manifestation of HELLP but is not life threatening. Life threatening complications are neurological complications and hepatic hematoma. HELLP syndrome is a Thrombotic Microangiopathy that occurs in pregnancy. It is usually associated with pre-ecclampsia. It is different from other TMAs by the presence of liver injury that defines its severity. Liver sub capsular hematoma can be life threatening as it can cause rupture of liver. Neurological complications include cerebral infarction, hemorthage in brainstem and cerebral edema. aHUS and TTP can also be triggered by pregnancy and hence be a differential diagnosis of HELLP syndrome. In HELLP syndrome anti thrombin III will be decreased and D Dimer will be elevated. ADAMTS 13 activity may be reduced to 30-60%. DIC can be considered as a DD, but it causes prolongation of PT and aPTT. In TTP, there will be a classical pentad of fever, neurological symptoms, renal failure, thrombocytopenia and MAHA. It is due to decreased activity of ADAMTS 13 to Acquired TTP can occur due to antibodies to ADAMTS13 which inhibits its activity. It is common in females. It is very severe with mortality of >90% if untreated. TRERATMENT OF TMAs: Plasma infusion or plasma exchange is enough to treat congenital TTP. Acquired TTP and DEAP HUS requires immunosuppression in addition to plasma exchange. Caplacizumab is the monoclonal antibody approved for the treatment of acquired TTP. Atypical HUS is treated with Eculizumab Neuraminidase associated HUS is treated with antibiotics and plasma exchange. Blood should not be given as it has IgM. Reference: Harrison's Principles of internal medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:317, Pg: 2365-2367.

text: A 34-year-old woman has been admitted to hospital for investigation of progressive weakness in her legs. For the past 5 years. The patient's mother has similar difficulties with weakness and sensory problems. Examination revealed power of 3/5 distally in the upper and lower limbs with a glove and stocking pattern sensory loss to pain and touch. What is the likely diagnosis?
expl: In view of the family history, this patient is most likely to have hereditary sensory motor neuropathy type I (Charcot Marie Tooth disease). CMT 1 is the most common form of hereditary neuropathy. Hallmarks of the disease include - Severely and uniformly slowed nerve conduction velocities (NCVs) Primary hypertrophic myelin pathology with prominent onion bulbs Secondary axonal changes Motor symptoms predominate over sensory symptoms. Often, patients report loss of balance, muscle weakness, and foot deformities. Onset in the first decade of life is typical, but disease develops in some patients in young or mid adulthood. Friedreich's ataxia is an autosomal-recessive genetic disease that causes difficulty walking, a loss of sensation in the arms and legs, and impaired speech that worsens over time. Complications of the disease include hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, scoliosis and diabetes mellitus. Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP) is an acquired autoimmune disease of the peripheral nervous system characterized by progressive weakness and impaired sensory function in the legs and arms. CIDP is closely related to Guillain-Barre syndrome and it is considered the chronic counterpart of that acute disease. Its symptoms are also similar to progressive inflammatory neuropathy. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Ch: 446, PG: 3483-3485

text: A 22-year-old man presents with tremor, sweating, flushing and weight loss. On examination his pulse is 135 bpm and his blood pressure is 160/110 mmHg. Which of the following is the least likely diagnostic possibility?
expl: Pheochromocytomas are catecholamine secreting tumours arising from the adrenal gland. Pheochromocytoma may occur in patients with von Recklinghausen's disease (NF-1) and von Hippel-Lindau syndrome. Skin neurofibromas and multiple cafe au-lait spots occur in peripheral (NF1) neurofibromatosis, while haemangioblastomas are commonly seen in those with the von Hippel-Lindau syndrome. Carney's triad includes Pheochromocytoma /paraganglioma, pulmonary chondroma and Gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST) Ataxia telangiectasia is not associated with pheochromocytomas. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 2976

text: A 55-year-old man presents with weakness, general malaise and ankle swelling. He has been unwell for 4 months, the ankle swelling having developed quite rapidly over the previous 3 weeks. Further investigation reveals a paraprotein band in his serum with kappa light chains demonstrated on immunofixation. What is the probable cause of the proteinuria?
expl: Multiple myeloma causes tubular dysfunction due to Complete occlusion of the renal tubules by the light chains-Cast Nephropathy Tubulointerstitial disesase due to immunoglobulin and hypercalcemia Proximal tubular dysfunction Tubular dysfunction causes mild proteinuria without hypertension and hematuria. Glomerular involvement includes Light chain deposition disease Amyloidosis Both cause massive proteinuria with variable hypertension and hematuria. So our patient is having either Amyloidosis or Light Chain Deposition Disease or Amyloidosis, since there is massive proteinuria. So what is the difference? Since the patient has circulating Kappa light chains, the biopsy is most likely to show LCDD. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st edition, Ch:314, Pg:2345.

text: A 16-year-old male presents with cardiac tamponade. On examination his peripheral pulse volume fell during inspiration. Which one of the following is the most likely explanation for this clinical sign?

options.A: The cardiac effect of high dose beta agonist bronchodilator drugs
options.B: A falling heart rate on inspiration
options.D: Reduced left atrial filling pressure on inspiration

ansText: Reduced left atrial filling pressure on inspiration
expl: This patient is demonstrating pulsus paradoxus . The right heart responds directly to changes in intrathoracic pressure , while the filling of the left heart depends on the pulmonary vascular volume . At high respiratory rates, with severe air flow limitation (eg cardiac tamponade, acute asthma) there is an increased and sudden negative intrathoracic pressure on inspiration and this will enhance the normal fall in blood pressure. Reference: Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Principles, 20 th edition, ch:265 pg:1843

text: Which of the following investigations should be conducted in a 7-month-old child who has a hemoglobin level of 6.3, a history of recurrent blood transfusions, an MCV of 70 fl, normal MCH, normal MCHC, and a peripheral smear indicating a hypochromic microcytic image?
expl: Explanation: In an infant with severe microcytic hypochromic anemia requiring transfusions, the most likely diagnosis is beta-thalassemia major . Hemoglobin electrophoresis is the definitive test, which would show a significant increase in Hemoglobin F (HbF) and possibly Hemoglobin A2 (HbA2) , with absent or reduced Hemoglobin A (HbA). Explanation of other options: Serum iron (Option A): Would be normal or elevated in thalassemia (due to transfusions), but low in iron deficiency. It is not the definitive test. Direct coomb's test (Option B): Used to diagnose autoimmune hemolytic anemia. Osmotic fragility test (Option C): Used to diagnose hereditary spherocytosis, which causes a normocytic or macrocytic anemia, not microcytic. Key Takeaways: Thalassemia major presents in infancy with severe transfusion-dependent microcytic anemia. Hemoglobin electrophoresis is the key diagnostic test.

text: A 37-year-old lady has developed progressive weakness in the hands and feet over a week. There is some associated numbness and tingling in the hands and feet. She complains of breathing difficulty. She had several episodes of diarrhea two weeks ago. On examination, there is slurring of speech. Her reflexes are all absent and there is sensory loss in a glove and stocking pattern. Which is the next appropriate step?
expl: This patient is having an LMN quadriparesis that is antedated by a history of diarrhoeal diasease. Guillain Barre syndrome is the likely diagnosis. As she is complaining of breathlessness, vital capacity measurement would be essential to access respiratory function and determine the need for ventilation. ICU admission is recommended when FVC is less than 20 mL/kg and intubation is recommended in most cases when FVC is less than 15 mL/kg. Diaphragmatic weakness occurs in 30% of patients with patients with GBS and involvement of the neck muscles, tongue and palate leads to further respiratory compromise. Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS): (Post-infectious polyradiculoneuropathy) - Immune -mediated demyelination of the peripheral nervous system often triggered by an infection such as viral (CMV), viral pneumonia or bacterial (classically Campylobacter jejuni ). CSF findings - Elevated protein with no pleocytosis - (albuminocytologic dissociation). Glucose is normal. Pathogenesis - Cross reaction of antibodies with gangliosides in the peripheral nervous system. Anti GM1 antibodies positive in 25% of cases. Clinical features - The characteristic features of GBS is progressive symmetric ascending weakness. It begins in the legs and progressively ascends to involve the trunk, upper limbs and finally the bulbar muscles. However it tends to affect proximal muscles earlier than the distal ones. Sensory symptoms tend to be mild (e.g., distal paraesthesia, peripheral sensory neuropathy) with very few sensory signs (NO sensory loss). Usually there is painless progression over days or weeks. Areflexia - All tendon reflexes are absent and the plantar responses were flexor. Cranial nerve involvement e.g., bilateral facial palsy Autonomic dysfunction : e.g., urinary retention and postural hypotension & tachycardia. Management - IVIG (IV immunoglobulins) or plasmapheresis. Regular monitoring of FVC (Forced vital capacity ) to access respiratory function. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 447, Pg: 3501-3504

text: A 32-year-old man presents with a 5-day history of weakness in the arms and legs, accompanied by tingling. He had several episodes of bloody diarrheal illness two weeks ago. On examination there was leg and arm weakness and flaccid deep tendon reflexes. Which test would best help confirm the diagnosis?
expl: The diagnosis is likely to be Guillain Barre syndrome. The two best tests are - NCS: Shows prolonged distal latencies and reduced CMAP in AIDP. In AMAN or AMSAN, there will be reduced CMAP without prolonged distal latencies. CSF analysis - Shows raised protein. Campylobacter serology should also be sent for this patient as he has history of bloody diarrhoea. GBS is often seen following Campylobacter infection. Previous history of a diarrhoeal illness (specifically Campylobacter jejuni) is a poor prognostic feature. Other poor prognostic features include Age > 40 years High anti-GM1 antibody titre Poor upper extremity muscle strength Need for ventilatory support Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 ST Ed, Ch: 447, Pg: 3503

text: The antibodies detected in Acute Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyneuropathy are of which immunoglobulin class?
expl: Explanation: The antibody seen in Guillain-Barre Syndrome (GBS) , also known as Acute Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyneuropathy (AIDP) , is predominantly IgG . Guillain-Barre Syndrome (GBS) is an autoimmune condition in which the body's immune system mistakenly attacks the peripheral nervous system, leading to acute paralysis. The main antibodies involved are of the IgG class, which target myelin in the peripheral nerves. This immune response causes inflammation and demyelination, producing typical features such as muscle weakness, sensory disturbances, and progressive ascending paralysis. Explanations of other options: IgM (Option B): Although IgM antibodies may play a role in some autoimmune disorders, they are not commonly linked to Guillain-Barre Syndrome (GBS). IgM is generally involved in the initial stages of the immune response and is not the characteristic antibody type seen in GBS. IgE (Option C): IgE antibodies are mainly linked to allergic responses and defence against parasitic infections. They are not typically involved in Guillain-Barre Syndrome (GBS), as their role is centred on hypersensitivity reactions rather than autoimmune activity. IgA (Option D): IgA antibodies are predominantly present in mucosal surfaces and are crucial for protecting mucous membranes. They are not commonly linked to the immune mechanisms of GBS, since their main role is mucosal defence rather than systemic autoimmune activity.

text: A 26-year-old man, who had a respiratory infection 4 weeks earlier, has been unable to stand or walk for the past 2 weeks due to progressive, symmetrical, ascending weakness. The weakness started in the lower limbs and later involved the upper limbs. On examination, reflexes are absent, while pain and position sense remain intact. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The patient shows hallmark signs of Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS) , namely a preceding respiratory infection, gradually worsening ascending symmetrical weakness, and loss of reflexes. Guillain-Barre syndrome is an autoimmune polyradiculopathy that leads to patchy, segmental demyelination of the spinal roots and peripheral nerves. Its link with recent infection, the pattern of ascending weakness, and the preservation of sensory function are typical features of the condition. Explanation of other options: Myasthenia gravis (Option B): In myasthenia gravis, muscle weakness usually becomes more pronounced with repeated activity and improves after rest. The condition often begins by involving the eye and facial muscles before progressing to the limbs. An ascending pattern of weakness with absent reflexes is not characteristic of this disorder. Polymyositis (Option C): Polymyositis is characterized by symmetric weakness of proximal muscles, mainly involving the shoulders and hips, leading to difficulty in tasks such as climbing stairs or lifting the arms overhead. Reflexes remain intact, and sensation is preserved. Since this case lacks proximal muscle involvement, shows absent reflexes, and does not follow the typical ascending pattern, polymyositis is unlikely. Multiple sclerosis (Option D): Multiple sclerosis usually progresses in a relapsing-remitting pattern with varied neurological signs. Typical features include visual disturbances such as optic neuritis and sensory issues like numbness and tingling. Affected individuals more often show increased reflexes rather than absent ones.

text: In a child diagnosed with Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS), which of the following statements is incorrect?

options.A: Areflexia of the affected limb is a mandatory diagnostic criteria
options.B: Plasmapheresis is not preferred in refractory cases
options.C: Intravenous immunoglobulin is the first line of management
options.D: Albuminocytological dissociation in CSF is characteristic

ansText: Plasmapheresis is not preferred in refractory cases
expl: Explanation: Plasmapheresis is actually preferred in refractory cases of Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS), especially when the condition does not improve after initial treatment with intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG). The standard treatment for GBS involves the use of either IVIG or plasmapheresis, depending on the patient's condition and response to initial therapy. Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS) Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS) is a n acute autoimmune disorder that affects the peripheral nervous system . It often leads to ascending paralysis , starting from the lower limbs and spreading upwards. GBS is considered a neurological emergency due to its potential to cause respiratory failure, autonomic dysfunction, and death without timely treatment. Epidemiology and Triggers Incidence: 1-2 cases per 100,000 persons per year. Often follows an infection or vaccination (molecular mimicry). Common triggers: Campylobacter jejuni (most common) Cytomegalovirus (CMV) Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) Mycoplasma pneumoniae Zika virus, Influenza virus These infections lead to molecular mimicry , where the immune system attacks nerve structures , particularly the myelin sheath , causing demyelination. Variants of Guillain-Barré Syndrome: Autoantibodies in Guillain-Barré Syndrome: Diversity: GBS patients exhibit a range of autoantibodies targeting nerve cells and structures. Common Antibodies: The most common are anti-ganglioside antibodies , which appear in up to 50% of GBS cases . Prognostic Implications: The presence of anti-GM1 antibodies correlates with poorer clinical outcomes , especially in pure motor variants and Miller Fisher Syndrome . Clinical Features: Motor Symptoms Symmetrical, ascending paralysis (starts in lower limbs → progresses proximally). Hypotonia or flaccid paralysis. Areflexia or hyporeflexia (deep tendon reflexes lost early). In severe cases: Facial nerve weakness. Bulbar or respiratory muscle involvement (respiratory failure in 25-30%). Sensory Symptoms Paresthesias and numbness in distal limbs ("glove and stocking" pattern). Loss of proprioception and vibration sense. Pain in shoulders, neck, or back. Autonomic Dysfunction Orthostatic hypotension. Cardiac arrhythmias (sinus tachycardia/bradycardia). Blood pressure fluctuations. Bowel and bladder dysfunction. Diagnostic Findings: Brighton Criteria for Diagnosis of GBS: Treatment: Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG) First-line therapy for both adults and children. Dose: 2 g/kg total, administered over 2-5 days. Mechanism: Neutralizes autoantibodies, blocks Fc receptors, and modulates immune response. Plasmapheresis (Plasma Exchange) Equally effective as IVIG , especially useful in refractory cases or rapidly progressive weakness . Removes circulating pathogenic antibodies and immune complexes. Typically performed as 4-6 exchanges over 10-14 days. Not recommended immediately after IVIG (should be spaced by ≥48 hours). Supportive Care Respiratory monitoring (FVC Autonomic monitoring (for arrhythmias and BP fluctuations). DVT prophylaxis and physiotherapy. Corticosteroids: Ineffective in GBS and not recommended.

text: A patient presents with pigmented spots around the mouth and lips, along with abdominal pain and vomiting. History reveals that pigmentation has been present since childhood. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS) is an autosomal dominant disorder characterised by mucocutaneous pigmented macules (especially on lips, mouth, fingers) and hamartomatous polyps in the GI tract . Patients often present with abdominal pain, vomiting, or intussusception due to polyps. Pigmentation starting in childhood and gastrointestinal symptoms strongly support PJS . Explanation of other options: Familial adenomatous polyposis (Option A): Caused by APC gene mutation with hundreds of adenomatous polyps in the colon, but no mucocutaneous pigmentation . Juvenile polyposis syndrome (Option C): Presents with multiple hamartomatous polyps and rectal bleeding, but pigmentation is absent. Cronkhite-Canada syndrome (Option D): A rare non-hereditary disorder with GI polyps, alopecia, and nail atrophy, not pigmented spots around the lips.

text: A 39-year-old lady has difficulty walking. On examination, she has an ataxic gait, increased tone in the legs with hyperreflexia and motor weakness. What diagnostic investigation should be arranged?

options.A: CT scan of the brain and spine

expl: The patient in this question has involvement of the pyramidal tract as evidenced by the hyperreflexia, hypertonia and the weakness. She also has ataxia, which could be either due to the involvement of the posterior column or the cerebellum. For imaging of the spinal cord and the structures in the posterior fossa MRI is the best investigation compared to CT. The diseases that can present like this are Multiple sclerosis, Vitamin B12 deficiency etc. Lumbar spine X ray will help to reveal only the bony abnormalities and hence is not useful here. EMG is used if a muscle disease is suspected, which is unlikely in this case. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 423,Pg: 3284

text: A 45-year-old man presents with recurrent episodes of dysuria and suprapubic discomfort over the past 3 months. He has been treated multiple times with antibiotics for suspected urinary tract infections. He denies fever or hematuria. On examination, his prostate is non-tender and normal in size. Lab reports show leukocyte count (>50/UI) in Urine analysis with no growth in urine culture. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: In this case, the patient presents with persistent urinary symptoms over the past 3 months , including increased frequency and suprapubic discomfort , along with a normal prostate examination . Urine analysis reveals a high leukocyte count (>50/μL) , yet urine cultures remain negative for bacterial growth . These findings are most consistent with a diagnosis of sterile pyuria . Explanations for other Options: Chronic Bacterial Prostatitis (Option A): Chronic bacterial prostatitis usually presents with recurrent UTIs , perineal or low back pain, and sometimes a boggy or tender prostate on digital rectal exam. Granulomatous prostatitis (Option B): This is a rare form of prostatitis usually due to tuberculosis , fungal infections, or after intravesical BCG therapy. It often presents with prostate enlargement, nodularity, or tenderness , which are absent here. Diagnosis typically requires a biopsy Acute UTI (Option C): Acute UTIs generally present with dysuria, frequency, urgency , often accompanied by fever, chills, or flank pain , and show positive urine cultures . This patient lacks systemic symptoms and has repeatedly negative cultures , which rules out a typical UTI.

text: Which of the following is true regarding Behcet disease?

options.A: The most common and the earliest lesion of Behcet disease is genital ulcers
options.B: The most specific lesion is oral ulcer
options.C: While oral ulcers do scar, genital ulcers usually do not
options.D: Pathergy test is a non-specific hyperreactivity test to trauma

ansText: Pathergy test is a non-specific hyperreactivity test to trauma
expl: The most common symptoms are associated with mucocutaneous tissues. Oral ulcers are seen in virtually all patients and are commonly the first manifestation. Commonly, like ordinary cancer sores, they are usually multiple. They scar only uncommonly. Genital ulcers are the most specific lesions, most commonly occurring on the scrotum or labia. They are larger and deeper and take longer to heal than oral ulcers and tend to form scars. Pathergy reaction is a nonspecific hyperreactivity of the skin to trauma. Typically, a papule or pustule forms in 24–48 h after a needle prick. It is rather unique for Behçet syndrome and is part of the ISG diagnostic criteria. Eye involvement is seen in half of all patients and in ~70% of males. It is most commonly a bilateral panuveitis. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Ch:364 Pg:2817

text: A diabetic patient came to you and wished you namaste. While doing namaste you as a doctor observe his hand has this deformity?
expl: The patient in the given question is unable to oppose the palmar surfaces of the hands and fingers(prayer sign). This is due to limited joint mobility syndrome or diabetic cheiroarthropathy or stiff hand syndrome. It is not an arthropathy, but a process that involves the periarticular structures. It is a fibrosing syndrome resulting in thick waxy and tight skin on the dorsal aspect of MCP, PIP and DIP of fingers. Larger joints can also be involved. It is seen in both type i and type ii diabetes and increases in frequency with age, disease duration and poor glycemic control. NSAIDs and steroids are ineffective in management. Physical therapy and glycemic control are the treatment.

text: A 75-year-old woman comes to the clinic for advice. Over the course of the past year or two she has had increasing problems with regurgitation of rotten food, has lost weight and acquired a chronic cough. According to her partner she has problems with halitosis which have not improved on multiple visits to the dentist. On examination her BP is 145/82 mmHg, pulse is 70 and regular and her BMI is 27. She has a neck mass which appears to gurgle when she swallows. Investigations show: Haemoglobin 13.2 g/dl (11.5-16.0) White cell count 7.3 x 10^9/L (4-11) Platelets 161 x 10^9/L (150-400) Sodium 141 mmol/l (135-146) Potassium 4.0 mmol/l (3.5-5) Creatinine 0.7 mg/dl Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: The history of regurgitation of rotten food, coupled with chronic cough and a gurgling mass on examination fits best with a pharyngeal pouch (Zenker's diverticulum) . Aspiration of food from the pouch may lead to pneumonia in some cases. Zenker's diverticulum is a pulsion diverticulum where pharyngeal mucosa herniates through the weak area between two parts of the inferior constrictor. Management involves either diverticulectomy for larger lesions, or Dohlman's procedure for smaller pouches. Whilst GERD is a possible alternative diagnosis, a pouch would not be found on examination. Achalasia is usually associated with progressive dysphagia to both liquids and solids, oesophageal carcinoma with progressive dysphagia first to solids then liquids. Plummer-Vinson's disease is associated with progressive dysphagia due to oesophageal webs. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 323, Pg: 2426

text: Where is the defect in multiple sclerosis?
expl: Multiple sclerosis is a disorder of the CNS characterized by chronic inflammation, demyelination and scarring. Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune disease of the central nervous system (CNS) characterized by chronic inflammation, demyelination, gliosis (plaques or scarring), and neuronal loss; the course can be relapsing or progressive. MS plaques typically develop at different times and in different CNS locations (i.e., MS is said to be disseminated in time and space). Demyelination New MS lesions begin with perivenular cuffing by inflammatory mononuclear cells, predominantly T cells and macrophages, which also infiltrate the surrounding white matter. At sites of inflammation, the blood-brain barrier (BBB) is disrupted, but unlike in vasculitis, the vessel wall is preserved. At the leading edge of lesions, large numbers of cytotoxic CD8 cells are found. Involvement of the humoral immune system is also evident; small numbers of B lymphocytes infiltrate the nervous system, myelin-specific autoantibodies are present on degenerating myelin sheaths, and complement is activated.

text: A 32-year-old man has a painful right eye. On examination, there is decreased visual acuity and a relative afferent pupillary defect of the right eye. What is the diagnosis?
expl: A painful eye with loss of vision, and also RAPD suggests optic neuritis . Optic neuritis describes any condition that causes inflammation of the optic nerve; it may be associated with demyelinating diseases, or infectious or inflammatory processes. It is also known as Optic papillitis(when the head of the optic nerve is involved), Neuro-retinitis(when there is a combined involvement of optic disc and surrounding retina in the macular area) and Retro bulbar neuritis (when the posterior part of the nerve is involved). Cause TREATMENT : Steroids are the mainstay of treatment of Optic neuritis. There is no difference between oral and Iv steroids in the outcome of optic neuritis. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 32, Pg: 223

text: A 35 year old man has difficulty with his vision. On examination he has impaired adduction of the right eye looking left. The left eye has jerky nystagmus. Which investigation is most likely to yield a diagnosis?

options.C: Paired CSF and serum for oligoclonal bands

ansText: Paired CSF and serum for oligoclonal bands
expl: The clinical scenario is internuclear ophthalmoplegia. This is most commonly seen in multiple sclerosis . MRI of the brain and CSF are the best diagnostic tests. In this scenario the lesion is in the right medial longitudinal fasciculus. Internuclear ophthalmoplegia - patient looking to the left MR imaging of the brain showed multiple abnormal high signals on T2WI involving bilateral deep white matter, corpus callosum, occipital periventricular regions, and periaqueductal regions of the pons and medulla Diagnostic tools in MS: MRI Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and spine may show areas of demyelination (lesions or plaques). Gadolinium can be administered intravenously as a contrast agent to highlight active plaques and, by elimination, demonstrate the existence of historical lesions not associated with symptoms at the moment of the evaluation. Central vein signs (CVS) have been proposed as a good indicator of MS in comparison with other conditions causing white lesions. Brain atrophy is seen as an indicator of MS. Cerebrospinal fluid Testing of cerebrospinal fluid obtained from a lumbar puncture can provide evidence of chronic inflammation in the central nervous system. The cerebrospinal fluid is tested for oligoclonal bands of IgG on electrophoresis , which are inflammation markers found in 75-85% of people with MS.
