text: A 33 year old female comes with a 3 month history of multiple neurological symptoms. It started with a blurring of vision on the right eye. She has noted that the visual blurring increases when she takes a hot shower. She also has multiple episodes of electric shock like sensation radiating from her spine down to both lower limbs. On examination, she has afferent pupillary defect in the right eye, with a pale disc. She also has bilateral lower limb spasticity and hyperreflexia, with extensor plantar response. What will be the likely findings in the MRI of the brain and spinal cord in this patient?

options.A: Chronic infarct in the occipital lobe on the left side
options.B: Demyelination of the optic nerve of the right eye with multiple demyelinating patches in the brain and the spinal cord
options.D: Space occupying lesion in the occipital lobe

ansText: Demyelination of the optic nerve of the right eye with multiple demyelinating patches in the brain and the spinal cord
expl: Lets analyze the symptoms of this young female. She has a blurred vision in the right eye with Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect, which is suggestive of optic neuritis. A pale disc suggests optic atrophy secondary to a long standing optic neuritis. Her visual symptoms increase on taking hot shower. This is known as Uhthoff's Symptoms. Also she has electric shock like sensation that radiates down her spine to both lower limbs. This is known as Lhermitte's symptoms. She has UMN signs in the form of spasticity, hyperreflexia and extensor plantar. All these point to the diagnosis of Multiple Sclerosis. The likely MRI finding that we will see will be demyelination of the optic nerve and other demyelinating patches, which may or may not be symptomatic, scattered in the brain and the spinal cord. SYMPTOMS OF MS: Sensory symptoms, girdle like sensation, pain. Cranial nerve symptoms: Optic neuritis, Facial palsy with sparing of taste sensation in anterior 2/3 rd of tongue, gaze disturbances like INO, one and a half syndrome, 6 th nerve palsy, pendular nystagmus. Motor symptoms: Weakness and spasticity Ancilliary symptoms: which include Paroxysmal symptoms( brief and self limited neurological symptoms caused by hyperventilation or movement, without any loss of sensorium), Lhermitte's symptoms, Uhthoff's Symptoms, Bilateral trigeminal neuralgia, hemifacial spasm, glossopharyngeal neuralgia, facial myokimia, bladder dysfunction, constipation, fatigue, sexual dysfunction. IMAGING IN MS: MRI typically shows areas of hyperintensity in T2 and FLAIR images perpendicular to the ventricles, called Dawson's Fingers. There will be transient enhancement of these lesions on contrast appearance, but the enhancement disappears in one month. The lesion persists life long in MS. >90% of the lesions visualized in the MRI are asymptomatic. Evoked potentials of the visual, auditory, somatosensory or motor pathways may be abnormal in 80-90% of patients. CSF oligoclonal bands may be seen in> 90% of cases of MS Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 444, Pg: 3462-3467

text: A 24 year old man came from South America 5 years ago. Since a year ago, he has had two tonic clonic seizures a week. On examination, he appears well, with no focal neurological deficit. A CT scan shows multiple calcified cystic lesions in the brain. Which diagnosis is likely?
expl: Neurocysticercosis is caused by Taenia solium (pork tape worm). This disease is found in South America and Asia It is typically benign, and most lesions resolve spontaneously within 2-3 months. There may be seizures due to localised inflammation that accompanies their degeneration in the cerebral cortex when calcified cysts occur.. An enzyme linked immuno transfer blot (EITB) assay of a patient's serum may confirm the diagnosis. Albendazole is the recommended treatment. Neurocysticercosis Here's why the other options are less likely: A) Neurosarcoid (Neurosarcoidosis): Neurosarcoidosis is a condition where sarcoidosis, an inflammatory disease, affects the nervous system. It can cause various neurological symptoms. However, the presence of multiple calcified cystic lesions in the brain, as described in the case, is not typical of neurosarcoidosis. C) Multiple sclerosis (MS): Multiple sclerosis is an autoimmune demyelinating disease of the central nervous system. MS does not typically present with multiple calcified cystic lesions in the brain. Instead, it is characterized by demyelinated plaques. D) Cerebral toxoplasmosis: Cerebral toxoplasmosis is an opportunistic infection often seen in individuals with weakened immune systems, such as those with HIV/AIDS. While it can cause brain lesions, these lesions are usually not calcified cystic lesions. Toxoplasmosis lesions are more commonly ring-enhancing on imaging. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:235 Pg: 1791

text: A 37-year-old male patient with a long history of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis, develops double vision. On examination of his eye movements abduction of either eye elicits nystagmus in that eye. Adduction is impaired in both eyes. On MRI scanning, where will a new white matter lesion probably be evident?
expl: Impairment of adduction in both eyes signifies an internuclear ophthalmoplegia . This is often accompanied by nystagmus of the abducting eye. The area of the brain affected is the medial longtitudinal bundle in the brain stem which connects the third and sixth nerve nuclei. The main causes of internuclear ophthalmoplegia are Multiple sclerosis tumour of the brainstem (glioma, for example) Brainstem vascular lesions or Wernicke's encephalopathy. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 32, Pg: 321

text: Which of the following is the most common initial symptom of Multiple Sclerosis (MS)?
expl: Explanation: Sensory loss is the most common initial symptom of Multiple Sclerosis (MS). Multiple sclerosis is a chronic autoimmune disorder characterized by demyelination within the central nervous system (CNS) . It affects various neural pathways, leading to a wide range of neurological symptoms that often fluctuate in severity. Common Clinical Features of MS: Sensory disturbances : These include numbness (hypesthesia) and tingling or "pins and needles" sensations (paresthesia) , often affecting the limbs or trunk. Optic neuritis : Typically presents with blurred vision , reduced color perception , and decreased visual acuity , usually on one side (unilateral), but can also be bilateral. Motor symptoms : Patients may develop limb weakness , often with spasticity , abnormal gait , and a positive Babinski sign , indicating upper motor neuron involvement. Cranial nerve involvement : This may manifest as facial weakness and occasionally hearing impairment . Cerebellar signs : Ataxia and vertigo are common, reflecting cerebellar or vestibular involvement. Bladder dysfunction : Often seen as urinary urgency , frequency, or incontinence due to neurogenic bladder. Lhermitte's phenomenon : Described as a sudden electric-shock-like sensation that travels down the spine when the neck is flexed. Uhthoff's phenomenon : Worsening of existing neurological symptoms when exposed to heat , such as during exercise or a hot shower. Imaging in MS: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is the preferred diagnostic tool for MS due to its high sensitivity in detecting CNS lesions . A characteristic MRI finding is the presence of periventricular, ovoid lesions that extend perpendicularly from the ventricular surface , known as Dawson fingers . These findings are essential for diagnosis and monitoring disease progression. Explanations for other Options: Motor weakness (Option A): Motor weakness is a common feature in MS, especially as the disease progresses. However, it is less likely to be the initial symptom compared to sensory disturbances. When present, motor symptoms often involve spasticity, stiffness, or weakness in the legs or arms. Ataxia (Option C): Ataxia, or lack of coordination, may occur in MS due to cerebellar involvement. While it is a recognized manifestation, it is not typically the first symptom . It usually appears later in the disease course or during relapses affecting the cerebellum or its connections Seizures (Option D): Seizures are relatively rare in MS , occurring in only a small percentage of patients. Although cortical lesions in MS can potentially lead to seizures, they are not a common presenting symptom and are far less frequent than sensory or motor signs.

text: A 59-year-old woman presents with poly-symptomatology. On examination she has prominent fasciculations. From which of the following conditions is she unlikely to suffer?
expl: Fasciculation suggest lower motor neurone disease . It is seen usually in diseases affecting the anterior horn cells of spinal cord. It can also be seen in diseases of the nerve roots and peripheral nerves. However, it is absent in diseases of the muscles or neuromuscular junction. Cervical spondylosis is a disease which affects the spinal cord as well as the nerve roots. So it can cause fasciculations. Motor neurone disease is the prototype illness that presents with fasciculations. Spinal muscular atrophy is an LMN type of MND and hence can cause fascicuations. Multiple Sclerosis is a disease causing demyelination of the white matter of the central nervous system and hence presents with predominant UMN symptoms and can have sensory symptoms as well. Hence MS is the less likely cause. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 447, Pg: 3411-3415

text: A 35 year old female comes to you with paraplegia of one day duration, with a sensory level at T10, she has bladder involvement and is catheterized. She gives a history of loss of vision in her left eye, one year back, with residual defective vision. She was not on any follow up. Her MRI brain and spinal cord shows multiple T2 hyperintense lesions. What will be the treatment of this patient?
expl: This patient who has a background history of an defective vision, now presents with symptoms suggestive of a spinal cord transection and MRI showing T2 hyperintense lesions. This is typical of Multiple Sclerosis. The acute episodes of Multiple Sclerosis is treated with steroids. Methylprednisolone 500-1000mg for 3-5 days, followed by a taper with oral steroids 60-80mg/day for two weeks. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 444, Pg: 3468

text: A 54 year old man has slowly progressive weakness of his upper limbs. On examination of the patient the physical signs are wasting and weakness of the small muscles of the hand, flattening of the muscles of the ulnar border of the forearm. The upper limb reflexes are absent. Pain and temperature sensation are reduced over the upper limbs and upper chest whereas light touch and proprioception remain intact. Lower limb reflexes are exaggerated and plantars are extensor. What is the likely diagnosis?
expl: Arnold-Chiari Malformation is a condition in which the cerebellum portion of the brain protrudes into the spinal canal. It may or may not be apparent at birth. Arnold-Chiari I type malformation usually causes symptoms in young adults and is often associated with syringomyelia, in which a tubular cavity develops within the spinal cord. Arnold-Chiari II type malformation is associated with myelomeningocele (a defect of the spine) and hydrocephalus (increased cerebrospinal fluid and pressure within the brain), which usually are apparent at birth. The patient described has the features of an intramedullary lesion of the spinal cord. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 442, Pg: 3453

expl: Complicated dental procedures or other forms of trauma can lead to a form of atypical facial pains which is also known as post traumatic facial pain/ neuralgia. text: A 47 year old woman complains of 12 months of mid and lower back pain associated with stiffness in her shoulders, wrists, small joints of the hands, hips knees and feet. The joint stiffness is more pronounced in the morning and lasts 2-3 hours and is associated with severe fatigue. She also experiences occasional pins and needles affecting all of the right hand and frequent frontal and temporal headache. Clinical examination demonstrates no synovitis but tenderness around the base of the cervical spine, across the shoulders, over the costochondral cartilages, greater trochanter and the knee. Investigations are as follows: CRP <5 g/l, ESR 20 mm in the first hour; CK, serum immunoglobulins and protein electrophoresis normal. What is the diagnosis?
expl: A young female with multiple joint pains and fatigue without any signs of joint involvement but with tender trigger points are characteristic of fibromyalgia. The inflammatory markers and CK are not raised, making the other diagnoses unlikely. Polymyalgia rheumatic may have shoulder girdle pain, but it occurs in elderly and inflammatory markers will be raised. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 373 Pg: 2868-2870

text: A 54 year old man has left sided hearing loss and vertigo. On examination, he has an absent corneal reflex on the left. There is also mild left sided facial weakness. Which one of the following is most likely?
expl: Cerebellopontine angle (CPA) tumours can cause vertigo, unilateral hearing loss. Large tumours may cause subtle facial weakness, decreased corneal reflex, and facial dysesthesia. If there was ophthalmoplegia or chemosis, then a cavernous sinus thrombosis would be more likely (it can also cause absent corneal reflexes). Option A: Frontal lobe tumour would present with prominent behavioural and personality changes, apraxia and headache. Option B: The clinical presentation of CVT is highly variable. The onset can be acute, subacute, or chronic. Headache (of gradual, acute, or thunderclap onset) is the most frequent symptom, occurring in almost 90 percent of patients, and may occur as part of an isolated intracranial hypertension syndrome, with or without vomiting, papilledema, and visual problems. Option C: The major otologic complication of VZV reactivation is the Ramsay Hunt syndrome, which typically includes the triad of ipsilateral facial paralysis, ear pain, and vesicles in the auditory canal or on the auricle Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st ed, Ch: 22, Pg: 161

text: A 61 year old man has had 6 seizures over the past week. The seizures are generalised tonic clonic. He has complained of a severe headache, and examination shows increased tone on the left with mild hemiparesis. There is papilledema in both eyes. An emergency MRI scan shows a mass in the right cerebral hemisphere. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: The rapid onset of symptoms make it likely that this is a malignant lesion, and the most common malignancy of the central nervous system is a glioma. Glioblastoma multiforme is by far the most common and most malignant of the glial tumours. Glioblastoma Craniopharyngeomas are suprasellar tumors that present with pituitary insfficiency or visual field defects. Meningiomas are extra axial tumors located at the cerebral convexities. Medulloblastomas are the most common primary tumors of childhood and are one of the small round cell tumors. They are seen in the posterior fossa. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 90, Pg: 702-707

text: A 20-year-old student presents with a 5-day history of fever and sore throat. His doctor started him on penicillin, but there was no improvement. On examination his temperature is 38.8°C. He has grey plaques on his tonsils, cervical lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Infectious mononucleosis is associated with kissing. The disease is acquired when a healthy carrier, who is shedding virus in his/her saliva, passes it during close buccal contact directly into the oropharynx of a partner who was not primarily infected as a child. Classic infectious mononucleosis may follow some days of vague indisposition or may start abruptly. It presents with sore throat, fever with sweating, anorexia, headache and fatigue, together with malaise quite out of proportion to the other complaints. Dysphagia may be noticed and also brief orbital oedema. Erythematous and maculopapular rashes occur in a small number of untreated patients, but in many more who have been taking ampicillin for a sore throat before infectious mononucleosis has been diagnosed. Rarely, tonsillar and pharyngeal edema can cause pharyngeal obstruction. The fever may rise to 40°C but high levels and swings are not seen. There is redness and oedema of the pharynx, fauces, soft palate and uvula, and about half the patients develop grayish exudates. Generalized lymphadenopathy is almost always present, most marked in the cervical region; the glands are symmetrical, discrete and slightly tender, and are accompanied by splenomegaly in about 60% of cases and an enlarged liver in 10%. There is usually a moderate bradycardia. Besides the rash, characteristic palatal exanthematous crops of reddish petechia are found in about one-third of patients, and jaundice occurs in about 8%. & Borrelia vincenti infection causes acute necrotising ulcerative gingivitis. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Ch:194, Pg: 1483-1484, 1486.

text: A 72-year-old woman presented with an acute, severe occipital headache, unsteadiness of her gait and vomiting. She had a history of poorly controlled hypertension. On examination there was nystagmus to the left, ataxia of the left limbs and gait ataxia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Cerebellar haemorrhage The most common symptoms are of severe nausea and vomiting and ataxia. Headache may be severe. Patients with cerebellar haemorrhage can rapidly become comatose within hours after the onset from herniation, because of its limited space in the posterior fossa. Pontine haemorrhage There are numerous nuclei located within the pons. Rapidly deteriorating level of consciousness, impaired extraocular movement and extensive sensorimotor deficits are clinical clues to pontine haemorrhage. Basal ganglia haemorrhage Contralateral hemiparesis, hemisensory loss, or hemi-inattention. Aphasia, especially non-fluency and impaired comprehension, is frequently seen if haemorrhage occurs in the posterior limb of the left internal capsule. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 428, Pg: 3350

text: A 18-year-old female presents with three headaches over a six month period.She describes the headaches as severe, right-sided and lasting for twelve hours and associated with nausea and photophobia. Each is preceded by spots before her eyes. What is the most appropriate initial treatment for this patient?

options.A: Diclofenac at the onset of the next attack
options.B: Ergotamine suppository at the onset of the next attack
options.C: Paracetamol plus metoclopramide at the onset of the next attack

ansText: Paracetamol plus metoclopramide at the onset of the next attack
expl: First line treatment of acute migraine consists of simple analgesic (either soluble paracetamol or aspirin) and an antiemetic (usually domperidone or metoclopramide). Second line treatment includes the use of non-steroidal-anti-inflammatory drugs such as diclofenac, Ibuprofen or Naproxen. Dopamine receptor antagonists are adjuncts to the treatment of migraine. They can improve nausea as well as improve the absorption of analgesics by improving the gastric motility. Mild to moderate attacks are relieved by oral medications. Sever attacks may need parenteral drugs. If the above measurements fail to alleviate the attacks, then triptan therapy (for example, sumatriptan) is indicated, other agents like 5HT 1B/1D agonists(Triptans), CGRP receptor antagonists(Gepants), or 5 HT 1F agonists( Ditans) are available. Triptans are available in oral, nasal or parentral formulations. They are contraindicated in those with major cardiovascular risk. They have to be taken early as possible. They are not effective in migraine with aura, unless given after the aura before the headache. CGRP receptor antagonists that are approved for treatment includes Remigepant and Ubrogepant. They are oral agents. 5 HT 1F antagonist Lasmiditan is orally active and has a better cardiovascular safety and free of major adverse effects. Parenteral opioids are moderately effective in treating acute migraine. Single pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation and non invasive vagal stimualtion is an approved treatment for acute migraine. It is important for patients to take the treatment as early as possible. Long term prophylaxis with drugs (for example, propranolol) is only indicated if the attacks are frequent, 4 or more in a month (more than two a month). propranolol, timolol, rimegepant, sodium valproate, topiramate, CGRP receptor antagonists(eptinezumab, erenumab, fremanezumab, and galcanezumab) are FDA approved for prophylaxis. amitriptyline, candesartan, nortriptyline, flunarizine, phenelzine, and cyproheptadine also display preventive efficacy Once effective stabilization is achieved, the drug is continued for ~6 months and then slowly tapered. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 430, Pg: 3361-3364

text: A 78-year-old lady presents with a 5 day history of severe left temporal headache radiating from her eye to the scalp. She had also experienced jaw discomfort during eating. Which of the following drugs should be given while awaiting results of diagnostic tests?
expl: The history suggests temporal arteritis. In view of the vision threatening nature of disease, the patient should be commenced on steroids, pending the confirmatory tests. Typically 60 mg of prednisolone per day is recommended. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Ch:363 Pg:2811-2812

text: A 66-year-old woman presents with dysphagia and intermittent vomiting. Endoscopy shows a tight lower oesophageal sphincter suggestive of achalasia. Which of the following medical therapies is most effective?
expl: Explanation: Botulinum toxin , when injected into the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) under endoscopic guidance, acts by inhibiting the release of acetylcholine from excitatory nerve endings. This inhibition results in the relaxation of the LES. It is considered the most effective non-surgical/non-pneumatic medical therapy for achalasia, typically providing relief from dysphagia for at least 6 months . However, the effect is often temporary, and repeated injections are frequently required. It is generally reserved for patients who are poor candidates for pneumatic dilation or surgery (myotomy). Explanation of Other Options: Diltiazem (Option A) & Glyceryl trinitrate (Option C): Calcium channel blockers (like Nifedipine or Diltiazem) and long-acting nitrates (like Isosorbide dinitrate or Glyceryl trinitrate) can decrease LES pressure. However, they are generally less effective than botulinum toxin or invasive procedures. Their use is often limited by side effects such as hypotension, headache, and dizziness. Bismuth (Option B): Bismuth is used in the treatment of H. pylori infection and peptic ulcer disease. It has no role in the management of esophageal motor disorders like achalasia.

text: A patient presents with high-grade fever, arthralgia, and myalgia, with symptoms persisting for the past 24 hours. On examination, petechiae are also noted. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The patient's symptoms of high-grade fever, arthralgia, myalgia, and petechiae align well with the clinical presentation of dengue . since there is no suggestion of hemodynamic instability therefore it is unlikely to be dengue shock syndrome. The symptoms and clinical presentation of dengue include: Febrile Phase: Characterized by sudden onset of fever, headache, severe muscle pain (myalgia), and bone pain, earning it the nickname "break-bone fever." Petechiae: The presence of scattered petechiae can be noted during the febrile phase and is consistent with dengue. A positive tourniquet test, indicating microvascular fragility, is a common finding in dengue. Diagnostic Tests: The diagnosis of dengue is confirmed through laboratory tests such as IgM ELISA, antigen-detection ELISA, or RT-PCR during the acute phase. Shock: Incubation Period: After dengue virus infection, there is an incubation period averaging 4-7 days. Phases of Dengue: The illness evolves through three phases - a febrile phase, a critical phase, and a recovery phase. Symptoms and Signs: Sudden onset of high fever, severe headache (often frontal), retroorbital pain, back pain, and severe myalgias. Early symptoms may include a transient macular rash, adenopathy, palatal vesicles, and scleral injection. Critical and Recovery Phases: Critical recognition is essential for managing severe dengue (previously termed "dengue hemorrhagic fever"). The recovery may feature defervescence and a spreading maculopapular rash. Petechiae and Epistaxis: These are common, with the tourniquet test helping to reveal microvascular fragility associated with the disease. Laboratory Findings: Often show leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and slight elevations in serum aminotransferases. Diagnostic Methods: Dengue is diagnosed using IgM ELISA, antigen-detection ELISA, RT-PCR, or virus isolation from blood during the acute phase. Explanation of other options: Dengue Shock Syndrome (Option A): Patient lacks shock signs (hypotension, tachycardia, cold extremities, organ dysfunction). DSS occurs in severe dengue , with significant plasma leakage leading to shock. Malaria (Option C): Malaria typically presents with cyclical fevers (tertian or quartan) rather than continuous fever. Petechiae are uncommon in malaria. Confirmed via thick and thin blood smears or malaria antigen test . Typhoid (Option D): Typhoid fever has a gradual onset , often with stepwise fever progression. Relative bradycardia may be seen, unlike the high fever of dengue. Rose spots (faint rash), rather than petechiae, are characteristic. Diagnosed via blood culture (Widal test is less reliable). Key Takeaways: Dengue presents with high fever, severe myalgia, arthralgia, and petechiae, without signs of shock. Laboratory confirmation includes NS1 antigen, IgM ELISA, or RT-PCR.

text: A 38 year old man with a history of depression is brought to the accident and emergency department after being found unconscious in a garage. A friend said that he complained of a headache, then had nausea and vomiting. He then became unarousable. Oxygen saturations are 95% on air and breath sounds are clear on auscultation. What is the likely diagnosis?
expl: The patient has a clear lung field with normal oxygen saturation which rules out primary lung of vascular pathologies like pneumonitis, pulmonary embolism and eosinophilia. Carbon monoxide poisoning is produced by the incomplete combustion of carbon containing fuels such as gas, coal, oil, wood and coke. CO increases the affinity of O 2 to Haemoglobin which results in cellular hypoxia in spite of a normal saturation. The O2 Hb dissociation curve shifts to the left. Headache is the most common symptom (90%) followed by nausea & vomiting, vertigo, alteration in consciousness and weakness. The cherry red skin colour occurs when COHb concentration exceeds 20% but it is rarely seen in life. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch:459 Pg 3593

text: A 52-year-old man presents with a history of panic attacks, palpitations, sweating, headache and flushing. On examination his pulse rate is 120 bpm, BP 190/110 mmHg. A blood test shows high levels of noradrenaline. Which of the following tests would be most useful in establishing the diagnosis?
expl: This patient most probably has a pheochromocytoma . The presence of noradrenaline alone usually indicates an extra-adrenal tumor. Scanning with [ 131 I] metaiodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) produces specific uptake in sites of sympathetic activity with about 90% success. It is particularly useful with extra-adrenal tumours. CT and MRI scans are useful in detecting adrenal tumours. An ultrasound scan is the least sensitive modality and is thus not preferred. Secondary hypertension may occur due to unilateral renal artery stenosis but is unlikely to be associated with these clinical features. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine 20 th edition Chapter:380 Page number:2739-41

text: A 49-year-old man presents with flu-like symptoms and a palmoplantar rash. On examination, epitrochlear lymphadenopathy is noted. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The classic rash and accompanying symptoms strongly suggest a diagnosis of secondary syphilis. Key Features of Secondary Syphilis: Mucocutaneous and cutaneous lesions along with generalized, non-tender lymphadenopathy. The primary chancre may still be present in about 15% of cases, particularly more common in HIV-positive individuals. Skin Rash: Presents as macular, papular, papulosquamous, or sometimes pustular lesions (syphilides). Lesions can be subtle, and up to 25% of patients with visible rash may not notice it. Typically begin as pale red or pink, non-itchy macules on the trunk and limbs. Progress to papular lesions, often involving the palms and soles. In HIV patients, severe necrotic lesions known as lues maligna can occur. Hair and Mucosal Involvement: Patchy hair loss on the scalp, eyebrows, or beard occurs in about 5% of cases. Condylomata lata- moist, highly infectious lesions can develop in skin folds such as the perianal area, vulva, or scrotum (seen in 10% of cases). Mucous patches, painless silver-gray erosions, commonly appear on oral or genital mucosa in 10-15% of patients. Constitutional Symptoms: Sore throat (15-30%), fever (5-8%), weight loss (2-20%), malaise (25%), anorexia (2-10%), headache (10%), and meningismus (5%). Acute meningitis may occur in 1-2% of patients, with cerebrospinal fluid abnormalities seen in up to 40% of early syphilis cases. Ocular and Ear Involvement: Ocular symptoms include pupillary changes, optic neuritis, iritis, or uveitis, which can cause permanent vision loss if untreated. Ear symptoms may include sensorineural hearing loss, vertigo, or tinnitus. Less Common Complications: Hepatitis, kidney disease, gastrointestinal conditions (such as hypertrophic gastritis and proctitis), arthritis, and periostitis. Liver involvement is often asymptomatic, while renal issues arise from immune complex deposition, leading to proteinuria and nephrotic syndrome. Resolution: Most signs and symptoms of secondary syphilis resolve spontaneously within 1 to 6 months. Options A, C and D are incorrect.

text: A 60-year-old man presents with central crushing chest pain radiating to the back. He has a weak pulse in the right arm and systolic BP is 120 mmHg in the left arm, 80 mmHg systolic in the right arm. Which one of the following is a feature of severity requiring immediate (surgical) action?

options.D: Loud diastolic murmur in the aortic area

ansText: Loud diastolic murmur in the aortic area
expl: In aortic dissection, hypertension should be treated with an infusion such as labetalol. A loud diastolic murmur in the aortic area suggests aortic regurgitation. Aortic regurgitation and pericardial effusion (hemopericardium) suggest dissection down to the aortic root . These features, or persisting chest pain suggest that the patient requires prompt surgery. text: A 33-year-old female was admitted to the hospital after experiencing a sudden and severe episode of headache. No precipitating factor was identified. Except for mild neck stiffness, general physical and neurological examinations were unremarkable. On admission, a computed tomography (CT) scan showed a thin collection of blood on the right sylvian cistern, establishing the diagnosis of subarachnoid haemorrhage. The admitting doctor is considering further management. Which of the Following medications have been shown to decrease the incidence of cerebral infarction in patients with subarachnoid haemorrhage?
expl: The medical management of SAH focuses on protecting the air way, managing blood pressure before and after aneurysm treatment, preventing rebleeding prior to treatment, managing vasospasm and Delayed Cerebral Ischemia(DCI), treating hydrocephalus, treating hyponatremia, limiting secondary brain insults, and preventing pulmonary embolus (PE). DCI remains the leading cause of morbidity and mortality following aneurysmal SAH. Treatment with the calcium channel antagonist nimodipine (60 mg PO every 4 h) improves outcome, perhaps by preventing ischemic injury rather than reducing the risk of vasospasm. Osmotic agents can worsen the cerebral perfusion and can worsen ischemia and hence should be given only to those with features of raised ICP. Vasopressors and hydration also helps to prevent cerebral ischemia. Steroids may be used to reduce head and neck pain caused by blood in the sub arachnoid space. It does not reduce cerebral ischemia and is hence not routinely recommended. So the most appropriate answer is Nimodipine Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 429, Pg: 3355

text: A patient came with cherry red discolouration of the skin. What is the likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The most likely diagnosis in a patient presenting with cherry red discoloration of the skin and mucous membranes is carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning . Carbon monoxide is a colorless, odorless gas produced during incomplete combustion of hydrocarbons (e.g., car exhaust, faulty heaters, fires). It binds to hemoglobin with an affinity >200 times that of oxygen , forming carboxyhemoglobin (COHb) . This not only reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity of blood but also shifts the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve to the left , impairing oxygen release to tissues. The combination of severe tissue hypoxia and bright red coloration of blood due to COHb explains the classic finding of cherry red discolouration in CO poisoning. The brain and heart are most sensitive to hypoxia, and symptoms can range from headache and lethargy to confusion, seizures, coma, and even death. Management includes immediate 100% oxygen or hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBO₂T) , which dramatically shortens the half-life of COHb and helps reduce both acute and delayed neurocognitive sequelae. Arsenic poisoning (Option A) presents with gastrointestinal distress, neuropathy, and skin changes, not cherry red skin. CO₂ poisoning (Option B) causes hypercapnia and respiratory acidosis; it does not cause cherry red discolouration. Cyanide poisoning (Option D) may cause bright red venous blood (due to blocked cellular oxygen utilization) but not cherry red skin appearance as classically seen in CO poisoning.

text: A patient presented with a headache for 6 months. She took analgesics regularly. The headache has been increasing and became severe for the past 3 days, but discontinued the analgesic. Likely diagnosis?
expl: If a person uses analgesics for a prolonged period of time, the headache becomes increasing in frequency and is resistant to preventive medications. After stopping the analgesic, they feel improved, especially if they have been using opioids or barbiturates. The residual headache that they experience after stopping the drug is probably the primary headache that is the underlying problem for the medication use. The treatment of medication overuse of headache is to reduce the dose of the analgesic by 10% every 1-2 weeks. Small dose NSAID can be given for residual headache and the preventive medication can be started. If opioids is the culprit medication, it has to be gradually tapered and stopped and then preventive should be introduced. Clonidine is used for opioid withdrawal. For day time pain, aspirin can be used. For nocturnal pain, chlorpromazine is used. IV hydration and antiemetics are used. The medication can be successfully withdrawn in 3-5 days, followed by institution of a short course of dihydroergotamine for 5 days, after which the preventive medications can be started.

text: A 22-year-old woman with a history of migraine is prescribed a progestin-only pill. What is the main contraceptive mechanism of action of this drug?

options.C: Creates an unfavorable endometrium for implantation

expl: Progestin-only pills are useful for women who are unable to take regular oral contraceptives that contain estrogen due to their side-effects or to the exacerbation of existing conditions like migraine. Daily intake thickens the cervical mucus thus preventing the entry of sperm. The dose of progesterone is not sufficient to inhibit ovulation or reduce luteinising hormone (LH) secretion. Although it decreases tubal motility, this is more related to the occurrence of ectopic pregnancy. It may make the endometrium out-of-phase but not unfavorable for implantation. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 3034

text: A patient presents with a new-onset headache. Which of the following makes the diagnosis of migraine least likely?
expl: This question deals with two major concepts: Primary vs Secondary headache New-onset headache Primary headache is not associated with structural problems of the head, whereas secondary headache occurs due to structural diseases. New-onset headache is a new and severe headache in a patient. These are mostly due to secondary causes . The presence of the following makes the possibility of secondary headache more likely: Age >55 years Worst-ever headache Sudden onset Vomiting preceding headache Focal neurological deficits (including papilledema ) Associated systemic illness Fever Headaches worsened on bending, lifting, and coughing Early morning headaches or sleep-disrupting headaches Scalp tenderness with pain In this case, papilledema is a red flag suggesting raised intracranial pressure and points to secondary causes like a brain tumor, meningitis, or cerebral venous sinus thrombosis. Therefore, the presence of papilledema makes migraine less likely . Related important points and concepts: Photophobia , unilateral headache , and throbbing pain are classical features of migraine and can also be seen in some secondary headaches. Migraine is a primary headache disorder and does not present with papilledema. Primary vs Secondary Headache Key Takeaways: Papilledema is a red flag pointing to secondary headache. Migraine is a diagnosis of exclusion for new-onset severe headache. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Chapter 16, Pages 112-113

text: A 42-year-old man has a 5-year history of recurrent right sided headaches which last for 2 hours. There is a pattern of daily occurrence for 2 to 3 weeks, followed by a month or so without headaches. The headaches were described as "explosive" and were graded 9 to 10 in severity on a visual analogue scale of 1 to 10. The quality of the head pain was reported to be throbbing, sharp, shooting, as well as aching. The pain was localized around the right eye, behind the right ear, and in the occipital region. There are no associated visual symptoms, but occasionally flushing is associated. He gets these headaches frequently during the winter. What is the likely diagnosis?
expl: This question is the classical description of a Cluster Headache. Bouts of frequent attacks, known as cluster periods , can last from weeks to months, usually followed by remission periods when the headaches stop. During remission, no headaches occur for months and sometimes even years. Common signs and symptoms Pain: Usually retro-orbital Deep, excruciating in intensity Non fluctuating And explosive. Ipsilateral cranial parasympathetic activation: Conjunctival injection Lacrimation Aural fullness Rhinorrhoea or nasal congestion Cranial sympathetic dysfunction such as ptosis Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 430, Pg: 3366

text: A 40 year old male presents with history of recurrent episodes of left retroorbital pain. It occurs one or two times in a day and lasts for around 1 or two hours. During the episodes the patient seems agitated and is associated with lacrimation. He gets such attacks for around 1 or two months after which he remains asymptomatic, just to get recurrence of such attacks in the future. Which of the following statements is false

options.A: Cluster headache is more common in males than in females
options.C: Indomethacin is an effective treatment modality
options.D: Non invasive vagal stimulation is an approved abortive therapy of cluster head ache

ansText: Indomethacin is an effective treatment modality
expl: This question deals with the clinical features of Cluster head ache. Cluster head ache has a male preponderance among the Trigeminal Autonomic Cephalagias. The other TACs are Paroxysmal Hemicrania and SUNCT/SUNA occur in equal frequency in males and females. Cluster head ache has a definite association with alcohol intake, whereas, the other two does not have any association. Among the TACs Paroxysmal Hemicrania is the only head ache having a responsiveness to Indomethacin. Treatment of Cluster Head ache: Acute attack: Respond well to oxygen inhalation as 100% oxygen at 10-15 L/min for 15-20 minutes. Sumatriptan 6 mg SC is rapid in onset and will usually shorten an attack to 10-15 min. Sumatriptan (20 mg) and zolmitriptan (5 mg ) nasal sprays are both effective in acute cluster headache, offering a useful option for patients who may not wish to self-inject daily. Oral sumatriptan is not effective for prevention or for acute treatment of cluster headache . Neurostimulation therapy: When medical therapies fail in chronic cluster headache, neurostimulation strategies can be employed. Deep-brain stimulation of the region of the posterior hypothalamic gray matter has proven successful in a substantial proportion of patients. Non-invasive vagal nerve stimulation is FDA approved using three 2-min stimulation cycles applied consecutively at the onset of headache on the side of pain. This may be repeated after 9 minutes Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 430, Pg: 3366-3367

text: Which of the following statements are true regarding the Trigeminal Autonomic Cephalagias? 1. All the TACs have migrainous character and autonomic disturbance. 2. SUNCT/ SUNA presents with stabbing pain that lasts for very short duration and occurs multiple times a day. 3. Cutaneous triggers are seen in all the three TACs 4. Trigeminal Neuralgia is a close differential diagnosis of SUNCT/SUNA 5. Indomethacin effect is seen only with Paroxysmal Hemicrania
expl: So this question basically deals with the different types of Trigeminal Autonomic cephalagias and their differences. The three TACs are Cluster Headache, Paroxysmal Hemicrania/ Hemicrania continuua and SUNCT/SUNA All the three TACs have autonomic disturbances and migrainous features. Duration of Attack: Each episode of cluster head ache lasts longer , but the number of aattacks during a bout will be less, where as SUNCT/SUNA, each attack is brief lasting for 1-2 minutes with 100s of episodes occurring in a bout. Paroxysmal Hemicrania lies in between the spectrum. Indomethacin effect : Is seen only with Paroxysmal Hemicrania and Hemicrania Continuua, and not with any other TACs. Cutaneous Trigger: SUNCT or SUNA is the only TAC with cutaneous trigger. This makes Trigeminal neuralgia a close DD. But the main difference is that autonomic symptoms will be more prominent in SUNCT/SUNA and there will be no refractory period to the cutaneous trigger Abortion of acute attacks: Cluster head ache has been described in the previous question Paroxysmal hemicrania : There is n o effective abortive treatment. Indomethacin and non invasive vagal stimulation are preventive. SUNCT/SUNA: Due to the very brief attack, the role for abortive treatment is limited, but IV Lignocaine is very effective in hospitalized patients. Lamotrigine, Topiramate and Gabapentin are preventive. Reference : Harrison's principles of Internal medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 430, Pg: 3366

text: A 27-year-old old woman presents with four hours of a unilateral temporal headache increasing in severity. The pain is of a throbbing character and is exacerbated by light.There are no abnormal signs on examination. What is the diagnosis?
expl: The patient presents with unilateral throbbing head ache with photophobia and with a normal neurological examination. Among the options the most appropriate answer is Migraine. Acute Subarachnoid hemorrhage presents with a thunderclap head ache and will have neck stiffness on examination. Cluster head ache is common in males and may have migrainous features, but will be associated with cranial autonomic symptoms like lacrimation or conjunctival congestion. Intra cranial tumor will have focal deficits or papilledema which is not mentioned here. CLINICAL FEATURES OF MIGRAINE: Phases of migraine: Premonitory or prodromal phase: Neck discomfort, cognitive impairment, yawning, food cravings etc Aura phase: Seen only in 25% patients. Neurological disturbances like scintillating scotomas Head ache phase: associated with photophobia, phonophobia, nausea, vomiting, vertigo, allodynia, osmophobia Postdrome phase: Fatigue, disturbance in concentrating. Types of Migraine Migraine with aura (complicated migraine): Around 15% to 20% of people with migraine headaches experience an aura. Migraine without aura (common migraine): This type of migraine headache strikes without the warning an aura. The symptoms are the same, but that phase doesn't happen. Migraine without head pain: "Silent migraine" or "acephalgic migraine," as this type is also known as, includes the aura symptom but not the headache that typically follows. Hemiplegic migraine Retinal migraine (ocular migraine) Chronic migraine: A chronic migraine is when a migraine occurs at least 15 days per month. Migraine with brainstem aura. With this migraine, you'll have vertigo, slurred speech, double vision or loss of balance, which occur before the headache. The headache pain may affect the back of your head. These symptoms usually occur suddenly and can be associated with the inability to speak properly, ringing in the ears and vomiting. Status migrainosus. This is a rare and severe type of migraine that can last longer than 72 hours. The headache pain and nausea can be extremely bad. Certain medications, or medication withdrawal, can cause this type of migraine. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, CH: 430, Pg: 3357-3359

text: A patient presents with unilateral throbbing headache, associated with photophobia, nausea and vomiting. She reports that each episode lasts for 24 hours maximum. What is the management of an acute episode?
expl: Explanation: The correct option for the management of an acute episode of Migraine in the patient described is Sumatriptan . Sumatriptan is part of a class of medications known as triptans, which are specifically designed to treat acute migraine attacks. Sumatriptan works by stimulating serotonin (5-HT1B/1D) receptors in the brain, which leads to the constriction of blood vessels surrounding the brain. This action helps to alleviate the headache as well as other symptoms associated with a migraine, such as nausea, photophobia (sensitivity to light), and phonophobia (sensitivity to sound). Sumatriptan is effective because it addresses the pathophysiological changes in migraine, specifically vasoconstriction in the cranial arteries. It is usually prescribed for rapid relief during the acute phase of the migraine, making it an appropriate choice for the symptoms described. Sumatriptan has been found to be effective in relieving headache pain during migraine attacks, as well as reducing the associated symptoms like nausea and sensitivity to light and sound. Explanation of other options: Acetaminophen and caffeine (Option A): While this combination can be effective for mild to moderate migraine attacks, it is generally less effective than triptans for severe migraines. Hence, Incorrect for severe attacks . Propranolol (Option C): Propranolol is a beta-blocker used primarily as a preventive treatment for migraines, not for acute symptoms. Hence, Incorrect for acute management. Topiramate (Option D): Topiramate is used as a prophylactic treatment to decrease the frequency of migraine attacks, not for the immediate relief of acute symptoms. Key Takeaways: Sumatriptan is the first-line treatment for acute migraine attacks because it directly targets the underlying pathophysiology by causing cranial vasoconstriction and reducing neurogenic inflammation.

text: A female presents with a unilateral headache accompanied by nausea, photophobia, and phonophobia. Which of the following is the drug of choice for acute treatment?
expl: Explanation: The triad of unilateral headache, nausea, and sensory hypersensitivity (photophobia/phonophobia) is classic for an acute migraine attack. Sumatriptan , a 5-HT1B/1D receptor agonist, is the drug of choice for acute migraine management . Mechanism of action: Causes cranial vasoconstriction and inhibits trigeminovascular nociceptive pathways, rapidly relieving migraine symptoms. Acute management of migraine: First-line: NSAIDs, Triptans (e.g., sumatriptan). Other options: Gepants (rimegepant), Ditans (lasmiditan). Supportive therapy: Antiemetics (e.g., domperidone, metoclopramide) for associated nausea. Prophylaxis for recurrent migraine attacks: Flunarizine (Option A): Calcium channel blocker. Propranolol (Option C): Non-selective β-blocker. Topiramate (Option D): Anticonvulsant with preventive benefit. Other options: Amitriptyline (TCA). Explanation of other options: Flunarizine (Option A): Used for prophylaxis, not acute attacks. Propranolol (Option C): Effective in prevention, but not for acute relief. Topiramate (Option D): Preventive therapy, not used during acute episodes. Key Takeaways: Sumatriptan is the gold standard for acute migraine therapy. Preventive therapy is reserved for frequent or severe migraine attacks.

text: A patient comes to the ER with a history of cluster headaches. What is the treatment of choice for acute relief?
expl: Explanation: Cluster headache is a severe unilateral headache associated with autonomic symptoms such as lacrimation, nasal congestion, and conjunctival injection. The first-line treatment for acute attacks is subcutaneous sumatriptan , which provides rapid relief within minutes due to quick systemic absorption. High-flow oxygen inhalation is also effective, but among pharmacological options, subcutaneous triptans are the most effective . Explanation of other options: IV Acetaminophen (Option A): Provides general analgesia but is not effective in aborting cluster headache attacks. Oral Sumatriptan (Option B): Onset is too slow for cluster headaches, which require rapid-acting therapy. Oral Propranolol (Option D): Used as prophylaxis in migraine , not for the acute treatment of cluster headaches.

text: A 27-year-old old woman presents with two hours of a unilateral temporal headache increasing in severity. The pain is of a throbbing character and is exacerbated by light.There are no abnormal signs on examination. What is the diagnosis?
expl: The patient presents with unilateral throbbing head ache with photophobia and with a normal neurological examination. Among the options the most appropriate answer is Migraine. Acute Subarachnoid hemorrhage presents with a thunderclap head ache and will have neck stiffness on examination. Cluster head ache is common in males and may have migrainous features, but will be associated with cranial autonomic symptoms like lacrimation or conjunctival congestion. Intra cranial tumor will have focal deficits or papilledema which is not mentioned here. CLINICAL FEATURES OF MIGRAINE: Phases of migraine: Premonitory or prodromal phase: Neck discomfort, cognitive impairment, yawning, food cravings etc Aura phase: Seen only in 25% patients. Neurological disturbances like scintillating scotomas Head ache phase: associated with photophobia, phonophobia, nausea, vomiting, vertigo, allodynia, osmophobia Postdrome phase: Fatigue, disturbance in concentrating. Types of Migraine Migraine with aura (complicated migraine): Around 15% to 20% of people with migraine headaches experience an aura. Migraine without aura (common migraine): This type of migraine headache strikes without the warning an aura. The symptoms are the same, but that phase doesn't happen. Migraine without head pain: "Silent migraine" or "acephalgic migraine," as this type is also known as, includes the aura symptom but not the headache that typically follows. Hemiplegic migraine Retinal migraine (ocular migraine) Chronic migraine: A chronic migraine is when a migraine occurs at least 15 days per month. Migraine with brainstem aura. With this migraine, you'll have vertigo, slurred speech, double vision or loss of balance, which occur before the headache. The headache pain may affect the back of your head. These symptoms usually occur suddenly and can be associated with the inability to speak properly, ringing in the ears and vomiting. Status migrainosus. This is a rare and severe type of migraine that can last longer than 72 hours. The headache pain and nausea can be extremely bad. Certain medications, or medication withdrawal, can cause this type of migraine. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, CH: 430, Pg: 3357-3359

text: A 30-year-old woman presents with a unilateral, throbbing headache that worsens with bright light and reports occasional skipped meals. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The clinical manifestations indicate a migraine headache . Migraine Migraine is defined as a recurring syndrome of headache associated with other symptoms of neurologic dysfunction in varying admixtures. It is the second most common cause of headaches and the most common headache-related cause of disability globally. A migraine attack has three phases: premonitory (prodrome), headache phase, and postdrome Diagnostic Criteria for Migraine by International Headache Society Repeated attacks of headache lasting 4-72h in patients with a normal physical examination, no other reasonable cause for the headache, and: At least 2 of the following features: Unilateral pain Throbbing pain Aggravation by movement Moderate or severe intensity Plus at least 1 of the following features: Nausea/vomiting Photophobia and phonophobia Explanation of other options: Hunger headache (Option A): Hunger headaches are typically bilateral rather than unilateral and do not present with photophobia or throbbing pain. These headaches are diffuse and associated with hypoglycemia due to missed meals, improving rapidly with food intake. Tension headache (Option C): Presents with bilateral, steady, pressing pain rather than unilateral throbbing pain, described as a tight band around the head and are not characteristically aggravated by light or accompanied by photophobia. Cluster headache (Option D): Cluster headaches present are severe, strictly unilateral pain centred around the eye, often accompanied by autonomic symptoms such as lacrimation and nasal congestion. These headaches occur in clusters lasting weeks to months, with multiple short-duration attacks per day, and typically do not have the strong association with photophobia seen in this case. Reference: Migraine: Symptoms, Causes, and Treatment Migraine Medications - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf

text: A woman reports having headaches for the past 9 months that become worse when lying down and improve later in the day. She also has a history of oral contraceptive use. Fundus examination reveals papilledema, and no focal neurological deficits are present. What is the likely cause of her headaches?
expl: Explanation: The clinical picture, marked by typical headaches that intensify when lying flat, papilledema on eye examination, and no focal neurological deficits, is suggestive of pseudotumor cerebri, also referred to as idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) . Explanation of other options: Myasthenia gravis (Option A): Myasthenia gravis typically manifests with muscle weakness and fatigue, most often involving the eye and bulbar muscles . Since this patient does not have muscle weakness or headache but does present with papilledema, the diagnosis is unlikely. Temporal arteritis (Option B): Temporal arteritis usually occurs in individuals over the age of 50 and is characterised by symptoms such as temporal headaches , scalp tenderness, and jaw claudication. However, papilledema is not a common manifestation of this condition. Chronic migraine (Option C): Chronic migraine is defined as headaches happening on 15 or more days each month for a minimum of three months. Although the duration fits, papilledema and position-related headache patterns are not characteristic of migraine.

text: Acute treatment of cluster headache
expl: The treatment of acute episodes of cluster headache is Oxygen inhalation @10l/min. Since it is not in the options, the next best option would be Sumatriptan SC. Sumatriptan 6 mg SC is rapid in onset and will usually shorten an attack to 10-15 min; there is no evidence of tachyphylaxis. Sumatriptan (20 mg) and zolmitriptan (5 mg) nasal sprays are both effective in acute cluster headache, offering a useful option for patients who may not wish to self-inject daily. Noninvasive vagus nerve stimulation (nVNS) is FDA approved for the acute treatment of attacks in episodic cluster headache using three 2-min stimulation cycles applied consecutively at the onset of headache on the side of pain; this may be repeated after 9 min. Oral sumatriptan is not effective for prevention or for acute treatment of cluster headache.

text: A 42 year old obese woman presents with gradual onset severe headache and visual blurring. On examination, she has bilateral papilloedema, without any focal deficits or seizures. Which of the Following may help improve the condition?
expl: A chronic head ache with papilledema can occur with ICSOL or IIH. Given the presence of obesity and the absence of focal deficits or seizure, the possibility of IIH should be considered. Vitamin A, prednisolone, minocycline and cyclosporin make idiopathic intracranial hypertension (used to be known as benign intracranial hypertension worse. Acetazolamide is used to treat IIH. IIH is likely to be due to high pressure caused by the buildup or poor absorption of cerebrospinal fluid in the subarachnoid space surrounding the brain. The disorder is most common in women between the ages of 20 and 50. Symptoms include headache, nausea, vomiting, and pulsating intracranial noises, closely mimicking symptoms of brain tumors. Acetazolamide may be used in vasogenic edema due to tumors also Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, ch: 307, Pg: 2270

text: A 26 year old lady presents with a severe headache, which woke her up from sleep. She is not pregnant and was on no drugs. On examination she was afebrile and alert. On examination of the optic fundus the cup of the optic disc was filled and the medial margins of the disc were blurred. There was no other CNS abnormality, in particular no neck stiffness. A CT scan was as normal. What is the likely diagnosis?
expl: This is the most likely cause, despite not being pregnant or on the OCP. In only 10% of cases is cerebral venous thrombosis due to damage to the vessel wall by infection, tumour or trauma. Commonest causes are inherited disorders of coagulation of which factor V Leiden mutation is found in around 20% of cases. Often there is a combination of causative factors: e.g. protein S deficiency and childbirth, pregnancy and Behcet's disease, OCP and factor V Leiden mutation. A CT is often normal in VST, diagnosis requires MR with Venography A meningioma presents often insidiously with symptoms depending on the location involved; CT may reveal a calcified extradural mass. Benign intracranial hypertension: A typical presentation of idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) is that of a female of childbearing age who presents with headaches and is found to have papilledema on fundoscopic examination. MRI findings that suggest, but are not diagnostic for, IIH include empty sella, flattening of the posterior aspect of the globe, distension of the perioptic subarachnoid space (with or without a tortuous optic nerve), and transverse venous sinus stenosis. Migraine presents with a unilateral throbbing headache with photophobia/phonophobia which may be preceded by a visual aura; there are no features of raised intracranial tension. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 427, Pg: 3342

text: A patient developed a severe headache after a lumbar puncture performed in the sitting position. Which of the following is not an appropriate management strategy for a post-lumbar puncture headache?
expl: Explanation: The patient's symptoms are consistent with a post-dural puncture headache (PDPH). Restricting fluid intake is not recommended for managing PDPH. Post-dural puncture headache results from intracranial hypotension due to cerebrospinal fluid leakage at the puncture site, causing traction on pain-sensitive structures. PDPH is more likely with traumatic needles such as Quincke or Babcock and with lower-gauge needles. Management of PDPH: Conservative Measures: Bed rest 8-12 hours Lying in supine position reduces cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leakage and allows the dural puncture to seal. (Option A ruled out) Analgesics Pain relief with acetaminophen or NSAIDs. Intravenous caffeine Acts as a cerebral vasoconstrictor, reducing headache severity and increasing CSF production. (Option B ruled out) Definitive Treatment for Persistent Headache: Epidural Blood Patch For headaches unresponsive to conservative therapy, 10-30 mL of the patient's autologous venous blood is injected into the epidural space at the puncture site. This forms a patch over the dural tear, reducing CSF leak or increasing intracranial pressure. (Option D ruled out) Reference: Postdural puncture headache

text: A 44 year old bank clerk presents with a headache, nausea and ptosis of the left eye with blurred vision. She does not have fatiguability of her eye movements. Examination revealed swelling on the left side of face, proptosis and chemosis of the left eye, left mastoid swelling and left ophthalmoplegia involving cranial nerves. The pupil sizes were equal. A CT of her head is normal. What is the likely diagnosis?
expl: A history of headache and no other obvious cause of ptosis is suggestive of cavernous sinus thrombosis. Third nerve palsy is associated with dilated pupil and Horner's syndrome is associated with miosis. A CT can be normal, and diagnosis is confirmed with MRI. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st ed, Ch: 441, Pg: 3444

text: A 47-year-old woman presented with a severe sudden onset headache, describing it as the worst headache she could imagine, but denying any head trauma. On examination of her cranial nervous system she had a partial ptosis of her right eye, which was unable to look up or medially, and her right pupil was dilated. Her only past medical history is polycystic kidney disease. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Subarachnoid haemorrhage caused by a ruptured right sided posterior communicating artery aneurysm
options.B: Subarachnoid haemorrhage caused by a ruptured left sided posterior communicating artery aneurysm
options.C: Subarachnoid haemorrhage caused by a ruptured right sided anterior communicating artery aneurysm
options.D: Subarachnoid haemorrhage caused by a ruptured left sided anterior communicating artery aneurysm

ansText: Subarachnoid haemorrhage caused by a ruptured right sided posterior communicating artery aneurysm
expl: Posterior communicating artery aneurysms can compress the third cranial nerve. If the aneurysm ruptures it can cause the classic picture of an ipsilateral painful third nerve palsy, with the eye down and out, ptosis, and pupil dilation. Cerebral aneurysms may be associated with polycystic kidney disease. Regarding the options: A is correct. It is the ipsilateral posterior communicating artery aneurysm that is compressing the third nerve. B is incorrect as posterior communicating artery aneurysms do not cause contralateral compressive symptoms. C and D are incorrect as anterior communicating artery aneurysms do not compress the third nerve. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 429, Pg: 3354

text: A man presents with his father, who collapsed while working outdoors in the hot sun at 42°C in May. On arrival, the patient was unconscious. There were no signs of dehydration, and serum electrolytes were normal. His body temperature measured 106°F. Which of the following findings is least likely in this scenario?
expl: Explanation: This presentation is consistent with heat stroke , defined as a failure of thermoregulation with a core body temperature exceeding 40.5°C (104°F). In severe heat stroke, sweating ceases due to impaired thermoregulation and depleted sweat function. The absence of sweating and the presence of dry, hot skin are hallmark features, unlike other hyperthermic disorders where sweating is usually present. Explanation of other options: Nausea (Option A): Commonly occurs in heat exhaustion and heat stroke due to systemic stress. Hypotension (Option B): Results from vasodilation and dehydration, frequently observed. Headache (Option D): Prominent neurological symptom in heat stroke. Key Takeaways: Sweating is absent in classical heat stroke. Heat stroke is a medical emergency with multi-organ dysfunction risk .

text: A 65 year old woman has several episodes of dizziness particularly when she turns her head. 2 months ago, she had an attack of vertigo, without deafness or tinnitus, lasting for a few minutes. Over the last month, she had five further attacks of vertigo, accompanied by moderate headache and a left homonymous hemianopia, lasting for about a quarter of an hour. After the last episode she developed persistent unsteadiness of gait, and was admitted to hospital. On examination there was normal visual fields. were full. There was rhythmic horizontal nystagmus, slight weakness of the right external rectus muscle without diplopia, and ataxia of gait, provoked by turning. The blood pressure was 160/80 mmHg. What is the diagnosis?
expl: Vertebrobasilar (posterior) circulation constitutes the arterial supply to the brain stem, cerebellum, and occipital cortex. Bilateral visual loss, dizziness, speech disturbances, drop attacks and transient global amnesia are features of vertebrobasilar insufficiency. MRI / MRA are good investigations to investigate for vertebral or basilar arterial disease. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 426, Pg: 3328

text: A male patient presented to the emergency room with seizures. He has a history of fever, headache, and confusion. An MRI brain was done, and it showed inflammation involving the bitemporal lobes. What is the most likely aetiology for this presentation?
expl: Explanation: HSV encephalitis classically involves the bitemporal lobes and presents with fever, seizures, confusion, and behavioural changes. Explanation of other options: Cytomegalovirus (Option A): Typically seen in immunocompromised individuals; MRI shows periventricular calcifications and ventricular enlargement, not bitemporal lobe involvement. Toxoplasma gondii (Option B): Common in immunocompromised hosts; presents with multiple ring-enhancing lesions in the basal ganglia or corticomedullary junction, not the temporal lobes. Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Option D): TB meningitis or encephalitis presents with diffuse cortical involvement and basal exudates; bitemporal localisation is not characteristic. Reference: Radiopaedia: Tuberculous Encephalopathy

text: What is the preferred medication for the presented case? A male patient, 54 years old, was brought to the emergency room with symptoms of fever, headache, and a focal seizure. The EEG results indicate the presence of spikes in the temporal lobe. Analysis of the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) sample reveals the presence of 50 cells, with 90% lymphocytes and 10% neutrophils.
expl: Explanation: The presentation of fever, headache, focal seizures , temporal lobe spikes on EEG , and a lymphocytic-predominant CSF pleocytosis is highly suggestive of Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) encephalitis . Intravenous Acyclovir is the empiric and first-line treatment of choice and must be initiated immediately to reduce mortality and morbidity. Diagnosis of HSV encephalitis involves CSF analysis showing lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal glucose, and mildly elevated protein. CSF PCR for HSV is the gold standard, with 96% sensitivity and 99% specificity. MRI is the preferred imaging modality, detecting early T2 and diffusion-weighted lesions in the orbitofrontal and temporal lobes. EEG may demonstrate periodic slow-wave activity in the temporal regions. Explanation of other options: Valacyclovir (Option A): An oral prodrug of acyclovir, used for outpatient management of herpes zoster and genital herpes, but not for the initial, critical treatment of HSV encephalitis. Ganciclovir (Option C): First-line treatment for Cytomegalovirus (CMV) CNS infections, not HSV. Foscarnet (Option D): It is used for CMV infections resistant to ganciclovir or for acyclovir-resistant HSV strains, which are rare. Key Takeaways: HSV encephalitis is a neurologic emergency characterized by temporal lobe involvement. Empirical intravenous acyclovir should be started immediately upon suspicion, before confirmatory PCR results.

text: A 50 year old male presents with unsteadiness of gait of one year duration. On examination, he has sensory loss in the stocking and glove pattern, with absent ankle jerk and pyramidal signs and sensory ataxia. Which of the following statements is false?

options.A: Cobalamine deficiency may be a cause of the above findings.
options.B: Dietary deficiency of copper may also lead to similar clinical features.
options.C: Haematological abnormalities if present points to the diagnosis of Vitamin B12 deficiency.
options.D: Excess Zinc is an known factor that reduced copper absorption.

ansText: Haematological abnormalities if present points to the diagnosis of Vitamin B12 deficiency.
expl: Symmetric sensory loss with distal areflexia and UMN signs is seen in Vitamin B12 deficiency, Copper deficiency and Vitamin E deficiency. It is also seen in adrenomyelkoneuronopathy. So all these can cause symptoms similar to subacute combined degeneration. Haematological abnormalities are known to occur not only in B12 deficiency, but also Copper deficiency and Vitamin E deficiency. In Vitamin B12 deficiency, there will be macrocytic anemia, hypersegmented neutrophils and pancytopenia. In copper deficiency, there will be microcytic anemia, neutropenia and occasionally pancytopenia. In Vitamin E deficiency, there will be acanthocytosis. Excess zinc upregulates intestinal metalothionine and decreases copper absorption. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Intrenal medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 446, Pg: 3496, 3497

text: A 40-year-old male presents with chronic back pain that has progressively worsened over the past few months. He also reports fever, night sweats, and unintentional weight loss. On examination, there is localized tenderness over the lower thoracic and lumbar spine. MRI spine is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: Characterized by chronic back pain, fever, night sweats, and weight loss . MRI often shows involvement of two or more adjacent vertebral bodies , typically affecting the lower thoracic and upper lumbar spine in adults. A hallmark feature is the destruction of the intervertebral disc space and adjacent vertebrae with potential abscess formation . The patient's symptoms of systemic infection (fever, night sweats, weight loss) combined with localized spinal tenderness and the typical MRI findings strongly suggest Pott's spine. Explanation of other options: Osteoporotic Vertebral Fracture (Option B): Common in older adults or those with osteoporosis, presenting typically as a sudden onset of back pain after minimal trauma or even no apparent cause. The patient's systemic symptoms like fever and weight loss are not typical of osteoporotic fractures. Metastatic Spinal Tumor (Option C): Can cause back pain and may involve vertebral bodies, but is more likely to cause widespread or multifocal pain and neurological deficits. Lacks specific systemic symptoms such as fever and night sweats that are associated with an infection like tuberculosis. Ankylosing Spondylitis (Option D): A chronic inflammatory disease primarily affecting the spine and sacroiliac joints, leading to pain and progressive spinal stiffness. Typically lacks systemic symptoms like fever and weight loss unless there is a concurrent secondary inflammation or infection. Key Takeaways: Pott's disease (spinal TB) should be suspected in patients with chronic back pain, systemic symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss), and MRI findings of vertebral destruction with possible abscess formation. Early diagnosis and anti-tubercular treatment are essential to prevent complications such as neurological deficits and spinal deformity.

text: A person experiences slight imbalance while trying to stand after getting off a roller coaster. Which neural tract is primarily responsible for maintaining balance in this situation?
expl: Explanation: The vestibulospinal tract plays a crucial role in maintaining balance and posture. This neural pathway originates in the vestibular nuclei, which are located in the brainstem and are part of the vestibular system, crucial for processing sensory information related to motion, equilibrium, and spatial orientation. The vestibulospinal tract influences motor neurons that control the muscles of the limbs and trunk, enabling quick and reflexive adjustments to maintain balance and posture, particularly during unexpected movements. When a person experiences an imbalance, especially after an activity like riding a roller coaster that significantly stimulates the vestibular system, the vestibulospinal tract is vital in helping to stabilize and orient the body correctly. Vestibulospinal tract: Receives inputs from the vestibular apparatus which detects changes in the position of the head relative to gravity and acceleration. Sends outputs to spinal motor neurons that innervate muscles, particularly extensor muscles, which are activated to maintain posture and balance. This neural pathway's activation is crucial when sudden adjustments are needed, such as after dismounting from a roller coaster, making option C the correct and relevant choice. Explanation of other options: Corticospinal tract (Option A): Primarily involved in voluntary motor control. Rubrospinal tract (Option B): Helps with motor input, largely redundant in humans, and plays a role in the control of hand movements. Vestibulocochlear tract (Option D): Incorrect terminology but closely related to the vestibulocochlear nerve, which is involved in hearing and balance; does not directly influence motor control for balance maintenance. Key Takeaways: The vestibulospinal tract is responsible for maintaining posture and balance by transmitting signals from the vestibular system to spinal motor neurons, ensuring quick adjustments to unexpected movements, such as after riding a roller coaster.

text: A 59-year-old man was previously diagnosed with pernicious anemia. He was non-compliant with medication for several years. He now has unsteadiness and difficulty walking. Lesion in which of the following is likely to be present?
expl: This patient has a long history of pernicious anemia and now presents with neurological symptoms. In pernicious anemia, antibodies against intrinsic factor are produced that lead to impaired absorption of vitamin B12. The diagnosis is Subacute Combined Degeneration (SACD) of the spinal cord due to vitamin B12 deficiency. Signs and symptoms of SACD - The onset is gradual and uniform. The posterior columns and corticospinal tracts are specifically damaged. Patient presents with subacute paresthesias in the hands and feet, loss of vibration and position sensation, and a progressive spastic and ataxic weakness. A positive Babinski sign may be seen. Loss of reflexes due to an associated peripheral neuropathy. Treatment - Replacement therapy , beginning with 1000 μg of intramuscular vitamin B12 daily for 5 days and then continued as a once monthly maintenance dose; oral maintenance is also reasonable, except in cases of pernicious anemia. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page Number-3496.

text: The image was given of a clinician performing an ankle jerk. It is exaggerated in which type of lesion?
expl: Lower motor neurons are those whose axons terminate on skeletal muscles. Damage to these neurons is associated with flaccid paralysis, muscular atrophy, fasciculations (visible muscle twitches that appear as flickers under the skin), hypotonia (decreased muscle tone), and hyporeflexia or areflexia. The development of cerebellar ataxia. Upper motor neurons typically refer to corticospinal tract neurons that innervate spinal motor neurons, but they can also include brainstem neurons that control spinal motor neurons. Damage to these neurons initially causes muscles to become weak and flaccid but eventually leads to spasticity, hypertonia (increased resistance to passive movement), hyperactive stretch reflexes, and abnormal plantar extensor reflex (positive Babinski sign).

text: A patient presents with tingling sensations in the hands and feet, generalized weakness, easy fatigability, pallor, and ataxia. Deficiency of which vitamin is responsible for these findings?
expl: Explanation: The constellation of symptoms described - paresthesias in the extremities, generalized weakness, fatigue, pallor, and ataxia - are classical for Vitamin B12 deficiency . Cobalamin plays a critical role in neurological health and red blood cell production. Its deficiency results in megaloblastic (pernicious) anemia and neurological complications like subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord, producing ataxia and peripheral neuropathy. These features highlight its essential role in maintaining the myelin sheath . Explanation of other options: Vitamin B1 (Option A): Deficiency leads to beriberi and Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, but does not present with combined anemia and neuropathy as in this case. Vitamin B2 (Option C): Deficiency manifests as ariboflavinosis, causing glossitis and cheilitis, without significant neurological deficits. Vitamin B3 (Option D): Deficiency causes pellagra with the 3D's (dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia), unrelated to the neurological and hematological findings here. Key Takeaways: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia with neurological manifestations . Neuropathy and ataxia point strongly toward subacute combined degeneration due to B12 deficiency. References: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9710417/
