text: At which level the lesion is located if all Extraocular muscles are paralyzed?
expl: Explanation: A lesion affecting both the midbrain and pons would damage the nuclei of cranial nerves III (oculomotor), IV (trochlear), and VI (abducens), which collectively innervate all the extraocular muscles. This would result in complete paralysis of eye movement. Such an extensive lesion is typically seen in severe brainstem pathology. Explanation of other options: Frontal eye field (Option A): A lesion here would impair voluntary conjugate eye movements (saccades) but would not paralyze individual extraocular muscles. Cerebral surface (Option B): A diffuse cortical lesion would not cause isolated, complete ophthalmoplegia. Spinal cord (Option D): The spinal cord does not contain the cranial nerve nuclei responsible for eye movement. Key Takeaways: The brainstem (midbrain and pons) houses the nuclei for CN III, IV, and VI. Complete external ophthalmoplegia localizes to the brainstem.

text: Which sign is being elicited?
expl: The plantar reflex is elicited by stroking, with a noxious stimulus such as a tongue blade, the lateral surface of the sole of the foot beginning near the heel and moving across the ball of the foot to the great toe. The normal reflex consists of plantar flexion of the toes. With upper motor neuron lesions above the S1 level of the spinal cord, a paradoxical extension of the toe is observed, associated with fanning and extension of the other toes (termed an extensor plantar response, or Babinski sign). However, despite its popularity, the reliability and validity of the Babinski sign for identifying upper motor neuron weakness is limited, it is far more useful to rely on tests of tone, strength, stretch reflexes, and coordination.

text: A 44 year old man has severe episodes of dizziness with associated vomiting and pain in the right ear. This occurs once or twice a week. During these attacks he feels the surrounding environment spinning around. He also mentions a high pitched sound frequently being present. On examination, during an attack, he has right horizontal nystagmus. Audiological testing reveals right-sided sensorineural deafness. What is the diagnosis?
expl: Meniere's disease is caused by distension of the endolymphatic compartment of the inner ear. The symptoms of Meniere's disease include vertigo, hearing loss and tinnitus . The dizziness is described as a spinning or whirling feeling and may cause problems with balance. Some people feel nauseated and vomit during an attack. Tinnitus refers to a ringing or roaring sound in the ear. Others may notice some hearing loss, especially with sounds that have a low frequency. Horizontal nystagmus is more commonly seen on examination, but vertical nystagmus may also occur. Option A: Vestibular neuritis presents with acute onset of vertigo with nausea, vomiting, and gait impairment. Option C: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) presents with recurrent episodes of vertigo lasting one minute or less that are provoked by specific types of head movements. BPPV does not cause prolonged or sustained vertigo, hearing loss, tinnitus, or neurologic deficits; these suggest an alternative diagnosis Option D: The most common clinical manifestations of vestibular schwannomas are unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, often in association with tinnitus Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 22, Pg: 160

text: A 64 year old man has symptoms of lethargy and vomiting. He drinks 10 pints of beer a day. He was started on an intravenous glucose infusion and chlordiazepoxide. For a day, he symptomatically improved. However, the next day, he became confused and started vomiting several times. He also had diplopia and was unable to stand. What is the likely diagnosis?
expl: This is a case of Wernicke's encephalopathy . It is a neurological disorder of acute onset caused by a thiamine (B1) deficiency . People who are at risk for acute thiamine deficiency are: Alcoholism, chronic diuretic use, bariatric surgery, hyperemesis, thiaminases in food Symptoms include: Ocular abnormalities (horizontal nystagmus, ophthalmoplegia) Ataxia Confusion . The episode may be precipitated by intravenous dextrose administration which exhausts vitamin B reserves, especially in alcoholics and malnourished .Supplementation with vitamin B should be done in all alcoholic patients before dextrose administration. Treatment is 200mg thiamine 3 times daily until there is no further improvement, followed by oral thiamine till complete recovery. Cardiovascular and ophthalmoplegia recovers in 24 hours. Psychosis may be permanent or persist for months. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch:333, Pg: 2526

text: A 27-year-old female presents with drooping of the left side of her face and an inability to close her left eye. She had a viral illness in the preceding week. There is no past medical history.On examination, there is a left VIIth nerve palsy. The remaining cranial nerves are normal. Power, tone and reflexes are normal in the limbs. What is the best course of treatment?
expl: This is the classical history of a post-viral Bell's palsy . There is some evidence to support a short course of steroids in the acute stages of the illness (NEJM 2007;357:1598-1607). This study suggests improved recovery of facial function with early treatment. No benefit was seen in acyclovir added to prednisolone in this study. Oral valaciclovir has been evaluated with an RCT but consensus supports steroids (with some clinicians continuing to support the concomitant use of acyclovir). You need to be confident that there are no features of Guillain-Barré (test reflexes), or brain stem vascular disease or space occupying lesion. The neurological examination of the cranial nerves thus needs to be completed with care. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 441, Pg: 3441

text: A patient with loss of the right half of the visual field loss on both sides. What would the probable diagnosis be?
expl: Lesion of the optic tract and beyond will lead to contralateral homonymous hemianopia Damage to the optic radiations in the temporal lobe (Meyer's loop) produces a superior quadrantic homonymous hemianopia (lesion marked as J). Lesions of the optic nerve will result in total blindness in the ipsilateral eye. Lesion of the optic chiasm will lead to bitemporal hemianopia. Injury to the optic radiations in the parietal lobe results in an inferior quadrantic homonymous hemianopia (K). Lesions of the primary visual cortex give rise to dense, congruous hemianopic field defects. Occlusion of the posterior cerebral artery supplying the occipital lobe is a common cause of total homonymous hemianopia. Some patients have macular sparing, because the central field representation at the tip of the occipital lobe is supplied by collaterals from the middle cerebral artery (L). Destruction of both occipital lobes produces cortical blindness. This condition can be distinguished from bilateral prechiasmal visual loss by noting that the pupil responses and optic fundi remain normal.

text: A 24-year-old anorexic is admitted for parenteral nutrition and has a tunneled line inserted. A few days after parenteral feeding has begun you are asked to see her as she has begun complaining of diplopia, lethargy and muscle weakness. She also has paraesthesia affecting her hands and feet. Examination confirms global muscle weakness and peripheral sensory loss. Which of the following electrolyte abnormalities is the most likely to have occurred?
expl: This patient is suffering from refeeding syndrome, where patients complain of a range of symptoms which can include Muscle weakness Peripheral neuropathy Neurological impairment Myocardial depression. It is characterized by a fall in phosphate, magnesium, potassium and fluid accumulation, which in combination can lead to cardiac failure. Patients at risk from re-feeding include those who are fed after a prolonged period of starvation , such as those with anorexia, and those with chronic alcoholism. Reference: Harrison;s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 335, Pg: 2546

text: A 48-year-old man presents with headaches and low libido. He is found to have hypopituitarism. The CT scan shows a pituitary tumour with suprasellar extension. Which of the following structures is likely to be compressed?
expl: In this case, with a pituitary tumor and suprasellar extension, the structure most likely to be compressed is the Optic chiasma . The optic chiasma is located near the pituitary gland and is particularly vulnerable to compression by pituitary tumors expanding upward. Compression of the optic chiasma can lead to visual disturbances, including bitemporal hemianopia, due to the partial crossing of optic nerve fibers at this location. The optic chiasm lies 5-10 mm above the diaphragm sellar and anterior to the stalk. Adenomas larger than 1.5 cm frequently have suprasellar extension, and a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan will show compression and upward displacement of the optic chiasm. Other options: Abducens nerve (Option A): The abducens nerve controls the movement of the lateral rectus muscle of the eye. Compression of this nerve can result in lateral rectus muscle weakness and difficulty moving the eye outward. Hypothalamus (Option B): While the hypothalamus is located near the pituitary gland and is important for regulating many endocrine functions, it is less likely to be directly compressed by a pituitary tumor with suprasellar extension. Superior extension of the tumour can lead to compression of firstly the optic apparatus and later the hypothalamus. Oculomotor nerve (Option C): Lateral extension of the tumour with compression or invasion of the cavernous sinus can compromise third, fourth, or sixth cranial nerve functions, manifest as diplopia in 5 to 15% of pituitary tumour patients. The oculomotor nerve controls several eye muscles and plays a role in eye movement. Compression of this nerve can lead to eye movement abnormalities, including ptosis (drooping of the eyelid) and diplopia (double vision). In this case, the most likely structure to be affected based on the tumor's location is the optic chiasma, causing visual disturbances. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st Ed, Ch: 380 Pg: 2901

text: Which of the following will not be affected by a lesion of the facial nerve in the internal auditory meatus?
expl: The extent of dysfunction depends on the level of injury. If it is proximal to geniculate ganglion, for example, internal auditory meatus, taste is lost in the anterior 2/3 of tongue. Also secretion from submandibular, sublingual and lacrimal glands is impaired. Hyperacusis is due to paralysis of stapedius. Orbicularis oculi is affected causing inability to blink/close eyelids. Sensation over the face is supplied by the trigeminal nerve, and sweat glands are controlled by the sympathetic nervous system, for example, anhidrosis in Horner's syndrome. tests used to assess the lesion of the facial nerve clinically are as follows: Blink test (corneal reflex) - when tapping on the patient's glabella, a suspension in blinking will occur on the affected side (the ophthalmic division of trigeminal nerve controls afferent limb, the efferent limb is the temporal and zygomatic branch of the facial nerve) Schirmer test (assessing lacrimation of the lacrimal gland) - lacrimation will be decreased by 75% compared to the normal side using a folded strip of blotting paper in the lower conjunctival fornix. It is important to note that a unilateral lesion within the geniculate ganglion can produce bilateral lacrimal deficiencies. Stapedial test - This involuntary reaction in response to high-intensity sound stimuli causes contraction of the stapedius muscle and gets mediated by the facial nerve. Testing of the stapedius reflex can be performed using tympanometry. Salivary Test - Salivation rate is assessed from a submandibular duct following stimulation with a 6% citric acid solution. If positive, there will be a reduction in salivation by 25% at the affected side and indicate a lesion at or proximal to the root of the chorda tympani. Taste test - though using salt sweet, sour, and bitter tastes along the lateral aspects of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. A positive result will indicate a lesion at or proximal to the root of the chorda tympani. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed,Ch: 441, Pg: 3439

text: A 41 year-old male presents to his family doctor with a two week history of numbness and a burning sensation on the lateral aspect of the left upper thigh. Examination reveals sensory loss over the anterolateral thigh. Which one of the following nerves is most likely to be involved in this patient?

options.D: Lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh

ansText: Lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh
expl: The pure sensory loss makes the diagnosis of meralgia paraesthetica and is a consequence of damage to the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh. It is usually a consequence of entrapment at the lateral inguinal ligament or less likely, trauma, ischaemia or a retroperitoneal lesion. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 446, Pg: 3498

text: A 27-year-old male is admitted following an altercation in which he is stabbed in the thigh by a bottle. Which of the following features suggests injury to the femoral nerve?

options.B: Loss of sensation over lateral aspect of thigh
options.C: Weakness of abduction of the hip
options.D: Weakness of adduction at the hip

expl: A lesion of the femoral nerve (L2,L3,L4) is characterised by weakness of the quadriceps femoris muscle and hence weakness of extension of the knee, loss of sensation over the front of the thigh and loss of the knee jerk. The obturator nerve (LB-4) supplies adductors of hip and lateral cutaneous nerve to thigh supplies sensation to the outer part of the thigh. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 446, Pg: 3498

text: A 27-year-old woman presents with new double vision. On examination she experiences horizontal diplopia on looking to her far right. Covering her left eye only obscures the innermost image. Covering her right eye only obscures the outermost image. In the neutral position her right eye is deviated medially. She has no problem on looking to the far left.Her neurological examination is otherwise normal. What is the most likely problem?
expl: The VIth nerve is motor to the lateral rectus muscle. It is responsible for abduction of the ipsilateral eye. In the neutral position the affected eye is deviated medially due to unopposed action of the medial rectus. In patients with diplopia the 'cover test' can be used to determine the eye that has the problem. On covering the affected eye the outermost image disappears. After finding a VIth nerve palsy the cause should always be looked for, it is not a diagnosis in itself. Due to the long course and anatomy of the VIth nerve it can be damaged in any condition causing raised intracranial pressure. It can therefore be a 'false localising sign'. Regarding the options: Concomitant right esotropia is not the answer. An esotropia is a squint where one or both eyes turn inwards. This may alternate between the eyes or may be a problem in just one eye. A concomitant esotropia is a squint where the degree by which the eye turns inwards does not vary in any direction of gaze (as opposed to an incomitant esotropia where the direction of gaze does affect the size or presence of deviation). Concomitant esotropias usually begin early in childhood. The patient has diplopia in all directions of gaze if vision is normal in both eyes. Left sided IVth nerve palsy is not the answer. The IVth nerve controls the superior oblique muscle. Lesions of it typically cause a vertical diplopia, usually noticed on going downstairs or reading. Left sided VIth nerve palsy is not the answer. This would cause a horizontal diplopia but it would be on far left gaze. The outermost image would disappear with the cover test over the left eye if it was affected. A medial longitudinal fasciculus lesion is not the answer. This connects the IIIrd and VIth cranial nerve nuclei in the pons and co-ordinates conjugate horizontal eye movements. Its lesions typically cause internuclear ophthalmoplegia. There will be impaired adduction on the side of the lesion with nystagmus of the contralateral eye. In the neutral position the eyes appear normal. Right VIth nerve palsy is the correct answer (see above). Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 441 Pg: 3444

text: A 2B-year-old man presents to the Emergency department after punching a window. He has lacerated the medial aspect of his wrist, damaging the ulnar nerve. What is he at risk of developing?

options.B: Inability to pinch paper between his thumb and index finger
options.C: Loss of sensation over the lateral three and a half fingers
options.D: Wasting of the second lumbrical muscle

expl: Ulnar nerve damage at the wrist results in wasting of the intrinsic hand muscles (other than the lateral two lumbricals) and the hypothenar eminence. This produces the classic claw hand. It supplies sensation to the medial one and a half fingers. The median nerve innervates the lateral two lumbricals and the thenar eminence (opponens pollicis, abductor pollicis and flexor pollicis brevis). It supplies sensation to the lateral one and a half fingers. Damage to the motor branch, the anterior interosseous nerve results in inability to form and pinch grip, tip to tip, instead holding the paper between the pulp of the thumb and index finger. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 446, Pg: 3498

text: A 19-year-old male presents with blurring of vision in his right eye. Examination reveals visual acuity in the right eye of 6/18 and in the left eye 6/6. Visual fields to confrontation reveal a right temporal visual field defect and partial loss of the superior part of the temporal field of the left eye. Where is the most likely position of the lesion responsible for this defect?
expl: The most likely localisation of the lesion is around the optic chiasma spreading up the right optic nerve. The signs indicate a bitemporal visual field defect with involvement of the right optic nerve (decreased visual acuity). Occipital lobe lesion causes a congruous homonymous hemianopia whereas an optic tract lesion causes an incongruous homonymous hemianopia. Temporal lobe lesion causes an upper homonymous quadrantanopia. Optic nerve lesions in isolation lead to unilateral visual signs. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 32, Pg: 219

text: A 4B-year-old civil servant attends the clinic stating that she has difficulty swallowing. She gives a two months history of difficulty with solids which has progressed to difficulty tolerating liquids in the previous two weeks. She has noticed some weakness in her right arm which has affected her ability to lift certain objects like the kettle. Previously, she has enjoyed good health with no hearing loss or facial weakness. She describes no visual symptoms.On examination, she has an absent gag reflex on the right, with reduced palatal movements. There is weakness on rotating the head to the left with flattening and weakness of elevation of the right shoulder. Eye movements, visual acuity, hearing and tongue movements are all normal. Where is the likely site of the lesion?
expl: The clinical scenario is that of a right sided pathology affecting the IX, X and XI cranial nerves. This produces the palatal weakness and the swallowing difficulties (IX/X), while the shoulder and sternocleidomastoid weakness are due to accessory nerve (XI) involvement. The absence of hearing loss or facial weakness makes a cerebello-pontine angle lesion unlikely. A lesion outside the skull may also involve the XII nerve (tongue). The most likely site, therefore is the jugular foramen. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 441 Pg: 3444

text: A 2D-year-old man suffers a deep laceration to the forearm resulting in transection of the median nerve. Following this injury, the nerve will undergo which of the following pathological processes?
expl: Wallerian degeneration is degeneration of the portion of the nerve distal to the injury. It occurs following axonal injury in both the peripheral and central nervous systems and usually begins within 2D24-36 hours of injury. Coagulative necrosis is cell death following ischaemia or infarction. It is characterised by a 'ghostly' appearance of affected cells unders light microscopy. Fibrinoid necrosis is a form of necrosis in which there is an accumulation of material in the affected tissue with a staining pattern reminiscent of fibrin. It is associated with Henoch-Schönlein purpura, malignant hypertension and hyperacute transplant rejection. Segmental demyelination is a feature seen in axons in the central nervous system with multiple sclerosis. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 437, Pg: 3411

text: Which of the following is true of tetanus?

options.A: Failure to culture Clostridium tetani from the wound would make the diagnosis doubtful

expl: A. Absence of a culture positivity from wound does not exclude tetanus. B. Patients need to be actively immunised after recovery. C. The toxin tetanospasmin does not cross the blood brain barrier, it diffuses through the blood to bind to receptors containing gangliosides on the neuronal membranes of presynaptic nerve terminals in muscles. The toxin does reach the brain by axonal transport. D. Cephalic means involving the cranial nerves usually from a wound on the head and neck. text: A 66 year old lady presents to the hospital with an ataxic gait. On examination, the patient had difficulty standing without assistance and minor movements of her head and body caused vertigo. There was mild postural tremor and marked hypotonia of the right limbs, mostly the arm. Finger to nose testing elicited marked intention tremor and dysdiadochokinesia in the right arm. Speech was dysarthric but comprehension was good.Where is the lesion likely to be?
expl: Lesions of the cerebellum (intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia) lead to motor signs ipsilateral to the lesion. Right pons or left medulla can also cause ipsilateral cerebellar sign, but there will be associated cranial nerve involvement. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 426, Pg: 3332-3333

text: A 45-year-old male presents with right-sided facial weakness. On examination, the patient is able to wrinkle his forehead on the right side but is unable to close his right eye completely, and his mouth droops to the left side when smiling. Based on these findings, which of the following statements best describes the type and location of the lesion?

options.A: Upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion on the right side
options.B: Upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion on the left side
options.C: Lower motor neuron (LMN) lesion on the right side
options.D: Lower motor neuron (LMN) lesion on the left side

ansText: Lower motor neuron (LMN) lesion on the right side
expl: Explanation: The presentation described in the question indicates a pattern of facial weakness that involves an inability to fully close the right eye and a mouth droop to the left side when smiling, while still being able to wrinkle the forehead on the right side. This pattern suggests involvement of the facial nerve on the right side of the face. Forehead Movement Preservation: In cases of lower motor neuron lesions affecting the facial nerve, the entire side of the face will show weakness, including the forehead. However, in upper motor neuron lesions, typically seen in strokes, the forehead receiving bilateral upper motor neuron inputs remains spared (patients can still wrinkle their forehead). Facial Nerve (Cranial Nerve VII) Involvement: The facial nerve controls the muscles of facial expression. A lower motor neuron lesion affecting this nerve will impair its function on the affected side, leading to inability to close the eye and drooping of the mouth. Side of Lesion: Since the patient cannot fully close the right eye and the mouth droops to the left (indicating weakness on the right), the lesion is on the same side as the deficits observed (right side). The symptoms described are consistent with a classic presentation of Bell's Palsy or another form of peripheral facial nerve palsy, which are types of lower motor neuron lesions. Explanation of other options: Upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion on the right side (Option A): A right UMN lesion would affect the contralateral (left) lower face , not the right side. Forehead sparing would be seen, but in this case, the right forehead is affected. Upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion on the left side (Option B): A left UMN lesion would cause lower facial weakness on the right , but the forehead would be spared. Since the patient has complete right-sided facial weakness (including the forehead), this is not a UMN lesion. Lower motor neuron (LMN) lesion on the left side (Option D): The patient has right-sided facial weakness , indicating a right-sided lesion, not a left-sided one. Key Takeaways: A lower motor neuron (LMN) lesion of the right facial nerve (e.g., Bell's Palsy) causes complete right-sided facial weakness, including the forehead, and inability to close the eye.

text: A 75-year-old female is noted to have sustained hypertension with a blood pressure of 196/80 mmHg. Which of the following is the most appropriate strategy for this patient?

options.A: ACE inhibitors would be contraindicated in association with a creatinine above 1.5 mg/dl
options.B: Antihypertensive therapy would be associated with only a minor reduction in risk of stroke in this age group
options.C: Beta blockers are less effective in this age group than in younger patients
options.D: Doxazosin would be the most appropriate initial treatment for this patient

ansText: Beta blockers are less effective in this age group than in younger patients
expl: This patient has isolated systolic hypertension with a persistent systolic BP over 140mmHg and diastolic BP below 90. This is associated with increased risk of stroke and coronary events in those over 60 years. This systolic hypertension should be lowered if persistent and is not responding to non-pharmacological measures, with calcium-channel blockers and thiazides as drugs of first choice . Elderly patients have a higher absolute cardiovascular risk than younger individuals and therefore benefit more from control of blood pressure. ACE inhibitors are not contraindicated when the serum creatinine is greater than 150umol/L but should be commenced under specialist supervision. There is evidence that beta blockers maybe less effective in elderly patients. Reference: Harrison’s Principles of Internal Principles, 20 th edition, ch:271 pg:1903

text: A 45-year-old male has a history of 6 months of cutaneous symptoms in the form of Raynaud's Phenomenon and livido reticularis. He recently has history of numbness of the hands and feet. expl: The patient in this question has a vasculitis as evidenced by the presence of involvement of multiple symptoms. The catch in the question is the presence of testicular pain, which is seen in Polyarteritis Nodosa. Polyarteritis nodosa is a medium vessel vasculitis which is characterized by the absence of pulmonary involvement and glomerulonephritis. Microscopy shows transmural fibrinoid necrosis without granulomas. Renal impairment can occur due to involvement of branches of renal artery. Mesenteric ischemia and bowel infarction can also occur. text: Which of the following is true regarding the action of clopidogrel?

options.B: It is a glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor
options.C: It is a hydroxymethyl coenzyme A inhibitor
options.D: It is an ADP receptor antagonist

ansText: It is an ADP receptor antagonist
expl: Clopidogrel prevents platelet aggregation through antagonism of the adenosine diphosphate (ADP) receptor. It has been shown to reduce mortality from stroke and ischaemic heart disease (IHD) in primary prevention studies. Vorapaxar is an anti-platelet agent that reduces platelet aggregation through reversible antagonism of Protease Activated Receptor-1 (PAR 1), also known as thrombin receptor. text: A 52-year-old woman develops sudden-onset facial droop, slurred speech, and inability to raise her right arm. The symptoms gradually improve and completely resolve within 24 hours. On examination, she has a mid-diastolic murmur over the left side of the heart and an irregular heart rhythm. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The patient developed sudden-onset focal neurological symptoms that completely resolved within 48 hours , indicating transient cerebral ischemia without infarction , which defines a Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA) . The presence of irregular rhythm and mid-diastolic murmur is suggestive of atrial fibrillation with mitral stenosis pointing to a cardioembolic source , but since the symptoms resolved completely , the episode is classified as a TIA (Option C ruled out) Transient ischemic attacks Transient Ischemic Attacks (TIAs) are brief episodes of stroke-like symptoms that resolve completely , typically lasting less than 24 hours, without evidence of brain infarction on imaging. Transient ischemic attacks (TIAs) represent brief vascular insults that can affect: Brain → focal neurological deficits Retina → amaurosis fugax (transient vision loss) Cochlea → transient hearing loss or vertigo Spinal cord → rare transient myelopathy TIAs share the same etiologies as ischemic stroke , including: Embolic events (from the heart or large arteries) In situ thrombosis of intracranial vessels In TIA, the occluded vessel reopens spontaneously , restoring neurological function. Imaging and diagnosis If brain imaging shows an infarction, the event is classified as a stroke , regardless of symptom duration. A normal imaging study does not rule out TIA, as the diagnosis is primarily clinical . Clinical significance TIAs are important warning events , signaling high risk for subsequent stroke. Risk of stroke after TIA: ~10-15% within the first 3 months, with most events occurring in the first 48 hours . Treatment For TIA, start dual antiplatelet therapy (Aspirin + Clopidogrel) for 21 days , followed by single antiplatelet therapy long-term for secondary prevention. Explanation of other options Thromboembolic stroke (Option B): A thromboembolic stroke results in persistent neurological deficits due to brain infarction and is diagnosed when symptoms last more than 24 hours or when brain imaging confirms infarction. Paradoxical embolism (Option D): Paradoxical embolism occurs when a venous thrombus enters the arterial circulation via a PFO or ASD. The mid-diastolic murmur in this patient is instead associated with mitral stenosis , not the shunt.

text: A 60-year-old woman presents with weakness in her right arm lasting for 6 hours. The weakness gradually improved and eventually resolved. She has a history of diabetes, hypertension, and obesity. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: Based on the clinical presentation, the most likely diagnosis is Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA). Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA) Defined as a brief episode of neurological dysfunction caused by focal ischemia in the brain, spinal cord, or retina, without resulting in permanent tissue damage or infarction. Symptoms usually last less than an hour, often just minutes, and resolve completely within 24 hours. The risk of stroke is highest within the first 48 hours after a TIA. Etiology: Common risk factors include diabetes, hypertension, advanced age, smoking, obesity, alcohol use, poor diet, psychosocial stress, and lack of physical activity. A history of prior stroke or TIA significantly increases the risk of recurrence. Pathophysiology and Subtypes: Large artery atherothrombosis (most common): Involves narrowing or blockage of large intracranial or extracranial arteries due to atherosclerosis, leading to reduced blood flow or artery-to-artery embolism. Small vessel ischemic disease: Caused by lipohyalinosis or arteriolosclerosis of small vessels, commonly linked to hypertension, diabetes, and aging. Cardiac embolism: Usually from clots forming in the heart chambers, often related to atrial fibrillation. Cryptogenic: Ischemic events with no clear source, sometimes termed Embolic Stroke of Unknown Source (ESUS). Other causes: Less common reasons include arterial dissection and vasculitis. Explanation for other options: Compressive neuropathy (Option A): usually causes persistent symptoms, unlike the transient symptoms described in this case. Ischemic stroke (Option C): leads to longer-lasting neurological deficits due to sustained disruption of blood flow, and symptoms typically do not resolve within 24 hours. Diabetic neuropathy (Option D): is unlikely to present with sudden, transient weakness affecting only one side of the body, as observed in this patient. Reference: TIA

text: A stroke patient presents with an inability to identify objects but can determine the colour, texture, and shape of objects. Which of the following lobes is involved?
expl: Explanation: Visual agnosia is the inability to recognize objects despite intact vision, while preserving the ability to perceive their color, shape, and texture, typically resulting from lesions in the temporal lobe. Temporal lobe stroke can cause memory impairment, difficulty recognizing faces or objects (prosopagnosia), fluent aphasia in left-sided lesions, visual agnosia, problems with visual perception and sound processing, and emotional or behavioral changes such as aggression, passivity, or trouble interpreting facial cues. Explanantion of other options: Frontal lobe (Option A) : It may result in difficulties with learning, visual-motor coordination, executive functions, and attention, including challenges in planning, focusing, and self-control. Parietal lobe (Option B): Right - Damage to this area can cause visuospatial deficits (e.g., the patient may have difficulty finding their way around new, or even familiar, places). Parietal Lobe, Left: Damage to this area may disrupt a person's ability to understand spoken and/or written language. Unilateral occipital lobe (Option D): Lesions of the occipital lobe, often from a posterior cerebral artery infarct, result in contralateral homonymous hemianopia a visual field loss on the same side in both eyes opposite to the lesion typically sparing the central (macular) vision.

text: A 65-year-old is investigated for dyspnoea and is shown to have an ejection fraction of 45% on echocardiography. How is the left ventricular ejection fraction calculated?
expl: The left ventricle pumps only a fraction of the blood it contains. The ejection fraction is the amount of blood pumped (stroke volume=end diastolic volume - end systolic volume) divided by the amount of blood the ventricle contains (end diastolic volume). A normal ejection fraction (EF) is more than 55% of the blood volume. Based on ejection fraction, heart failure is divided into: HF with reduced EF (HFrEF) : EF > 40% HF with preserved EF (HFpEF) : EF > 50% HF with mid-range EF (HFmrEF) : EF 40-50% Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page

text: A 7D-year-old woman presents with a two month history of episodic loss of vision in her right eye. Her electrocardiogram was normal and carotid ultrasound reveal a 49% stenosis of the right internal carotid artery, as assessed by the NASCAT criteria. What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
expl: The combination of aspirin and clopidogrel was found to prevent stroke following TIA better than aspirin alone in a large study(POINT STUDY). Current NICE guidelines recommend that patients who have had a suspected TIA who are at high risk of a stroke (ABCD score of 4 or above) should have aspirin (300mg OD) started immediately. They also need specialist assessment and investigation within 24 hours of onset of symptoms. Secondary prevention measures should be introduced as soon as the diagnosis is confirmed, with consideration of individual risk factors. The ABCD scoring system uses: Age > or equal to 60 (1) BP > or equal to 140/90mmHg at initial evaluation (1) Clinical features (unilateral weakness 2, isolated speech disturbance 1, other 0) Duration of symptoms (> or equal to 60 minutes, 10-59 minutes, Diabetes mellitus (1) Although you cannot calculate the ABCD score with the information given in this question, aspirin remains the most appropriate answer. Carotid endarterectomy has been established as an effective treatment for both symptomatic patients and asymptomatic patients who are shown to have carotid artery stenosis. It reduces the risk of disabling stroke or death by 48% in a person with severe symptomatic carotid stenosis (>70%) who has had a TIA. The peri-operative risk of disabling stroke or death is approximately 3%. Current guidelines recommend endarterectomy for symptomatic patients with greater than 70% stenosis, based on the North American Symptomatic Carotid Endarterectomy Trial which showed clear benefit. The endarterectomy should be performed as soon as the patient is fit for surgery, preferably within two weeks of a TIA. The benefit is marginal for symptomatic patients with 50-69% stenosis, but may be greater in male patients. NICE recommends these patients are also considered for endarterectomy. There is significantly less benefit for asymptomatic patients, even those with greater than 60% stenosis. Patients with less than 50% stenosis should not be considered for carotid surgery . Recurrent stenosis can occur in 1-20% of patients following endarterectomy, and re-operation is needed in 1-3% of cases. Ipsilateral strokes occur in 9% of patients following endarterectomy, and 26% of those treated with medical management alone (within 2 years). All patients with suspected non-disabling stroke or TIA who are considered as candidates for carotid endarterectomy should have carotid imaging within 1 week. If the patient has had a disabling stroke there is no real benefit in them undergoing the procedure. Modified-release dipyridamole is indicated in combination with aspirin only once a TIA has been confirmed by a specialist. Alone, it is recommended only if aspirin is contraindicated or not tolerated. Clopidogrel is recommended in patients who have had an ischaemic stroke, rather than a TIA. Warfarin is only indicated with cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, or if the patient has atrial fibrillation. Please note for this explanation, North American Symptomatic Carotid Endarterecomy Trial (NASCET) criteria have been used. Carotid imaging reports will state which criteria are being used. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 427, Pg: 3345

text: A 67-year-old male with a history of diabetes, hypertension and hypercholesterolemia presents with dizziness. He reports that he woke up this morning and attempted to get out of bed but felt dizzy. He vomited and was unable to get out of bed to go to the bathroom. His wife was concerned as this had never happened before and called for the ambulance. On arrival at the emergency room his blood pressure was 180/70 mmHg, pulse was regular at 60 beats per minute and he was apyrexial. Blood sugar was within normal limits.On neurological examination his visual fields were full, and fundoscopy was notable for grade 2 hypertensive retinopathy. He had left jerk nystagmus on looking to the left and left jerk nystagmus on looking to the right. He was able to perform finger to nose and heel to shin in the bed. On standing the patient felt dizzy. His blood pressure was 170/80 mmHg after three minutes standing. He refused to walk for fear of falling. The rest of his examination was unremarkable.What is the leading diagnosis at this time?
expl: Although there is no dysmetria a patient can have vertigo in isolation from a stroke. Typically however the patient has direction changing nystagmus. You would be more reassured if the patient were able to walk. A trial of meclizine prior to walking may help. A cerebrovascular accident should be considered and an MRI obtained of the brain. The patient is not orthostatic on examination by definition. Labyrinthitis typically has associated tinnitus and a history of infection or head trauma. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st ed, Ch: 22, Pg: 160

text: During a scorching summer afternoon, a man, who had been toiling in a field, unexpectedly collapsed. Upon examination, there were no apparent physical indications of dehydration, although his radial pulse was detectable. The doctor determined that the man's serum electrolyte levels were within the normal range. Shockingly, the man's body temperature measured 106 degrees Fahrenheit. Considering these circumstances, which of the following should be administered as an initial form of immediate assistance?
expl: Explanation: The patient has heat stroke , defined by a core body temperature >40°C (104°F) with central nervous system dysfunction (collapse). The presence of a radial pulse indicates a perfusing rhythm, so CPR is not needed. The immediate life-threatening priority is rapid cooling . Covering the patient with cool, damp sheets (often combined with fanning) is an effective initial cooling method Explanation of other options: Inject epinephrine immediately (Option A): Epinephrine is used in cardiac arrest (ACLS); it is not indicated for heat stroke and could be harmful. Cover with hot damp sheets (Option B): This would worsen hyperthermia. Start CPR: Indicated only if the patient is pulseless and apneic, which is not the case here. Key Takeaways: Heat stroke is a medical emergency characterized by hyperthermia and CNS dysfunction. The cornerstone of initial management is rapid cooling to prevent irreversible organ damage.

expl: CSF sugar . If LP is delayed in pyogenic, empirical antibiotic therapy should be initiated after blood cultures are obtained. Centrifuged sample has more yield.

text: A patient presented with fever, headache, mental confusion, nausea and neck stiffness. Lumbar puncture was performed and CSF analysis reveals proteins 45 mg/dl, glucose 7 mg/dl and increased neutrophils >80%. What is the most appropriate treatment?
expl: Explanation: The patient's presentation and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) findings are indicative of bacterial meningitis. The most appropriate treatment for bacterial meningitis, given the clinical and CSF findings, would be Ceftriaxone + Vancomycin . This combination is recommended to cover a broad spectrum of potential bacterial pathogens, including resistant strains such as penicillin-resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis, until the specific organism can be identified and sensitivities are determined. Based on the provided text and the diagnosis of bacterial meningitis is supported by: Symptoms : Fever, headache, mental confusion, nausea, and neck stiffness. CSF Findings : Increased neutrophils : Predominance of polymorphonuclear cells (neutrophils) in the CSF is typical in bacterial infections. Low glucose levels (7 mg/dL) : Significantly reduced CSF glucose, compared to normal (40-70 mg/dL), which is common in bacterial meningitis due to glucose consumption by bacteria. Elevated protein levels (45 mg/dL) : Protein levels are elevated due to increased permeability of the blood-brain barrier. These findings align with the classic signs of bacterial meningitis, which include low CSF glucose, high protein concentration, and a high percentage of neutrophils. Immediate Actions : Obtain blood cultures and start empirical antimicrobial therapy along with adjunctive dexamethasone to reduce complications. CSF Diagnosis : The diagnosis is confirmed by CSF analysis showing high protein, low glucose, high white blood cell count with a predominance of neutrophils, and positive results on Gram stain or culture. Bacterial Meningitis Diagnosis: Empirical Therapy Initiation : Start treatment immediately after obtaining blood cultures, before lumbar puncture if necessary, especially if neuroimaging is required. Classic CSF Abnormalities in Bacterial Meningitis : High white blood cell count : Mainly neutrophils. Low glucose : Less than 40 mg/dL and a CSF/serum glucose ratio of less than 0.4. High protein : Greater than 45 mg/dL. Increased intracranial pressure : Opening pressure often above 180 mmH2O. Gram Stain and Culture : More than 60% positivity in Gram stain and over 80% in culture, reinforcing the presence of bacterial pathogens. PCR Testing : Useful for detecting bacterial DNA, which can help identify the specific causative organism. Differential Diagnosis : Includes other conditions that can present with similar CSF findings but may require different management, such as viral, fungal, tuberculous, and carcinomatous meningitis. Treatment Considerations : The administration of high-glucose solutions prior to lumbar puncture is unlikely to affect CSF glucose levels significantly unless there is a considerable delay. Explanation of other options: Ampicillin + Acyclovir (Option B): Ampicillin is used for Listeria monocytogenes , which is a concern in neonates, elderly, or immunocompromised-not the most common pathogen in this case. Acyclovir is used for herpes simplex encephalitis (HSE) , which presents with temporal lobe involvement , seizures, and lymphocytic (not neutrophilic) CSF . Cefotaxime + Ampicillin(Option C): Cefotaxime is an alternative to ceftriaxone but does not cover penicillin-resistant S. pneumoniae unless combined with vancomycin. Ampicillin is used for Listeria , which is less likely in this patient. Penicillin + Azithromycin (Option D): Penicillin alone is ineffective against penicillin-resistant pneumococci . Azithromycin is a macrolide used for atypical pneumonia and has no role in bacterial meningitis. Key Takeaways: For bacterial meningitis, the best empirical treatment is Ceftriaxone + Vancomycin to cover common pathogens, including resistant pneumococci.

text: A patient presented with an 11-day history of fever and neck stiffness. Lumbar puncture revealed lymphocyte predominance, glucose of 50 mg/dL, and protein of 3000 mg/dL, along with the presence of a cobweb-like coagulum. Gram stain was negative. Chest X-ray demonstrated upper lobe disease with hilar lymphadenopathy.
expl: The combination of subacute fever with neck stiffness, typical CSF profile (lymphocyte predominance, reduced glucose, markedly elevated protein), cobweb-like clot formation, and chest X-ray revealing upper lobe disease with hilar lymph node enlargement are hallmark findings of tuberculous meningitis . A negative Gram stain favors a mycobacterial infection over c ommon bacterial causes. Explanations of other options: Bacterial meningitis (Option B): Bacterial meningitis usually has a rapid onset (within 24-48 hours), shows neutrophil predominance in the CSF, and often yields a positive Gram stain. The slower progression and lymphocyte-rich CSF in this case argue against bacterial meningitis. Fungal meningitis (Option C): Although fungal meningitis may show comparable CSF findings such as reduced glucose and elevated protein, it is more commonly seen in immunocompromised individuals and usually lacks the classic upper lobe changes on chest X-ray. Pulmonary involvement in this context strongly favors tuberculosis. Viral meningitis (Option D): Viral meningitis is generally characterized by normal or only slightly raised protein, normal glucose, and no cobweb coagulum. The very high protein level (3000 mg/dL) together with low glucose makes a viral cause unlikely.

text: A 19-year-old boy was diagnosed with meningococcal meningitis. What is the drug of choice (DOC) for prophylaxis to be given to his contacts?
expl: Explanation: Rifampicin is the drug of choice for chemoprophylaxis of close contacts of a patient with meningococcal meningitis. Meningococcal meningitis caused by Neisseria meningitidis is highly contagious and spreads through respiratory droplets. Close contacts-such as roommates, family members, or anyone with prolonged exposure-are at high risk of acquiring the infection. Chemoprophylaxis is essential to prevent secondary cases. It is the drug of choice for adults unless contraindicated (e.g., pregnancy, resistance concerns). It effectively eliminates Neisseria meningitidis from the nasopharynx, thereby reducing secondary cases. Alternatives (such as ciprofloxacin or ceftriaxone) can be used in special situations, but rifampicin remains the standard recommendation in most guidelines. Rifampicin 600 mg twice daily for 2 days in adults is the standard regimen Explanation of Incorrect Options: Ethambutol (Option B): Used for tuberculosis, not effective against Neisseria meningitidis. Doxycycline (Option C): Used for a variety of infections, but not recommended for meningococcal prophylaxis. Amoxicillin (Option D): Not suitable for meningococcal chemoprophylaxis.

text: For MDR-RR TB, what is the indication of short course bedaquiline?

options.A: Resistance to rifampicin and sensitive to fluoroquinolones
options.B: Mutation only to INH A and kat G gene

ansText: Resistance to rifampicin and sensitive to fluoroquinolones
expl: Explanation of answer: Short-course bedaquiline-containing regimens are indicated for MDR/RR-TB patients who are rifampicin-resistant but fluoroquinolone-sensitive. Multidrug-resistant / Rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (MDR/RR-TB) is defined by resistance to rifampicin, with or without resistance to other first-line drugs. The short-course bedaquiline-containing regimen (typically the 6-month BPaLM regimen) is indicated when the strain is resistant to rifampicin but remains sensitive to fluoroquinolones. BPaLM Regimen Components: Bedaquiline Pretomanid Linezolid (600 mg) Moxifloxacin WHO Endorsed Regimen Use: Indicated when: Confirmed Rifampicin resistance (MDR/RR-TB) Confirmed Fluoroquinolone susceptibility Age ≥14 years Non-CNS involvement No prior exposure to any BPaLM drugs >1 month unless drug resistance to them is ruled out Not recommended in: TB meningitis or CNS TB Pregnancy and lactation Age Known exposure to BPaLM drugs for over 30 days without confirmed susceptibility Explanation of other options: Mutation only to INH A and katG gene (Option B): Indicates isoniazid resistance, but rifampicin resistance is required to define MDR/RR-TB. Without rifampicin resistance, the patient does not qualify for bedaquiline-based MDR therapy. Rifampicin sensitive (Option C): First-line anti-TB drugs are used for rifampicin-sensitive TB. Short-course bedaquiline regimens are specifically for rifampicin-resistant cases. Extrapulmonary TB like tubercular meningitis (Option D): Bedaquiline has poor CNS penetration, and tubercular meningitis is a contraindication for short-course regimens due to limited efficacy. text: A child presents with two weeks of poor feeding and marked irritability. The sibling has confirmed tuberculosis and is receiving antitubercular therapy. As part of the evaluation, a lumbar puncture is done. Which of the following findings is most likely in the CSF?

options.A: Lymphocytosis with low sugar and high protein
options.B: Lymphocytosis with high sugar and high protein
options.C: Neutrophils with low sugar and low protein
options.D: Neutrophils with low sugar and high protein

ansText: Lymphocytosis with low sugar and high protein
expl: Explanation: The history of two weeks of poor feeding and irritability, along with close contact with a tuberculosis case, points toward a diagnosis of tuberculous meningitis . In tuberculous meningitis, cerebrospinal fluid usually demonstrates lymphocytic pleocytosis (up to 1000/μL), increased protein levels (100-800 mg/dL), and reduced glucose. This classic combination of findings represents the chronic inflammatory reaction seen in CNS tuberculosis. Explanations of other options: Lymphocytosis with high sugar and high protein (Option B): Although lymphocytosis and elevated protein are consistent with CNS infections, increased glucose (hyperglycorrhachia) is not characteristic of tuberculous meningitis. In TB meningitis, *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* typically lowers CSF glucose through heightened utilization. Therefore, elevated glucose would argue against this diagnosis. Neutrophils with low sugar and low protein (Option C): A pattern of low glucose together with low protein is unusual in CNS infections, since infections generally cause protein to rise as part of the inflammatory process. In addition, neutrophilic predominance is more indicative of acute bacterial meningitis. Neutrophils with low sugar and high protein (Option D): Although neutrophils may appear in the CSF during acute bacterial meningitis, their predominance is not typical of tuberculous meningitis, which is usually characterized by a lymphocytic response.

text: A young individual presents with an unusually severe headache, unlike any previous episodes. Examination reveals high blood pressure and neck stiffness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The sudden onset of an intense headache described as the 'worst ever,' together with hypertension, neck stiffness, and a CT scan demonstrating the classic ' Star of Death' pattern from blood in the basal cisterns, is indicative of a subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). A subarachnoid hemorrhage happens when blood collects in the subarachnoid space, the area between the brain and its delicate coverings, most often caused by a ruptured aneurysm, and has a mortality rate of about 35% if left untreated. Explanations of other options: Cluster headache (Option A): Cluster headaches present as intense, one-sided pain usually located behind the eye, accompanied by autonomic symptoms. They appear in cyclical patterns or clusters, but unlike subarachnoid hemorrhage, they are not associated with neck stiffness or the 'Star sign' on CT scans. Encephalitis (Option C): Encephalitis usually manifests with fever, confusion, seizures, and localized neurological signs. Since fever is absent and CT shows typical SAH features, encephalitis is an unlikely diagnosis. Meningitis (Option D): Although meningitis may cause headache and neck stiffness, it usually also presents with fever and light sensitivity. The CT scan findings do not match meningitis, and the classic 'Star of Death' pattern on CT is specific for SAH.
full: a young individual presents with an unusually severe headache, unlike any previous episodes. examination reveals high blood pressure and neck stiffness. what is the most likely diagnosis? cluster headache subarachnoid haemorrhage encephalitis meningitis  explanation: the sudden onset of an intense headache described as the 'worst ever,' together with hypertension, neck stiffness, and a ct scan demonstrating the classic ' star of death' pattern from blood in the basal cisterns, is indicative of a subarachnoid hemorrhage (sah). a subarachnoid hemorrhage happens when blood collects in the subarachnoid space, the area between the brain and its delicate coverings, most often caused by a ruptured aneurysm, and has a mortality rate of about 35% if left untreated. explanations of other options: cluster headache (option a): cluster headaches present as intense, one-sided pain usually located behind the eye, accompanied by autonomic symptoms. they appear in cyclical patterns or clusters, but unlike subarachnoid hemorrhage, they are not associated with neck stiffness or the 'star sign' on ct scans. encephalitis (option c): encephalitis usually manifests with fever, confusion, seizures, and localized neurological signs. since fever is absent and ct shows typical sah features, encephalitis is an unlikely diagnosis. meningitis (option d): although meningitis may cause headache and neck stiffness, it usually also presents with fever and light sensitivity. the ct scan findings do not match meningitis, and the classic 'star of death' pattern on ct is specific for sah.

text: What is the confirmatory test for the given condition?
expl: Explanation of answer: The given condition is Tuberculoma. NMR spectroscopy detects specific lipid peaks and metabolic profiles that help confirm tuberculoma and differentiate it from neurocysticercosis. NMR spectroscopy (Nuclear Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy) is a non-invasive biochemical imaging technique that analyzes the chemical composition of brain lesions. It is especially helpful when CT or MRI shows ring-enhancing lesions, where the differential diagnosis includes tuberculoma vs. neurocysticercosis. Key Spectroscopic Finding in Tuberculoma: Prominent lipid peak at 1.3 ppm. This is the hallmark finding of caseating tuberculoma. Helps differentiate from neurocysticercosis, which lacks a strong lipid peak and may show other metabolites like lactate. Intracranial Tuberculoma - Diagnostic Imaging: Explanation of other options: CBNAAT of CSF (Option A): Useful in diagnosing tuberculous meningitis by detecting MTB DNA, but not confirmatory for parenchymal tuberculoma and does not distinguish it from other ring-enhancing lesions. PET scan (Option B): Shows increased metabolic activity, but is non-specific and cannot biochemically differentiate tuberculoma vs. neurocysticercosis. MRI aerial scan (Option D): Not a recognized term in clinical radiology. Standard MRI provides anatomical detail, but lacks metabolic resolution offered by spectroscopy. Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4845155/

text: The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) specimen of a patient is shown below, along with microscopy. The report reveals mononuclear cytosis, raised protein levels, and reduced glucose. What is the most probable etiology?
expl: Explanation: The combination of clinical details with CSF findings - lymphocytic predominance, elevated proteins, hypoglycorrhachia (low sugar), and the presence of a characteristic cobweb-like clot - points towards tuberculous meningitis (TBM) . Features of Tuberculous Meningitis (TBM): Etiology: Caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis via hematogenous spread or rupture of subependymal tubercles into the subarachnoid space. Presentation: Subacute onset with fever, headache, meningismus, and cranial nerve palsies (especially ocular nerves from basal meningeal involvement). Complications: Hydrocephalus, elevated intracranial pressure (ICP), and ischemic infarcts. CSF Findings: Lymphocytic predominance Elevated protein (100-500 mg/dL) Decreased glucose ( Cobweb-like pellicle formation Diagnosis: Gold Standard: CSF culture for M ycobacterium tuberculosis. Supportive Tests: AFB staining, CSF ADA levels, or PCR for TB DNA. Management: Early initiation of antitubercular therapy (ATT) . Corticosteroids to minimize inflammation and reduce complications. CSF Findings in Different Types of Meningitis: Explanation of Other Options: Aseptic meningitis (Option B): Typically viral, presents with lymphocytic predominance but normal glucose and near-normal protein levels. Bacterial meningitis (Option C): Usually shows neutrophilic pleocytosis, very high protein, and markedly reduced glucose, with turbid CSF. Chemical meningitis (Option D): Results from rupture of intracranial tumor contents (e.g., dermoid, glioma) into CSF. Shows variable inflammatory response, elevated protein, but absence of microbial organisms. Reference: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8425579/ https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8425579/

text: A 16-year-old girl presented with a 12 hour history of fever and diffuse headache. On examination she was febrile (37.5°C). She was fully conscious. Mild neck stiffness was noted but there were no other neurological signs. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed: Cell count 200/mL(60% lymphocytes) Protein 0.8 g/L(0.15-0.45) Glucose within normal range Gram stain No organisms seen What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Enteroviruses and mumps are the commonest causes of viral meningitis. Cryptococcal meningitis is an infection of severely immunocompromised individuals, especially advanced human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection. Tuberculous meningitis is an insidious illness, presenting over weeks and months. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st Ed, Ch: 138 Pg: 1106

text: Whole blood is stored at which temperature for maintaining erythrocyte viability?
expl: Whole blood provides both oxygen-carrying capacity and volume expansion. It is the ideal component for patients who have sustained acute hemorrhage of ≥25% total blood volume loss . Whole blood is stored at 4°C to maintain erythrocyte viability , but platelet dysfunction and degradation of some coagulation factors occurs . In addition, 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate levels fall over time , leading to an increase in the oxygen affinity of the hemoglobin and a decreased capacity to deliver oxygen to the tissues, a problem with all red cell storage. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 113, Pg: 885

text: A 22 year old man is admitted following a severe road traffic accident. He suffered significant blood loss at the scene. He is resuscitated with IV crystalloid and group O negative packed red cells. Intra-operatively the anesthetist phones you for advice. Bloods show: Hb: 6.6 g/dL; WBC: 11200/μL; platelet count 83000/μL; PT 28 seconds; APTT: 72 seconds; fibrinogen: 1.9 g/L. What is most appropriate to use to reduce his bleeding risk?
expl: The likely diagnosis is a disseminated intravascular coagulation following a road traffic accident. His PT and APTT are significantly prolonged; therefore, FFP is indicated at a dose of 15 mU/ kg. He will likely require platelets; however, at present, they are greater than the recommended threshold of 20000/μL. Cryoprecipitate is primarily used to replace fibrinogen when below 1.5 g/L. Prothrombin complex concentrate is used to reverse warfarin. For these situations, fibrinogen level should be maintained at >1.50 g/L and PT prolonged no more than 3 s above the upper limit of normal. Vitamin K should be given. Reference: Harrison's Principles of internal medicine 21st ed chap 116 pg. 917

text: Factor VII deficiency should be considered with which of the following coagulation abnormalities?

options.C: Prolongation of both PT and aPTT

expl: Commonly used tests of hemostasis provide the initial screening for clotting factor activity, and disease phenotype often correlates with the level of clotting activity. An isolated abnormal prothrombin time (PT)suggests factor VII deficiency, whereas a prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) indicates most commonly hemophilia or factor XI deficiency. The prolongation of both PT and aPTT suggests deficiency of factors V, X, and II, or fibrinogen abnormalities. The addition of the missing factor at a range of doses to the subject's plasma will correct the abnormal clotting times; the result is expressed as a percentage of the activity observed in normal subjects. Reference: Harrison's Principles of internal medicine 21st ed chap 116 pg. 911

text: Antiparasitic action of Metronidazole on E. histolytica is via :
expl: E histolytica lacks glutathione and glutathione reductase, it relies on its thioredoxin reductase system to prevent, regulate, and repair the damage caused by oxidative stress. Metronidazole inhibits this antioxidant system. Metronidazole is the drug of choice for the following parasitic infections: Amoebiasis Giardiasis Trichomoniasis Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch: 223Pg 1718

text: A 12 year old male was admitted to the emergency department with significant lethargy which had worsened over the past year. On examination he was conscious and oriented. His heart rate was 70 beats per minute, blood pressure was 120/70mmHg and he was afebrile. Clinical examination of the abdomen revealed no organomegaly. His haemoglobin is 11.2 g/dL, white cell count of 8200/mm3 and a platelet count of 365000/mm3. The plasma urea was 30 mg/dL, creatinine 1.3 mg/dl, sodium 132 mmol/L, potassium 2.3 mmol/L, bicarbonate 38 mmol/L. The plasma liver function tests were within normal limits. His electrocardiogram demonstrated U waves. Which one of the following is the likely diagnosis?
expl: So the given patient has hypokalemia with metabolic alkalosis as evidenced by a high bicarbonate. But his blood pressure is high. So barter and Gitleman are ruled out. ACE inhibitor causes hyperkalemia. Hypokalemia with hypertension and alkalosis is caused by Liddle syndrome in the given options. Others include: Conns syndrome(primary hyperaldosteronism), renal artery stenosis(secondary hyperaldosteronism), Apparent mineralocorticoid excess, Cushing's syndrome. Lets see how: So in all these there will be excess sodium reabsorption mediated by the ENaC. In Liddle syndrome it is due to activating mutation of the channel, while in others, it is due to aldosterone excess. To maintain electrical neutrality of the interstitium, potassium and H+ ions are secreated. So the result is hypertension, hypokalemia and alkalosis. In Liddle syndrome, the Renin and Aldosterone levels will be low, since the receptor is activated by a mutation, the sodium reabsorption will inhibit RAAS. There are two other conditions that will behave like Liddle syndrome. The first one is Cushing Syndrome, where the ENaC is activated by endogenous steroid, remember that glucocorticoids have mineralocorticoid action too. So that Renin and aldosterone will be suppressed. The second one is Apparent mineralocorticoid excess, due to 11β hydroxy steroid dehydrogenase which converts Cortisol to Cortisone, so that there will be excess cortisol that acts on the ENaC. So in all these conditions, the renin and aldosterone levels will be low. Liddle's Syndrome and Apparent Mineralocorticoid excess are single gene mutations causing hypertension. Hypertension and hypokalemia in these can be treated with potassium sparing diuretics. In Conns syndrome, there will be high aldosterone due to aldosterone secreting adenoma, which will inhibit Renin. In Renal Artery stenosis and renin secreting tumors, there will be the same finding of hypokalemia, alkalosis and hypertension. But the Renin and aldosterone levels will be high. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st edition, Ch: 53, Pg:353.

text: A 34-year-old woman has presented to the emergency department for the third time with abdominal pain which typically lasts several days. The previous two occasions she has been discharged home without a firm diagnosis. Between episodes the patient is symptom free. She complains of feeling anxious. She has recently re-started the combined oral contraceptive pill after completing her family. On examination she is anxious and hypertensive at 155/98 mmHg with a pulse of 102. She has no rashes. Her abdomen is diffusely tender. Investigations show Haemoglobin 12.8 g/dl(13.5-18) White cell count 8.1 x 10^9/L (4-10) Platelets 220 x 10^9/L (150-400) Sodium 135 mmol/l (134-143) Potassium 3.9 mmol/l (3.5-5) Creatinine 0.6 mg/dl Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) is a rare disorder characterised by abdominal pain and neuropsychiatric symptoms which usually presents in the 20-40 age group. Rash is not a feature of AIP like other porphyrias. Hypertension and tachycardia are common examination findings. The progesterone component of the combined oral contraceptive pill is known to precipitate porphyria attacks. Many other drugs have been described in association with an attack. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 416 Pg: 3237-3248

text: A 16 year old boy with known sickle-cell disease is brought to the emergency department profoundly unwell. He has a reduced conscious level, temperature 39 ° C, pulse rate 160 beats/min and blood pressure 70/40 mmHg. Investigations: Hb: 7.8 g/dL; MCV:68 fl; WBC: 17000/7mu;L; platelet count 480000/μL , Reticulocyte count: 10 X 109/L(NR:50-100 X 109/L ) Blood film: neutrophilia with toxic granulation; RBC consistent with sickle cell disease and hyposplenism. What is the most likely clinical diagnosis?
expl: Patients with sickle-cell disease have compromised splenic function resulting from microvascular occlusion. This puts them at risk of life-threatening infections from capsulated organisms.hyposplenism (through reduction in phagocytic capacity) increases the risk of meningococcal disease. Aplastic crises produce a very low hemoglobin with a reticulocytopenia. There is no history of joint pain or shortness of breath to suggest a vaso-occlusive painful crisis or sickle chest syndrome. text: Which one of the following proteins defect is most likely to be associated with very high levels of plasma chylomicrons?
expl: Dietary triglycerides in cholesterol are packaged by gastrointestinal epithelial cells into large lipoprotein particles called chylomicrons . After secretion into the intestinal lymph and passage into the general circulation, chylomicrons bind to the enzyme lipoprotein lipase, which is located on endothelial surfaces. This enzyme is activated by a protein contained in the chylomicron, apoprotein CII, liberating free fatty acids and monoglycerides, which then pass through the endothelial cells and enter adipocyte or muscle cells. Patients with familial lipoprotein lipase deficiency usually presents in infancy with recurrent attacks of abdominal pain caused by pancreatitis. They also have eruptive xanthomas resulting from triglyceride deposition. Treatment should consist of a low fat diet that may be supplemented by medium-chain triglycerides, which are not incorporated into chylomicrons. The absence of functional apoprotein CII, with consequent failure to activate lipoprotein lipase, presents with a similar phenotype, although the affected patients are typically detected at a somewhat later age than are patients with familial lipoprotein lipase deficiency. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 20 th edition Chapter: 400 Page number:2889-90

text: A 70-year-old woman is referred for investigation of a creatinine of 2.5 mg/dl. She mentioned several episodes of haematuria with symptoms of ureteric colic. She has a long history of low back pain treated with a combination of painkillers. An ultrasound shows two irregular shaped kidneys size 8.5 and 9 cm and renal papillary calcifications. Which of the following is the most likely?
expl: Our patient is an elderly female with renal impairment, with a background history of use of combination analgesics for low back ache. She also reports ureteric colic with hematuria episodes. There is bilateral scarred kidneys with papillary calcification. This constellation of symptoms is known as analgesic nephropathy. NSAID induced tubulointerstitial disease will not present with colic and hematuria. There is no other information given in the question which suggests a myeloma other than low back ache. Myeloma does not produce colic and hematuria. It will not cause shrunken kidneys. Myeloma causes CKD with normal sized kidneys. Chronic obstructive uropathy due to calculi is possible, but the history of analgesic intake is specified in the history which cant be ignored. Analgesic nephropathy is usually a result of prolonged or chronic ingestion of combination analgesics, that contain phenacetin or acetaminophen and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs(NSAIDs) including aspirin or ibuprofen and caffeine. There will be papillary necrosis and shedding of the necrosed papillae causing colic and hematuria. There will be normal anion gap metabolic acidosis due to loss of tubular function. The patients are at increased risk of urothelial malignancy. Ct scan will show garland calcification. Usual NSAIDS does not cause Analgesic nephropathy A useful mnemonic device for the conditions associated with RPN is POSTCARDS, which stands for the following: Pyelonephritis Obstruction of urinary tract Sickle cell Tuberculosis Cirrhosis of the liver Analgesic abuse Renal transplant rejection Diabetes mellitus Systemic vasculitis Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st edition, Ch:316, Pg:2362

expl: Ans. is 'b' i.e., Replacement of glutamate by valine in 13 chain of HBA Sickle cell anemia Sickle cell anemia is a hereditary hemoglobinopathy, i.e., the type of disease characterized by production of defective hemoglobin. text: A 70-year-old man presents with lower back pain and increasing pallor. Investigations show abnormal renal function, normal liver function with preserved albumin, but markedly elevated gamma globulins. Spine X-ray reveals multiple lytic lesions. Which cell type is most likely responsible for this presentation?
expl: Explanation: The combination of low back pain, pallor, impaired renal function, elevated gamma globulins, and lytic bone lesions is characteristic of multiple myeloma, which arises due to the accumulation of plasma cells . Multiple myeloma develops when malignant plasma cells build up in the bone marrow and secrete large quantities of a monoclonal protein , resulting in widespread systemic effects. Explanation of other options: Lymphocyte (Option A): Although lymphocytes can lead to lymphomas, these usually present with lymph node enlargement and may affect organs such as the spleen and liver. The lack of lymphadenopathy, along with lytic bone lesions and elevated gamma globulins, makes a lymphocytic origin unlikely. Histiocytes (Option C): Histiocyte-related disorders, such as Langerhans cell histiocytosis and hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, usually present with distinct clinical findings like skin rashes, enlarged liver and spleen, and blood cell deficiencies. Monocytes (Option D): Monocytes, a type of white blood cell, can mature into macrophages and dendritic cells as part of the immune system. Disorders of monocytes usually show features such as skin involvement , gum enlargement, and blood abnormalities. However, the rise in gamma globulins is more indicative of a plasma cell disorder.

text: All of the statements regarding 'beer potomania' are true, except?

options.A: It occurs in alcoholics whose sole nutrient is beer
options.B: Typically urine Na+ concentration is > 20 mM
options.C: AVP levels are expected to be suppressed in this condition
options.D: Resumption of a normal diet and/or saline hydration will correct the causative deficit

ansText: Typically urine Na+ concentration is > 20 mM
expl: Hyponatremia can occasionally occur in patients with a very low intake of dietary solutes. Classically, this occurs in alcoholics whose sole nutrient is beer, hence the diagnostic label of beer potomania; beer is very low in protein and salt content, containing only 1-2 mM of Na+. The syndrome has also been described in nonalcoholic patients with highly restricted solute intake due to nutrient-restricted diets, e.g., extreme vegetarian diets. Patients with hyponatremia due to low solute intake typically present with a very low urine osmolality ( urine Na+ concentration that is The fundamental abnormality is the inadequate dietary intake of solutes; the reduced urinary solute excretion limits water excretion such that hyponatremia ensues after relatively modest polydipsia. AVP levels have not been reported in patients with beer potomania but are expected to be suppressed or rapidly suppressible with saline hydration; this fits with the overly rapid correction in plasma Na+ concentration that can be seen with saline hydration. Resumption of a normal diet and/or saline hydration will also correct the causative deficit in urinary solute excretion, such that patients with beer potomania typically correct their plasma Na+ concentration promptly after admission to the hospital. Reference: Harrisons Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:53 Pg: 343

expl: Explanation: Hereditary spherocytosis is a genetic condition where red blood cells are sphere-shaped rather than biconcave, and the main treatment is elective splenectomy. In hereditary spherocytosis , splenectomy is highly beneficial since the spleen is chiefly responsible for destroying spherocytes. The timing depends on disease severity: In severe cases it is done electively at 4-6 years, in moderate cases, it may be postponed until adolescence , while mild cases are usually managed with folic acid supplementation alone. Explanations of other options: G6PD deficiency (Option A): In G6PD deficiency, splenectomy can aggravate anaemia since the spleen plays a key role in clearing damaged red blood cells. Management mainly focuses on preventing exposure to oxidative triggers and treating acute hemolytic crises. Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (Option B): In paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH), hemolysis results from a complement system defect, making stem cell transplantation the only curative option. Splenectomy is not useful since the red cell destruction is complement-driven and occurs in the entire circulation. Hairy cell leukaemia (Option D): In hairy cell leukaemia, the primary treatment is chemotherapy , while splenectomy is reserved for patients with significant splenomegaly or those who do not respond to standard therapy, rather than being the first-line approach.

text: A 71-year-old man is admitted to hospital in a comatose condition. His wife gives a history of past episodes of sweating and palpitations, confusion, and occasional abnormal behavior that improves with intake of glucose.. On examination his pulse is 92 bpm and his blood pressure is 140/90 mmHg. His plasma catecholamine level is normal and blood glucose is 65 mg/dl. What is the most probable diagnosis?
expl: This patient is suffering from hypoglycemic episodes as evidenced by the classical autonomic and neuroglycopenic symptoms which gets relieved with intake of glucose. (Whipple’s triad). Insulinomas may be sporadic or associated with MEN1 syndrome. Pheochromocytoma, either isolated or as part of the MEN-II syndrome, is unlikely as his blood pressure and catecholamine levels are normal. Pseudodementia is associated with severe depressive illness. Memory impairment, slowed thinking and lack of spontaneity are characteristic features. Hypoglycemia is not associated with this disorder. Hypoglycemia may be documented by Whipple's triad: symptoms consistent with hypoglycemia a low plasma glucose concentration measured with a precise method relief of symptoms after the plasma glucose level is raised. The lower limit of the fasting plasma glucose concentration is normally ~70 mg/dL (~3.9 mmol/L), but lower venous glucose levels occur normally, late after a meal, during pregnancy, and during prolonged fasting (>24 h). Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 20 th edition Page number:608, 2748, 2887
