text: Which cell is primarily involved in causing structural damage to joints in RA?
expl: Osteoclasts are the cells that are ultimately responsible for the structural damage in RA. The chief pathology of RA is bone not only bone destruction, but also decreased bone formation. The first cells that are activated are CD4 + T cells. Macrophages are the chief inflammatory cells involved. But the bone damage is mediated by activated osteoclasts. Bone erosions: The damage is typically located at the regions where the synovium is inserted to the periosteal surface at the edge of bone, at the rim of the articular cartilage. This also explains the development of bone erosions at the radial aspect of the MCP. Juxtra-articular osteopenia is another pathology that is seen in the adjacent bone due to inflammation of marrow. It results in substantial thinning of bone trabeculae. TNFα inhibits bone formation by inhibiting osteoblasts. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 358, Pg: 2756-2757

text: A 65 year old man has been confirmed to have lung cancer. Which form of cancer has the worst prognosis?
expl: Small cell lung cancer has the worst prognosis out of all lung cancers and is rarely suitable for surgical resection. Even when diagnosed early the 2-year survival is in the order of 20-25%. The main form of therapy is chemotherapy. Small cell cancer is associated with syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (ADH) and squamous cell cancer is associated with paraneoplastic hypercalcaemia through increased parathyroid-related hormone. 75% of small cell cancers arise in the proximal airways. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch:78 Pg 599

text: A 68-year-old male came to the physician with complaints of chronic back pain, easy fatigability, and a past history of multiple urinary tract infections in the last 3 months. His ESR is elevated, x-ray of his skull is shown below. Which of the following investigations is useful for diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: The clinical picture (bone pain, fatigue, recurrent infections) with lytic bone lesions is highly suggestive of multiple myeloma . The most useful initial diagnostic test is serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP) , which detects the presence of a monoclonal (M) protein or "M-spike" produced by the malignant plasma cells. Multiple myeloma is a malignant plasma cell disorder characterized by uncontrolled proliferation of plasma cells in the bone marrow, often presenting with anemia, bone pain, recurrent infections, and renal impairment . Skull X-ray classically shows 'raindrop' lytic lesions . Screening and Diagnostic Tests: Serum and urine protein electrophoresis: Detect monoclonal M-protein spike ; urine may show Bence Jones proteins . Hematology: Anemia is common; ESR elevated , rare plasma cell leukemia (>2000 plasma cells/μL). Biochemistry: Hypercalcemia, increased creatinine and urea, decreased albumin, decreased A/G ratio, elevated β2-microglobulin. Serum alkaline phosphatase usually normal. Peripheral smear: Rouleaux formation. Imaging: X-ray: Lytic lesions, osteopenia. MRI: Assesses marrow infiltration, cord or nerve compression. PET/CT: Detects bone damage and extramedullary involvement. Additional Tests: Serum free light chain assay: Elevated kappa or lambda chains. Immunofixation: Determines light chain subtype. 24-hour urine: Bence Jones protein excretion. Fat pad biopsy: Detects amyloid deposits. Flow cytometry: CD138+ plasma cells. FISH: Detects chromosomal abnormalities; del(17p) and translocations indicate poor prognosis. Bone marrow biopsy: Plasmacytosis >10% (often >30%), presence of flame cells , Mott cells , Russell bodies , Dutcher bodies . Explanation of other options: MRI brain and Head CT scan with contrast (Option A and C) : It is not first-line for myeloma diagnosis. MRI spine is useful for evaluating cord compression from vertebral lesions. PET scan (Option B): Used for staging and assessing metabolic activity of lesions, but not the primary test for establishing the diagnosis. All options A, B, and C are imaging studies. While important for staging, the diagnosis is confirmed by laboratory tests demonstrating a clonal plasma cell disorder. Key Takeaways: Serum protein electrophoresis is a key screening test for multiple myeloma to identify a monoclonal paraprotein. Lytic bone lesions on X-ray are a classic feature.

urine may show bence jones proteins . hematology: anemia is common; esr elevated , rare plasma cell leukemia (>2000 plasma cells/μl). biochemistry: hypercalcemia, increased creatinine and urea, decreased albumin, decreased a/g ratio, elevated β2-microglobulin. serum alkaline phosphatase usually normal. peripheral smear: rouleaux formation. imaging: x-ray: lytic lesions, osteopenia. mri: assesses marrow infiltration, cord or nerve compression. pet/ct: detects bone damage and extramedullary involvement. additional tests: serum free light chain assay: elevated kappa or lambda chains. immunofixation: determines light chain subtype. 24-hour urine: bence jones protein excretion. fat pad biopsy: detects amyloid deposits. flow cytometry: cd138+ plasma cells. fish: detects chromosomal abnormalities; text: You review a 55-year-old woman in the clinic. She has a thyroid mass, which was diagnosed as lymphoma on core biopsy. Which of the following is the best choice therapy in this case?
expl: Radioiodine therapy is useful in management of differentiated thyroid cancer (papillary and follicular thyroid cancer). But it is not useful in lymphoma as the cells don't concentrate iodine. Iodine 131 is a radioactive isotope of iodine (RAI) that is selectively concentrated in the thyroid tissue and metabolized by the same pathways as naturally occurring iodine. This, together with its long half-life (8 days), allows it to deliver high doses of radiation to the thyroid gland (b-radiation) sufficient to destroy thyroid follicular cells. So, 131I is used in the treatment of Grave's disease, toxic multi-nodular goiter and differentiated thyroid cancer. External beam radiotherapy is used in the treatment of thyroid lymphoma, but not all tumours are responsive and treatment may only be effective for a short time. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition page 2952

text: A 39-year-old woman gives an eight month history of bloody diarrhoea. On average she has six bowel motions per day with associated urgency. She also reports weight loss of approximately 3 kg. On examination she is dehydrated and tachycardic. There is evidence of pallor and abdominal examination reveals left-sided tenderness. Which of the following pathological features would you expect to find given the likely underlying diagnosis?
expl: Chronic bloody diarrhoea in a young patient is very suggestive of a diagnosis of ulcerative colitis (UC) . The time course is too long for an infective cause and whilst Crohn's disease (CD) may cause a colitis, this is less frequent. CD often presents watery diarrhoea. The predominant left sided symptoms (urgency and anatomical distribution of the tendency) should also point towards UC. The answer here therefore is diffuse mucosal inflammation . All the remaining options are histological features of Crohn's disease . Transmural inflammation is seen in CD. Sub serosal lymphoid aggregates are seen in CD Normal crypt architecture is found in CD while crypt abscesses and goblet cell depletion are seen in UC. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st Ed, Ch: 326 Pg:2474-2475

text: The Barium swallow of the Oesophagus of a HIV patient shows this. What is the causative organism?
expl: The flow of barium along the mucosal surface is grossly irregular in Candida . A characteristic feature of it. Esophagitis in HIV may present with odynophagia and retrosternal pain. Upper endoscopy is generally required to make an accurate diagnosis. Esophagitis in HIV: Esophagitis in individuals with HIV may present with symptoms like odynophagia (painful swallowing) and retrosternal (behind the breastbone) pain. Upper endoscopy (esophagogastroduodenoscopy or EGD) is often necessary to accurately diagnose the cause of esophagitis in HIV patients. Possible causes of esophagitis in HIV include Candida, CMV (Cytomegalovirus), and HSV (Herpes Simplex Virus). Each of these infections can have distinct characteristics. CMV infection typically results in a single large ulcer in the esophagus. HSV infection is more commonly associated with multiple small ulcers in the esophagus. Additionally, esophageal involvement in HIV can also be related to Kaposi's Sarcoma (KS) and lymphoma. Sometimes, there may be large, painful esophageal ulcers of unclear origin, and these may respond to treatment with thalidomide. Gastric Issues in HIV: While achlorhydria (lack of stomach acid production) is a common problem in individuals with HIV, other gastric (stomach) problems are generally rare. Neoplastic conditions involving the stomach in HIV-infected individuals can include Kaposi's Sarcoma (KS) and lymphoma. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition Ch: 202 Pg 1568

text: Following are causes of hypokalemia. Which one of the four items listed does not cause hypokalemia?
expl: Hypokalemia may result from renal losses, gastrointestinal losses, or intracellular redistribution of K. Renal losses that result in hypokalemia include K-wasting diuretics, osmotic diuresis, glucocorticoid excess, mineralocorticoid excess, and leukemia. Gastrointestinal losses that result in hypokalemia include diarrhea, vomiting, nasogastric suction, and laxative abuse. Redistribution of K may occur, resulting in hypokalemia, in patients who have been administered insulin or glucose, in patients treated with beta-adrenergic stimulation, and in patients with alkalosis. Acidosis, on the other hand, causes hyperkalemia making answer B the choice that does not result in hypokalemia. References: Harrisons Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch:53 Pg: 348

expl: t(11,14), is seen in Mantle cell lymphoma, which leads to over-expression of Cyclin D. SOX11 encodes for SRY related HMG box family of transcription factors. Mantle cell lymphomas that express SOX11 are more indolent and require only observation. They present with circulating disease and splenomegaly, but with no lymphadenopathy and very low Ki67. text: What is the diagnosis of a 50-year-old man who presents with symptoms of anemia, fever, and recurrent nosebleeds? The patient has hepatosplenomegaly and lab investigations indicate a hemoglobin level of 6g/dL, a total leukocyte count of 40,000/cu.mm with 10% blasts, and a platelet count of 12,000/cu.mm. Further investigation reveals the presence of t(8;21) in the blasts.
expl: Explanation: The presentation of pancytopenia (anemia, thrombocytopenia), hepatosplenomegaly , high white count with circulating blasts , and the specific cytogenetic abnormality t(8;21) is diagnostic for Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) . The t(8;21) translocation is a common and specific finding in a subtype of AML. Explanation of other options: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) (Option A): More common in children and is characterized by lymphoblasts, not myeloblasts. It is associated with different cytogenetic markers. Preleukemia (Myelodysplastic Syndrome)(Option C): Involves dysplastic hematopoiesis and cytopenias but does not typically have a high blast count (>20%). Aleukemic leukemia (Option D): A rare form where the white cell count is normal or low, which contradicts the high leukocyte count in this case. Key Takeaways: AML presents with signs of bone marrow failure (anemia, infection, bleeding) and organ infiltration. Cytogenetic studies like t(8;21) are crucial for diagnosis, classification, and prognosis in AML.

text: A 60 year old man is investigated for weight loss and dyspepsia. Endoscopic examination reveals an ulcerated lesion in stomach. Biopsy shows the presence of a low grade mucosa associated lymphoma and Helicobacter pylori. CT of chest & abdomen shows no metastases. What is the best treatment option for this patient?
expl: Helicobacter pylori colonization of the Upper GIT is associated with the following outcomes: Peptic Ulcer disease. It is more commonly associated with duodenal ulcer than gastric ulcer. Non cardio gastric adenocarcinoma Low grade gastric B cell MALT lymphoma H Pylori provides protection against Reflux esophagitis and its sequelae like Barret esophagus and esophageal adenocarcinoma. The diagnosis here is a gastric MALT (Mucosa Associated Lymphoid Tissue) tumour . These are usually marginal zone B cell lymphomas associated an excellent prognosis. MALT lymphoma is the third most common type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma . MALT lymphomas are most commonly found in the gastrointestinal tract ( stomach is the commonest). But they can be found in any extranodal site. Low grade gastric MALT tumours are associated with Helicobacter Pylori infection and respond in over 80% of cases to helicobacter eradication. A proportion of patients will not respond to eradication therapy alone and will go on to more conventional anti-lymphoma therapies such as cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil, nucleoside analogues or radiotherapy. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 163, Pg: 1280-1283

text: Which of the following mutations is associated with the Philadelphia chromosome?
expl: Explanation: The Philadelphia chromosome is a cytogenetic abnormality caused by a reciprocal translocation between chromosome 9 and chromosome 22 . This translocation places the ABL oncogene from chromosome 9, which encodes a tyrosine kinase , next to the BCR (breakpoint cluster region) gene on chromosome 22. The resulting BCR-ABL fusion gene produces a protein that activates signal transduction pathways , driving uncontrolled cell growth independent of normal external signals . The Philadelphia chromosome is associated with chronic myeloid leukemia (CML). Explanation of other options: Inversion (Option A): Inversion occurs when a segment of DNA breaks away from the chromosome, flips around, and reattaches in the reverse orientation. A mutation caused by inversion of the intron 22 sequence, which is present in about 40% of severe Hemophilia A cases. Insertion (Option B): Insertion involves the addition of extra nucleotides into a DNA sequence, which can cause frameshift mutations. For example: Cri-du-chat syndrome is caused by a deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5. Deletion (Option D): Results in the loss of a segment of DNA from a chromosome.

text: A 60-year-old man presents with fatigue, pallor, weight loss, and left hypochondrial heaviness. Splenomegaly is present. Hemogram: Hb 10 gm/dl, WBC 165,000/cu.mm, Platelets 3 lakhs/mm 2 . Peripheral smear: 15% metamyelocytes, 30% promyelocytes, 45% myeloblasts. What is the diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: Marked leukocytosis with left-shifted myeloid precursors and splenomegaly point to CML , caused by BCR-ABL1 fusion gene (t(9;22), Philadelphia chromosome). Pathophysiology: BCR-ABL1 tyrosine kinase promotes uncontrolled proliferation and inhibits apoptosis. Phases: Chronic: Blasts Accelerated: Blasts 10-19%, basophilia >20%. Blast crisis: Blasts >20%, AML-like. Investigations: FISH/PCR for BCR-ABL1 (IOC). NAP score: Decreased. Bone marrow: Hypercellular with granulocytic proliferation. Treatment: Imatinib, Dasatinib, Nilotinib (TKIs, DOC). HSCT: For resistant/blast crisis. Explanation of Other Options: Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (Option A): Characterized by lymphocytosis (increased lymphocytes) rather than myeloid precursors. Peripheral smear shows smudge cells and mature lymphocytes , not myeloblasts. Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (Option C): Mainly involves lymphoblasts , not myeloid cells. More common in children , though it can also occur in adults. Acute Myeloid Leukemia (Option D): Diagnosed when >20% blasts are present in the bone marrow or blood. In this case, 45% myeloblasts are seen only in the peripheral smear , making AML less likely. AML usually presents acutely with fever, bleeding, and pancytopenia, whereas CML has a chronic course .

text: A 50 years old male presented with fatigability for one year. Evaluation showed mild anemia, massive splenomegaly. Hb- 10gm%, ILC of 120 x 10(3), platelet 500 x 10(3), neutrophils 60, basophils 4, eosinophils 6, lymphocytes 15. Also seen were myeloblasts, myelocytes metamyelocytes and bands. M: E ratio 8:1. What is the most sensitive investigation?
expl: The age, the symptoms and the presence of massive splenomegaly points towards a myeloproliferative disorder. From the peripheral smear, we can see that there is an increase in neutrophils with a shift to left having band forms, myelocytes and metamyelocytes and an increase in myeloid erythroid ratio classical of Chronic Myeloid Leukemia. The cytogenetic abnormality seen in 90% of patients with CML is the reciprocal translocation between chromosome 9 and 22. This translocation can be identified by the technique of FISH and PCR. Immunophenotyping is a process used to identify the cells based on the antigens on their surface. It cannot be used for identifying chromosomal anomalies. FDG PET is the imaging technique used to identify areas of increased metabolism as in malignancy or infections. It can help us to identify the organ involved, but doesn't help in identifying the type of disease. Leukocyte alkaline phosphatase measures the alkaline phosphatase in neutrophils. Its value is high in leukemoid reaction, tissue damage, steroid use, OCP, aplastic anemia, hodgkin's lymphoma and Down syndrome. It is elevated in myeloproliferative disorders, but is low in the chronic phase of CML. It is low in PNH and hereditary hypophosphatemia.

text: Which microorganism causes cat scratch disease?
expl: Explanation: Cat scratch disease (CSD) is an infection caused by Bartonella henselae , a Gram-negative, facultative intracellular bacterium. It is transmitted by the bite or scratch of cats (especially kittens) or via fleas carrying infected feces. In immunocompetent patients, it causes localized lymphadenopathy and fever, while in immunocompromised individuals, it can lead to bacillary angiomatosis, peliosis hepatis, and endocarditis. Transmission: Primarily from cats; via scratches, bites, or fleas (Ctenocephalides felis). Clinical presentations: Cat scratch disease (immunocompetent): Papule/pustule at site, tender lymphadenopathy, fever, malaise. Bacillary angiomatosis (immunocompromised): Vascular skin lesions resembling Kaposi sarcoma, systemic symptoms. Peliosis hepatis: Blood-filled cavities in liver/spleen, hepatomegaly. Endocarditis: Culture-negative, seen in immunocompromised patients. Diagnosis: Serology (IgM/IgG via ELISA/IFA), PCR, Warthin-Starry silver stain, culture (difficult). Treatment: CSD: Often self-limiting. Severe → azithromycin or doxycycline. Bacillary angiomatosis/peliosis: Doxycycline or erythromycin for months. Endocarditis: Doxycycline + rifampin. Explanation of other options: B. quintana (Option B): Causes trench fever, spread by lice. B. bacilliformis (Option C): Causes Carrion's disease, transmitted by sandflies. Borrelia burgdorferi (Option D): Causes Lyme disease via tick bites. Key Takeaways: Bartonella henselae is the causative agent of cat scratch disease. In immunocompromised hosts, the infection manifests as bacillary angiomatosis or peliosis hepatis .

text: Spot diagnosis in HIV patient?
expl: Oral thrush, Aphthous ulcer, hairy cell leukemia and Kaposis's sarcoma are common oral lesions in HIV patients. Oral thrush is seen as white, cheesy exudate, often on an erythematous mucosa in the posterior oropharynx. While most commonly seen on the soft palate, early lesions are often found along the gingival vestibule. The diagnosis is made by direct examination of a scraping for pseudohyphal elements. Oral hairy leukoplakia presents as white, frondlike lesions, generally along the lateral borders of the tongue and sometimes on the adjacent buccal mucosa Aphthous ulcers of the posterior oropharynx also are seen with regularity in patients with untreated HIV infection. The etiology is unknown Oral Kaposi Sarcoma is seen as reddish purple nodular lesions which appear highly vascular. So among the options, Kaposi Sarcoma is the best choice Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 202, Pg: 1569

text: Which of the following statements concerning the relationship of tuberculosis (TB) and HIV infection is correct.

options.A: Levels of plasma HIV RNA decrease in the setting of active TB.
options.B: TB usually develops only when the median CD4 count is 200/L.
options.C: Extra pulmonary disease is more common than pulmonary disease in the HIV-infected individual
options.D: Therapy for TB is the same in the HIV-infected patient as in the HIV-negative patient

ansText: Therapy for TB is the same in the HIV-infected patient as in the HIV-negative patient
expl: In the US, up to 5% of patients with AIDS have active TB infection, which is more commonly pulmonary than extra pulmonary. It is important to recognize and treat TB early in the course of disease in patients with HIV infection, since TB can increase the level of HIV RNA in the plasma. Skin testing is helpful for predicting who is at risk for TB but is not helpful in the diagnosis of active infection. The epidemic of TB associated with HIV infection is probably the greatest health risk to the general public and the healthcare profession. Though atypical mycobacterial infection occurs relatively late in HIV infection in patients with low CD4 counts, active typical TB may develop relatively early in the course of the disease. Patients with relatively high CD4 T cell counts may exhibit typical pulmonary reactivation with the clinical syndrome of weight loss, fever, cough, and dyspnea and with a chest x-ray revealing apical cavitary disease. In patients with lower CD4-+T cell counts, disseminated disease, including extrapulmonary manifestations are more common. Fortunately, the treatment of active TB in an HIV patient can be quite successful, and the recommended therapy is generally the same as it would be in a patient who does not have HIV infection. However, rifabutin should be substituted for rifampin in patients who are receiving the protease inhibitors or non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors because of adverse interactions. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 178 Pg: 1369-1379

text: A 50-year-old HIV patient presented with a painful lesion, as shown ?in the image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Explanation: Kaposi sarcoma presents as violaceous lesions on the skin or mucosa, commonly seen in HIV-positive individuals due to HHV-8 infection. The lesion shown in the image is a violaceous plaque located on the hard palate in an HIV-positive patient, which is highly suggestive of Kaposi sarcoma (KS). KS is a vascular tumor associated with human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8) and is classified as an AIDS-defining illness. It typically involves the skin, oral mucosa, and internal organs like the lungs and GI tract. Clinical stages: Patch stage: Flat, pink or red macules. Plaque stage: Raised purple or brown lesions. Nodular stage: Firm, raised nodules that may ulcerate. Variants of KS: Classic KS: Older Mediterranean or Eastern European males. Endemic KS: Seen in younger individuals in sub-Saharan Africa. Transplant-associated KS: Occurs in patients on immunosuppressants. AIDS-associated KS: Occurs in HIV/AIDS, especially with low CD4 counts. Pathophysiology: HHV-8 infects endothelial cells, promoting angiogenesis and spindle cell proliferation. Diagnosis: Biopsy showing spindle cells, angiogenesis, and extravasated RBCs. PCR or serology for HHV-8 may support the diagnosis. Management: Antiretroviral therapy (ART) is the cornerstone, as immune reconstitution leads to regression. Chemotherapy (liposomal doxorubicin, paclitaxel) for extensive disease. Radiotherapy or cryotherapy for localized lesions. Explanation of other options: Basal cell carcinoma (Option A): Typically presents as pearly nodules on sun-exposed skin, not as violaceous mucosal lesions. Malignant melanoma (Option C): Presents as dark, irregular pigmented lesions, not characteristic violaceous plaques. Squamous cell carcinoma (Option D): Can occur in the oral cavity but appears as ulcerated, keratotic growths, not violaceous patches. Reference: PubMed - 23679875

text: A 45 year male presents with weight loss and watery diarrhea for several weeks. Investigations reveal hypokalaemia. Which of the following would support a diagnosis of a VIPoma?
expl: VIPomas in adults are usually neuroendocrine islet cell tumors of the pancreas that produce high amounts of VIP. Other secreted hormones may include secreted gastrin and pancreatic polypeptide. Achlorhydria (lack of acidity from the stomach) is classically associated with VIPoma. It can be diagnosed by measuring acid output from nasogastric contents (NG tube). Features of VIP syndrome include watery diarrhea, hypochlorhydria, hyperglycemia, hypercalcemia and flushing. Hypoglycemia is associated with insulinoma Pellagra a condition caused by niacin deficiency occurs in carcinoid syndrome Migratory erythema associated with glucagonoma. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st Ed, Ch: 84 Pg: 665

text: A 28-year-old woman presents to the Emergency department very agitated, complaining of abdominal pain. This has been her third attendance over the past six months, and each time there have been no significant findings. Her only medication of note is the oral contraceptive pill. On this occasion her BP is elevated 155/90 mmHg, her pulse is 92, and her temperature is 37.8°C. Her abdomen is generally tender but soft, and she has active bowel sounds. She complains of lower limb weakness, and she appears to have 4/5 power weakness below the knee.Investigations show: Hb 13.4 g/dl(13.5-18) WCC 10.2 x 10^9/L (4-10) PLT 194 x 10^9/L (150-400) Na 132 mmol/l (134-143) K 4.4 mmol/l (3.5-5) Creatinine 1.1 mg/dl Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
expl: Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP) is associated with: Hypertension A mild increase in temperature Non-specific abdominal pain Patients feel normal between attacks , and the disease itself is due to accumulation of both porphobilinogen and amino-levulinic acid. In general, drugs that lead to increased activity of the hepatic P450 system, such as phenobarbital, sulfonamides, oestrogens, and alcohol, are associated with increased risk of acute attacks. text: A 34 year old lady presents with a long history of abdominal pain and diarrhoea. She also gives a history of recurrent mouth ulcers. Recently the pain has become more intense, she has begun to lose weight and has developed fever with night sweats and she also complains of a rash over her legs. On examination she is thin, she has clubbing and erythema nodosum. On examination of the abdomen a firm tender mass can be palpated in the right iliac fossa. In this patient, which of the following investigations is most appropriate?
expl: The clinical features in this patient points towards a diagnosis of Crohn's disease . However, the features of increased pain, fever, sweats and a mass suggest the patient may have developed an abscess in the right iliac fossa . Hence, imaging this area with CT scan to detect and treat the collection is the investigation of choice. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 326, Pg: 2477

text: A 31 year old gymnast has sudden onset vertigo and dizziness. On examination, there is horizontal nystagmus, with a full range of eye movements. Her speech is slurred. There is intention tremor and dysdiadochokinesia which is asymmetrical. She has an ataxic gait. Which of the Following investigations would be most appropriate?

options.B: MRI and MRA of head and neck

ansText: MRI and MRA of head and neck
expl: The clinical picture is of an acute onset cerebellar syndrome, which suggests a vascular cause. This would involve the posterior (vertebrobasilar) circulation. If headache or neck pain were associated, a vertebral artery dissection would be most important to exclude. A Magnetic Resonance Angiography (MRA) will help to diagnose dissection, stenosis or thrombosis. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 423, Pg: 3283

text: A 60-year-old man presents with pain in the lower back. The pain begins in the lower back and radiates to the lower abdomen. He has not been on any medications recently. Investigations reveal a normocytic normochromic anemia, raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein. Renal function is impaired. Ultrasound scan shows bilateral hydronephrosis. Which of the following investigations should be done?
expl: The presence of hydronephrosis points towards obstruction at the level of ureters on both sides. The cause is likely retroperitoneal fibrosis. It is also supported by the raised ESR and CRP. It is characterized by low back ache and lower extremity edema. It is often associated with IgG4 Disease. But IgG4 levels will be normal as the disease often presents in the fibrotic stage. Ct abdomen will show inflammation around the aorta extending to the iliac vessels. CT PET will help differentiate between lymphoma and retroperitoneal fibrosis. 24 hour urine for creatine clearance may be used to asses the function of kidney, but it will not throw light to the diagnosis. 24 hour urine protein is also not useful. Intravenous urogram is used for diagnosing obstruction, usually intraluminal. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st edition, Ch: 368, Pg:2838.

text: A 52 year old man presents with lower back pains and lethargy. Investigations subsequently confirmed obstructive nephropathy and retroperitoneal fibrosis. His medication is reviewed on the ward round. Which medication is well known to cause retroperitoneal fibrosis?
expl: Retroperitoneal fibrosis is a disease featuring the proliferation of fibrous tissue in the retroperitoneum, the compartment of the body containing the kidneys, aorta, renal tract and various other structures. It may present with lower back pain, renal failure, hypertension, deep vein thrombosis and other obstructive symptoms. It may have an autoimmune etiology. 1/3 rd cases are secondary to malignancy, medications, aortic aneurysm or certain infections. Methyldopa, methysergide, amphetamines, beta blockers, cocaine and LSD are drugs which cause retroperitoneal fibrosis. Azathioprine is used to treat the condition. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st ed, Ch: 319 Pg: 2375

text: A 48-year-old woman is undergoing investigations for secondary amenorrhoea and joint pains. Blood tests show her follicle-stimulating hormone level to be 40 IU/l (> 30 in postmenopausal women). What would be the best method for diagnosing osteoporosis in this patient?
expl: This patient is most probably menopausal judging by her FSH level. All the options are non-invasive techniques for estimating skeletal mass or bone mineral density. Dual energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) is the 'gold standard' for diagnosing osteoporosis. A DXA scan provides a T-score reflecting fracture risk, which may influence treatment decisions. T score of less than -2.5 obtained by DXA is labelled as osteoporosis while the value between -1 to -2.5 is termed osteopenia. Fractures are readily detected by bone scintigraphy even if plain films are normal. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 3196

text: A farmer presents with high-grade fever, rash, vomiting, retro-orbital pain, and myalgia for 5 days. Dengue hemorrhagic fever is suspected. Which of the following investigations is most appropriate for diagnosis at this stage?

options.D: Viral isolation of Aedes albopictus (C6/36) culture

expl: Explanation: The patient presents after 5 days of fever onset , which means the viremic phase has subsided, and the antibody response (IgM) has begun. Therefore, IgM ELISA is the preferred diagnostic test at this stage for confirming dengue hemorrhagic fever (DHF) . Early-phase tests such as NS1 antigen and RT-PCR are most effective within the first 5 days of illness, whereas IgM ELISA becomes the test of choice after day 5 .

text: Which of the following investigations is most likely to indicate that ovulation is imminent?

options.A: Follicle size of 20 mm on ultrasound scan

expl: Sudden increase in luteinizing hormone (LH) -the LH surge - is of particular significance as it indicates that ovulation will occur about 24 hours after the LH peak. Follicle size is usually around 22 mm prior to ovulation but an ultrasound scan gives no indication that ovulation is about to occur. An increase in basal body temperature and secretory changes in the endometrium occur after ovulation. A positive Spinnbarkeit test is used to demonstrate oestrogenic activity on the cervical mucus. Elasticity of the cervical mucus is greatly enhanced prior to ovulation, but does not provide a clue as to when ovulation will occur. Reference : Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21 st edition Page 3031

text: A 27-year-old shop worker is referred with a three month history of recurrent episodes of disorientation and confusion. Her friend has found her wandering around the house on several occasions, apparently with no idea of where she is or how she got there. Her mood has been very low, with frequent emotional outbursts, and she has considered leaving her job because of problems with working the computer and managing customers' queries. Her friend feels her condition is significantly worsening. Physical examination is normal, apart from recurrent, asymetrical, jerks in all four limbs. Which of the following investigations is likely to be most useful in reaching a diagnosis?
expl: This kind of rapid cognitive decline in a young person with myoclonus is strongly suggestive of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD). A definitive diagnosis of any form of CJD requires pathological examination of brain tissue, which is usually only done post-mortem. During life, investigations are undertaken for two reasons: to exclude other possible diagnoses, and to support the diagnosis of CJD. Supportive investigations are EEG, CSF examination and MRI. The EEG in sporadic CJD may show significant abnormalities involving deep brain areas such as the thalami. The normal rhythms are gradually lost. Initially the changes are diffuse, and non-specific, developing into generalised bi- or triphasic periodic sharp wave complexes with a frequency of 1-2 per second. High voltage sharp waves may be synchronous with myoclonic jerks. In an appropriate clinical context, this EEG pattern is strongly suggestive of a diagnosis of CJD. Neither CSF examination nor MRI are options here, but both can also give supportive information. The CSF typically contains no inflammatory cells, but the total protein content may be raised. Analysis for brain specific proteins, particularly 14-3-3, is supportive in the right clinical context. In a proportion of cases, abnormalities of signal in the anterior basal ganglia (caudate/putamen, and sometimes the cortex) can be seen on MRI, which can also support the diagnosis. Chest x ray and liver function tests may help to exclude other diagnoses, but do not give supportive information for CJD. Visual evoked potentials may be altered in CJD, but no specific pattern has yet been identified to support the diagnosis. CT head generally demonstrates brain atrophy in CJD, but this is not a specific finding and is therefore less useful than an EEG. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21 st ed, Ch: 438, Pg: 3420 20th edition Chapter:430 Page number:3152-3153

text: A 27-year-old woman presented with a history of sudden onset right-sided weakness and dysphasia lasting 8 hours. She had returned to India from US 2 days previously. There was no significant past medical history and physical examination was normal. Chest X-ray, ECG and a CT head scan were all normal. Which one of the following investigations is most likely to reveal the underlying cause of this episode?
expl: The history here suggests a lower limb deep vein thrombosis with peripheral embolus through a patent foramen ovale, leading to a left sided cerebrovascular event. This is termed the paradoxical embolus - so-called because a thromboembolus arising from the venous circulation can end up in the systemic circulation. Transoesophageal echocardiography is the investigation of choice to investigate for a patent foramen ovale, although transthoracic echocardiography with contrast may be an alternative. expl: Biosafety levels (BSL) are used to identify the protective measures needed in a laboratory setting to protect workers, the environment, and the public . The levels are defined in Biosafety in Biomedical Laboratories (the BMBL). BSL-3 laboratories are used to study infectious agents or toxins that may be transmitted through the air and cause potentially lethal infections. Researchers perform all experiments in a biosafety cabinet. BSL-3 laboratories are designed to be easily decontaminated Cultures of SARS-CoV-2 should be handled in a biosafety level 3 (BSL-3) laboratory using BSL practices Inoculation of animals with infectious wild-type SARS CoV-2 should be conducted in an animal biosafety level 3 (ABSL-3) facility using absl-3 practices and respiratory protection. text: Which of the following is not an evidence-based measure for preventing the transmission of COVID-19?
expl: Explanation: While several proven public health measures including vaccination, masking, and respiratory hygiene significantly reduce the transmission of COVID-19, ivermectin has not been shown to be effective for either prevention or treatment of the disease. Initial small-scale studies suggested a possible antiviral effect, but subsequent large randomized trials and meta-analyses failed to confirm any clear clinical benefit. Consequently, major health authorities such as the WHO, CDC, and NIH do not recommend ivermectin for COVID-19 prophylaxis or therapy outside of approved clinical trials. Measures to Prevent the Spread of COVID-19: Cough Etiquette (Option A ruled out) Always cover your mouth and nose with a tissue or your elbow when coughing or sneezing. Dispose of tissues immediately. Wear Masks (Option B ruled out) Practice Physical Distancing Wash Hands Regularly Use Hand Sanitizer Avoid Touching Face Get Vaccinated (Option D ruled out) Follow Local Guidelines Avoid Large Gatherings Monitor Symptoms and Get Tested Reference: WHO - COVID-19 Vaccines Advice https://www.who.int/emergencies/diseases/novel-coronavirus-2019/covid-19-vaccines/advice WHO - Advice for the Public https://www.who.int/emergencies/diseases/novel-coronavirus-2019/advice-for-public WHO - The Race for a COVID-19 Vaccine https://www.who.int/news-room/feature-stories/detail/the-race-for-a-covid-19-vaccine-explained CDC - Prevention and Treatment https://www.cdc.gov/coronavirus/2019-ncov/about/prevention-treatment.html

text: SARS-CoV-2 is
expl: SARS-CoV-2 is the cause of a respiratory disease called COVID-19. The virus is a member of lineage B of the Betacoronavirus genus that not only includes the highly pathogenic viruses SARS-CoV-1 (which caused a smaller epidemic in 2002-2003) and MERS-CoV (a lineage C virus that caused small epidemics in 2012, 2015, and 2018), but also contains the lineage A common cold viruses CoV-OC43 and CoV-HKU1 and MERS-CoV. These are enveloped, positive-sense RNA viruses encoded by a viral RNA genome that is quite large, a single linear RNA segment that encodes four structural proteins, designated the S (spike), E (envelope), M (membrane), and N (nucleocapsid) proteins, and a large polyprotein that is cleaved into 16 nonstructural proteins in infected cells. Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal medicine, 21st edition page Ch: 199 Pg 1507

text: In patients affected by COVID-19, which of the following patterns is frequently observed in chest CT scans?
expl: Explanation: Bilateral, peripheral, and basal-predominant Ground Glass Opacities (GGOs) are the most common and characteristic early finding on chest CT in patients with COVID-19 pneumonia. GGOs appear as hazy areas of increased lung attenuation that do not obscure the underlying bronchial and vascular markings. CT- chest of COVID-19 patient shows widespread faint ground glass opacity upper lung lobe as well as reticular shadowing bilaterally in the image below. Explanation of other options: Interlobular septal thickening and Crazy paving pattern (Option A and D): This pattern (GGO + interlobular septal thickening) can be seen in COVID-19 but is less common and typically appears later in the disease course. It is more classically associated with conditions like Pulmonary Alveolar Proteinosis. Air bronchograms (Option B): Can be seen within areas of consolidation in COVID-19 but are not the primary or most frequent pattern. Key Takeaways: The classic CT finding in COVID-19 pneumonia is bilateral, peripheral ground-glass opacities. This pattern reflects the underlying alveolar damage and inflammation.

text: A 75-year-old man died because of a cardiac arrest in the intensive care unit. The treating doctor believed that he was responsible for the patient's death despite knowing that the patient had a poor prognosis. Which is the most likely cognitive distortion?
expl: This refers to relating external events to oneself when there is no reason to do so. All events that can be brought into consciousness are associated with a sense of personal possession , although this is not usually in the forefront of consciousness . This ‘I’ quality has been called personalisation : and may be disturbed in psychological disorders. There are two aspects to the sense of self-activity/personalisation; the sense of existence and the awareness of the performance of one’s actions. The individual blames him or herself for the consequences of others’ actions. In this scenario, the treating doctor is personalising the death of an elderly patient who had a sudden cardiac arrest and a poor prognosis . Reference: Synopsis of Psychiatry, eleventh edition, chapter 28, page no. 875

text: Which of the following is not seen in cocaine intoxication?
expl: Cocaine intoxication is known to stimulate the central nervous system and cause various physiological effects. The symptoms typically seen during cocaine intoxication include: Hyperthermia : Cocaine use can increase body temperature due to its stimulant effects on the central nervous system. Agitation : Cocaine is a stimulant, which can lead to agitation, restlessness, and hyperactivity. Myocardial infarction : Cocaine use can cause vasoconstriction, which increases the risk of myocardial infarction (heart attack), especially in individuals with preexisting cardiovascular disease. Why Bradycardia is Incorrect: Bradycardia (slow heart rate) is not typically seen in cocaine intoxication. Instead, tachycardia (rapid heart rate) is common. Cocaine stimulates the sympathetic nervous system, leading to an increase in heart rate and blood pressure. Key Takeaways: Cocaine intoxication often leads to tachycardia , agitation , hyperthermia , and myocardial infarction due to its stimulant effects. Bradycardia is not typically a feature of cocaine intoxication; instead, it is associated with conditions like opioid toxicity or vagal stimulation .

text: A year after her husband died due to myocardial infarction, the wife again started exhibiting symptoms like feeling depressed, guilty, lonely and was not able to sleep. She developed these symptoms exactly on the same day that her husband died a year ago. This is termed as:
expl: When the trigger for an acute grief reaction is a special occasion, such as a holiday or birthday, the rekindled grief is called an anniversary reaction . It is not unusual for anniversary reactions to occur each year on the same day the person died or, in some cases, when the bereaved individual becomes the same age the deceased person was at the time of death. Although these anniversary reactions tend to become relatively mild and brief over time , they can be experienced as the reliving of one's original grief and prevail for hours or days. Reference: Kaplan and Sadock’s Synopsis of Psychiatry, Chapter 34 End-of-life issues, Page number 1355.
